en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati. Salutations to the illustrious Rāmacandra. Salutations to the illustrious Kṛṣṇa. Salutations to Sarasvatī. Salutations to the illustrious teacher Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Oṃ, [salutations] to the one known through the Vedas, the beloved of Umā, adorned by the two feet of Krama.
I bow to Him who is served by Nandīśa and others, for the attainment of my desired goal. || 1 ||
I bow again and again to Śaṅkara, to Śaṅkarācārya, to Vyāsa who is of the nature of Nārāyaṇa, and to Sarasvatī and Brahmā.
Crying out "Govinda!", the one afflicted by fear obtained protection;
let everyone daily worship that Govinda, who is the very embodiment of compassion. || 3 ||
Having resorted to this protection, she has attained that which is very difficult to obtain;
O Kṛṣṇa, the queen of Kṛṣṇa takes refuge in that Kṛṣṇa every day.
I perpetually bow to the Guru who has revealed the reality of Brahman, who is endowed with preeminent qualities, and who is the instructor of the Praṇava.
I worship him who is known as Vāṇī, the Lord of the Universe, who himself dwells in my field (heart), who is a Guru equal to Viśveśvara, and who is self-luminous light.
I always take refuge at the feet of that omniscient Guru, by whose disciples, grand-disciples, and others the entire earth is currently pervaded.
I salute that ocean of bliss named Advaitānandavāṇī, who is more venerable even than his own guru, who is adorned with all the arts (kalās), and who is the one to be known.
I am that Imperishable (Akṣara) in whose nature of Being-Consciousness-Bliss everything is woven like warp and woof, and wherein all the Vedāntas find their ultimate culmination.
Having prostrated before the pair of feet of Śrī Kṛṣṇa,
I shall explain this composition entitled *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha*.
Making me, the scribe, the very form of the remembrance of the pair of the Teacher’s feet, he composes this commentary; for I am not the master here.
[He bowed] to Śaṅkara— namely, Śaṅkarācārya Bhagavatpāda, who is an incarnation-form of Śiva— and to the two Kumāras, Vighneśvara and Subrahmaṇya; likewise,
while elucidating the words of the *Śivapurāṇa*, [he explained] the meaning of the *Vyāsasūtra* and the meaning of the *Śruti*.
As he has said: "The meaning of the Śruti is correctly established as this very one: 'Śaṅkara is the face of Savitṛ,'" and so forth.
[He spoke of] Vyāsa, the author of the Sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa, who is identical with Nārāyaṇa and is an incarnation of Nārāyaṇa; and likewise there is a statement regarding the Dvāpara age.
"Viṣṇu, the great sage in the form of Vyāsa— indeed, no one other than the lotus-eyed Lord could be the author of the Mahābhārata"— saying such things, Sarasvatī, the consort of Brahmā,
approached Hiraṇyagarbha in the assembly hall.

Having encountered the calamity caused by the theft of her garments, Draupadī— whose name means "black"— sought protection for the sake of obtaining ten million garments from that teacher who had revealed the Brahman-principle to Kṛṣṇa (Arjuna) and taught it to hundreds of disciples; he is thus described.
He is known by the name Svayaṃjyotirvāṇī; He is known by the name Svayaṃprakāśasarasvatī.

He is the weightiest Guru. All this—in which imperishable Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss—is woven like warp and woof and situated within—that imperishable reality is where the Vedāntas find their ultimate rest.
I shall now explain how they become causes for awakening through their intended meaning.

Oṃ. May there be well-being. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. Victorious is the [commentary] that removes rebirth, which issued from the lotus-like mouth of the venerable Bhagavatpāda; it has reached the feet of Śauri (Viṣṇu) like the great river that, having attained a thousandfold divisions by following previous teachers, flows as a single stream after its divisions have ceased.
This well-spoken teaching has as its sole ultimate goal the non-dual Brahman. || 1 ||

Oṃ. May there be well-being. Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa. This is the connection [of the text]. By the statement that the Imperishable (akṣara) is the warp and woof of everything, the extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) of Brahman—consisting in its being the substratum of all—is stated. By the phrase "consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss" (*saccitsukhātmaka*), the intrinsic definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*)—consisting of the nature of truth, knowledge, and bliss—is stated. In that regard:

By stating that the Vedāntas culminate in the imperishable Brahman of the aforementioned nature, it is declared that the Vedāntas alone are the authority regarding this; in the commentary on the verse "I am not capable here," the word *prabhuḥ* means "capable. For the sake of the unimpeded completion and the widespread dissemination of the work he intends to compose—

By way of praising the commentary of the venerable Bhagavatpāda, he performs the auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) characterized by an inquiry into the reality of Brahman, which is the subject matter of that commentary, beginning with the words "adhigatabhidā" (having understood the distinctions).
Through the medium of a simile, [he describes] the Gaṅgā of the two lotus-feet of the venerable form...

It also performs the auspicious rite of reconnection (*saṃdhāna*). Regarding the word "Śauri": just as the river Mahī, having emerged from the foot of Śauri (Viṣṇu), attains a thousandfold division upon reaching its various branches;

even so, the pearl-like utterance (*sukti*) issuing from the lotus-face of the venerable feet of the Blessed One—which has non-dual Brahman as its sole refuge—is that which effects both the production and the dissolution [of all things].

The connection is as follows: "Victorious is [this work], which, having accepted the explanations of the former teachers as subjects to be explained by the heart, possesses a thousandfold distinctions in its meaning. Here, by the qualification of the *sūkti* (well-spoken teaching) as "possessing a thousandfold attained distinctions," the various differences of the established doctrines (*siddhānta*) that will be demonstrated in his own treatise are indicated.

It is indicated that for all of them, the very root is the well-spoken word (sūkti) issuing from the lotus-like mouth of the venerable feet of the Blessed One. The Gaṅgā river, which has attained division— that is, reached various distinctions—
having emerged from the foot-lotus of Śauri, the illustrious Mahāviṣṇu, triumphs with supreme excellence over the divisions, that is, the various regions of the earth.

"Proceeds" is a praise. The "lotus" (*ambuja*) is the very lotus-like face of the venerable teacher (*bhagavatpāda*); the qualification "glorious" (*śrīmat*) is used to indicate that the reason for superimposing the nature of a lotus upon the face is its possession of splendor (*kāntimat*). [The word] *jananaharaṇī* means that which removes birth; "birth" (*janana*) refers to *saṃsāra*, and it is that which is produced by itself...

It is called *jananaharaṇī* because it removes [the cycle of] birth by means of the knowledge of Brahman. A well-spoken work (*sūkti*) is a commentary that is faultless both in its composition and its meaning. "The non-dual Brahman as the sole refuge" (*brahmādvayaika-parāyaṇā*):
that which is Brahman and non-dual is "non-dual Brahman" (*brahmādvaya*); that which is non-dual Brahman and the one is "the non-dual Brahman alone" (*brahmādvayaika*), and that is the refuge.

That well-spoken verse whose ultimate purport has as its object Brahman, which has the non-dual alone as its final resort— by this qualification, it is stated that the subject matter of the scripture consisting of the commentary, which is subsumed under the words of the aphorism, is Brahman, which is devoid of the second [the world-appearance], uniform, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss.

By the qualification "the remover of birth" (jananaharaṇī), it is stated that liberation (mukti) is the purpose of the scripture. By implication, one who desires liberation is indicated as the qualified student (adhikārī) of the scripture; and for the qualified student of liberation, the relationship (saṃbandha) characterized by the nature of the goal and the seeker is also indicated. || 1 ||

Ancient scholars, exerting themselves to the utmost to establish the oneness of the Self regarding matters already proven by worldly experience, have demonstrated various diverse paths with indifference.
Here, for the sake of the intellect, I shall briefly present some of the different established conclusions (siddhānta-bheda) rooted in those [paths].
O Father, I shall compile for the sake of purification those words explained in the commentary on the *Caryāpadas*.

Thus, by directly stating the subject matter and other elements of the Vedānta scripture— which consists of the Bhāṣya— in these eight verses through both the words and their meaning, the author indicates that since his own work is a treatise (prakaraṇa) belonging to the Vedānta scripture, its subject matter and so forth are likewise identical to those of that scripture.
Now, he declares his intended undertaking with the words "by the ancients. By the ancient teachers— who were exceedingly intent and devoted to establishing the identity of the Self—
he [established] that which is conventionally established as a means for attaining the realization of the identity of the Self.

Regarding objects that are established merely through delusion— namely, those appearing in the forms of the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśvara*), and the world (*jagat*)— various kinds of paths, mutually contradictory, have been shown due to a lack of regard [for their ultimate reality]. By the phrase "due to a lack of regard," [it is implied] that among these mutually contradictory views regarding the oneness or plurality of the individual soul (*jīva-ekatva-nānātva*)...

The doubt that those teachers who insist upon various modes such as being a reflection might themselves be non-Self— just like the proponents of duality— is thereby dispelled. For the teachers' presentation of various seemingly contradictory modes is merely a means for the comprehension of the intended reality.

It does not lead to a fault; rather, it serves solely as an ornament for the discernment of certain listeners, because they attain the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self—the means to liberation—through some particular mode of understanding characterized by the diversity of their own intelligence. As it has been said by Sureśvarācārya:
"By whatever means the realization of the inner self may arise for men, that very method should be considered valid here;
and yet, that [method] is not fixed."
*Vyutpatti* means understanding; *pratyagātman* refers to the inner self, the conscious self that is within all.

In regard to that subject, the method or manner (*prakriyā*) presented here in this Vedānta scripture is excellent, flawless, subordinate [to the goal], non-contradictory, and manifold. Regarding this, Dīkṣita has also stated in his *Parimala* that the reality is unimagined (*akalpita*).
When entities are conceptualized as means for realization (*pratipattyupāya*), contradiction does not constitute a fault. For example,

when the true Arundhatī is conceptualized by various persons through various stars situated to her east, north, and so forth as coarse substitutes for Arundhatī, the contradiction among these [substitutes] does not constitute a fault.
From that root— the source of the various paths previously demonstrated— here, in this work of my own,
for the purification of the intellect and the refinement of one's own understanding, it should be understood that the actual purpose is indeed the welfare of the world.
[This is] proclaimed by the words in the form of commentaries of the venerable feet of my father.
Having received from him his own knowledge of Brahman, the teacher [Śaṅkara] demonstrates it by means of those very [scriptures],
providing supporting arguments as best as he can, in order to establish the acceptability of his own work.
Establishing this through reasoning, I shall write in no great detail. In that regard,

for one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*) and has attained a preliminary understanding of Brahman as the Self through the Vedāntas— and who, having thus aroused the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), seeks the knowledge of that [Brahman]— the Vedāntas...
The nature of the injunction (*vidhi*) perceived in the act of hearing is now considered. There are indeed three types of injunction:

the original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), and the exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*). Among these, the first is an injunction whose fruit is the attainment of something that has not been attained in any way whatsoever throughout the three periods of time. For example:

"Sprinkles the rice-grains. Here, there is no way for the sprinkling of the rice-grains—which is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarma*)—to be established by any other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*) except through an injunction (*niyoga*).
The second type of injunction is that which fulfills the unestablished portion of what is already partially established as an alternative; for example, "He threshes the rice-grains."
While explaining what was already stated—that "here, in this compendium, I shall summarize the various systems of tenets"—one might object:

"Is it not improper to say that your summary in your own work consists only of the tenets established in ancient texts, when you have also provided logical demonstrations for things not even found in those ancient works? [To this, the author replies: "It is not so. [Reason: Because...

He dispels the doubt that [this might be so] because it is observed here and there in the *Saṃgraha* by stating, "In those [works]. He says, "Among them," meaning that first, the rule for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) is investigated in his own work. Therein, he first points out the qualified person (*adhikārī*) for the rule of hearing with the words, "One who has studied... [meaning] one who has produced an initial comprehension (*āpāta-pratipatti*) through the Vedāntas.

The meaning is: one for whom there has arisen—through the prolonged [practice] of the object being the Self non-different from Brahman—a desire for knowledge (*jijñāsā*), which is a wish for knowledge in the form of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). Even for one who has studied the Vedas, if there is an absence of study of the Vedāṅgas such as Śikṣā, Kalpa, and Vyākaraṇa, there is an absence of proficiency, and thus no *jijñāsā*.

Intending to show that even the practice of [scriptural study] would not be possible if it were merely superficial, it was stated "of one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs. Nor should it be asked: "How can the realization of Brahman as the Self, which arises from the faultless Vedānta, be considered superficial? For [the realization] is "I am not Brahman."

The sense is that because of the suspicion of contradiction with perception and so forth, even in the realization of Brahman as the Self— which is of the nature of valid knowledge— there arises the possibility of it being subject to doubt regarding its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
The connection is that the injunction "one should hear" (*śrotavya*) is perceived in the hearing of the Vedāntas.

"For the sake of that knowledge" means for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman as the Self, which is not a locus for any suspicion of invalidity. By the word "khalu," the fact that the three types [of injunctions], such as the *apūrvavidhi*, are well-established in the *Pūrvatantre* (the Mīmāṃsā system) is indicated.

"Even in the three times" means: in any manner whatsoever—whether as having a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*) or an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatva*), and by whatever means—in all three times, at no time is there any attainment [of the act] without an injunction. An injunction that effects the attainment of such acts as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and the like is the first type; this is the meaning of an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction). By the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) in the word "rice-grains" (*vrīhīn*), the rice-grains [are indicated].

This is because it is understood that [the object] is to be refined (*saṃskārya*). It should be understood that sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) has been stated to be a ritual act of refinement (*saṃskārakarma*). "Injunction" (*niyoga*) refers to an injunctive word (*vidhāyaka-śabda*).

In this case, even in the absence of an explicit injunction, the threshing of the materials that serve as the source-substance (*prakṛtidravya*) for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) will be obtained simply through the implication (*ākṣepa*) of the production of rice grains; therefore, this injunction is not for the purpose of obtaining that [threshing]. Rather, it is [for another purpose] because, despite the obtainment of threshing through implication, it is just like that [other case].
Since there is no difference in their being recognized as causes by the world, even [methods such as] tearing with the fingernails would apply to the subject; therefore,
because there is a possibility that the threshing is not already established, the result is the fulfillment of that specific portion.

The third type of injunction is that which results in the exclusion of one of two principal elements (*śeṣin*) or one of two subordinate elements (*śeṣa*), when there is a constant application of either one principal element or two subordinate elements;
for example, in the Agnicayana sacrifice, the mantra "imāmagṛbhṇan raśanāmṛtasya" [is prescribed].

"Subsequently, he takes the reins. Or, for example, as in the case of the Gṛhamedhīya, a specific sacrifice within the Cāturmāsya, where one performs the two Ājyabhāga offerings; and in the Agnicayana, both the taking of the horse's rein and the taking of the donkey's rein are to be performed.

In that context, regarding the taking up of the horse's reins, the mantra "imām agr̥bhṇan raśanām" (they have taken this rein) applies invariably due to its *liṅga*— that is, its inherent capacity to manifest the manner of taking up the reins. Therefore, the injunction is neither for the purpose of obtaining that [application], nor for the purpose of fulfilling an unobtained portion thereof.

However, because the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is non-specific, the mantra would apply even to the grasping of the donkey’s halter; therefore, it is for the purpose of excluding that. Likewise, since the *Gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice has the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), the two *ājyabhāga* offerings would necessarily apply there by extension (*atideśa*) alone; thus, [the rule] does not apply there.

The injunction is for the purpose of obtaining that [result], or for the purpose of restricting it; however, since [the details] would also apply by extension (*atideśa*), such as the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the [injunction] is intended to exclude those.

Regarding the term *puroḍāśa*: in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, substances such as the *puroḍāśa* dedicated to Agni and others have been prescribed. However, rice (*vrīhi*) is prescribed by way of reference to the sacrifice once it has already arisen; thus, for rice—which is prescribed as a subsequent element (*utpannaśiṣṭa*)—there is no application in a sacrifice that is already occupied by the *puroḍāśa* prescribed as an original element (*utpattiśiṣṭa*).

Because direct instrumentality is impossible, [the status of being a means] culminates in being a means to the sacrifice by way of being the material substance for the *puroḍāśa* cake. Furthermore, the status of the rice grains (*vrīhi*) as the material cause of the *puroḍāśa* is mediated through the production of the rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), and the production of the rice-grains necessitates its own causes; and in the production of the rice-grains...

The meaning is that since the reason for threshing has been ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is no attainment of the desired threshing even in the absence of an injunction. Now, one might object: "If threshing is obtained from worldly practice (*loka*), then its constant attainment would also follow from that very practice. To this, he says, beginning with "But... (*kiṃtu*), [stating] "from implication" (*ākṣepāt*).

The meaning is: "because of the implication of the production of rice. However, the connection is that since the portion [of the action] such as threshing is already established, its result is the fulfillment of that specific portion. Regarding the phrase "of the two": when one subsidiary (śeṣa) is permanently established for two principals (śeṣin), it has the result of excluding the other principal; or, when there are two [subsidiaries] for a single principal.

The construction is as follows: since the two remaining [options] are already established as permanent, the third rule is one whose fruit is the exclusion of the other remaining option. "Not that" means: it is not for the purpose of establishing that [option], because it is already established;
nor is it for the purpose of filling out an unestablished portion, because it is permanently established. "Precisely from the extended application (atideśa)"—thus [it is concluded].

The meaning is that the modification (vikṛti) must be performed according to the model (prakṛti). Regarding the statement "there is no injunction there," the injunction "he performs the two ājyabhāga offerings" does not serve as the means of obtaining (prāptyartha) the two ājyabhāgas, because they are already obtained even without that injunction;
nor does it serve to fulfill an unobtained portion, because they are eternally obtained. Rather, [it serves another purpose].
The construction is: "for the purpose of its cessation."

This example is cited according to the position of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the section concerning the *gṛhamedhīya* sacrifice; it is cited as an instance where something must be illustrated somewhere. Nor is it the case that even in a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), once the unestablished portion has been fulfilled by the threshing that was already partially established, [the purpose of the rule is exhausted].

It might be argued that because the other means, such as tearing with the nails, is already excluded by that [injunction], its cessation is also obtained; thus, since there is no difference in their resulting in the fruit of cessation (*nivṛtti*), it is not proper to distinguish between restriction (*niyama*) and exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) based on their results. This objection is untenable, for the carrying [of the firewood] is not established through implication (*ākṣepa*) without a restrictive injunction (*niyama*).

Because it is impossible to turn one away from acts such as tearing [the grain] with the nails, the *niyama* (restrictive injunction) consisting in the fulfillment of what has not been previously attained is primary; and because it is proximate— since it pertains to the very act of threshing (*avaghāta*) which is the object of the injunction— it is accepted that this *niyama-vidhi* alone constitutes the result.
Because the exclusion of others (*itaranivṛtti*), which arises as a secondary consequence (*tadanuniṣpādinī*) and is remote due to its non-prescriptive nature,

cannot appropriately be considered the result when a proximate result is possible. Thus, among these three distinct modes of injunction, what kind of injunction for hearing (*śravaṇavidhi*) is intended there?
Certain authors, such as the author of the *Prakaṭārtha*, say: "This is an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) because [the matter] was not previously established.

But [one might object]: does this not rather serve as a restrictive exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*) of the entire collection of other subsidiary elements obtained through extended application (*atideśa*), based on the injunction "he performs the two butter-portions" (*ājyabhāgau yajati*)?

Since this is not an established conclusion, he says: "In the section concerning the *grahamedhīya*. The phrase "even in a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)" means that it is just as in the case of an exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*). "Because it is already occupied by that" means that because the requirement for producing rice-grains is already satisfied by threshing alone, [the need for other means] has been stilled.

Thus, although the distinction between restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*) and exclusive injunctions (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) is obtained by way of their essential nature— since a restrictive injunction prescribes an action such as threshing when it is only optionally established, whereas an exclusive injunction prescribes an action that is already invariably established— their difference is established by way of their results.

The meaning is that it is not logical. He states two reasons for accepting that the result of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is the restriction itself, beginning with the words "Because of being primary" (*prāthamyāt*).
The phrase "because of proximity" (*pratyāsannatvāt*) means because of its proximity to the injunction. [This applies] when [the result] resides in the action to be enjoined (*vidheyakriyā*).

Regarding the reason for its proximity, he states the cause for its being "first presented"—that is, its priority—by means of the passage beginning with "vidhitaḥ" and ending with "aśakyatayā. He states two reasons for not accepting that the exclusion of others (*itaranivṛtti*) is the fruit of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*): [the first is] by means of that which is produced as a secondary consequence (*tadanuniṣpādinyā*).

By [the words] beginning with "ityādinā" (and so forth). The meaning is: of that which has arisen immediately after the presence of the fulfillment of the unattained portions. By this, it should be understood that one reason stated is its having a delayed presence (*vilambitopasthitikatva*). Regarding the second reason, he states the cause for its being remote (*viprakṛṣṭatva*) with the word "avidheya" (uncontrollable).

"Exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) means that something is not to be performed or is not an auxiliary part; and its scope extends to such things as the non-depositing [of the sacrificial cake] and the tearing of the nails, which is the meaning. Now, he begins the discussion concerning the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*), which is the subject at hand. "In this way," [he says], because hearing the Vedāntas is not already established with respect to the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman.
The meaning is that, because it is not established by any other means of knowledge, [the word "iti"] has the sense of non-attainment with respect to its being a means of proof.

For there is no evidence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to prove that hearing the Vedānta is the cause of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; for even in this world, such realization does not frequently arise in one who has performed the hearing, nor does it fail to arise in one who has not performed the hearing, as in the case of Vāmadeva while still in the womb.

Because there is deviation from both sides regarding its arising; nor is there a general rule established in other treatises that mere hearing is the cause for the direct realization of the object to be heard,
by virtue of which the status of being a cause could be obtained here through a general principle even in the absence of a specific apprehender of causality.

Thus one might suspect [the following]: even if it were accepted that hearing the treatises on music (*gāndharva*) and so forth is a cause for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the six musical notes (*ṣaḍja*) and so on, there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because one does not observe the direct realization of *dharma* and other such objects through hearing the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and its meaning.
Therefore, this is indeed an original injunction (apūrvavidhi).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the claim "not being apprehended through other means of knowledge" is unestablished, since its apprehension is possible through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)?

For instance, when there is hearing of the Vedānta, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is observed; and when that [hearing] is absent, it is not observed. To this, he replies: "Not indeed."

"Because of its non-arising" means because of the non-attainment of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). "Of Vāmadeva" refers to the Śruti passage: "Even while lying in the womb, Vāmadeva spoke this. Thus, in the manner previously described, the meaning is that he spoke of his own liberation through the birth of this knowledge of Brahman.

Now, it is observed that upon hearing the science of music (gāndharva-śāstra), there is a direct perception of the musical notes such as ṣaḍja and so forth, whereas in the absence of that [hearing], there is an absence of that [perception]; in that case, regarding the direct perception of the specific notes which are the objects to be heard, [it depends on] the music...

At the time of apprehending causality, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the specific act of hearing (*śravaṇa*) consisting of scriptural inquiry is grasped as the cause for that which is delimited by being a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the object to be heard. And thus, [it follows that] the direct realization of Brahman—
Even though there is no apprehension of a specific causal relationship between the hearing of the Vedānta and [the result],
the direct realization of Brahman is indeed a direct realization of the object to be heard;
and since the hearing of the Vedānta is also "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) in its aforementioned general sense, [it serves as the cause].

One might argue that since the status of being a cause for the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) is already established [by other means], this is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); to this he says: "Nor is it mere hearing. In the context of hearing about *dharma*, there is the status of being a means to a transcendental good (*alaukikaśreyas*) in the form of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), as qualified by sacrifices and the like.

Alternatively, because there is no perception of the direct realization of form (*rūpa*) or phenomena (*dharma*) despite their being capable of such realization, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the aforementioned general relation of cause and effect; thus,
even if one grasps through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth that the hearing of the *Gāndharva-śāstra* is a cause for the direct realization of musical notes, [the general rule fails].
He states that the hearing of Vedānta does not result in the attainment of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman:

"The [knowledge of] Gandharva music, etc. Regarding the word "karma," the phrase "etc. here includes the collection of scriptural passages that set forth deities such as Hiraṇyagarbha; and by the phrase "dharma, etc.," [deities such as] Hiraṇyagarbha and others are included.
The deity is grasped; therefore, it is said: "because of the absence of attainment"—this is the meaning.

In the Bhāṣya as well, in the section [Sūtra 3.4.47] stating "There is an injunction of another auxiliary for one who possesses that [knowledge], optionally, like the beginning of the injunction," it is maintained that silence (*mauna*), which is an auxiliary to knowledge, must be understood as an injunction—
just like childhood (*bālya*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*)— because it constitutes a new requirement (*apūrvatva*). Thus, what is designated by the term "scholarship" [is itself the subject].
Thus, it is accepted that regarding the hearing [of the Veda], there is only a prior injunction (pūrvavidhi).
Regarding this point, he states the consensus: "In the Bhāṣya as well. The connection is that even in the Bhāṣya, only a *pūrvavidhi* (an original injunction) is accepted.

This is the meaning: it is heard in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka [Upaniṣad], "Therefore, having discarded scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), a Brāhmaṇa should abide in the state of a child (*bālya*); and having discarded both childhood and scholarship, then..."

He is called a *muni* because, having known the Self through the means of hearing and so forth, the Brāhmaṇas have transcended [worldly life] and attained the stage of the Paramahaṃsa, which is free from all mental distractions and manifests liberation while living; therefore, even now, a Brāhmaṇa who seeks the direct realization of Brahman should [attain] scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*).

Having become disillusioned with childhood, one should desire to attain [the state of] "pāṇḍitya" (scholarship). The intellect that takes the form of an initial inquiry is his "paṇḍā" (scholarship); thus he is a "paṇḍita," and his activity is "pāṇḍitya," which means the act of hearing [the scriptures]. "Childhood" (vālya) refers to the activity of a child—that is, being free from hypocrisy, pride, and so forth—but it does not refer to the child himself.

The form of "acting as one pleases" (*yatheṣṭaceṣṭā*) is well-known; because it brings about outward-directedness, it is opposed to *vidyā*. Therefore, by the word *bālya*—which denotes purity of being (*bhāvaśuddhi*) consisting in the absence of hypocrisy and the like—the reflection (*manana*) that is to be accomplished through purity of being is indicated. This is because it occurs subsequent to hearing (*śravaṇa*).

Having become indifferent to both childhood and scholarship—that is, having properly practiced both—thereafter one should become a *muni*, characterized by right reflection; this is the injunction. For Vyāsa and others who are established in meditation, "reflection" (*manana*) here refers specifically to meditation (*dhyāna*).

Because we observe the employment of the word "muni" [in the context of meditation], and because that word is not employed when one rests merely in the *mātrā* (the syllable) without *vicāra* (reflection) following *dhyāna* (meditation), it follows that, due to its being something previously unknown (*apūrvatva*), just as there is an injunction (*vidhi*) for hearing (*śravaṇa*), so too must an injunction be accepted for silence (*mauna*)— which is an auxiliary to knowledge— as a means for the arising of knowledge. This is because of its being something previously unknown.

"Devā" (the gods) is the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*). As for the meaning of the Sūtra: for the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*) who possesses that [knowledge]—namely, the knowledge consisting of the determination of reality born from hearing and reflection—and who desires the direct realization of reality, the third stage, called "muni," is enjoined by the statement "then he is a muni," in comparison with scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*) and childlike innocence (*bālya*). Now, as for scholarship...

One who, through the two types of learning (*bālya*), has ascertained the reality and seeks its direct realization, engages in meditation spontaneously, just as one seeking a jewel engages in the continuous stream of cognitions directed toward the reality of that jewel. Nor would it follow that one seeking the direct realization of reality would also engage spontaneously in hearing the means to that realization and so forth.

One might argue that even in that case, the suspicion of the injunction being purposeless is equal; however, this must be addressed by noting that it has already been established that without an injunction, engagement in the hearing of the Vedāntas is impossible. Thus, regarding the claim that the injunction for silence (*mauna*) is useless, he says: "By way of an alternative" (*pakṣeṇa*). An injunction for silence as an auxiliary (*sahakārin*) must be accepted, because it is not obtained [otherwise] as a matter of course.
For the sake of realization through cultivation, [it is practiced] in meditative absorption.

The fact that the hearing of Vedānta is the cause of the eternal, direct intuition (*aparokṣa-sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is not unestablished; for it is established as a cause of direct intuition by virtue of its being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whose object is a perceptible reality (*aparokṣa-vastu*). This is because the possibility of verbal direct intuition (*śābdāparokṣa*) has been established, and it is precisely for that purpose [that the inquiry is undertaken].
The introduction to that.

Even for one who is proceeding spontaneously, there is the possibility that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) might occasionally fail to be attained due to the intensity of the perception of sense objects. Thus, even if the injunction regarding silence (*mauna-vidhi*) lacks the status of an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), its status as a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*) is indeed established; and when such a restrictive injunction exists, [the fault lies] in its transgression.

The intention of this portion of the Sūtra is as follows: fearing that realization might fail to arise due to the acquisition of visible objects, one restrains with effort even the perception of objects that has occurred naturally and applies oneself solely to meditation; this is the position [of the opponent]. Now, [the author asks]: "But..."

One might ask: "In a section primarily concerned with the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), how can there be an injunction for meditation and the like, given that this would entail a split in the sentence? To this he says: "Like the injunctions for the subsidiaries. This means: "Like the injunctions for the auxiliary parts. Just as in a section devoted to the primary injunction, there is an injunction for the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries through a subordinate division of the sentence, so it is here.

The meaning is that the injunction regarding meditation and so forth is an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Since, according to the stated reasoning, the injunction of silence (*mauna-vidhi*) is established as a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*), the commentators’ statement regarding its "novelty" (*apūrvatva*) should be understood as intending that it was not necessarily obtained [as a requirement] in every case (*pākṣikāprāpti*) with respect to the portion concerning the injunction of silence. This is just as [the commentators state] regarding the aphorism (*sūtra*): "because there is no obtaining [of it] in one alternative" (*pakṣeṇa prāptyabhāvāt*).

Regarding what is to be said: the statement in the *Bhāṣya*, "because it is unprecedented" (*apūrvatvāt*), is for the purpose of making known that the injunction to hear [the Vedas] is indeed an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

Furthermore, the intention of the author of the *Prakaṭārtha* and others is that the relationship between the example and the exemplified is intended to apply merely to the case of non-attainment (*aprāpti*). He now refutes the position that it is an original injunction.

Regarding the phrase "of the hearing of Vedānta": the meaning is that the status of hearing—consisting of Vedānta characterized by inquiry—as the cause of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman is established even without an injunction. Now, one might ask: how can a verbal statement be the cause of direct realization?
Since directness (*sākṣātkāratva*) belongs only to knowledge produced by the sense organs, he says: "an object that is not indirect" (*aparokṣavastu*).
The directness of a cognition consists in its having an object that is not indirect; it does not consist in being produced by the sense organs.
Furthermore, the non-indirectness of an object consists in its non-difference from the consciousness that is conducive to the practical transaction (*vyavahāra*) regarding that object.

This will be explained in the discussion on the directness of verbal knowledge (*śābdāparokṣavāda*). Thus, the meaning is that because the knowledge produced by the Vedānta has as its object a reality whose nature is established by scripture as being eternally immediate, its status as a direct realization (*sākṣātkāratva*) is established. To the question, "But what is the relevance of the doctrine of the directness of verbal knowledge in this treatise? he says:

The phrase "for that very purpose" means that it is well known that the connection of those doctrines is for the sake of establishing that the Vedāntas produce immediate valid knowledge of Brahman, and not for any other purpose.

Nor does it follow that, merely by virtue of being a means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman, hearing (*śravaṇa*)— though it attains the status of being a cause for the direct realization of Brahman common to those with superficial insight— does not also attain the status of being a cause for that direct realization in its form as a certainty regarding existence, which is desired for the purpose of removing ignorance.

It must be stated [as follows]: since it is established that mere inquiry is the cause for determining the object of inquiry, and that the means of knowledge regarding Brahman is the cause for its direct realization, it follows that *śravaṇa*—consisting of the knowledge of the words of the Vedānta once they have been investigated—is the cause of that [realization]. Nor has it been said...
There is deviation from both [sides], because deviation in positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) due to the deficiency of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) is not a fault;

and because there is no deviation in negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), since for one who remembers past lives, the attainment of the fruit is possible through hearing [the teachings] in another birth.

Surely, by establishing in the doctrine of verbal immediacy (*śābdāparokṣavāda*) that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is an immediate entity is the cause of direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) regarding its own object, it follows that the Vedāntas likewise possess the status of being a cause for immediate knowledge in general with respect to Brahman— which is eternally immediate as their own object— and not merely [a cause] for the existence [of that knowledge].

The state of being the cause for the direct realization of that [Brahman] consists in its nature as a definitive certainty (*niścaya*); and this is appropriate only for *śravaṇa*, which is the hearing of the Vedānta texts qualified by inquiry (*vicāra*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such certainty existing even prior to inquiry.
Nor is it the case that the result characterized by the cessation of ignorance can arise from the mere direct realization produced by the [Vedic] sentence alone while [inquiry] exists.

It should not be said that the nature of direct realization as being of the form of certainty need not be sought; for in each of those various passages teaching Brahman, it is indicated by the sign of repeated questions and answers until the cessation of doubt.

By the scriptural passage beginning with "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the realization of Vedānta," and by the sign consisting of the non-cessation of ignorance— inferred from the persistence of transmigratory existence as before even in one who has heard of Brahman— it is established that [the means] such as hearing,
reflection, meditation, tranquility, self-control, devotion, and dispassion are the causes for the maturation of knowledge.

And since, by the mark of the perception of the injunction, it is precisely the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman—characterized as a certainty—that is desired for the purpose of removing ignorance, [the opponent] raises an objection: "Nor can it be so," etc. The words "of the Vedāntas" are to be supplied. Thus, the fact that hearing the Vedāntas is the cause of such a direct realization remains unestablished.

The meaning is: merely by establishing that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whose object is an immediately present thing (*aparokṣa-vastu*) is the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) with respect to its own object; and once it is established that a means of valid cognition whose object is an immediately present thing is the cause of immediate knowledge, and it is further established that inquiry (*vicāra*) is the cause of the determination (*nirṇaya*) regarding what is to be investigated.

He states that by combining the two types of causal relationships, it is established that in the present context, *śravaṇa*—consisting of knowledge of Vedānta qualified by inquiry—is the cause of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, which takes the form of a certainty regarding what exists.
He says: "Of mere inquiry" and "as a cooperative factor. The meaning is: due to the absence of the cooperative factor consisting of one-pointedness of consciousness (*citaikāgrya*).

Once it has been established— by the force of the two-fold means of valid cognition consisting of the nature of cause and effect— that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the cause of the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), it is inferred that Vāmadeva’s hearing and so forth occurred in a previous birth;
just as, for example, the cause of the enjoyment seen in a creature immediately upon birth is [inferred to have existed previously].

He states that for one who speaks thus, there is no deviation from the rule regarding karma belonging to a previous birth; this refers to "one who remembers his former births," meaning Vāmadeva, who remembered his prior state.

Otherwise, because the status of being a cause would be sublated by deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it would be impossible to know that [the means] is a means of accomplishment even through scripture; for just as the tactile sense-organ is unnecessary for the direct perception of a jar, so too [other means] are unnecessary for the direct realization of Brahman.

Furthermore, regarding the doubt that there might be another means in addition to hearing [the scriptures], the presence of a deviation from the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*) does not constitute a fault. Thus, since [the goal] is already attained, this is not an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*). Therefore...
In the commentary on the sūtra "Thus repetition [is required], because of the repeated instruction," it is shown that hearing and the other means culminate in direct perception;

for when hearing and so forth are repeated, they become purposeful in a perceptible sense, just as threshing and other such acts culminate in the production of rice grains. This refers to the case of hearing.

The instruction regarding subsistence (vṛtti) is obtained through the principle of the threshing at the New and Full Moon sacrifices, because the purpose of seeing Brahman is one whose result is perceptible (dṛṣṭārtha). However, it would not be appropriate as an original injunction (apūrvavidhi), like the threshing of all herbs; for in the Agnicayana sacrifice, having filled [the vessel] with all herbs—
It has been established in the *Tantravārttika* that since the threshing— which is enjoined for the purpose of preparing the mortar—
is not for a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), there is no repetition [of the action]. Therefore, this is indeed a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

"Otherwise" means: the failure to accept the avoidance of the two kinds of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the manner previously stated. The meaning is that, due to the certainty of deviation—which constitutes the certainty of a sublation (*bādha*) consisting in the absence of the nature of being a valid reason—the injunction to listen would result in a lack of informative power (*abodhakatā*); consequently, even for you, there would be no "injunction of what is not previously known" (*apūrva-vidhi*).

At the time of raising the doubt that, just as hearing (*śravaṇa*) is a cause for the direct realization of Brahman, there might be another cause— such as specific austerities (*tapas*) and so forth, or the attainment of a superior birth— the [objection] is made that Vāmadeva’s knowledge arose from such another cause. Thus, because of the possibility of this doubt, there is an absence of the means of hearing (*śravaṇa*) in the case of Vāmadeva.

The knowledge of deviation (vyabhicāra) does not constitute an obstacle to the apprehension of hearing as the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Furthermore, since it is impossible for two mutually independent causes to produce the cognition of a single object, no suspicion whatsoever arises regarding the existence of another cause for the direct realization of Brahman.

It must be stated that this is because such is observed in the world; thus he says, "the jar," etc. Since hearing the Vedānta is established as a cause for the direct realization of Brahman even without an injunction, he states the resulting conclusion: "And so," etc. He further remarks that the *Vṛttyadhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the Vṛtti) is consistent only if the injunction regarding hearing and so forth is understood as a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

"Exactly for this reason" means precisely because there is no status as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*). The connection is: "for this very reason, there is the instruction of repetition. Regarding the commentary beginning with "ending in vision" and concluding with "ending in the production of rice-grains," the following is the interpretation: hearing and the other [means] have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), and thus they are to be repeated.

They culminate in vision (*darśana*). Just as actions such as threshing, when repeated, culminate in the production of rice grains and are thus considered to have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), here too the "visible fruit" is the very vision of the Self (*ātmadarśana*); this is the meaning. [As it is said: "Indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, is to be heard..."
By such statements as these, hearing and other practices are prescribed with the aim of realizing the Self; in that regard, what [is the case]?

For in the absence of that [conceptualization], when something is being observed by the eye according to its actual state, if some other subtle particularity not yet grasped therein is pointed out by someone else, then for the sake of understanding that [particularity], there occurs once again the very same [operation] of that eye.
A resolve indeed proceeds toward action; thus, when the living self (jīva) is perceived by the mind as "I," one hears—
through the Vedāntas acquired through study— the teaching that its true nature is the non-dual consciousness of Brahman, and applies the mind with vigilance toward that realization.
In this way, since a person might at some time engage in such a deposit, their engagement in hearing the Vedānta would be merely occasional.
Regarding the doubt as to whether these [preparatory rites] are to be performed only once or should be repeated until the realization of the Self (ātma-darśana),
[the prima facie view is] that they are to be performed only once, since the injunction is fulfilled by that much. This is just like the case of the Agnicayana sacrifice,
where the statement "having filled [the vessel] with all herbs, one threshes them" prescribes [a single performance].
Just as the threshing of all medicinal herbs— which constitutes the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the mortar—

is performed only once, so too the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other means when performed once becomes the cause for the vision of Brahman (*brahmadarśana*) in another birth; thus, the injunctions for hearing and so forth constitute an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction).
When [the truth] has been attained, the conclusion is that repetition of hearing and so forth must be performed. Why? Because of repeated instruction;

for instance, in the Bhṛguvallī, the father instructs Bhṛgu repeatedly, saying, "Seek to know Brahman through austerity," where austerity means reflection, that is, the inquiry into Brahman. Likewise, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya, [the father instructs] his son Śvetaketu.
He instructs [the disciple] repeatedly with the words "That thou art," preceded by reflection and meditation.

Furthermore, since the fruit of the vision of the Self is to be produced through hearing and the other means, and since a visible means in the form of the repetition of hearing and so forth is possible, it is improper to postulate an invisible means; therefore, one should apply the repetition of hearing and the rest to the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam*.

Furthermore, because it is difficult to understand [otherwise], repetition is indeed required—just as in the case of threshing which results in the production of rice—but there is no repetition as in the case of threshing performed within the fire-altar (*agnicayana*); for there is a disparity, since the threshing performed therein has an invisible (*adṛṣṭa*) purpose.
This was established in the *Āvṛttyadhikaraṇa*.
This does not accord with those who maintain that it is an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction); therefore, the eleventh chapter [of the *Tantravārttika*] defines the *tantra*.

For this very reason—the meaning being "because it is already established"—this reason is connected with the sense of the particle *eva* (only/just) through the absence of being an *apūrva-vidhi*. He states the reason for its being a *niyama-vidhi* (a restrictive injunction).

Regarding the phrase "in the absence of that": the connection is that, in the absence of that [external object], a person might at some time engage in placing the mind itself attentively upon that [object]. He provides an example for the exertion involved in the mental operation directed toward grasping the specific qualities residing in the self, which are not being grasped by the mind through ordinary means. He says: "Just as..."

"Something" means such things as jewels and so forth. "Therein" means in those jewels and so forth. "Of that very [object]"—the sense of the particle *eva* is that it does not [proceed] toward another operation. The connection is: "it proceeds again toward the operation of the eye. "Proceeds" means it proceeds in such a way that there is focused attention (*praṇidhāna*).

The *praṇidhāna* (mental orientation) is an adverbial adjunct; it is the effort conducive to the subsequent act of opening the eyes by fixing them toward an object such as a jewel. Thus, there is a distinction between *praṇidhāna* and *pravṛtti* (activity). Regarding the Vedāntas: "There is no diversity whatsoever here; I am Brahman, pure consciousness."

The meaning is: by means of [the realization] "I am Brahman" and so forth. Here, in this Brahman, there is not even the slightest collection of differentiated particulars in the form of various knowers, cognitions, and objects of knowledge. Prajñāna is supreme knowledge—the eternally self-luminous consciousness of the living being (jīva-caitanya), which is the conscious Self (cid-ātman) acting as the witness to the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties. I am that Brahman.

"I am Brahman" (*brahmāsmi*) is the meaning of the Vedas (*śrutīnām*). The term "study" (*adhyayana*) refers to the study of the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*). "Having heard" means having known [it] through indirect cognition; "one who has faith in the Śruti" means for the sake of attaining that [direct realization]. "Therein" (*tatra*) means in the Self (*ātman*) as grasped by the notion of "I" (*aham*).
In such a way that there is attentiveness and one-pointedness of mind.

The scriptural statement "not attained by the mind" suggests that [the Self] is not an object of the mind; yet, because there is also the scriptural hearing that "it is to be seen by the mind alone" and "it is seen by the highest intellect," a doubt arises that it might still be an object for an uncollected mind.

It is incorrect to suggest that, just as upon hearing a specific [instruction] regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) grasped through the notion "I am," there might occasionally be an engagement of the mental faculty even independently of Vedāntic inquiry— as occurs when hearing the Vedāntas—
because the Śruti denies that Brahman is an object of the mind; for one who has studied the scriptures, this denial is understood.
He says "no" because of the possibility [of such a relation]. The connection is that the scriptural statement "without reaching" refers to the object of the mind when it is not attentive.

The meaning is that words such as "Truth," "Knowledge," and so forth, being unable to reach Brahman through their primary power (*śakti*), turn back along with the mind and resort to indication (*lakṣaṇā*). By the phrase "along with the mind," [it is shown] that even the mind [cannot reach Brahman directly].

The meaning is that attainment is negated. Just as the status of Brahman as an object of the mind is negated, its being an object [of other faculties] is also stated by Śruti. Thus, when there is a contradiction between two Śrutis, regarding the Śruti that establishes that Brahman is accessible to the intellect (buddhi) denoted by the word "mind" (manas), [the former] is superior.

On account of the force of the qualifying attribute, the scriptural negation of being an object is understood to mean the negation of being an object for an uncollected mind; thus, since it is possible for one who has completed the study of the Vedas with their auxiliary branches to understand this established rule, he states "by the mind alone" to show that activity in the operation of the mind itself is unavoidable. "Uncollectedness" means the state of being devoid of one-pointed concentration (*ekāgratā*).

Regarding the phrase "because doubt arises": although one ought to say that the aforementioned determination of the established order is possible through the force of the qualification "foremost," the statement "because doubt arises" has this underlying intention:

that the mind does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*), as indicated by the scriptural text on its being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*).

Due to the contradiction arising from the presence of an *upādhi*, even in the case of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Self, the mind does not possess the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*), because that realization is of the nature of the eternal witness (*nityasākṣin*). Furthermore, in passages such as "it must be witnessed by the mind alone" (*manasaivānudraṣṭavyam*), the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is intended to signify that the mind is a means (*sādhana*) toward the direct realization produced by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising from the sentence; all such points belong to the domain of verbal testimony (*śābda*).

This will be explained in the section on *parokṣavāda*. Furthermore, since in reality the mind lacks the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the imagined object to be excluded by a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*)— namely, that "the person might at some time engage in the operation of the mind itself"— is indeed inconsistent.

Alternatively, since there is the possibility of the delusion that liberation arises from the knowledge of a distinct self— based on scriptural passages such as, "When he perceives the other, the Lord, and His greatness, he is freed from grief"—
one might even study another scripture consisting of an inquiry into a distinct self for the sake of obtaining the knowledge that is the means to liberation.
Let there be an injunction for the rule of hearing the Vedāntas concerning the non-dual Self, so that activity may occur toward that [Self].

For this very reason, he states another alternative to be excluded: "Or rather... Through such scriptural passages as "For one who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs, joy and sorrow depart from him who knows the Self," it is understood that knowledge of the Self is the means to liberation.
Moreover, even for one who has studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary branches (*sāṅga*), the knowledge of the reality of the Self does not arise in this world without inquiry (*vicāra*);

for it is established by experience that doubts regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*) and so forth persist due to the possibility of various interpretations (*yojanā*) within the Upaniṣads (*vedānta*) which expound the Self. Consequently, one who seeks the knowledge that is the means to liberation [must engage in inquiry].

Just as one who engages in the inquiry into Vedānta proceeds toward the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* scripture in order to dispel misconceptions, doubts, and the like regarding the purport that obstructs the knowledge of That [Brahman], so too might one at times engage in the inquiry into scriptures such as Nyāya and Sāṃkhya, interpreting them according to their own preferred method of reconciliation.

Because there exists the investigation into the Vedānta; and because the investigation of the Self found in the systems of logic such as Sāṃkhya lacks the nature of an investigation into the non-dual Self, it does not remove errors, doubts, and the like regarding such a Self, since the Vedāntas themselves would otherwise be subject to the error of attributing their own purport to that [dualistic] Self.

Furthermore, it should not be said that the engagement of one seeking knowledge is impossible therein because [the Self] is the cause [of bondage]; for even in that case, engagement is possible through delusion, based on the view that knowledge of the Supreme Self as distinct from the individual soul (jīva) is the means to liberation. Nor does this apply only to one who has completed the study of the Vedas along with its auxiliary sciences.

The delusion that the knowledge of a distinct self (*bhinnātma-jñāna*) is the means to liberation cannot arise. It must be stated that in the Vedāntas, such as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*), the knowledge of the supreme Self as non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*) is perceived to be the means to liberation; for [it is said]: "When he sees the other, the Lord, as the one who is worshipped... (*juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyaty anyam īśam asya*).

Regarding the phrases "the greatness" and "he who is free from sorrow," since there is a possibility of error due to the word "other" occurring in the scripture, one might mistakenly perceive the Lord—
who is the impeller of the intellect and other faculties through His mere proximity— as a separate entity distinct from the intellect and so forth;
for, through delusion, the conscious Self has been grasped as non-different from the intellect and its functions.

The teaching regarding difference is purposeful, but it does not mean that the individual soul (jīva) is different [from Brahman]. Since the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is established by direct perception, it does not require a scriptural teaching; for from another Śruti text, "juṣṭam" means served or resorted to by the hosts of seers (*ṛṣi-saṃgha-juṣṭam*), one perceives: "I am the Lord."
The true meaning of the Śruti is that when one directly realizes the glory of this Lord— that is, His essential nature characterized by greatness— one attains it and becomes free from sorrow.

In this context, the word "self" (ātman) refers to the second [kind of self], as determined by a thorough consideration of the surrounding passages such as, "All this is what this self is. For it is not a matter of established tradition that a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) applies only when there is a possibility of obtaining the object through other means in reality. By which...

Since it must be admitted that the direct realization of Brahman— which consists of the ascertainment of its existence— is achievable solely through the hearing of Vedānta, by means of the removal of the impurities that obstruct it and which are produced by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the observance of the rule of hearing Vedānta, [it follows] that in reality...

One might suspect that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is not appropriate because there is no other means of accomplishment; however, a restrictive injunction applies in cases where the optional attainment of the intended means cannot be prevented due to the possibility of another alternative means being conceived as a potential option.

[Objection: But surely, in the injunction "the Self is to be heard," only the investigation of the Self in general is understood, and not the investigation of the non-dual Self; therefore, how can the exclusion of the investigation of a differentiated Self be obtained through this injunction? To this, he says: "Here," etc.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the statement of the proposition—"When the Self is seen, everything becomes known"—is included.
For when the Self, by virtue of being the substrate of all, is the self of all, then upon the knowledge of that Self, everything distinct from it becomes known in its true nature;

furthermore, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) expressed as "all is indeed the Self" is established, and not otherwise. Thus, the word "Self" occurring in the sentence to be heard must refer exclusively to the non-dual Self.

The intended meaning is that by means of the rule for investigating that [Brahman], the exclusion of the investigation of a distinct self is obtained. Now, an objection: just as threshing is a means for the production of rice, even though fingernail-picking and other such methods are in fact also means, it is appropriate to have a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) whose fruit is the exclusion of those other methods. But here, in the case of the direct realization of non-dual Brahman—

Since the investigation of a distinct self does not possess the status of a means [to liberation] in reality, a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) whose fruit is its exclusion is not tenable. Nor is there an inconsistency in the restrictive injunction merely because the investigation of a distinct self cannot be excluded; for there exists the possibility of an investigation that is independent of a teacher and conducted in a vernacular tongue.

It should not be argued that there is no possibility of exclusion [from the definition] because works such as treatises (*prabandha*), histories (*itihāsa*), and Purāṇas— which will be cited— possess the quality of being causes for the direct realization of Brahman in the form of a certainty regarding reality (*satā-niścaya*).
For even those [works], according to the method to be explained immediately hereafter, are [ultimately] causes for the cessation of ignorance through the certainty regarding reality.

Anticipating the objection that—just like the inquiry into Vedānta dependent upon a teacher—the direct realization [of Brahman] is not a means [to liberation] because it does not remove the impurities that obstruct the direct realization of form (*rūpa-sākṣātkāra-pratibandhaka-kalmaṣa-nivṛtti*), and thus lacks actual status as a *sādhana*, and therefore a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is impossible—he says: "Not so. "Family custom" (*kuladharma*) means that which has come down through the lineage of one's family.
The meaning is that while there is a necessity for Dharma, in reality there is no such necessity for the attainment of other means to it. "By which" (yena) means "by way of necessity.
"For the sake of the meaningfulness of the restrictive rule" (niyamārthavattvāya) refers to the Vedānta [teaching] dependent on a Guru, which is intended to be enjoined.

Since it is possible for the nature of direct realization in the form of certainty to arise even through investigation and other means independent of a teacher— merely by hearing [the scriptures]— there would be no necessity for the rule of hearing the Vedānta under the guidance of a teacher.

The meaning is that, since there is no visible purpose [for the ritual], an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) must be accepted; furthermore, its status as a means for the removal of ignorance (*avidyā*) by way of the cessation of impurity (*kalmaṣa*) must necessarily be postulated. The phrase "being produced by the unseen merit" is an attribute of the cessation of impurity, while the word "itself" (*sva*) refers to direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), lest one should suspect [otherwise].
For by that much alone, the connection is established, since the accomplishment of its fruit— the fulfillment of the portion not yet attained— is achieved; or rather,
it is like [the acquisition of knowledge] dependent on study from the mouth of a teacher.

For a person of keen intellect, the immediate, determinate knowledge of Brahman— which is of the nature of direct realization— is possible even from the inquiry into Vedānta accomplished through one’s own effort alone. However, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the rule of hearing the Vedāntic statements from the mouth of a Guru is required for the removal of ignorance and its latent impressions.

It is employed by means of renunciation (*nirāsa*). In the absence of that [renunciation], it remains as if indirect (*parokṣakalpa*), not removing ignorance because it is obstructed by its non-existence. Nor is there any logical impossibility of the non-removal of ignorance upon the arising of knowledge;
for the absence of an obstacle is required in all cases, even when [knowledge exists].
Because, upon the perception of a specific instance of direct perception, there is an obstruction caused by a limiting condition (upādhi);
thus, the non-cessation of that [delusion] is logically established, just as the delusion regarding the form of a reflection does not cease.

He states the reason for the rule that "where the non-attainment of the intended means of accomplishment is occasional and cannot be prevented, there is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi). The phrase "by that much alone" means by the mere attainment of the portion not previously established.
He states the reason for the occasional non-attainment of the intended means of accomplishment: "by way of being an alternative means."
Since the direct realization of Brahman, which consists of certainty for the virtuous, is a visible fruit, it is possible—

according to the previously mentioned method— that through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one may conceive of even literary compositions in vernacular languages as being means to that realization, just like the inquiry into the Vedānta.
Since there is, in reality, no status as a means [to liberation], he states another point to be excluded by saying "by way of possibility" (*saṃbhāvanayā*).
Alternatively, by the word "only" (*mātra*), the Guru is excluded; in that case, it is said that ignorance is removed solely by the direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman.

[The opponent] objects: "Since the attainment of the fruit characterized by the cessation [of ignorance] occurs [through other means], what is the use of the injunction for hearing [the scriptures] which is dependent on a teacher? [The author] replies with the words "But... (kiṃtu).

To ensure that the injunction regarding the restriction of hearing is not purposeless, it must be assumed that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from that restriction is required for the realization of its own fruit, namely the immediate intuition (*aparokṣajñāna*) of Brahman; therefore, the cessation of ignorance does not result from the aforementioned indirect knowledge.

He resolves [the objection] with the words "attainment" (*siddhi*), meaning "from the mouth of the Guru. The term "by means of non-attachment" (*nirāsenā*) means "by means of the door of non-attachment.
After the word "thus" (*iti*), the phrase "as something to be conceptualized" (*kalpanīyatvena*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the phrase "by its absence":
this means "by means of impurity," in the sense that there is an absence of the removal of impurity (*kalmaṣa*). The word "kalpam" means "equal" (*tulyam*). And not...

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of making the restrictive rule meaningful" and so forth: previously in the text, it was stated that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule serves as a cause for the arising of knowledge by means of the removal of impurity (*kalmaṣa*); whereas here, it is shown that once knowledge has arisen, it brings about the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of eliminating the impurity that acts as an obstacle therein.

It should not be said that there is a contradiction between earlier and later statements in asserting that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule of hearing (*śravaṇa-niyama*) is a means [to liberation],

for there is no contradiction due to the difference in philosophical perspectives. Now, even if this were so, it would be incorrect to claim that the Brahma-knowledge, once arisen, requires the removal of impurities— which is accomplished by the unseen merit of the restrictive rule— in order to fulfill its own effect, which is the cessation of ignorance.

Thinking that [the cognition] is valid because it possesses the nature of validity (*pramātva*), like the valid cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth, he raises an objection: "And there is no arising of knowledge.

[The phrase] "the impossibility of non-cessation" means that there would indeed be the cessation of ignorance. Even in the case of the valid cognition of mother-of-pearl, although there is no dependence on another [means of knowledge],...

He offers a rebuttal, stating that since even in cases of the delusion of a reflection one observes a requirement for the perception of specific features as an absence of obstacles, it is likewise logical that the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) requires that same perception.

And thus, since the undertaking of self-study (*svādhyāya*) would also apply through means such as reading from a written text, there exists the inquiry into Vedānta even when preceded by one's own effort alone, just like the rule prescribing study dependent on the mouth of a teacher (*gurumukha*).

Since this [injunction] would apply to the case as an injunction of the rule of hearing (*śravaṇa*) dependent on the mouth of a guru for the purpose of the direct realization of Brahman in the form of certainty, it might be argued that it is redundant; for the exclusion of inquiry devoid of a guru is already established by the very injunction of approaching a guru, namely: "For the sake of knowing That, one should approach a guru alone."
It should not be suspected that this is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi).
Regarding the phrase "of the absence of an impediment":

although, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the absence of an impediment never functions as a cause (*hetu*) anywhere, nevertheless, because it is accepted that an unimpeded causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause of the effect, it indeed possesses such a delimiting property (*avacchedakatā*).

The meaning is that there is a dependence on the absence of obstacles. "Because its non-cessation would otherwise result" means that it would follow that ignorance could not be removed by the knowledge achieved through inquiry devoid of a guru.
He establishes the rule for the necessity of hearing (śravaṇa) along with an illustration, saying: "And thus..."

The meaning is: "when there is the attainment of that which is to be excluded, namely, reflection devoid of a teacher. [Regarding the word] "written": for one who desires worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), there is no accomplishment of prosperity and so forth without the performance of the Vedic rites;
and such performance is not possible without knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas; and that knowledge of its meaning...

The attainment of the Veda, which is denoted by the term *svādhyāya*, is not possible without [the acquisition of the Veda]. Regarding the acquisition of the Veda, both study—characterized by the repetition after the utterance from the mouth of a teacher—and reading from a written manuscript are well known in the world as the means for its attainment. Thus, by the sentence enjoining study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the study of the Veda [is established].

The meaning is that just as it is enjoined by the very act of study that one should accomplish the acquisition of the syllables (akṣara), and thereby the exclusion of methods such as reading from a written manuscript is obtained, so it is in the present case as well. [Objection: But for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman...
It is heard that reverence for the guru is required; however, it does not possess the status of being a direct means (*sākṣāt-sādhana*) toward the knowledge of Brahman produced by scripture.

Therefore, when a means is required for the production of that knowledge, the inquiry dependent upon the guru alone is postulated as the means by virtue of its suitability, rather than some unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), since a visible means (*dṛṣṭa-dvāra*) is available.

Because it is improper to assume the unseen (adṛṣṭa) when [the result] is already possible [through other means]. Since approaching the teacher is established as a means to knowledge by way of inquiry dependent upon the teacher through the very injunction for approaching him, the exclusion of inquiry conducted without a teacher is already established by that alone; therefore, the restrictive injunction of "listening" (*śravaṇa*) in the statement "one should listen" would be fruitless.

He raises an objection with the words "And not... [The text continues: "A Brahmin should attain detachment (*nirveda*)," where the word "he" (*saḥ*) refers back to the Brahmin mentioned in the preceding sentence, "There is nothing uncreated through what is created. To the question "In what manner?", the Śruti says: "The uncreated, eternal liberation (*mokṣa*) [is not attained] by means of created action (*karma*)."

"It does not exist. Therefore, having understood that liberation is to be accomplished through the knowledge of Brahman, one should approach a teacher for the sake of that knowledge; this is the meaning. Since the investigation dependent upon a teacher is already established by the scriptural injunction "that [Self] is to be heard," approaching the teacher is enjoined as a subordinate part of that process. However, in the absence of such an injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*), it would be optional.

Since approaching the guru (*gurūpasadana*) is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) of hearing (*śravaṇa*), and since there is no injunction for hearing [independent of it], there is no such injunction [for approaching the guru] at all; therefore, its futility does not arise.

Otherwise, by the very injunction for approaching [the teacher] which is a subsidiary element of Vedic study (*adhyayana*), [prohibitions against] writing, reciting from a manuscript, and so forth, would [already apply].
