If exclusion were the meaning, then even the rule of study would become futile;

or rather, since the hearing of non-dualistic treatises concerning the Supreme Self is already possible as an alternative, let there be an injunction for the rule of hearing the Vedāntas. Nor does this contradict such rules as "one should not speak like a Mleccha," and so forth.
Precisely because of that prohibition, there is no attainment [of the goal];
thinking that hearing the Vedānta is impossible due to the dullness of one's training in the scriptures,
he disregards even the prohibition regarding human goals and desires to know non-duality through literary compositions in the vernacular.
For even in that case, since the possibility of pride arising exists, the restrictive injunction is established as purposeful.
He offers a rebuttal, stating that because the procedure for going (*gamanavidhi*) attains its own existence, it does not result in the futility of the injunction to hear (*śravaṇavidhi*).

[He says] "of the approaching of the teacher" (*gurūpasadanasya*). He states an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the case where an auxiliary injunction (*aṅgavidhi*) would render the principal injunction (*pradhānavidhi*) futile, [saying] "otherwise" (*anyathā*).

The sense is that since the approach to a teacher can serve as a visible means for the acquisition of syllables by way of study, it is improper to abandon that [visible means] when it is available; thus, [the injunction] must be "by the prescribed rule alone.
He states another alternative [exclusion]: "Or rather," let it be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*).

The meaning is that there should be a restrictive injunction regarding the subject of inquiry, stating that one who desires to know non-duality (*advaita*) must investigate the Vedāntas alone, and not vernacular compositions (*bhāṣā-prabandha*). [Objection: But surely, a person must not utter the clear speech of what is called "Mleccha" (barbarian) vernacular compositions; otherwise—

He raises the objection: "What is the need for an injunction, since the exclusion of vernacular compositions for those qualified to hear [the scripture] is established by the force of the prohibition itself—that the person [who violates it] would incur sin? He says: "And not so.
For if the prohibition of vernacular were an auxiliary part (*aṅga*) of knowledge, then, having transgressed that prohibition, one would [be liable to sin] therein.

One might argue that, out of fear that knowledge will not arise, one would not engage in that [activity], since it lacks human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) and is therefore prohibited; and thus, even by transgressing that prohibition, engagement in listening to poetry and the like might occasionally occur. To this, he replies: "removes" (*harati*).

Regarding the phrase "mastery of the scriptures": he states the reason for [the necessity of] transcending [the literal meaning] with the words "it is impossible. The reason for this impossibility is the paucity of mastery.
Now, one might object: what of that qualified seeker for whom hearing the Vedānta is impossible due to a paucity of mastery?
If it is argued that the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) for the investigation of Vedānta is untenable because an injunction cannot apply to an impossible object, we say no;

for although an investigation of the Bhāṣya and such works may be impossible for one of dull intellect, an investigation of a Vedānta manual (*prakaraṇa*) is possible even for one who is a dull-witted candidate (*adhikārin*). As it has been said in the *Pañcadaśī* regarding one of dull intelligence: [text follows].
One should awaken the seeker through the bliss of the Self; that is to say, Yājñavalkya awakened his own beloved Maitreyī by means of the section titled "The Bliss of the Self" (Ātmānanda).
For it is indeed accepted [in the *Kartradhikaraṇa*] that,

although there is a prohibition against speaking untruth for the sake of a human purpose as established therein, the prohibition is nonetheless acknowledged for some reason during the interval of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, lest the performance of the sacrifice be rendered defective by such [speaking].

Since there might be a tendency for one who desires [the result] to speak untruth, the prohibition "one should not speak untruth" is established as being for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) by virtue of its context within the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*); thus, the prohibition possesses purposefulness by way of serving the sacrifice. Alternatively, it is just as the recollection of the meaning of a mantra occurs through the mantras themselves.

The restriction "only that which is to be proven" applies because, by that very principle, there is the possibility— under one alternative— that even the Kalpasūtras, the *ātmiya* (one's own) texts, and the *grahaṇaka* (introductory) statements might be included; likewise, there is the possibility under another alternative that even the Vedānta-based Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and human-authored compositions might be included.
Let this restriction exist because of its occurrence.

He states that even the Mīmāṃsakas accept that for the sake of achieving a great fruit, one may engage in what is prohibited— even by transgressing the prohibition of human goals— and that such a prohibition makes the injunction meaningful:
"For this is indeed admitted here."

He who has accepted the transgression of a prohibition is described as such. He states the reason indicated by the phrase "from whatever cause" with the words "unimpaired" (*avikalām*) and "possessing purpose" (*arthavattvam*).
The connection with the preceding [text] is that this has been "explained. He states another alternative exclusion with the words "or else" (*yadvā*) and "by means of mantras alone" (*mantrair eva*).

Regarding the doubt as to whether mantras such as "Agnirmūrdhā" (Fire is the head), which are enjoined for use in a sacrifice by the Śruti and other authorities, assist the sacrifice by producing an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) through mere recitation, or rather through the visible means of reminding one of the ritual action— since even the Kalpasūtras and similar texts serve to remind one of the actions to be performed— [the conclusion is that they assist through the visible means].
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that mantras are for the sake of what is unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), because [otherwise] they would be meaningless.

The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since mantras assist the sacrifice by way of manifesting its meaning, and because it is illogical to postulate an unseen purpose when a visible purpose is possible, they serve the action required for the performance of the rite which yields the fruit.
The mantras serve as auxiliary elements (*aṅga*) to the ritual action by way of causing the recollection of the means for that action.

It should not be argued that the recollection of the means is not the mediating factor (*dvāra*) because such recollection can be accomplished through *kalpasūtras* and other texts just as well as through mantras; for there is an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*) stating that the meaning of the mantra must be recollected by means of the mantra alone.

Because it is possible [for the result to arise from other means]. However, the restriction will serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). As it has been said: "Where a visible [result] is not obtained, there the postulation of an invisible [result] (*adṛṣṭa*) should occur. And thus, just as by the restrictive injunction regarding mantras (*maṃtra-niyama-vidhi*), the exclusion of the *Kalpasūtras* and other texts based on mantras is effected, so too by the study of one's own Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*).

The meaning of the illustrative example and the illustrated subject in this text is as follows: when the restriction that "only the Vedāntas are to be investigated by one desiring to know Brahman" is established, the exclusion of their source—the Itihāsas and so forth—is obtained. This [text] is a compendium of the ritual matters associated with the performance [of sacrifices] as composed by the Yājñikas.

The "sentence" (vākya) refers to the *grahaṇaka-vākya*; the two "histories" (itihāsau) are the *Mahābhārata* and human-authored compositions (*pauruṣeya-prabaṃdha*) such as the *Prabodhacandrodaya*, which have been cited as examples.
In the *Adhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*, it is stated that this is in every respect a rule of non-restriction (*aniyama-vidhi*) and a rule for an additional auxiliary (*sahakāryantara-vidhi*);

however, the description of it as an "original injunction" (*apūrva-vidhi*) is intended to mean that even if it is a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*), there exists a partial non-attainment (*pākṣiky aprāpti*). In that very context, the phrase "by way of an alternative" (*pakṣeṇa*) refers to this partial non-attainment.

"It has been made clear by the application of the words of the sūtras devoted to exposition"—thus say the followers of the Vivaraṇa. For one who has performed the hearing (of the scriptures), first of all, there arises from the word itself a non-doubting, indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). For the word [produces] indirect knowledge.
Because its capacity is determined by its nature as a producer, it cannot overstep that [nature].
The mention of "the wick" (*vartyāni*) is an illustration, as other things to be excluded are also possible.

For instance, in the Śruti passage, "Its cause is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga," two means for attaining That by way of realizing Brahman are specified; the meaning of the term *sāṃkhya* consists of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditation (*dhyāna*).
One is the path of meditation (*upāsanā-mārga*) mentioned in the third chapter, which is expressed by the term "yoga";

the other is the primary cause under discussion, characterized as the cause of the universe, which is attained through direct realization (*pratyak-tvena*) by means of knowledge reached via Sāṃkhya and Yoga— this is the meaning of the Śruti.

Likewise, it is well-established in the Brahma-mīmāṃsā that the meditation upon Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahmopāsanā) is the cause for the attainment of Brahman by the meditator who has gone to the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), through the means of the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra); similarly, specific forms of austerity and so forth are established in the Purāṇas and other texts as direct means for the knowledge of reality.

An established example should be cited: likewise, for one who is devoted to the Vedāntas under a teacher, who is skilled, and who possesses the qualification for hearing (*śravaṇa*), there might occasionally arise an inclination toward the path of yoga, the practice of meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*), specific forms of austerity (*tapas*), and so forth—just as toward the hearing of Vedānta—for the sake of attaining the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore, [the following] has the purpose of removing that [inclination].
Since a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible, he concludes the position of the restrictive injunction with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*).

Now, one might object that if it is a restrictive injunction, there would be a contradiction with the commentary on the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*), which states that it is an injunction of another auxiliary (*sahakāryantara-vidhi*); to this he replies:
"of another auxiliary," etc. The sense is that the possibility of it being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*) has already been refuted. Regarding the phrase "in that very [context]":

The meaning is that this is stated specifically in the *Bhāṣya* on that very section. By the sentence "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*), hearing is enjoined with the aim of producing a non-doubting, indirect verbal knowledge; it is not enjoined with the aim of producing a verbal direct realization, because by its very nature, a word generates only indirect knowledge. This remains true even when [the word] is assisted by inquiry (*vicāra*).
Furthermore, since it is never observed that a word is a cause for direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*),
this [injunction] does not constitute an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction) even if its fruit is mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). This is because, even in the absence of an injunction,
the status of a word as a cause of verbal cognition and the status of deliberation as a cause for the determination of the object of inquiry are already established.

Since it has been established that hearing the Vedānta texts, characterized by inquiry through the power of both [hearing and reflection], serves as the cause for indubitable verbal knowledge; however, adopting the aforementioned objects of exclusion, he states the view that this is indeed a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). Thus: "For one who has performed hearing, at first..."

However, for one who has subsequently performed reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises from that very [scriptural testimony] once it is endowed with these specific auxiliary factors;
for even a sense organ, though incapable of cognizing the aspect of "thatness" (*tattva*), acquires that capacity [through such auxiliaries].
Recognition arises from the association with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); it is not the case that a word— which, like [the sense organ], is incapable of producing direct knowledge by itself—
is established as capable of doing so in instances such as the direct perception of a beloved woman who has been contemplated during a state of separation.
It is logical that meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), through its accumulation and conjunction, generates immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*); consequently,

the capacity of a word to generate indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding its own object is inherently contradicted by its status as a means of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*) when conjoined with the accumulation of meditative cultivation, just like [the sense organs] which are instruments of cognition.

And since the capacity to produce indirect knowledge has already been established, it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) as before; such is the view of those who hold a partial position (*ekadeśin*).

Now, are *manana* (reflection) and *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) not prescribed for the purpose of attaining a certain, yet indirect, verbal knowledge? Or are they prescribed for the sake of direct [knowledge] arising from the verbal [testimony]? It is not the first, because that [direct knowledge] is established by mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone prior to the performance of reflection and so forth; nor is it the second, because the word produces only indirect knowledge.
He dispels the doubt that "capacity [for action] is what you intend" by adopting the second alternative, beginning with the word "paścāt" (afterwards).
This means: immediately after verbal, non-doubting, indirect knowledge; that is, once reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) have been performed.

By which [reason] he was so described. "From that very [source]" means "from the word itself"; the sense is that the diversity of effects is observed due to the diversity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). He demonstrates this very point by means of an example: "the parts thereof" and "its capacity."
In this context, the meaning is "the capacity for generating knowledge whose object is a partial aspect.
Regarding the phrase "of the word," the connection with what follows is that it is logical for a word to be the producer of immediate (non-conceptual) knowledge.
Now, even if the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is established as an auxiliary to the sense organ in that case, [what of] the accumulation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?

Anticipating the objection that the capacity to produce direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) by way of being an auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) for the instrument of knowledge has not been established anywhere, he says: "In the absence... (*vidhura*).
In the phrase "capable of that" (*tatsamartha*), the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is the production of direct perception. But even so—

He says "no" [to the objection] because it would follow that the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and so forth would be *apūrva-vidhi*s (injunctions of something previously unknown), on the grounds that the accumulation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consisting of reflection and meditation—by virtue of its cooperation with verbal testimony—is not established as a cause for verbal direct perception (*śābda-sākṣātkāra*) by any other means of knowledge; therefore, he says: "And thus... (*tataśca*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because both the production of mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) and the production of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) have already been established. It should be understood that the statement regarding the cause of mediate knowledge is for the purpose of establishing the *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction) of the rule of hearing (*śravaṇavidhi*). This refers to [the meditation] performed together with the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the "city" (*pura*).

The direct realization of Brahman does not arise from hearing the Vedanta, but rather through the mind alone, according to the scriptural text: "It is to be perceived by the mind alone. Furthermore, this is supported by the statement in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*: "The mind, refined by the teachings of the scriptures and the preceptor, as well as by tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues, is the instrument for the vision of the Self."

Some, however, maintain that since hearing [the scriptures] is for the purpose of attaining indirect knowledge free from doubt, the restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) exists solely for that purpose.
In the context of showing that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a beloved woman—

even though it is not independent externally— the specific causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established such that the internal organ, when assisted by the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of an external object, becomes the cause of its direct perception.

The sense is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and the absence of sublaters (*bādhaka*), the causal relation is grasped as follows: "That which is delimited by being a means of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇatva*) assisted by the accumulation of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāpracaya*) is the cause of immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*). In this regard, it is unestablished that the nature of verbal testimony (*śabda*) is simply to generate mediate cognition (*parokṣajñāna*).
Since the view that the mediacy (*parokṣatva*) and so forth residing in knowledge is caused by a specific defect of the sense organ will be refuted later,

the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*)— just as for reflection (*manana*) and so forth— is not untenable with respect to verbal immediate intuition (*śābdāparokṣa*). Thus, he indicates his own dissatisfaction [with this view] by referring to "those who hold a single part" (*tadekadeśinaḥ*), which means those who hold a single part of the *Vivaraṇa*.
He states another opinion: "The direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman does not arise from the hearing of Vedānta.

In this view as well, the reason should be understood as being that the capacity of the word (*śabda*) to produce indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is already established by its inherent nature, and thus it cannot be exceeded. He then asks: "What, then, is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the direct realization of Brahman?"
"What then? [The author] says "by the mind alone" (*manasaiva*), considering that the mind itself is the instrument (*karaṇa*) [of knowledge], and thus states the proof for that.

In some versions, there is a separate reading of "by the mind alone" immediately after "what then?"; in that case, there is no inconsistency. Regarding that very point, he cites the agreement of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "the scripture," which refers to sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and the instruction of the teacher.

The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include [virtues] such as patience toward the teacher's exposition of the meaning of the sentences. Thus, by establishing here that the direct realization of Brahman is mental in nature, the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are understood as being auxiliary to the mind— which is the instrument of that realization— and not as being independent acts as in the previous view.

The distinction of this view from the previous one is indicated by the phrase "by being an auxiliary to the word which is the cause of verbal direct intuition. Regarding *śravaṇa*, however, he states that there is no difference from the previous view: "But *śravaṇa*...
The phrase "precisely for that purpose" means "precisely for the sake of indubitable, verbal, mediate knowledge."

The restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding hearing (*śravaṇa*) is to be understood precisely as being for the sake of immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), because of the mention of that result in the statement "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*). Furthermore, its purposefulness (*tādarthya*) is established only through its being an auxiliary to the mind which serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*), and not directly;
for it is not accepted that immediate knowledge arises from the word alone. Nor does [immediate knowledge] arise from that [word] by itself.
Since the purpose [of the scripture] would not be achieved by the form [of the object] alone, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*).

In the case of the six notes (*ṣaḍja*, etc. heard through the ear, for the sake of removing the superimposed mutual non-discrimination, [the mutual distinction is established] by the ear aided by the hearing of the science of music (*gāndharvaśāstra*).

Because of its state of being mixed up, when a thing is manifesting through indirect perception (*parokṣadarśana*) as it truly is, the hearing of the scripture— given that the scripture exists— is useful by way of acting as an auxiliary to the sense organs for producing the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of that thing, in order to remove the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) that has been superimposed upon it. This is [the meaning].
Some say it is because [the order] has been established.

He states another opinion: "In the case of immediate knowledge," and so forth. Now, one might object: since hearing (*śravaṇa*), which consists of inquiry in the form of reasoning (*tarka*), cannot by itself have direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) as its fruit, it must be stated what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) it assists; in response to this expectation, he says: "And being for that purpose. This means: and having direct realization as its purpose.
"Of that" means "of the hearing of the Vedānta.

"Functioning as an instrument" means "functioning as the instrument for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman. However, the word "instrument" does not mean "as a cooperative cause" for the direct realization of Brahman; this is the meaning of the particle *eva*. It is not "directly."

The sense is that the hearing of Vedānta does not possess the capacity to produce direct realization independently or directly, because, being of the nature of reasoning (tarka), it lacks intrinsic validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya). He states the reason for the emphatic particle "eva" (only) in the phrase "only by way of the mind's assistance," namely: "from the word" (śabdāt).
The word "of that" means of the hearing of the Vedānta. "In that form" means in the form of being an auxiliary to the mind which is the instrument of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
Even though there is no attainment [of the object] by way of being an auxiliary to the mind which is the instrument of direct realization, [it functions] as an organ for that realization.

He states that there is attainment through cooperation: "In the case of audible [objects]. This means: in the objects of perception produced by the auditory organ. "In the case of the six notes (*ṣaḍga*, etc. means:
regarding those specific qualities of sound such as the six notes, for one who is devoid of the study of the science of music (*gāndharva-śāstra*).

A mutual non-discrimination (aviveka) is superimposed; it should be understood that what is called "mutual non-discrimination" consists of the form of mutual identity and the form of the appearance of each other's attributes.
And for one who possesses an investigation into the Gāndharva-śāstra, this [non-discrimination] is assisted by that very investigation.

Just as the six notes and so forth are experienced by the auditory faculty alone as mutually distinct, so too is there an experience among living beings of a lack of discrimination— such as identity and the like— among the conscious self, the vital breath, the body, and so forth, when these are being experienced by the internal organ, the mind.

The fruit of *śravaṇa*— which consists of a specific mental modification (*ceto-vṛtti*) characterized by an inquiry into the principles conducive to determining the purport (*tātparya*) of Vedānta statements regarding non-dual Brahman— is neither a mediate nor an immediate cognition of Brahman, since that [cognition] arises from the word [itself].

Because it is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor can it be argued that hearing (*śravaṇa*) should consist merely in the knowledge of words qualified by the intended meaning as determined through the investigation of the nature [of those words], for it would then be logical for the fruit of that [hearing] to be the knowledge of Brahman.
It must be stated that [the injunction] does not apply to knowledge, because an injunction is untenable with respect to knowledge. Furthermore,

since it is accepted that the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) is rooted in the *Jijñāsā-sūtra*, which enjoins the necessity of performing inquiry (*vicāra*), "hearing" is nothing other than inquiry in the form of mental activity consisting of reasoning and refutation (*ūha-apoha*).
Even here, if there exists a scripture that removes superimposition (*āropa*),

then the internal sense-organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), aided by that [scripture], would directly cause the realization of the Self— which is distinct from intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth and is perceived as the nature of Brahman through the Vedāntas; thus, the person engaged in inquiry [attains this] through the six means (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and so on.
He states that [the scripture] postulates a causal relationship in the case of the direct realization of its own nature (*svarasākṣātkāra*). "While being manifest" refers to the hearing of that;

"hearing of that" means the hearing of the scripture. "In the direct realization of that" means in the direct realization of the manifest object. It is utilized for the direct realization of the object as something distinct.
The meaning is that it serves as a cause. Regarding the phrase "of this":

the meaning is that since this state of being an auxiliary to the sense organ—which functions as the instrument of direct realization—is already established even without an injunction for hearing the Vedāntas in the manner described, there is no contingency of it being an *apūrvavidhi* (an original injunction).

It has been established that among the positions stated, the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) is intended either with reference to verbal knowledge as non-perceptual (*aparoakṣa*) or with reference to verbal knowledge as perceptual (*parokṣa*). Now, he states another view according to which that injunction is intended solely for the purpose of removing obstacles:
"Of the Vedānta sentences," and so forth.

In order to exclude *manana* (reflection), which consists of an inquiry into reasoning conducive to removing doubts regarding the possibility of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the phrase "conducive to the determination of the purport" (*tātparya-nirṇayānukūla*) has been stated. It should be understood that the reasonings conducive to that determination are the [six marks] beginning with the introduction (*upakrama*).
By the term "specific modification of consciousness" (*citovṛtti-viśeṣa*), a modification in the form of an action to be accomplished through effort is intended, and not [a mere mental state].

What is intended here is the concealment in the form of ignorance that is incurable, because it will be stated later that knowledge is unfit for injunction. The term "in Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*) is a locative of object (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The word "of that" (*tasya*) means "of knowledge. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including perception and so forth, with reference to knowledge.
He refutes the meaning of the word *śravaṇa* as it is accepted by the opponent’s view— that "listening" (*śravaṇa*) is what is enjoined— by stating, "And not in the form described [above].
This refers to the fact that, according to the *Brahmajijñāsā* Sūtra, one who is endowed with the fourfold means [of qualification] seeks the knowledge of Brahman.

The meaning is that an inquiry into Vedānta must be performed. This is because the word *jijñāsā* in the Sūtra indicates (*lakṣaka*) "inquiry" (*vicāra*). And since the scriptural passage "That [Self] is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) is the source of that Sūtra, if in that "to be heard" passage hearing (*śravaṇa*) consists of knowledge (*jñāna*), then the meaning of "it is to be heard" is that the performance of hearing in the form of knowledge is what must be done.

He says [this] because, if the subject matter were the same, there would be no relationship of root and derivative between the words "desire to know" (*jijñāsā*) and "should be heard" (*śrotavya*) in the two sūtras, due to the absence of a single unified meaning. He states: "Because of the injunction to hear. *Ūha* is the extraction of valid principles (*nyāya*) from fallacious arguments (*nyāyābhāsa*), while *apoha* is the rejection of those fallacious arguments.

Nor should it be argued that the fruit of inquiry itself is the knowledge of Brahman— either by means of determining the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*), or by means of removing obstacles such as errors regarding the intended meaning caused by human fallibility; for [the required] knowledge of the intended meaning is [already present] in verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*).

Because it is not accepted that [the absence of an obstacle] is a cause, and because it is not accepted that the absence of an obstacle is a cause for an effect in any instance, it is untenable for those two to serve as mediating factors (dvāra). Furthermore, if the knowledge of Brahman were produced by causes other than the form of inquiry (vicāra), its validity would result in being extrinsic (parataḥ-prāmāṇya).
Is it not the case that the collection of statements beginning with "That, my dear, is the Real" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and ending with "That is the Truth; That is the Self;
That art thou" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), which establishes the non-dual supreme reality because it possesses a consistent opening and conclusion, results in an inference of this nature?

The determination of the purport (*tātparya-nirdhāraṇa*) is the direct fruit; through that, the removal of obstacles such as the notion of *Umā* and so forth is the fruit of inquiry. Once those [obstacles] have been removed, the sentence, being unimpeded, generates the realization of non-dual Brahman. This is the actual state of affairs regarding other scriptural passages as well. And thus:

He raises an objection: even though hearing does not have the direct result of knowledge of Brahman, it may nonetheless have that as its result through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*). He says: "And [it is] not [the case that] only of inquiry... Here, the particle *eva* has the sense of "also" (*api*); thus, just as knowledge is the fruit of the means of valid cognition consisting of verbal testimony (*śabda-pramāṇa*), let it be the fruit of its inquiry (*vicāra*) as well.

The meaning is that even with respect to the knowledge which is the fruit of verbal testimony (*śabdapramāṇa*), deliberation (*vicāra*) can function as a cause either by means of determining the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*) or by means of removing obstacles dependent upon that [determination]. The qualification "produced by that" [is applied] to the exclusion of error and the like; for it is precisely error and so forth that constitute the "human fault" (*puruṣāparādha*) regarding the knowledge of the intended meaning.

He states the reason for the absence of [tātparya-jñāna] being a door [to verbal comprehension]: "of the knowledge of the intended meaning (tātparya-jñānasya)," etc. The sense is that [the knowledge of the intended meaning] is otherwise established by its producing the removal of obstacles. If the knowledge of the intended meaning were not a cause with respect to verbal comprehension, then inquiry [would serve no purpose], since it would merely result in the removal of obstacles through the determination of the intended meaning.

Considering that the status of being a cause for verbal cognition has long since vanished, he states the reason why the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*) is not a cause: "In no case [is it a cause] with respect to an effect. This is because it would contradict common worldly experience (*lokavyavahāra*), which holds that even when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is present, an effect does not arise due to the force of an obstruction. [This applies to] the absence of an obstructer...

The inclusion [of the cause] within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not accepted. Rather, the intention is that by accepting that the unobstructed causal complex is the cause of the effect, the status of being "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) is itself accepted—just as in the case of "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so on—as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) within that complex.
This is the meaning according to the intended purport (*tātparya*).

Therefore, according to the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, the injunction of hearing (*śravaṇa*), which consists of inquiry, is a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) solely for the purpose of removing human error by means of determining the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*). As for the phrase "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), it is merely a praise based on its fitness for being seen; it is not a mention of the fruit of hearing. This is the summary.

For one who has set out to hear the Vedānta for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman, there arises the possibility of engaging in other activities midway, just as one engaged in hearing texts such as the Caraka and Suśruta for the sake of medical knowledge might do; therefore, the injunction "one must hear [the Vedānta]" is a restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā-vidhi) intended to preclude that [diversion].
He states the refutation of the view that inference, which consists of deliberation on the grounds of cognition, is the cause of verbal valid knowledge:

"of the knowledge of Brahman," etc. "Extraneous" (atirikta) means extraneous to the means of verbal valid knowledge. "Because of the consequence of extrinsic validity" (paratastvāpattiḥ) means that, regarding the production of validity, there would be the state of the knowledge serving as the locus of validity being produced by an additional cause.

The meaning is that there would be dependence on another (paratastva). Consequently, the implication is that this would contradict the established tenet (apasiddhānta). If the fruit of hearing (śravaṇa) is not the knowledge of Brahman, then for what purpose is it enjoined? To this he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt).
This means because it is impossible for the fruit to be the knowledge of Brahman. [Objection: In that case, how is it that [the scripture] says "it must be seen" (draṣṭavya)?

He states the praise of the fruit of hearing [the scripture] therein: "But it is to be seen," and so on. Regarding the phrase "merely a eulogy," the word "of the Self" is to be supplied as the remainder; the sense is that the eulogy is for the purpose of inducing engagement in hearing that [scripture] and so forth. He states the position of the restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*): "for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman."

Now, it might be argued that in the view of Vācaspati Miśra, having established the obligatory nature of hearing the Vedānta according to the method to be explained, one must speak of the application of the restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*). And this being the case, for one who performs the hearing of the Vedānta with the goal of attaining knowledge—
Anticipating the objection— namely, how another activity could possibly be entailed such that a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) aimed at its cessation would be possible—
it is argued that although no other activity is entailed by virtue of [the inquiry] being a means to the knowledge of Brahman,
another activity is nonetheless possible due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality.

He states this with an illustration: "Cikitsā," etc. Medical treatment (*cikitsā*) refers to medicine; for the sake of knowing it—which can only be accomplished through medical treatises—one engages in hearing the texts known as the *Caraka*, *Suśruta*, and so forth, for that specific purpose.

The meaning is that even when one is engaged in other activities, just as there is an inclination toward those [objects], so too is there an inclination toward that [object] solely by the power of the latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding the object.

For the *Chāndogya* establishes that being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃstha*) leads to immortality, thereby determining that the state of having no other activity is the means to liberation; since the root *sthā* preceded by the prefix *sam* denotes completion,
the term "established in Brahman" refers to [the state] within Brahman.

Because completion consists in the state of having no other activity; and because in the Atharva Veda there is an explicit prohibition of other activities, stating: "Know that one alone as the Self; abandon other words"; [and] from the time of sleep until death.

This is also because of the Smṛti passage beginning with "One should lead [the mind] by means of reflection on Vedānta," and so forth. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of combining other activities— which are not conducive to the knowledge of Brahman— with "hearing" (śravaṇa) toward a single goal, it is not appropriate to maintain that the restrictive injunction (parisaṃkhyā-vidhi) is intended for the purpose of excluding those other activities.
It should be stated.

Now, just as for one engaged in listening to texts such as the *Suśruta*, medical knowledge arises without obstacle even while other activities are present, so too for one who practices the daily hearing of Vedānta, [knowledge arises] even when worldly and Vedic activities occur from time to time in the interim.

Anticipating the objection that [the injunction] would be fruitless because the arising of the knowledge of Brahman occurs spontaneously, and thus it would be a *parisaṃkhyā-vidhi* (an injunction of exclusion), [the author] intends the following resolution: for the sake of making the injunction to hear [the scriptures] meaningful, it is only hearing performed in accordance with the injunction that serves as the means to knowledge—not occasional hearing; therefore, there is no fruitlessness. With this in mind, regarding the aforementioned point...
He cites the statements of the Śruti and Smṛti: "One who is established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*). This means one for whom no other activity exists;

the state of being such is "that-ness" (*tattvam*), which refers to that person. That is to say, it is the state of being devoid of any other activity than the operations of hearing and so forth concerning Brahman, which are augmented by tranquility, self-restraint, and the like. Likewise...

And the commentary on the section concerning renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) establishes that being established in Brahman—augmented by tranquility, self-control, and so forth—is his own duty (*svadharma*), and that there is transgression for him if he deviates from it. To the question, "How is this meaning obtained through the term 'established in Brahman' (*brahmasaṃstha*)?", he says: "Of that which is preceded by *sam*. Nor is it...

It should not be said that "completion" in Brahman refers merely to dissolution into the form of Videha-kaivalya; for if that were the case, the phrase "he attains immortality" would be redundant. Therefore, it must be stated that being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthatā*) is enjoined as the means for the attainment of immortality; hence, completion in Brahman is nothing other than this.

The conclusion regarding the nature of activity is established in the Bhāṣya. Thus, the sense is that by means of the statement indicating that the state of having no other activity is the means to liberation, the cessation of all other activities for one desiring liberation is effected as a matter of course. He cites the scriptural passage directly indicating such cessation: "Him alone, the one... and so forth.
Know that very substratum— the single-natured Self— upon which this entire world, beginning with the earth, is superimposed, or upon which the gods reside.

In the sūtra beginning with "sahakāryantaravidhiḥ," since [the practice] would not be obtained in a view where the perception of difference is predominant, it is therefore a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi); and in its commentary, it is stated that for one who has performed the hearing [of the scriptures] but considers himself to have achieved his purpose through mere verbal knowledge alone, there remains ignorance.
Since there would otherwise be no inclination toward *nididhyāsana*— which is useful for the direct realization [of truth] that follows upon *tarka*—

it is accepted that this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding *nididhyāsana*, based on the mere fact that what is not a means to that end is already included among the possible options. By that same logic,

even though it is not established through a rule of combination (*samuccaya*) that something which is not a means [to realization] should be practiced alongside it, [the injunction] serves the purpose of excluding that [non-means].

Some, following the statement of the Vārttika— "Since the purpose of the injunction here must be either a restrictive rule (niyama) or an exclusive specification (parisaṃkhyā), because an exclusive specification is possible"—
say that [the injunction] "The Self is to be heard" means: "By the very non-perception of the non-Self, we worship the Supreme Self."

Śravaṇa, which is enjoined as having the Self as its object— just like manana and so forth— is indeed the knowledge of the Self arising from the scriptures and the teacher's instruction; it is not, however,
the investigation into the intended meaning (tātparya), and there is no injunction whatsoever regarding that.

He states that those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) must renounce the utterance of words and so forth that convey the non-Self (*anātman*), as these are not means for knowledge (*jñāna-sādhana*); thus says the Śruti: "Abandon other words. One who maintains that this is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) objects: "But [these words] are not useless for the knowledge of Brahman," and he answers this objection with a counter-objection (*prativandya*).
Regarding the phrase "by another auxiliary means," the ellipsis is "he does not attain silence.
The proponent of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) presents the intended meaning of the cited Sūtra and Bhāṣya;
then, the proponent of the exclusive injunction (*parisaṃkhyāvidhi*) shows it as follows: "of one who has already performed the hearing (*śravaṇa*)."

The word "of one who considers" (*manvānasya*) is followed by the ellipsis "even while engaged in another activity. This is connected [to the previous statement] because a restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) is accepted in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya merely on the grounds that the alternative possibility of its accomplishment (*tatsādhanapakṣaprāpti*) arises. In the Vārttika, the meaning of the word "here" (*atra*) is "in the sentence to be heard" (*śrotavyavākya*). Here, the restriction is the purpose of the injunction.

"Would be" constitutes one connection [to the following]. If, because [the object] is eternally attained, a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is not possible, then the meaning of the injunction would be an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*); this is the connection. The reason why exclusive specification serves as the purpose of the injunction is expressed by the words "since," and so forth. [This refers to the fact that] we [should be] free from other activities during the meditation on the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) have set out from this [knowledge]. Having shown the position that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are to be enjoined according to different views, he states the position that there is no injunction for them, beginning with "The Self is to be heard" (*ātmā śrotavyaḥ*). Regarding the phrase "being bound":
The meaning is that, just as reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), which are described as having the self as their object, are of the nature of knowledge,

so too hearing (*śravaṇa*) is indeed of the nature of knowledge. The intention is that it is not the case [that hearing is a mere action], because an investigation (*vicāra*) in the form of a ritual act to be performed cannot directly have the self as its object.

Is it not the case that the example "like reflection (*manana*) and so forth" is untenable, because reflection and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are not forms of knowledge? For reflection is an activity consisting of the investigation through reasoning;
and as for meditative absorption, according to the grammatical rule *dhya-ai cintāyām* ("the root *dhyai* is used in the sense of thinking"), it is... [meditation].

If it is argued that meditative practice (*dhyāna-kriyā*) is not knowledge, and therefore how can it be said to be like reflection (*manana*) and so forth— thus indicating that reflection (*manana*) and contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) are established as being knowledge— it is replied:
the Self (*ātman*) has the nature of Brahman because its essence is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).

The intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth are imagined [to be Brahman] because they are objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; for it is accepted that this very inference is the means of realization (*anupramāṇa*). As it is stated in the *Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa-vārtika* (Chapter 4): "Having ascertained the meaning of the scripture, it is said that 'it must be reflected upon' (*mantavya*)."
In this context, even reasoning (tarka) is employed in accordance with the words of the Veda. Reasoning concerns the meaning of the words;
thus, reflection in the form of reasoning is enjoined for the sake of strengthening the meaning of what has been heard, so that there may arise an inference exactly as it is.
That reasoning, too, is enjoined as reflection precisely when it is not in contradiction with the Śruti. And that...

Reflection (*manana*) has as its object only the meaning of the constituent parts (*padārtha*), and not the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), because the latter is to be known solely through the sentence. Likewise, the word "and" (*tathā*) has the sense of conjunction. The meaning is that just as reasoning consisting of reflection is non-contradictory to the Vedas, so too it possesses the nature of inference (*anumiti*). Therefore...

The same is the case in the Nyāya system as well. There, reflection (*manana*) is accepted as being of the nature of inference (*anumiti*). Furthermore, according to the author of the *Vārttika*, even meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) is indeed knowledge (*jñāna*). To illustrate this, it is recorded in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* within the two Maitreyī-brāhmaṇas found in the fourth and sixth chapters.
"Verily, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
Immediately following this, in the fourth [chapter], it says: "Verily, by the seeing, hearing, thinking, and knowing of the Self, my dear Maitreyī...
And in the sixth [chapter], however: "Verily, when the Self, my dear, has been seen, heard, thought, and known..."

Thus, there is an objection (*ākṣepavārtika*) regarding both of these points: [the first] concerning the restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has been said regarding the practices such as "seeing" (*darśana*) and so forth; [the second] concerning how, when those have commenced, it is said that [the goal] is attained "through knowledge" (*vijñānena*), and then how "meditative contemplation" (*nididhyāsana*) is further mentioned. Now...

When the restatement of what was previously stated in the passage beginning with "The Self is to be seen" has commenced, how is *nididhyāsana* (meditative reflection), which was mentioned among seeing and the other means, expressed by the word "by means of realization" (*vijñānena*)?
Is it not rather that the restatement of seeing and the others is made using synonymous terms for each, such that *nididhyāsana* is also restated by the term "seeing"?

In that same way, the phrase "by means of *nididhyāsana*" would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), but not so the term "by means of *vijñāna*"; this is the meaning. The *Vārttika* provides the following resolution: the term "by means of *vijñāna*" is stated for the purpose of removing the suspicion that it refers to meditation (*dhyāna*). For the word "*nididhyāsana*" might give rise to the suspicion that it denotes meditation. As for the word "since" (*yataḥ*): [it introduces the reason].
Since the opponents raise the objection that the word *nididhyāsana* denotes meditation (*dhyāna*),
and that meditation is enjoined by the phrase "it should be meditated upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) as the means for attaining direct experience following hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*),
this [text] addresses that doubt.

Having paused at the occasion of restatement for the purpose of exclusion, the Śruti— intending that in the preceding sentence knowledge in the form of *nididhyāsana* (contemplative realization) was intended, and not mere meditation (*dhyāna*)— therefore leaves no room for the suspicion of an injunction to meditate, as expressed by the term "realization" (*vijñāna*).

The meaning of the Vārttika is that it restates *nididhyāsana* (reflective meditation). To the question, "What fault is there in meditation being a constituent part of direct experience (*anubhava*), such that this doubt is dispelled by the Śruti? he states the second half of the Vārttika: "Upon the arising of realization... (*vijñānotpatti*).

The meaning is as follows: since I have previously stated that meditation and so forth possess causality, whatever refutation must be offered against the claim that meditation or its application is the cause for the arising of consciousness, I have already stated it earlier in the discussion on "relation" (*saṃbandha*) and so forth. For there, the reality of the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* was explained.

When the referents of the *tat* and *tvam* words have been determined through the practice of hearing and reflecting upon the *gocara* (the object of study), and since the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha-jñāna*) alone has then reached its proper occasion,
there is no room for the injunction to meditate (*dhyāna-vidhi*). Nor [can it be said that] by those two [means], the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)...

It should not be argued that even when misconceptions (*saṃbhāvanā*) have ceased, the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārthabodha*) does not arise due to the obstruction of contrary cognitions (*viparītapratyaya*); for it is possible for even contrary cognitions to cease through the power of repeated practice in hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*), since [the contrary cognition] is something to be removed by the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence.

Furthermore, because a contrary cognition does not act as an obstacle to that [correct cognition], and because in the world it is not observed that an error acts as an obstacle to the arising of the perception of its own opposite.
Now, if nididhyāsana is not meditation (dhyāna), what then is it? To this he says in the Vārttika: "Now..."
The manifestation of knowledge is called *tṛṇididhyāsana*. It is the state of not requiring effort, like a person who has already grasped [the object],
and the state of not being dependent on anything else, until the aforementioned realization becomes manifest.

The radiant [Self] is first to be realized through the diligent performance of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth as an action here; reflection (*manana*) is the primary means for the object [of knowledge]. Having heard and reflected, one then directly realizes that Self.
Thus, immediately after the determination of the meanings indicated by the terms *tat* and *tvam*, which arises from the ripening of hearing and reflection—
By means of the sentence, one attains the knowledge of Brahman as the Self directly and non-empirically;

the meaning is that one experiences it. He states that for one who possesses the knowledge of the meaning of the sentence, all duties are fulfilled: "No further effort is required once [that knowledge] has arisen from the means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth."
The knowledge of the modification (*vṛttijñāna*) arises subsequent to some slight posterior experience.
For this very reason, in the *Samanvaya Sūtra*, immediately after the refutation of the injunction to know the Self, the Bhāṣya states:

"What then is the purpose of such statements as 'The Self, indeed, is to be seen'? We reply that they have the appearance of injunctions for the purpose of causing one to abandon natural inclinations toward worldly objects," and so forth.
The meaning is that once [knowledge] has arisen, nothing further is required after the manifestation of Brahman as the inner self (*pratyag-brahmatva*) by means of that [knowledge].

Thus, according to the view of the Vārttikakāra, since *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) is accepted as being knowledge itself, there is no failure of the illustrative example [of "not like reflection, etc.,"] as there would be if it were merely like *manana* (reflection) and so forth.

Nor should it be said that, according to the view of the author of the Vārttika, there would be a tautology between "one should meditate upon" (*nididhyāsitavya*) and "one should see" (*draṣṭavya*); for after the injunctions for hearing and reflection have been prescribed with the aim of seeing,
the subsequent mention of the fruit is logically understood as being intended to conclude that section— or else, [it refers to] "one should see."

The repetition is avoided because the statement "one should reflect" (*nididhyāsitavya*) is a restatement of the initial insight prompted by inquiry, whereas [the injunction] is a restatement of the direct realization that is the fruit of inquiry. He cites the commentary’s agreement regarding the absence of an injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth with the words "for this very reason."

The meaning is that, because hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—like the direct vision (*darśana*) itself—are of the nature of knowledge, they are eternally established according to the method to be described hereafter; thus, they are unfit for injunction (*vidhi*).
"For what purpose? means that they would be purposeless.

The word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including [the injunctions] such as "it should be heard. "Having the appearance of an injunction" means they are similar to well-known injunctions such as "it should be studied. Here, by means of the suffix *tavya*, the praise inherent in seeing, hearing, and so forth is indicated; and thus, for one who desires liberation and [seeks] the vision of the Self...

Even though one has understood that hearing [the scriptures] and so forth are indeed the means to liberation, if— after reflecting upon the hardship of practicing hearing and so forth together with renunciation, celibacy, and the like— one does not apply oneself to them with all one's energy,
but rather performs only those actions or meditations appropriate to one's caste and stage of life as they happen to arise; [that is the case].

Even there, one does not find final liberation because of the realization that those [means] do not result in the attainment of the ultimate human goal; therefore, he engages in the praise of the direct perception and hearing of that [Self], with the intention that, through his total enthusiasm, his engagement may occur specifically in hearing and so forth—hence, the statement beginning with "The Self, verily," and so on. Thus, it is not...

The author of the Bhāṣya refutes the objection that injunctions would be redundant by stating, "It is natural," etc. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), he refers to the person who acts with an outward orientation, thinking, "May what is desired be mine; may what is undesired not be mine," yet who does not thereby attain the ultimate human goal—that ultimate [goal]...
One who desires the goals of human life.

The commentary is summarized as follows: [the scriptures] such as "The Self, indeed, is to be seen" turn one away from the sphere of activity consisting of the natural aggregate of cause and effect, and cause one to proceed toward the inward current of the Self. This is its inherent nature (*svābhāvikatvam*).

The commentary on the summary (*saṃgrahabhāṣya*) explains the qualification of the object: "He who... and so forth, meaning "he performs various kinds of ritual acts and meditations. By the thought, "May what is desired be mine; may what is undesired not be mine," [there arises] a commonality of suffering.

The desire for touched pleasure (*spṛṣṭasukha*), which has as its object the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*) consisting of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), is what is intended here. For this very reason, he says: "And there one does not obtain the ultimate human goal. In that context, the meaning of the word is "external means"; [the phrase] "from the natural" (*svābhāvikāt*) refers to *avidyā* (ignorance) as the inherent nature.

The meaning is that it has that [the aggregate] as its effect. "Activity of the aggregate" means the performance of ritual action (*karma*) and meditation (*upāsana*); "from the sphere of that" means from the form consisting of the deities to be worshipped, mantras, and so forth. He is one whose "stream"—that is, the inclination of the mind—is directed toward the object, which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*).

The meaning is that its nature is a stream directed toward the inner self (*pratyagātman*). The sense is that it turns one away from external means and causes one to engage in hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth. And if "hearing" consists of the investigation into the purport of the Vedānta, then, by means of determining that purport, [it leads to realization].
The result is precisely the removal of obstacles consisting of error, doubt, and misconception regarding the intended meaning of the Vedānta.

Thus, it has been stated that because hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the rest are of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), there is no injunction (*vidhi*) regarding them. Now, even while accepting that hearing and the rest are of the nature of action (*kriyā*), he says that there is still no injunction regarding them: "And if...
The fact that they are of the nature of action has indeed been stated by the author of the Vārttika himself: "Hearing and the rest are actions that must be performed here."

By the phrase "with effort" (*prayatnataḥ*) and so forth, there is an inclusion of *manana* (reflection), but not of *dhyāna* (meditation), because according to the view of the author of the *Vārttika*, it has been stated that the practice of *dhyāna* does not occur after *śravaṇa* (hearing) and *manana*. Nor [is it the case that *dhyāna* is not to be practiced], for [the scripture says]: "Meditate on the Self thus: 'Om'; know this knowledge... (*om ity evam dhyāyatha ātmānam vidyām etām*).
It should not be argued that there is a contradiction with many scriptural passages such as "and the entire method of yoga" (yogavidhiṃ ca kṛtsnam),

because it will be explained in the third chapter— in the manner set forth in the *Dhyānadīpa*— that those passages teach a different path indicated by the word "yoga" occurring in the Śruti text, namely, the application of Sāṃkhya-yoga.

Nor should it be said that, because it is not the cause [of that], there is no inclusion of meditation (dhyāna) within the path of inquiry indicated by the word "Sāṃkhya" occurring in the Śruti; for its inclusion therein was stated with the intention of the view that the term *nididhyāsana* has the meaning of meditation (*dhyāna*). As for meditation...

The author of the Bhāṣya also agrees that [Sāṃkhya] lies outside the path [of the Vedas], and thus Yoga is refuted by this; for in the *Adhikaraṇa-bhāṣya* on the passage "that cause which is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga," it is stated that both knowledge and meditation are exclusively Vedic.

The meaning of the sūtra is as follows: since [the two systems] are expressed by the terms "Sāṃkhya" and "Yoga," the word "jñāna" refers to the practice of knowledge that is Vedic—that is, declared in the Vedas.
By this, the Yoga-śāstra is refuted on account of its contradiction with the Vedas and so forth. In the Sāṃkhya path...

Intending precisely the absence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), even the sages beginning with Sarvajñātman have not stated that the word *dhyāna* has the meaning of "knowledge" (*jñāna*). That fruit which arises from hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) is declared by those of sharp intellect to be for the sake of direct vision (*darśana*); the understanding that it is exactly thus for one who lacks direct experience is indeed [the case].

"At the completion of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*manana*), there is indeed that meditation (*nididhyāsana*). Regarding this verse, the venerable Āśrama-caraṇas offer this explanation, which states another alternative view concerning meditation: "Hearing," etc.
It is said loudly by those of keen intellect that the fruit which arises from the cognitions of hearing and reflection is for the purpose of [attaining] direct realization (*darśana*).
Such is the connection [of the words]. He clarifies this very point with the phrase "not devoid of experience" (*anubhavavihīna*).

"Śruta" means hearing; the meaning is: when hearing and reflection have reached maturity through practice performed for a long time, with devotion, and without interruption. "Not devoid of experience" means lacking direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
"Distinct from the direct realization that removes ignorance" means as follows: the cognition that "it is exactly thus"— namely,

the cognition consisting in the determination of the referents (*lakṣya*) of the words *tat* and *tvam*, namely, "I am indeed the conscious Self whose nature is Brahman, and Brahman is indeed the inner Self whose nature is the single essence of consciousness"— that alone is called *nididhyāsana*, and nothing else.

In this view, meditation (*dhyāna*) consists solely of the practices of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*); however, contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) is not to be practiced as a separate act, because direct realization arises at the very moment the intellect (*buddhi*), which is the fruit of long-term practice of hearing and reflection, comes into being.

Neither the removal of other obstacles nor the realization of Brahman [is the object of the injunction]; and since its being the fruit [of that realization] is already established by common worldly experience, and since no other means— whether optional or cumulative—
is established [as required], there is no room for even the three types of injunctions in this case.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), however, there is a distinction in that even *nididhyāsana* (contemplation) must be practiced separately. With the intention of showing the absence of meditation (*dhyāna*) in the path of Sāṃkhya, the teacher Vidyāraṇya also stated in the *Dhyānadīpa* that one must perform inquiry (*vicāra*) alone until the dawn of direct realization (*bhānodaya*). Having thus inquired, [one attains] immediate perception.
If one does not know the Self as Brahman, one should investigate further until direct realization (*aparokṣya*) is attained.

If, despite such investigation, one does not attain the Self even unto death, one will certainly attain it in another birth once the obstacles have been destroyed. This same principle applies to the fivefold bliss (*ānandapañcaka*), culminating in the bliss of the Self (*ātmānanda*).

In brief, it has been explained in many ways that even though the path of Sāṃkhya is devoid of meditation (*dhyāna*), its meditation does not yield an equal result in all respects. The word "eva" (only) serves to exclude [other paths], while the particle "na" is for the purpose of drawing in the preceding negation. This is by way of removing obstacles to inquiry (*vicāra*).

The sense is that even though the means for the realization of Brahman may be available, knowledge does not have that as its direct fruit, because it has been stated that [knowledge] is the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: although it follows that inquiry is useful for the direct intuition that removes ignorance by way of dispelling the aforementioned obstacles, such an intuition— [...is not produced by the Vedas... (Note: This sentence fragment appears to be part of the original text's logical flow).
Since the means of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) by way of the removal of obstructing sins is not established through any other source of knowledge (*māna*),

the statement "it should be heard" (*śrotavya*) teaches that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is a means to knowledge (*vidyā*) by way of the removal of sin. Nor is the removal of the sin that obstructs knowledge [attained] through sacrifices and the like.

It should not be argued that the injunction is redundant because [liberation] is already established; for it is reasonable to assume a distribution according to which some obstacles in the form of sins are removed by the performance of sacrifice, while others are removed by the performance of hearing (the scriptures), since such obstructing sins are infinite. And thus:

He dispels the doubt that "it would again result in being an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), and thus there would be an injunction of another auxiliary," as well as the statement regarding its novelty (*apūrvatva*) in the *Bhāṣya* on the section concerning hearing, which is designated as "erudition" (*pāṇḍitya*). He does so by stating: "It is not for the purpose of removing other obstacles."

Since there is another obstacle in the form of sin, distinct from the obstacles consisting of misconception, doubt, and error regarding the intended meaning (tātparya), the removal of that [sin] is not the fruit of *śravaṇa*; therefore, it does not lead to knowledge by way of removing that [obstacle].

The meaning is that listening (*śravaṇa*) is what must be performed. This is the underlying intention: it is improper to regard the injunction "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) as an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), because that has been refuted in the *Āvṛttyadhikaraṇa*;

furthermore, according to the method set forth by the *Vivaraṇa* and other works, the necessity of hearing the Vedānta is established by the evidence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Since it is possible for these [injunctions] to function as restrictive injunctions (*niyamavidhi*)— by depending on their visible fruit, which consists in the removal of obstacles such as delusion regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya-bhrama*), and by accomplishing both knowledge and the removal of obstacles through hearing alone—
we state that they are intended to turn one away from the objects of natural inclination, and so forth.

According to the Bhāṣya, since it is possible for the means of realizing Brahman— such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth— to be included within the context of Brahman merely by being a cause for a specific inclination toward it through the medium of praise,
there is no possibility of it being an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction); this is because the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that it is indeed an *apūrva*.

"And because there is the possibility of intending [the act] as optional (*pākṣika-śamy-abhiprāyaka-tva*). The phrase "and having that as its fruit" means "and having the removal of obstacles such as delusion (*bhrama*) and so forth as its fruit. Now, one might object: "Even if [the act] is already established, since the status of a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) and so forth is possible, how can there be an absence of the three types of injunctions? To this, he says: "And another means... (*sādhanāntaraṃ ca*).
Even though there is no injunction for inquiry (*vicāra*), the approaching of a teacher (*gurūpasadana*), being enjoined for the sake of knowledge (*vijñāna*), must—

since it is possible for it to function through a visible means and thus it is improper to assume an invisible one— culminate in the purpose of knowledge solely by way of the inquiry into the Vedānta dependent upon the mouth of the teacher. For this very reason, [the text mentions] one's own effort...

This is the exclusion of the investigation into the object of proof (*sādhya*). However, in the absence of an injunction for study (*adhyayanavidhi*), the act of approaching [the teacher] (*upagamana*), even if enjoined, is not for the sake of that [study], because it is not enjoined as being for the purpose of acquiring the syllables (*akṣarāvāpti*). Therefore, [it does not serve as the basis for the inference of the injunction].

Since the rule of study— which consists in reciting [the text] immediately after it has been uttered by the teacher— is established as excluding reading from written manuscripts and the like, this restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding study is fruitful. Furthermore,

for one who seeks the inquiry into Vedānta in order to dispel misconceptions regarding its purport (*tātparya*) and so forth, there might occasionally be an inclination even toward dualistic (*dvaita*) treatises.

It might be argued that even in that case, since the inquiry into the Vedānta exists through the application of what is accepted by them, the injunction prescribing inquiry into the Vedānta— which reveals the non-dual Self— is meaningful. However, this is not so, because that [inquiry] itself is a cause for the delusion regarding the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Because there is no absence of a refuter of that [objection], there is no occasion for another means of proof.
Now, one might object: "Since there is the possibility of obtaining [knowledge] through inquiry conducted independently of a teacher by means of an alternative [to inquiry under a teacher], he says:
'Even in the absence of an injunction for inquiry.
'For this very reason' means: precisely because of the injunction regarding approaching [the teacher]. After the word 'exclusion,' the word 'is obtained' (*labhyate*) is to be supplied."

The implication is that the injunction prescribing the rule of inquiry dependent upon a teacher within the sentence is purposeless. Nor should it be argued that because the injunction for approaching the teacher (*upagamana*) is a subordinate part of the injunction for inquiry, the injunction for approaching the teacher cannot even come into existence in the absence of that [inquiry]; for approaching the teacher [is required] for the sake of the knowledge of Brahman.

The sense is this: when looking for a means (*dvāra*), since it is appropriate to accept the very deliberation (*vicāra*) established in the world—which is dependent on a teacher—as the means, there is no requirement for an injunction to "listen" (*śrotavya*); thus, its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) [of that injunction] is not established.

Consequently, just like deliberation, the act of approaching [the teacher] (*upagamana*) is also logically established as a constituent part of knowledge (*vidyā*). This concludes the previously mentioned [point].
He dispels the objection with the words, "But in the absence of the injunction for study. The connection is as follows:

since the exclusion of reading from written texts and the like would not be established in the absence of the injunction for study, the restrictive injunction regarding study is one that possesses a fruit. [The phrase] "for that purpose" means...

The meaning is "for the sake of obtaining the syllables" (the Veda). The word "but" (*tu*) expresses a distinction between approaching [the teacher] as an auxiliary to Vedic study and approaching him for the sake of knowledge; he states that very distinction with the words beginning "approaching," etc.

The sense is that the fact that the fruit of Vedic study is the acquisition of syllables has been established in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works. He refutes another possible counter-argument: "Nor [is it the case] that because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) and so forth...
Now, even if in reality there is an absence of a capacity to negate that [duality], [one might argue that] the knowledge of a distinct self is the means to liberation.
It has been stated that activity toward that [object] arises from the delusion regarding the door of delusion; however, [the author] says "no" to this.

Nor is it correct to claim that the injunction "one must listen" (*śrotavya*) is accepted merely on the grounds that someone might still engage in listening there [in the case of the *Brahmasūtra*] under the pretext that it excludes others;
for even regarding the statement "one must listen," one who lacks faith in non-duality— which is the fruit of the Lord’s grace— might still apply the interpretation favored by the opponent.

Because there is the possibility of the delusion that [the text] is intended for the injunction of investigating a self accompanied by a second entity, an activity initiated by such delusion cannot be averted even by a hundred injunctions.

"By means of the delusion that [the world] is its remover. Here, there is no dispute that the qualification for the injunction of hearing (*śravaṇa*) belongs to one who possesses the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*) and has a firm desire to know (*vividiṣā*) produced by the performance of sacrifices and other rites in this life or in another birth. Furthermore, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by sacrifices and so forth [leads to the realization of] the non-dual, undifferentiated [Brahman].

Having established the certainty that the direct realization of Brahman is the means to liberation through the Vedāntas acquired by the study of the scriptures along with their ancillaries, and having generated a firm desire for such a realization of Brahman— known as *vividiṣā* (the desire to know)—
one thereby attains the means for the direct realization of the non-dual Self.
It impels the seeker of liberation toward the very hearing and other means of knowing the non-dual Self that truly exists; it does not,

however, produce a desire for or engagement in the inquiry into the knowledge of a separate self or its means by way of creating the delusion that knowledge of the individual self (jīva) or the self as father is the cause of liberation.

Therefore, because [the practice of] desire and so forth lacks the capacity to cause the direct realization of Brahman—which is free from phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)—as a result of sacrifices and other rites through the medium of inquiry into the distinct nature of the self; and thus, as the *Smṛti* states: "The impression of non-duality arises for men only through the grace of the Lord. It is precisely through the grace of the Lord, accomplished by means of sacrifices and other such acts, that [non-dual realization occurs].

The meaning is that for men, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from the desire for the knowledge of non-dual Brahman; therefore, for one who possesses the aforementioned delusion and lacks desire, faith, and so forth regarding the direct realization of the reality of non-dual Brahman,
there is no qualification for the injunction to listen (*śravaṇa*), nor does the restrictive rule (*niyamavidhi*) apply to him, nor is it mandatory (*nitya*).

Regarding the phrase "the grace of the Lord" as being intended by the opponent, the word *ātman* in the Śruti refers only to the individual soul (*jīva*) and not to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is because in the preceding sentence—"But for the sake of the self, everything becomes dear"—the individual soul is the subject under discussion; furthermore, in the complementary passage—"This whole world has the self as its essence"—it is the one who is the self of all that is meant.
Because it aims to establish the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the word "Self" (*ātman*) found in the scriptural passages must be understood as referring to the non-dual Self. Even in that case,
since its establishment is not yet proven, the identity between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and the Supreme Self is not possible, for [the two] are conscious and...

The intended interpretation of the phrase "and so forth" should be understood as follows: because the identity of the two volitions (*cetanā*) is contradictory; and because it is logical that the scripture (*śruti*) is intent on enjoining meditation (*dhyāna-vidhi*) based on non-difference, and so on. The word "elsewhere" (*anyatra*) means in the investigation of a different [type of] self (*bhinnātma-vicāra*).

Nor is it reasonable to claim that this is an *aparisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) intended for the purpose of excluding other activities; for it is impossible for one who is not a renunciant to exclude other activities,
whereas for a renunciant, such exclusion is already established by the injunction for renunciation itself, which is concurrent with being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*).
Since it is established by another scriptural passage that "one who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality," any other scriptural injunction enjoining renunciation would be redundant;
