for, in light of that [established fact], the instruction in the text to be heard regarding the cessation of other activities would be purposeless. Nor is there an injunction for inquiry...

It might be argued that even though [the study of] other subjects is possible, a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the Vedāntas is still possible because it serves to exclude works such as compositions in vernacular languages (*bhāṣāprabandha*).

However, this objection is untenable; since the restriction to the Vedāntas is already obtained through mere proximity (*sannidhāna*), it cannot be the object of a restrictive injunction. [The rule] "one's own [Veda] should be studied... [is established by context].

Thus, for the sake of understanding this meaning, by the force of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) itself, the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayanavidhi*) is understood to have produced the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas through the Upanishads; since the fact that this knowledge culminates in its fruit— being produced by no other cause— is thereby established, [it follows] regarding Brahman, the meaning of the Vedas...
For the sake of liberation, since discourses in common speech and other such compositions are not attained when that which is to be known [is realized].

He refutes the restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā-vidhi*) with the words "Not so" (*na ca*). Keeping in mind the dilemma— whether the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) teaches the cessation of other activities for a householder and others, or for a renunciant whose status is already established by the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-vidhi*)— he refutes them in succession, beginning with the words "not for one who is not a renunciant."

The phrase "because of impossibility" means that the occurrence of a contradiction with another injunction is the reason for that impossibility. The connection is as follows: since its cessation is already established, the instruction would be purposeless. Furthermore, the other scriptural passage, "One who is firmly established in Brahman attains immortality," establishes the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa-āśrama) characterized by being firmly established in Brahman.

The meaning is that this is clear from the *bhāṣya* on the section [beginning with] "Jaimiti [holds that there is] *parāmarśa*. He refutes the position that the Vedāntas are an *niyamavidhi* (restrictive injunction) by virtue of being the subject matter of inquiry, stating: "And not by inquiry... and "Precisely because of proximity... [This refers to one] who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*) and has attained a preliminary understanding through the Vedāntas.

When the inquiry has arisen as something to be undertaken for the sake of reaching a definitive conclusion that terminates the desire to know Brahman and the Self, a person seeking the subject matter of that inquiry perceives that the Vedāntas are present in their mind; thus, the thought arises: "The Vedāntas alone are to be investigated by me. And so, even without an injunction, there is a restriction to the Vedāntas.

The meaning is that its restriction by means of an injunction would be useless because it is already obtained [by other means]. He states another reason for obtaining the restriction of the Vedānta even without an injunction: "svādhyāya" (one's own Veda). This was stated relying on the Mīmāṃsaka position that there is comprehension of the meaning; however, according to the Siddhānta, the injunction for study has the attainment of the syllables as its fruit.

Nor should it be said that, in the section concerning the injunction of other auxiliary means (*sahakāryantara-vidhi*), an injunction is accepted for hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)— which are designated by the terms "childhood," "maturity," and "silence" (*mauna*)— because [it is established that] such inquiry is the cause for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of what is to be investigated.
Furthermore, since reflection (*manana*)— which consists in the investigation of reasoning conducive to the establishment of the reality—

and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*)— which consists in the repeated practice thereof— are well-known in the world as causes for the clarity of the realization of that reality, there is no need for injunctions regarding them; they function like explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) cast in the form of injunctions, by way of praise.
Because the designation "injunction" (vidhi) is applied there merely on account of its producing an excellence in activity, and because there is likewise no injunction for hearing [the Vedānta],
the inquiry into the Brahma-kāṇḍa, like the inquiry into the Karma-kāṇḍa, is rooted in the injunction to study (adhyayana-vidhi).

Thus, according to the school of the teacher Vācaspati, the definition of Brahman— the object of inquiry— as the cause of the origin, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe has been stated by the scripture beginning with, "From which indeed these beings are born. Herein:

If it is argued that even the state of being the sole cause of the world’s creation, maintenance, and dissolution must constitute a defining characteristic, because it does not apply to anything else;

Of those beloved sentences, the attainment of the human goal (puruṣārtha) is possible through the knowledge of their meaning acquired via study and reflection; the knowledge of the meaning of those sentences,
produced by the very sentences obtained through study, culminates in its fruit, whereas other compositions such as vernacular works do not.

The meaning is that, according to the principle of "produced cognition" (*janitamiti*), since the injunction to study culminates in the attainment of its fruit—the acquisition of syllables—it does not follow that compositions such as non-Vedic literature (*bhāṣāprabandha*) would be subject to that injunction.

In this context, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. This is said assuming that hearing and the other [means of knowledge] are not themselves objects of injunction.

He raises the objection regarding the contradiction with the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya: "If not... The words "is accepted" imply that it is accepted by both the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya. To resolve this contradiction, [the author] first states that although hearing and so forth are actions suitable for injunction, they are not already established as obligatory (*nityaprāpta*).
He states that it is "subservience. Regarding the term "investigation" (*vicāra*), in the phrase "cognition of that" (*tat-pratyaya*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the object (*vastu*).

The clarity and lucidity of that realization, as well as its freedom from obstacles, constitute what is designated as "injunction" (*vidhi*) in the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya; this usage of the term "injunction" is figurative, not primary.
He resolves the contradiction by stating, "because its possibility has been shown," meaning "just like an explanatory passage (arthavāda) that has the appearance of an injunction.

This refers, for example, to passages such as "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a low voice" (*viṣṇur upāṃśu yaṣṭavyaḥ*). For instance, after the text has first prescribed, "One performs the Upāṃśu sacrifice between [the two offerings]," it is then recited again.
"Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to in a whisper; Prajāpati is to be sacrificed to in a whisper;
Agni and Soma are to be sacrificed to in a whisper.
Herein, the intermediate sentence concerns the offerings to Agni and Agni-Soma.
In the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, it has been established that the three sentences concerning Viṣṇu and others— which enjoin a sacrifice characterized by the time interval between the two *puroḍāśa* offerings—

are merely *arthavāda*s (explanatory praises) intended to glorify the sacrifice enjoined by the sentence regarding the interval, by way of restating the optional deities already obtained from the wording of the mantras. This is the case here as well.

It should be understood that this has been cited as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). As for the phrase "that cause which is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga," since there exists a possibility of excluding those who are excluded by the term "Yoga" mentioned in the Śruti,
[this statement] serves the purpose of excluding them with respect to a qualified seeker capable of inquiry.

Regarding the statement that a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) is possible: it is not so; for when a qualified seeker capable of inquiry experiences a renewed doubt concerning reality—either due to an inconsistency raised by himself or one raised by another—it is impossible for him to possess a definitive knowledge of the meaning revealed by the Veda. This is the [required] capacity.

Because, in the absence of that specific counter-measure, non-investigation itself would necessarily follow by its own force. As for the objection that the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahmopāsana*) was mentioned as something to be excluded, even in the case of including such qualified meditation— which is a means to liberation via the attainment of the world of Brahmā— for one who is eligible for the injunction to hear (*śravaṇa-vidhi*) and is free from desire for everything else;
Since there is no possibility of its occurrence, it cannot be excluded; furthermore,

because even the meditation on qualities (*guṇopāsana*) is a means to knowledge only through the gateway of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— just as the tearing of nails and the like [are not means]— and since there is no possibility of its attainment as an alternative (*vikalpa*) alongside hearing and so forth due to their being of equal status, there is no exclusion of that [meditation].

It may be argued that the rule of discipline (*niyamavidhi*) applies only to the fruit [of the practice]. However, it should not be said that the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the attributeless [Brahman] can arise—just as the direct realization of the qualified [Brahman] arises—without hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means, through the meditation on the qualified [Brahman].

This is because [the realization of the attributeless] occurs by way of removing obstacles such as the lack of conviction regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Because hearing and the other [limbs] are understood to be means for the knowledge of Brahman in the form of a certainty regarding its existence,
and because of the aforementioned authoritative evidence as well as the indicative mark of their being restated as obligatory,
the scripture which teaches that supreme liberation is attained gradually through the meditation on the qualified Brahman (saguṇopāsanā) also [prescribes] hearing and the other [limbs].

Because it is stated that [meditation] is not incompatible with the arising of door-like knowledge (*dvāraka-jñāna*); and because if one were to accept the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) through the power of meditation on Brahman with attributes (*saguṇopāsana*) alone, without hearing and so forth, there would be a contradiction with the *Devatādhikaraṇa*.
For in that section, since gods and others lack bodies and so forth, [it is argued that they cannot perform] meditations on Brahman with attributes.

Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that they lack the capacity for the means of attaining the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman— such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth— and therefore have no qualification for them, the established conclusion (siddhānta) was reached that they do indeed possess such qualification because their bodies and other faculties exist, based on the authority of mantras, arthavādas, itihāsas, and purāṇas. In this regard, the following [is stated]:

The purpose of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been stated: if the gods lack the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, then even for one who has attained the state of a god through the meditation on Brahman—which yields the fruit of gradual liberation—it would be impossible for knowledge to arise due to the impossibility of hearing and so forth; consequently, the possibility of returning [to the cycle of rebirth] would follow for one who desires gradual liberation.

In the Siddhānta, however, the purpose shown is that because the gods possess the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, their engagement in the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) is established. This purpose is also shown in brief in the concluding commentary (*bhāṣya*) of the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. And thus says the Bhāṣya:

Therefore, since the desire for liberation and other such conditions are possible, the qualification of gods and others for the knowledge of Brahman is established; likewise, the scriptural accounts of gradual liberation are also consistent only in this way.
The phrase "only in this way" (evameva) means precisely when gods and others possess the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.

Regarding their qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, there are scriptural indications (*śrautaliṅga*) that were previously set forth, such as: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he alone became it," and likewise, "One hundred and one generations of ṛṣis, O Maghavan,
dwelt in the state of a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacarya*) under Prajāpati," and so on.

The meaning of the word "tathā" (thus) is that they are born [in that state]. Now, it might be argued that there is no fixed rule that for all those who meditate on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇa-brahma*), knowledge arises only through hearing and so forth; for even Hiraṇyagarbha, a meditator on the qualified [Brahman], attained knowledge—as stated in the *Puruṣavidha Brāhmaṇa* commentary on the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*.

If it is argued that knowledge arises even in the absence of hearing [the scriptures], prostration, and so forth, at the time of the actual exposition [of the teaching], we say no; for even in the case of Hiraṇyagarbha, as with Vāmadeva, the arising of knowledge was possible only through hearing and other means in a previous birth. This is stated in that very commentary (*bhāṣya*).

In the statement, "Because hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) have as their direct object that which is to be known," the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) indicates the necessity of hearing and the other means— which reveal the Brahman that is to be known— compared to such acts as prostration; thereby, it suggests the possibility of [the requirement for] hearing and so forth in previous births, according to that commentary.

Since it is understood that this is the intended meaning of the statement, the assertion in the preceding commentary— that knowledge arises merely through the purification of causes and effects without hearing and so forth—
is justified as a provisional statement (*abhyupagama-vāda*), just as [the case of] Hiraṇyagarbha or Vāmadeva, who attained knowledge through the means for knowledge in a previous birth.

Furthermore, since that which is to be postulated already exists, it is more logical to postulate what has already been established, namely the hearing [of the scriptures] and so forth. Nor should it be argued that an inquiry into the attributeless (nirguṇa) is impossible for Hiraṇyagarbha because he was devoted to the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) in a previous birth; for Hiraṇyagarbha, due to the difference in births across different kalpas...

Regarding the possibility of both qualified and unqualified worship: it is not the case that the state of Hiraṇyagarbha is attained merely through qualified worship performed in a single lifetime; for if that were so, it would follow that all worshippers of the qualified [Brahman] [would attain it].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the Lord] being Hiraṇyagarbha himself; rather, [Hiraṇyagarbha] possesses lordship over the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka),
is the husband of Sarasvatī, has attained the direct realization of reality from birth, is omniscient,
and possesses the power to create the entire material universe and so forth for his devotees.

The capacity to bestow sovereignty over the three worlds, the agency in specific cosmic functions such as the initiation of Śiva, Viṣṇu, and others, the cause of the manifestation of Rudra from his forehead,
and the sovereignty consisting of being born from the navel-lotus together with Viṣṇu— all these are established by the Śrutis and other authorities.

Having resolved to attain the state of Hiraṇyagarbha as described for the coming kalpa, that Great Person— like Dhruva, Prahlāda, Viśvāmitra, Agastya, Bhṛgu, and others— performed throughout many births the means for that attainment, namely the meditations on the qualified and unqualified Brahman, as well as various forms of austerity.
Since the status of Hiraṇyagarbha is attained by a certain individual through the unsurpassed grace of the Lord, it is not untenable—
just as in the case of Vāmadeva— to postulate that even Hiraṇyagarbha performed [such acts as] hearing and so forth in a previous birth,
provided they were practiced by him in his prior life.

Since hearing and the other [limbs of yoga] are obstructed by the desire to attain the station of Hiraṇyagarbha, it is logically established that they do not produce the direct realization of reality at that time; as it has been said by the elders: "When the longing for the world of Brahmā is truly present, let it be restrained; one should investigate [the Self]."

"One does not, however, directly realize the Self [merely by that]. Nor should it be argued that the rule of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth does not apply in every instance where knowledge arises, because it is accepted that the dawn of the direct realization of reality occurs even in the absence of hearing and so forth for one who has engaged in the path of Yoga.
[This is not so,] because [the scriptures state]: "One should unite the Self with 'Om'," and "Meditate thus upon 'Om'."
Regarding the passage beginning with "the self" (*ātmānam*), by the power of the rules for meditation, one attains that cause which is reached through Sāṅkhya and Yoga;

and since it will be stated in the third chapter that those incapable of inquiry are qualified for the path of Yoga— by means of such Vedic indicators (*śrautaliṅga*) as "this knowledge and the entire rule of Yoga"— [it follows that this refers to them].

Because it is not admitted that knowledge arises for one capable of inquiry without inquiry; thus, whatever means is established by the scriptures as a means to the knowledge of reality through an unseen (adṛṣṭa) medium— all of that, like the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa), serves as an auxiliary cause when one is unable [to proceed] by way of the Sāṃkhya path, which consists of the seen (dṛṣṭa) materials.

Alternatively, it may be postulated that the means for attaining knowledge of reality occurs through the path of yoga. It is more reasonable to postulate that the attainment of knowledge arises from the mere perception of reality; otherwise, one would have to postulate that activities such as suckling at the breast arise solely from the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living, which would necessitate the assumption of a memory of being a means to a desired end from a previous birth.

It would not be necessary to postulate a cause consisting of *saṃskāras* for everything that is universally accepted, because the impossibility of an effect arising without a cause already established and observed is equal in both cases; for this very reason, in the *Pañcadaśī*, a restriction to two paths is stated regarding the knowledge of reality: Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

Having thus deliberated upon the two paths with the words "by nature," the author of the *Saṃgraha* will also state in the third chapter that only the two paths designated as Sāṃkhya and Yoga are the means for the nourishment of knowledge (*vidyāvṛddhyupāyatvena*), concluding with the words "the Supreme Lord said.
Thus, for one who is intent on the practice of the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).

Since the fact that the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāvāpti*) is universally accepted as the goal remains established, the author states in the passage beginning with "The venerable Tīrthas, in the *Dhyānadīpa*,
have also mentioned another means for the attainment of knowledge" that this is the final conclusion:
in the absence of any prohibition, for one who is qualified for knowledge and capable of inquiry...

When there is a prohibition [against hearing the Vedas], the hearing of the Vedānta is what must be practiced; however, for one who is qualified for knowledge but incapable of inquiry, the hearing of Itihāsas, Purāṇas, compositions in vernacular languages, and so forth, is what must be practiced;
and for a member of the three higher castes who is incapable of inquiry, the practice of the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman denoted by the term "Yoga" is what must be performed.

And since neither of the two paths is possible [for him], he attains knowledge by means of practicing one or the other of them, through obtaining a birth suitable for their realization. Thus, because hearing (*śravaṇa*) is necessarily incumbent upon one qualified for hearing, there can be no other means of equal status to it.

It is established that there is no scope for an injunction (vidhi) in this regard, because there is no possibility of attainment through either conceptual construction or accumulation [of merit]. Likewise, with respect to the direct realization of Brahman, since hearing and so forth are already invariably attained, it occurs even without an injunction.

It has been established that the performance of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is accomplished; now, even though there is a requirement for an injunction regarding the performer of inquiry, just as the hearing of the *Karmakāṇḍa* and the inquiry into the ritual sentences are accomplished through the force of the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) alone— even in the absence of a separate injunction— so too [is this case].

He concludes with the words "And thus" (evam ca), intending that since even the hearing of the Vedānta is accomplished by the force of that [inquiry] alone, there is no need for a separate injunction of inquiry regarding the sentences to be heard. The literal meaning is: since hearing and so forth are already established through worldly practice, there is no requirement for an injunction of hearing.

The meaning of the first sūtra has been summarized through an investigation into the meaning of the sentences to be heard. Now he summarizes the meaning of the second sūtra as it follows in sequence: "And of that which is to be investigated. The word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of emphasis; it is connected with the word "by scripture" (śrutyā), and thus it means: "the definition has been stated by scripture itself."

The meaning is that [the relationship] is not something imagined by a person, like the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. The phrase "that from which beings are born, by which they live, and into which they enter at death—desire to know that; that is Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) is the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*); in this scriptural passage, the pronoun *yat* refers to that which has been defined in the *Brahmavalī*.

Brahman is understood as consisting of existence, consciousness, bliss, and infinity, because it is the inherent nature of all pronouns to refer back to the subject under discussion that has been previously introduced. Consequently, by the force of the scriptural statement itself,
the essential definition (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa) of Brahman— consisting of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss— is obtained.

And the fifth [meaning], "primordial nature" (*prakṛtitva*), expresses either the state of being a cause or causality in general. The word *bhūta*, which denotes both the five primordial natures and the agent of causality, is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for the great elements (*mahābhūta*) such as earth and so forth, as well as for the three [qualities]. This is because there is no definitive restriction [of its meaning] to the primordial natures alone.

Because they do not manifest [as distinct from their source], the word *bhūta* denotes everything that is an effect, according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "they come into being" (*bhavanti*). They "live" (*jīvanti*) in the sense that they obtain stability;
they "depart" (*prayanti*) in the sense that they are dissolving; and they "enter into" (*abhisaṃviśanti*) that into which they attain identity (*tādātmya*).

"Desire to know that Brahman which is the cause of all"—that is, you should desire to know it through its specific attributes, as the very nature of the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) which is filled with the singular essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), and you should seek to realize it directly; for by the mere act of desiring this, the aforementioned direct realization is attained. By the suffix *-san*, inquiry (*vicāra*) is indicated by way of the definition already stated.
The meaning is "investigate Brahman. Here, since there is the scriptural reading: "That from which beings are born is Brahman; that by which they live is Brahman;

that into which they enter is Brahman," the state of being the cause of the world's birth, the cause of its maintenance, and the cause of its dissolution are each [established] individually by the scripture.
The definition of Brahman has been stated, but not that [of the individual soul].

The author of the Kaumudī holds that these three characteristics alone are mutually independent; for this very reason, in the *adhikaraṇas* beginning with "Because of the inclusion of the moving and the unmoving" (Brahma-sūtra 1.3.1), attributes such as being the destroyer of all are presented individually as marks of Brahman.

It appears that the text "from which [the world] is born" (janmādi) states that being the cause of that [world] is the definition of Brahman according to the Śruti. He raises an objection to that: "In the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the world. The locative case here has the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*); for, beginning with "from which beings are born," the Śruti identifies the causality of Brahman within the very Brahman that is to be defined.

Because it establishes the existence of sentient beings, there is no impossibility [of the definition]. Since the singular number in the phrase "That Brahman" (tad brahma) makes known the oneness of the individual Brahman that is the object of definition, there is no room for the fault of under-extension; thus, having established the absence of these two faults, he states that there is also no over-extension: "because it does not apply to anything else."

The meaning is: because of the absence of the state of being directed toward Brahman. Now, an objection: there is a pervasion with "Pradhāna" (the Primal Matter), since the Sāṃkhyas accept it as the material cause;
for as the material cause, it is the cause of the world's birth, as its substratum, the cause of its maintenance, and as the locus of dissolution, the cause of its dissolution.

If it is argued that [the definition] applies there as well because of existence (*sattvāt*), we say no; for since agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended as a qualifying attribute within the definition, it is incompatible with the insentient *pradhāna*. Nor should it be said that agency alone should be the individual definition, without the qualifying term "being its material cause" (*tad-upādānatva*); for [agency] exists in the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the agent of the world's birth and so forth by means of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*).
Because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*); and because a limited individual soul (*paricchinna-jīva*) cannot possibly be the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [world].

Nor is it intended here that the definition consists of being the direct agent of the world's birth, being the cause of the world's maintenance by way of governance, and being the destroyer of the world through the desire to withdraw it; for [if this were so], it would apply to the individual soul (*jīva*).
It should not be argued that because [the definition] is over-pervasive (*vyāpta*), the qualified term "being the material cause" (*upādānatva*) is redundant; for in that case,

let "being the material cause" itself be a separate definition of *māyā*, since it does not attain the status of a distinct material cause merely by being a constituent of Brahman’s status as the material cause, given the existence of other causes such as *pradhāna*.

The sense is that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) because [the definition] lacks any basis in authoritative means of knowledge (aprāmāṇikatva). He accepts the possibility of each [cause] being a definition individually by saying, "True. Then, having raised the objection as to how the triad of causes is stated as a definition in the scripture (śruti), he explains that even the scripture intends each one individually as a definition, rather than their combination.

With the intention that there is no purpose [in defining it otherwise], he says: "This is indeed the threefold definition. This causality of the world—among birth and the others—is each defined individually and independently of the others;
this alone is intended by the Śruti as the threefold definition, not a single unity consisting of causality defined by all three together.

The meaning is "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*). It should be understood that the phrase "three terms" refers to multiple [attributes], but not to a restriction to exactly three, because it has been shown that there is the possibility of even more than that. He cites the consensus of the author of the Sūtras and others regarding the fact that each [attribute], such as being the destroyer of the world, constitutes a definition of Brahman. This is indicated by the words "for this very reason," where the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)...
This is a summary of the *Antaryāmy-adhikaraṇa* and the *Jagadvācitva-adhikaraṇa*. The meaning is as follows:

in the *Kaṭhavallī*, it is recited: "He for whom both Brahminhood and Kṣatriyahood are food, and for whom death is the condiment—who indeed knows where He is? Here, the terms "Brahminhood" (*brahma*) and "Kṣatriyahood" (*kṣatra*) are employed.
The word *odana* (rice/food) is not used here in its primary sense, but rather in a figurative one;

for in common worldly usage, the word *odana* is well known to have as its primary referent that which is edible, and thus the word *odana* is applied to those two [the *brahma* and *kṣatra*] by virtue of the quality of being edible. And so, when it is stated that "for whom the *brahma* and *kṣatra* are like food, being edible," [it is understood figuratively].
The non-existence of the referent of the word *yat* is perceived. With this very intention, it was stated in the Sūtra: "ateti" (it is not).

Regarding the meaning expressed by the word *odana* (rice), there are two kinds of edibility: one consists in being the object of the action of eating (*bhujikriyā*), which is the nature of being food (*bhojyatva*), and the other consists in being subject to destruction (*vināśyatva*). However, edibility is a quality (*guṇa*).
[The word] is well-known [to denote fire], but the quality of perishability is not; and in figurative usage, only a well-known quality is taken up.

For example, in the expression "the boy is fire," only qualities such as purity belonging to fire are employed because they are well-known, and not even qualities such as perishability that belong to it. The same applies to the present case according to worldly convention.

The quality of being fit for consumption (*bhojyatva*) is understood from the word *odana* (boiled rice) precisely by virtue of its force; and since the state of being fit for consumption exists even in the Brahmin and Kṣatriya when they take the form of female bodies, and since the state of being fit for consumption is perceived in the Brahmin and Kṣatriya with respect to a male, the quality of being a mother (*mātṛtva*),
which was previously perceived, [resides] in the referent of the word *yat* (which) that stands in a correlative relationship to them.
The mark of the individual soul (jīvaliṅga) in the form of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) is set aside when, due to the proximity of the word "mṛtyūpasecana" (moistened by death),
the quality of being perishable is attributed to the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya,
rather than the quality of being an object of enjoyment (bhojyatva) in the act of eating whose objects are the female bodies of the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.

Because death cannot possibly be a "sprinkling" (upasecana), there would otherwise result the logical inconsistency of the phrase "death is whose sprinkling. However, since death acts as an auxiliary in the destruction of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, no such inconsistency arises;
thus, in that context, the previously understood meaning of "non-truth" (anṛtatva) applies to the sense of the word *ṛta* when it refers to that [destruction].

The nature of being a destroyer culminates in this specific distinction: that which is to be destroyed is grasped as a quality. For in the world, condiments such as curd are seen to be the means for the destruction of the food mixed with them; thus, by the force of using the term "condiment" (*upasecana*) for Death, [it follows that] for all things consisting of the moving and the unmoving, which are accompanied by Death—

The destruction of the world is understood from that [statement]; and by means of *ajahallakṣaṇā* (non-exclusive indication), the terms "Brahmin" and "Kṣatriya" are understood to refer to the entire world. Consequently, even in the referent of the pronoun *yat* (which is correlative to that), there appears a characteristic mark of Brahman (*brahmaliṅga*) consisting in the power to withdraw the entire world. This being the case:

Because of the connection with the quality of being "not to be eaten" (*prathamamadanīyatva*), a doubt arises as to whether the one perceived there is the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows:

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is the individual soul (*jīva*), because, according to worldly convention, the state of being an "eater" (*atṛtva*) is understood as the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*); furthermore, by the statement "the Supreme Self does not eat," its status as an enjoyer is negated. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of the inclusion of both the moving and the non-moving (*carācaragrahaṇāt*). This is in accordance with the phrase "death as the sprinkling" (*mṛtyūpasecanapada*).

According to the manner previously stated, since *atṛtva* (the state of being an eater) is understood as the nature of the destroyer of the entire world consisting of both the moving and the non-moving, it is not possible for anyone other than the Supreme Self to be the destroyer of the world; nor should it be argued that, by the force of worldly convention, *atṛtva* appears in the form of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).
Because the establishment of the quality to be destroyed depends on the remainder of the sentence,
it is more powerful due to its greater speed; therefore,
the conclusion is that "the other" refers to the Supreme Lord, the Destroyer, in whom [all distinctions] are non-distinct.

It exists through the conceptualization of difference. It should be understood that the fourth quarter of the mantra intends to illustrate its difficulty of comprehension by stating, "Who knows Him, the undifferentiated Supreme Self, thus and so? This is because His attributes are designated in the sections concerning the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmin), the presiding deities (Adhideva), and so forth.

Having begun with "He who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within," and having stated several successive passages beginning with "He who dwells in the earth," and concluding that section with the words "with respect to the deities" (*adhidaivata*), [the text] continues again with "He who [dwells] in all..."

"He who dwells in all beings," "he who [dwells] in all worlds," "he who [dwells] in all gods," "he who [dwells] in all sacrifices," and so forth— certain synonymous expressions are recorded according to the differences between the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions. Therein, regarding the divine and other spheres, such as the gods, beings, worlds, Vedas, and sacrifices:
The one heard [in the scripture] is the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Why? Because of the designation of His attributes (taddharmavyapadeśāt).

This is because at the beginning of the passage, there is the specific designation of His attributes—namely, the attributes of the Supreme Self consisting of being the sustainer of all and the controller of all, as established by the Śruti text: "By whom, once born, all things live. And this... [imaṃ ca]... [text fragment].

The meaning of the sūtra is that the inner controller (antaryāmī) is not the individual soul (jīva) or others, because of designations such as "the world" (*loka*), since the aforementioned attributes are impossible in those [others]. [This is established] because of the reference to the universe (*jagadvācitvāt*). In the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Jātaśatru, Bālāki—

The words of Ajātaśatru addressed to the Brāhmaṇa are heard: "O Vālāka, he who is the maker of these persons, and whose work this is—he indeed is to be known as the Person. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the "Person" mentioned as the object to be known is the individual soul (jīva) or the Supreme Self (para). [The prima facie view is: it is the individual soul.

The prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the term *dharma*] is established through its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) as a synonym for the word "person" (*puruṣa*), because in the Veda and in common worldly usage— such as in passages like "one indeed becomes meritorious (*puṇya*) by means of meritorious action (*puṇyena karmaṇā*)" and "they said this regarding action alone"—
the word "action" (*karman*) is used in the sense of merit (*dharma*) and so forth, as in the expression "this person is meritorious because he exists in happiness."

They spoke because it was established there through the observation of usage; that is to say, Ārtabhāga and Yājñavalkya [spoke]. The person connected with ritual action is indeed the *jīva* (the individual soul) and not the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because the latter lacks qualities such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; this is established by the statement, "nor is he the agent of these persons."

It must be explained how the agency attributed to the Puruṣas such as Āditya and Candra—which belongs to the Supreme Puruṣa by nature—can possibly belong to the individual soul (jīva). [The answer is: Because the individual soul, who is the experiencer, possesses agency toward those Puruṣas who constitute the instruments of experience through the medium of its own unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa); for this very reason, it belongs to him...

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the statement "this is action" (*caitatkarma*) is purposeful because it establishes the agency of the person under discussion through the medium of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). To this, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

the word "action" (*karman*) does not possess a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for dharma and so forth, in accordance with the well-known etymological derivation that action consists of motion (*calana*).
Because [the term "action"] is conventionally established in the sense of physical movement (*parispaṇda*). How, then, is the application of that term to *dharma* and so forth justified?

It is justified through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since *dharma* and so forth are produced by movements such as the body, which consist of prescribed or prohibited forms. Nor [is it unjustified] in the case of what is produced by mental activity alone, such as the meditation on a deity.

It should not be argued that since merit (*dharma*) and the like lack the quality of being produced by motion (*parispaṃda*), when the term is used metaphorically (*lakṣaṇayā*), a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) must necessarily be admitted for merit just as it is for motion. For, in the present case, since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*) to favor one over the other, conventional usage does not arise; thus, [the term] "action" (*karma*) is derived from the sense of "that which is performed" (*kriyate*).
The word *vyutthāya* (having emerged) expresses merely an action;
this word also expresses merely an object presented through perception and so forth, because there is no [object] under discussion that is fit to be referred back (*tatparāmarśa*). And thus:

This entire world is the effect of his action; by the attainment of this meaning, it should be understood that the Puruṣa’s status as the creator of the entire world without exception is established. Furthermore, that [creatorship] which is a characteristic of Brahman—namely, the creatorship of the Puruṣa regarding the sun and so forth—is not possible for the individual soul (jīva) in a primary sense. Of these Puruṣas...

In this context, since it is possible to understand the term "agent" (*kartṛ*) in its primary sense, it is improper to understand it in a secondary sense. Nor should it be argued that because the creatorship of the entire universe has been stated, the creatorship of the sun and other deities is already implied therein, making their separate mention redundant; for in the mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth, the sun, the moon, and others [are specifically mentioned].

Because the separate mention [of the *puruṣa*] is purposeful as it removes the delusion that those [beings] possess the nature of the Supreme Brahman— which arises from proclaiming their great majesty— the term *puruṣa* does not refer to the individual soul (*jīva*) either.

[This is] conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). Since the term "person" (*puruṣa*) is derived through the etymological derivation (*kḷptayoga*) from "filling" (*pūraṇāt*), its application is justified even for the individual soul (*jīva*) who pervades the entire body, just as it is for Brahman who pervades the entire universe. Therefore, one should not assume a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) for it [in the case of the *jīva*]; even if such a convention were assumed, that convention—like the etymological derivation—would be common to both the individual soul and Brahman.

Furthermore, since the conceptualization [of the Self] is possible as mere consciousness (*cetanāmātra*), the scriptural mention of "Person" (*puruṣa*) does not favor the position of the individual soul (*jīva*). Moreover, in some scriptural recensions, the word "Person" is not even heard. Thus, the meaning of this Sūtra is as follows:
the "Person" who is to be known is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because He is the creator of the entire universe; nor is the reason unestablished.

Since the word *karma* denotes the world (*jagat*), it is established that the Puruṣa is the Supreme Self; and thus, by the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the expression "the power of being the destroyer of all, etc.," the nature of being the controller of all and the sustainer of all— as stated in the *Antaryāmi-adhikaraṇa*— is also included.
The agency mentioned in the section concerning the designation of the world (Jagadvācitvādhikaraṇa) is understood here as the agency of the creation of the entire universe.

Others, however, maintain that because the status of being the cause of origination and the cause of subsistence is common to efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*), the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) into Brahman is shown in order to indicate its material causality (*upādānatva*). Let it be that Brahman is the material cause of the world.
And regarding its birth, like a potter in the production of a jar;

and regarding its maintenance, like a king in the stability of a kingdom— it has been stated that He alone is the director of the world's birth and sustenance, in order to eliminate the doubt that some other deity might be the cause for these, distinct from the material cause (upādāna).

Is it not the case that the interpretation of the purport— that the passage beginning with "from which" (*yataḥ*) states the definition of Brahman, the referent of the term *tat*, who is the Lord distinguished from the individual soul (*jīva*)— is incorrect? For, in accordance with the remainder of the sentence, "Desire to know that Brahman" (*tadvijijñāsasva tadbrahma*), the meaning of the scriptural statement is the definition of Brahman as the non-dual object of inquiry.

Anticipating the objection that [the text] conveys only the state of being the agent of creation (*pratipādākatva*), he states the view of those who accept that the Śruti has as its purport the definition of Brahman as it truly is: "But others...
For the realization that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*) of all beings, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient, constitutes its non-duality (*advitīyatva*).

It is the cause of awakening. Nor can it be said that [the self] is not so because consciousnesses are eternal; for although they are eternal in their own nature (*svarūpa*), they are admitted to be effects by virtue of being qualified by the two bodies. And even so, there remains a second thing relative to Brahman, namely its effect.

Since it exists, how can its status as the material cause (upādānatva) be understood as indicating non-duality? It must be said that for an effect, its material cause alone is its real nature; there is no real nature other than that, whereas the form of the world consisting of name and form is not real.
This is because it has been established in the *Ārambhaṇa-ādi* and other sections that [the world] is illusory (*mithyā*).

Therefore, by means of teaching that being the material cause of all things is the actual nature (*svarūpa*) of everything—that Brahman alone is such—it becomes the cause for realizing the actual non-duality (*advitīyatva*) of Brahman. And the realization of non-dual Brahman—

He states that the dissolution of all beings into Brahman is shown by the scriptural passage, "That toward which they go and into which they merge," for the purpose of communicating that Brahman is the material cause— the cause of the realization of non-duality with Brahman, which has liberation as its goal. [This is expressed in the phrase] "upādānatve" (as the material cause).

[Objection: But surely, since the material cause (upādāna) such as clay—which is the locus for the dissolution of a jar and so forth—is also the cause of its birth and other states, the cognition of it as the material cause would arise by virtue of that [causality] as well; [Response: No, he says: "of the causality of birth."

The "efficient cause" (nimitta) refers to the potter’s staff, wheel, and so forth. [Objection: In that case, the teaching in the Śruti regarding Brahman as the cause of birth and so on would be useless, since the desired goal is accomplished merely by teaching dissolution; [Response: No, he says, "Let it be. Just as in the production of a jar there is a potter distinct from the clay which is the material cause (upādāna), so too in the production of the world there must be a material cause.
To eliminate the delusion that there might be some other causal agent distinct from Brahman,
the scripture declares that Brahman alone is the creator of the world; likewise,

for the maintenance of the world, [Brahman is the cause] beyond the material substrate of the subjects to be protected, just as a king is distinct from the subjects he protects during the stability of his kingdom.

The meaning is that, in order to eliminate the doubt that there might exist another efficient cause or controller distinct from Brahman— the material cause of the world— sacred scripture declares that this very Brahman is the sustainer and director of the world's life.

And thus they say that this single definition alone characterizes Brahman as non-dual by virtue of its being both the non-distinct efficient cause (nimitta) and material cause (upādāna). Furthermore, the causality of Brahman— which is of the nature of non-dual,
immutable consciousness— is not of the form of being a productive cause (ārambhakatva), as is the case with atoms, nor is it...

Unlike the *prakṛti*, its nature is not one of undergoing transformation (*pariṇāmitva*); rather, it is characterized by appearing as the manifold world of ether and so forth through illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) due to ignorance (*avidyā*).

The meaning is as follows: "And thus" (*tathā ca*) refers to the fact that once it is established—through the Brahman's being both the cause of the world's birth and the sustainer of its life—that Brahman alone is both the material cause (*upādāna*) and the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of the world; this single definition stated in the Śruti, culminating in the non-difference between the Lord and the material cause, defines Brahman as the second [type of] characteristic.

The meaning is that it makes known [the truth] by way of dispelling the doubt regarding the existence of any entity apart from Brahman, but it does not mean that each individual definition is "existent. Furthermore, the term *nimittopādānam* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*)," and this is again a *karmadhāraya* with the preceding term.

It should be understood that although the non-difference between the deity and the material cause is already established, the term "non-distinct" (*abhinnapada*) is used again to indicate that the non-difference understood through the *karmadhāraya* compound is characterized solely by identity (*aikya*), and not of the nature of an essential identity (*tādātmya*) as found in cases such as "blue lotus," where there is a distinction between quality and the possessor of the quality. Now, [one might object] that because of the ablative case-ending in the word "yataḥ" (from which),...
Nor is it established by the *liṅga* (inferential mark) that Brahman is the substratum for the dissolution of all beings; nor is its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*) of Brahman certain—
whether in the form of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) like *pradhāna*, or in the form of being a producer (*ārambhakatva*) like atoms,
or like a rope which is the material cause of a superimposed snake and so forth.

Alternatively, it may be stated that [Brahman] has the nature of being the substratum for the illusory manifestation (vivarta) in the form of the world. Regarding this, the first [position] is not tenable because Brahman is immutable (kūṭastha). For if one accepts a real non-difference between the modification (pariṇāma) and the subject of modification (pariṇāmin), then if Brahman were subject to modification, birth and other states resulting from that modification would also belong to Brahman.

[Otherwise] they would follow as logical consequences. And in that case, its immutability—established by scripture and characterized by being free from modifications such as birth and death—would be undermined. Furthermore, because of that immutability, its undergoing transformation is impossible. Nor is the second [alternative] possible, because Brahman is non-dual; for if Brahman were to possess a second, [it would no longer be Brahman].

With the intention that [the effect] might possess the status of being an originator (*ārambhakatva*) because it is possible for it to obtain a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), as in the case of the conjunction of two atoms, he says: "And of Brahman. He states that the third alternative remains by saying:
"But rather," and so forth.

Transformation (*pariṇāma*) is the alteration of a thing through its becoming existent or non-existent in a manner identical to itself; or, transformation is an alteration characterized by being non-different from the cause. Alternatively, transformation is the effect being non-different from the cause. Manifestation (*vivarta*), on the other hand, is an alteration characterized by being distinct from that [cause], or it is an appearance without that non-difference [from the cause].
The distinction between *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* (real transformation) is that an effect which cannot be described as distinct from its cause is called *vivarta*.

Now, if pure Brahman is accepted as the material cause (*upādāna*), does it exist in the form of Īśvara or in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*)? Regarding this, some who follow the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* say that pure Brahman alone is the material cause.
Because the *janmādi-sūtra* and its commentary state that being the material cause (*upādānatva*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman as the object of knowledge;

thus, in causal statements such as "from the Self, space was produced," words like "Self" which denote the variegated [conditioned] reality function only as indirect indications (*lakṣaṇā*) for the pure [Brahman].

Is it not the case that in the Siddhānta, the non-difference between Brahman and its illusory transformation (*vivarta*) is accepted, whereas in the theory of origination (*ārambhavāda*), the product is held to be absolutely distinct from its material cause? Thus, the difference between the produced (*ārabhya*) and the illusorily transformed (*vivarta*) is clear. Is this not the case even in the theory of modification (*pariṇāmavāda*) as maintained by the Sāṃkhyas and others?

Anticipating the objection—"Since the transformation (*pariṇāma*) and that which undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) are accepted as non-different, how is the distinction between *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* to be understood?"—he states, "By the difference in their definitions," namely: "The object is not [the same]... This means that the object designated as the material cause (*upādāna*) does not exist otherwise; that is, its existence does not consist in appearing in another form while depending upon its previous form.

"Becoming" (*bhāvanam*) means abiding. "Otherwise-becoming" (*anyathābhāvaḥ*) means a particular state of abiding; such is the sense. "Having the same ontological status as that" (*tatsamasattākaḥ*) means that which has the same ontological status (*samāsattā*) as that entity (*vastu*)—that is, the otherwise-becoming. And thus, it is when there is identity of ontological status with the existence of the entity intended to be the material cause (*upādāna*).
The definition of transformation (*pariṇāma*) thus culminates in this: being a specific state of that [original substance] is its transformation.

In that context, the word "real" (*satyam*) is used to exclude illusory appearance (*vivarta*). To exclude the transformation-status of a jar (which is not real), the qualified term "specific state" (*avasthā-viśeṣa-rūpatvam*) is employed. He states the definition of illusory appearance (*vivarta*): "That" refers to the manifestation of a thing in a different form through an unreal nature.

The connection is with the term "vivarta" (illusory manifestation). The definition of vivarta is: being a particular state of that [substratum] while having a degree of existence (sattā) different from the degree of existence of the entity accepted as its material cause (upādāna).
Since the entity of clay, accepted as the material cause, has a degree of existence different from that of consciousness, this [definition] applies to it as well.
The qualificand is included to exclude soft objects; "real" is included to exclude dimension.

That [reality] belongs to the Brahman-consciousness as ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattā*), while the phenomenal world of jars and so forth possesses conventional reality (*vyāvahārika-sattā*). Only the latter is excluded here.
Since liberation is not something distinct from that [state], he states another definition based on what is common to both [the liberated and the bound]:

"The cause is characterized by being *salakṣaṇa*. This means that a thing regarded as the material cause (*upādāna*), while possessing the characteristic of being *salakṣaṇa*, is a particular state of that [cause]. Here, the definition of transformation (*pariṇāma*) is that which is *salakṣaṇa*.

The object to be realized (*bodhya*) must be of an insentient nature, because it is a rule that both the substrate of transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and the transformation (*pariṇāma*) are insentient. There is no suspicion of over-extension (*avyāpti*), for the qualification [“insentient”] excludes the possibility of clay being the transformation of a pot,
while the substantive [“real”] excludes the possibility of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) being a transformation of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

He states the definition of *vivarta* (illusory manifestation): "That" (*tad*). The definition of *vivarta* here is: being a particular state of that [substratum] while being distinct from the entity regarded as its material cause (*upādāna*).
In this context, the intended distinction consists in the difference between consciousness (*cit*) and insentience (*jaḍa*), as in the case of the ether (*viyat*) and so forth.
Since, like the world of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*), even illusory silver and the like are admitted to be superimposed upon consciousness as delimited by those very objects,

there is consistency with the definition [of Brahman] because it possesses a nature distinct from mere insentient matter (*jaḍa*)— that is, it is a transformation (*vivarta*) of consciousness. This applies to consciousness which is distinct from the insentient matter considered to be the material cause (*upādāna*).

The qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is for the purpose of excluding [the appearance of] insentient matter (*jaḍa-vivarta*). The term "real" (*satyam*) is for the purpose of excluding the appearance of clay (*mṛd-vivartatva*) in the case of a jar or the like, which are transformations of clay (*mṛt-pariṇāma*). He states the definitions of *vivarta* and *pariṇāma* by another method: "non-different from the cause" (*kāraṇābhinnam*). [This refers to that which is] regarded as the cause...

Since being an effect of that [Brahman] and being a transformation of that [Brahman] exist in the ether and other elements when there is non-difference from the reality, yet being a transformation of that does not exist [in the case of the ether etc.], in order to exclude that [unwanted application], the word "real" (satyam) is used. Even though a superimposed identity between Brahman and the phenomenal world exists, it is the intended substratum (dharmin) that is meant in the definition.

There is no over-extension (ativyāpti) because there is no difference in the common nature between the two. In the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), since even clay possesses non-difference from the jar, the qualifier [in the definition] is included to exclude the possibility of clay itself being a transformation into a jar or the like. "Non-different from that" means, in reality, even without such non-difference.

Differentiation (*vyatireka*) means difference (*bheda*). In this definition, "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not intended [as a necessary condition], because even beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are admitted to be illusory transformations (*vivarta*). Alternatively, this definition applies specifically to illusory transformations that are of the nature of effects. And thus, [the transformation] is [different] from the object regarded as the material cause (*upādāna*), in reality.
Since it is difficult to define [the relationship] in terms of either difference or non-difference, the effect—

characterized as a transformation (vivarta) of the form of the effect— is here [regarded] with respect to ignorance (avidyā), which is intended to be the material cause (upādāna) in relation to consciousness (caitanya) that is in fact impossible to define as either different or non-different from that ignorance.

The qualifier "distinct" (*bheda*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the effect that is difficult to define as non-different from its material cause (*upādāna*) according to the theory of creation (*ārambhavāda*). When "non-distinct" (*abheda*) is stated, it is to exclude over-extension to the effect that is difficult to define as distinct from its material cause according to the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*). The term "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) is included to prevent over-extension to other things.

In the Siddhānta, because the difference between cause and effect is accepted, the phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is stated in order to avoid the charge of impossibility. Now, one might ask: how is it that difference and non-difference between cause and effect are difficult to define? It is said in reply: first of all, their difference is difficult to define. [This is evident in cases such as] depressions and elevations, and so forth.
A jar [is perceived] as distinct from its constituent material substance.
In the view that accepts a threefold division of existence—wherein silver and the like possess a phenomenal (prātibhāsika) reality—the distinction of their definitions has been stated:
in Brahman, in objects such as a jar, and in illusory silver such as that [perceived] upon mother-of-pearl, [the essence] is everywhere the very nature of Brahman.
Because of non-perception [of the whole as distinct from its parts], and because the cloth is not perceived apart from the threads joined in a particular way;

and because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such expressions as "clay is the jar," "threads are the cloth," and "gold is the earring. Indeed, coreferentiality does not exist between two things that are distinct in reality.

Furthermore, a causal condition is possible [only if the effect exists in some form]; for otherwise, since the jar and so forth do not exist in the clay and other materials prior to the operation of the causal factors, their production would be impossible—just like the horn of a hare. Moreover, it is impossible for an effect that is non-existent prior to the moment of its production to function as the agent of the act of being produced.

Because agency is observed only in that which is already established; and because at the moment of origination, a connection with a material cause as a cooperative factor is untenable, since the effect does not exist in the preceding moment. Indeed, a connection is only possible between two things that are already established prior to it.

Otherwise, since even for things like a hare’s horn, a connection with causes would be unavoidable; and because if one does not admit that the effect prior to the operation of the causal factors is distinct from a mere non-entity (tuccha), then—just as in the case of the hare’s horn—it would be impossible for it to acquire its own nature later on. Furthermore, [this is so] once [the effect] is established as existing previously...

The proponents of the non-difference of cause and effect (kāryakāraṇābhedavādins), such as the Sāṃkhyas and others, maintain that since there is no evidence for a difference between cause and effect at the time prior to the existence of the effect, their non-difference is established; therefore, even subsequently, their non-difference must be accepted.
The logicians and others who maintain the doctrine of difference, however,

argue that the non-difference between cause and effect is impossible because their natures are contradictory; for it is not possible for the very same thing to be both its own effect and its own cause.

Furthermore, it would follow that there is no difference in their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); for the causal efficiency of fetching water and so forth is not possible for the clay substance prior to the production of the jar, as that [efficiency] would have to be present even before. Nor is the causal efficiency of the clay possible for the jar, because, like the clay itself, the jar would also have to be a producer of the jar.

Because it would follow [as an absurd consequence] that the effect exists prior to the operation of its cause, which would render the activity of the causal factors (kārakas) useless; and because it would follow that it would be perceived just like the clay itself. As it is said in the *Pañcadaśī*: "That jar is not different from the clay, for it is not seen when separated [from it]."

"Nor is it non-different, because it was not so even previously in the state of the lump [of clay], nor because of its being perceived as distinct. This means that when there is a separation from the clay, and when a discrimination is made by the intellect— thus has the mutual relationship between cause and effect been demonstrated by both those who maintain their difference and those who maintain their non-difference.

Because it is impossible to refute through logical arguments that the effect is neither different nor non-different from its cause prior to its production, and because it is difficult to determine whether it exists or does not exist [at that time], its unreality is established; however,
the cause [remains real] both prior to the production of the effect and at the time of the effect's existence.
Furthermore, because it persists at the time of the destruction of the effect and can be defined as existing with a distinctness from the effect,
it is indeed real; thus it applies to the intermediate cause, such as clay, in relation to its effect.

Although reality is established in relation to its respective effects, ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satyatva*) is not admitted for anything other than Brahman, because everything apart from Brahman is sublated by the Śruti. However, the ultimate reality of Brahman is accepted, because it is the eternally existent Self and is devoid of sublation. Therefore...

Thus, when the cause of the world is real, clay and the like are real; and when the world is illusory, the effects such as jars made of clay are likewise unreal. This is adopted by the Śruti as an illustrative example, as it is stated in the *Pañcadaśī*: "In this way, through its nature as Māyā, the modification has the character of unreality."

In the verse beginning with "The Śruti has declared that the substance which is the substratum of modification is real," the collection of arguments previously stated regarding the unreality of modifications and so forth [is applied here]. Thus, the meaning of the words is as follows; the word "as an illustration" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And it has been stated in the *Bhāmatī* commentary on the section concerning bondage: "By this..."

The Śruti reiterates by way of illustration through the continuous passage beginning with "clay alone is real" that the unreality of the entire collection of modifications is established by their being indefinable according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), while the reality of the cause is established by its being definable; thus, "modification is a mere verbal handle."

The meaning of the Śruti is that "only the name 'clay' is real. A modification (*vikāra*), such as a jar and so forth, is "an undertaking" (*ārambhaṇa*)—meaning it is commenced or dealt with by speech through words such as "there is a jar" or "there is a bowl"; it is merely dealt with by speech, and nothing more.

The sense is that, in reality, there is no modification (vikāra), because such a thing is impossible to define. If one asks, "How then does the production of jars and the like arise from the substance of clay, and how is the conventional usage of difference between cause and effect maintained?"—to this he replies: "Name" (nāmadheya) refers to the conventional usage of difference; it is merely a name, devoid of objective reality.

The sense is that, just as there is the conventional usage "Rāhu’s head" or "a person’s consciousness," so too difference, like modification, is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*). What, then, is real? To this he says: "clay.
By this, [he means] that which is perceived in modifications such as jars and bowls by way of its form as clay.

The reality of the cause is distinguished from the reality of the modification by the very fact of its being a cause; thus it is established that it is difficult to express [the nature of] the effect in relation to the cause, whether through difference, non-difference, or both.
He asks, "Now" (*atha*). But surely, in the Śruti, it is the pure Brahman itself, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence...

The definition has been stated [in the sūtra], and the remainder of the sentence is "let one desire to know that," because it declares that Brahman, which is the object defined, is what is to be known. If it is argued that a question regarding a matter already ascertained is inappropriate, we say no; for just as the pure [Brahman] is to be known, so too is its true nature (tattva).

The individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are both constituent categories (*padārtha*), are also objects of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) because they serve as the means for attaining the realization of the pure Brahman; likewise,
according to the method to be explained, they both possess the nature of being the non-different material and efficient cause (*abhinna-nimittopādānatva*).

"It is possible" means that because the qualities of being an object of inquiry (*jijñāsya*) and not being a cause (*akāraṇatva*) are common to both [the individual soul and Brahman], the question is justified; this is the intended meaning. As stated in the words of those who know the tradition: "The individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), pure consciousness (*viśuddhācit*), the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord (*jīveśayorbhidā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the connection between that [ignorance] and consciousness (*taccitoryoga*)—these six are beginningless for us."
Since the threefold nature of consciousness alone is well-established, the question is posed accordingly in three ways.

Because the desire to know the specific follows from the knowledge of the general, the meaning of the word "atha" (now/then) is the inquiry following the knowledge that Brahman is the material cause in its general form.

Or rather, that is its meaning: the sense of the particle *eva* is that Brahman alone, whether in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*) or in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), is the material cause (*upādāna*).

In the aphorism "From which the birth, etc., of this [proceed]," the term *janmādi* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which birth is the beginning"; the referent of the other member of the compound is birth, maintenance, and destruction. This is indicated by the neuter singular form *janmādi*.

Because the *samāhāra-dvandva* (collective compound) indicates a sense other than the constituent members (*anyapadārtha*), whereas if one were to resort to the *itaretara-yoga-dvandva* (copulative compound) regarding birth, subsistence, and dissolution— which constitute the sense other than the members— the result would be the undesirable conclusion that the sūtra should have read "janmādayaḥ" (birth and so forth). Furthermore, "being the beginning" (*āditva*) belongs to birth, which occurs among those things that are being born.

In the Sūtra, the statement "it is seen with reference to stability and destruction" indicates that birth is the first among the [three] forms; by the pronoun "of this" (asya), there is a reference to the entire phenomenal world present in the mind of the author of the Sūtra; and by the genitive case, [there is a reference] to the world.

The mention of "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*) is an indication of their relationship. The word "from which" (*yataḥ*) is an indication of the cause. In the sutra, there is the ellipsis of the word *tat* (that), and from the preceding sutra, the word *brahma* (Brahman) is to be supplied. Thus, the meaning of the sutra is: "That from which this world originates, etc., is Brahman. Brahman is that which is to be known.

Because it is the pure Brahman, which constitutes the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), that is primarily intended to be indicated (*lakṣya*); therefore, its definition is stated in the aphorism concerning "birth and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*). This is because, in the preceding aphorism—"Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*)—the term *brahman*, which presents the subject matter of the scripture, refers to pure Brahman.

The sense is that, because it is [the self] thus appropriated, it is precisely that which is expected as the definition. However, in the causal passages such as "From the Self, space was produced" and "He desired; He, being omniscient and all-knowing," it is Brahman in the form of the Lord (Īśvara) that is stated to be the cause, not the pure [Self].
The state of being a desirer is the agent of all cognitions.

According to the *Vivaraṇa*, however, [the cause] is indeed the form of the Lord (*īśvara*) characterized by omniscience and so forth, which is variegated by *māyā*; for the Śruti states: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge—from Him this Brahman, name-and-form, and food are born," and so on.

The material cause is Brahman. For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya, in the sections beginning with "Because of the teaching of its attributes" and "Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere," it is stated: "That same Ṛg-verse, that Sāman-chant, that Uktha-hymn, that Yajus-formula, that Brahman—it possesses all works, all desires, and all odors."

It has been described that the state of being the self of all, which results from being the material cause of everything as stated in such scriptural passages as "consisting of all tastes," is a characteristic of the Lord that distinguishes Him from the individual soul (jīva).

Because the [notions of] "you" (tvam) and so forth are untenable, the words *ātman*, *tat*, and "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) occurring in those sentences denote the *śabala* (the qualified or variegated Self). Therefore, it is not established that the pure [Self] is the material cause based on the causal sentences;
thus he says, "And so," in accordance with the natural sense of the *janmādi-sūtra* and its commentary.

The meaning is: "given that the pure [Brahman] is understood to be the material cause. The intention is that since figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) alone is accepted, it is logical that the understanding of the pure [Brahman] as the cause arises from the causal statements. Now, regarding the question, "Is the pure Brahman the material cause? and so forth, he sets forth the response by adopting the second alternative.

Regarding the term *vivaraṇa*: for that aforementioned source of beings (*bhūtayoni*), "consisting of knowledge" (*jñānamaya*) refers to austerity (*tapas*) previously mentioned in the mantra; it is a modification of the knowledge of its own nature, meaning it is in the form of a reflection within the veil of *māyā*.
From that omniscient source of beings, that which is proximate to it—occurring at a subsequent time—is [the subject].

The meaning is as follows: according to the Śruti, "that which has the form of the effect—namely, that called Brahmā and Hiraṇyagarbha—is born," the connection is that Brahman in its form as the Lord (Īśvara) alone is the material cause (upādāna). The word "alone" (eva) excludes the idea that it is either the pure [Brahman] or the form of the individual soul (jīva). By the phrase "omniscience and so forth," the qualities of being all-knowing, having all desires, and being the father of all are intended.

The meaning is this: that very Brahman-consciousness which constitutes the form of Īśvara—characterized by omniscience and other qualities, and distinguished by the nature of a witness as defined by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Māyā—is the material cause (upādāna), because its attributes such as being the Lord of all are included. Now, at the point of answering the question as to whether pure Brahman is intended to be the material cause, it is stated that it is indeed the form of Īśvara.

While it would have been sufficient to say merely "Brahman as the material cause" (*brahmopādānam*), the qualification of it as being "mixed with Māyā" (*māyāśabalatva*) is for the purpose of dispelling the delusion that the Lord (*īśvara*) is also pure consciousness (*śuddhacaitanya*) alone. Furthermore, the employment of various qualifications such as "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*) is [intended] to show that when Brahman in the form of the Lord is the material cause, He is the one who is omniscient.

It should be understood that this is for the purpose of demonstrating the unanimity of all such causal statements regarding the Brahman that is the Lord, who is distinguished from the individual soul (jīva) and the pure Brahman.
If pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), which is the underlying thread of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), were the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything,

then that [consciousness] would not be a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the Lord distinct from the individual soul. Furthermore, the refutation of the Lord’s being the material cause found in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* is intended to refute His being the material cause as qualified by *māyā*, but not [His being the material cause as pure consciousness].

This [verse] is intended to refute the view that consciousness, in its extracted form as the Lord (īśvara), is the material cause; for at the end of the first chapter of that very [work], it is stated that the status of being the material cause of the world resides in the referent of the word "That" (tatpadārtha).

He states the support of the Bhāṣya regarding its being the material cause (*upādānatva*) with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: precisely because it is accepted that Brahman, in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*), alone is the material cause.

The connection is as follows: the Bhāṣya describes the state of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*), which is occasioned by the status of being the material cause of all as stated in such scriptural passages (*śruti*), as a characteristic mark of the Lord (*īśvaraliṅga*).

It is undisputed that for whatever possesses the nature of being the material cause (upādāna), it must possess the nature of being the self of all (sarvātmaka), because of the identity between the material cause and its effect; this applies to nothing else.
