This is so provided that the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of consciousness qualified by the state of being a reflection, and the Lord (Īśvara) is of the nature of consciousness qualified by the state of being the original object (bimba).
If it is maintained that Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness and which is the underlying substrate as the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*), is the material cause (*upādāna*) of all,

then since He alone possesses the nature of being the Self of all (*sarvātmakatva*), there would be no justification for the introduction in the Bhāṣya of the exclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a mark (*liṅga*) of the Lord (*īśvara*) regarding this "being the Self of all. Nor [is it the case] that the pure [consciousness], which serves as the qualificandum...

It should not be said that the state of being the Self of all, which resides in Brahman, is described in the Commentary as a mark (*liṅga*) of the Lord in the form of consciousness qualified by freedom from attributes; for if that were the case, it would not serve to distinguish [the Lord] from the individual soul (*jīva*), since [freedom from attributes] is a property of the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

With the intention that, just as being the self of all is an attribute of Īśvara, it is likewise an attribute of the *jīva*, he says: "Pervading both the *jīva* and Īśvara. This is heard in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*: "That golden person who is seen within this sun, with a golden beard and golden hair, is entirely golden down to his fingernails."

Having begun thus, it is said that "the *ṛc*, the *sāman*, and the *geṣṇas* belong to him"; then, regarding the three subsequent [limbs], it is said: "This person who is seen within the eye—that indeed is the *ṛc*, that is the *sāman*, that is the *uktha*, that is the *yajus*, that is the *brahman*.
And it is further stated: "Those who sing upon the lute, they sing of this [person]. The meaning of this is: the person who is within the sun.

This is seen from the scriptures as golden (*hiraṇmaya*), consisting of light; the meaning is that its essential nature is self-luminous consciousness (*caitanya*). To facilitate meditation upon Him, the text describes His body with the words "golden-bearded" (*hiraṇya-śmaśru*) and so forth.
Here, the words "gold" (*hiraṇya*) and "gold" (*suvarṇa*) refer to light. The phrase "up to the tips of the nails" (*praṇakhāt*) indicates pervasion.
The *Ṛk* and *Sāman* are the two eyes of that golden person; according to the *Parimala*, they have become the wealth of praise.

He states another location for the worship of that very same person, as if it were the station of the sun, saying: "He who is within the eye. In the passage beginning with "That indeed is the Ṛg," there is a change of gender for the sake of the predicate.
That very person is the Ṛg, he is the Sāman, he is the Uktha, he is the Yajus, and he is the Brahma-Veda.

The *brahmapada* is superior to the *ṛc* and other [Vedic meters], and thus transcends the Vedas. Likewise, by the statement regarding its "limbs" (*geṣṇa*), its nature as the self of all the gods is declared; and by the statement "That indeed is the *ṛc*," its nature as the self of all the Vedas is declared.
Similarly, those who are well-known singers of songs upon the lute are worldly persons.

By the statement "they too sing this Person," just as His nature as Indra and others is established, so too is His nature as the ordinary person established. Thus, by combining His nature as all the gods,
His nature as all the Vedas, and His nature as all ordinary persons, there is His nature as the Self of all (*sarvātmakatva*).
They conclude thus, since the nature of being an animal has also been largely established [as a possibility]. This being the case, a doubt arises:
Is the golden person heard of within the sun and the eye a particular deity presiding over the orb, or is he the eternally established Supreme Lord? In this regard—

The golden person (*hiraṇmaya-puruṣa*) is indeed a particular deity; for it is logical that he possesses the nature of a transmigrating being (*saṃsārin*) through his having golden hair and so forth, and because the attribution of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*) can be superimposed upon him for the sake of meditation. Therefore, he is not the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), since a body is impossible for Him.

This being so, we reply to the objection raised: "Because of the teaching of His attributes within, and because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere," the golden person situated within the sun and other such objects is none other than the eternally established Supreme Lord. Why? Because of His attributes; for He possesses the quality of being the Self of all, as indicated by the passage: "That same [Self] is the *ṛc*... and so forth.
In passages such as "That is Sām," the quality of being the self of all belongs exclusively to the Lord,
because His being the self of all is established by His being the material cause of everything; furthermore, when a primary sense is possible, it is improper to assume a figurative attribution.

Even for the Supreme Lord, by the power of His will for the sake of favoring His practitioners, there arises a body consisting of the transformation of a portion of pure *sattva* within *māyā*; thus, the Śrutis speak of "the Lord, the Supreme Lord, accompanied by Umā," and so forth, as well as "my birth and action are divine," and so on.

And because it is well-known in the Smṛtis, this is the conclusion. Having enjoined meditation—denoted by the word *kratu*—in the passage beginning "All this, indeed, is Brahman," with the words "one should perform the sacrifice" (*kratuṃ kuryāt*), the text reads, upon the arising of the expectation for an object of meditation: "Consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body, whose form is light."

"His resolve is true; his nature is space; he performs all actions; he possesses all desires; he possesses all odors; he possesses all tastes; he has pervaded this entire universe; he is without speech and without regard; this is my Self within the heart. This is the meaning: [the Self] consists of mind.

The meaning is this: this quality of being praised by the *Ṛg* and *Sāman*— which consists in being praised by all the *Ṛks* and *Sāmans*— is an attribute of the golden person (*hiraṇmayapuruṣa*), and it culminates in his identity with Indra and others, who are well-known in the Veda as being praised by the *Ṛks* and *Sāmans*.
If the Golden Person were distinct from Indra and others as well as from space, then that qualification would not be established; for it would otherwise refer to something other than them.
He whose body is the vital breath (prāṇa), which has the mind as its primary faculty, is "one whose body is prāṇa" (prāṇa-śarīra).
He whose form is consciousness (bhā) is "one whose form is light" (bhā-rūpa). His volitions (saṃkalpa) regarding creation and so forth are true and unimpeded, like space (ākāśa).
Its essential nature is endowed with qualities such as non-pervasiveness and subtlety;

its "effects" (karmāṇi) are so called either by way of the etymological derivation that "all actions are performed [in relation] to it," or else, because of the proximity of the qualities, odors, tastes, and so forth of the elements, the word *karman* refers here to vibratory motion (*parispanda*).

The meaning is that all flowings belong to Him. All desires—whether in the form of longing or as specific forms of happiness—belong to Him. All fragrances, which are of the nature of merit, belong to Him, according to the Smṛti: "And His is the meritorious fragrance on the earth. All tastes belong to Him. This entire visible world is [subordinate] to Him.
Because of its direct identity with that [the Supreme], it is the "Vyoman" (the Sky). Alternatively, "vāka" means speech;
one who possesses such speech is "vākī," while one who lacks it is "avākī"—meaning, in effect, one devoid of the organ of speech.
The mention of "speech" here is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the organs of action and the vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*).
Because there is no difference in their possession of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). "Lack of regard" (*anādara*) means that he has no desire (*kāma*);

by the negation of regard, the mind (*manas*), which is its transformation, is negated. And by the negation of the mind, the negation of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) is established, because there is no difference in their possession of the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*).
In this context, motion, desire, and the possession of odor and taste cannot occur without identity with the specific elements— wind, earth, and water— which serve as their substrates; thus,
by the statement regarding "all activity" and so forth, there is identity with everything without distinction.

Furthermore, by the statement of the teacher, "All this is known through meditation," it is understood that the quality of being the self of all belongs to that which possesses the attributes of consisting of mind (*manomaya*) and so forth. And that [status] is possible only for Brahman, because its being the self of all is established by its being the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything. The individual soul (*jīva*), however, does not possess the qualities of consisting of mind and so forth.

The [objection] that its possession of qualities is impossible because of its being the Self of all is not valid; nor should it be said that the nature of consisting of mind (*manomayatva*) and having vital breath as a body (*prāṇaśarīratva*), which are attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*), are impossible in Brahman,
for [these are possible] through identity with the individual soul, just as [the earth] possesses fragrance and so forth through identity with the elements.

"Because of the possibility of [qualities] such as consisting of mind (*manomayatva*)," etc. The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: Brahman alone, characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind, is indicated here as the object of meditation. Why? Because it is Brahman that is well-known throughout all the Vedāntas, as seen in the preceding passage: "All this, indeed, is Brahman."

Because it is taught by its own specific term, and because in this sentence— as well as in the analytical phrases such as "prāṇaḥ śarīram asya" (breath is its body)— there exist the presence of pronouns that draw back the previously mentioned Brahman, it is established that Brahman itself, endowed with qualities, is the object of meditation here. As for the phrase "but in the case of being the material cause of all":

Even if one accepts that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the material cause of everything just like pure Brahman, the characteristic of the Lord (*īśvara*)—namely, being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*), which distinguishes Him from the individual soul—would not exist; this is the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*). Now, an objection is raised: since the status of the material cause belonging to Brahman as qualified by *māyā* has been refuted in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, there is a contradiction with that [text].
To this he says: "In the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*.
Even Māyā, by virtue of being a qualification of the Lord who is the prototype (*bimba*), does not fall within the category of that which is not the material cause (*anupādānatva*).

The meaning is that only the [conceptual] "settling" (*niveśa*) therein is refuted; however, that which consists of the Lord as Consciousness qualified by the nature of being the prototype (*bimbatva*) is not rejected, and thus there is no contradiction with that. Now, having rejected the status of the variegated (*śabala*) as the material cause, [the author proceeds] to support the argument that being the material cause of the world is the definition of Brahman as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).

How can it be possible to conceive such an intention for the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* text, given that its natural sense is understood to be devoted to establishing that Brahman, as the underlying reality (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), is the material cause (*upādāna*)? To this he says: "In that very [work]," referring to the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*.

This is the meaning. Furthermore, "residing in the referent of that word" (tatpadārthavṛttitva) is intended to mean "residing in the indicated referent of that word" (tatpadalakṣyārthavṛttitva), and since the indicated referent is pure Brahman, there is no contradiction between the earlier and later parts of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* text; nor is it the case that [the reflection] is not the original object (*bimba*).

It should be stated that the status of being the material cause (upādānatva) belongs to Bhūteśvara; for, since the property of being the indicated meaning (lakṣyārthatva) is common to both the sentence-meaning and the word-meaning, the qualification "residing in the meaning of that word" would otherwise result in being redundant. Therefore, [the definition] is "residing in the meaning of that word."

It must be stated that [the cause] resides precisely in the referent of the word "That" (tatpadavācyārtha); therefore, in order to avoid contradiction with that, and to avoid contradicting the many Śrutis which establish that the Lord— possessed of attributes such as omniscience— is the cause of the world,
the doctrine of a variegated material cause (śabalopādānatva) is refuted.

The point is that since it must be stated precisely as the refutation of the view that Māyā is the qualified material cause (*upādāna*), there is no contradiction with the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*. [An objection: "In that case, does this not contradict the statement in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa* Sūtra and its Bhāṣya that [the world] is the definition of Brahman as the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)? He replies, "Not so," by saying, "And thus... (*evaṃ ca*).

The meaning is: since it has been established that [the two] are indeed of the nature of the original image (*bimba*), by examining the *Bhāṣya* passage which states that they are the substrata of those attributes and possess the characteristic of having non-different material causes; the word "also" (*api*) implies that, in this way, even the causality residing in the Lord (*Īśvara*) [is understood].

They maintain that the undivided consciousness (akhaṇḍacaitanya), which follows after that [intellect], is capable of being characterized as standing apart (taṭasthatayā) like the moon in relation to its branches; thus, they consider it to be the definition of Brahman as the object of knowledge (jñeyabrahmalakṣaṇatva).
Furthermore, the phenomenal world (prapañca), beginning with suffering and so forth, is a transformation (pariṇāma) of Māyā resting upon the Lord (īśvara); therein, the Lord...
Clinging.

This [term] "caitanya" (consciousness) is connected with the preceding word "kāraṇatva" (causality); the word "sat" (being/existent) is to be understood as a supplement, which makes known the Lord as distinguished from others. "Tadanugatam" (inherent in that) means inherent in the Lord, whose nature is consciousness qualified by being the prototype (bimba). "Akhaṇḍacaitanyam" (indivisible consciousness).

The meaning is that it refers to the pure consciousness which is the substantive (viśeṣya). Furthermore, "being incidental" (taṭasthatva) should be understood as either being external to the nature of the object to be defined (lakṣya), or not pervading the object to be defined, or being a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa). For example, when the question "Where is the moon? is asked, the answer is "On the branch. In that case, just as...
Just as one perceives the moon— which is distinct from the stars— by means of its location on the branches and so forth, so too,

the causality residing in the Lord makes the Lord known by way of His distinction from others; thus, it serves to indicate that which is inherent in the Lord, namely the undivided Consciousness (caitanya), by way of its distinction from others, for the sake of defining Him as the "subsidiary" (taṭastha) indicator.

The meaning is that it is indeed capable [of this]. When there is an understanding of its distinction from the individual soul (jīva)—which lacks the possibility of being the material cause of the world because it does not possess the nature of consciousness qualified as a reflection due to its non-differentiated causal materiality residing in God—and from primordial matter (pradhāna) and the like, which are devoid of the possibility of being its creator; [the following is understood: "It is indeed capable. This refers to the possibility of God’s status as the material cause of the world through His nature as consciousness qualified as a reflection, by virtue of His being the non-differentiated efficient and material cause. This occurs when there is an apprehension of His distinction from the individual soul—which is devoid of the possibility of being the material cause of the world because it lacks the nature of consciousness characterized as a reflection—and from primordial matter and so forth, which lack the possibility of being its agent.

The intention is that even for Brahman, which is the object to be qualified (*viśeṣya*), its distinction from primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and other such entities is understood; thus, the fact that this [distinction] constitutes the definition of the knowable Brahman has been stated in the *Janmādyadhikaraṇa-sūtra* and its commentary, as well as in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*. The sense is that, in this way, Brahman is apprehended through its extrinsic definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*) as being distinguished from primordial matter and the like.

When there arises a specific desire to know what the nature of Brahman is like, the definition of its essential nature (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa) proceeds: "Brahman is of the nature of Truth, Knowledge, and Bliss.
With this very intention, the Commentators have stated: "And the determination of that..."
By the statement beginning with "From Bliss indeed,

these beings are born," which says "from whom [they are born]," it is meant that these beings are born from that reality whose nature is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity— namely, from Bliss alone, and not from any other cause.

For this is well-known from the previous section; such is the meaning of the scripture (*śruti*). By means of this definition of essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), Brahman—which is the object signified by the word *tat* (That), which conforms to the Lord who exists as the archetype (*bimba*), and which is in reality the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*)—is specifically determined as that which is to be known. And this [definition] is rooted in the intention to express the definition of essential nature.
By the word "khaṇḍa" (fragment/part), Īśvara is indicated as the reflection of Māyā, which is the material cause of the world;
and Māyā rests upon Īśvara, for the state of being a reflection is produced by Māyā. He [Īśvara] is qualified by that [Māyā].

It should not be argued that it is impossible for Māyā to be dependent on consciousness because its dependence on consciousness must be stated even prior to the conceptualization of it as a reflection; for since Māyā, like the state of being a reflection, is beginningless, its dependence on consciousness qualified by that [Māyā] is logically established. In reality, [consciousness] is without distinctions.

Regarding consciousness, because the state of being a conceptualized reflection has existed from beginningless time, the status of being a reflection exists merely by virtue of its dependence on indeterminable *māyā*. Regarding consciousness, because the state of being a conceptualized reflection has existed from beginningless time, the status of being a reflection exists merely by virtue of its dependence on indeterminable *māyā*.

That [reflection] is considered to be imagined by Him (tatkalpita), but it is not accepted as a transformation of Māyā like the ether and so forth; for if that were the case, it would follow that the Lord, who exists as a reflection, is beginningless. Nor does Māyā, from time immemorial, effect the state of being a reflection in Consciousness such that it could be considered imagined by Him.

It must be asked: how can it be possible for consciousness (*caitanya*) to take as its substrate that which is qualified by that [limitation]? [The answer is: because Māyā possesses the power to bring about the impossible. Nor should it be asked: "Why not assume that Māyā, residing in pure consciousness itself, effects the state of reflection therein? For [the scripture says]: "But Māyā..."

This is because it contradicts the Śruti passage: "One should know Prakṛti as Māyā and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā. By the word "māyinam," it is understood that Māyā has its locus in Īśvara. The individual souls (jīvas), however, are reflections in ignorance (avidyā), according to the Śruti: "He creates the soul and the Lord by means of the appearance [of duality]. Thus, Prakṛti...

The meaning is that the primordial nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) produces the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) as distinct reflections. For a distinction between reflections is not possible without a distinction between limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor can it be argued that because multiple reflections are seen even in a single mirror, the distinction between reflections is not pervaded by a distinction between limiting adjuncts; for [this would contradict the observation] in the case of a single mirror...

Even when there is a difference in reflections due to a difference in the original object (*bimba*), it is observed that where the original object— such as the sun— is one and the same, no difference in reflections occurs in the absence of a difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, since the consciousness that constitutes the original object is unitary,
one must therefore accept that the ignorance (*avidyā*) which serves as the limiting adjunct for individual souls (*jīva*) is indeed distinct from *māyā*, the limiting adjunct of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nor does [the Lord] create the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) by means of a reflection while proceeding from the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti);

for the Śruti states, "Māyā and Avidyā become themselves," whereby it is indicated that Māyā and Avidyā— the substrata for the reflections in the forms of the Lord and the individual soul— become themselves.

It should not be argued that the demonstration of [the world] having the nature of the primordial material cause (*prakṛti-mūlaprakṛti*) contradicts the position that *māyā* and *avidyā* are distinct; for while *māyā* is the material cause of ether and the rest, it will be shown that *avidyā* is likewise the material cause of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) and so forth. Thus, *māyā* and *avidyā* are unified by their common status as material causes.

Since there is no contradiction in establishing that [the Self] is "itself alone" as being of a single primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and since it is also reasonable to interpret the singular number in the word "ignorance" (*avidyā*) as referring to the genus, there is no contradiction with its multiplicity either; for it has been demonstrated that in the case of a reflection, a distinction between reflections is impossible without a distinction between limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Regarding the reflection...
And because of the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*).

Furthermore, in the commentary on the section concerning the "Invisible" (*adṛśyatvādhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*), it is stated that the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) rests upon the Lord (*īśvara*) and serves as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); thus, it is taught that Māyā is both the limiting adjunct of the Lord and its substratum (*āśraya*). Likewise...

In the *Ānumānikādhikaraṇa* of the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated that there is no rebirth for the liberated; for it is clearly asserted therein that the seed-potency of ignorance (*avidyā*) has been consumed by knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, in the *Bhāmatī* commentary on that *Bhāṣya*, [it is explained] that the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) and the plurality of the ignorances (*avidyā*) which serve as their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)...
Furthermore, because it has been explained that [the reflection] is merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*) precisely by way of being negated by knowledge (*vidyā*),
and because the reflection-nature of individual souls (*jīva*) is clearly stated in both the Sūtra and its Commentary,
he sets forth the view of those who believe that the distinction between Māyā and Vidya is established by Śruti and other authorities.

By the words "the manifold of misfortune and so forth," etc., [the author] intends that while in the previous view it was stated that Brahman in the form of Īśvara is the material cause (*upādāna*), that is indeed true; however, in certain respects within the world, the status of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a material cause must also be accepted. This is the intention behind this view.

The process of manifestation (*pravṛtti*) is to be understood as the transformation of *māyā* which rests upon the Lord (*īśvara*), based on the scriptural text: "One should know *māyā* to be *prakṛti*.
This is the intended meaning. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*), it means that the Lord alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) in the case of ether and the other elements.
However, regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, he shows the specific distinction indicated by the word "but" (*tu*) with the words "the Lord... and so on.

"Being possessed by the elements" (*bhūtopasṛṣṭatva*) means being conjoined with the elements characterized by supporting [the body]. And that [possession] belongs to the individual souls (*jīva*), specifically regarding the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). The subtlety of the elements consists in their being limited in size. "For this very reason": [it refers to] the transformation of the soul's ignorance (*avidyā*) within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.

Because Māyā has entered into the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*) as their supporter and into the gross elements (*mahābhūta*) as their material cause (*upādāna*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are effects of the subtle elements produced by the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is itself supported by the Lord and conditioned by the gross elements resulting from the transformation of Māyā.

In that regard, both [the subtle body and the elements] possess the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*). For this very reason, the Śruti states: "Thus, for this seer, these sixteen parts (*kalā*), which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and dissolve away. Here, the term "parts" (*kalā*) refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and so forth.

O Videha, at the time of the wise one's attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*), the severance of the effects of ignorance (*avidyā*) through knowledge is shown by way of referring to the portions that are products of ignorance, as stated in another Vedic text: "The fifteen constituents (*kalā*) have returned to their foundations. This refers to the great elements (*mahābhūta*), which are the effects of *māyā* that are not to be removed [by knowledge].

The proponents of the distinction between Māyā and Vidya maintain that the dissolution of those [elements] into their respective primal sources (prakṛtis) was taught with reference to the portions that serve as the support for the forms of transformation.

This is the meaning: just as rivers such as the Gaṅgā and others go to their setting upon reaching the ocean, even so, for this wise person who perceives the Self as complete everywhere, the *kalās*—which constitute a portion of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*)—have the Puruṣa as their goal; the Puruṣa is the "resting place" (*ayana*), that is, the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Those which are tranquil, having reached the Puruṣa, go to their rest; that is to say, they dissolve into the Puruṣa. The word "darśita" (shown) implies "the Puruṣa. The term "pratiṣṭhāḥ" is a feminine accusative plural. The meaning of the accusative plural is "the Māyās," namely, the great elements consisting of transformation. [These are] the fifteen kalās.

"Pratiṣṭhāḥ" means they have returned [to their source], that is to say, they are dissolved therein. "Tadanivartyā" (not removable by that) means that the *māyā*, which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Īśvara, cannot be removed by the knowledge (*vidyā*) residing in the individual soul (*jīva*). This is the sense. If the *kalās* were merely transformations of the individual soul's ignorance (*avidyā*), then their dissolution would occur entirely within the person (*puruṣa*) alone; and thus...

The statement establishing their dissolution into the gross elements would otherwise be rendered meaningless; therefore, it must be asserted that Māyā is the material cause (*upādāna*) even of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), or else that the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is the material cause of them. In this regard, the purpose of both [Māyā and the subtle body] being the material cause is simply the establishment of the consistency between the two scriptural passages. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of *māyā* would not be established if it were not sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); for its falsity is established through the force of the scriptural texts (*śruti*) that negate all objects of perception (*dṛśya*) in Brahman, as well as by inferential marks (*liṅga*) such as being an object of perception. Nor...

It must be stated that since there is no cessation of *māyā* through knowledge (*vidyā*), and because there is no other means of its removal, it would follow that *māyā* persists even when all beings are liberated. However, this is not the case; for at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), when the karmas that bestow enjoyment upon all living beings cease simultaneously, the entire phenomenal world [is withdrawn] by the mere will of the Lord (*īśvara*).
Like a householder, there is liberation from everything.

Just as the phenomenal world (prapañca), such as space and so forth, is a transformation of Māyā resting upon Īśvara, and thus Īśvara is the material cause (upādāna) therein; likewise, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the rest are merely transformations of ignorance (avidyā) resting upon the individual soul (jīva), and thus the jīva alone is the material cause therein. Furthermore, the internal organ and the like are not effects of Māyā.

Furthermore, if there were no entry [of the elements] into the great elements (*mahābhūta*), the inconsistency of the two cited scriptural passages would arise. As for the scriptural statement regarding the destruction of the *kalās* by knowledge, it refers to the perspective of one who knows reality—that the *kalās* have passed away. When the knower of reality is dying, people standing nearby perceive that they are perishing.

Since it is stated clearly in the *Kalālayādhikaraṇa-bhāṣya* that "they consider even his body and so forth to dissolve into earth and the other elements, like a jar," this is established as being an object of perception for an external observer (*taṭasthapuruṣa*). Thus say the partial adherents (*ekadeśinaḥ*) among those who maintain the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā*.

From this point forward, there is no further need for that Māyā which serves as the instrument of action. For the Lord, who possesses true resolve and is endowed with creative contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*), there arises a [volition] in the form: "May Māyā, along with its effects, undergo a complete dissolution within Me, who am in reality of the nature of pure Consciousness alone. It is precisely from such a volition that the characteristic transformation of Māyā occurs.

Because its dissolution occurs through [the cessation of] volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*). In the collections of texts such as the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas that establish the cessation of *māyā* through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the intention is the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Alternatively, although the mere knowledge of reality is capable of removing *māyā* just as it removes *avidyā*, for various living beings...

The summary is as follows: due to the obstruction of karma, that [knowledge] does not remove [ignorance] for one who is not yet liberated; however, for one who is being liberated at the very last moment, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) removes it because of the absence of obstructions—such points should be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, the claim that both [ignorance and karma] are the material causes (upādāna) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth is unestablished, given the systematic arrangement of the two scriptural passages.

Thinking that the commentators themselves have explained it otherwise, he shows another view with the words "as in the case of ether and so forth. The "vision of the knower of reality" (*tatvavid*) is the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). Here, by the word "vision," its result, namely the dissolution of the *kalās*, is intended. The meaning is that there is a scriptural statement regarding the dissolution of the *kalās* in the *puruṣa* when that [realization] is the object. [This applies] to the elements (*bhūteṣu*).

The meaning is that the statement regarding the dissolution of the *kalās* is merely a restatement of an object established through delusion for those who mistakenly believe that even the *kalās* are effects of the great elements, which are themselves transformations of *māyā*. The literal meaning of the words is: "They think [it is] just as the destruction of a jar, ending in its reduction to powder, is seen on the ground. This is the perception.
Regarding the term "object" (*viṣaya*):
here, "cognition" (*pratīti*) means a cognition that is of the nature of an error, having that [object] as its object, yet not having it as its object. Regarding "because of clarity":
the sūtra on that topic states, "Those [senses], for the other [the Puruṣa], because he says so"; that is, those [senses], such as the mind (*manas*) and so forth, [belong] to the other, the Puruṣa.
They dissolve without remainder. For thus the Śruti says: "In this very way, of him... and so forth;

such Śruti indeed declares dissolution without remainder—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. [Otherwise], if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth were not effects of Māyā, the Śruti that establishes the Lord as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the internal organ and so forth would be contradicted.
The term "contradiction" (virodha) indicates the fault [of the argument],
while "not a partial proponent" (na ekadeśī) [indicates the subject].

Even among those who maintain non-difference [between Brahman and the world], some hold that although God is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) such as ether and so forth, nevertheless,

because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the rest are perceived as identical with the individual soul (*jīva*), the individual soul alone is their material cause. For this very reason, in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the internal organ and the rest is shown to reside in the individual soul alone.

And they say that in the *Vivaraṇa*, regarding the determination of the specific relation to each object (*pratikarma-vyavasthā*), it is described how the consciousness of Brahman possesses connection with jars and other objects by virtue of being their material cause (*upādāna*), while the individual soul (*jīva*), though not connected to those, possesses connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth. [From this] is born the vital breath, the mind, all the sense organs, and space.
Based on such scriptural passages as, "Air, fire, water, and earth, the supporter of the universe," it follows that Brahman alone is the material cause of the entire empirical world.

Some who maintain the non-difference of *māyā* and *avidyā* hold that while *māyā* is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord alone, for the individual souls (*jīvas*), who are of the nature of reflections, the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇas*) themselves are the limiting adjuncts; thus, they ascribe the status of material cause (*upādānatva*) to the soul itself with respect to the internal organ and so forth.

He says, "They speak as if they were proponents of that difference," [referring to] "even among those who maintain non-difference. The word "api" (even/also) indicates similarity with the previous view in certain respects. That similarity will become clear through the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth. Now, [an objection]: even in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether and the rest, the individual soul (*jīva*)...

To the question, "Why then should the individual soul (*jīva*) not be the material cause (*upādāna*)?", he says: "Even though... This means that because [the world] is a transformation of *māyā* resting upon the Lord (*īśvara*), the Lord alone is the material cause of the ether and so forth, and not the individual soul. Now, if one accepts the non-difference between *māyā* and *avidyā*, then [it would follow that] the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other things, which are transformations of *avidyā*, [would also be the material cause].

It might be argued that since there is no difference in the fact that Māyā is a transformation dependent upon Īśvara, it is more appropriate to say that Īśvara alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) even of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth; to this he says "nevertheless," etc. Regarding "the individual soul" (*jīva*): the internal organ and the rest [are perceived] in such modes as "I am the agent," "I breathe," "I am the ego," and "I am gross."

The identity of the living self (*jīva*) with things ending with the body is perceived; and since that is not possible without those things being superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon the living self, the meaning is that the living self alone possesses the status of material cause (*upādānatva*)—in the form of being the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—and not the Lord (*īśvara*).
This refers to the "regulation according to each action" (*pratikarmavyavasthā*).

The meaning is as follows: since it has been stated that Brahman’s omniscience consists in its nature as the illuminator of all things at all times within the consciousness of its own essential nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*), a defect might then arise—namely, that the individual soul (*jīva*) would likewise possess the capacity to perceive everything at all times within the consciousness of its own essential nature. Therefore, this section of the text is intended to establish the specific determination (*vyavasthā*) regarding the objects of perception for the individual soul. In this context, "Brahman" refers to the original archetype (*bimba*).

The meaning is that, because Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, is the material cause of everything, its relation with pots and other objects is established as one of identity (*tādātmya*). Although the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of that [Brahman], is all-pervasive due to the all-pervasiveness of ignorance (*avidyā*), it does not possess identity with pots and the like, because it lacks the status of being their material cause; however, it does have such identity with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.
Regarding the individual soul (jīva), however, in the section concerning the illusory nature of the dream-world,

it was established that if Brahman were the material cause of the world, its transformation into the form of the world in its entirety would result in either total exhaustion [of Brahman] or the contradiction of scriptural texts stating its partlessness.

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it follows that either Brahman would be non-existent apart from its modifications, or else, if there were a partial transformation, there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning [Brahman's] partlessness; this is addressed by the sūtra: "And so it is in the case of the Self, for [the world] is manifold" (*ātmani caivaṃ vicitrāśca hi*).

Others maintain that, according to the intention of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), the creation of the ether and other elements within Brahman is possible— just as the manifold dream-world is created within the dreaming individual soul (*jīvātman*) without the destruction of its own nature; for this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
The meaning is that it has been established in the *Vivaraṇa* that there exists for [the individual soul] a relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*).

By this, it is stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth; otherwise, the soul would not possess the aforementioned state of being conjoined with the internal organ and other such things, just as it does not with jars and the like.

The sense is that it would be so because there is no distinction in the absence of being the material cause (*upādāna*). In this regard, if one accepts the non-difference of ignorance— which is the transforming material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth— from the *māyā* residing in the Lord (*īśvara*), then the Lord alone would possess the status of the material cause with respect to the internal organ and the rest.
It is appropriate to say this: if, by the aforementioned reasons such as the realization of identity with the individual soul (*jīva*),

it must be stated that the individual soul alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, then the internal organ and the rest would reside in the transforming ignorance (*avidyā*) that rests upon the individual soul, rather than in the *māyā* that rests upon the Lord (*īśvara*).

Furthermore, a distinction from the immediate cause must be stated; since there is no causality residing in consciousness apart from its being based on primordial nature (prakṛti) as it undergoes transformation into the form of an effect,
the non-difference of Māyā and avidyā is thus accepted.
The assertion that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth is mutually contradictory;
this underlying unease is indicated by the word "also" (*api*), which implies that it applies even to those who maintain the non-difference [of the soul and Brahman].
Even if one accepts that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the material cause of the internal organ and so forth, [there remains the problem] regarding His being the cause of all effects...

He introduces another school of thought in order to state the distinction that [the world] does not have [the Lord] as its material cause (*upādāna*). "From this" means from the aforementioned Lord; the sense of the ablative case is "material causality" (*prakṛtitva*);
the word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of emphasis.

After the phrase "of the dream-phenomenon," the word "material cause" (*upādāna*) is to be supplied by ellipsis. Does the entire Brahman transform into the form of the world, or only a part of it? It is not the first case; thus he says: "Of that" (*tasya*).
Just as there is a falling away from its prior nature for milk that has transformed into the form of curd, so too it would be for Brahman.

The meaning is that there would be a falling away from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). He refutes the second alternative—that a single part (*ekadeśa*) of Brahman undergoes transformation—by means of the phrase "by a single part" (*ekadeśena*), as explained previously.

Some maintain that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the cause of everything, acting as the creator of the Lord (*Īśvara*) and so forth within itself, like a dreamer. Alternatively, based on such scriptural passages as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," and because insentience (*jāḍya*), which is characteristic of Māyā, is observed in jars and other objects, Māyā is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.

How is it understood that Brahman is the material cause? On this point, the authors of the *Padārthatatvanirṇaya* say: both Brahman and Māyā are the material cause; thus, the compatibility of both [types of] scriptural statements is established. Furthermore, there is the compatibility of the persistence of both characteristics—existence and insentience—within that [cause].
Brahman is the material cause by way of its undergoing transformation, while ignorance is the material cause by way of its undergoing modification.
Regarding the term "pakṣa" (the prima facie view): it means that when the prima facie position has been reached— that Brahman’s status as the material cause is impossible in either way—

if one were to admit that Brahman’s status as the material cause consists in its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), like milk or the earth, then [the objection of] the total transformation of everything and so forth would follow.

A fault would follow [if it were taken literally], but it is not accepted in that way; rather, just as a rope and the like are the material cause (*upādāna*) of a snake and so forth, Brahman is accepted as the illusory material cause (*vivartopādāna*).

Therefore, there is no room for the aforementioned fault—this is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding the phrase "and in the Self" (*ātmani ca*), the single *ca* (and) functions as follows:

The word "hi" has the same meaning as "śabda"; the second [occurrence] has the sense of emphasis, while "hi" here signifies the reason. Consequently, just as within the self—the living soul (jīva), the dreamer—diverse creations such as chariots and so forth occur without any destruction of the essential nature of the consciousness of the jīva, even after the state of dreaming has ceased, it remains as the witness of the intellect and other faculties.

Just as the consciousness of the living being (jīva-caitanya) persists as it was before, so too do the diverse creations beginning with space (viyat) arise within Brahman without any loss of its own essential nature (svarūpa). This is because the persistence of Brahman in the forms of existence, consciousness, and bliss (sac-cid-ānanda) throughout creation, maintenance, and dissolution is established by the Śruti, as indicated by the Sūtra.
The meaning of the Sūtra: Now, regarding the question, "Is pure Brahman the material cause? and so forth, he introduces the reply by adopting the third position: "The individual soul (jīva).

This refers to the fully perfect conscious Self (cidātman), which, even without undergoing limitation or becoming a reflection due to ignorance (avidyā), has [already] attained [the state of being the cause].
Existing as a living being, it imagines itself to be the Lord of All before the state of lordship has been attained;

from itself alone, it imagines the creation of the ether and so forth, and it imagines its own distinction from that imagined Lord as well as its subordination to Him. Likewise, it gradually imagines the state of being a human being and so on, just as follows:

In the view that the phenomenal world beginning with space (*viyat*) is conventionally real (*vyāvahārikasatya*), whereas the dream-world is illusory (*prātibhāsika*), the dreaming individual soul (*jīva*) alone imagines itself as a god, animal, or human; as its controller, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*); and as distinct from it. And so, in that same manner, [it imagines] within itself alone...

The meaning is that the proponents of the *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* (the theory that the world is created at the very moment it is perceived) state that Brahman, having assumed the state of the individual soul (*jīva*), is the material cause of everything because it imagines all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*). In this position— that Brahman, having assumed the state of the individual soul, is the material cause of everything— there is no Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from the individual soul.

This indicates the fault that [the doctrine] contradicts the Śruti, Smṛti, Nyāyasūtra, Bhāṣya, and other texts which establish the Lord as the controller of all living beings, and that it renders the distinction between bondage and liberation untenable; thus say some.

And thus, because of the pervasive presence of the term "living" (*jīva*), it is established that Brahman, whose nature is that of the Lord (*īśvara*), is indeed the material cause (*upādāna*) of all.

Now, he raises the objection regarding the impossibility of this causality being a defining characteristic of Brahman, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). In the Śruti, however, the word "but" (*tu*) emphasizes that Māyā is the material cause (*prakṛti*), as follows:

Because smoothness and other qualities residing in clay and the like are followed through (anugama) in the jar and so forth, clay and the like possess the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the jar and so forth. Similarly, because insentience (*jāḍya*) residing in Māyā is followed through in the universe, she possesses the status of being its material cause; thus he states the reasoning as well: "of the insentience of Māyā."
How so? [The opponent asks: "But surely, the fact that Brahman is the material cause (*upādānatva*) was previously demonstrated by citing numerous scriptural passages.

True, it was demonstrated; however, that is not possible, because for Brahman—which is partless—it is impossible to be a transformative material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) like clay or other such substances, nor can it be an illusory material cause (*vivarta-upādāna*)."

It should not be argued that [superimposition] occurs even in the case of partless things, such as the sky, because we observe the superimposition of blueness and so forth upon them; for in the world, the status of being a material cause (upādānatva) is not established for substrata of illusory transformation (vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna), unlike in the case of things that undergo real modification (pariṇāmin).
Therefore, the acceptance of that status [of being a material cause] in those cases is untenable.

The intention of the objection is that [the definition] is merely a verbal designation. With the words "here they say," etc., he refutes the impossibility of the definition of Brahman as being constituted by its status as the material cause (*upādānatva*). Regarding the word "existent" (*sat*):

Nor should it be argued that it is improper to speak of existence as a property of Brahman, since that existence—which is its very nature and incapable of being sublated—is identical with the nature of Brahman itself; for the point is that such a conventional usage regarding its being a property is possible through the conceptualization of difference, just as one speaks of "the head of Rāhu. Now, [an objection]:

He says "no" to the objection that there are two kinds of material cause (*upādāna*). Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*): or rather, he says "no" to the objection that it is impossible for Brahman, which is partless, to be a material cause. The meaning of "therein" is "between Māyā and Brahman. Having restated the intention of the objection, he refutes it with the words "not so" (*na ca*), citing the examples of clay and so forth.

The meaning is that because the well-known characteristic of being a material cause (*upādāna*) exists even in the substrates of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna*), the acceptance of those as material causes is merely a technical convention (*paribhāṣā-mātra*) and not [an actual fact].
Regarding the phrase "in its own self" (*svātmani*): here, the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the entity intended to be the material cause; and thus...

The definition of *upādānatva* (material causality) is "being the substrate of an effect while being the cause of the production of that effect. The term "while being" (*sati*) is included to exclude efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). The term "substrate" (*ādhāra*) is included to exclude things like the ground (*bhūtala*), which are substrates of effects but not their material causes. The phrase "even there" means even in the case of the locus of an illusory manifestation (*vivartādhiṣṭhāna*).
"Exactly as stated": in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), both Māyā and Brahman possess the status of material cause (*upādānatva*).

Furthermore, in that context, the status of material cause is not merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*) with respect to the locus of illusory manifestation (*vivartādhiṣṭhāna*), because the definition of a material cause is "that which is the cause for the production of an effect within itself."

Some say that this is because there is no distinction even in that case. Accepting the very process already described, they state another definition that is common to both *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* (transformation):

"The nature of being a material cause (*upādānatva*) is the capacity to produce an effect non-different from itself; and this exists for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in its form as Being (*sat*)."
There is non-difference [of the world] from Brahman as it undergoes transformation, which is insentient and subject to modification;
for there is the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such expressions as "the jar exists" and "the jar is insentient."

The meaning is that Maya possesses the status of material cause (*upādānatva*) by way of being the transformed substrate (*pariṇāmitayā*), while Brahman possesses the status of material cause by way of being the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatayā*); thus, both together constitute the material cause, which is consistent with both scripture (*śruti*) and logic (*nyāya*).

Regarding the phrase "non-different from itself" (*svābhinna*): by the word "itself" (*sva*), one refers to the clay and so forth, which are the material causes of jars and the like, as well as the world’s transformative material cause.

The world is real ignorance (*bhūtamajñāna*). And Brahman, which is the material cause of the illusory manifestation (*vivartopādāna*), is also apprehended as real. In that regard, the non-difference of the jar and so forth from clay and the like is evident, because of the experience that "the jar is indeed clay. [The author] demonstrates through experience the non-difference of the effects from ignorance and Brahman with the words "it exists" (*asti ca*). Now, [an objection]: clay and the jar...

Just as there is no such experience as "the pot is Brahman" or "the cloth is Brahman," so too there is no such experience as "ignorance is the pot" and so forth. Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt as to how there can be non-difference between the world (prapañca), ignorance, and Brahman, the qualification "being whose nature is existence" (sadrūpatva) is given to Brahman.

Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is insentient (*jaḍa*). Thus, although there is no experience of non-difference between Brahman and ignorance on the grounds of their respective forms as "Brahman-ness" and "ignorance-ness," there is an experience of non-difference between the world (*prapañca*) and those two on the grounds of their common nature as "existence" (*sat*) and "insentience. This he states with the words "the pot exists" (*san ghaṭaḥ*), and so forth. Now, [an objection]:

Since the nature of clay is experienced in the causal substance prior to the production of the jar, and the nature of clay is thus established as a property of the cause, it is logical that the perceptual experience "this is a clay jar" apprehends the non-difference between the causal and resultant substances.

If it is asked: "What is the proof that existence (*sat*) and insentience (*jaḍatva*) are attributes of the cause, by virtue of which—on the strength of the experience 'the pot exists' and 'the pot is insentient'—the non-difference of the phenomenal world from Brahman, whose nature is existence and whose nature is insentience, could be established? It is replied: Brahman’s nature as existence is [established] by such texts as "He is Being" (*sa deva*), and so forth.
This very point—that it consists of insentience and delusion—is established by scripture (*śruti*). Through scripture, the insentience of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established.

And so, just as there is the experience of "clay-ness" in a jar and the like due to its non-difference from the causal substance of clay, the experience of existence and insentience in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is logically accounted for precisely because of its non-difference from the causal substance whose nature is the Real Entity (*sadvastu*); [it does not require] anything separate.

A property such as existence (*satva*) is not admitted [as distinct from the substrate]; likewise, even the experience that "the pot exists" or "the pot is insentient" (*jaḍa*) apprehends the non-difference between the effect, the cause, and the substance.

Furthermore, regarding the non-difference [of the world from Brahman] in the Sūtra, "And its non-difference [from Brahman], because of such terms as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa)," the commentary (*Bhāṣya*) and the *Bhāmatī* state that this "non-difference" does not mean non-existence through separation, nor indeed do we say that "non-difference" means identity; rather, we intend to exclude difference. Thus, [they establish] the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

It should not be argued that the acceptance of non-difference [between the individual soul and Brahman] results in a contradiction of one's own tenets (apasiddhānta) because of the negation of non-difference from Brahman;

for the intention [of the scripture] is the negation of a non-difference that possesses the same ontological status as the substratum which is Brahman, even while accepting a phenomenal non-difference— just as in the case of "this" and "silver."
Because there is no contradiction.

The meaning is that it should not be argued: "Even if the non-difference of the world from ignorance—which is insentient by nature—is established, what follows for Māyā? This is because their non-difference is accepted.
Regarding the acceptance of the non-difference between cause and effect, he raises this doubt with the words "na ca" (and not).
The non-difference of those two—the cause and the effect—must be accepted. Why?
From such terms as "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*). The meaning of the term "originating from speech" is found in the scriptural statement: "All this has its origin in speech.

Furthermore, there are scriptural passages establishing the universal nature [of the cause], such as "All this is indeed the Self," and prohibitive passages such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here."

The meaning of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) is *śruti* (scriptural authority). The *śruti* concerning "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) has been explained on the occasion of describing the definition of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*).

If the effect were a different reality from its cause, the scriptural teaching that Brahman, the cause of the world, is the self of all would be untenable. Likewise, if the world, which has Brahman as its material cause, were real...

The meaning is that since the negation of the world within Brahman would otherwise be impossible, one must accept the non-difference of the phenomenal world from Brahman, who serves as its cause. Now, an objection may be raised: by the term "non-difference" used in the Sūtra, the identity of effect and cause is understood; however, that is untenable.

The Commentator explains the word "non-difference" (*ananyatva*) from the Sūtra in order to dispel the doubt that consciousness and insentience—the Brahman and the phenomenal world—cannot be one due to their causal relationship and their mutual opposition.
He states: "Non-difference means non-existence as something distinct [from the cause]. And it is not the case that, if the effect were non-existent apart from the cause...

It must be explained how there is the relation of cause and effect; for, since what is intended is the absence of the existence of the effect apart from the existence of the cause, there is no room for the suspicion that the very nature of the effect is being denied.
He cites a passage from the *Bhāmatī* commentary which demonstrates the intended meaning of the word "non-difference" (*ananya*) in the Sūtra:

"Not indeed" (*na khalu*). By the word "non-difference" (*ananya-tva*), we do not assert the identity of cause and effect; rather, the impossibility of identity between the conscious and the unconscious is the reason for its negation, as indicated by the particle "indeed" (*khalu*). If that were so, the scriptural teaching that "through the knowledge of the causal Brahman, all is known" would not be established.
He raises an objection with the words "But what... because [the opponent] does not admit non-difference. He replies: "Difference.
The meaning is that we deny a difference in existence (*sattva*) between cause and effect. And thus, [that which is] the very nature of the causal Brahman...
Existence alone is the true nature of any effect; when that is known, everything inseparable from it becomes known in reality.

Thus, there is no contradiction with the proposition that through a single cognition all things are known. Nor does the contradiction of the proposition remain, because even though the true nature of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is known when the nature of Brahman is known, it is still impossible to know the specific, individual characteristics of each particular thing.

It must be said that this is so; for in propositional statements such as "when the Self is known, everything becomes known," the word "all" refers to all principles (*tattva*), and thus the knowledge of all things in their unique, specific forms is not intended. Nor is there any determining factor (*vinigamaka*) against such an interpretation.

It must be said: since the knowledge of non-dual Brahman, which is the means to liberation, is obtained merely through the knowledge of the reality of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the futility of knowing the specific, individual forms of those [objects] is itself the refutation [of their necessity]; for even when the cause, Brahman, is known, [the knowledge of] each respective [form within] the entire phenomenal world...

Furthermore, since the cognition of a common form is impossible, there would be the undesirable consequence that the scriptural statement regarding "all-cognition" would lack authority if it were intended to mean that; and because the perception of difference is condemned here and there in the scriptures as being a cause of evil, the scriptural declaration does not have the intention of teaching the cognition of manifold forms.

This has been stated in the *Pañcadaśī*: "In this context, the realization of all through the realization of the One is taught solely for the purpose of making non-duality (*advaita*) manifest; it is certainly not intended to convey multiplicity. The meaning of this is as follows:
here, in the Vedāntas, by the realization of the one Brahman, there is the realization of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) within non-duality.

The meaning is that the Śruti exists solely to turn the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) toward Brahman, and for the sake of the seeker’s realization of non-dual Brahman alone. The point is that the realization of non-dual Brahman is accomplished merely through the knowledge that everything has Brahman alone as its real nature. Now, [an objection]:

The meaning of the scripture—that "when Brahman is known, everything becomes known"—is naturally understood as the knowledge of everything in its respective unique form. To the question, "Why might this not be so?
he says: "Not at all. This is because the knowledge of everything was not intended by the scripture with the desire to convey a cognition of manifoldness (*nānātva*).

The construction [of the compound] is due to the absence of purpose; the meaning is that it refers to the two—the *Bhāṣya* and the *Bhāmatī-nibandha*—because they are sublated and because they are established. Nor should it be argued that if the real non-difference between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman is denied, then a real difference would necessarily follow.
For the reality of a difference depends upon the reality of either the substratum (*dharmin*) or the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); in that regard,

although Brahman is real, since the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is understood from such terms as "merely a beginning" (*ārambhaṇa-śabda*), the difference between the two [is not real].

The sense is that [the distinction] is untenable because of its lack of reality. Regarding the term "apparent" (*prātītika*): just as in the error "this is silver," the non-difference between the object "silver" and the substrate "this" is established by delusion; likewise, since there is no contradiction with our own tenet (*siddhānta*) in accepting the non-difference established by such errors as "the pot exists," this is the intended meaning.

By the Śruti passage, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," which contains the word "tu" (but/only) for the purpose of restriction, it is understood that Māyā alone is the material cause; however, the author of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* maintains that Brahman alone is the material cause, since [Brahman], though immutable (*kūṭastha*), [is the cause] by its own nature.
They say that because a [direct] causal status is untenable, Māyā is the instrumental cause; for even though it is not the [material] cause,
it follows through into the effect, just as clay does, since we observe that qualities residing in it, such as smoothness, also follow into the jar.

Mena [the author] addresses the doubt that, because Brahman lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), the definition of Brahman—which includes being the material cause—is impossible; he states that both Māyā and Brahman possess the nature of being the material cause (*prakṛti*), since there is no distinction between them according to scripture and reasoning, and as for the scriptural passage "But Māyā... (*māyāṃ tu...*)— [The rest of the sentence continues: ...in that [passage], [it is stated that Māyā is the material cause].
The word "but" (*tu*) is not for the purpose of restriction; rather, it is intended to highlight the distinction of *māyā* from Brahman, whose nature is existence (*sadrūpa*).

This distinction consists in *māyā* being the material cause (*prakṛti*) by virtue of its being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*). This is according to the differing views of authors such as Padārthatattvanirṇaya-kāra and others who hold this intention.

The doubt regarding the impossibility of the definition has been dispelled. Now, the author of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* states two views held by those who believe that Brahman alone is the material cause and not Māyā, and therefore there is no room for the doubt concerning the impossibility of the definition, beginning with the words "But the author of the Saṃkṣepaśārīraka... and so forth. To the objection that Māyā would then be useless, he replies, "No."
Regarding the term "of the immutable" (kūṭasthasya):

if Brahman were the material cause without Māyā, then Brahman itself would necessarily undergo transformation. And thus, by those who advocate the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavādins) [it is said]: "transformation..."

Because the real non-difference between the transformer (the substrate) and the transformation is admitted, Brahman would likewise be subject to modification through the transformations such as birth and so forth; yet it cannot be argued that this is an undesirable consequence, for in many Śrutis, such as "It is not born," Brahman's state of being immutable is established by its freedom from modifications like birth and the rest.

The meaning is that because there is a contradiction in [Brahman] being the material cause [directly], it must be stated that Brahman’s causality is through the medium of *māyā*; thus, *māyā* is not useless. Just as, although the substance of clay is the material cause, the refinement such as smoothness residing in it is an instrumental cause, for the substance of clay in its unrefined state [cannot serve as such].

The status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) of jars and so forth is thus established. Likewise, the meaning is that *māyā*, which is superimposed upon Brahman—which is of the nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*)—is accepted as a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), effecting its status as the primordial source (*prakṛti*) of the world therein.
Nor does the absence of *māyā*’s status as the material cause contradict the scriptural statement: "One should know *māyā* as the material cause" (*māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vidyāt*).

It should not be said that there is a contradiction with the Śruti; for the Śruti’s mention of her as "prakṛti" (primordial matter) is justified merely by her being the sustainer (*nirvāhakatā*) of Brahman’s status as prakṛti.

It is precisely with the intention that Māyā possesses the status of prakṛti only as a sustainer and does not possess the status of prakṛti inherently, that the usage of the term "śakti" (power) is observed for her in the Śruti.

"His power is heard to be indeed manifold"— for the material causality (*upādānatva*) of the power inherent in substances such as clay toward any particular effect is not [the same as the power of Brahman].
Vācaspatimiśra, however, maintains that Brahman itself— conditioned by Māyā residing in the individual soul (jīva) and having that as its object—

is the material cause (upādāna) by way of undergoing illusory transformation (vivarta) into the form of the world based on the channels (nāḍīs); thus, Māyā is merely an auxiliary (sahakāri), not an instrumental cause (dvārakāraṇa) that persists in the effect.

Because it is well-known in the world, the argument that— due to the absence of any decisive factor (*vinigamakābhāva*)— both Māyā and Brahman are the material cause (*upādāna*) is refuted; for since Māyā is the power (*śakti*) of Brahman, it cannot be a material cause in its own right, and if one does not admit that she is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there would be no [material cause] for the world.

It should not be argued that the material cause (upādāna) would be subject to transformation, for Brahman’s state of undergoing transformation has been repeatedly refuted as being contradictory to its immutability (kūṭasthatva); rather, as in the view of Vācaspati,
the phenomenal world is the object of Māyā superimposed upon Consciousness.

This is because it is logically consistent to accept that [the world] is merely an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman. Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the usage of the term "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) regarding *māyā* found here and there in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, for such usage can be explained as being intended from the perspective of another philosophical school. But [an objection may be raised]: if [the world] does not have *māyā*—which is insentient—as its material cause (*prakṛti*), [how can this be so]?

He says "no" [to the objection] that the insentience (*jāḍya*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would not exist. The phrase "even without a cause" means even without a material cause (*anupādāna*). Insentience, which is pervasive throughout the world, is not a quality of a cause; rather, it is the inherent nature of the world itself. Therefore, for the sake of establishing that [insentience], Māyā is the material cause.

With the intention that one should not postulate a causality mediated by following from the effect (*kāryānugatadvāraka*), he says: "Vācaspati Miśra, however... [and] "residing in the individual soul (*jīvāśritā*). Now, an objection: in the Akṣara Brāhmaṇa, it is stated that Māyā—denoted by the word "ether" (*ākāśa*)—resides in eternal consciousness (*nityacaitanya*).
Because it has already been established [that Brahman is the locus of Māyā], how can it be accepted that the individual soul (jīva) is the locus of Māyā?

Furthermore, this contradicts the Śruti text, "But [they worship] Maheśvara, the wielder of Māyā," because by the word "akṣara" (the Imperishable), the fact that [Māyā] rests upon Brahman—denoted by the term Maheśvara—is established. Moreover, if the individual soul were the locus of Māyā, then for that very [soul]...

The world would have the status of being the material cause [of itself] because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of *māyā*. For Brahman’s status as the material cause of the phenomenal world consists precisely in its being the substratum (*āśraya*) of the *māyā* that transforms into the phenomenal world. However, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the substratum of *māyā*, then that soul alone would be the material cause of the world, and not Brahman. Furthermore, [if *māyā* were] the object (*viṣaya*) of *māyā* residing in the soul...

If it is argued that, according to the view that Brahman is "created," there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of its status as a controller and creator of the world due to the non-acceptance of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for Brahman— it is replied: by the phrase "residing in the individual soul" (jīvāśrita), what is meant is residing in consciousness qualified by the state of being an individual soul (jīvatva).

This is not what is intended. Rather, in accordance with the *Akṣarabrāhmaṇa*, the state of being a *jīva* consists precisely in being dependent upon consciousness (*caitanya*). However, because *avidyā*—which is to be known as the sphere of *māyā*—acts as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) within the manifestation of consciousness, it is said that *māyā* resides in the *jīva*. Furthermore, it is not the case that *māyā* alone is the delimiting factor for the manifestation of the state of being a *jīva* within consciousness.

It should not be said that there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). For, just as between the state of being a substance (*dravyatva*) and the state of being a substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*), their mutual dependence—characterized by being the cause for each other's existence—is not a fault. Mutual dependence [is not a fault].

There would be a fault either in its production (*utpatti*) or in its manifestation (*jñapti*); however, that fault does not apply here, because both ignorance (*avidyā*) and the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) are beginningless and are manifested by the eternal witness (*sākṣin*). Nor should it be said that the assumption of the state of being a living soul as a regulator for the persistence of ignorance is redundant; for [it serves this purpose] in Brahman...

Because it prevents that [superimposition], Brahman is faultless; for since the Śruti states that Brahman is "stainless" (*nirañjana*), it is understood to be devoid of defects, and thus it is impossible for it to be the substratum of a defect in the form of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nor should it be argued that the Śruti is merely concerned with the factuality of being faultless, for such a restriction would [contradict the text].
Because there is an absence of proof, and because the individual soul (*jīva*), like Brahman in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*), is in reality free from defects;

nor does this contradict the Śruti text, "But [He is] the Great Lord who possesses *māyā*," for just as in expressions such as "Devadatta is a house-owner" or "a wealthy man," the suffix is used even though Devadatta is not the actual substratum of the house or wealth.

Just as [the term "possessor"] indicates another relationship characterized by the relation of owner and owned, so too— even though Brahman, denoted by the word *Maheśvara*, is not the substratum of *māyā*— the scriptural statement "the Illusionist" (*māyinam*) is justified because it indicates another relationship between *māyā* and Brahman characterized by the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*). [This applies] to the phenomenal world...

Furthermore, because it is accepted that the world is merely an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman as made an object of Maya which rests upon the individual soul (*jīva*), there is no contingency of the individual soul being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world; and because the scripture exists which establishes Brahman’s status as the universal controller, omniscience, and so forth, even in the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, this is established.

Māyā, which rests upon the individual soul (jīva) and has the Brahman as its object, is the material cause (upādāna) by virtue of its transformation (vivarta) into the form of the phenomenal world (prapañca). As stated in the commentary on the *Vācārambhaṇa* section:
"The very root cause itself, through that form of the final effect, [becomes] everything in the form of an effect, like an actor."

"It attains the status of being the locus of empirical transaction. "From the final effect" means up to and including the final effect. For an actor, while his own true nature remains unrecognized by the spectators, attains the state of reality through various roles he enacts. In the same way, the Reality remains unrecognized by individual souls (jīvas).

The meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is that the existent Brahman, through its states such as truth and falsehood, attains the form of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca*) and becomes the object of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Here, by the mention of the analogy of the actor (*naṭa*), the view of Vācaspati is [presented].

The view favored by the Bhāṣya is adopted. As stated in the Kalpataru: "Śaṅkara declared that Brahman is the cause [of the world] while remaining unknown, like an actor; likewise, Vācaspati proclaimed that the seed of the world is the ignorance (ajñāna) of the individual soul (jīva). However, the author of the Siddhāntamuktāvalī maintains that the power of Māyā alone is the material cause (upādāna).

"O Brahman, this Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without exterior; for it neither has an effect nor an instrument," according to such scriptural passages. However, it is figuratively designated as the material cause (*upādāna*) by virtue of being the locus of *māyā*, which is the material cause of the world. It is precisely this kind of causality that is intended in the definition.

They say this is what was intended to be expressed. Now, who is the Lord (Īśvara) and who is the individual soul (jīva)? Regarding this, it is stated in the *Prakaṭārthavivaraṇa*: "Māyā is beginningless, indeterminable, unmanifest, and inherent in pure consciousness; the reflection of consciousness within that [Māyā] is the Lord."
