The reflection of consciousness (cit) in those very [powers] called ignorance (avidyā), which possess the capacities for veiling (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa) within their delimited and infinite portions, is the individual soul (jīva).

Now, even while accepting that Māyā alone possesses the primary status of material cause (*upādānatva*) in accordance with the natural sense of the Śruti text, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," [the author] dispels the impossibility of the definition of Brahman.

Regarding the view of the author of the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*: "That which is under discussion" refers to this aforementioned intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, whose nature is that of the Witness (*sākṣin*).

That for which no cause exists is "without prior" (*apūrvam*); that for which no further effect exists is "without posterior" (*anaparam*). For that Brahman, the "effect" (*kāryam*) and the "instrument" (*karaṇam*)—meaning the means for the creation of the world—do not exist. This is because of such scriptural passages as these.

The meaning is that Brahman is the material cause (*upādāna*). If that is so, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti, Sūtras, Bhāṣya, and other texts which establish that Brahman is the material cause of the world; to this he says: "the world," etc. The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. It means: "exactly such [a cause]"—that is, being the locus of Māyā while serving as the material cause of the world.

In the preceding section, the Lord’s status as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the universe was stated; furthermore, in passages such as "the *māyā* residing in the individual soul" (*jīvāśritā māyā*), the individual soul (*jīva*) was also mentioned. Now, in order to define the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of these two, he introduces a question with the word "atha" (now).
Regarding that *māyā* which is well-known from the scriptural text, "But *māyā* is indeed *prakṛti*," as being the material cause of the elements (*bhūta-prakṛti*): [the question follows].

"Īśvara is the reflection of consciousness. Now, one might raise the objection: "Since the supplementary statement 'But [He is] the Great Lord who possesses Māyā' establishes that Māyā rests upon Īśvara, it is impossible for Īśvara to be a reflection of Māyā, because an adjunct (upādhi) is never observed to reside within its own reflection. To dispel this doubt, he says:

The meaning is that [Māyā] rests upon pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). By the word *mātra*, there is an exclusion of its being a reflection (*bimba*) and so forth. The intention is that even in the supplementary portion of the text, the term "Maheśvara" is indicative (*lakṣaka*) of pure consciousness. He negates the reality of Māyā—as held by the Sāṃkhyas regarding *prakṛti*—by describing it as "indescribable" (*anirvācya*). Māyā, first of all, is not distinct from the Brahman-consciousness...

It is not different in reality, because it is impossible for that [individual soul] to be different from Brahman, as this would contradict the scriptures which establish the falsity of everything apart from Brahman. Nor is it non-different, because consciousness and insentience cannot be identical. Nor is it both different and non-different from consciousness, because difference and non-difference are mutually contradictory in a single locus.
Because it is possible; thus, it is not merely that much.

It cannot be real, because that would contradict the scriptural teachings on non-duality (*advaita*); nor can it be unreal, because that would make it impossible for it to be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the world.

Nor can it be both real and unreal, because reality and unreality are mutually contradictory in a single locus. Furthermore, Māyā cannot possess parts, as that would entail its being a finite, beginningless entity, which in turn would imply that the Lord, who is its reflection, is likewise finite.

Because it would entail the consequence of having a beginning; for if Māyā had a beginning, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress due to the requirement of another Māyā as its material cause (*prakṛti*). Nor is it partless, because that would entail the absence of being a material cause, since in the world material causality is observed only in the case of objects that possess parts.

Nor can it possess both forms, because possessing parts and being partless are contradictory in one and the same thing. Therefore, the meaning is that *māyā* is "indefinable" (*anirvācya*) because it cannot be defined in any way whatsoever. The individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*) upon its finite and infinite regions. It is not...

The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that the reflection of consciousness (*cit*) in this very [intellect] is the individual soul (*jīva*). The qualification of the locations as "limited" (*paricchinnatva*) is for the purpose of obtaining the limited nature of the individual souls who consist of those reflections. And thus, in various places in the Bhāṣya, regarding the individual souls—

The determination of finitude is consistent [with this]. For instance, in the section beginning with *sarvatra prasiddhopadeśāt* (Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere), the commentary—which takes the form of an explanation of the word *śārīra* found in the Sūtra—states:
"The word *śārīra* means 'that which exists in the body' (*śarīre bhavaḥ*). Now, one might object: "But the Lord (*īśvara*) also exists in the body."

It is true that [the Self] exists in the body, but it does not exist *only* in the body; for its all-pervasiveness is heard in scripture as being "all-pervading and eternal like space. The individual soul (jīva), however, exists only in the body, because the body is the locus of its experience and because it has no functioning outside of the body.

Likewise, the commentary (bhāṣya) concerning the section beginning with "Heaven and Earth" states: "And it is not possible for the individual soul (prāṇabhṛt), which is non-omnipresent and limited by adjuncts (upādhi), to properly be the abode of heaven, earth, and so forth; thus, it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva) to be the primary abode of the world denoted by the terms 'heaven, earth, etc.'"

The meaning of the commentary is "due to the lack of pervasiveness. Just as for you [the Naiyāyika], the cloth has no parts that serve as its constituent causes (*ārambhaka*), so too for Māyā there are no spatial parts (*pradeśa*), because she is beginningless (*anādi*). Rather, because the powers of projection (*vikṣepa*) and concealment (*āvaraṇa*) within Māyā are infinite, the very portions possessing these powers of projection and concealment are what constitute her "parts."

With the intention that these [powers] are intended to be expressed, he says: "possessing the powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa). The power conducive to the concealment of the consciousness of Brahman is the power of concealment. And concealment is the state of being fit for the empirical usage [expressions] such as "Brahman does not exist" or "Brahman does not manifest. By the word "projection" (vikṣepa)...

The meaning is that the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) refers to the capacity conducive to the various sufferings and so forth common to each individual soul (*jīva*), which is intended here. Now, an objection may be raised: the description of the portions (*pradeśa*) of *māyā* as being the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the souls is untenable, as seen in the commentary on the *Ānumānikādhikaraṇa* and other such passages.
Since it would follow that there is a contradiction with conventional usage if ignorance were the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), he says:
"In the designations of ignorance," etc.

The sense is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural statement], because it is the regions of *māyā* themselves—referred to by the term "knowledge" (*vidyā*) in the Bhāṣya—that are being sublated. However, in the *Tattvaviveka*, it is stated: "Māyā and avidyā, which consist of the three guṇas, constitute the root nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); they bring about [the world] through their own manifestation as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)."

Since it is established by scripture that [the Lord] exists, two distinct forms are postulated: Māyā, which consists primarily of pure *sattva* unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*, and *avidyā*, which consists of *sattva* that is impure because it is overpowered by those two. Having thus conceived this distinction between Māyā and *avidyā*, the Lord is the reflection in Māyā.

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection of consciousness (*vidyā*). There is but one fundamental nature (*mūlaprakṛti*); when characterized primarily by its power of projection (*vikṣepa*), it is called *māyā* and serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord (*īśvara*).

When characterized primarily by its power of concealment (*āvaraṇa*), it is called *avidyā* or *ajñāna* and serves as the limiting adjunct of the individual soul. For this very reason, of that [nature]...
Although pure consciousness (cinmātra) is common to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara),

the experience of the connection with ignorance (ajñāna)— characterized as being "ignorant" and "warm"— belongs to the jīva alone and not to the Lord; thus, the distinction between the jīva and the Lord is established in certain contexts.

Having postulated an indefinable difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) within the single primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) by way of the relationship between a part and the whole, their nature as reflections was stated. Now, he establishes that same point by postulating a different kind of distinction in form within that very [nature], as follows: "In the Tattvaviveka... etc.
The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of indicating a distinction; the ellipsis is "the difference in form," etc.

Purity (*śuddhatva*) of *sattva* consists precisely in its not being overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*. *Māyā* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*) dominated by pure *sattva*. [That which is] impure *sattva*...
The meaning is that *pradhāna* is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*). The impurity of *sattva* consists precisely in its being overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*.

Having thus defined the two distinct forms mentioned in the Śruti—namely, *māyātva* and *avidyātva*—according to the purity and impurity of *sattva*, [the author] now defines those very same forms mentioned in the Śruti through the distinction between the powers of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) and concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). "It is one alone," etc.

"From this very reason" means: precisely because the individual soul (jīva) possesses an adjunct (upādhi) that has the power of concealment. "Of that" means: even though Prakṛti—which serves as the adjunct for both the individual soul and the Lord—is dependent upon the mirror-like consciousness (bimba-caitanya) common to both the individual soul and the Lord. "Not [the concealment] of the Lord": here too, the phrase "from this very reason" is to be supplied.
The meaning of that [statement] is precisely because the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) does not enter into the category of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of Īśvara. And thus,

regarding the doubt as to how the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Īśvara— established by both scripture and experience, wherein one is omniscient while the other is ignorant— is possible given that *prakṛti* is common to both:

The sense is that there is no room [for such an objection]. He states another opinion: "In brief," etc. Considering that in the Śruti the word "cause" refers to *avidyā* and the word "effect" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he says:
"In *avidyā*," and so forth. Now, [it may be objected]: "By means of reflection, it creates the Jīva and the Īśvara; and it is both *māyā* and *avidyā*."

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the Śruti because that scripture perceives the individual soul (jīva) as having the causal adjunct (kāraṇopādhika), it is replied: "By means of reflection, He makes [the distinction] between the individual soul and the Lord. For by the first part [of the verse], both the individual soul and the Lord are indeed presented.

In the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, however, following the Śruti which states that this individual soul (*jīva*) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) while the Lord (*īśvara*) has the cause as His limiting adjunct, it is held that the Lord is the reflection of consciousness (*cit*) in ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas the individual soul is the reflection of consciousness in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nor [is the soul] by means of the substance in the form of the internal organ...
It cannot be argued that consciousness delimited by the body— just as space is delimited by a jar—

is the individual soul (jīva); for since the portion of consciousness delimited as the soul would differ here and there, this would entail the fallacy of the loss of what was done (kṛtahāna) and the acquisition of what was not done (akṛtābhyāgama).

However, since a reflection does not differ from that which is delimited by the movement of its delimiting adjuncts— just as the delimited object does not differ from the movement of its delimiting adjuncts— it has been stated that this fault does not apply to the position of the reflection.

The state of being a reflection is perceived; however, in a case where there is identity with the original object (*bimba*), a difference between reflections is not possible without a difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because no difference between reflections is observed in cases such as the reflection of the sun and so forth in the absence of a difference in the limiting adjuncts. Thus it is stated in the cited scripture:
The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are of the nature of reflections, are respectively established by the terms *māyā* and *avidyā*.
Furthermore, in this context, the term *māyā* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is an effect of *māyā*. Nor does it refer to the primordial material nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction in the statement "Māyā and Avidyā become [the two] themselves" within the scriptural passage "Jīva and Īśvara," which seeks to establish the non-difference of both Māyā and Avidyā from the root-prakṛti;
for [this refers to] the internal organ designated by the term "Māyā," just as [it does to] the root-prakṛti and Avidyā.

The sense is this: although there is no primary identity between the root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) and [the individual], since there exists a distinction necessitated by their relationship as material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*), the supplementary statement "Māyā and Avidyā become themselves" is thereby justified. Nor should it be argued that the Lord is simply the Consciousness delimited by Avidyā, and likewise that [the individual soul] is simply the Consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Let it be the individual soul (*jīva*). With the intention that the state of being delimited by ignorance and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is already established for the two consciousnesses (the substrate-consciousness and the consciousness reflected therein), and that postulating a reflection distinct from those would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), he raises an objection with the words "If not," etc.
It is not, however, simply the case that [the *jīva*] is the consciousness as a reflection.

This is the meaning of the verse. The mention of the "individual soul" (jīva) is also an elliptical reference to the Lord (Īśvara), since the status of both the individual soul and the Lord as reflections is established by scripture;

thus, intending that there is no fault of excessive conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava), he states the defect in the position that the individual soul is limited (avacchinna) with the word "here" (iha).

In this world, because the portion of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) residing in the body of a Brāhmaṇa or others possesses the status of both agent and enjoyer of karma; whereas in another world, the portion of consciousness delimited by the internal organ residing in the body of a god or others is an enjoyer who is not the agent—there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the loss of what was done and so forth. [This is avoided] by that through which the karma was performed...

The meaning is that there would be the accrual of the fruit of an action not performed by him, which constitutes his experience. Nor can it be argued that since it is accepted that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) residing in a body such as that of a Brāhmaṇa travels to another world, it is therefore the very locus of consciousness delimited by that organ which must travel there as well.

It must be stated: the point is that even when a jar moves to another location, no movement is observed on the part of the portion of space delimited by it. The word "tu" (but/however) is used to highlight the distinction of the reflection from the consciousness that serves as its delimiting locus (*avacchedya-caitanya*). Regarding the phrase "of going and coming":

The meaning is that even when going and coming occur, [the reflection] does not become divided, just like the delimited space [within a vessel]. The intention is that in a water-filled jar or similar object containing the reflections of the sun and so forth, no division of the reflection is observed even when the vessel is carried to another location.

When these views regarding the specific nature of the reflections of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) have been stated, that Brahman which stands as the original prototype (bimba) is the pure consciousness (śuddhacaitanya) to be attained by the liberated; this is so provided one sets aside the threefold system found in the *Citradīpa*, which posits the triad of the individual soul, the Lord, and pure non-consciousness (viśuddhācit). As it is said:

The space delimited by a jar is the "jar-space" (*ghaṭākāśa*); that which is reflected in the water resting within it is the "water-space," which includes the clouds and stars. The unconditioned is the "great space" (*mahākāśa*).
Within the mass of clouds situated in the midst of the great space, there exist those [clouds] whose nature as rain is to be inferred from their effects.
But when reflected in the water-form and its parts that take the shape of frost, it is the space of the clouds; thus, in reality, there is a fourfold nature of a single space.

But surely, when one among several water vessels containing reflections of the moon and so forth is destroyed, the merging of the reflection perceived as residing within it with its original source (the *bimba*) is experienced through direct perception; likewise, [this occurs] with another reflection. In the same way, at the time of disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*), for the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is that of a reflection— [The text continues: ...there is a merging with the original source, which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is because, like the reflection, the individual soul is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Supreme Self, and because the Supreme Self is omnipresent. Furthermore, since the individual soul is of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya-rūpa*), it is not subject to destruction even upon the destruction of the body, just as fire is not destroyed by the destruction of the fuel. Therefore, there is no contradiction in the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self. Thus, the statement that "the individual soul merges into the Supreme Self" is established. This is the view of the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha. However, others hold that the individual soul is an eternal, partless entity (*nityo 'navayavaḥ*) distinct from the Supreme Self. According to them, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means its becoming one with the Supreme Self through the cessation of all distinctions (*bhedopamardena*). This is because, although the individual soul is eternal, it is subject to bondage due to the presence of beginningless ignorance (*anādya-vidyā*), and thus its true nature remains unmanifest. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its true nature becomes manifest, and it attains liberation. This is the view of the venerable Rāmakaṇṭha. Now, the venerable Bhaṭṭa argues that the individual soul is a part (*amśa*) of the Supreme Self, just as a spark is a part of fire. He maintains that the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means the individual soul’s attainment of the state of being a part of the Supreme Self, which is its own essential nature. This is because, while the individual soul is indeed a part of the Supreme Self, it is not a part in the sense of being a portion (*avayava*) like a limb of a body; rather, it is a part in the sense of being a manifestation (*vibhūti*) or a specific power (*śakti-viśeṣa*). Therefore, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is simply the realization of its own inherent nature as a part of the Supreme Self. This is the view of the venerable Bhaṭṭa. However, the venerable Sadyojyoti holds that the individual soul is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Supreme Self, just as curd is a transformation of milk. He maintains that the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means the individual soul’s reversion to the state of the Supreme Self, which is its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). This is because, just as gold ornaments revert to the state of gold when melted, the individual soul, which is a transformation of the Supreme Self, reverts to the state of the Supreme Self upon the cessation of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). This is the view of the venerable Sadyojyoti. But how can the individual soul, which is a transformation of the Supreme Self, be eternal? It is eternal because it is of the nature of consciousness, and because consciousness cannot be destroyed even when the body is destroyed, just as fire is not destroyed by the destruction of the fuel. Therefore, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is established. This is the view of the venerable Sadyojyoti. However, others hold that the individual soul is a reflection (*pratibimba*) of the Supreme Self, just as the moon is reflected in water. They maintain that the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means the individual soul’s merging with the Supreme Self through the cessation of all distinctions, just as the reflection of the moon merges with the moon itself when the water vessel is removed. This is because, although the individual soul is a reflection of the Supreme Self, it is not a separate reality; rather, it is the Supreme Self itself appearing as a reflection due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, the reflection merges with its original source, the Supreme Self. This is the view of the venerable Somānanda. Now, the venerable Utpaladeva argues that the individual soul is identical with the Supreme Self, just as the sun is identical with its rays. He maintains that the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means the individual soul’s realization of its identity with the Supreme Self, which is its own essential nature. This is because, although the individual soul is indeed the Supreme Self, it appears as a separate entity due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its true nature as the Supreme Self becomes manifest, and it attains liberation. This is the view of the venerable Utpaladeva. But how can the individual soul, which is identical with the Supreme Self, be subject to bondage? It is subject to bondage because, although it is essentially the Supreme Self, it identifies with the body, senses, and mind due to the influence of beginningless ignorance, just as a person identifies with a dream-body. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its true nature as the Supreme Self becomes manifest, and it attains liberation. This is the view of the venerable Utpaladeva. However, the venerable Abhinavagupta holds that the individual soul is a limited manifestation (*saṅkoca*) of the Supreme Self, just as a crystal is a limited manifestation of light. He maintains that the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self means the individual soul’s expansion (*vikāsa*) into the state of the Supreme Self, which is its own essential nature. This is because, although the individual soul is essentially the Supreme Self, it is limited by the influence of beginningless ignorance. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its limitations are removed, and it expands into the state of the Supreme Self, just as a crystal, when freed from its coverings, expands into the state of pure light. This is the view of the venerable Abhinavagupta. Thus, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is established according to the various perspectives of the masters. This concludes the discussion. Now, regarding the question of whether the individual soul is a part, a transformation, or a reflection of the Supreme Self, the venerable Abhinavagupta says: "The individual soul is neither a part, nor a transformation, nor a reflection of the Supreme Self; rather, it is the Supreme Self itself, appearing as a limited manifestation due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. This is because, if the individual soul were a part of the Supreme Self, then since the Supreme Self is omnipresent, the individual soul would also have to be omnipresent, and there would be no distinction between the liberated and the bound. If it were a transformation, then since the Supreme Self is eternal and changeless, the individual soul could never attain liberation. If it were a reflection, then since a reflection is not a real entity, the individual soul would be unreal, which contradicts scriptural authority. Therefore, the individual soul is the Supreme Self itself, appearing as a limited manifestation due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its true nature as the Supreme Self becomes manifest, and it attains liberation. This is the final view of the venerable Abhinavagupta. Thus, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is established. This concludes the discussion. Now, regarding the question of whether the individual soul is a part, a transformation, or a reflection of the Supreme Self, the venerable Abhinavagupta says: "The individual soul is neither a part, nor a transformation, nor a reflection of the Supreme Self; rather, it is the Supreme Self itself, appearing as a limited manifestation due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. This is because, if the individual soul were a part of the Supreme Self, then since the Supreme Self is omnipresent, the individual soul would also have to be omnipresent, and there would be no distinction between the liberated and the bound. If it were a transformation, then since the Supreme Self is eternal and changeless, the individual soul could never attain liberation. If it were a reflection, then since a reflection is not a real entity, the individual soul would be unreal, which contradicts scriptural authority. Therefore, the individual soul is the Supreme Self itself, appearing as a limited manifestation due to the influence of beginningless ignorance. Upon the cessation of that ignorance, its true nature as the Supreme Self becomes manifest, and it attains liberation. This is the final view of the venerable Abhinavagupta. Thus, the merging of the individual soul with the Supreme Self is established. This concludes the discussion. Now, regarding the question of whether the individual soul is a part, a transformation, or a reflection of the Supreme Self, the venerable Abhinavagupta says: "The individual soul is neither a part, nor a transformation, nor a reflection of the Supreme Self; rather, it is the Supreme Self itself, appearing as a limited manifestation due to the influence of beginning

He dispels the objection—that the state of pure Brahman alone constitutes the original image (*bimba*), and not the attainment of the status of the Lord as a reflection (*pratibimba*) due to contradiction with observed reality—by accepting it as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*). [This is shown in the passage beginning] "When it has been stated thus... and "That which stands in the place of the original image... and so forth.
The meaning is that it stands in the place of the reflected image, such as the moon well-known in the world. Now, one might ask:

"How can consciousness qualified by being an image be pure? If this is asked, the answer is no; for by the term "pure," what is intended is the absence of attributes such as omniscience and omnipotence. Furthermore, in the *Citradīpa*, a threefold division [of consciousness] is taught.

The connection [of the passage] is as follows: having set aside the [conventional] process and postulated a fourfold nature of consciousness (*caitanya*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is demonstrated. And so says the *Citradīpa*: "The immutable (*kūṭastha*), Brahman, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*)—thus consciousness is fourfold, just like the space within a jar, the great space, the space in water, and the space in a cloud. This is stated in that verse.

He summarizes the illustrative portion of the analogy with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*). "Dependent on me" (*madāśrita*) means dependent on the space (*ākāśa*) situated within the jar. The qualification "together with clouds and stars" is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that there might be no reflection of space in water.

And thus, this is the intended method for refuting that [objection]: when the reflection of water, elephants, and stars is perceived, the reflection of space is necessarily perceived along with them; therefore, there is no room for the suspicion that the reflection of space does not exist. [The term] "unlimited" (anavacchinna) [is used].

The meaning is "unconfined by a jar. The connection is that [the reflection] is reflected in those water-form components which exist within the mass of clouds. The word "tat" (that) refers to the mass of clouds. One should not raise the doubt: "If there is water in the mass of clouds, why is it not perceived? For they are like frost.
With the intention that it exists in a subtle form, he says: "By frost. He states the proof for the existence of water therein:
"characterized by rain. He summarizes the portion of the verse consisting of the example and its application with the word "likewise" (*tathā*).
[The senses] are subtle; smell, taste, and so forth are not perceived by the eye or the ear.

Likewise, consciousness delimited by that [intellect], which manifests as the substratum for the two bodies— the gross and the subtle— and which remains changeless like a peak (kūṭa), is the "immutable" (kūṭastha). Consciousness reflected therein in the imagined internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the individual soul (jīva), which is subject to transmigratory existence.

Unconditioned consciousness is Brahman; the consciousness reflected in the mental impressions (*dhīvāsanā*) of all living beings, which reside within the darkness of *māyā* supported by that [Brahman], is the Lord (*īśvara*).
Having thus postulated this fourfold nature of consciousness, [that which is] colored by the mental impressions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)...

The distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been shown through the difference in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of knowledge; this is another specific point stated therein.

Having taken together the five organs of cognition known as hearing and so forth; the five organs of action known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa and apāna;
and the two-fold internal organ consisting of mind (manas) and intellect (buddhi)—this constitutes the seventeenfold subtle body (liṅga-śarīra).

In the context of the illustration, the term "subtle body" (*sūkṣma-deha*) corresponds to the jar; the term "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) refers to consciousness delimited by the two bodies, which corresponds to the space within the jar. The reason for consciousness being delimited by the two bodies is its existence as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The meaning of the word *kūṭa* is a specific iron ball fixed to a particular piece of wood; that which remains immovable like that is *kūṭastha*. The intended meaning is that [the Self] is reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is superimposed upon that *kūṭastha* and is comparable to the water contained within a jar. [This reflection occurs] apart from the consciousness of the *kūṭastha*.

He states the purpose of the conceptualization of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) with the words "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*). The meaning is that immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) cannot be the locus of transmigration; for if it were the locus of transmigration characterized by birth, death, and so forth, its immutability would be contradicted. [This occurs] when [consciousness] is supported by Brahman, which stands in the place of the great ether (*mahākāśa*).

The meaning is that [the reflection] is reflected in those mental impressions (*adhīvāsanā*) situated within the darkness called *māyā*, which stands in the place of the circle of clouds. Those [impressions] belonging to the two states of waking and dreaming consist of the gross internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*); their subtle states belong to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

The impressions (*vāsanā*) are intended [here]. Regarding the phrase "the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*): the internal organ is colored by the impressions of cognition (*dhīvāsanā*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) is likewise; the meaning is that they are distinct due to their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Because the impressions of cognition are infinite, the phrase "colored by impressions" is used to dispel the suspicion that the Lord—whose nature is consciousness reflected in them—might be manifold.

The state of having cognition as an adjunct (*jñānopādhikatva*) has been stated. Having established the fact that in the previous systems only the difference between the original image (*bimba*) and the reflected image (*pratibimba*) is imagined, while their essential non-difference (*abheda*) remains, he states the distinction from those [systems] in this present system with the words "And this... In this system, first, the fourfold nature of consciousness (*cic-cāturvidhya*) was characterized.

One distinction has been stated; in relation to that, another distinct distinction consisting of the falsity of the reflection (*pratibimba-mithyātva*) has been mentioned—meaning it was stated there in the *Citradīpa*.

Among these four types of consciousness, that which manifests as "I am the living soul" (jīva) is superimposed upon the immutable (kūṭastha), with its specific aspects of knowledge, bliss, and association being concealed by ignorance. It is thus superimposed like silver on mother-of-pearl;
for this very reason, it is superimposed upon the general aspect of the substratum, just as the properties of "this-ness" and "silver-ness" are superimposed [upon the same substrate].

Regarding the two forms consisting of the specific parts: the simultaneous manifestation of "I" and "you" occurs in the expressions "I myself" and "I act. Indeed, "I" and "you" are superimposed forms of specific parts;
because there is an absence of linguistic usage [of one person's terms] by another person, they are mutually excluded. "I myself"—

And you [assert] that the common element (*sāmānyāṃśa*), which is the substratum for the counter-correlate of otherness, is itself Devadatta, because it persists even when the linguistic usage "Devadatta goes" is applied to another person.

He shows yet another distinction: "In the fourfold [categories]," etc. The connection is as follows: the individual soul (*jīva*), which manifests as "I," is superimposed [upon Brahman], just as silver is upon mother-of-pearl. Now, it is observed that the superimposition of silver and the like occurs upon mother-of-pearl and the like when they are known in their general form as "this" (*idantvena*), but not known in their specific forms such as "mother-of-pearl-ness."

But here, one might object: "In this case, no substratum is perceived that is known in its general form yet unknown in its specific form. Anticipating this, he says: "The immutable" (*kūṭastha*). [One might ask: "However, since the immutable is untouched by ignorance, how can its specific aspects—such as being unattached, blissful, and complete—be concealed?"
Just as the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*) is not perceived even when it is cognized— just as the "this-ness" (*idantva*) of the mother-of-pearl is [perceived]—
no manifestation of the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self is seen through any common form whatsoever. Furthermore,
in the cognition "this is silver," there is a simultaneous manifestation of both the general aspect of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the specific aspect of the superimposed object (*āropya*).

It is observed that in the present case, however, it is the specific aspect consisting of the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) itself that shines forth as "I," and not some general aspect; therefore, the hypothesis that the referent "I" is superimposed—like a silver [shell]—is not tenable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "For this very reason," [referring to] the superimposition of the referent "I" upon the immutable substrate (*kūṭastha*).
The meaning is "simply from conceptual construction" (*kalpanādeva*). Regarding the phrase "of *svayam* and *tvam*":

for the immutable (*kūṭastha*), *svayam* is its generic form, whereas *kūṭasthatvam* (the state of being immutable) is not, because that [state] is knowable solely through scripture (*śāstra*). Furthermore, both *svayam* and *tvam* manifest together with the immutable at the time of the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*).

Even prior to that [state of liberation], its own manifestation is not contradictory, because it is admitted to have the nature of an immutable (*kūṭastha*) essence consisting of eternal consciousness (*nityacaitanya*). Furthermore, since the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmibhāva*) is established through the conceptualization of a distinction— such as "the head of Rāhu" or "the consciousness of a person"— between the self and non-eternal consciousness, therefore [this is so].

The point is that because the immutable (kūṭastha) Self is always manifest by its very nature as a universal form, it is not contradictory for it to be the substratum for the superimposition of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) in the form of the "I-sense" (ahamartha).
He shows that the "I-sense" has a particular form, like a piece of silver, in the words: "I, you, indeed... (ahaṃ tvaṃ hi).
The meaning is "the referent of the word 'I'.

Regarding the phrase "having the form of the superimposed particular aspect": this means having the form of, or resembling, that particular aspect such as silver which is superimposed upon mother-of-pearl and the like. And "resemblance" here means the state of being excluded [from others].
"Because of being excluded" (*vyāvṛttatvāt*) means "because of the cognition of being excluded. Therefore, there is no identity between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*);

for while the reason for the cognition of being excluded is the absence of linguistic usage (*vyavahārābhāva*), its own nature, on the other hand, shows that it has the form of a universal (*sāmānyarūpatva*). This is what [the author] indicates by the words "but its own nature" (*svayaṃ tu*).

In common worldly usage, "self" (svayam) is well-known as being distinct from "other" (anya); to demonstrate that it is established as such a duality, the term "counter-correlative of other" (anyapratiyogī) is used as a qualifier for "self. As it has been said in the *Citradīpa*: "Devadatta goes himself; you, look! (devadattaḥ svayaṃ gacchetvaṃ vīkṣasva).
Likewise, [the word] *svayam* is used in the world in such ways as "I myself am not able."

Thus, it is precisely due to this mutual superimposition that worldly people fail to distinguish between the immutable (kūṭastha) and the individual soul (jīva); however, their distinction is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad with reference to the individual soul: "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them."

By demonstrating that [the self] perishes only upon the destruction of its illusory adjuncts (*māyopādhi*), and by demonstrating its indestructibility with the intention of establishing it as immutable (*kūṭastha*)— as in the statement, "Indeed, this Self is indestructible"— it is clear that if the *jīva*, whose essence is the "I-notion" (*ahamartha*), were destructible, how could there be non-difference from the indestructible Brahman?

[Objection: But surely, since the immutable Self (kūṭastha) and the individual soul (jīva)—which manifest as "I" and "myself"—are distinct from each other like mother-of-pearl and silver, why is their difference not perceived by everyone? To this, he says: "In this way. This means that while the individual soul, whose essence is the "I," is superposed upon the immutable Self like silver upon mother-of-pearl... [he says] "mutually," etc.

The meaning is that non-discrimination (*aviveka*) arises precisely from the superimposition of non-difference (*abhedādhyāsa*) between those two; that is to say, it is the absence of discrimination, which is the absence of the experience of difference.

Now, in the case of an error such as "this is silver," through the perception of the specific feature—"this is mother-of-pearl"—there occurs [the cognition of] the two categories of the general and the particular, namely *śuktitva* (mother-of-pearl-ness) and *rajatatva* (silver-ness).

The difference between two things is accepted based on the certainty that they possess mutually contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavatva*). But here, how is the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the immutable reality (*kūṭastha*) to be understood? For in the absence of such [contradictory properties], since the two manifest themselves through the relationship of the general and the particular—just as in the case of "real silver" where the "this-ness" (*idamartha*) and the "silver-ness" are in fact one—the two would result in being essentially identical.

Raising the objection that the jīva, whose nature is the referent of the word "I," cannot be established as being superimposed upon the kūṭastha—which is the very meaning of the word "Self"—the author demonstrates their distinction by means of scripture. The word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "But the discrimination...
(*vivekastu*) serves to set aside this doubt. "Discrimination" (*viveka*) is the experience of difference from these [entities] mentioned nearby, such as the body and so forth.

The meaning is: having arisen from those elemental adjuncts (upādhi-rūpa-bhūta) in an aggregated form—that is, having arisen in a state of equilibrium—and having attained birth through the emergence of the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties;
then, when those elemental adjuncts such as the intellect and so forth perish through the knowledge of reality (tattva-jñāna), [the self likewise ceases].

The scriptural statement, "They perish after it perishes," establishes the perishability of the conditioned self; and this is possible only if that individual soul (jīva), which consists of a reflection in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and is thus dependent on its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), is illusory (mithyā).
However, if the conditioned jīva were real (satya), a statement asserting its perishability would be untenable.

In the same way, this Self, which is a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), O Maitreyī, is indeed imperishable; it is truly imperishable and does not perish even through the destruction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, the scripture establishes the non-perishing nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthacaitanya*). This is what is meant: this Self is consciousness...
From the scriptural passage beginning with "Having arisen from these very elements," it follows that the Self, which is of the single essence of pure consciousness,
appears to arise following the arising of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and perishes following their destruction; thus,
apart from the arising and destruction of the limiting adjuncts, no arising or destruction of the conscious Self is taught.
Because of the use of the prefix *anu* in the phrase "it perishes along with" (*anuvinaśyati*), it is not possible for that [intellect] to possess destruction and so forth by its own nature;

for this would contradict the scriptural statement, "Verily, this Self is indestructible," which establishes the absence of destruction for the Self that is a mass of consciousness. [Therefore, the intellect cannot be identical to the conscious Self, which is devoid of arising and destruction.]

By assuming identity with the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is consciousness as a reflection, the statements regarding destruction and so forth are to be explained; consequently, just as in the case of the silver and the "this" object at the locus of an illusion, here too there is a distinction between perishability and imperishability.

Since the difference between the *jīva* and the immutable (*kūṭastha*) Self is clearly manifested by the very certainty that they possess mutually contradictory attributes, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), which is the nature of the *jīva*, upon the immutable Self is established. [The author] now raises an objection regarding the contradiction with other scriptural passages that might arise if one were to accept, on the basis of the cited scripture, that the *jīva* as a reflection is subject to destruction: "The 'I-sense'... and so forth.

The ellipsis to be supplied after "non-difference" (abheda) is that it is established by the statement "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi). The underlying sense is that non-difference is impossible between that which is to be destroyed and that which destroys.

This grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not occur in the sense of non-difference; rather, it occurs in the sense of sublation (*bādhā*). For example, in the statement "This post is a person," the cognition of being a post is set aside by the cognition of being a person. In the same way, in the realization "I am Brahman," the nature of being the immutable Brahman [sublates the limited self].

Through awakening, the superimposed nature of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) is sublated; for as stated in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "Just as the cognition of a post is sublated by the cognition 'this is a man,' so too the entire notion of 'I' is sublated by the cognition 'I am Brahman.'"

He sets aside [the objection], saying: "This is not so. Just as non-difference is seen to be the sentence-meaning of a co-referential statement such as "This is that," likewise, in a co-referential statement such as "That which is a post is a man," the sentence-meaning is seen to be of the nature of a sublation (*bādha*). For in the case of "That which is a post is a man," [it refers] to the man...

The non-difference between a perceived illusory post (*prātibhāsika-sthāṇu*) and a conventional person (*vyāvahārika-puruṣa*) is not the meaning of the sentence, because it is sublated (*bādhita*). Rather, the meaning of the sentence is the absence of the identity with the post—which exists in reality—in the person who serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition of the post; this constitutes the non-sublation (*abādha*). Likewise:

And from the sentence "This is a post, not a man," there arises the cognition that "this man actually lacks identity with a post"; by that cognition, the superimposition of a post upon the man—which previously had an object—is sublated.

In the same way, by the sentence "I am Brahman," [the superimposition] of identity with the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the referent of "I," [is sublated]. This [soul] is devoid of identity [with Brahman].

The knowledge "I am Brahman" arises; by that knowledge, the superimposition of being a knower, an agent, happy, miserable, and so forth—along with the ego-sense (*ahamartha*) characterized by attributes such as agency—is entirely sublated together with its own object. And when the superimposed ego-sense has ceased, for the individual soul (*jīva*)...

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with other scriptural passages (śruti) because this form, which is the immutable consciousness-essence (kūṭastha-caitanya), abides as the nature of the full Brahman (pūrṇa-brahma).
As for the literal meaning: "this" (idam) and "Brahman" (brahma) possess the same case-ending (sāmāna-vibhakti), forming a state of identity.

Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is accepted on the basis of a meaning consisting of non-difference (*abheda*), such that there would be no fault of the impossibility of non-difference. [The opponent] objects: "But if non-difference is not the sentence-meaning, then what is it? [The author] replies with the word "but" (*kiṃtu*). He states that it is not intended as the sentence-meaning because of sublation (*bādha*). [He says this] regarding the word "personhood" (*puruṣatva*) in the context of sublation.

What is intended is the absence of identity with the imagined post (*sthāṇu*), because it is accepted that [the absence of identity] constitutes the meaning of the sentence in the context of sublation (*bādhā*). In the phrase "I am Brahman," the words "by that which is produced by the sentence" are to be supplied after the word "here. This is because the knowledge of the sentence-meaning here does not have the form "I am Brahman."

By the phrase "the nature of the immutable Brahman" as well, what is intended is the state of being the immutable Brahman while actually lacking identity with the referent of "I," precisely for the purpose of sublation.

And if this grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in non-difference were according to the reasoning set forth in the Vivaraṇa and other works, then let the word "I" (ahaṃ), which denotes the individual soul (jīva), refer by secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) to the immutable (kūṭastha), since that [immutable self] is capable of non-difference with Brahman, which is unsublatable.

This is because it is accepted as being the object of the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence. It should be understood that this was stated by us by relying on the view that, between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) possesses the absence of the superimposed object, and that the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the superimposed is distinct from the substratum.
"The superimposed nature of the sense of 'I'":
this states the fruit of realization—that the identity with that superimposed sense of "I" is removed.
That the Great Sentence (mahāvākya) has the purpose of sublation (*bādhārthakatva*) is not a fabrication of my own imagination; rather—
He states that this was said by Sureśvarācārya: "This which... In dim darkness, a post (*sthāṇu*) is apprehended.

By means of the cognition of a person (*puṃdhiyā*) produced from the words of a trustworthy person—namely, the cognition that "this is indeed a person," and not "this is a post"—but rather "in reality this is not a post, but a person"—just as the cognition "this is a post" [is sublated] along with the identity with the superimposed post...
It is thus revoked. By the cognition (*buddhi*) produced by the sentence "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*),

which takes the form "I am indeed Brahman alone, devoid of identity with the *jīva* who is the referent of 'I'," the entire complex of cognitions such as "I am the agent," "I am the enjoyer," and so forth— accompanied by the superimposed referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*)— is revoked by the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākyārtha*).
The word "hi" (for/indeed) is used for the purpose of illuminating that the cessation of all misfortunes for the knower through knowledge is established by experience.

Now, in sentences of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), since the sentence-meaning consisting of identity is primary, the sentence-meaning consisting of sublation is the general rule; therefore, in the present case [of the Vivaraṇa and other texts], it is of the nature of identity.

Furthermore, because it is precisely the meaning of the sentence that is accepted [as the primary import]. This is because even the venerable Bhagavatpāda, in his *Vākyavṛtti*, accepts that in the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) it is indeed non-difference—designated as the identity (*tādātmya*) between the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*—that constitutes the meaning of the sentence, as stated in the verse: "In this context, the meaning of the sentence is the identity of those two very word-meanings."

Since it can be argued that even the sublation (*bādhā*) of the Vārttikakāra’s statement constitutes the meaning of the sentence in this context— and since the engagement [with the text] is justified by resorting to such boldness (*prauḍhi*)— it is established that in the statement "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*), non-difference (*abheda*) is the sentence-meaning; thus, the non-perishing Brahman's non-difference with the perishing individual soul (*jīva*) is logically possible.
Since that objection remains exactly as it was, he says "yadi ca" (if, however) out of a sense of dissatisfaction [with the previous position].
That which is called Īśvara— the reflection of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) in the intellect (*dhī*), comparable to a cloud in the sky—

is established in the *Māṇḍūkya Śruti* as being in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*), unified, a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and indeed the enjoyer of bliss (*ānandabhuj*). It is that very same one who consists of the bliss of deep sleep.

Immediately following that, [the text states]: "He is the Lord of all, He is the omniscient, He is the inner controller (antaryāmī), He is the source of all, the immutable (kūṭastha)... Thus, among the four—the immutable, Brahman, the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara)—which are summarized in the verse beginning with "Consciousness is fourfold" (ciccaturvidhā), the consciousness of Brahman (brahmacaitanya) is first [discussed].
Since [the nature of Brahman] is well-known from statements such as "Truth, Knowledge," a scriptural passage was not cited there as the authority;

rather, the passage "indeed, it is imperishable" is shown as the authority for the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*). Furthermore, the statement regarding arising and destruction that conforms to the arising and destruction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) refers to what is situated in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The proof for the individual soul (*jīva*), which is of the nature of a reflection of consciousness, has been stated. By means of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), the proof for the previously mentioned Lord (*īśvara*) must now be stated; he states that with the words "But he who... (*yastu*). The word "that" (*saḥ*) is used for emphasis; the meaning is that this very Lord who was mentioned is none other than the one described in the Śruti as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). He whose state is deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is [the *suṣuptisthāna*].

In the waking state, which is the locus of deep sleep, there exist forms such as being "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), and "agency," due to the superimposition of identity upon the internal organ (antahkarana) designated as "consciousness.
Likewise, due to the superimposition of non-difference such as "I am fat" regarding the body, there exist [attributes] such as fatness, leanness, and Brahminhood.

Forms exist. Likewise, through the superimposition (adhyāsa) of forms such as "I am blind" or "I am mute" upon the eyes and other organs, forms such as blindness and muteness exist. Similarly, for the individual soul (jīva), there exist infinite forms—such as "consisting of space," "consisting of air," and "consisting of water"—which are established by superimposition upon objects like space and are subsumed under scriptural texts (śruti).

However, in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because the adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*) have dissolved, all forms established by delusion (*bhrānti*) dissolve as well due to the dissolution of every kind of delusion; with this in mind, it is said that [the Self] has "become one. As it has been stated:
"He who was previously joined with the principal forms consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), now, through that dissolution, has attained oneness."

"Like a mass of rice flour": "before sleep," meaning at a time prior to falling asleep; "by dissolution," meaning by the dissolution of forms. Consciousness (*prajñāna*), which is sentience, exists in the waking state and others as having a differentiated form due to the distinctions among mental modifications (*vṛtti*);
however, having attained a state of relaxation, it returns to oneness in deep sleep due to the dissolution of those modifications.

Intending to convey that [Brahman] has been attained, the state of being a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*) is mentioned. Here, "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers to the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), which exists as the original image (*bimba*). The individual soul (*jīva*), who is the reflection (*pratibimba*) of that, is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*);
and because he experiences the bliss that constitutes his own essential nature during the state of deep sleep through the removal of veils, he is called "the enjoyer of bliss" (*ānandabhuk*).

This is the meaning of the scripture. Now, an objection may be raised: the *jīva* consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is the reflection of the gross internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) during the states of waking and dreaming, because the gross internal organ is denoted by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
That very same *jīva* consisting of consciousness, at the time of deep sleep, exists in a subtle form within the dissolved state of the internal organ.

For, according to the Vedic scripture, "He is indeed the origin and the dissolution of beings," that [Self], which is conditioned by the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of the cognitions of all living beings and has all things as its object, possesses omniscience; and from that very fact, its status as the creator of all is also established. Furthermore, no one who is conditioned merely by the mental impressions of our own intellects can possess omniscience.
It cannot be said that [the object] is not experienced, because since the latent impressions (vāsanās) are imperceptible, that which is conditioned by them is likewise imperceptible.

Thinking that because [the self] is conditioned by the instruments of action (karaṇa) it is called "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya), and thus its being the Lord (Īśvara) is unestablished since the one consisting of bliss is the individual soul (jīva), he states that the remainder of the passage shows that the one consisting of bliss in deep sleep is indeed the Lord. "In that very [passage]" means in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti itself.

"Sovereignty over all" means being the agent of the origin of the entire world; "womb" means the material cause. He states the reason why that which consists of bliss is the material cause of everything: "from whence," etc.
For it is from the blissful Self (ānandamaya) that the origin and dissolution—the birth and absorption—of all beings proceed.

Therefore, the meaning is that You are the source of all. He also provides a logical argument for the omniscience of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) as stated in the Śruti: "All things... Each individual cognition takes on a particular object;
thus, when all [cognitions] are combined, the entire universe is made their object. And so, of all cognitions—

Once it is established that [the Self] has all things as its object, it follows that the latent impressions (vāsanās) of all cognitions—which consist of the subtle states of all cognitions—also have all things as their objects. And thus, the omniscience of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), which is conditioned by the latent impressions of the cognitions of all living beings, is established; this is the meaning.

Now, as for what was stated—that the Lord (Īśvara) has ignorance conditioned by mental impressions (*vāsanā*) as His adjunct—is it that ignorance itself is the adjunct of the Lord who is the reflection? Or is it ignorance colored by mental impressions? Or is it all mental impressions collectively? Or is it each individual impression? Not the first; [for] if He were reflected in the mental impressions...

This is because it would contradict the statement that "consciousness is the Lord" (*caitanyaṃ īśvaraḥ*). Furthermore, if ignorance alone were the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord, the pursuit of the impressions of knowledge (*dhīvāsanā*) would be rendered futile. Nor can it be argued that the Lord, having ignorance as His adjunct, attains omniscience [thereby].

It should not be said that "the pursuit of the latent impressions (vāsanās) of all objects" [is required], because omniscience can be established by means of mental modifications (vṛttis) directed toward all objects— which are themselves transformations of the *sattva* aspect residing in ignorance— and thus there is no need for the latent impressions of the intellect (*dhīvāsanās*) for that purpose; for this reason, the second [alternative] is also rejected.

Because it is possible for ignorance alone to serve as that limiting adjunct (upādhi), and because, since deep sleep cannot occur simultaneously for all living beings, it is impossible for the latent impressions (vāsanās) of all their cognitions to exist simultaneously; therefore, it is not possible for those [impressions] to serve as the limiting adjunct of the Lord by way of being qualifiers of ignorance. This is because of them...

Precisely because simultaneity is impossible, even the third alternative is not tenable; for, since [the mind] is occupied with all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cognition, a single reflection in the form of the Lord (*īśvara*) is impossible, as no such distributed reflection is observed in the world. Therefore, the fourth alternative remains, in which there is experience.

He anticipates an objection: "And not ours... This means that for us living beings, there is no experience at the time of sleep of any [self] consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—which is conditioned by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of individual cognitions—in the form "I am omniscient. [The phrase] "of the impressions" refers to those [impressions] present in the waking state and so forth.

The meaning is that, just as the gross internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are not fit for perception by the witness-consciousness during deep sleep, so too the internal organs consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) are not fit for such perception;
consequently, the states consisting of bliss (ānandamaya), which have those as their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), are likewise not fit for the experience of "I" (aham).

Regarding the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), it is stated that the "blissful one" (*ānandamaya*) mentioned in the *Māṇḍūkya* is the individual soul (*jīva*) due to its association with deep sleep (*suṣupti*). For instance, when the karma that bestows experience during the waking state and other stages is exhausted, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) dissolves in the form of sleep; then, by the power of karma that again bestows experience, it awakens.

When [the intellect] becomes condensed (*ghanībhavati*), the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by that [intellect] is called "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*). That same [soul], when its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is in a state of dissolution at the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), is called "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
This is always shown in the *Māṇḍūkya* [Upaniṣad] by such passages as, "In the state of deep sleep, he has become one," and so forth.

This being the case, how can statements regarding his being the Lord of all and so forth be reconciled? In this way, there are three specific forms of the Supreme Self: the Adhidaivata (the divine), the Adhyātma (the internal), and [the third]. Among these, the Adhidaivata consists of four forms, including pure consciousness as the third.
These have been established by means of the analogy of the painted cloth in the *Citradīpa*.

Since the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) described in the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*—which is conditioned by all the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the intellect (*dhī*)—cannot exist as a single entity according to the reasoning already stated, it must be asserted that the *ānandamaya* conditioned by the latent impressions of the intellect is indeed individual; and that [individual] is precisely the *jīva*. Thus he says: "But in the *Brahmānanda*," referring to the Lord as described by the venerable teacher Vidyāraṇya in the *Citradīpa*.
By those very [authorities], the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) has been asserted for the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) in the work titled *Brahmānanda*.

However, the word used there is intended to convey a specific meaning regarding its nature as a *jīva*. Furthermore, the phrase "due to connection with deep sleep" (*suṣupti-saṃyogāt*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for its state as the Lord (*īśvara*) when conditioned by latent impressions (*vāsanopādhika*).

It should also be observed that [the Lord] would follow as a non-entity at the beginning of the waking state and so forth; furthermore, because there would be a plurality of Lords due to the multiplicity of those conditioned by individual latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and because it is impossible for anyone to possess all latent impressions simultaneously. In this regard, he demonstrates the aforementioned method with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
The meaning is: "when that karma which bestows experience (*bhoga*) during the waking state and so forth has been exhausted. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the dreaming state;

the plural number, however, is used with reference to the various individual instances of waking and dreaming. "In the form of sleep" means "in the form of deep sleep" (*suṣupti*). This has been stated in the *Pañcīkaraṇa* regarding the intellect (*buddhi*).

"Susupti" (deep sleep) is the state of abiding in the form of the cause. [The author] raises an objection regarding the contradiction with the subsequent portion of the text which establishes the Lord-hood of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) if that were the individual soul (*jīva*): "If this were so. This means that although the one consisting of bliss, who is the individual soul in the state of deep sleep, lacks Lord-hood in reality, there is nonetheless non-difference from the Lord.
He provides a rebuttal, stating that the statement regarding his lordship is consistent with the intended meaning (*vivakṣā*), beginning with the words "In this way" (*ittham*).

He establishes the introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) in order to demonstrate the intention to show the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti,
beginning with the word "Exist" (*santi*).
The connection is that there are three qualified forms of the Supreme Self as *adhidaivata* (the divine), and likewise there are qualified forms of the Supreme Self as *adhyātma* (the internal).
The term "of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmanaḥ*) means "of the undifferentiated consciousness" (*nirviśeṣa-caitanya*). As for the term "*adhidaivatam*":
The meaning is that they have the deities as their essence (*devatātmaka*). And the meaning of the term *adhyātma* is that they have the individual soul (*jīvātman*) as their essence.

The two terms *adhidaivata* and *adhyātma* are indeclinables (*avyaya*). He elaborates on what has been stated with the word "therein" (*tatra*). The meaning is: among those forms consisting of the individual soul and the deities. For the individual soul, there are three forms characterized by distinctions.

The form of the Fourth State (*turyapāda*), which is devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣarūpa*), has been explicitly shown by the *Māṇḍūkya Śruti*. However, although the Lord’s forms—both those devoid of distinctions and those possessing distinctions—are intended by that scripture, they have not been stated explicitly by the *Śruti* itself; rather, these have been [elucidated] by Śrī Vidyāraṇya, who is well-versed in the purport of the scriptures.
By the teachers, in the *Citradīpa*, with illustrative examples.

Just as a cloth that is naturally white undergoes four stages— being washed, smeared with ink and the like, marked, and finally colored by the application of pigments— all belonging to a single painted cloth; so too is the Supreme Self, which is pure when devoid of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of Māyā and its effects.
The Lord conditioned by Māyā is Hiraṇyagarbha, conditioned by the subtle body which is the aggregate of the effects of the unquintuplicated elements;
the Virāṭ Puruṣa is conditioned by the gross body which is the aggregate of the effects of the quintuplicated elements.
Thus, these four states belong to the one and only Supreme Self.

He says that they have been described [in the verse beginning] "variegated cloth" (*citrapaṭa*). In this regard, there is this summary verse: "It may be naturally white, or washed here; it may be fashioned by being smeared with clay;
it may be marked with forms of ink, or colored by the filling in of pigments. He explains the illustration summarized in this verse.

Regarding the word "yathā" (as): the verse beginning with "svataścid antaryāmī tu... ("The Self-luminous One is the Inner Ruler by His own nature... presents the illustrative example (*dārṣṭāntika*) summarized therein. Regarding the word "tathā" (so too): the connection in the verse is "the Supreme [Self] is the Self-luminous One by His own nature. He explains this specific portion as follows:

Regarding the term "Supreme Self" (paramātman): in the verse, the word "tu" (but/indeed) serves for emphasis. Thus, the connection is that the Supreme One alone, being the possessor of *māyā*, is called the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*). He states this aspect as: "The Lord (*īśvara*) conditioned by *māyā*.
In the verse, the connection is that the Supreme One alone, through subtle creation, is the Thread-Self (*sūtrātman*). He states this aspect...

He explains this with the words "this [is] composed of the five-fold elements" (*pañcīkṛta*). The meaning is that he is conditioned by the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), which is the pervasive effect of the unevolved (*apañcīkṛta*) elements. Nor [does this apply] to the Sūtra-self, who is designated by the term Hiraṇyagarbha.
It may be asked: "Since the status of being a *jīva* (individual soul) is well-established for him in both Śruti and Smṛti, how can he have the nature of the Lord (*Īśvara*)? To this it must be said:

because we accept that Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the *jīva*, the lord of Satyaloka, and characterized by the conceit of the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-sūkṣma-śarīra*), is distinct from the Lord; whereas the Lord is [distinct] from the collective...
Even in the absence of identification with the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), because [the individual] is governed by the collective subtle body (*samaṣṭi-sūkṣmaśarīra*),

it is intended here that he be designated by the terms *Hiraṇyagarbha* and *Sūtrātman* through the quality of being conditioned by that collective subtle body as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). And thus:

The intention is that Hiraṇyagarbha’s status as the Lord (Īśvara) is merely figurative. For this very reason, it should be understood that in the *Citradīpa*, when enumerating the various deities accepted by other schools as the Lord, Brahmā—the ruler of Satyaloka—is mentioned separately from Hiraṇyagarbha who is the form of the Lord. In the verse, he alone is the Supreme.

The connection is that Virāṭ is said to be the gross creation. Explaining this point, he summarizes it with the words "pañcīkṛta" (composed of the five elements). This Virāṭ Puruṣa, who is the form of Īśvara, is to be understood as established by the Śrutis, such as the Puruṣasūkta and the Vaiśvānara-vidyā passages.

It should also be understood that the *vivāṭapuruṣa*— the individual soul (*jīva*) who identifies with the gross aggregate (*samaṣṭisthūla*), appearing in the form of a son of Hiraṇyagarbha, the lord of Satyaloka— is indeed distinct [from the Supreme Self], as established by the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*.
"Thus it is concluded" means that, according to the manner described, one should perceive that which is in reality a single entity as possessing four forms.

And within this Supreme Self, which stands in the place of a canvas, there exists the entire phenomenal world consisting of the stationary and the moving, which stands in the place of a painting. Just as the clothing-like appearances of men depicted in a painting are painted so as to resemble the garments of the actual people who served as the models for the canvas; so too is this world.

Likewise, for embodied beings upon whom the Supreme Self is superimposed, reflections of consciousness (cidābhāsas) similar to pure consciousness are postulated; these, known by the name "jīva," undergo transmigration.
With respect to the inner self (adhyātma), however, there are three forms distinguished as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. Among these, in deep sleep (suṣupti)...

The *prājña* is the witness of pure consciousness within the expanded internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This very one who is described here as consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the *taijasa* during dream, identifying with the individual subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), and the *viśva* during waking, identifying with the individual gross body (*sthūlaśarīra*).
Having thus shown the fourfold form relevant to the present subject, he speaks incidentally [in the verse beginning] with "In this.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the entire world were to have the status of being supported by that [Brahman], then everything would likewise be insentient; consequently, the distinction between the sentient and the insentient would not exist. He dispels this doubt by means of an illustration, [beginning with] "Just as..."

"Resemblances of clothing" means that although garments consisting of specific colors may share a similarity of form with the cloth upon which a painting is based, they are called "resemblances" because they lack the capacity to ward off cold, wind, and so forth. "Of embodied beings" means those possessing a gross body; it refers to the *ahaṃkāras* (ego-senses) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

He states the purpose of the conceptualization of the reflection of consciousness: "And those... Thus, the sense is that the distinction is established—namely, that the aggregates of causes and effects (the bodies) are conscious when joined with the illumination of knowledge (*vidābhāsa*), whereas others, such as mountains and oceans, are unconscious. In this way, the forms of the Lord have been shown, as well as those of the individual soul (*jīva*).
He shows the forms with attributes and without attributes as declared in the Śruti: "But with reference to the self" (*adhyātmaṃ tu*).

The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate the distinction between the forms with attributes of the individual soul (*jīva*) and those of the Lord (*īśvara*). He demonstrates that very distinction [with the words] "the universe" (*viśva*) and "forms" (*rūpāṇi*).
The word "saviśeṣāṇi" (with distinctions) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding the word "tatra":

the meaning is "in the midst of the three forms. Regarding the word "vilīne" (dissolved): the sense is that when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has dissolved, [the self] becomes characterized by the internal organ which has dissolved in a subtle form; [this refers to] the gross internal organ and so forth.

The inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding [any other] witness-ship. Now, an objection is raised: previously it was stated that the soul in deep sleep is the *ānandamaya*, so how can it now be said that he is the same as the *prājña*? To this, he replies: "This very one... Here, the word "here" (*iha*) means in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti.

The meaning is that this is because we see the completion of the sentence immediately after "therein he is the enjoyer of bliss" with the words, "the conscious one (prājña) is the third foot, having consciousness as its mouth. Here,
"consciousnesses" refers to the states of ignorance which take the form of veils and serve as the "mouths"— that is, the means— through which the experience of bliss during the time of sleep occurs.

He whose means of realization are such is "ceto-mukha" (one whose face is consciousness). Now, one might ask: how is it possible for the soul in deep sleep (*sauṣupta-jīva*) to both experience bliss and possess the state of being "ceto-mukha," even though this is taught in the scriptures?
In that regard, the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti* [speaks] of the Self manifesting in the experience of "I" (*aham-anubhava*).
Having begun with the statement "This Self has four quarters," [the text] describes the four quarters consisting of the distinctions of the states of Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña,
and Turīya, in order to facilitate the realization of the fourth quarter— the non-dual Brahman-Atman— by means of the progressive negation of each preceding quarter.

Because of the similarity of their gross, subtle, and subtler limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the author] included Virāj and the others within Viśva and the rest; thus, by stating "the waking state is the locus of Viśva," "the external [state] is Prājña," and so forth, he defined the feet as Viśva and the others. Therefore...

Intending to express the inclusion of the unmanifested Īśvara within the "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) which is designated as "the wise one" (prājña), the statement of its attributes such as being the Lord of all is made therein.
