It is said in response: For one who has arisen from deep sleep, there is observed the recollection of pleasure characterized by the time of sleep, in the form "I slept happily. And that [recollection] is not possible without an experience of pleasure at that time, because it is impossible to remember a pleasure that was not experienced. Nor...

It must be stated that in deep sleep, the experience of the bliss that is the nature of the Self occurs precisely through modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*); for at that time, the internal organ, having dissolved, lacks the capacity to produce such a modification. Nor can it be argued that, as in the case of liberation, the experience occurs through the consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpa-caitanya*) alone during the time of sleep.

It should not be asked why one should postulate a mind in the form of a reflection within the activity of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*), given that the experience of pleasure arises [directly]. For since the experience of bliss is observed through activities endowed with the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*) during both waking and dreaming states, it is impossible to abandon this [explanation] even in the case of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), as it is possible there as well. This remains so at the time of liberation (*muktikāla*).

Because it is accepted that only the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) dissolve, there is a disparity [between the states] due to the impossibility of a mental modification (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, if the experience of bliss in deep sleep were merely the nature of the eternal witness (*sākṣin*), it would follow that no impression (*saṃskāra*)— which consists in the destruction of the experience— could exist, and consequently,
the subsequent recollection "I slept happily" would be impossible.

Therefore, the scripture (*śruti*) which conveys the aforementioned meaning is indeed appropriate; "vyavasthiti" means "delimitation. He states that these quarters are directly declared by the scripture with the word "therein" (*tatra*). This means: provided that the conceptualization of the quarters is established in the manner described. The scripture, having introduced the four quarters...

The connection is that [the author] described the Viśva and the other quarters (pādas). They are called "quarters" (pāda) because by means of them Brahman—the identity with the Self—is reached, understood, and comprehended; Viśva and the others are so named. With this etymological derivation in mind, he states the purpose of the conceptualization of the quarters according to the Śruti: "Each preceding... The meaning is as follows.
By the statement, "This Self has four quarters," the fact that the individual soul (jīva) possesses four quarters is introduced;

then it is stated, "Vaiśvānara, whose sphere is the waking state, is the first quarter. Since the intention here was to speak specifically of the quarters of the individual soul, one would have expected it to be said that Viśva is the first quarter, rather than using the term Vaiśvānara.
In the form of the Virāṭ Puruṣa.
The statement that the Lord (Īśvara) has four feet indicates the inclusion of Viśva and Vaiśvānara within the Lord.
Nor should it be asked what restrictive principle, intended by the Śruti, dictates that Vaiśvānara alone—and not Hiraṇyagarbha and Īśvara—should contain Viśva; for [the reason lies] in those two...

Since the similarity consisting in having a gross adjunct (*sthūlopādhikatva*), which distinguishes [the Vaiśvānara] from Īśvara and Hiraṇyagarbha, is intended as the regulating factor, it is stated in the sentence expounding the second quarter that "the Taijasa,
whose station is the dream state, is the second quarter"; here, [the distinction is] having a subtle adjunct (*sūkṣmopādhikatva*).

By way of similarity, the inclusion of Hiraṇyagarbha within the Taijasa state is intended, in accordance with the introductory statement, "Vaiśvānara is the first foot. Likewise, the passage establishing the third foot—beginning with "becoming one in the place of deep sleep"—has already been cited above. Here too, [the same applies].

By stating that the one denoted by the word *prājña*— the self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)— is the third foot, the intention is to include Īśvara within it on the basis of the commonality of possessing an extremely subtle limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Thus, since the remainder of the passage,
beginning with "He is the Lord of all," intends to express the non-difference between the self consisting of bliss and Īśvara.
Because it has already been established, there is no inconsistency. Thus, this sentence sets forth the fourth quarter:
"Invisible, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without marks, unthinkable, indefinable, the essence of the oneness of the Self, the cessation of phenomenal expansion, auspicious, non-dual."
They consider it the fourth.

"Invisible" means not being an object of the eyes and other [senses]. "Beyond conventional usage" means not being within the scope of worldly activity characterized by engagement and withdrawal. "Ungraspable" means not being within the scope of the organs of action.

It is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), empty (*śūnya*), inconceivable (*acintya*), beyond the scope of dry logic (*śuṣkatarkāgocara*), inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*), and beyond the scope of the power of words (*śabdaśaktyagocara*). It has as its essence the realization of the single self (*ekātmapratyayasāra*). This is an internal *karmadhāraya* compound consisting of the four terms beginning with "one" (*eka*).

Oneness is the state of being devoid of division; fullness is the nature of the Self in all bodies; and consciousness is the nature of the witness. "The essence is bliss" means that bliss is the core. This is according to the commentary on the *Ānandamaya-Adhikaraṇa*, [which describes] the cessation of the phenomenal world (*prapañcopaśama*).

It is of the nature of the absence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), because the absence of imagined objects does not exceed the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); or rather, it is of the nature of the destruction of phenomenal proliferation, because it will be stated that the cessation of duality—along with its causes, which is to be accomplished through knowledge—is identical with the substrate. It is *śiva*, meaning pure.

The meaning of the Śruti is that they meditate upon the fourth state— which is free from all defects, non-dual, and devoid of duality— as the foot that completes the number four in relation to the three feet consisting of the forms of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña. Here, among these feet characterized as Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña—
Furthermore, there is the inclusion of Vaiśvānara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Īśvara within these [states], as well as the contemplation of their unity;
likewise, there is the unity of the quarters beginning with Viśva and the morae (mātrās) that constitute the components of the syllable Om.

What is intended here is reflection (*cintana*). Thus says the Śruti: "The quarters are the *mātrās*, and the *mātrās* are the quarters. Likewise, there is also the statement of Gauḍapāda: "One should know the syllable Om by its quarters; the quarters are the *mātrās*, without a doubt. The intention of the word "without a doubt" (*na saṃśayaḥ*) is as follows:

The unity of the quarters beginning with Viśva and the measures (mātrās) must be contemplated until all doubt is removed; thus, the nature of the measures has been shown by the Śruti itself as "the letter A, the letter U, and the letter M. In this way, [the unity] of the quarters beginning with Viśva, such as Vaiśvānara and the others, [is to be understood].

The contemplation of the unity of the *mātrās* (the constituent elements) of all these [states] is for the purpose of dissolving them into the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) of the fourth quarter (*turyapāda*), which is the non-dual (*niṣprapañca*) Brahman-ātman. And therein, this is the sequence:
first, one should contemplate the unity of the forms of Viśva and Vaiśvānara, and subsequently [those of] Taijasa.

One should contemplate the unity of the causal principle, Hiraṇyagarbha. Thereafter, one should contemplate the unity of the principles Īśvara and Prājña, which correspond to the letter *a*. In that same sequence of contemplation, one should dissolve them: the triad beginning with *a* into *u*, and the triad beginning with *u* [into *m*].

One should dissolve the triad beginning with *ma* into the *makāra*, and that [in turn] into the fourth quarter, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Having dissolved the intellect (*citi*) into pure consciousness, one should cause it to abide in that very state. As for the dissolution into the *ukāra* and so forth, it means that the triad beginning with the form (*ākāra*) does not exist apart from the *ukāra*.

For one who, having thus resolved, practices *samādhi* every day in the manner described, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman occurs. Then, through the attainment of Brahman, one’s duty is fulfilled;
such is the intended meaning of the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*. All this [is derived] from the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti*.

In the *Vārttika*, which is a commentary on the *Bhāṣya* composed by Sureśvarācārya for the purpose of concisely stating its essential meaning (*tātparya*), after the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) has been performed, it is stated:
"The letter *a* alone is Viśva; the letter *u* is remembered as Taijasa; the letter *m* is Prājña—one should perceive them as one."

As for the sequence: it should be understood that here, regarding Viśva and the others, the inclusion of Vaiśvānara and the rest was not made separately because their internal presence within them is already established. Having reflected in this manner with great effort even before the time of meditative absorption (samādhi), one should contemplate everything—from the gross to the subtle—within the conscious Self (cidātman).

One should dissolve [the gross]. One should dissolve the letter *a*, which is the universal Puruṣa, into the letter *u*. Here, the Puruṣa is indeed Vaiśvānara. One should dissolve the subtle Taijasa, the letter *u*, into the letter *m*.
Here, the Supreme Lord is that which is conditioned by [the letter *m*], acting as the controller of the collective subtle body.

This is the subtle meaning of the word *kāraṇa*. One should dissolve the causal state (*kāraṇa*), which is the *prājña* (the deep-sleep state), into the conscious self (*cidātman*). Here, the meaning of the word *kāraṇa* refers to the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is *māyā* alone.
"I am the conscious self, eternally pure, awakened, liberated, real, non-dual, and an abundance of supreme bliss."

"I am Vāsudeva, Om. Since I remain as the pure conscious self (cidātman), therefore, in the sense that I am Vāsudeva whose nature is eternally pure, awakened, and so forth, the syllable "Om" signifies the nature of acceptance. The word "iti" connects with the subsequent verse.

"Having known the discriminating mind, one should dissolve it into its witness. According to the method stated thus, having known that only the pure conscious self remains, one should dissolve—that is, cause to settle—the discriminating and dissolving mind into the Witness, Vāsudeva, as previously described; and [the mind] dissolved into the conscious self—

One should not move that mind at all; seated as one who is full by nature of awakening, like a full, immovable ocean, one should maintain samādhi for a long time—this is the meaning of the Vārttika. Thus, the yogi, being composed, endowed with faith and devotion, having conquered the senses and subdued anger, [should remain].

One should perceive the Self as non-dual, since all this—from beginning, middle, to end—is suffering; therefore, having renounced everything, one should always be established in reality. Whatever is established in the world and in the scriptures as a means for achieving the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), all that is nothing other than being established in the Self.

Since it is inseparable from suffering throughout the three periods of time, one should therefore renounce everything according to the prescribed rule and, in the manner described, practice steadfastness in reality characterized by *samādhi*. He says this very thing:
"The yogi should always, with effort, [practice] this knowledge during the *sandhyās*."
One should practice detachment from enjoyments in this world and the next.

"One of refined intellect is a wise person" (*sudhīḥ*). The meaning is that one who is most firm in faith, having become dispassionate, should undertake this knowledge characterized by meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at the junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*) and practice it constantly.
He who perceives the all-pervading, peaceful, infinite Self as non-dual—
For him, nothing remains to be attained or known.
The wise one shall have accomplished all that was to be done and shall be eternally liberated while living;
he has transcended the darkness of ignorance and is devoid of all appearances.
Blissful, stainless, and pure, it is beyond the reach of mind and speech; it is free from the relationship of signified and signifier, and devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted.
"One has heard of the Vaiṣṇava state, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss. Thus [it is said].

The term *ābhāsa* refers to the reflection of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*). The words "the universe" (*viśva*) and so forth are the denoted (*vācya*), while the forms (*ākāra*) and so forth are the denoters (*vācaka*), as they are the subject under discussion.

The meaning is that what is to be abandoned is suffering, and what is to be accepted is the pleasure derived from sense objects. Likewise, in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti, there is a focus on meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
With this intention, it is also stated in the Gauḍapādīya:
"One should unite the mind with the *praṇava*; the *praṇava* is Brahman, free from fear.
For one who is constantly united with the *praṇava*, no fear exists anywhere. This is the summary.

Now, one might object: since the realization of reality is possible through the path of Sāṃkhya alone, consisting of hearing and so forth, what is the use of the method of Yoga for one who desires liberation? To this, he says: "Because of the ease of realization. This refers to that mendicant seeker of liberation who, due to dullness of intellect, lacks skill even when [the means] are present.

Because the path of Sāṃkhya is not possible due to the absence of teachers and others skilled in the exposition of logic (nyāya), the prescription of meditative absorption (samādhi) in the Māṇḍūkya and other texts serves as a means for realizing the reality of Brahman without effort, through the process of intentional dissolution.
The meditation on Brahman prescribed in the Māṇḍūkya, Tāpanīya, Pañcīkaraṇa, and other texts has been explained in the *Dhyānadīpa*.
This very point has been explained by the venerable Śaṅkarācārya in his commentary on Gauḍapāda’s *Kārikās* in the *Dṛg-dṛśya-viveka*.

However, the distinction is that in the *Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda*, the threefold process (*cittraividhya-prakriyā*)—in which the immutable Self (*kūṭastha*) exists within the range of the individual soul (*jīva*)—is adopted as the basis, as elucidated in the *Citrādvaitadīpa*. For it is stated therein: "Like waves in a reservoir of water..."
Due to the conception of [the self] as being situated one above the other according to the analogy of bubbles, the individual soul (jīva) is threefold:

the ultimate (pāramārthika), the empirical (vyāvahārika), and the apparent (prātibhāsika). Among these, the ultimate individual soul is that which is conditioned by the [individualizing] limitation (avacchinna).

The venerable Guru Vidyāraṇya has shown who is qualified [for inquiry]: "He who, due to extreme dullness of intellect or the impossibility of obtaining the requisite materials, does not obtain the jewel of inquiry, should constantly meditate upon Brahman. Regarding the term "of the unmanifest" (avyākṛtasya):

Alternatively, since the unmanifest world is designated as the "undifferentiated" (*avyākṛta*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and because the Supreme Lord is referred to by that term in various places, He is designated by it here; furthermore, the statement in the *Māṇḍūkya Śruti* that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is the Lord is intended to express non-difference from Him— this is the explanation of the *Māṇḍūkya Śruti*.
He states that this was said by the authors of the commentary themselves in their commentary (*bhāṣya*) on Gauḍapāda’s *Māṇḍūkya-kārikās*, which takes the form of an exposition (*vivaraṇa*).

"In this very way" refers to what was stated by the venerable Vidyāraṇya-guru in his *Cid-dīpa*, excluding the fourfold division of consciousness (*cic-cāturvidhya*) [that he himself had previously mentioned].

In another treatise (*granthāntara*), relying precisely on the threefold nature established by the statement of the elders—that "the individual soul (*jīva*), the Lord (*īśa*), and pure consciousness (*viśuddhā cit*) [are distinct]"—it is stated that there is a specific distinction for the individual soul called its "threefoldness. This is what he says with the words: "But in the *Dṛgdṛśyaviveka*," where the word "but" (*tu*) signifies the aforementioned specific distinction of the *kūṭastha*.

He demonstrates the inclusion [of Jīvakuṭāvalī] within this very [work]. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means in the treatise titled *Dṛkdṛśyaviveka*. The particle *hi* indicates well-known tradition. Regarding the phrase "waves in a reservoir of water":
just as waves exist on the surface of a reservoir of water such as the ocean, and bubbles exist on the surface of those [waves].

For the meaning of the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*) is a logical principle (*nyāya*) or an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). In this way, the empirical individual soul (*vyāvahārika-jīva*) is postulated as the reflection of the immutable [Self] upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which persists as long as empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) continues. Of that [soul]:

The meaning is that, through the state of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), at the time of dreaming, the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) individual soul (*jīva*)—which consists of a reflection in the *antaḥkaraṇa* (internal organ) composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is postulated, just like chariots and other objects consisting of latent impressions.
The word "therein" (*tatra*) means within the midst of the three types of souls. "Conditioned" (*avacchinna*) [refers to the *avacchinnajīva*].
The meaning is that the Self, which is the nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) delimited by the two bodies, is the ultimate individual soul (*pāramārthika-jīva*).

In the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) such as "I am Brahman," the non-difference between the individual soul and Brahman is propounded; and this [non-difference] is established only when the ultimate individual soul is postulated. Otherwise, [if one were to rely on] the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) or the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) [soul], [the non-difference would not hold].
In the case of two living beings, [the suffix] śu [is applied].

Even though the delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) in that case is imagined, the delimited (*avacchedya*) itself is unimagined; therefore, because it is non-different from Brahman, when Māyā remains enveloping that [Brahman], the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—
having attained identity with the imagined internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) within the internal organ— conceives of itself as "I."

The empirical [self] is so called because it persists as long as worldly transaction continues, even though it is illusory (*māyika*). The apparent [self] (*prātibhāsika*) is the one who possesses the conceit (*abhimānin*) regarding the dream-body and so forth, which are imagined by sleep— a state that is a specific variety of illusion (*māyā*) and which persists by veiling even that empirical self during dreaming.
Since [the individual soul] is false by its very nature—like a shell-silver or the like—it cannot be non-different from the real Brahman;

for even though the two bodies that serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the eternally unchanging (*kūṭastha*) and ultimately real soul are themselves imagined (*kalpita*), the soul itself is inherently real. Thus, non-difference from Brahman is possible in the ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*).

He shows the purpose of the conceptualization of the *jīva* with the words "in that" (*tasmin*). This means in the limited *jīva*. He defines the empirical *jīva* with the word "him" (*tam*). When the covering (ignorance) has arisen, veiling the immutable Self (*kūṭastha-ātman*), within that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is superimposed upon the immutable Self—there [is the empirical *jīva*].

The meaning is that the "reflected light" (yaścidābhāsaḥ) is the empirical individual soul (vyāvahārika-jīva). As it has been said: "The intellect (buddhi) is superimposed upon the immutable (kūṭastha), and therein lies the reflection of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "conceiving 'I'":

this means the agent of the conceit (abhimāna) that takes the form of "I," which is the nature of the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of "I. Now, [one might ask] in the form of the modification consisting of the "I"-aspect...

It is appropriate that the sense of "I" (ahaṃ-abhimāna) resides only in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as it undergoes transformation, and not in the reflection of consciousness; therefore, he says: "The internal organ... He provides the reasoning for its being of a transactional nature (*vyāvahārika*) by saying: "Of that...
Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for a transactional individual soul (*jīva*), for [there is evidence] such as "the agent of 'I'-making," "the enjoyer," and so forth.
Because "I" (the *aham*) is the subject of the experience of form (*rūpa*),

and because agency, enjoyership, and so forth— which constitute the locus of the self's transmigratory existence— cannot belong to anything else; nor is such [agency and enjoyership] possible in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
since that, being devoid of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), possesses the attributes of non-consciousness (*caitanya*).

Because it is impossible for [the Self] to be the locus of well-known agency and so forth; however, since the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)— though false— is a reflection of the conscious Self,
it is fit for the conventional usage of "consciousness," and thus its attributes are established as being the attributes of consciousness.

Because there is no contradiction. The point is that it is impossible for the ultimate (pāramārthika) jīva to be the locus of transmigratory existence, because it is immutable (kūṭastha). "That too" means even the empirical (vyāvahārika) jīva;
for the empirical jīva, during the waking state, considers itself to be a Brāhmaṇa, Devadatta, and so forth.

Yajñadatta considers his son to be a devotee of Viṣṇu; however, the dreaming self (svapnajīva) considers himself, in the state of dream, to be a Kṣatriya named Viṣṇuśarman, the son of Nārāyaṇa, and a devotee of Mahādeva. Therefore, the veiling (āvaraṇa) of the waking self is established.
The illusory individual soul.

Because that [reflection], along with its own phenomenal expansion, ceases upon the awakening of the individual soul (jīva) who perceives it. Thus have these [objections] been shown regarding the difference [between the two] in the view of those who maintain that the Lord is a reflection.
However, the followers of the Vivaraṇa say: "When the knowledge that produces differentiation has reached absolute destruction..."

Because the Smṛti states, "He will destroy the non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman," it is established that a single ignorance alone serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*); thus,

the distinction between the *jīva* and the *īśvara* occurs through the relationship of the original image and its reflection, and not because both [the *jīva* and the *īśvara*] are [separately conditioned by ignorance].
Because it is impossible for both to be reflections in the absence of two distinct limiting adjuncts (upādhi) acting as the basis for their reflection.

He says "by sleep. Now, one might object: "Since you have accepted that *māyā* is the creator of all conceptualizations (*kalpa*), how can sleep be the creator? This would lead to the fallacy of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Anticipating this objection, he says "māyā" with the intention that there is no such fault, because he accepts that sleep is merely a particular state (*avasthā*) of that [māyā]. It is not [independent].

Furthermore, it must be explained how sleep can be a specific state [of Māyā], given that Māyā lacks the defining characteristic [of being such]. For the definition of Māyā is indeed "possessing the powers of concealment (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). This definition applies to sleep, which conceals the waking consciousness and produces the projection consisting of the dream-world. Thus, [the definition] is not lacking in sleep.

The meaning is "because of its being real. He states the purpose for postulating the illusory (prātibhāsika) individual soul (*jīva*) with the words "in the case of the dream-body and so forth. The meaning is that since the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) soul is [considered] real, it is impossible for it to be the agent of the ego-identification (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*) during the time of a dream. He states the reason for its being illusory:

The meaning is that by the phrase "through the expansion of a dream," at the time of waking, there is an experience of sublation—such as the cognition "I am a Brahmin, not a Kṣatriya"—regarding the one who saw the dream, who appeared in the form of a Kṣatriya or the like.
He concludes [the section] regarding the Lord in order to provide knowledge of the distinctions between the modes already stated and those yet to be stated: "Thus."

The word "tu" (but) is intended to convey a specific meaning that will be explained later: namely, that the Lord is the original consciousness (*bimbacaitanya*) itself and not a particular reflection (*pratibimba*).

Furthermore, "causing division" (*vibhedajanakatva*) is intended to mean being the cause for the persistence of the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), rather than the literal sense [of creating the difference], because it is accepted that such a distinction is beginningless (*anādi*). The term "ultimate" (*ātyantika*) refers to its own...

At the beginning of dissolution (*pralaya*), due to the destruction of the effects of ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is also the destruction of its cause, ignorance itself, because of the non-difference between a modification (*pariṇāma*) and that which undergoes modification (*pariṇāmin*). However, that destruction of ignorance is not absolute, because [ignorance] arises again.
In liberation (*mukti*), however, through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is destruction even of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and that is absolute.
Thinking that [ignorance] would arise again, the qualification "absolute" (atyantika) was given to the destruction of ignorance.

Alternatively, even though at the time of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) the veiling aspect (āvaraṇāṃśa) of ignorance is destroyed, because the projective aspect (vikṣepāṃśa) has not been destroyed, that destruction is not absolute.
The sense is that the qualification [of the Self] is intended to show that in liberation in Videha there is the absolute destruction of knowledge;

this is because [the reflection] cannot logically be a reflection. Nor does this contradict the scriptural passage, "By means of a portion of His own self, He becomes the individual soul (jīva), and Māyā and Avidyā become [His portions] of their own accord," which establishes that both are reflections.

It must be said: since the status of being a reflection (*pratibimbatva*) as well as the status of being the original object (*bimbatva*) is equally imagined (*kalpita*), it is logical that the term *ābhāsa* (appearance) occurring in the Śruti includes both the reflection and the original object.

In that case as well, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection and the Lord (*īśvara*) is the original object (*bimba*); only when this is so is it logical, by means of the worldly analogy of the original object and its reflection, that the Lord possesses independence while the individual soul possesses dependence upon Him.

Is it not the case that in the world, because there is the conventional usage of the term "appearance of a face" (*mukhābhāsa*) with respect to a face qualified by being a reflection, whereas such usage does not occur with respect to a face qualified by being the original object (*bimba*), the word "appearance" (*ābhāsa*) cannot, in its primary sense, convey the original object-consciousness? Indeed, [the same applies] to the original object as it does to the reflection.

It might be argued that, because it is imagined in a specific form, the term *paramābhāsa* (supreme reflection) should be understood as referring to the *bimba* (original object) by virtue of its association with the quality of being imagined. However, this is not possible; for it is contradictory to assume that a single occurrence of the word *ābhāsa* can, in its primary sense, refer to a *pratibimba* (reflection) and, in a secondary sense, refer to a *bimba*. This would result in a confusion between the distinct categories of the original and the reflected.

Nor should it be argued that this contradiction is avoided by accepting that the term *ābhāsa* (appearance) refers to both the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) through a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*); for when it is possible for the term *ābhāsa* to have its primary meaning by taking both to be of the nature of a reflection (*pratibimba*).

If it is argued that this is because the conceptualization of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is itself groundless, it is replied: Just as it is not possible for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) to be reflections, since the consciousness that constitutes the original object (*bimba*)—being unitary like the sun—cannot have two reflections in the absence of distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor...

It should not be argued that the appearance of two reflections is untenable because the supplementary portion of the text states, "māyā and avidyā themselves become [the two]," thereby establishing two limiting adjuncts (upādhi) consisting of māyā and vidyā; for by that [statement],
the term "itself" (svayam) refers to the primordial root-nature (mūla-prakṛti) under discussion, which is of the nature of māyā.

Even though a distinction between the forms characterized as *vidyā* and *avidyā* has been set forth, since two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) required for two reflections have not been established, and because a difference between *māyā* and *avidyā* in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) would contradict the established doctrine (*siddhānta*),
it follows that, as the literal reading is untenable, a single ignorance (*ajñāna*) alone is the cause of the division between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Furthermore, in accordance with the *Pratipādaka-smṛti*, the followers of the *Vivaraṇa* maintain that in the scriptural passage "He creates by means of the reflection (*ābhāsa*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)," the term *ābhāsa* refers— by means of a non-abandoning secondary signification (*ajahallakṣaṇā*)— to both the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection. Regarding this point as well:
The meaning is "even between both the original object (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba). He states the reasoning for this: "only when that is so. This means:

only when the status of being the Lord (Īśvara) is accepted as belonging solely to the consciousness of the original object (bimbacaitanya). "Sovereignty" (svātantrya)—the remainder of the sentence being that this is established by such scriptural texts as "He is the Lord of all; He is the sovereign of beings," and so forth. "Dependence on Him" (tatpāratantrya) [is established].

For it is He indeed who causes one to perform good deeds; "He who dwells within the self controls it from within"—it is established by such scriptural and traditional texts that one goes either to heaven or even to hell, impelled by the Lord; this is the implied meaning.

Just as a person might play by observing the straight, curved, and other transformations occurring within a reflection, so too does the *jīva* undergo transformations; according to this reasoning stated in the *Kalpataru*, even the sūtra "The world is the sport of Brahman" (*lokavat tu līlā kaivalyam*) becomes consistent. [This applies] to that which is reflected in ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The specific manifestation of the soul's particularity is a distinct modification of knowledge in the form of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
serving as the locus for its expression, just as a mirror is for the light of the sun spreading in all directions.
He demonstrates this very worldly illustration by citing the verse on the *kalpataru* (wish-fulfilling tree): "Those residing in the reflection," and so forth.

Just as in the world a certain person, seeing the modifications such as straightness or curvature residing in his own reflection—which are actually produced by himself in the original object (*bimba*)—plays with them, so too does Brahman [perceive] the modifications residing in the individual soul (*jīva*).

The meaning is that, according to the method explained in the *Kalpataru* commentary on the phrase "seeing [beings] as they sport, being directed by their own karma," this *sūtra*—which establishes the sovereignty of the Lord—is also consistent, as it serves to demonstrate the Lord's independence. As for the meaning of the *sūtra*: because the Lord has all his desires fulfilled (*āptakāma*), [he acts without need].

Because there is no purpose or objective [to be attained], it is not possible for [the Lord] to engage in activities such as creation; this is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa). The word "but" (tu) serves to set aside that objection. The activity of the Lord characterized by creation and so forth occurs entirely without reference to any purpose, like mere play or the world itself. Just as in the world...

Just as play is observed even in one who is most abundantly endowed with all human enjoyments, such as a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*), and without any intention toward a specific purpose; furthermore, although the Lord lacks any aim for a purpose, His engagement in creation and so forth is established by His very nature. For it is indeed observed [in the world].

The play (*līlā*) of living beings—consisting of laughter, singing, and so forth, which is devoid of any purpose or objective and is prompted by the experience of an abundance of happiness—is natural;
for indeed, it is not possible even to conceive of a purpose in that regard. [Likewise,] crying is [prompted] by an abundance of suffering.
This is because the excessive outpouring of affection, laughter, singing, and so forth, being devoid of any ulterior motive, is established by the experience of everyone.

For this very reason, in cases such as laughing or weeping, one asks for the cause alone and not for a purpose. And it is said in the Māṇḍūkya Śruti: "This is the nature of the Divine; for Him whose desires are fulfilled, what longing can there be? This refers to creation and the rest.

The meaning is "conventional usage. Furthermore, we accept that the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consists of illusion (*māyā*), just like the creation in a dream. And in that regard, a question concerning its purpose is not appropriate, because no such question regarding a purpose is observed in the case of a dream-creation; this is the sense. Now, if ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), then...
Regarding the description in the Sūtras, Bhāṣya, and other texts that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), he says [in response]:

"ignorance" (*ajñāna*), etc. It is the locus for the manifestation of specific qualities. This refers to the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*), an agent (*kartṛtva*), and an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*), which belongs to the nature of consciousness reflected in ignorance (*avidyā-pratibimba-caitanya*) and is common even to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). By means of these specific forms, [the soul is distinguished].
Manifestation is apprehension; its locus is the limiting adjunct (upādhi)—this is the meaning.

Therefore, even though it is conventionally designated as having that [intellect] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there is no abandonment of consciousness as its limiting adjunct by this much alone;

for if consciousness were the individual soul (*jīva*) only when delimited by the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it would be impossible for the yogin to preside over a plurality of bodies (*kāyavyūha*).

This is what is meant: since the attributes such as agency do not exist as mere transformations of pure ignorance, the individual soul (jīva) does not acquire specific attributes such as agency merely through that limiting adjunct (upādhi);

rather, it acquires them only through the superimposition (adhyāsa) of identity with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which possesses those specific attributes such as agency. Thus, it is not [the case that the soul’s agency is real].

Therefore, the definition of that limiting adjunct (upādhi) is useless. "Hence" means because it is accepted that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the locus for the manifestation of distinctions. "Even in common usage" implies the scriptural statement, "This individual soul (*jīva*) has its limiting adjunct as its effect," as well as the *Sūtra-bhāṣya* and other such works. [The verse continues: "Having brought about the absolute destruction of the knowledge that produces differentiation..."

In the passage from the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, "Who will create a non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman?", the meaning is that it is like the conventional usage [of the term] "jīva" as having ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Now, one might object: by the force of the scriptural statement, "This jīva has a product (*kārya*) as its limiting adjunct," it is appropriate to abandon the view that ignorance is the limiting adjunct, since the qualifying term "having a product as its limiting adjunct" [is used].

Anticipating the objection that [the soul] is excluded because its limiting adjunct is a cause (*kāraṇopādhikatva*), [the author] states, "Not merely this much," with the intention that, due to contradiction with Smṛti, that [soul] does not have its exclusion based on a causal adjunct. The meaning is: "merely by the qualification of having an effect as an adjunct (*kāryopādhikatva*) in the Śruti. Now, if there is a contradiction with Śruti, the Smṛti itself must be interpreted otherwise...
The interpretation is appropriate. That method of interpretation is as follows:

the term "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is its effect; and although the internal organ, as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), is singular, the use of the singular number in the word "ignorance" is intended to denote the genus (*jāti*). Thus it is.

To dispel the doubt that the meaning of the Smṛti might be that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the factor effecting the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman— wherein the self conditioned by the internal organ is the *jīva* and the self unconditioned by it is the Lord (*īśvara*)— he refutes the idea that the internal organ alone, as a mere product-condition (*kāryopādhi*), serves as the condition for being a *jīva*.

The meaning of the word "only" (eva) is that [the capacity for simultaneous control] belongs only to one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is delimited by a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and not to one whose adjunct is ignorance (*ajñāna*).

As for the phrase "because it is untenable": the presiding over a plurality of bodies indeed consists in the simultaneous control of many bodies; and that must be predicated of a yogi who, through the power of yoga, is simultaneously present within all the bodies he has created.

Furthermore, this is not possible for a yogi whose form is delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because that [organ] is limited in its capacity. However, it is possible if the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) is that [intellect], since, owing to its pervasiveness, the presence of the yogi’s soul—which has that as its adjunct—simultaneously in all bodies is logically established; and thus:

Although Smṛti is weaker than Śruti, it is stronger when supported by the impossibility of [the Lord] presiding over a multitude of bodies (kāyavyūha); therefore, in accordance with that Smṛti, this statement in the Śruti— "this individual soul (jīva) has a body as its limiting adjunct" (kāryopādhi)—
is intended merely as a description of its nature (svarūpa), and does not exclude the causal limiting adjunct (kāraṇopādhi).
The intended meaning is that it is subordinate to the qualifier.

Nor can it be argued that, by the power of yoga, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the yogin attains such vastness as to become capable of manifesting a multitude of bodies, and that it is therefore logical for that [organ], thus delimited, to serve as the substratum for the manifestation of those bodies; for the penetration [of the self] occurs like a lamp. Thus it is said: "The penetration is like a lamp."

This is because, in the commentary on the penultimate section of the *Śāstra* and other texts, it is described that within the *kāyavyūha*, a distinct internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is created for each body through the power of yoga, just like the eyes and other sense organs.
"Vaipulya" means pervasiveness. "Adhiṣṭhānatva" means the state of being an impeller.

"Like a lamp": just as a single lamp may enter into many wicks, so too, through the power of yoga, a yogin may simultaneously enter into many [bodies], even though there is a distinction between the original lamp and the lamps that have entered the wicks.

However, there is a difference between the illustration and the illustrated: while the yogi possesses distinctness, [the lamps] possess oneness in all their bodies; thus, a disparity exists between the illustration and the subject of the illustration.
Nevertheless, the connection between the two must be understood through the superimposition of the non-difference of the universal (*jāti*) "lamp-ness" upon the individuals.
For the Śruti demonstrates the manifold manifestation of a single yogi: "He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold."

The meaning of the Sūtra is that states such as "fivefold" or "sevenfold" and so forth are not possible through the simultaneous occupation of multiple bodies by a yogin; rather, the manifold existence established by the Śruti is justified [otherwise]. This is because of the description of creation, and likewise because of the single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) belonging to one [individual].
The sense is that if one accepts the vastness [of the body] as being fit for the manifestation of bodily arrays (*kāyavyūha*), there would be a contradiction with the *Bhāṣya* and other texts.
In this regard,
although according to the yogi’s own established doctrine, it is his very internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that becomes vast through the power of yoga...

It is appropriate to state that the purport of the Bhāṣya and other texts is simply that [the Lord] effects the manifestation of the yogi’s manifold bodies, their presiding over them, and their enjoyment— wherein the yogi is of the nature of consciousness delimited by his own [body]— and not, as it might literally appear, the production of multiple internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).

If one were to accept that the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are created anew for each individual, it would result in the fallacy of *asatkāryavāda* (the doctrine that the effect does not pre-exist in the cause) and entail the fault of excessive conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).

Furthermore, since it is accepted that Hiraṇyagarbha and others possess, through the power of yoga, a collective internal organ (*samaṣṭi-antaḥkaraṇa*) that pervades the entire cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), [the internal organ cannot be a new creation]. Indeed, for Hiraṇyagarbha and the others...

There is no evidence for the pervasiveness of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) belonging to one who was in the state of a sacrificer in a previous birth; for if that were the case, it would follow that the internal organs of people such as ourselves are also pervasive,
and because the descriptions of the creation of the internal organs found in the Bhāṣya and other texts can be understood as referring to the views of other schools.

And this very [process] is the method for yogis in the Yoga-śāstras regarding the conjunction with multiple bodies, as shown in the Bhāṣya through the presentation of other views; and it is stated that "this is the method in the Yoga-śāstras. Nevertheless, because the connection with the hands is thus established, it is as in the penultimate section (adhikaraṇa) of the Śāstra.
It should be understood that this objection is based on the intention of the Śrutabhāṣya and other such works.

Since in a reflection only the difference from the original object (*bimba*) is superimposed, while its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) remains real, there is no impossibility of the individual soul (*jīva*), whose form is that of a reflection, being associated with liberation. Nor is there another soul, limited by a state associated with liberation, existing apart from that [reflection], nor a soul distinct from the reflected soul.

Either a consciousness distinct from the Lord of the individual soul (jīveśvara), designated as the "immutable" (kūṭastha), must be postulated; or else, the scriptural hearing that "indeed, this Self is indestructible" has as its purport the fact that even upon the cessation of the limiting adjuncts and the disappearance of the state of being a reflection, the essential nature of the individual soul does not perish. It is not intended otherwise.
That which is distinct from that [consciousness] is another consciousness called the *kūṭastha* (the immutable).

In reality, however, according to the position that the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is consciousness undelimited by it, there would be the following defect to be mentioned later: since the consciousness within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) is entirely delimited [by the internal organ], the Lord, who is consciousness in its undelimited form, would exist only outside the cosmic egg.

The intended meaning is as follows: Alternatively, if by the phrase "the Lord is consciousness unconditioned by anything" one intends to mean that the Lord is consciousness without attributes (*nirupādhika-caitanya*), then— although there is no fault regarding the contingency of [the Lord] existing only within the cosmic egg (since He exists everywhere)— there remains the fault of contradicting the Śruti which states, "The Lord has the causal adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*)."
Therefore, it is established that— just as in the case of the Lord— the soul must also be admitted to possess limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) caused by material factors,
in accordance with the *Smṛti*. As for the objection raised in the *Citradīpa* that the soul, being of the nature of a reflected consciousness,
is false by its very essence (*svarūpataḥ*) and thus incapable of participating in liberation— that [objection] applies only to the "immutable" (*kūṭastha*) one, which is fit for such participation.
Having postulated a certain consciousness distinct from both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*),
the fourfold nature of consciousness (*cic-cāturvidhya*) has been demonstrated. Furthermore, in the *Dṛgdṛśyaviveka*,
by relying on the very falsity (*mithyātva*) of the reflection, the ultimate reality of the limited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*)— which persists until liberation— is established.

The notion of "living-ness" (jīvatva) is imagined, and both [theories] are untenable; for since the mere difference between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is imagined, there is no evidence for their being inherently different. With this intention, he says: "In the reflection, [there is nothing] other than the original image.
The meaning of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is the exclusion of the imagined nature of the essential form (*svarūpa*). [He says: "Not as something distinct from that."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: one should not postulate another individual soul (jīva) distinct from the reflected soul, nor another consciousness designated by the term "kūṭastha. Likewise, apart from the empirical (vyāvahārika) soul, even an illusory (prātibhāsika) soul need not be postulated, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), just as there is no separate empirical soul during the time of a dream.
It must be said that the impossibility of its being an agent at that time due to its being veiled serves as the proof for postulating such a veil;
for, since the absence of obscuration in the consciousness of the living self will be explained during the discussion on the *sākṣin*,
it is possible for the waking living self to be an agent even in a dream— as in the case of one who [thinks], "I who [was dreaming]..."

"I saw Śrī Kṛṣṇa; that very same one I now see while awake," or "I remember him"— from such recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of non-difference between what was seen in a dream and what is seen while awake, and because the non-perception of [qualities like] Brahminhood and so forth can sometimes be explained by causes such as the absence of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is not the case that...

It must be stated that the observation of the sublation of the dreamer along with his own dream-creation serves as the proof for the conceptualization of the empirical (prātibhāsika) individual soul; for at the time of waking, there occurs a sublation in the form of "I am a Kṣatriya," and so forth.
Consciousness delimited by the internal organ and other adjuncts of the individual soul is indeed the Lord in the form of the original prototype (bimba),

because the scripture— starting with "He who dwells in knowledge" and so forth— declares that the Lord Himself, through His presence as the inner ruler (antaryāmin) in proximity to the individual soul,
abides within the various modifications.

Since the sublation of the dreamer consists merely in the sublation of the kṣatriya-hood and other attributes superimposed upon the self within the cognition, there is no sublation of the dreamer himself; otherwise, it would contradict the previously cited recognition of the identity of the perceiver. Therefore, even the conceptualization of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) is not authoritative.

This must be understood as follows: even that which was stated by those who maintain the fourfold nature of consciousness— namely, the two scriptural passages, "They perish along with it" and "Indeed, this Self is imperishable"—

since they establish two contradictory attributes, perishability and imperishability, within the subject at hand, the Self consisting of a mass of consciousness (*prajñānaghana*), for the sake of making that [duality] possible, [the Self] is perishable...

The claim that an immutable, indestructible consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya) is established as distinct from the reflection is also weak; for it is precisely within the individual soul (jīva), which consists of the reflection of consciousness upon ignorance (avidyā), that the statement regarding destruction refers to the perishable nature of the qualifying attribute— the state of being a reflection— while [the indestructibility] pertains to the substantive (viśeṣya).

With the intention of referring to the aspect of pure consciousness (*caitanyāṃśa*), he says "indeed imperishable" (*avināśī vai*), based on the consideration that the postulation of a difference between the substrates (*dharmibheda*) is precluded by the complexity (*gaurava*) involved, since the statement teaching the absence of destruction is thus rendered intelligible. Now, [the opponent may argue]: the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection of ignorance, while the Lord (*īśvara*) is its original image (*bimba*); and the consciousness that underlies both the original image and the reflection— The final sentence is incomplete in the source text. A full translation would continue with the conclusion of the argument regarding the nature of consciousness. However, based strictly on the provided fragment, the translation is as above.

In the view of the *Vivaraṇa*, where "pure consciousness" (*śuddhacaitanya*) is defined as the material cause of the two bodies, within what is that consciousness included— which is accepted by those who maintain a fourfold division of consciousness as being named the "transcendentally real self" (*pāramārthika-jīva*) and the "immutable witness" (*kūṭastha*), and which is delimited by those two bodies?
First of all, the inclusion of the individual soul (*jīva*)— which is pure consciousness as the object of attainment (*upeya*)—

within those two [the body and the intellect] is not possible, because, since those two lack the nature of being its material cause (*upādāna*), it is impossible for the immutable substrate (*kūṭastha*), which is the material cause of the two bodies, to be included within them. Nor is its inclusion possible within the Lord (*Īśvara*), who exists as the archetype (*bimba*).

Because there is no evidence for the Lord’s presence within the modifications such as the body through the proximity of the individual soul (jīva) and its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); and because those who maintain the doctrine of the Immutable (Kūṭastha) accept that the consciousness called the Immutable is [itself] such [unchanging], he says: "by means of the limiting adjunct of the individual soul."

The meaning is: by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which causes the manifestation of the specific qualities of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is of the nature of a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the eye (*cakṣus*), and so forth. "Only the Lord" (*īśvara eva*)—the force of the particle "only" (*eva*) is to indicate that neither pure Brahman nor the individual soul in the form of a reflection [is the cause]. [This applies to] that which consists of the sentient and the insentient.

The meaning is that there is no proof for the existence of a separate, immutable [self] distinct from that [Brahman], because the thousands of Śrutis and Smṛtis which establish the Lord as the material cause of the entire phenomenal world serve as the authority for His abiding within the modifications such as the body by way of being their material cause;
and because there is a lack of evidence for His difference from that [Brahman]. Not so.
In this regard, not only is scripture that establishes [Brahman] as the material cause the authority,
but also the Antaryāmī Brāhmaṇa, which establishes the Lord— who exists as the archetype— as the controller of the entire universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings.
He states the proof for [the Self's] abiding within the modifications [of the intellect] in the passage beginning, "He who, dwelling in consciousness... and so forth.
Others, however, maintain that a reflection not supported by a material form is not tenable, and the example of a reflection in the colorless sky is all the more inappropriate.

Regarding the phrase "by the scriptural statement": the expression "He who is within consciousness, whose body is consciousness, who controls consciousness from within," and so forth, is included by the word "etcetera.
Here, in the Mādhyandina recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the term "consciousness" (vijñāna) refers to the individual soul (jīva).

Regarding the phrase "standing," in the Kaṇva recension, where the sequence reads "standing in consciousness" (*vijñāne tiṣṭhan*) instead of "standing in existence" (*sthāne*), it is understood that the word *vijñāna* has the same meaning as the word *ātman*. Furthermore, since the word *ātman* here refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), [the term] is used in that sense there.

The sense is that, although the word *ātman* is commonly used for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), it must necessarily refer to the individual soul in this context due to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of being "that which is to be governed. Regarding the phrase "by the proximity of the individual soul":
for the Lord's status as the governor of the individual soul and so forth occurs just as a distant king exercises governance over his subjects.

However, the meaning is that [the Lord] exists within the self precisely by being the regulator of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth, because of the perception of His proximity in the statement, "He who dwells in the self. The citation of the *Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa* passage is also an elliptical reference to the *Smṛti*; thus, there is the *Smṛti* of the *Bhagavadgītā*:

"The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine. Here, "beings" refers to living creatures; "machine" refers to the body; and "being mounted upon it" refers to the sense of "I" therein.

The meaning is that [the Lord], causing my ego-sense to wander as if it were new, sets it in motion and turns it back according to [past] karma. With the intention that the Lord’s status as a controller is merely due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of *māyā* and is not real, the word "by *māyā*" is used. And thus, of consciousness...

The distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) has been shown according to those who accept the state of being a reflection. Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of the individual soul and so forth according to the view of those who do not accept that [reflection], he refutes the reflection of consciousness. He says, "Others... and "unconditioned by form... and so on.

In the world, a reflection is observed only of things possessing form, such as the moon and so forth, and not of formless things such as air and so forth; thus, because this pervasion (*vyāpti*) is observed, the meaning is that it is impossible for consciousness (*caitanya*), which is formless, to possess the nature of a reflection. Furthermore, he states that for this reason also, it is impossible for consciousness to be a reflection: "all the more so, being formless."

The phrase "in ignorance, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and so forth" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Although, according to the method to be explained later, there is a deviation from the rule that "only a substance possessing color has a reflection" in the case of the sky, the author says "all the more so" (sutarām) with the thought that there is no deviation whatsoever from the rule that "the reflection occurs only in an adjunct (upādhi) possessing color. Now, [an objection]:

Anticipating the objection that there is no rule stating that a formless substance cannot have a reflection—since the reflection of the formless sky is experienced in the water of wells, ponds, and the like—he says: "The sky... [and so forth].
First of all, the reflection of light in the water of wells and such is universally admitted; in that [instance],...

The delusion that there is a reflection of the sky [in water] is merely a conceptual construction of worldly people; however, in reality, no reflection of the sky exists therein, because that would contradict the stated rule.
For when the orb of the sun pervading the expanse of the sky is reflected in water,
the conventional designation "reflection of the sky" is rooted merely in error.
Likewise, the theory that phonemes are reflections in sound has also been stated on the grounds that sound is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*).

Because there is no evidence for the hypothesis that sound (dhvani) possesses the status of being a substrate for the reflection of phonemes (varṇa), based on the attribution of properties such as high pitch (udāttatva) belonging to sound onto the phonemes merely through proximity.

He states the defect that causes the error: "pervading the expanse of the sky" (*gaganābhogavyāpinī*). "Expanse" (*ābhoga*) means extension. The meaning is that because the orb of the sun’s rays and so forth, which exist pervading the upper region of the sky, are perceived as reflections in water, there arises the error of a reflection of that very sky in the water. Now, just as...

The sky is experienced in such forms as "the blue exterior" or "the vast sky," and so forth. Likewise, even in the water of wells, ponds, and the like, an experience in the form of "the blue sky" or "the vast sky" is universally acknowledged. Nor is it logical that the vastness and other qualities perceived in the water of a well and so on belong to the sky.

In reality, I am [the sky]; therefore, it is indeed of the nature of a reflection. In that regard, one must say that the sky which is being seen is present there. Consequently, how can the reflection of the sky be denied? Nor should it be argued that a reflection is impossible for that which is formless (*nīrūpa*), for even in the case of that which is formless, qualities such as color, number, and dimension [can be reflected].
Nor should it be said that, because of the observation of reflections, "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is also intended as a qualifying attribute;

for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the technical categories of substance, quality, and so forth are not accepted. Even if they were accepted, a reflection of a substance endowed with color (*rūpa*) cannot be accounted for by the case of the reflection of the sky (*gagana*); and as for that state of being "endowed with it" (*tadupahitatva*):
In reality, this is because it is logical to postulate a restrictive rule that [the reflection] occurs either in its own inherent form or in a form superimposed upon itself.

Thus, by accepting the reflection of the sky—qualified by blue color and other attributes superimposed externally—in water and the like, there is no contradiction whatsoever; nor is there anything [required] beyond the reflection of light already admitted in water and such.
It must be said that the objection regarding the complexity (gaurava) involved in accepting the reflection of the sky is itself a sublation;

for even if one accepts the error of perceiving the reflection of light as the reflection of the sky, the object of that error— which resides in the reflection of light— is indeterminable (anirvacanīya), just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

If it is argued that since the necessity of accepting the reflection of space makes the resulting complexity (gaurava) equal [to the alternative], and since complexity that follows from experience is not a fault, the rule that "only a substance possessing color reflects" is inevitably contradicted in the case of the reflection of space— this is true; nevertheless, regarding consciousness...

The intended meaning here is simply that a reflection is not possible [in this case], because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth, being formless, cannot serve as the substrate for a reflection. Now, one might object: even in the case of sound (*dhvani*), which is formless, there must be said to exist a reflection of the phonemes (*varṇa*), which consist of formless substance; for it is only by being so [that cognition occurs].

Just as the blackness of a mirror is superimposed upon the reflection of a face appearing in that mirror, so too can the properties such as high pitch (*tāratva*) residing in the sound be superimposed upon the phonemes (*varṇa*) by means of their reflection in the phonemes residing in the sound; it cannot happen otherwise. Thus...
Anticipating the objection that a reflection of the formless Self cannot occur within the formless internal organ and so forth,
he refutes the supporting example with the words "In sound":
even an echo is not a reflection of the preceding sound, according to the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).

Because sounds such as those of a drum, a lute, or a conch are [perceived] as the nature of earth, water, and so forth, while the echo itself is the nature of space, it is impossible for the latter to be a reflection of the former sound. Furthermore, even an echo in the form of a phoneme is not a reflection of a preceding phoneme.
Since it is established that the echo, caused by the sound that manifests the phonemes, functions as a manifester of the phonemes just like the original sound itself; therefore,
the individual soul (*jīva*) is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), like the space within a jar, whereas [the Supreme Self] is that which is not so delimited.
The Lord is consciousness.

Now, it may be objected that at the time of the production of sound from a specific musical instrument such as a drum, an echo is heard in the adjacent regions of space near specific stones and other objects; this [echo] is indeed a reflection of the original sound.
Since there is no cause for the production of a sound called "space" (namakhyadhvani), it must be so; and thus, just as...
One might ask: "In formless regions of space, there is a reflection of sound in the form of an echo; why should this not be the case here as well? To this he says, "No," adding: "Even an echo...
Nor should it be suspected that there is an absence of a cause for the production of the echo, since space itself serves as the material cause (upādāna).

This is because of the existence of the word "satvāt" [in the sūtra], meaning that the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) exists; and it should not be argued: "Even if an echo were a reflection, why could it not be a quality of space?
For, according to the view that the original object (bimba) and its reflection (pratibimba) are distinct, the reflection in the form of an echo is merely illusory (prātibhāsika).

The meaning is that, since it is impossible for [the echo] to be a quality in the conventional sense, and because there is no difference between the reflection (the echo) and the original object (the sound) as defined by the counter-sound—given the position that they are non-different—it is impossible for it to be a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*), with respect to the words "earth" and so forth which constitute the original source (*bimba*). Now, [one might object]: what about the echo in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*)?
It must necessarily be stated that [the cognition] is a reflection of the phoneme (varṇa), and not that it is the phoneme itself directly;
for in the case of the manifestation of each individual phoneme, the throat, palate, and other articulators that manifest the phoneme are absent.
Thus, just as in that case, there is a perception of formless [phonemes] within formless regions of space situated near mountains, caves, and so forth.

One might ask: "Why could there not be a reflection of phonemes (varṇa) in the same way as in the case of the material substrate (prakṛti)? To this he says: "Even the echo of the form of the phoneme," meaning that it is not like an echo even in the location of the throat, palate, and so forth.
The throat and other organs do not manifest the phoneme (varṇa) directly;

rather, it is the sound (dhvani) produced by the impact of the throat, palate, and so forth that does so. Thus, just as the primary sound manifests the phoneme, likewise, at the site of the manifestation of each individual phoneme, [the sound] is produced.

The meaning is that in this case, it is only the echo itself that can be the manifestor of the phonemes; therefore, one need not admit that the phonemes possess the nature of reflections. [The author] concludes the refutation of the reflection of consciousness with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Consciousness...
The meaning is that a reflection is impossible.

Nor does it follow that because consciousness existing within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) is delimited in its entirety as individual souls (*jīva*) by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of their respective internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the Lord (*īśvara*), whose nature is consciousness free from those specific delimitations, must exist only outside the cosmic egg; such is the view held by Vijñāna.

In passages such as "He remains," the scriptural teaching regarding His abiding in various modifications by way of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) would be contradicted; however, in the case of the reflection theory (*pratibimbapakṣa*), since the reflection of space is observed even while the natural space within the water exists, its existence in a single location in a doubled manner is logically established.

It must be stated: for even in the view that it is a reflection (*pratibimba*), what is called a reflection there is only of that consciousness which has entered into the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); it is not a reflection of the whole [consciousness] according to the analogy of the moon in water, because a reflection of the portion situated within it is impossible there. Indeed, not...
Just as the reflection of space or light, when separated by clouds, is seen in water,

so too is the reflection of that which is already within the water seen there; or rather, just as the reflection of the face and other features exists while they remain outside, does that reflection persist even when they are submerged within the water?

If the Lord (*īśvara*) were defined as consciousness (*caitanya*) unconditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), one might raise the objection that this contradicts the scriptures which teach that the Supreme Lord exists within all modifications, such as the internal organ, in the form of the inner controller (*antaryāmin*). This is expressed by the words: "And not thus" (*na caivam*) and "it would be contradicted" (*virudhyate*).
And thus, the sense is that the reflection theory alone must be accepted in order to avoid contradiction with scripture.
Anticipating the objection that even the adoption of the reflection theory contradicts scripture, he says: "In the reflection theory, however...
He demonstrates the very distinction indicated by the word "however" (tu) in the passage beginning with "situated in the water" and ending with "having doubled."
The meaning is that [the soul exists] both as a reflection and as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

He states that even in the case of the reflection theory, the contradiction with the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* is difficult to avoid, saying "since" (*yataḥ*). Since the absence of that [reflection] in the Lord is equal to [the absence of the inner controller], it should not be argued [that the contradiction does not apply].

The connection [is as follows]. Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it means within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth. Now, one might object: just as the reflection of the entire lunar disc appears in water, so too should there be a reflection of the entirety of consciousness (*caitanya*) within the internal organ and other such substrates; it would not be the case that a portion of consciousness situated outside the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), which is not contained within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), is reflected.

And thus, since the Lord who is the prototype exists even within the cosmic egg (aṇḍa), there is no equality with the contradiction found in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa; [the author] says "no" and replies: "But not... He demonstrates the impossibility itself: "For not...
The words "or of light" imply "of that which is situated outside," while the phrase "even of that which is within water" refers to... [etc.]
The phrase "of the kāśa grass, etc. is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. "Therein" means "in water, etc. He states another example: "Not indeed," etc.

Therefore, just as the reflection in water is that of the sky within each individual cloud, so too the reflection in the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) must be the reflection of that which does not itself reside within them; since it is impossible for the original object (bimba) to exist in a different location from its reflection, the Lord exists as the inner controller (antaryāmin).
The absence of the quality of being born from Brahmā (*brāhmaṇāṃjasya*) is equal [in both cases];

what follows from that? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that a reflection cannot occur there of a portion that is included within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). The words "of that which is not included therein" refer, by ellipsis, to consciousness (*caitanya*).
The meaning is that conceptualization follows what is observed. Regarding the phrase "another modification" (*vikārāntara*):

since the portion of consciousness contained within the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) is situated within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the status of being a reflection (*bimbatva*) must be attributed to the consciousness situated outside of it; thus, the Lord who exists as the original reflection (*bimbabhūta-īśvara*) would also have to exist outside the cosmic egg. And if...

In the reflection theory (*pratibimbapakṣa*), in accordance with the Śrutis and other authorities that establish the Lord (*īśvara*) as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of all, one disregards worldly perception and accepts the reflection of the entire consciousness (*kṛtsnacaitanya*);
thus, the consistency of the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa* is established. In that case, the Lord is the unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinnacaitanya*).
The intended meaning is that the Lord (Īśvara) is consciousness delimited by the absence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); for, since the internal organ is a mental construct (*kalpita*),
the absence of the internal organ— which is real— is indeed present even when consciousness is delimited by the internal organ and so forth.
The resolution should be understood as follows: it is not possible for the Lord, whose nature is consciousness delimited by that [upādhi], to abide within all modifications;
therefore, the scriptural authority (brāhmaṇa) establishing that [Lord] is equally applicable.
Furthermore, it has been stated in the *Tṛptidīpa* that even non-existence (*abhāva*) serves as an upādhi for the Lord.

The distinction between the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) and the state of being Brahman is determined by the presence or absence of association with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa); it is not otherwise. Just as a positive attribute (vidhi) may serve as a limiting adjunct (upādhi), why should a negation (pratiṣedha) not do so?

Does the nature of being a chain not remain the same whether it is made of gold or iron? [In this way], through the exclusion of what is not that (atadvyāvṛtti), it is directly a positive affirmation.
"And the activity of the Vedāntas proceeds in two ways," so it has been stated by the Teacher.

This is the meaning of the verses: the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of individuality (*jīvatva*) and Brahman-hood (*brahmatva*) are distinguished—that is, differentiated—by their association with or dissociation from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the presence of that [limitation] is the adjunct (*upādhi*) of being a living soul (*jīva*), while the absence of that is the adjunct of being Brahman; thus, there is a distinction between the adjuncts of the individual soul and the Lord. It is not otherwise—that is, there is no other way for the state of being a living soul to have an adjunct. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only a positive entity (*bhāva*) can be an adjunct?"

Anticipating the objection that this does not apply to non-existence (*abhāva*), he states the lack of a decisive reason for distinction with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). He provides an example for the claim that there is no difference in the case where non-existence, like existence, possesses a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that serves to differentiate it, using the phrase "gold [chain]" (*suvarṇa*). Here, "chain-ness" (*śṛkhalātva*) refers to the quality of being a differentiator from unrestricted movement. Now, [one might object]:...

Having raised the objection that it is logical for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth— which are positive entities— to serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), because they are the means for the soul’s perception in the form of the "seer" and so on, [the author] intends to show that, by the same logic, since the negation of the internal organ is also a means for the perception of Brahman,
it is likewise logical for it to be the limiting adjunct of Brahman. Thus:
He states that the commentators have declared that the negation of those limiting adjuncts (upādhis) is the means for the realization of Brahman:
"By the exclusion of what it is not" (atadvyāvṛtti).

Here, by the word "that" (tat), Brahman is denoted. That which exists therein—namely, the collection of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth—is its exclusion or negation. The meaning is: by means of making that [Brahman] known through the form of that [negation]. And [it is taught] both directly and by way of affirmation.

The witness of the intellect, the witness of the Buddha, and the witness of all— seeing, hearing, and thinking— in such a manner, their activity proceeds by virtue of being the illuminator within Brahman;
thus, through this, the states of agency and enjoyment belong to the limited self (jīva) therein.

In that regard, the objection that— because the locus of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is distinct— there would follow the fallacies of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*),
is refuted even in the theory of reflection (*pratibimbapakṣa*), since [the reflection] belongs to that which is not contained within oneself but is in proximity to oneself.
