Since it must be stated that the reflection of the locus of consciousness occurs within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there would necessarily be a plurality of reflections due to the plurality of the original objects (*bimba*) whenever the internal organ moves from place to place; thus, the fault remains equal. Nor can it be maintained that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection in the internal organ.
Even though the defect is equal in both cases, the individual soul (jīva) is a reflection of ignorance;
its internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which moves from place to place, is like the reflection of a great mass of clouds pervading a body of water upon it.
It might be argued that this fault does not apply to the position that [the light] is the cause for the manifestation of distinctions there, like a spreading and expansive light; however,
it must be stated that because ignorance, unlike the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), lacks mobility, distinct reflections cannot arise.

[The opponent says: "It is [the view of] limitation (avaccheda). And thus, since according to the aforementioned reasoning both positions—the reflection (pratibimba) and the limitation (avaccheda)—are equal in their lack of consistency with the *Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa*, and since the impossibility of the reflection of consciousness has been demonstrated all the more clearly by the statement "being formless" (*nīrūpa*) and so forth, the position of reflection is abandoned in favor of limitation.

The sense is that the position [of non-restriction] alone is to be accepted. Thus, he states "by this" (*eteneti*) that even another defect in the theory of restriction (*avacchedapakṣa*) has not been refuted, as it is equal to the defects that will be mentioned later. Regarding the phrase "of that which is not included within itself" (*svānantargatasya*), the reasoning previously stated should be kept in mind; the intention behind the qualification "of that which is proximate to itself" (*svasannihitasya*) is as follows.

If a single reflection of the portion of consciousness— which exists outside the cosmic egg and not within all internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa)— were to occur in all of them, then, because there would be no difference in the location of the reflected consciousness (bimba-caitanya), there would be no distinction between the locations of the reflected consciousness for each respective internal organ.
It might be possible [to claim] by means of producing a distinction between reflections; however, that is not possible because a reflection is impossible for that which is separated [by space].

Rather, it must be stated that in each respective internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), only that portion of consciousness (*caitanya*) which is in immediate proximity serves as the original object (*bimba*). Consequently, it is logical that there is a production of distinct reflections both here and elsewhere.
"Because the defects are equal" means because the defects—namely, the fallacy of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāna*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*)—are equal.

This refers to what was previously demonstrated: that God (*īśvara*) is the reflection of consciousness (*cit*) in ignorance (*avidyā*), while the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection of consciousness in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

He raises an objection, suggesting that even though the defects are equal in the views of the *Saṃkṣepa-śārīraka*, the latter view should be accepted because the aforementioned defects do not apply to the position of the *Vivaraṇa* and other works. [The phrase] "na ca" [is used for this].
"Gatvaram" means having the nature of moving; "tadupari" means above the reservoir of water. "Visṛtvareti" [is used next].

Just as in various water regions, a fragment of intense light emerging from the gaps in clouds— possessing a nature of spreading and moving— is the cause of the specific manifestation of the reflection of the great mass of clouds pervading the reservoir of water, so too here and in other worlds is [the sense of] agency, enjoyership, and so forth.

The meaning is that the position is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the cause for the manifestation of specific [qualities]. He states the reason why there is no fault such as the loss of what has been performed (*kṛtahāna*) and so forth: "like the internal organ."
Likewise, even in the view that [the self] is limited (*avacchedapakṣa*), it is possible to accept that the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Even in that case, in order to avoid the faults of "losing what was done" (*kṛtahāna*) and "gaining what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*)— namely, that one part of a single soul is the agent while another part is the enjoyer— it must be [understood] in reality...

Furthermore, since the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) must be accepted as the basis for refuge, by that same logic, even in the case of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*),
it is possible to dispel objections by admitting that, in reality, there is only one consciousness and that the limiting adjuncts which delimit it are likewise one.

If those who maintain the theory of reflection (pratibimbavādins), having abandoned the position that the individual soul (jīva) is the reflection in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) due to its equality with the aforementioned defects,
instead adopt the position that the jīva is the reflection in ignorance (avidyā); then, even for those who maintain the theory of limitation (avacchedavādins),
they must likewise abandon the position that the jīva is limited by the internal organ, as it is fraught with defects such as the loss of performed actions (kṛtahāna) and so forth.

He states that the view which holds the individual soul (*jīva*) to be the Consciousness limited by ignorance (*avidyā*), being free from the aforementioned defects, is accepted: "In that very way," and "the *jīva*. This is also to be understood as an illustration; for since ignorance is a mental construction (*kalpita*), it is possible to maintain that the Lord (*īśvara*) is the Consciousness-Self limited by the absence of that [ignorance]. Thus, the *jīva* is the reflection in ignorance.

Having accepted the absence of defects such as the loss of performed actions (*kṛtahāna*) in the position [that the individual soul is Brahman] limited by ignorance (*avidyā*), the equality [of the two views] was demonstrated; now, in order to support the absence of defects such as the loss of performed actions even in the position that the individual soul is the reflection in ignorance (*avidyā-pratibimba*), [the following is stated] regarding the position that it is limited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

He anticipates and refutes the fault of the loss of what has been acquired (*kṛtahāna*) and so forth with the words "even there" (*tatrāpi*). This means even in the position that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*). "In a certain location" (*kvacit pradeśe*) means in a location delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) residing within a body such as that of a Brāhmaṇa. "Another location" (*pradeśāntara*)...
Thus [it is said].
The meaning is: the region delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) residing within the bodies of gods and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in reality" (vastutaḥ):
even though there is a difference in location, it is because of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) as the reflection of ignorance (avidyā), both here and elsewhere.

The faults such as the loss of what has been performed (*kṛtahāna*) and so forth must be avoided; the meaning is that for the proponent of the reflection (*pratibimba*), there is no other [logical] alternative. He states that this method of avoidance is the same even in the position of the limitation (*avaccheda*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

"Because of that [shadow]," meaning "in reality. The meaning is that although there is a difference in the locations of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) here and in the other world, there is no fault such as the loss of what has been performed (*kṛtahāna*), because consciousness is one in reality. Now, [an objection]: if there is merely an identity of consciousness in reality...
Since [the self] is common to other living beings, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that one person experiences the fruits of karma performed by another; therefore, he says:
"limited by that" (tadavacchedaka). The word "that" (tat) refers to consciousness (caitanya). Thus, the consciousness limited by a single internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is one individual soul (jīva).

The intention is that there is no such over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because it is accepted that the individual soul (jīva) is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). In this theory of delimitation (avacchedapakṣa), according to the method previously stated, God (īśvara) is consciousness delimited by the absence of a real internal organ; thus, "God has the causal [upādhi] as His limiting adjunct."
It should be understood that, in accordance with scripture, the Lord is either consciousness delimited by ignorance (avidyā) or [consciousness delimited by māyā].

Nor is there any fault in the view that [the Self] is delimited; for it is said: "Just as this luminous Self, the Sun, though one, enters into many different forms, and by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) the Lord is made to appear as differentiated within various fields (*kṣetra*), so too is this unborn Self. And for this very reason, the scripture provides the analogy: "Like the sun and its reflections," and so forth.
There is a contradiction with both the Śruti and the Sūtra; [this is so] because of the immediately following Sūtra which states: "But it is not so, because [the soul] is not apprehended like water."

He raises an objection regarding the contradiction of this position with both scripture (*śruti*) and the aphorisms (*sūtra*), stating: "Nor is it the case that [the soul is] limited" (*na cāvachedapakṣaḥ*).
Just as the single sun, entering waters divided by the difference of vessels—meaning, being reflected in many water-vessels—is made to appear in many forms of distinction; so too [is the soul].

Thus, the Lord, the self-luminous Self, though being one by His own nature, attains apparent diversity; that is to say, being reflected in the various fields which serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), He is rendered in the form of difference and diversity is obtained.
Just as there is a distinction in the case of a single sun caused by its being reflected in many limiting adjuncts.

In this way, it must be stated that the multiplicity intended here for the Self as well is indeed established by virtue of its being reflected in various fields (*kṣetra*); otherwise, there would be a lack of correspondence between the illustration and the thing illustrated, resulting in an inconsistency. Thus, the position of limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*) is contrary to the Śruti; such is the meaning. In this manner, [the Self] is indeed one alone.

"The Self of beings is established in every being; it is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water. "In every form, He became the counterpart of that form," and "He acts through the appearance of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa).
Such scriptural passages are also to be understood as demonstrating the reflection of consciousness within beings.

The Supreme Self, which constitutes the essential nature of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is perceived in manifold ways while being established as a reflection within all those entities—where "being" is repeated distributively to include every limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that acts as a mirror. Yet, by its own nature, it is seen as one, according to the scriptures. This is the meaning of the word "form" (*rūpa*).

"Upādhiparaḥ. Here too, the prefix *prati-* is used for the purpose of including all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as seen in the usage "this is a reflection of the person" (*puruṣapratirūpaḥ*) regarding the reflection of a person (*puruṣapratibimba*).
He cites the sūtra found in the third chapter: "For this very reason," because [the reflection] is of the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*).

In the Śrutis, oneness is intended as being intrinsic (svābhāvika) and plurality as being conditional (aupādhika); for this very reason, reflections of the sun in water and other such things are cited in the Śrutis as illustrative examples for its conditional plurality.

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: regarding the phrase "form, form" (*rūpaṃ rūpam*), the word *pratirūpa* in the Śruti does not denote a reflection (*pratibimba*). This is because there are counter-examples (*vyabhicāra*) such as: "Just as the one wind, having entered into various forms, became the form and the counterpart-form (*rūpaṃ rūpapratirūpaḥ*)," and so forth. Therefore, [it refers to] the sun and so on.

Precisely because of the inherent force of the analogy of the reflection, it must be stated that there is a reflection of consciousness; the author of the Sūtras himself raises an objection to that reflection with the words, "Like water."

Just as, for instance, in the case of the sun which possesses form, water that possesses form and is located at a distance from it is apprehended as being suitable for the arising of its reflection; however, there is nothing whatsoever that is both suitable for the arising of a reflection and distant from the all-pervading self. Having thus stated the impossibility of a reflection, [the author proceeds:]

"Because it participates in increase and decrease through inclusion, and for the sake of the consistency of both, it is thus. By the immediately following sūtra, it is shown that just as the sun reflected in water appears to increase when the water increases,
to decrease when the water decreases, and to move when the water moves, so too its [the individual soul's] [participation in these states] is superimposed (ādhyāsika).
Just as the increase, decrease, and so forth, which follow the water, are figurative;

likewise, because the self is included within the limiting adjuncts through its delimitation by the internal organ and so on, the increase, decrease, and so forth that follow it are merely figurative. Thus is the correspondence between the illustration and the illustrated.
"There is no contradiction because of consistency"— thus the author of the Sūtras himself stated the intended meaning of those two [sūtras] regarding the position of delimitation (avaccheda).

He states the meaning of the illustrative portion of the Sūtra with the word "yathā" (just as). Transparency (*svacchatvam*) is the fitness for the arising of a reflection. With the intention that there is no reflection therein of what is situated within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he says "tataḥ" (from that), which means in relation to the sun, which is the original object (*bimba*). He explains the applicatory portion (*dārṣṭāntika-bhāga*) with the words "naivam" (not so).

The consciousness-self (cidātman) does not possess suchness—that is, it does not have the same nature as the sun and other objects reflected [in water]. Why? Because of non-apprehension; that is, because the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth lack the capacity for the arising of a reflection of the self. For the internal organ is not situated in a location remote from the self, since the self is all-pervading (sarvagata).

Nor is it [the case that the self is reflected], because we do not accept that it possesses manifested form (*udbhūta-rūpa*); and because the conscious self (*cidātman*), like the sun and so forth, is not perceived as being fit to be a reflection, since it is a substance devoid of form (*nīrūpa-dravya*). Therefore, by way of the analogy of the sun reflected [in water], the relationship between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*) is untenable. This is the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*).

Even though there is no equality between the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) in terms of the aspect of being reflected images, there is no contradiction regarding their essential nature, because equality in the intended aspect is possible even there. Indeed, complete equality between the two is not possible anywhere; for if that were the case, [the status of] the illustration and the subject of the illustration...

Intending to show the similarity of the intended portion [of the present sūtra] on the grounds that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the annihilation of existence (bhāvoccheda), the author of the sūtras demonstrates it with the words "increase and decrease" (*vṛddhihrāsa*). In the phrase "immediately after that" (*tadanaṃtaram*), he explains the word *tat* as referring to the preceding sūtra, "like water" (*ambuvad*), by saying "just as" (*yathā*). The term "internal" (*ādhyātmika*) means established through delusion (*bhrāntisiddha*). Likewise, [he speaks of] the conscious self (*cidātman*).

Because it is delimited by the intellect and so forth, it is included within the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the intellect; thus, when the body and internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of an elephant or similar being expand, the conscious self (cidātmā) appears as if it expands, and when the body and internal organ of a gnat or similar being contract, it appears as if it contracts. When they move, it appears as if it moves, and when they are divided, it appears as if it is divided.
And thus says the Śruti: "It thinks, as it were; it moves, as it were.
When the intellect thinks, the Self thinks, as it were; when it moves, the Self moves, as it were—yet in reality, it neither thinks nor moves. Such is superimposition (adhyāsa).

The meaning is that, in accordance with the *Siddhāntabindu*, the intended sense here is the equality of the Self in its possession of qualities such as growth (*vṛddhi*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of those two": it refers to the previously cited scripture (*śruti*) and the aphorism (*sūtra*) based upon it, which provide the evidence for consciousness being reflected [in the intellect].
Just as when a jar containing space is being carried away,
it is the jar that is carried and not the space, so too the individual soul (jīva) is like space.
In this view of limitation (avacchedapakṣa), there is not only an absence of contradiction with the Śruti and the Sūtras, but indeed the Śruti [supports it].
He says that there is also support from the Sūtras: "contained in a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃvṛtam*).

It is well known that space delimited by a jar (*ghaṭāvacchinnam ākāśam*) exists; and just as that [space] is not carried away even when the jar is being carried, such is the illustration. In the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*) is like space (*nabhopamaḥ*), meaning it is equal to space. This is what is intended.

By using the term "Yama" (the restrainer) for the individual soul (*jīva*), which denotes its similarity to space enclosed within a jar, it is stated that the soul is of the nature of consciousness delimited [by adjuncts]. Likewise, the scriptural texts concerning "entry" also show that the conscious Self acquires attributes such as being seen only through the limiting adjuncts of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; they do not [show it to be inherently possessed of such qualities].

It is produced by the state of being a reflection. For instance, beginning with the passage, "This very [Self] has entered here up to the tips of the nails," the *Puruṣavidha Brāhmaṇa* states: "Breathing, he becomes what is called breath; speaking, he becomes speech; seeing, he becomes sight; hearing, he becomes hearing; thinking, he becomes mind. This is the meaning of the Sūtra.
This [Self], well-known in all the Vedāntas, is present here as the differentiator of name and form;
it has entered this aggregate of cause and effect, having made the tips of the nails its limit. Now, one might object:
while the entry of Devadatta into a house or a snake into a hole is well known, such is not the case for the Self.

An entry [into the world] can be conceived; however, because He is omnipresent, an entry characterized by reflection—like that of the sun and other luminaries in vessels of water—is not possible. Since such an entry was already refuted by the Commentator (Śaṅkara) during the discussion of the passages concerning entry in the Taittirīyaka and other texts, what kind of entry is it then?

When the inquiry arises as to what is intended by the term "having entered," it is as follows: just as the sun and other luminaries, having entered into water by way of reflection, are perceived as possessing the attributes of that [water], so too the Self—
which was already established prior to this as the presiding substratum within the aggregate— is perceived as possessing the attributes of the vital breaths, the intellect, and so forth.

Thinking that what is intended by the word "entered" (*praviṣṭa*) in this context is merely the state of being perceived— and not a literal, primary entry— the Scripture itself explains the word "entered" through the passage beginning with "breathing indeed" (*prāṇann eva*).
By performing the act of breathing— that is, the movement of breath— through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is called "the breath of the breath," and so forth.

In the Śruti, that which is denoted by the second occurrence of the word *prāṇa* becomes [the agent]; speaking—that is, performing the function of the organ of speech—one becomes denoted by the second occurrence of the word *vāk*, as in "the speech of speech," and so forth. Seeing form—that is, performing the visual mental modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) whose object is form through the attainment of identity with the internal organ—one [perceives] by means of the eye.
In the scripture beginning with "The eye," that which is denoted by the second occurrence of the word "eye" is [the Self], who— while hearing— that is,

performing the function whose instrument is the ear and whose object is sound, does so precisely through the attainment of identity with the internal organ (manas), as stated in the scripture beginning with "The ear of the ear."

The second [state] becomes denoted by the term "ear" when one considers [the self] as performing a function in the form of thinking independent of the eyes and other organs; thus, in the Śruti, it becomes denoted by the second term "mind" (manas) when performing the function of the mind.
The mention of the activity of the eyes and so forth refers to the aggregate of cause and effect.
This is a mere indication of activity in general.
Furthermore, because the position of limitation (avacchedapakṣa) alone is adopted by both scripture and sūtra in the passage, "A portion [of Him], on account of the designation of diversity."

Since all composite entities are perceived within the self, even so, there is a contradiction with the sūtra "If it is argued that [the self] is merely an appearance" (Ābhāsa eva cet) and its commentary located in the second chapter, which concerns the position of limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*).

And [the objection that the soul is] difficult to ward off is invalid, because it has been stated by [Śaṅkara] himself that the soul is a reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*). The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows:

the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed a manifestation; it is precisely the reflection of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and not the Supreme Self itself without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). Nor is it absolutely different from the Supreme Self, as in the Nyāya system, for there is non-difference [established by such texts] as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

Because it contradicts scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, since the reflection is in reality non-different from the original object (*bimba*), there is no contradiction with the aforementioned scripture in the view that it is not a mere appearance; this is the meaning of the word "and" (*ca*) [in the verse]. [Objection: No, because the position of the reflection was stated in the cited Sūtra and its Bhāṣya, and because of the objection raised in the Sūtra: "If [the reflection were the enjoyer], there would be no distinction [between the two], as in the case of the world. (BS 2.3.50).
It should not be argued that there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) for such an assumption because it would result in the doctrine being merely another philosophical school (*matāntara*);

for the Sūtrakāra himself, in the third chapter, has already refuted the theory of the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya-pratibimba*) through reasoned argumentation, and this serves as the restrictive principle (*niyāmaka*), as does the *Ābhāsa-sūtra* regarding the individual soul (*jīva*).
Furthermore, because no logical justification for [the self being] a reflection has been presented, this is the meaning of the sūtra *bhoktrāpatteḥ*:

"All this is indeed Brahman"—by this scripture, the non-difference of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) from Brahman is established. And by the scripture "I am Brahman," the non-difference of the class of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-varga*), who constitute the referent of the word "I," from Brahman is established.

It is thus established: and so, according to the two-fold Śruti, if one accepts the non-difference of the enjoyer and the world of objects from the one Brahman, then the enjoyer would result in being the object of enjoyment, and the object of enjoyment would result in being distinct from the enjoyer;
likewise, the enjoyer would also result in being non-different from the object of enjoyment—[this being the case] for those two which are non-different from the one Brahman.

If it is argued that because there is necessarily non-difference between them, an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) does not follow, and that in such a case a lack of distinction would result—contradicting perception and other means of knowledge that inform us of a distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed—it is replied:
the non-difference of the enjoyer and the enjoyed from the one Brahman is established by scripture. Regarding those two...

Both the fact that [the elements] are established by perception and other means of knowledge, and their mutual distinctness, are tenable in accordance with the world. Just as in the world, foam, bubbles, and waves— which are transformations of a single ocean— are non-different from that one ocean, so it is with these modifications.

Because the distinction between transformations is established by experience; for it is precisely because difference is established by experience that those very things, such as foam and the rest, possess mutual distinctness.
In this same way, there is [a distinction] between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, which are both transformations of the one Brahman.

The claim that both non-difference from Brahman and mutual difference among things are possible—and thus that there is no contradiction between the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita*) and perception or other means of knowledge—is not an interpretation of the contradiction accepted by our own school (*siddhānta*). This is because it is not admitted that the eternally immutable (*kūṭastha-nitya*) Brahman undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*). Rather, [the correct view is as follows:]...

The declaration in the Bhāṣya and other works that this is according to the intention of another school (matāntara) is as well-known as the ringing of a bell; the same applies here, such is the summary.

Regarding the term "part" (aṃśa): the individual soul (jīva) is a part of the Lord (īśvara). Why? Because of various designations (nānā-vyapadeśāt), as seen in such scriptural passages as, "He who dwells within the Self and controls it from within," and so forth, due to the relationship between the governed and the governor, and so on.

The literal meaning of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "because of the designation of the plurality—that is, the difference—between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)" is as follows:

here, the "part-nature" (aṃśatva) intended for the consciousness of the individual soul is of the nature of being delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), like the space within a jar; it is not, however, a primary part-nature, for a primary part cannot exist in Brahman, which is partless.
The meaning is that this is clear from the commentary on that particular section (adhikaraṇa) regarding "because of possibility."

Therefore, since the limitation of all-pervading consciousness by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth is necessarily inevitable, they favor the position that the *jīva* is this very limitation. Others, however,
maintain that the *jīva* is neither a reflection nor a limitation, but rather...
Just as the son of Kuntī (Arjuna) is [essentially] the son of Rādhā (Kṛṣṇa), so too the state of being a jīva belongs to Brahman itself through ignorance;

thus he concludes the support of the position of limitation (*avacchedapakṣa*). "Therefore" means: because a reflection is impossible, and because there is no contradiction in the position of limitation and there exists evidence for it. This is the meaning of the limitation of consciousness.

With the intention that even in the theory of reflection (*pratibimba*), it is more appropriate to postulate the status of being the living self (*jīvatva*) and so forth for that very [reflection] which is accepted by both parties, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), he says: "Limitation (*avaccheda*) is inevitable. Regarding "limitation": the living self is that which is limited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); the mention of the "living self" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), [including] that which is limited by ignorance (*avidyā*).
"God has the effect as his limiting adjunct (upādhi), while this individual soul (jīva) has the cause as his limiting adjunct"—
so says the Śruti. And in the Śruti, "Māyā and Vidyā themselves become the manifestation (ābhāsa)," it is said that there is an appearance.

The term *pada* refers to that which is delimited (*avacchinna*), because it has been stated that [the state of] existence (*bhava*) consists in the appearance of a reflection. Furthermore, the term *māyā-pada* refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the individual soul (*jīva*) first encountered; for the scripture itself states, "This individual soul has a causal adjunct" (*kāryopādhir ayaṃ jīvaḥ*). And the internal organ, which is introduced by the term *māyā*, is of the nature of primordial materiality (*mūlaprakṛti*).

This is conditioned by the relationship between the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*). The previous statement regarding the Lord as unconditioned (*anavacchinna*), and the statement regarding the Lord as conditioned by non-existence (*abhāvāvacchinna*) according to the *Tṛptidīpa*, are mentioned merely for the sake of possibility;

they do not represent the intended meaning (*tātparya*), because that would contradict the Śruti which states: "The Lord has as His limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) the cause of that [non-existence]. Regarding the unconditioned...

However, in the case of the position that [non-existence] is the Lord (Īśvara), because it lacks limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the capacity for being the agent of all knowledge and so forth is impossible; thus, this same defect applies equally to the position that non-existence is the Lord’s limiting adjunct. [Non-existence] is designated by such terms as Māyā, Vidyā, the unevolved (avyākṛta), Power (Śakti), the Imperishable (Akṣara), Space (Ākāśa), and so on.

For, like a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), that [non-existence] cannot be the determinant (*prayojaka*) of omniscience and other such attributes. Therefore, in the *Vākyavṛtti*, the venerable teacher [Śaṅkara] demonstrated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the limiting adjunct that determines omniscience and so forth, with the underlying sense being:
"The source of the world has Māyā as its limiting adjunct and is characterized by omniscience and the rest. Now, what...?
In response to the question, "Who is the Lord (Īśvara) and who is the individual soul (jīva)?", he sets forth another opinion as a reply: "But others [say]...
He asks, "Then who is the jīva? and "But what...? He provides the answer that the jīva is indeed Brahman itself, preceded by an illustration:
"Of the son of Kuntī alone..."—that is, of the son of Kuntī specifically, and not [of anyone else].
The meaning of the word "evam" (thus) is "from its reflection and so forth. The meaning of "rādheya-tattvam" is "the state of being a descendant of Rādhā";
the sense is "like that. However, the connection is with the phrase "of the unmodified itself.
This means "devoid of the states of limitation and reflection. In this regard, there is the concurrence of the Bhāṣya and the Vārttika.

He demonstrates this by way of its cause through the verse beginning with "vyādha" and so forth. Just as Karṇa, though born into a royal family, was raised from birth amidst hunters and, due to living among those of that same class, considers himself— through ignorance characterized by the delusion of birth— to be the son of a charioteer (rādheya) and not [a prince].
Furthermore, O son of Kuntī, one experiences even that which is self-established.

This is because it is established in the *Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad-bhāṣya* through the illustration of the prince raised among hunters that Brahman itself transmigrates by its own ignorance and is liberated by its own knowledge;
just as the state of being a hunter ceases for the prince upon the recovery of his memory, so it is for the Self when it is known.

And because of the statement in the *Vārttika*, "By means of such sentences as 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*)," it follows that Brahman itself, having assumed the state of a *jīva* through its own ignorance, is the creator of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Thus, even the Lord (*īśvara*), along with attributes such as omniscience, is imagined by the *jīva* like a deity perceived in a dream.
Thus they say.
Fallen from the supreme good resulting from his status as a son of Kuntī, he experienced manifold sufferings everywhere, characterized by various kinds of curses and insults.
And once, the Blessed Lord Vivasvat gave him the instruction: "O Karṇa, son of Kuntī, you are not a woman, but a man worthy of honor."
By that recollection, having been made to remember his own true nature—which is free from being the locus of disease, being afflicted, and so forth—ignorance was removed;

and when that [ignorance] had ceased, he abandoned the manifold sufferings caused by being the locus of disease and affliction, and attained the highest good (śreyas) prompted by the recollection of his identity as the son of Kuntī. In the same way, Brahman also [attains liberation] through the beginningless, established [recollection].
Having its own true nature veiled by its own ignorance, it attains the state of being a living individual (*jīva*) and falls away from its self-established, eternal, and unsurpassed nature of bliss.
Consequently, it transmigrates; thus, while transmigrating, Brahman at times—like during the state of dreaming—[experiences various conditions].

The meaning of the commentary is as follows: when the ignorance that causes the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) and so forth is removed by means of the knowledge (*vidyā*)—which has a beautiful object (*sugocara*) and is produced by a teacher and scripture imagined through one's own ignorance—one is liberated and experiences the established, unsurpassed bliss solely through the consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*). Regarding the phrase "of the ignorant" (*ajñasya*): it means of one whose own true nature is veiled by ignorance.

The meaning is that when ignorance is removed by the knowledge produced by the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and others as instructed by the Guru, the state of being a *jīva* ceases for the Self. Having thus defined the *jīva*, he defines the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding the phrase "and thus": through a careful examination of the Bhāṣya and the Vārtika, [he describes the Lord] as being devoid of the nature of a reflection and so forth.

The meaning is: this being established—that the full Brahman alone exists as the individual soul (jīva). The connection is that even the Lord (Īśvara), along with attributes such as omniscience, is imagined by the individual soul.

He states the reason why the aforementioned individual soul alone is the imaginer of the Lord, beginning with the words "by its own ignorance" (svāvidyayā) and so forth, because there is no other imaginer.
To establish the intended meaning—that the individual soul (*jīva*) fashions the Lord—[the author] provides an illustration: "In a dream," etc.

Just as in a dream the dreaming individual soul itself fashions the Supreme Deity, endowed with attributes such as omniscience, and having fashioned Her, worships Her day and night; through that worship...

Thus one obtains the fruit characterized by both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). Such is the intended meaning of the illustration regarding staying awake and so forth.
Now, regarding this soul (*jīva*) being one, some who rely on the position just mentioned say:
"The soul is one; therefore, only one body possesses a soul, while others are soulless, like bodies seen in a dream. This is their ignorance.

The entire world is imagined; its entire empirical discourse exists as long as ignorance persists, like the perception of a dream. Furthermore, there is no established distinction between the bound and the liberated, because the individual soul (jīva) is one.
Even the liberation of Śuka and others is merely imagined, like the liberation of another person seen in a dream.

In the context of defining the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he begins another line of inquiry with the words "as stated immediately above. This means: as stated in the text beginning with "Brahman itself transmigrates through its own ignorance and is liberated through its own knowledge," and so forth. The term "one" (eka) means that because Brahman is one, and because the positions of limitation (avaccheda) and reflection (pratibimba) are not accepted therein.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the individual soul (*jīva*) is one, then only a single body would be endowed with life, and not all bodies. He dispels this doubt by accepting it as a desired consequence, saying: "And by that... One might further object: "Just as in a single body movement is observed in the form of activity for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, so too [should it be in all bodies]."

It is seen in all bodies. To the question of how only one body can be possessed of life, he says: "The others. Just as in the state of dreaming, the body of the dreamer alone is possessed of life, while the other bodies seen by the dreamer appear to possess specific movements [though they are not].

It should be understood that even though things appear as living beings while dreaming, they do not exist in that way; the same should be seen to apply to the waking state as well. Now, one might object: "While sleep is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the creator of the dream-world—since it exists when the dream occurs and is absent when it does not—there is nothing whatsoever established through such concomitance as the creator of the waking phenomenal world."
He says "no" to the claim that the world must be real; [he states] "because it is unknown by that [Self]. This means "because of the ignorance of the individual soul (jīva).
The point is that the fact that ignorance is the cause of the world is established by the scriptures.
Now, if all worldly activity were merely imagined—like the activity in a dream—then, just like that, [it would cease] all at once.

[Objection: There would be an abolition of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), and thus knowledge (*vidyā*) would be rendered useless. [Reply: He says "no," with the words "of that" (*tasya*). This means "of the individual soul" (*jīva*). Just as the continuity of dream-transaction persists until the exhaustion of sleep, so too the continuity of all transactions is logical until the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) through knowledge; therefore, there is no futility of knowledge.

The intention is that [the Lord] perceives this for the sake of removing ignorance (*vidyā-nivṛtti*). Now, one might object: "If there were only one individual soul (*jīva-eka-tva*), the established distinction—where one soul is bound and another soul is liberated—as proven by scriptures such as those concerning Śuka and the mother-of-pearl shell, would not be possible. Anticipating this doubt, he says "bound" (*baddha*) to show that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Just as one who has awakened from a dream [does not see the dream].

The meaning is this: just as one instructs another person regarding a liberation established through delusion, so too does one instruct the very person regarding the liberation of cloth and other objects established through the delusion that they are the self (*jīva*), for the purpose of engaging them in such practices as hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*).

And here, the washing away of all possible doubts must be performed by means of the stream of water that is the analogy of the dream. Others, however, failing to find conviction in this doctrine of one soul in one body, [cite the Sūtra: "But [the soul is] manifold, because of the designation of difference, as in the world."

By means of such sūtras as "Līlā-kaivalyam" (Sūtra 2.1.33), it is established that the Lord alone—who is superior to the individual soul—is the creator of the world, and not the individual soul; for although the Lord has no purpose to fulfill since His desires are already attained, the creation of the world occurs solely out of His divine play (līlā). Thus it is stated.
And those who, perceiving a contradiction [in other views], maintain that Hiranyagarbha alone [is the creator]...

An objection is raised: "In the doctrine of the identity of the individual soul (jīva), since there would be no one other than oneself to instruct in knowledge, the arising of that knowledge would not occur; furthermore, because of the absence of any distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, the practical activity of the soul, such as the worship of the Lord, would be impossible. Anticipating this, he says: "And here... Just as in the state of a dream, one perceives a certain teacher or even the Lord within the dream itself.

The sense is that one meditates upon those two after having conceptualized them, and through them one obtains knowledge and so forth; it is just like that. Thus he states another view within the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*). "Others, however" (*anye tu*); "a single body" (*ekaśarīra*)—that doctrine of a single soul in which there is only one body possessing a soul is described as such. "Based on the mind" (*manaḥ-pratyayam*)—of the mind...

The meaning is: "trust" refers to the certainty of its being authoritative. One might argue that there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) for the claim that only one body possesses a soul while all other bodies are soulless; nor should it be said that the identity of the soul (*jīvaikya*) serves as such a determining factor, because there is likewise no determining factor as to which specific body a single soul occupies.

The sense is that it is impossible to express [otherwise]. As for the phrase "moreover," the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas established in the first chapter—which posits the Lord as non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*)—is not tenable; for if that were the case, attributes such as the Lord’s status as the creator of the world would result in being properties of the individual soul, which would contradict experience.

The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of refuting the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). It is accepted that Brahman—which is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) due to its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—possesses attributes such as being the creator of the universe and omniscience. Therefore, there is no possibility of the attributes of Brahman applying to the individual soul, even though there is a distinction based on limiting adjuncts.

Because [the distinction] is established in the world by way of the determination of dharmas. He states the reason for accepting an imagined distinction: "because of the designation of difference. The meaning of the Sūtra is that in passages such as "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, and controls the self," there is a designation of difference regarding the relationship between the controller and the controlled, and so forth. "As in the world" means:

The Sūtra has already been explained previously. Here, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the Sūtra beginning with "But because of the impossibility, [it] is not the embodied one" (*anupapatter tu na śārīraḥ*) is understood. The meaning of the Sūtra is that [the one possessing qualities such as being made of mind (*manomaya*)] is not the embodied self (*śārīra*), precisely because of the impossibility of [attributes] such as "being the agent of all actions" (*sarvakarmatva*) in that [embodied self]. And [the phrase] "and contradiction" (*virodham ca*) [is also included].

In this doctrine which denies the existence of an Īśvara distinct from the individual soul (jīva), there is no Īśvara who possesses the capacity for the creation of the world and so forth, nor one characterized by empirical difference.

They maintain the doctrine of a single soul in multiple distinct bodies, asserting that the primary soul is the reflection of Brahman, while other souls are its reflections— mere semblances of souls comparable to the reflected image of a person seen on a cloth when that body is depicted in a painting— and it is these [semblances] that undergo transmigratory existence and the like. Others, however, [hold a different view].

Thinking that there is no determining factor as to which specific Hiraṇyagarbha possesses the primary status of being the *jīva* given the distinction [of Hiraṇyagarbhas] in every kalpa, they hold that there is only one *jīva* who presides over the entire body in a particular manner; and it is not as if there were a division of body parts in this way.
Even upon the dissolution of the body, there would be the undesirable consequence of mutual recollection of pleasure and so forth.

The meaning is that there would be a contradiction with those sūtras that establish qualities such as existence, being the creator of the world, and being the self of all. Regarding the phrase "the reflection of Brahman": according to this view, the original archetype (bimba), which is Brahman, exists as the Lord (Īśvara) who is superior to the individual soul (jīva); therefore, there is no contradiction with the cited sūtras.

It has been indicated. Regarding the word "tat" (that): the meaning is that other individual souls (*jīva*) and the semblances of non-sentient beings (*ajīva-ābhāsa*), which are reflections of the primary *jīva*—namely Hiraṇyagarbha, who is a reflection of Brahman and possesses the capacity for creation and so forth due to his material adjunct (*upādhi*) as the creator of the elemental world—are like that [Hiraṇyagarbha] in their lack of such creative power. The term "kalpāḥ" means "equal."

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "partaking of saṃsāra and so forth": by this, a distinction is indicated from the previous doctrine, which held that just as the body of Hiraṇyagarbha is endowed with life by the principal *jīva*, so too are other bodies endowed with life by the *jīvābhāsa*s (reflections of the *jīva*). Here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include liberation; for there is also liberation for the *jīvābhāsa*s.

It should be understood that there is the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha, who is one's own reflection, and subsequently the attainment of pure Brahman. Regarding the phrase "that with distinctions" (*sa-viśeṣa*): it refers to that [doctrine] in which, within the theory of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), there exist many bodies possessing distinctions and individual souls; the meaning is that they maintain or accept such a view.

Expressing dissatisfaction even with this [view], he states the doctrine of a single living being (*ekajīvavāda*) itself: "But others... and "There is only one... He explains that the living being (*jīva*), which is the reflection of Brahman in ignorance (*avidyā*), is indeed one because ignorance is one;
and that very same [being] presides over every body for the sake of its own experience and so forth, rather than there being a reflection of Brahman in [separate instances of] ignorance.

Hiraṇyagarbha presides over his own body, whereas other bodies are presided over by the appearances of his reflections. Why? Because there is no evidence for the status of other individual souls (jīvas) as being such reflections; this is the meaning of the word "only" (eva). [The phrase] "without distinction" means:

The meaning is: "without a distinction between primary and secondary. For only if there were a plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) would such a distinction be possible—namely, that one soul is primary while another is a secondary semblance of a soul (*jīvābhāsa*). But this is not the case, because it is accepted that [the Self] is one; this is the intended sense. Now, [an objection is raised]: "Devadatta’s head..."

It is observed that there is a coordination such as, "Just as there is pain in the head of one person, so there is pleasure in my foot," regarding hands and feet; likewise, if a single soul were the presiding controller of all bodies, [there would be a similar coordination] such as, "There is pleasure in Devadatta’s body for me, and [pain] in the body named Yajñadatta."

He raises the objection that there would be the undesirable consequence of everything being connected with everything everywhere in the form of "suffering" and so forth, stating: "And it is not thus."

Since it is observed that there is no recollection of happiness and so forth from other births, it is postulated that the difference of bodies is the cause for the lack of such recollection; therefore, the yogi’s recollection of happiness and so forth within his various bodily manifestations is a case of perceiving an object that is spatially or temporally remote.

Because [the case] is like that of grasping or like the manifestation of yoga, and because there is no destruction [of the individual], they do not accept that as an illustration; thus, they favor the doctrine of a single soul in multiple bodies (*aneka-śarīra-eka-jīva-vāda*).
Others, however, argue that since the absence of a distinction between bound and liberated states is equal even here, [it applies to] whichever among the gods...
If it is argued that this is because of the prohibition found in such scriptural passages as, "He alone awoke; he became that," and so forth.

Since it is accepted that the difference between bodies is the cause of the lack of recollection [of past experiences], the aforementioned over-extension does not occur. Nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of evidence for this; for even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is one and the same across past bodies and the present body, the fact that we do not observe the recollection of things such as pleasure from other births establishes the difference between those bodies.

He provides the rebuttal, "by that which belongs to another birth," because the status of being its instigator (*prayojakatā*) is commonly accepted. Now, one might object that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because we observe continuity of consciousness even when a yogi possesses different bodies; to this he says, "But in the case of the yogi... The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from people like us. He shows this by saying, "by the body... For it is not the case for people like us...
There is direct perception of an object that is spatially remote because of the absence of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) that would cause it;

thus, the mere difference of bodies is not the cause of that [non-perception]. Rather, it is the difference of bodies conjoined with a specific unseen force that is the cause of the failure to reconnect. Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases where there is a fit for recollection.

The state [of being]. "Yogaja" means born of yoga; "dṛṣṭaparam" means having seen the highest. That doctrine in which many bodies are presided over without distinction by a single soul—that is what is meant by "so. He raises the doctrine of multiple souls with the words "the others," etc. "In this case as well" means even in the immediately preceding view. If, in the doctrine of a single soul, the established order [of experience] is accomplished, then...

Anticipating the objection, "What is the fault?", he states that the fault is the inconsistency with the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and commentaries: "tadyo yaḥ" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.5). Among the gods, whichever god directly realized—that is, had the direct intuition of—that Brahman, he alone became that Brahman; no other, being devoid of the realization of Brahman. [This establishes] the liberation of the knower and the non-liberation of the ignorant.

Furthermore, by means of a scriptural text (*śruti*) that establishes [the soul's] growth, the distinction between bondage and liberation is demonstrated. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the scriptural text "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*)—which is accepted by the Commentator and others as establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation—is included. As for the mention of "scripture" (*śruti*), it refers to that which, having gone...

"Those do not return; that is my supreme abode," and so forth—this is an illustration of such scriptural passages (*śruti*). "Because of the prohibition" refers to this *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra. In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the Kāṇva recension, there is the statement:
"His vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart. This concerns the departure of the vital breaths for one who knows the reality of the Supreme Brahman.

The negation of its departure [is established] because its movement is preceded by departure; this is the meaning of the Sūtra's statement "If it be argued... which serves as the basis for the Siddhāntin’s objection.

Not being satisfied with the profound inconsistency of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) in the section beginning with "na śārīraḥ" (not the embodied one), which establishes the states of bondage and liberation, [the author] resorts to the doctrine of multiple individual souls (*anekajīvavāda*) by accepting that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth constitute the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).
They establish the distinction between the bound and the liberated; regarding this, some say as follows concerning the three [times].

The author refutes the prima facie view with the words, "Not from the embodied self. In the Mādhyandina recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad itself, within the same context, there is the statement: "From him, the vital breaths do not depart," referring to the embodied self who knows Brahman. Here, by the word "him" (tasmāt), the embodied self under discussion is meant.

The word "body" (śarīra) is understood here; because it is the primary referent in relation to the body, the sentence "not from that" (na tasmāt) negates the departure of the vital breaths from the embodied soul (jīva), not from the body. Therefore, even for the knower, there is indeed departure from the body.

Regarding the statement of the Kāṇvas, "There is no departure of the vital breaths (prāṇas) for him," the meaning should be understood as follows: for that wise one, the vital breaths do not depart from the body, but rather go to the world of Brahman together with him. As for the phrase "not ending" (nāntastham), it means the absence of an end, that is, the absence of logical consistency [in the opponent's position].

Regarding the phrase "of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth": one should not say that even in the doctrine of manifold individual souls (*nānājīvavāda*), there is an equal contradiction with the meaning that Brahman alone transmigrates through its own ignorance and is liberated through its own knowledge— as established in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya*—
because the demonstration in that *bhāṣya* concerns Brahman alone...

Through its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), which has transformed into the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [the Self] attains the state of various individual souls (*jīva*) and transmigrates; for it is logically consistent that the intended meaning is that it is gradually liberated through its own knowledge (*svavidyā*). This is because the commentary, which establishes the liberation of Śuka and others as supported by *śruti* and *smṛti*, states: "Brahman itself, through its own ignorance..."

It cannot be argued that the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*jīva-nānātva*) is not established from those [scriptural] passages, because it is improper to interpret them otherwise by following the mere literal sense of the word "transmigrates" (*saṃsarati*).

Nor can it be said that the cited Śruti, Smṛti, and Bhāṣya texts lack the purport (*tātparya*) of establishing the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikatva*), for they do indeed have that as their purport; thus, the doctrine of the plurality of souls is not proven from them. This is because even in the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), [the same applies].

Nor should it be argued that the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is established because the absence of intended meaning is equal [in all cases] and because ignorance (*avidyā*), which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the soul, is one; for, in accordance with the cited scriptural passages and their commentaries, it is possible to accept the multiplicity of ignorances. As for that unity...

The sense is that it is possible for the Śruti and other authorities to intend reference to the genus [of individual selves]; furthermore, even though ignorance (*avidyā*) is one, since there is the scriptural statement that "this individual self (*jīva*) is [defined] by its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are its effects," it is possible to accept that the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) themselves serve as the limiting adjuncts for the state of being an individual self. This is the case in the doctrine of manifold selves (*nānājīvavāda*), according to different philosophical views.

He begins to establish the system of bondage and liberation with the words "Among them" (teṣu). This means: among those who maintain the doctrine of manifold souls (nānājīvavādins); "some" (kecit) refers to a certain group within that category.

Although ignorance (*ajñāna*) has as its sole locus and object pure Brahman, and liberation consists precisely in that [locus], nevertheless, because a portion of ignorance remains in one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)— given the acceptance of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) arising from a trace of ignorance— ignorance possesses parts; thus, when the realization of Brahman arises with respect to a certain limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that very [portion of ignorance] is [removed].
It ceases with respect to other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as it previously continued through other parts; however, others argue:

"But even in the doctrine of manifold souls (*nānājīvavāda*), if the soul is conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-upādhika*), then since primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is one, it would have been removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) attained by Śuka and others, and consequently, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) should not be perceived at present."

With the intention of raising an objection, he asks: "Even though... [The phrase] "having the pure Brahman as its locus" means that it is not possible for ignorance to have the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—in their qualified forms—as its locus, because those two are themselves superimposed (*kalpita*).
Thus, the status of being an object, which consists in being veiled, belongs to the pure [Brahman] alone, and not even to the Lord.

The sense is that since non-perception is established solely through the distinction caused by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as in the case of one living being [perceiving another], it is useless to postulate for the Lord, with respect to individual souls (*jīvas*), the state of being an object characterized by being veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "only one": [it refers to] the unborn, single Māyā.

One should know that [ignorance] is indeed the material cause (*prakṛti*). The sense is that its oneness is understood from the hearing of the singular number in such scriptural and traditional texts as "in the knowledge which produces the distinction," as well as from the simplicity of the tradition. And "only upon its destruction" refers to such passages as "and again at the end, there is the cessation of the universal illusion (*viśvamāyā*)" and "having reached the absolute end through the destruction of ignorance."
The point is that, according to the Śruti and Smṛti, liberation is understood to be the cessation of ignorance, which is the root of all misfortune.
It is not accepted that the destruction of the entirety of ignorance occurs through the knowledge of reality regarding a single [object], by which there would be no systematic distinction;
rather, through the knowledge of that [object], only that specific portion of the root ignorance which has transformed as that particular internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth is destroyed.
Destruction is accepted [of ignorance]. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of evidence for its having parts;

for it is admitted that even when a portion of ignorance possessing the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) is destroyed in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), a portion of ignorance possessing the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) persists until final liberation (*videha-kaivalya*), as it has not been removed by knowledge. Thus, [ignorance] possesses parts.

Because it is understood that [ignorance] possesses parts; for thus, since there is the possibility of infinite parts in the form of portions belonging to the indeterminable ignorance itself, which are likewise indeterminable, he provides a resolution by establishing the distinction between bondage and liberation through their multiplicity, beginning with the words "Even so" (*tathāpi*). [This refers to] the existence of ignorance.

The view is that bondage is [the connection with ignorance] and its destruction is liberation; thus it is considered liberated. Now, for consciousness, the connection with ignorance is bondage and the lack of such connection is liberation. It is not, however, the cessation of that [ignorance], because the cessation of bondage is established by the mere absence of connection; rather, the cessation of ignorance occurs through knowledge.
Even for the explanatory scripture (*pratipādaka-śāstra*), its purport (*tātparya*) is established precisely through that lack of connection [with the ultimate]; otherwise,
upon the arising of the opposing knowledge that destroys the root ignorance, there would be no remainder, just as a tuft of cotton is consumed when it comes into contact with the opposing fire.

He states the view of others—those who think that [if liberation were not real], the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation as well as the scriptures on liberation while living (jīvanmukti) would result in being without foundation—with the words "But others... (anyetviti).

Just as, according to the view of the *anyathānyathā-ekadeśin*, the absence of the conjunction with a jar (*ghaṭa-saṃyogābhāva*) is the regulator for the existence of the absolute absence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāva*) on a surface, so too, when the absolute absence of a jar exists pervasively across many locations,
[it is determined] in a certain location...
Just as the conjunction of a jar ceases to connect with other locations upon the destruction of that jar, so too, when ignorance manifests within consciousness,

the mind acts as its regulator; thus, ignorance— which exists by connecting to specific regions of consciousness through that limiting adjunct (upādhi)— is pierced in certain places by the arising of the vision of Brahman.
According to the method stated in the Śruti, "The knot of the heart," when the mind ceases to function, one is no longer joined [to saṃsāra]; otherwise, one remains as before.
They say that bondage and liberation consist precisely in the association with or dissociation from knowledge. Others, however, maintain that ignorance does not have pure consciousness as its locus.

First, he states an example relevant to the subject at hand, beginning with "yathā" (just as). On the ground, the absence of a jar is established by experience; for it is accepted that this absence exists throughout the three periods of time. Thus, even after the jar has been removed, it continues to exist in its locus, namely the ground. Likewise, even when the ground possesses a jar, one perceives that "the jar does not exist [there]."
Fearing the consequence that [the cognition] would be invalid (*pramā*), the Naiyāyikas postulate this as a solution:

since there is no relation between the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar and its locus (the ground), it is established that the cognition of it [as existing] there is an error (*bhrānti*). Furthermore, prior to the production of the conjunction with the jar, on the ground...

It should not be asked how there can be an absence of the relation consisting in occurrence (*vṛti*) for that [absolute non-existence] which possesses a relation at the time of the conjunction of a jar; for, in accordance with our experience, when the absolute non-existence of a jar occurs in a location such as the ground,
the restrictive factor is the absence of either the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or the non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) of the conjunction of the jar.

Since, through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is possible for the absence of a jar to lack a relation with the ground that serves as the locus of the jar’s conjunction, he illustrates this very position [of the opponent] by saying, "the view of a certain Nyāya partisan. Regarding the phrase "in those [cases] likewise" (*tadvatsu*): it means "in those cases where there is an absence of the conjunction of a jar. Regarding the phrase "by that limiting adjunct" (*tadupādhinā*): it means "by the mind itself as the limiting adjunct."

"In some place" means in a locus of consciousness (*caitanya-pradeśa*). The connection is that [the mind] ceases upon the arising of the vision of Brahman. To provide the authority for the statement that "the vision of Brahman is what causes the cessation of the mind," he says, "it is split asunder. In the phrase "the knot of the heart," the word "heart" refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and that internal organ—
Because it is superimposed upon the conscious self (*cidātman*), it has attained identity with it; thus, it is called a "knot" (*granthi*) because it is like a knot.

And that [knot] dissolves into Brahman itself once the vision of Brahman has arisen—this is the meaning of the Śruti. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": the meaning is "in other regions of consciousness. Regarding the phrase "not ignorance": [it refers to] pure consciousness.

The meaning is that that which is propounded by the Vedānta scriptures cannot be the substratum of ignorance, because it is experienced solely as the object of ignorance in the form: "I do not know the reality known through the Vedānta."

However, that [knowledge] which has Brahman as its object and resides in the individual soul (jīva)— existing in all individual souls, which are reflections of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), like a genus (jāti) residing in each individual instance—
abandons one who has produced such knowledge, just as a genus abandons an individual instance that has perished; it is that very [knowledge].
Liberation; they say that the established rule is that it takes up another [basis] as before.
One experiences, "I am the living self (jīva)," and "I do not know. Since ignorance is experienced as having the living self alone as its substratum,
it should not be argued that it is untenable for ignorance to reside in the living self, which is consciousness qualified by its own effect, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

It must be stated that since consciousness which has become a reflection within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) alone is accepted as being the individual soul (jīva), and the qualified entity [the internal organ plus consciousness] is not accepted as the soul, and because the internal organ is beginningless, its reflection is also beginningless; how then could it be the locus of beginningless ignorance? This is what must be addressed.

Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is understood to have a beginning because its dissolution is heard of in states such as deep sleep and its birth is heard of at the commencement of waking, its beginninglessness in the form of gross and subtle states has been established in the Sūtra by the principle that what exists can only be manifested, just as in the case of masculinity and femininity.
Just as semen, blood, breasts, and other physical forms that are unmanifest in childhood become manifest in youth—
this being a manifestation of what already exists— it is likewise logical that this internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), while existing in an unmanifest state during sleep and so forth,
undergoes manifestation in the form of attaining a gross state; it is not [the manifestation] of something non-existent.
"Because the production of things such as a hare's horn is not observed"—this is the meaning of the sūtra.

For it has been established during the discussion on the distinction between Māyā and Avidyā that Avidyā is beginningless and resides upon the reflection of consciousness. [The term] "each" [is used] because ignorance, like duality or plurality, [belongs to each individual].

If ignorance were to exist as a pervasive property (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) across all individual living beings (*jīvavyakti*), then the direct perception "I am ignorant" would not occur for each individual. This is because the perception of a pervasive property depends upon the perception of all its substrates;
thus, for any single soul (*jīva*), there would be no perception of all souls. In reality, however, regarding ignorance...

It should be understood that even though [the cognition] has a distributed existence (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), because that cognition is of the nature of the eternal witness (*nityasākṣin*), it does not depend upon the perception of all its substrata; for the aforementioned rule applies only to the domain of produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*). Regarding the word "some" (*kañcit*): when the mind is withdrawn by means of the arisen knowledge (*vidyā*), [the cognition] is defined by that [mind].
The sense is that because even the state of being a reflection has ceased, there is the destruction of the individual manifestation whose nature is consciousness qualified by that [reflection].

And thus the Śruti says: "The other [Īśvara] leaves her behind once she has been enjoyed," meaning that he abandons this ignorance—denoted by the word *ajā* (the Unborn)—which has its enjoyment experienced by the *jīva*. She is called *bhuktabhogā* because she is the one whose enjoyment has been experienced.
The meaning is that, according to this etymology, the objects denoted by the term "enjoyment" (ābhoga) are transformations of ignorance (avidyā).

The sense of the scriptural passage is that the "unborn" (aja) is devoid of birth, while the "other" is the individual soul (jīva) who has arisen with knowledge. "He alone" means he alone [is the Lord]; "the other" refers to the ignorant one. And thus says the Śruti: "For the one unborn, rejoicing, lies near [the other]"—here, "one" [refers to the Lord].
Furthermore, the unborn [Self], devoid of discrimination, while embracing—that is, serving—ignorance which has transformed into the form of the aggregate of cause and effect, dwells within it;
that is, following after that [ignorance], it lies down, meaning it exists [in that state]. It possesses the conceit of "I" and "mine" therein.
That is to say, it does not abandon [them].

Others, however, while accepting a distinction of ignorance (*avidyā*) for each individual soul, justify the states of bondage and liberation through the persistence and cessation of that [ignorance]. If it is asked, "By whose ignorance was the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) created?"— since there is no determining factor, it is created by the ignorance of all [souls], and thus it is manifold.
It is like a cloth already begun; when one person is liberated through the destruction of their ignorance,

there is the destruction of the common phenomenal world— just as a cloth is destroyed by the breaking of a single thread— while at that very moment, other phenomenal worlds arise through the remaining ignorances, just as another cloth is produced from the remaining threads still present.
Some say that it is the production of an internal world common to both the complete and the other [categories].

By stating here that "one abandons some ignorance while remaining supported by another," it is also implied that bondage and liberation arise from the connection with and the disconnection from ignorance, respectively; for no other meaning is possible for that statement.
Both of these two views—that bondage and liberation consist in the connection with and the disconnection from ignorance—belong to him [the author].

Considering that [the view] contradicts the natural tenor of the Śruti, Smṛti, Bhāṣya, and other texts which establish that [avidyā] is destroyed by knowledge, he states the view that is not so contradictory: "But others... and "only having admitted... [meaning] even while not admitting the existence of difference due to avidyā.
Since it is impossible to establish bondage and liberation as being of the nature of destruction [of that unity], nor can it be argued that even though it is one,

liberation in the form of its destruction is established by postulating the existence of parts— as was previously suggested— it must be noted that it has already been stated that such persistence is untenable once the opposing knowledge (*vidyā*) has arisen; thus, there is no liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
It should not be said that this contradicts the acceptance of the persistence of a trace (leśa) of that [avidyā];

for the intention is that even when avidyā has been destroyed, its residual impression (saṃskāra), which persists until the exhaustion of the prārabdha, is intended to be designated as a "trace of avidyā," as will be stated with supporting examples. Thus...

Having established the manifold arrangements of bondage and liberation within the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*nānājīvavāda*), he introduces an objection by relying on the diversity of ignorance (*avidyānānātva*) which was incidentally introduced as being useful for that establishment, saying: "In this view..."

The meaning is: the position that there is a plurality of ignorances (*avidyā*). To the question "Of whom?"—does the commencement of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) proceed from the ignorance of a single individual soul (*jīva*), or from the ignorances of all? It cannot be the first, because there is no determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) [to establish it as such]. Nor can it be the second; for if one ignorance were destroyed, there would follow the destruction of the entire phenomenal world, and consequently, the liberated souls would [perceive] no other souls.

The intention of the objection is that [the world] would result in the non-perception of all manifold diversity (*prapañca*). Having taken up the second position, he refutes the inconsistency stated therein with the words "due to the absence of a determining factor" (*vinigamakābhāvāt*), etc.
The phrase "produced by all ignorance" (*sarvāvidyākṛta*) means that it is the transformation of all ignorance belonging to all individual souls (*jīva*). Alternatively:

The meaning is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman made the object of all ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the first explanation, he states the illustration: "commenced by many realities" and "common to those other than the Sakalas.
"Those other than the Sakalas" refers to those who are distinct from all the unliberated individual souls (*jīvas*). It is common to them.
The meaning is "of another conceptual proliferation."

Just as in the Nyāya system the illusory silver produced by various instances of ignorance is distinct for each individual— similar to the duality produced by various relative cognitions (*apekṣābuddhi*)— so too the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether and the rest, produced by various forms of ignorance (*avidyā*),
is distinct for every person. As for the silver seen by you in the mother-of-pearl shell:

Others say that, in this way, the claim that [the Lord] is "sinless" is merely a delusion of identity; for the māyā residing in the Lord, which is the cause of the phenomenal world, is distinct from the multitude of avidyās residing in individual souls.

Although the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is entirely the product of ignorance (*avidyā*), the author states—along with an illustration—the view that because there is a distinction between those ignorances, the phenomenal world itself is indeed distinct for each individual. He says: "That [and] that," etc. Now, one might object: where a delusion of silver occurs in a mother-of-pearl shell simultaneously for many people, there, due to the distinction between the individual ignorances, a corresponding distinction in the produced silver would also exist here.

It must be stated as an illustration, yet that is not possible; for even in that case, it is impossible for a single person who was previously ignorant to suddenly produce silver. If this is argued, we say no; because by the power of destiny, when a certain person first perceives the specific characteristic of mother-of-pearl, [the thought arises] "this is not silver."
