The point is that even when silver together with its substrate is destroyed by a subverting perception (*bādhakapratyakṣa*), the distinction from silver must necessarily persist because the error regarding silver continues in other things; thus, the illustrative example is established.

Regarding the phrase "in the Nyāya view": in the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, just like oneness, duality and so forth also exist as long as the substance exists, and not [as mere conceptual constructs].

In this regard, [duality] is produced by *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition). This is because it would be cumbersome to postulate an infinite number of dualities and their subsequent productions and so forth;
rather, it is accepted that *apekṣābuddhi* is the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of that [duality]. Thus, there is no consequence of its being perceived at all times.

The meaning is: "because of acceptance. Now, an objection: if that were so, then just as each respective silver is perceived by that very person alone and not by another, likewise the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) imagined by each respective ignorance (*avidyā*) would also be perceived by that very person alone and not by another; and thus, the very world-phenomenon that is experienced by you—[that same one...]

He dispels the doubt that recognition—such as "this is also being experienced by me"—would not be a form of perception, by means of an illustration: "the mother-of-pearl and the silver. This is merely an illustrative example. In the Nyāya system, the recognition "those very two, Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, who were seen by you have been seen by me too" is [an instance of] duality.

Just as it is seen even when there is a difference [between individuals], it should be understood that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ether (*viyat*) and so forth is not a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to individual souls (*jīva*). Rather, *māyā*—which is distinct from the collection of ignorances residing in individual souls—is accepted as the common material cause (*upādāna*) for the transformation into the phenomenal world of ether and so forth, which is shared by all souls. Therefore, ether and so forth...

Because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is one, he shows that the cognition of its unity is merely figurative by stating, "residing in the individual soul" (*jīvāśritā*). Since the evidence for Māyā being distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*) and for its residing in the Lord (*īśvara*) has already been presented previously, it is not stated here.

Others, however, maintain that the ignorance of individual souls (*jīvas*) serves both as a mere veil (*āvaraṇa*) and as an instrumental cause (*upādāna*) for illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika*), such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. The nature of being the material cause, along with its relevant corollaries, has thus been concluded.

Fearing that ignorance (*avidyā*) might be rendered useless if it lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he says: "Of the individual souls" (*jīvānām*).

The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to dispel the aforementioned doubt. The meaning of the word "only" (*mātra*) is the absence of being the material cause even with respect to any effect whatsoever. And [it is said]: "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own *yogamāyā*."

In the words of the Blessed One, I am not the Supreme Self who manifests as the light of the entire multitude of living beings in the form of perfect bliss and so forth; rather, this is due to Māyā, which constructs for me a collection of attributes such as omniscience, lordship over all, and being the self of all.

It should not be said that this contradicts [the scripture], because the meaning of "due to being veiled" is established as the māyā residing in Īśvara alone being the veiler of Brahman; for, in accordance with the experience that the veiler [of the thought] "I do not know Brahman in its true nature" resides in the jīva,
it must be stated that the avidyā residing in the jīva alone is its veiler.

The sense is that, since the word *māyā* occurring in the words of the Blessed One is logically justified as characterizing the ignorance (*avidyā*) that constitutes transmigratory existence within the individual soul (*jīva*) and consciousness (*caitanya*). For, just as in the case of concealment (*āvaraṇa*), ignorance is also admitted to be the modifying material cause (*pariṇāmī-upādāna*) even for illusory projection (*prātibhāsika-vikṣepa*); thus, there is no room for the suspicion of redundancy.

With this intention, he says: "prātibhāsika" (apparent). Now, an objection may be raised: while it is possible for the ignorance residing in individual souls (*jīva*) to serve a purpose there as the material cause of the dream-world—which is apparent and superimposed upon the consciousness of the soul—it is not possible for that same ignorance to be the material cause of nacre-silver and the like. This is because [nacre-silver] is superimposed upon the consciousness limited by the nacre and so forth.

If it is argued that these [three] do not exist in the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) of silver and so forth, [we reply: True; however, there is no fault, because by the word "etc. (ādi), dream and the like are intended here. Alternatively, as in the view of Vācaspati, even the case of shell-silver and the like is [an instance of] the limited [form of] shell (śuktyavacchinna) made an object of the individual soul's ignorance (jīvāvidyā).

There is no fault, for it is consistent to explain the utility of the individual souls (*jīvas*) and their ignorance (*avidyā*) in cases such as illusory silver by intending them to be transformations (*vivarta*) of pure consciousness. Furthermore, regarding the previously stated definition of Brahman as being both the non-different efficient and material cause, it has been established that its nature as a material cause consists in its being the substratum of the illusory transformation (*vivartādhiṣṭhānatva*).

In connection with that, the definition of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been reached; following that, the discussion of the oneness and plurality of the individual soul, as well as the bondage and liberation, and the oneness and plurality of the phenomenal world (prapañca), has become relevant. Since all of this has now been defined, he concludes [the section] for the purpose of facilitating the understanding of the subject matter to be discussed hereafter, stating: "It is concluded."
The meaning is "it is finished. Regarding the term *upādānatvam* (the state of being the material cause), the meaning is "a formal definition."

Now, what kind of agency (*kartṛtva*) do some say [the creator possesses]? Based on such scriptural passages as "It thought; it desired; it made itself by itself," they hold that it primarily consists in possessing knowledge, desire-to-act, and volition that are conducive to the effect, much like a potter. Others, however, [hold a different view].

If, in order to sustain the status of being an agent characterized by the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) and volition (*kṛti*), one were to require further instances of desire to act and volition, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Therefore, the agency (*kartṛtva*) of Brahman consists solely in possessing a knowledge that is conducive to the effect; and this same fallacy does not apply even to that knowledge, because [the knowledge]...
Because, being of the nature of Brahman, it is not an effect.

He raises an objection in order to define agency as included within the definition [of Brahman]: "The object," etc. The meaning is that agency is impossible as a property for Brahman, who is indifferent (udāsīna).
He refutes this by stating, "Some say," etc., on the grounds that although such agency is impossible by its own nature, it is possible through the influence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi).

Alternatively, one might object that it is not possible for Brahman, as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, to be its agent (*kartṛ*), because we do not observe that the clay and so forth, which are the material causes of jars and other objects, are their agents. To this, [the author] replies with the word "Now" (*atha*).
For we observe that in the case of the conjunction between a jar and God, it is God alone who, being the material cause, acts as the agent. Thus, [it applies] to Brahman.

He refutes [the objection] by stating, "Some say," and so forth, on the grounds that its agency is possible due to the force of the scriptural texts (*śruti*) establishing its authorship. Alternatively, what kind of agency is intended here in the definition of Brahman? Is it of the nature of possessing knowledge, desire to act, and volition, or rather...

[The definition of agency] as "possessing knowledge conducive to the effect" or "possessing knowledge consisting in the contemplation of what is to be created that is conducive to the effect": the first [option] is not [correct], because there is no evidence for such agency on the part of Brahman.
Nor are the second and third [options correct], because if the knowledge conducive to the effect were itself an effect, then [one would require] another agent to account for its agency.

The point is that if there were a dependence on another cognition, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress; and if that [cognition] were not an effect, then Brahman—whose very nature is eternal cognition—could not possess agency in the form of possessing such a cognition. Regarding this, he demonstrates the proof for the first position:

Some say that in the Śrutis, the words "that" (*tat*) refer to Brahman itself; the meaning of "by itself" (*svayam*) is that it did not require any other agent. "It made itself in the form of the world" means that it acted as if it were an agent. By these Śrutis, knowledge, will, and action are shown to be conducive to creation.

The sense is that [these qualities] are being established. Nor should it be argued that since knowledge and the other [qualities] are also effects, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because they would require further instances of knowledge and so forth to account for their agency; for the intended meaning of "agency" (*kartṛtva*) is restricted to effects distinct from the triad of knowledge and the rest, and thus no infinite regress follows. Knowledge and the rest...

The intention is that, by refuting the first position—that there will be another creator for the triad—he establishes the second position with the words "But others... [stating] "because it would lead to an infinite regress.
This is because, in order to avoid the failure to conform to the definition of agency, one must acknowledge [agency] in every effect whatsoever.
The sense is that if agency were defined as possessing the triad [of will, knowledge, and action], there would indeed result the fallacy of infinite regress.
"Possessing knowledge alone"—by the word *eva* (only/alone), desire and action are excluded from those two;

the sense is that it is because of the complexity [gaurava] involved in including them within the definition of agency. Nor is this so in the case of the two cited scriptural passages regarding desire and action...
It should not be said that the demonstration would be futile.

And thus, the statement in the *Vivaraṇa* that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the agent of pleasure and so forth is consistent with the *Kalpataru*'s explanation: for the creation of ether and the rest is accomplished by mere observation (*vīkṣaṇa*), whereas the material creation is accomplished through effort exceeding mere observation, being effected by means of Hiraṇyagarbha; therefore, it is described as "smiling" (*smita*). Thus, the statement of the *Kalpataru* is also reconciled.

The meaning is that although those two [the *śruti*s] establish them as the cause of creation, there is no evidence for the claim that they are presented as such specifically to justify their status as agents; this is because [the Self] is not an effect (*akāryatvāt*).

The fact that Brahman, whose very nature is eternal consciousness, possesses such knowledge must be understood by taking into account a distinction conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*). Nor should it be argued that even so, this contradicts the scriptural statement "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), which establishes that the knowledge which is the cause of creation is not occasional; for [the nature of] Brahman...

The sense is this: although cognition is impermanent, it is occasional because it is qualified by an occasional auxiliary characterized by the ripening of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of living beings; it is with this in mind that the scriptural statement [of its being an agent] occurs.
He states the means of knowledge for the claim that agency consists merely in possessing a cognition conducive to the effect: "In this way..."
And thus: the meaning is that when it is intended not to include agency within the definition of desire and volition, [it refers to] "of the individual soul" (jīvasya).

Just as that [soul] possesses a witness-form of knowledge conducive to the arising of pleasure, pain, and so forth, likewise there is no desire and so on conducive to those [states], because of the lack of experience and because it is not admitted. Not [so].

It should not be argued that this is untenable because the production of pleasure through the performance of its means by one desiring pleasure is established by experience; for what is intended here is the absence of desire-to-act (*cikīrṣā*) and volition (*kṛti*) directed toward the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the locus of pleasure and so forth. Thus, it is merely the possession of knowledge conducive to the effect [that is meant].

The meaning is that the statement in the *Vivaraṇa* is consistent only if agency (*kartṛtva*) is accepted, and not otherwise. "His breath is the Vedas; his glance is the five elements; his smile is the moving and the unmoving; his sleep is the great dissolution."
In the *Vācaspati-śloka*, it is stated that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are perceived by Brahman; likewise, in the *Kalpataru* commentary—

which is devoted to explaining the purport of both [texts] regarding the fact that the material world of moving and non-moving beings is the very smile of Brahman— it is established that the great elements are to be accomplished by the mere perception of Brahman.

The objective basis for the mention of that [Brahman] being "desirous" has been shown. And this is consistent with the admission that Brahman possesses knowledge conducive to the creation of the great elements, as well as the volition and effort conducive thereto;
for there is no contradiction with the qualifying term "mere," which serves to exclude volition and so forth other than the act of looking (*vīkṣaṇa*). For in the world...
A smile in the form of a gentle laugh is well known to be achievable through an effort exceeding that required for mere knowledge. Likewise,

just as Brahmā requires a specific act of observation (*īkṣaṇa*) toward the material creation, so too is an additional effort required for the activity characterized by the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha within the creation of the moving and unmoving world.

Since the agency of Hiraṇyagarbha, like that of the Supreme Brahman, is established by Śruti and Smṛti, it has been shown that the dependence on further activity— namely, the contemplative vision (īkṣaṇa) conducive to the creation of the non-manifest— that belongs to the Supreme Brahman, is the basis for the designation of the moving and unmoving world as having Brahman as its sole reality.

Furthermore, that [agency] is not possible for the Sacrificer (yajvan) even when there is a requirement for greater effort on the part of those who behold the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). The meaning of the statement "by means of Hiraṇyagarbha" is "in dependence upon the birth of Hiraṇyagarbha," but it does not mean Hiraṇyagarbha himself.
The meaning of the scriptural text should be understood as follows: Brahman is both the direct agent (*sākṣātkartā*) and the efficient cause (*prayojakakartr*).

This is because, in the final section of the second chapter, the status of the Supreme Lord as the direct agent even in the creation of the material world has been established; such is the intended sense. Furthermore, the verse by Vācaspati is intended for the praise of Brahman.

For Brahman is most highly praised; for it is from that Brahman that all the Vedas arise as effects without effort, like the breath of a person, and by whose mere glance the great elements come into being,
and with whom Hiraṇyagarbha [abides] the universe consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
The sense is that the mere gentle smile of Him for whom even the great dissolution is like deep sleep is itself a singular marvel of His excellence.

Others, however, maintain that agency (*kartṛtva*) consists in possessing a cognition in the form of an intention regarding what is to be created that is conducive to the effect; it is not merely the possession of a cognition conducive to the effect. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the individual soul (*jīva*) is an agent even in cases such as the illusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell or dreams, since the soul possesses the knowledge of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which is conducive to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*). It is not [merely that].

It should not be argued that the individual soul (jīva) is the creator of the dream-world, because the scripture itself states, "He who creates chariots, horses, and roads is indeed the maker," and so forth;
for the author of the Bhāṣya has explained that this is merely a figurative attribution of agency, like saying, "The plow carries the ox."
They say that because it has been explained as being the cause for the manifestation of chariots and so forth,
by this very fact— the state of being the creator of the entire cosmic manifestation— the omniscience of Brahman is established as a matter of course.
Pointing out the defect even in the second position, he supports the third position with the words "apare tu" (others, however).

Regarding "sraṣṭavyālocanā" (the observation of what is to be created): the meaning is that it takes the form "this is to be created by me. Regarding "adhyāsa" (superimposition): it refers to the knowledge of the substratum which is favorable to the object of superimposition, such as silver.
The meaning is "by virtue of possessing that [nature]. As for the phrase "nor is this an undesirable consequence" (*na ceṣṭāpatti*), the word *na ca* is to be connected with the word *vācyam*.

The word *atha* means "at the time of dreaming. He states the reason why the individual soul (*jīva*) is the creator of the chariot and so forth: "For he is the agent" (*sa hi kartā*). The meaning is: because the individual soul is the agent of the karma that causes the chariot and other things in dreams, therefore [he is the creator]. [This is] by the authors of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāraiḥ*).

In the expression "the plough carries the oxen," the primary sense—that the plough is the agent of the oxen's standing or that it is what pulls the oxen—does not exist; rather, it is said figuratively because, when the plough exists, there is the acquisition of straw and other fodder through agriculture, which serves as the cause for the oxen's maintenance. Thus, one says, "it carries the oxen."

In the same way, his status as the agent is figuratively attributed to him by means of the cause consisting in his being the creator of merit (*dharma*) and so forth— which are the causes for perceiving objects such as chariots in a dream— and by means of the cause consisting in his being the basis for the appearance of those chariots and other things; for it is said in the Śruti, "He is indeed the agent," and thus the commentators [explain] that this agency is of a figurative nature.

The meaning is "because it has already been stated. By this, the statement in the *Vivaraṇa* that pleasure and so forth possess agency is also explained as being merely figurative; for even in the absence of the knowledge consisting of the reflection "I am this pleasure, pain, and so forth," [the experience of] pleasure and so forth [occurs].

It should be understood that there is no contradiction with the *Kalpataru*, which states that because primary agency is impossible through mere vision (*darśana*), and because [creation] is accomplished by "mere looking" (*vīkṣaṇa-mātra*),
what is intended here is "looking" in the form of the contemplation of what is to be created.
Furthermore, by the *Janmādi-sūtra*, Brahman is defined as the cause of the entire universe, being both its agent (*kartṛ*) and its material cause (*upādāna*).

When this has been established, his omniscience is proven by implication; for the status of being the creator of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the entire world is impossible without omniscience. Thus he says: "By this very [fact]."

In the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Because the Veda has its source in Him" (Śāstrayonitvāt), it was established that Brahman is also the author of the Veda. Now, how can the omniscience of Brahman be consistent? For, unlike the individual soul (jīva), the absence of an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) makes even the status of being a knower impossible. To this, [the answer is: regarding all objects... [all-knowledge]... *(Note: The provided fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical flow of the argument as presented in the source text.)*
Īśvara is conditioned by ignorance colored by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of his own volition (prāṇidhi).
Therefore, His omniscience arises from being the witness to all objects and their latent impressions; this is the position of Bhartṛhari, Tīrtha, and others, which has already been shown previously.
He states another reason for the establishment of omniscience: "Because He has the scripture as His source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*). He explains the meaning of this aphorism:

"Also by virtue of being the author of the Veda. Now, just as the authorship of the Veda establishes omniscience according to the manner described in the *Bhāṣya* and other works, so too does the status of being the creator of all things, which is included in the [aphorism] beginning with "birth and so forth" (*janmādi*), establish it.

This establishes that [point]. And so, one might ask: "What is the reason for saying that while [the quality] was established by implication in the previous sūtra, it is here being formally established? It is said in reply: Because of the difference in intent (*tātparya*) and the presence of [explicit] existence [of the probandum], the previous sūtra was concerned with the definition (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas this [sūtra] is concerned with the formal proof (*sādhana*) of omniscience; thus it is so.
This is the conventional usage. Consequently, the application of the aphorism is: "Brahman is omniscient because it is the author of the scripture. Now, one might object:

"The omniscience of Brahman is established directly by such scriptural passages as 'He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, the possessor of qualities, the knower of all sciences'; so what need is there for a formal proof? This is true; however, regarding what is stated in the scripture...

Because the firmness of the path toward omniscience is established through such scriptural authority and logical reasoning, [the author] introduces an objection in order to define the omniscient being as proven by both scripture and reason. He begins with the word "Now" (*atha*).

For the individual soul (*jīva*), the state of being a knower consists in its being the substratum of knowledge in the form of the modifications of its own limiting adjunct, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The status of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is not possible for Brahman, as established by valid means of knowledge, because of the absence of an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in it. Nor should it be argued that Brahman also possesses an internal organ; for scripture restricts this internal organ to being the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), stating, "This individual soul has the effect [the body] as its limiting adjunct. Furthermore, the state of being a knower is pervaded by omniscience.

Because omniscience is a specific form of the nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Thus, by the cessation of the pervader—which is Brahman’s nature as a knower—there follows the cessation of the pervaded, which is omniscience; this is the meaning. The sense of the word "only" (*eva*) is that in the absence of the nature of being a knower, omniscience is cast far away. Even though the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), [the same principle applies].
He offers a rebuttal, stating that omniscience is somehow possible because those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) constitute the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of God.

Regarding the phrase "here, all things," the word "here" means "in this objection. The phrase "the latent impression of all objects as the witness" refers to the latent impression that constitutes His own limiting adjunct.
The meaning is: by virtue of its illuminating all objects as its domain.

The proponents of the theory of the pre-eminence of the object (*prakaṭārthakārāḥ*) say: just as for the individual soul (*jīva*), the transformations of its own limiting adjunct, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are the receptors of the reflection of consciousness, and through that connection, [the soul] possesses the status of a knower; so it is for Brahman.

Since there exist reflectors that take as their substrate the transformations of *māyā*, which is its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)— though existing throughout the three periods of time— is apprehended through direct perception by means of the manifestations reflected therein; thus, [the Lord] possesses omniscience.

The authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, however, maintain that because it is possible for Brahman to have direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the entire existing universe according to the method described above, and because recollection is established through the presence of impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by that perception,
the existence of all past objects is proven; thus, prior to creation, [Brahman perceives] the entire universe being created within Māyā.
This is because [the world] manifests as the appearance of objects in accordance with the unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) of individual souls;
and because Brahman, being the witness of that [world] and having it as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), is established as its prover.
Keeping in mind the lack of satisfaction regarding the previously mentioned solution, he states another solution:

"The authors of the *Prakaṭārtha*, however," and so on. Just as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the knower-ship, so too is *māyā* the limiting adjunct for knower-ship; and thus, in Brahman—

The meaning is that there is no possibility of suspecting the cessation of omniscience, because there is no cessation of the quality of knowing—which is pervasive—within that which has *māyā* as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is because of the scriptural statement, "He who is measured by his own limiting adjunct, *māyā*" (*svopādhimāyāmāpīnam*), and because of the declaration in the *Vākyavṛtti*: "The source of the world, characterized by omniscience and so forth, has *māyā* as its limiting adjunct."

The sense is that it is established that *māyā* is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord (*īśvara*). The meaning of "characterized by omniscience and so forth" is that He possesses unique attributes such as omniscience, universal sovereignty, and being the self of all. "Because of discerning" means because of making [it] an object of cognition.

Regarding the phrase "the authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, however": according to the view of the authors of the *Prakaṭārtha*, even with respect to the manifold objects of the past and future, the Lord's knowledge—which is a form of direct perception—is free from the veil of *māyā*.
According to the view of the authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi*, the Lord's knowledge regarding objects such as the past is [direct], just like that of individual souls (*jīvas*).

The word "only" (*eva*) has the sense of specification, meaning "only that which is beyond the senses. The term "existing" (*vidyamāna*) is used because, in the world, it is observed that the nature of perceptual cognition is to have as its object only present things; since there is no reason to deviate from this established nature, [perception cannot apprehend the past or future]. Furthermore, the scripture that establishes omniscience belongs to God (*īśvara*).

The sense is that [the Lord] is indifferent toward whether knowledge is mediate (*parokṣa*) or immediate (*aparokṣa*). "Produced by that" means produced by the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of an existing object. He establishes the cognition of a future object with the words "prior to creation. The term "manifestation" (*sphuraṇa*) refers to a mental modification (*vṛtti*); it denotes the state of being undergoing illusory transformation (*vivartamānatva*) or the state of undergoing real transformation (*pariṇamamānatva*).
"Of that which has that as its limiting adjunct" means "of that which has māyā as its limiting adjunct. But how [is this so]?

They establish omniscience by asserting that it is the arising of consciousness whose object is a thing that has come into being. The authors of the *Kaumudī*, however, say that Brahman’s omniscience consists in its own essential nature as knowledge, because it illuminates everything with which it is connected; this includes even the past and the future within [the scope of] ignorance (*avidyā*).

In the case of a variegated reflection, just as a variegated color is perceived through the manifestation of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too is its conjunction [with the substrate] possible because it exists in the form of a latent impression. Now, one might object that [the Lord's] omniscience would consist in the cognitions of his states (*vṛttijñāna*).
This is not so, because it contradicts the exclusive scriptural statement: "Everything shines only after Him who shines" (*tameva bhāntamanubhāti sarvam*). Regarding creation...

Because of the restrictive statement "in the beginning, one alone, without a second," the dissolution of even the functional cognitions (vṛttijñāna)— just as that of the great elements— must be asserted; otherwise, it would follow that Brahman lacks omniscience at that time.
Therefore, he states that [the Lord] possesses adjuncts (*dupādhikatva*). "By being its witness" (*tatsākṣitayā*) means by being reflected in that *māyā*.
Regarding the phrase "of creation," it refers to that which exists prior to it. He states the cause of transformation: "by the unseen merit and demerit of the individual soul" (*jīvādṛṣṭa*).

"Because its status as the means of accomplishment is established"—this means that agency is established through the function (*vṛtti*) of *māyā*. "Regarding the future," etc.—the meaning is that the existence of knowledge concerning future objects, which consists of a reflection in the function (*vṛtti*), is possible within Brahman.
Just as in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), the omniscience of Brahman is likewise described by means of functional cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*) endowed with the reflection of consciousness.
By means of two views. Now, he defines that [world] by means of knowledge of its own nature (svarūpa-jñāna) alone, stating: "But according to the author of the *Kaumudī*... [Objection:

But since there is no evidence for the existence of the past and future worlds during the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) or prior to creation, Brahman’s omniscience would not be established at those times; for consciousness cannot relate to what is non-existent.

He says "no" because of the impossibility of their being mixed together; [he explains] "even of the past and the future. This is because it has been established by the authors of the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas in the Devatādhikaraṇa that the past phenomenal world exists in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) at the time of dissolution, and likewise, the future world exists in the form of latent impressions alone prior to creation.

The meaning is that since [the existence of] the sentient being has been established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* and other sections, the omniscience of the Brahman-consciousness conjoined with past and other objects is proven even then.
The "unopened state" (*anunmīlitatva*) of the variegated [world] means its non-manifestation; the reason for that is its "emission," which is none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the phrase "citra-miti" (the cognition of the variegated): a metaphor (*rūpaka*) is to be seen here. This is the intended meaning: at the time when the gross phenomenal world (*sthūla-prapañca*) exists, the subtle phenomenal world consisting of latent impressions (*saṃskāra-ātmaka sūkṣma-prapañca*) does not exist; and at the time of dissolution (*pralaya-kāla*) and so forth, the gross phenomenal world does not exist.
Thus, because the consciousness of Brahman (*brahma-caitanya*) is never always conjoined with the entire phenomenal world, it is eternally [unconditioned].
"His omniscience cannot exist [otherwise] than as uncontracted.
He states what is excluded by the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) in the phrase "by the knowledge of its own nature alone" (*svarūpajñānenaiva*), namely:
"but not by means of modifications of consciousness" (*na tu vṛttijñānaiḥ*). This restriction in the scripture excludes that which is distinct from the self-luminous Self (*svaprakāśātma*).

The meaning is that the world, beginning with the sun, is being illumined by the nine [suns]. Here, this must be considered: if the Vedic restriction (avadhāraṇa) is contradicted by the requirement of a modification of *māyā* (*māyāvṛtti*) for the purpose of the manifestation of the world by the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacaitanya*), then [the same applies] to the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*).

Even if there is a dependence on the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) for the manifestation of objects such as a jar, this [dependence] is indeed contradictory [to the thesis], because those modifications of the internal organ are insentient (*jaḍa*). Even with that dependence, the meaning of the restrictive scripture— that "all insentient things are manifested by consciousness alone" (*caitanyamātrāvabhāṣya*)— is not [contradicted].
In that case, the same resolution applies even when there is a dependence on the veil of māyā.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that the Lord lacks the status of a creator with respect to the initial illusory manifestation (*māyā-vivarta*) consisting of the act of seeing (*īkṣaṇa*), as well as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth which follow it. This being the case, Brahman would consist merely of knowledge regarding all objects, but would not possess the nature of being an omniscient knower.

If it is argued that [Brahman] is omniscience, that is true; Brahman consists solely of the knowledge of all objects, but it does not possess the nature of a knower consisting in the agency of producing all knowledge.

He states the objection regarding what fault there would be if omniscience were absent at the time of dissolution: "The initial," etc. That is to say, if omniscience were absent at that time, then at the beginning of creation, the "seeing" (īkṣaṇa) described in the Śruti—"He thought"—which is conducive to the creation of the elements, [could not occur] due to the absence of agency.

The meaning is that there would follow the consequence of Brahman lacking agency with respect to the creation of the elements and so forth preceded by [His] observation. Here too, this must be considered: even in this case, at the time prior to creation, Māyā and its connection with Brahman exist as something distinct from the consciousness of Brahman.

A primary determination of non-duality (advaita) is not possible. If it is argued that, by the force of scriptural passages and other authorities establishing the beginninglessness of *māyā* and so forth, those statements are intended to determine the absence of a second entity consisting of unmanifested effects (*avyākṛta-kārya*), then [the text] would always be concerned with all objects.

The hypothesis that the statement regarding the Lord's being "accompanied by another" (sadvitīyatva) is intended to establish the absence of any effect other than the continuous stream of the veil of *māyā*— which constitutes omniscience— on the strength of scriptural passages (*śruti*) and other authorities that teach omniscience as consisting in the agency of knowledge,
is equally [untenable]. Indeed, the support of omniscience through the veils of *māyā* alone is what is accepted by the *Bhāṣya*.

And likewise, the commentary on the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* states: "Moreover, for one who is a transmigrating soul possessing ignorance and so forth, the arising of knowledge would depend upon a body and other such factors;
but this is not the case for the Lord, who is devoid of any cause that obstructs knowledge—at the time prior to creation."
This [verse] is intended to refute the Sāṃkhya objection that it is impossible for Brahman’s contemplation of what is to be created to take the form of "seeing" (īkṣaṇa),
because it is established in the world that seeing in the form of a functional cognition (vṛttijñāna) must be accomplished by causal factors such as a body,
and Brahman lacks such a body and so forth.

The commentary states that for the individual soul (jīva) alone, the arising of knowledge as a mental modification (vṛtti-jñāna) is dependent on the body and other factors; however, for the Lord (īśvara), the arising of knowledge in the form of a modification of Māyā is independent of the body and so forth. Thus, even prior to creation during the period of dissolution (pralaya), His vision in the form of a modification of Māyā and His eternal omniscience persist.
"It is possible" (saṃbhavati) is the intended meaning of the commentary's resolution (*samādhāna*).
This commentary has been interpreted by the commentators in exactly this way;
it should be understood that ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are the causes of the obstruction to knowledge (*jñāna-pratibandha-kāraṇa*) according to the commentary. And therefore—

It should be understood that the refutation of the position which seeks to establish omniscience through the veil of *māyā* is inconsistent. He raises an objection: "This being so" (*evaṃ sati*) means that this is so when omniscience is established by the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) alone.

[The opponent replies: "But not..."—the sense being that this is not the case because the knowledge of one's own nature is eternal. It is not, however, of the nature of being the agent of all cognitions.

The word "of Brahman" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, although the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) is a general form while the status of being the agent of all cognitions (*sarvajñānakartṛtva*) is a specific form— and thus their non-difference is not possible— nevertheless,
the intended meaning is precisely that Brahman does not possess the state of being a knower, and not [anything else].
Even though non-difference is stated between those two, there is no contradiction.

For this very reason, in the section on *vākyānvaya*, the authors of the Bhāṣya stated that "being the knower" (*vijñātṛtva*) is a characteristic mark of the individual soul (*jīva*); thus, even scriptural passages such as "He who is all-knowing" (*yaḥ sarvajñaḥ*) must be interpreted solely with the intention of [the Self] having the nature of knowledge (*jñānarūpatva*). Although...
By the very consciousness that is the nature of Brahman, it illuminates everything with which it is in contact.

"Precisely for this reason" means: precisely because Brahman lacks the status of being a knower. "Thus it is stated" refers to what is recited in the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "It is for the sake of one's own self that everything becomes dear; therefore, indeed, the Self, my dear, should be seen," and so forth. Here, is the individual soul (*jīva*) presented as the seer? Or rather—

The doubt is whether the inner Self, which is non-different from the Supreme Self, is by nature devoid of phenomenal manifestation (*niṣprapañca-svabhāva*). Regarding this, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: because the individual soul (*jīva*), the enjoyer, was the subject under discussion in the preceding passage, and because even in the concluding statement—"By knowing whom one would know this knower, O Maitreyī"—the quality of being a knower, which is an attribute of the individual soul, is mentioned, [it must be the soul].

Thus, it might be argued that what is taught here as the object to be seen is [the individual soul]. However, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*), alone is taught as the object to be seen. Why? Because of the syntactical connection of the passage (*vākyānvaya*). To explain: here it is propounded that by knowing the Self, everything becomes known; and this [knowledge of everything] is possible only by accepting Brahman as the substrate of all.

Likewise, even such statements as "All this is the Self" (*sarvam ātmā*) are seen to be connected with the intention of teaching Brahman alone, which is the Self of all, through the process of figurative implication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on the effort of construing them. As for the reference to the individual soul (*jīva*) in the preceding passage, "But everything is dear for the sake of the Self," that refers to the soul as it is established in common worldly experience.
Having referred to the enjoyer, the statement "the knower" (*vijñātāram*) is intended to teach that he is to be seen as pure Brahman;

it does not, however, refer to the attribute of being a knower belonging to the individual soul (*jīva*), because that statement refers to the liberated soul (*muktajīva*). Furthermore, since the liberated soul is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that [attribute] is impossible in its case. Rather—
The mere restatement of the lack of being a knower based on past states of existence does not independently establish anything for anyone.

Therefore, it is established that the Maitreyī Brāhmaṇa is consistent with the view that the Self to be seen is non-different from the innermost Self (pratyagātman) and devoid of attributes (nirviśeṣa). Herein, if the quality of being a knower were common to Brahman, then [it could not serve] as a mark of the individual soul (jīva).

The meaning is that the commentators would not have introduced [this argument] if it were not the case; yet since they did introduce it, it is understood that Brahman does not possess the status of a knower.

Anticipating the objection that there would be a contradiction with scripture if one does not accept the Lord’s agency in the production of knowledge regarding all objects, he says: "He who is omniscient."

Thus [it is said]. Now, since pure eternal consciousness alone cannot be the denotation of the verbal root *vid* because it is the object (*lakṣya*) in all instances, it must be admitted that qualified consciousness is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). And so, since a qualified entity can be an effect, there is no contradiction for Brahman in being the agent (*kartṛ*) whose status is expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*).

Because it is established that the statement identifying "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*) as a characteristic of the individual soul (*jīva*) is merely a secondary or figurative assertion, due to its contradiction with scriptural texts (*śruti*) that establish the omniscient creatorship [of Brahman];
for knowership is [merely] distinguished from the non-differentiated Brahman intended as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of that specific section [of the *Brahma-sūtras*].

Furthermore, because the presentation of the marks of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is appropriate, and because the author of the Commentary himself has established in the *Īkṣaty-adhikaraṇa* that the primary agency of knowing— which encompasses all objects— is the act of seeing (*īkṣitṛtva*),

and because it is improper to abandon the possibility that the suffix (*pratyaya*) heard in the text refers to its own primary meaning, he speaks [as follows] out of dissatisfaction [with the previous position].

By the words "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth, [the author] states "by consciousness alone" (*caitanyenaiva*). The restrictive particle *eva* (alone) has the sense of "not by the veils of *māyā*.

Nevertheless, although that [consciousness] is not an effect in its essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*), it is an effect of Brahman in its form delimited by the visible world (*dṛśyāvacchinnarūpeṇa*); thus, even according to the Śruti which speaks of the agency in producing knowledge, as in "He who is all-knowing," [there is no contradiction].

"There is no contradiction," says the teacher Vācaspati Miśra. But [one might object]: why does the individual soul (*jīva*), like the Lord (*īśvara*), not manifest objects by its own essential consciousness (*svarūpa-caitanya*) without depending on a mental modification (*vṛtti*)? To this, it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that the consciousness of Brahman...

By being the material cause of all, it has attained identity with everything and illumines all that is conjoined with it. The consciousness of the individual soul (jīvacaitanya), however, although omnipresent due to its having ignorance (avidyā) as its limiting adjunct, does not so illumine because it is not the material cause and is therefore non-attached. It is just like the universal "cowness" (gotva), which, though omnipresent, does not illuminate everything.
Just as the universal (sāmānya), such as "cowness" and the like, becomes associated with individual instances (vyakti) by its very nature even in the absence of actual contact,
so too the individual soul (jīva), though not in contact with objects, becomes associated with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) by its own nature. And thus,
when a modification of the internal organ takes the form of a mental state (vṛtti) through the eyes and other senses—

Having emerged through the gateway, the visual ray transforms instantaneously into the form of a long beam extending to the limits of the object-field; having pervaded the object-field, it then ascends that [beam] and perceives the object.

In that case, there would be a contradiction regarding the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). He says "no," explaining with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). This means "of that [consciousness], namely, of the consciousness whose nature is self-luminous.

Regarding the phrase "delimited by the visible" (*dṛśyāvacchinna*): one should not argue, "How can the status of being the qualified agent (*adhikāritva*) be established for consciousness delimited by the visible—such as beginningless *māyā* and so forth—in the manner described? For even *māyā* and the like...

The point is that once the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is established through the attainment of identity with its respective effects, it is easily accomplished even for that which is delimited by *māyā* and so forth. He raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*).
[He says] "it does not manifest"; nor can one maintain here that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because if that were the case, ignorance (*avidyā*)...
Because the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is consciousness as a reflection, would— due to its all-pervasiveness—

be subject to the contingency of knowing everything by illuminating the entire universe with which it is in contact, [the opponent argues that] the consciousness of one's own essential nature (*svarūpacaitanya*) does not depend on instruments such as the eyes.

The sense is that [otherwise] there would be the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthya*). Regarding the phrase "it has been stated here," the meaning is that the resolution to this objection has been stated. As for "the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*)," the meaning is that just as the world is not conjoined with Brahman in the same way it is conjoined with the individual soul, therefore the consequence of its being omniscient does not arise. Now, [an objection]:

Just as there is no connection between the individual soul (jīva) and objects such as a jar, so too the absence of a connection with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and the like is equal, precisely because [the soul] lacks the status of being their material cause (upādānatva). Consequently,

the internal organ and the rest cannot be manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣi), which is the nature of the individual soul's consciousness, without the mediation of a mental modification (vṛtti).

Anticipating this objection—that even in the absence of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), there might be a contradiction regarding the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth being manifest to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsyatva*) due to the relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) with the living consciousness—he provides an illustration: "Just as [space], though all-pervading... and "it becomes associated...
The point is that, therefore, there is no contradiction in the internal organ and so forth being manifest to the witness; otherwise, the eyes and other sense organs would be rendered useless.

He dispels the objection with the words "And thus," and so forth. The meaning of "And thus" is: while the individual soul (*jīva*) lacks an inherent connection with objects. As for the example "like the rays of the eye," it refers to the sudden pervasion of the object by the transformation of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The word "that" (*tam*) means that transformation. "Makes [it] its object" (*gocarayati*) means...
The remainder [of the sentence] is "the consciousness of the living being" (jīvacaitanya).

Just as grass and other things that cannot be burned by fire alone are nevertheless burned by fire when mounted upon a mass of iron, so too [is it with] that which cannot be illuminated by the consciousness of the living being alone.
It is logical that objects such as a jar are manifested by consciousness when it has ascended upon a modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ;
however, since the individual soul (jīva) is limited by having the internal organ as its adjunct (upādhi),
it does not manifest objects like a jar due to the absence of contact, except through the medium of a mental modification.

When the non-difference from the Brahman-consciousness, as delimited by the object associated with that [mind], is manifested, it illuminates that object. Alternatively, although the individual soul (jīva) is all-pervading, because it is veiled by ignorance—

Regarding the fact that the consciousness of the living self (*jīvacaitanya*), even though it exists in the location of the object, does not possess the capacity to illuminate that object by itself, whereas that capacity does exist for it when it is mounted upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*), he provides an illustration: "By fire alone," etc.

In the phrase "the state of being illuminated by that" (*tatprakāśyatvam*), the word *tat* refers to the consciousness of the living self. Now, [an objection might be raised: is it not the case that...?

Even though [the consciousness] exists in the location of the object, there is no contact with the object; therefore, it does not possess the capacity to manifest that object. And if one were to accept the capacity to manifest the object upon obtaining contact between the two through the modification (*vṛtti*), why is the consequence of omniscience not avoided, given that the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is all-pervading and thus contact with objects exists even when [it is not manifesting them]?

The sense is that by demonstrating that the individual soul (jīva) lacks the capacity to illuminate objects precisely because it is veiled— just as the Brahman-consciousness existing as the archetype (bimba) [is not so illuminated]— it is possible to avoid the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the jīva would be omniscient.

In the view that the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvacaitanya) is limited because it has the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) as its limiting adjunct, there is no possibility at all of the objection regarding the consequence of omniscience. This is because, since that [consciousness] lacks an inherent connection with objects, it is impossible for it to consist of the manifestation of those objects without the mediation of a mental modification (vṛtti). Thus, he states another solution: "Or rather" (yadvā), etc. Therefore...

The meaning is "because it is thus delimited. Regarding the phrase "conjoined with that": when there is the manifestation of non-difference between the Brahman-consciousness—which is conjoined with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) through the medium of its modification (vṛtti) and is delimited by the object—and the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) which has the internal organ as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), then that individual soul [perceives] that object.

The meaning is that it "illuminates. Having adopted the first position—that the *jīva* is a reflection of ignorance—he states another solution, even though the *jīva* lacks the status of being a material cause (*upādāna*), by accepting its connection with objects such as jars and the like. He says, "Alternatively," and "even though [the Self] is all-pervading."
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that [the soul] is "even when in contact with objects.

Otherwise, since the soul's lack of illumination regarding objects would be established simply by the absence of contact with objects, the postulation of its being veiled (*āvṛtatva*) would result in futility; this is how it should be understood. Nor [is it the case that] "he does not perceive me... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

It must be stated that since there is no experience [of the Self] as "I know," how could its being veiled be established? For the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the object of the experience "I am"; thus, although that [consciousness] is absent in the pervasive consciousness of the individual due to the limitation of the internal organ, it is present in the location of the object.
The sense is that there is no sublation (bādhaka) to the postulation of its being veiled, and because there exists the experience: "I do not know [the Self] in Its form as all-pervading."

Being itself non-luminous and thus not manifesting objects, it manifests only that specific object when— through the coloring of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding a particular object and by means of the removal of its own veiling— its manifestation occurs precisely therein. Thus...

Because the individual soul (jīva) depends upon the emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti) for the purpose of coloring its own conscious nature, for the purpose of manifesting the non-difference between the consciousness of the object and [the self], or for the purpose of overcoming the veil [of ignorance], it illuminates only that object with which it has come into contact.

"some degree of identity (jatva) is also possible. Regarding this, in the first position, what kind of coloring by objects (*viṣayoparāga*) could there be for the all-pervading individual soul (*jīva*), which depends upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*)? For even by means of a modification, there can be neither identity nor conjunction between the object and the consciousness of the individual soul, both of which are already established and inactive.
The installation is possible.

"Even by itself" (svayamapi): objects do not manifest by themselves because they are insentient; as for the individual soul (jīva), although it is self-luminous, it does not manifest because it is veiled—this is what the word "even" (api) is intended to express.
Alternatively, the word "api" has the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa); thus, [the meaning is] precisely because of its being veiled.

The meaning is: "by its own lack of self-luminosity. Regarding the phrase "due to the reflection of the mental mode (*vṛtti*)," when there is a reflection of the mental mode upon a particular object, the locus of the object—the individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*)—also undergoes that reflection. By means of this, the veil covering the individual consciousness is removed; and thus, the individual consciousness...
That which is the first category of the coloring of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is [the object]. "In that very [place]" means in the particular object itself.
"That very [one]" means not another object; therefore, the consequence of [the self] being omniscient does not follow—this is the sense.

He reveals this very point [with the words] "And thus. When it is established that the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) does not manifest objects without a mental modification, [then...]

The meaning is "being existent. "Conjoined with that" means conjoined with the function (*vṛtti*). "Even the state of being limited to something" refers to the sense that the state of being limited to something is established by experience, as is the non-omniscience established by experience.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that the conformity to the eyes and other [senses] is thereby established. He raises an objection with the word "here" (*atra*).

The meaning is: "among the positions previously stated. What is the referent of the word "what" (*ka*)? Is it characterized by essential identity (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*), or characterized by oneness (*tādātmyalak�ṣaṇa*), or characterized by conjunction (*saṃyogalakṣaṇa*)? Regarding this, first of all, it cannot be the first [option], because it depends upon a function (*vṛtti*);

for since the consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*) is omnipresent, it is already in proximity to the location of the object. Thus, between the consciousness of the living being and the object—

With the intention that a relationship consisting of essential identity (*svarūpātmaka-sambandha*) is established even without a further operation (*vṛtti*), the term "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*) was stated. He refutes the second and third [alternatives] in sequence with the words "even by an operation. In the world, when the identity of two objects is experienced, it is experienced from the very beginning, not in the middle.
With the intention that [the conjunction] is adventitious (*āgantuka*), he says "of the two already established.

One must state that a conjunction is produced by the action of one or by the action of both; since neither of these is possible in the present case, he says "of the two inactive. Furthermore, even though the two kinds of action are absent in gold and the like, there is fire...

It must be stated that the conjunction of two earthly portions is observed; likewise, if one were to admit from the very beginning a conjunction between the object and the consciousness of the living being, it would contradict the demonstration that such [conjunction] is dependent upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*). This is the intended meaning.
The connection is that even by means of a mental modification, the production [of the conjunction] is not possible.

Since the consciousness of the living being (jīvacaitanya) is not a material cause and is partless, identity and conjunction between the object and the consciousness of the living being do not exist inherently; likewise, it is also the meaning of the word "even" that their production through a mental modification (vṛtti) is not possible. It should be understood that "production" (ādhāna) means "bringing into existence" (utpādana).

On this point, some say that the relationship is precisely that of the object and the subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*). Others, however, maintain that if the function (*vṛtti*) is the regulator merely by being the relation between object and subject, then even a sensory function that has not emerged [from the sense organ] could serve as its regulator; thus, they accept the emergence [of the function] to avoid the fault of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyāpatti*). They say: "That [direct contact] is not what is intended; rather, when there is a conjunction with an object that has become non-obscured by attaining identity (*tādātmya*) with the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) present in the object, a mediated relationship (*paraṃparāsaṃbandha*) involving that [consciousness] as its medium is obtained for [the self] as well. Therefore, it is precisely that [mediated relation], the 'reflection upon consciousness' (*ciduparāga*), which is intended."

Others, however, maintain that since pleasure and the like are observed to be immediate precisely because they are in direct contact with immediate consciousness, a direct contact must be admitted in the case of an immediate object.

With the intention that, although the relationship characterized by the subject-object relation did not exist prior to the arising of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) for the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) present in the location of the object, such a relationship arises once that [modification] has arisen— because of the possibility of that [relationship], which is distinct [from the two] and indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*)— he says:

Regarding this, some say: the meaning of the word "but" (*tu*) is that it is not accepted that the relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*), identity (*tādātmya*), or conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is dependent upon a mode of existence (*vṛtti*), such that the aforementioned fault would arise. In the case of an imperceptible object, [the object] such as the inferable is [revealed] by the limited conscious self (*jīvacaitanya*) through the mode of inference and so forth.

Since, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the relationship characterized by the status of object and subject is admitted even without the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), [the author] states "merely the relation of object and subject" to show that this relationship is not intended by the authors of the *Vivaraṇa*, who maintain the necessity of the emergence of the *vṛtti*. This refers to the case of indirect perception (*parokṣa*).

The meaning is that there is a relationship of object and subject [between the two]. "The state of being its regulator" means that the relationship of object and subject is the referent of the word *tat* (that). Even in the absence of the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), the rule is established that whatever object the modification of the individual soul (*jīva*) possesses is what is illumined, and not anything else; thus, there is no contingency of it becoming the illuminator of other objects.

The meaning is that there is no such contingency, since even conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations have been refuted; therefore, he asks: "Of what is that [consciousness] the substrate? He states the intended relation with the words: "By being present in the object" (*viṣayasannihita*). This means that because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) has arisen by pervading the object, the individual self-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*), as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is present in the object.

The meaning is as follows: identity (*tādātmya*) with that [modification] must be understood for the [consciousness] as well; thus, even for the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*)—which is intended as the illuminator of the object and which is present [within the body]—there is obtained an indirect relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*) with the object, mediated by the contact between the modification and the object, characterized by identity with the modification that is in contact with the object.

The sense is that since the aforementioned relationship is possible without the emergence [of the object] from [the internal organ], the Teacher Vivaraṇācārya has stated its emergence. Because objects such as pleasure are immediate (*aparokṣa*),
they are connected with the individual self-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) which illumines them.

The relationship is established as the determinant factor (*prayojaka*). Thus, even regarding the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) of external objects such as jars, it is not possible for there to be a uniformity [of the determinant], because a direct relationship serves as the determinant in some cases of the immediacy of an object, while in other cases a mediated (*paraṃparā*) relationship serves as the determinant, resulting in a lack of consistency (*vairūpya*).
Furthermore, because a mediated relationship cannot be postulated when a direct relationship exists, this [relationship] is also not intended by the Teacher; thus he says, "others [say]."
Therefore, when the mental modification (*vṛtti*) comes into contact with an object, it acquires that modification as its limiting adjunct; by means of that adjunct,

a conjunction born of conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) is possible between the Jīva, which is your material cause (*upādāna*), and [the object], just as there is a conjunction of the effect [with the object] arising from the conjunction of the cause and the non-cause.

They say that because the logic is the same, the conjunction of the instrument with its non-instrument must also be accepted as a consequence of the conjunction of the effect with its non-effect. However,
the proponents of the "one-part" (ekadeśin) view [hold that] the consciousness which illuminates the object, being conditioned by that internal organ, has attained identity with the object.

The intended meaning of "the reflection of consciousness" (ciduparāga) is precisely the production of identity with the object by means of the manifestation of the non-difference between Brahman and consciousness.

"Therefore" means that a mediated (paraṃparā) connection is not accepted. Regarding "of the modification" (*vṛtteḥ*): when there is a conjunction of the modification with the object, a "conjunction-born-conjunction" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) is possible between the object and the living-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*), which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the modification. This is what is meant: the modification belongs to the living-consciousness.

The object of the mental modification (vṛtti) is the effect, while the object of the concealment (āvaraṇa) is not the material cause of that concealment; rather, the living consciousness (jīvacaitanya) is the material cause of the mental modification.
Thus, there occurs a conjunction of the mental modification and its object with the living consciousness, as between an effect and its non-effect.

In this context, the conjunction intended is "conjunction-born conjunction" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*), which occurs between the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) and its object, where [the former] is the cause with respect to the body and [the latter] is the non-cause with respect to that same body. Now, [one might ask]: how can there be a conjunction of the hand—which is the cause of the body—with the tree, given that the hand is a non-cause of the body? [The answer is: because the hand is indeed a non-cause of the body with respect to that [tree]. The hand is the effect of the body, yet it is the tree that is the effect of the hand.

Anticipating the objection that direct contact (*sahasamyoga*) is accepted because, at the time of the hand-tree contact, there is the experience that "the tree is conjoined with the body" by way of the hand being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the tree, [the author replies: in the present case as well, regarding an object such as a jar, at the time of the contact between the jar and the mental mode (*vṛtti*),
the jar shines forth by way of the mental mode being the delimiting factor for the jar-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*).
With the intention that [the reflection] does not arise because of being mixed, he says "cause and non-cause. Regarding "by the equality of reasoning":

the meaning is by the equality of the reasoning consisting of conceptualization and experience in both cases. Now, an objection: even for the living self-consciousness (jīvacaitanya) which is present in the location of the object, the status of having the mental modification (vṛtti) as its limiting adjunct (upādāna) is accepted by the teacher Vivaraṇācārya.

It is not so. Even though the individual soul (jīva) lacks the status of being the material cause (upādāna) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth, there is a connection between the soul and the internal organ by its very nature, just as the universal of cowness (gotva-sāmānya) is connected to the individual cow characterized by the dewlap and other features. In this same way, although the soul is unattached to objects, it is connected with the internal organ by its own nature.

Because in the passage beginning with "it is conjoined" (*saṃsṛjyate*), this has been established as being without a covering (*aprāvivaraṇa*); and consequently, since the individual soul-consciousness lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) with respect to the mental modification (*vṛtti*), the aforementioned connection would not be established.

Therefore, because even a "conjunction born of conjunction" (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) is not accepted by the Teacher, he says [the following] out of dissatisfaction: "But for the partial adherents (*ekadeśinaḥ*)."

The meaning is that what is intended by "the coloring of consciousness" (cid-uparāga) is precisely the establishment of a relationship of identity between the living-consciousness (jīva-caitanya), which manifests objects such as a jar, and that object, the jar itself. Now, an objection might be raised: even through a mental modification (vṛtti), it is not possible to bring about the production of identity between the object and consciousness, both of which are already pre-established.
Since this has been stated previously, one might ask how its accomplishment is achieved; therefore, he says: "having attained identity with the object.

Because the Brahman-consciousness, which exists as the prototype (*bimba*), is the material cause (*upādāna*) of objects such as jars, the identity between Brahman and the object is already established. Thus, it has attained identity with the object.

When the distinction between the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) and the consciousness of Brahman is manifested by the modification (*vṛtti*) produced from the non-apprehension of objects through the consciousness of Brahman, the identity of the object with the consciousness of the individual soul is obtained by means of that modification.
The manner in which this manifestation of non-difference occurs will be explained later; therefore, there is no inconsistency in the production of this identity.
The state of being.

Even though the individual soul (jīva), by virtue of its omnipresence, is in proximity to all objects and thus capable of manifesting them, it cannot be established as the direct perception of a specific person because of its commonality [to all].

For it is precisely by virtue of being conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that [the Self] illumines objects. And thus, the established doctrine—that superimpositional relation (*adhyāsika-sambandha*) is the regulator for the direct perception of objects—is also consistent.
Nor does this lead to a confusion of the two Yakṣas (the individual soul and the Supreme Self) regarding the all-pervasiveness of the individual soul (*jīva*), as in the first case.
They say that because of the difference between those two— namely, that one side is delimited while the other is not— it is indeed "the second."

He states the purpose of the qualification provided—namely, that the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) is conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and limited by its objects—in the words "by being all-pervading. The phrase "but those" means "by way of being all-pervading. The word "of that" means "of the individual soul (*jīva*). The phrase "by way of commonality" means "by way of being common to all persons."

In the view that the "word *puruṣa*" refers to the knower (*pramātṛ*)—the individual soul (*jīva*) being a reflection of supreme ignorance—there is no difference between various souls. Therefore, regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*), it means "of the soul. Consequently, although the consciousness of the soul is all-pervading, whatever object that soul causes to appear by means of its internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) by that soul alone.

The meaning is that the qualification "being conditioned by the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇopahitatva*) must be stated in order to establish the restriction that [the reflection] belongs to none other [than the individual self].

He states the advantage for the view of a certain school (Ekadeśin) with the words "And thus": this means provided that it is accepted that the consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*), which illuminates objects, attains identity with the object through its mental modification (*vṛtti*). [The term used is] "superimposed" (*adhyāsika*).
The meaning is that the relationship is one of identity established through superimposition (*adhyāsa*). As for the phrase "and not thus":
even in the first position—that there is a repetition of the word for the sake of indicating the relationship—it is accepted that the repetition serves to manifest non-difference;
this is the intended meaning. He removes the objection regarding confusion: "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*) refers to the view that the individual soul is all-pervading (*sarvagata*).

"Repetition is for the sake of connection" refers to the first position; "repetition is for the sake of manifesting non-difference" because the individual soul (jīva) is limited by the adjunct of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—this is the meaning of the second position. The underlying sense is that, although the author of the *Vṛtti* maintains the same manifestation of non-difference in both the first and second positions...

In the first alternative, the function (*vṛtti*) serves to bring about a relationship of identity between the object and the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), which illuminates the object by means of manifesting its non-difference [from Brahman].
In the second alternative, however, the function [serves] the consciousness of the individual soul that illuminates the object [directly].
It is for the purpose of manifesting non-difference from the consciousness delimited by the object; thus, there is no confusion between the two positions.

Alternatively, in the first position, since the individual soul (*jīva*) is all-pervading, the consciousness of the individual soul—which is always already present in the location of the object—attains identity with the object as it delimits that object.
In the second view, however, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is limited,

the mental modification (*vṛtti*) brings about proximity with the object and thereby also effects the manifestation of the non-difference between the soul and the Brahman-consciousness which is its substrate; thus, there is a distinction between the two cases.
This solution, which avoids the confusion between the two positions, is indicated in the root text by the two terms "all-pervasive" (*sarvagatatva*) and "limited" (*paricchinnatva*);
however, the previous solution was indicated by the terms "first position" (*prathama-pakṣa*) and "second position" (*dvitīya-pakṣa*).
In the first position, it is held that there is a repetition of the meaning of the connection (*saṃbandha*).

In the second position, it is because the purpose for which the repetition is made is understood to be the manifestation of non-difference (*abheda*), since the relationship itself is understood to be the objective (*uddeśya*). In this view, by distinguishing between what is intended and what is not,
the purpose of the repetition ultimately results in the manifestation of non-difference alone, as is the case in both the first and second positions.
It should be understood that the term "Ekadeśin" was used at the very outset with the intention that the confusion between these two [positions] would otherwise be unavoidable.

Now, regarding the second position, what is this manifestation of non-difference? Some say it is like the water of a pond and the water of a field [flowing together] by means of a canal; [likewise, it occurs] by means of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) between the consciousness delimited by the object and the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
"Unification" (ekībhāva) is the manifestation of non-difference. And thus, although it is the very consciousness of Brahman, as delimited by the object, that illumines the object;
The intention of the Teachers who maintain that "the function [of the mind] has for its object the relation [between consciousness and the object]" is as follows: here,

the relationship characterized by the state of the manifested and the manifestor between the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya)— which is intended to be the illuminator of objects— and the object such as a jar, depends upon the mental function (vṛtti) conjoined with each respective object.

This is what is intended. For instance, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), being a transparent substance, is by its very nature capable of manifesting consciousness; a jar or similar object, however, is not so, because it is an opaque substance.
Through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) that pervades objects such as a jar, the opacity existing therein is overcome.
The capacity for the manifestation of consciousness is imparted [to the object].

As it has been stated by the Vivaraṇācāryas themselves: "For the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), by means of its own nature, imparts the fitness for the manifestation of consciousness not only within itself, but also to objects such as jars with which it is in contact. And it is observed that even an opaque substance [becomes manifest] through a transparent medium.

From contact: [it is] the capacity for receiving a reflection.
