Just as a wall or similar object possesses the capacity for receiving a reflection at the time of contact with water, so too does a jar or similar object possess the capacity for manifesting the living consciousness (jīvacaitanya) present near it, which constitutes its "receiving a reflection. For consciousness as well, there is the state of being manifested; in that case, it is simply the state of being reflected.

Thus, it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is for the very purpose of establishing the relationship characterized by the indicated (*vyaṅgya*) and the indicator (*vyañjaka*). And so, when the aforementioned relationship between the object-consciousness and the consciousness of the mental modification has been established by means of the mental modification that has emerged outward, [the consciousness] is reflected upon the jar and other objects.
"The consciousness residing therein (the heart) illumines that [Self]," he says. He then objects to the second position with the word "atha" (now/if).

As for the question "What is this?": according to the second position, the removal of the veil is for the purpose of manifesting non-difference; indeed, it has been stated that in this view, the individual soul (*jīva*) is considered to be limited.
In this view, the soul, which has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct, is delimited by the object.
Furthermore, the manifestation of non-difference through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is not possible for the Brahman-consciousness that exists as the substrate (*bimbabhūta*),

because— unlike a modification in the form of the undivided whole (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*)— a modification directed toward an object such as a jar lacks the power to remove the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Consequently, while the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the object remain as distinct limiting adjuncts, the individual soul (*jīva*)...

The meaning is that the manifestation of non-difference from Brahman is impossible [in that case]. He offers a rebuttal, saying "Some say," on the grounds that even when two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that differentiate are present, if they occupy the same location, the manifestation of non-difference can occur through their power, as such a thing is observed in the world. A *kedāra* is a place where grain is produced. And thus:

Just as in the world it is well known that the identity between the water residing in a pond and the water residing in a field is manifested through the channel, so too the identity between the individual self (*jīva*), which is consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and the consciousness of Brahman delimited by the object is manifested through the mental modification (*vṛtti*), provided that the modification reaches the location of the object.

The meaning is that, because there is no difference between a fence and that which is enclosed by it, it is established that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva), also resides in the location of the object.

Nevertheless, because the door of its enclosure (the body) has become one [with it], the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*) has come about; thus, the manifestation of objects for the living soul is possible. Others, however, say that [it occurs] through the reflection of Brahman—which occupies the position of the original object (*bimba*)—as delimited by the object.

The unification with the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the manifestation of non-difference; for as long as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that distinguishes them remains present—just as in the case of a mirror—a unification of the two is impossible. According to the author of the *Vṛtti*, if the Brahman delimited by the object were to attain the state of being the individual soul through the manifestation of non-difference, then at that time, because Brahman would lack contact with that object, [the manifestation of non-difference] would be...
Furthermore, if its status as a seer were impossible, it would follow that it lacks omniscience.

"Thus" means: when the manifestation of non-difference has become possible. Now, it may be objected that the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) cannot possibly be the illuminator of objects, because, lacking the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) with respect to the object, it lacks the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). Nor can it be argued that the consciousness of Brahman alone should be the illuminator of objects.

It must be stated that this is because [the object] attains a direct identity-relation with [the self] by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna*). If that were so, it would contradict the understanding that the individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) alone is the illuminator of the jar—as expressed in such statements as "the jar is illuminated by light" and "the jar was understood by me. Thinking thus, he raises an objection once again.

In order to state the purpose of manifesting non-difference, [the author says] "even though" (*yadyapi*). Regarding the phrase "that which illumines the object," the ellipsis is that it must be stated thus because of the attainment of the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*).

The meaning of the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) is that it is not the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*); and if that were so, there would be a contradiction with the experience: "This jar is known by me."
This is the sense; he refutes [the objection] with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

Regarding the phrase "of that": when the Brahman-consciousness, which illuminates the object through the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*), attains the state of being conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇopahitatva*) by means of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it becomes the individual soul (*jīva*).

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with experience in the conclusion that the Brahman-consciousness’s capacity to illuminate objects belongs to the *jīva* alone, because the state of being a *jīva* has not arisen from a complete merging [of the two]. As for the phrase "like a mirror":
just as in the case of a reflection in a mirror, there is no manifestation of non-difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

The meaning is that, just as there was then an experience of difference between those two, so too in the present case, when there exists a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as the form of the object and so forth, identity is possible. Now, one might object: "When all limiting adjuncts have ceased through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), the manifestation of non-difference that occurs there is not what is intended here; rather, it is like [the merging] of milk and water."
Just as in the case of two objects situated in a single location by way of being contained within a vessel, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the object reach a state of being in one place,

what is intended is the manifestation of a figurative non-difference between the consciousness delimited by them, based solely on that [proximity]. And in this manifestation of non-difference, there is no contradiction caused by the existence of distinguishing limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as in the case of a mirror.

Even in the state of a reflection of the face, one perceives the manifestation of non-difference between the original object and its reflection by thinking, "It is my very face that appears in the mirror. In this view as well, the explanation must be made in this very manner; for the manifestation of non-difference between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its modification (*vṛtti*), and the reflection is not primary.
Because a relationship of cause and effect is possible between a covering (vṛtti) and that which possesses the covering (vṛtimat), and because identity between these two is impossible,

identity between their respective reflections is likewise impossible; for this reason, he states [the following], as it would contradict the demonstration— made in the passage beginning with "If there were identity"— that in this system there is no confusion (sāṅkarya) among the knower (pramātṛ) and the other factors.

The author of the *Vṛtti* states that there is an "manifestation of non-difference. Regarding the phrase "then, having that as its object": when Brahman, delimited by an object, attains the state of being a *jīva*, its status as the Lord (*īśvara*) must necessarily be admitted to cease;

for it is impossible for both the state of being a *jīva* and the state of being the Lord to coexist within a single consciousness under one and the same delimiting condition (*avaccheda*). And thus, at that time, during the state of being a *jīva*—
The meaning is that, due to the absence of contact with that object, it is not possible for Brahman to be its seer.
The word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied after the word "of that" (*tasya*).

Rather, the Brahman-consciousness delimited by an object projects a reflection that illuminates the object onto the front surface of the non-manifesting (avṛti) which is in contact with that object; thus, there is a unification of that reflection with the individual soul (jīva). And so it is with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)...

Furthermore, in that which possesses [the property], the non-confusion of the cognizer, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge among the various consciousnesses delimited by their respective objects is also established. Nor does it follow that, if the consciousness conditioned by the mental mode (*vṛtti*) were the means of knowledge regarding the object, it would— like the consciousness that is the substrate of the object— be non-different from the object through superimposition.

It should not be argued that because there is no [natural] relation, the superimpositional relation (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) cannot be the governing factor for the direct manifestation (*aparokṣya*) of an object; for the very consciousness that is the substrate of the object, when delimited by that object and reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*),
exists in a state of non-difference from it, and thus the relation with it is established.

Now, it may be argued that at the time when consciousness, which has the object as its locus, is in contact with a mental modification (*vṛtti*), just as there is the status of being a *jīva* caused by being conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), so too the status of being the Lord (*īśvara*) caused by being conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*) would be non-contradictory; and thus, even then, for the Lord who exists as the original prototype (*bimba*), [the reflection would exist].

Omniscience remains unimpaired; otherwise, since the state of being a *jīva*— which is conditioned by the consciousness presiding over the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth— would persist forever,
the Brahman that constitutes the original archetype (*bimba*) would never possess contact with the internal organ and the like.

Thinking that the objection—that if such a vision were impossible, there would be the fault of the consequence that omniscience could never exist—applies equally to this view as well, he maintains an internal dissatisfaction and asks: "What then is the manifestation of non-difference intended by you?
He asks this with the words, "But what [is it]? He states that [manifestation] with the words, "[It is] delimited by the object," for [the term] "front part" refers to the modification (*vṛtti*).

Beginning from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) situated in the heart and extending as far as the sense objects, it exists as an uninterrupted stream that has attained lengthening like the radiance of the Kaustubha jewel and other gems. Of that veil, the portion in contact with the sense objects is called the "front part" (agra-bhāga). Within that [front part], there is the reflection of Brahman, which is the illuminator of the sense objects.

The meaning is as follows: "non-identity with the individual soul" here intends the manifestation of non-difference; since there exists a non-difference in the form of identity between the possessor of the reflection (the substrate) and the reflection itself, the manifestation of non-difference between those two reflections is possible. "And thus," etc.

The meaning is: when it is accepted that the reflection in the mental mode (*vṛtti*)—which is in reality distinct from the reflection in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—manifests as non-different from it, thereby illuminating the object.
Regarding the phrase "non-confusion also": because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the mental mode and its possessor, there is a manifestation of non-difference between their two reflections.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that the "admixture of the two" (*vaṃdasaṃkara*) is likewise possible.

Just as a face is delimited by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a mirror, so too is the consciousness reflected therein (*pratibimbacaitanya*) delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct;

this is the knower (*pramātā*). The consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is likewise delimited by that very [modification] as its limiting adjunct; this is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

"Brahman-consciousness delimited by an object is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). The meaning is that their non-confusion (*asāṃkarya*) is established because of the existence of delimiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that serve to differentiate them. By stating that "non-confusion is established in this view," [the author implies] that in the previous view, [non-confusion was not established] regarding the object-delimited [consciousness].

It has been indicated that because the attainment of the status of a *jīva* by Brahman-consciousness is accepted, the non-confusion between the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the consciousness of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not logically tenable; however, in reality, even in the previous view there is no confusion, since the existence of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that differentiate the *jīva* from Brahman— and the resulting attributes such as omniscience— is dependent upon them.
And it should be understood that this is because the systematic arrangement has already been shown. He raises an objection with the words "If not. Regarding the phrase "of that":
the connection is that [the reflection] does not [arise] because of the absence of an illusory (adhyāsika) relationship between that [reflection] and the object.

Since the reflection within the mental modification (*vṛtti*), which is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), lacks the status of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of the object, an identity (*tādātmya*) between the two is impossible; and thus...
In the case of the direct perception of an object, the relation of superimposed identity (*ādhyāsika-tādātmya*) is the regulating factor.

Others, however, say that the consciousness which is the substrate of the object in its form as a reflection is itself the illuminator of the object, because it directly acquires a superimpositional relationship with it; thus,

although there exists a distinction [between the self and the object] insofar as the consciousness is qualified by its state as a reflection, they are one in their nature as consciousness characterized by that [reflection].

Existence (*bhāva*) is the manifestation of difference. This being the case, there is no confusion between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, nor is there any contradiction with Brahman’s omniscience, because it remains as it was before in its nature as the prototype (*bimba*). Now, in the third position, what indeed is this "overcoming of the veil" (*āvaraṇābhibhava*)?

If it is argued that ignorance is destroyed by the very knowledge of a jar, and thus the phenomenal world (prapañca), which has ignorance as its root, would cease to exist, some here respond: [Ignorance] which veils pure consciousness exists in a portion delimited by an object, like a firefly [in the sky].

Others, however, maintain that "overpowering" (abhibhava) means either the destruction of ignorance by a portion of knowledge— just as great darkness is destroyed by light— or its envelopment like a mat, or its retreat like a frightened soldier;
yet [they argue] that if there were destruction by a portion of knowledge, there would be an absence of material cause (upādāna).
The intention of the objection is that this contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).

[However, there is no contradiction] because the non-difference between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) is accepted; thus, the very same relation of identity with the object that belongs to the consciousness of the original image also belongs to the reflection in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*).

He refutes [the objection] by stating that there is no *apasiddhānta* (departure from an accepted tenet). He says: "By the non-difference from that," meaning "by the non-difference of the reflected consciousness (*pratibimba-caitanya*) from the original source (*bimba*). Even though there is non-difference between the original source and its reflection, because a conceptualized difference (*kalpita-bheda*) exists, the relation belonging to the original source becomes the relation belonging to the reflection.

Indicating by the word "non-existent" that there is a lack of intrinsic flavor [in the previous view], he states the manifestation of non-difference through another method: "Others, however, say... [The phrase] "even though difference exists" [is used]; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "together with the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is consciousness qualified by the state of being a reflection. "That" refers to the state of being the original archetype (bimba).
The meaning is: "by that self" refers to pure consciousness (*śuddha-caitanya*) as characterized by both [the reflection and the original].

And as for the phrase "this being so": the meaning is that if one accepts the manifestation of non-difference through the nature of the consciousness characterized [by the reflection], the two previously mentioned defects do not exist. Here, this should be considered: [is it] unification through the nature of the consciousness characterized [by the reflection]?

Nor is there an ontological non-difference, because that [non-difference] does not depend upon its manifestation (*vṛtti*). Nor is there a conventional non-difference, because since the difference between the original image (*bimba*) and the reflected image (*pratibimba*) is conventional, a non-difference identical to it is impossible. Nor...
The illusory non-difference [between the two] arises merely from the two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) being located in the same place;

since such an illusory non-difference between the consciousness of the original (*bimba*) and the reflected (*pratibimba*) is possible on that basis alone, it would be useless to employ "pure consciousness" (*caitanyamātra*) as a defining characteristic for that purpose. He objects to the third position with the word "atha" (now/if). [He says] "it would cease," because ignorance (*ajñāna*) is one.

The meaning is as follows: it does not cease; therefore, there is no destruction of ignorance, but rather the suppression of the veil. Nor is any other mode possible, because none is perceived—this is the sense. He refutes [the objection] by relying on the very unity of ignorance, beginning with "On this point some say" and "mere consciousness. The word "mere" (mātra) excludes anything other than the Witness (sākṣin).
The sense is that [the witness-consciousness] is the supreme, all-pervasive sentience, because the non-obscuration of its nature will be explained later.

As for the phrase "destruction by a single part," the sense is that there would not follow the cessation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) which has that [consciousness] as its root. With the intention of showing that no other mode [of destruction] is perceived, he says, "like a mat," and so forth.
Refuting the etymological explanation [of *nirvāṇa*] as "overcoming obscurations," he explains it in another way, beginning with the words "anyathā" and so forth.

Furthermore, in that case, since it would follow that there is an absence of obscuration even at another time once [the light] has departed all at once through the process of contraction (*kaṃdalanā*), and because movement and envelopment are impossible for that which is inactive, the aforementioned form of suppression is not possible.

Therefore, even for ignorance (*ajñāna*), which veils pure consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), its very nature is such that it veils the consciousness delimited by an object in its state of being conjoined with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of a particular form;
this [nature] itself is what constitutes "overpowering" (*abhibhava*). Nor is there a delimitation by the object...

One might object: "How is it logical that ignorance, which exists by depending upon consciousness as its object—just as a cloth depends upon a wall—should not obscure that very consciousness? This doubt is raised; however, [the answer is that] based on the cognition "I am ignorant," that [ignorance] indeed has as its substratum the very consciousness that is manifest in the experience of the "I."

They say that this is because it does not conceal that [object]. Others, however, maintain that what is experienced as being opposed to the knowledge of a jar— as in "I do not know the jar"— and as being removable by that knowledge— as in "the ignorance of the jar has ceased when the knowledge of the jar arises"— is not the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

Since it is impossible for that [ignorance]— which has pure consciousness as its object and which is to be removed by that [knowledge]— to be of such a nature, rather, it is another form of ignorance,
consisting of a specific state (avasthābheda) of the root-ignorance, which has the consciousness delimited by the jar as its object; therefore, it is the destruction of that [specific ignorance].

Such is the overcoming [of the veil]. And it is not the case that, when one cognition destroys that [veil], there would follow the consequence that other cognitions having the same object would also lack the capacity to overcome the veil; for they maintain that there are as many ignorances as there are cognitions. Thus they say.

"Furthermore, 'therein' means by way of the removal of the veil from the consciousness delimited by the object (*viṣayāvacchinna-caitanya*). 'That and that' means the state of not veiling that consciousness delimited by the object which exists in the condition of being conjoined with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of this or that object. Now, just as [one perceives] a jar..."

Just as a cloth being pervaded by darkness indeed covers it, so too ignorance, existing as it pervades the Brahman-consciousness delimited by an object, certainly covers that consciousness; therefore, the assumption that it does not cover it is untenable. [The opponent] objects: "But not... [and continues: "In the case of ignorance, like a cloth..."

He states that this objection does not arise because the distinctness [of the Self] is established by experience: "I... and so on. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): it means of ignorance (*ajñāna*). Even though ignorance rests upon the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), it does not veil it; for if it were to veil it, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), as this has been established in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Dahara-adhikaraṇa*. [The witness...]
The underlying intention is that the unobstructed nature of consciousness will be explained later;

furthermore, since the ignorance that veils consciousness as delimited by objects is distinct from the root-ignorance which is the material cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), even when that [object-specific] ignorance is removed by the knowledge of a jar or similar object, there is no removal of the phenomenal world.
He shows the view that [the world] would persist because of that, due to the non-cessation of ignorance which is the root of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), by saying "But others...
He states the proof for the plurality of ignorance with the words "the jar... and "by way of opposition...
Here, by the word expressing the experience and verbalization of ignorance—"I do not know"—...

Because it has a contradictory object, even the experience expressed as "I do not know" is indeed an object of knowledge that contradicts [the absence of] knowledge; nor should it be argued that the experience "I do not know" has only the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge as its object and not positive ignorance (*bhāvarūpājñāna*), for the reason that the very concept of prior non-existence is not accepted—this is the sense. [The phrase] "because such a state is impossible" means:

The meaning is that it is impossible for [the object] to be the content of consciousness delimited by the pot (ghaṭāvachinnacaitanya) and simultaneously to be removable by its destruction. Rather, the connection is that it is "another ignorance" (ajñānāntara). Regarding the phrase "in the form of a modification" (avasthābhedārūpa), the purpose of this qualification will be stated later. Not... [sentence fragment].
And the passage beginning with "caivam ekena" has a clear meaning.

Some maintain that these forms of the states of existence, like fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), are beginningless because they are of the nature of ignorance; [they hold that] sleep, having veiled the empirical world and individual soul, projects the dream-world and dream-individual soul.

To that extent, due to its association with the power of obscuration and distraction, it exists in the state of ignorance; likewise, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth have dissolved, there is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), characterized by the subsequent reflection: "I slept happily, I did not know anything."
The state of ignorance experienced during deep sleep by those possessing root-ignorance is indeed a specific modification (bheda-rūpa) of that very ignorance.
Now, are these states of ignorance beginningless, or do they have a beginning? Not the first, because there would be no proof for it;

nor the second, because it would contradict the established doctrine that ignorance is beginningless—if this is argued, [the author] says "And these... to show that some establish the first position: these states of ignorance are beginningless.

The meaning is that because it is ignorance, there is no failure of the illustrative example— just as in the case of root-ignorance— since in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the deities), the beginninglessness of root-ignorance was established through both scripture and reasoning. Nor is being "root-ignorance" the determining factor for the beginninglessness of a particular instance of ignorance, but rather merely "being ignorance."

It should be stated: the sense is that, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), that alone [the ignorance of the state] is the efficient cause. Others establish the second position—that there are various types of ignorance regarding states—and says: "They are empirical," etc. Nor is there any contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
The meaning is that the acceptance of the beginninglessness of ignorance has as its object the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). [The inference is:

"The various states of knowledge under dispute have a beginning, because they are states of ignorance, like sleep and like deep sleep. The phrase "by way of repetition" (*āvṛttyā*) is intended to exclude any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the root-ignorance. [This refers to] those occurring at the time of waking.

The world and the individual souls (*jīva*) are not perceived during the time of dreaming in the same manner as they are known to be; therefore, the sense is that because they are not perceived as they are, an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) must be postulated for them. "Vikṣipanti" means "they create. [The phrase] "in the form of a particular state of ignorance" refers to ignorance itself.

Its definition is the possession of the power of veiling (*āvaraṇa*) and projection (*vikṣepa*). Since it exists in sleep (*nidrā*), which is the cause of dreaming, its nature as ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established; for, since sleep is attained through the manner to be described later, it cannot be the root-ignorance itself, and thus it is established that it is a specific state (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of that [ignorance].

The sense is that by the first illustration, there is a deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalpya*). Similarly, the connection is as follows: the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is experienced at the time of deep sleep just like the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), is indeed of the nature of a specific state of ignorance. Now, [an objection]: as for deep sleep...

It is not the case that the persistence of root-ignorance and deep sleep at that time is unestablished because of the observation of such experiences as "I am ignorant" and "I am sleeping"; for this reason, he says: "I [experienced] happiness. This refers to the recollective reflection (*parāmarśa*).
Thus, by the fact that the reflection observed upon waking would otherwise be inexplicable, [it follows that there was experience] at that time.

The experience of deep sleep and its root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is postulated as being of the nature of the witness (*sākṣin*). For, when there is the mention of "I" (*aham*), the conjunction of the self with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the causal factor; since that [conjunction] has dissolved at that time, there is no mention of "I"—with this intention, he says: "dissolved in the internal organ and so forth."

The term "the eye and so forth" (*cakṣurādikamādi*) refers to the first category of objects; the presentation of the experience of deep sleep, which is inferred through retrospective reflection (*parāmarśa*), is intended to establish the true nature of deep sleep. For if there were an absence of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) at the time of deep sleep, the state of deep sleep would not be established as having that specific character; therefore, this experience is presented.

Therefore, for the purpose of proving the existence of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), it must be understood through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) consists of that very state; for at the time of deep sleep,
[the self] is not connected with anything other than root-ignorance, such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.

The mention of the dissolution of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth is intended to indicate that it is impossible for [the Self] to have that state as its nature by way of being dissolved; thus, even in the illustration of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is no deficiency in the common property (*sādharmya*). This is the sense.
Furthermore, since the karma that bestows the experience of waking arises only when the Supreme Reality exists, those two [the waking state and its experience] are also beginningless.
Similarly, others hold that other instances of ignorance in the form of various states are likewise beginningless. But [an objection may be raised]:
if they were beginningless, then all that ignorance would be destroyed by the very first cognition produced regarding a jar.

Because there is no determining factor [to distinguish between them], and because it would be impossible for the object to be manifested if all ignorance covering that limited consciousness were destroyed, subsequent cognitions do not overcome their respective veils.

If it is argued that [the state] remains exactly as it was, some here say: just as when many prior absences of knowledge exist, yet upon the arising of a single cognition, only one prior absence is removed; so too in the case of those things which are of the nature of obstructions, by virtue of their possessing the capacity to produce doubt and the like.

Even though other prior absences (prāgabhāva) exist, when a single cognition arises, only one ignorance is removed; likewise, even while other ignorances remain, there is the manifestation of the object.
He dispels the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in both examples. "Of those two" means of sleep and deep slumber (*nidrā-suṣupti*).
"Even other [ignorance]" means even the ignorance that veils the consciousness delimited by objects such as a jar.
This is because, according to the view that the ignorances of the various states are beginningless, that [specific ignorance] is produced by the first arising cognition of a jar.

The established position is that the ignorance existing previously as the veil over the jar, upon the destruction of that [specific] cognition, is subsequently covered again by the ignorance of the state that has arisen thereafter. He raises an objection, saying "But," [suggesting] that this would not be established under the view that those [ignorances] are beginningless. [This is countered] by the initial cognition of the jar.

There is the destruction of all those ignorances. Nor does he refute the second alternative with the example "the jar. Since there is no determining factor (vinigamaka) to establish that by the first cognition only one ignorance is destroyed and not the others, it must be stated that all ignorances are destroyed; thus, the meaning is that the second alternative is untenable.
In the second alternative (*dvitīyakalpa*), he states another defect, similar to the absence of a differentiator (*nirvikamaka*): "tadavacchinna" (delimited by that).
The meaning is that all ignorance would be destroyed by the first cognition. "Tadavastham eva" (remaining in that very state):
for, in order to establish that subsequent cognitions possess the power to overcome the veil (*āvaraṇa*), as many cognitions as there are...

It is accepted that there are as many instances of ignorance to be removed as there are [objects]; however, even if that is admitted, if all ignorance were destroyed by the first cognition alone, that same defect remains exactly as it was.
This is just as, in the Nyāya system, there are as many cognitions of a jar as there are jars.

There exist prior absences (*prāgabhāva*) of the cognition of a jar. Among these, by the first cognition, only one prior absence of that cognition is removed; the others remain exactly as they were before. Even while they exist, the illumination of the object is still achieved through those [other cognitions]. This should be applied here in the same way; thus he provides the resolution. Regarding this, some say:

[Objection: Is it not the case that the example is dissimilar? For the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge does not obscure an object, whereas ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) does obscure the object; and as long as an obscuration exists, the manifestation of the object is not possible. [Reply: He says "no," stating "doubt and so forth" (*saṃśayādi*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has the meaning of "error" (*viparyaya*) and other such states.
In our own system (siddhānta), the obscuring nature of ignorance in its positive form consists in its capacity to produce doubt and other such states regarding an object that is considered ignorant;
and this capacity is equally present in the opponent's view regarding ignorance in the form of the prior non-existence of knowledge. Therefore, there is no disparity between the two examples.
The state is indeed one; this is the sense [of the phrase] "by virtue of the result."

Others, however, maintain that when there is no direct perception of what is present and when a single cognition arises— despite the existence of other prior absences— the "obscuration" (āvaraṇa) consists of the totality of absences of the perceptions of specific features; and this obscuration ceases upon the perception of those specific features.
They say: whenever ignorance veils [the self], it is destroyed by that very knowledge; however, since [knowledge] veils everything at all times, such [veiling] would be useless.
Rather, when the concealing ignorance is destroyed by the modification (vṛtti) of knowledge, [then the self shines forth].

Upon the cessation of that particular function, it veils another instance of ignorance. And this being the case, there is no undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of those instances of ignorance—which remain as non-obscuring at the time of the arising of the realization of Brahman—not being removed even from that [realization]; for although they lack direct opposition to it, [they are nevertheless removed].

Because it is dependent upon the primal ignorance (mūlājñāna) which is to be terminated by that [knowledge], its cessation is logically possible only through the cessation of that ignorance, just like the relationship with ignorance and so forth.

Having raised an objection with the passage beginning "Now, in the case of beginninglessness," etc., he provides a resolution by another method, saying "But others... This is connected with the phrase "they say.
He himself demonstrates the lack of satisfaction in the intention of others regarding the previous solution, saying "of that which is veiled" (āvṛtasya). Even for that which is veiled...

In the Siddhānta, because non-perceptual knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is accepted [as arising] from mountain fires and the like, it is stated that [this is] "non-perceptual knowledge" (*aparokṣajñāna*). Regarding the word "yāvat": the mere prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of a perception that contradicts doubt and so forth with respect to a post (*sthāṇu*) or similar object is not capable of producing doubt and the like.

Regarding the statement "this is a post": even at the stage of certainty (*niścaya*), since there exists the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of another certainty regarding the same object, there would again arise the contingency of doubt for one who possesses the memory of "human-ness" (*puruṣatva*).
However, this applies only to certainties that have the same object as the doubt and so forth.

The collection of as many absences as there are must be described, according to the opponent's view, either as that which has the capacity to produce doubt and the like, or as the obscuration of the object. And at the time of a single certainty, the aggregate consisting of the absence of the perception of all particularities— which is accepted by the opponent as the obscuration— [is likewise present].

Because there is an absence of the non-perception of specific differences, there is no resulting doubt or the like; nor is there, according to the opponent's view, an impossibility of the manifestation of the object at the time of the first cognition of a jar or similar thing, since the aggregate of prior absences—which are considered to be veils—is absent. Therefore, even for an object that is veiled, at the time of the first cognition—
The meaning of "illumination does not occur" here is that this illustration is not possible.
And as for the phrase "this being so": it means that if ignorance were not an obscuring factor at all times for everyone.
And as for "for that reason too": it means even from the realization of Brahman. The reason for the consequence of non-cessation is its lack of obscuration.
Regarding persistence: if, at the time of the arising of the realization of Brahman, the various states of ignorance (*avasthājñāna*)— just like the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—

were to remain veiling the consciousness of Brahman within the regions of their respective objects, then, by virtue of being a veil over that consciousness, they would be removed by the realization of Brahman in the same manner as the root ignorance which has the same object.
The meaning is that there would be a cessation even of those [impressions] remaining in an unmanifest state, because there is no difference in their having the same object.

However, if they remain without veiling that [knowledge], cessation is not possible, as they lack the quality of having the same object as it. Consequently, the implication is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their persistence even in the state of disembodied liberation (videha-kaivalya).
The connection is that [the objection] "if this were so, there would be the consequence of non-cessation" is not valid. He states the reason for this with the words "of them" (*teṣām*).

Here, the second and third occurrences of the word *tat* refer to the realization of Brahman, while the fourth occurrence of the word *tat* refers to the primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), as follows:
Upon the cessation of knowledge, the relationship between consciousness and ignorance ceases, because that relationship is dependent upon its relatum, which is knowledge; such is the meaning.
It is for this very reason that their dependence on it [the Self] is maintained, insofar as they exist in the form of specific states [of consciousness].
Others, however, hold that because ignorance has the nature of having objects, it necessarily veils everything at all times by its very nature; and it does not [wait] for the arising of an object.

It should be stated that its status as an obscuration is not tenable due to the prior absence of anything to be obscured; however, thinking that it still exists in a subtle form even then, they postulate [its existence], just as one might in a place crowded with many people.

A falling meteor, while striking one person's head, causes others as well to move away; or just as a single medicine that cures a derangement of the humors (sannipāta) removes one disorder while driving other disorders far away,
so too knowledge, in destroying one instance of ignorance, dispels other instances of ignorance as well.
And "obscuration" (tiraskāra) is the obstruction of the power of that [knowledge] which persists as long as the knowledge remains.

Now, if this were the case, then in the instance of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika*), the second and subsequent cognitions would be fruitless, since they would not overcome the obscuration; for [the obscuration] was already overcome by the first cognition.
Obstruction does not occur through either removal or rejection, because it is merely overcome [by the light].

Anticipating the objection that it is unestablished that the ignorance of the various states is dependent upon the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), he says: "For this very purpose. The sense is as follows: just as the dependence of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) upon that [root-ignorance] is postulated because its cessation is established through the cessation of ignorance, so too is it in the present case. As it has been said:

It should be understood that the purpose of the qualification "having the nature of distinct states" will be explained later, and thus it is indicated here. Now, with the words "But in the case of the position of beginninglessness," etc., he shows the resolution of the very objection previously raised by way of another method. The connection is: "Others, however, imagine."

He shows their intention with the words "of ignorance" (*ajñānasya*). Now, one might object: there is no rule that all ignorance always veils its objects during its own duration at the time of a single cognition; for while one ignorance is being destroyed, there is a suppression—consisting in the obstruction of the power of concealment—of others even though they exist at that time.
Since it will be explained later that they do not act as veils at the time of a single cognition, he says:

"In general" (*utsargataḥ*). Now, if it is said that [ignorance] veils at all times, one might object that since objects such as jars arise, the veiling of the consciousness delimited by the jar and so forth by the various states of ignorance is perceived even prior to that time.

That [objection] is untenable. He dispels the doubt—namely, that at that time, because of the absence of the delimiting object (*avacchedaka-viṣaya*), there would be no consciousness delimited by it (*tadavacchinna-caitanya*) to be veiled by the ignorance of the state (*avasthājñāna*)—with the words beginning with "na ca" and ending with "tadāpi. This refers to the period prior to the arising of any effect whatsoever, and the period subsequent to its destruction.

The sense is that the existence [of ignorance] in an unmanifest form has been established in various places by the ancient teachers through scripture (*śruti*), tradition (*smṛti*), and reasoning (*nyāya*). "In this way" means: knowledge (*jñāna*) is the agent; as long as knowledge persists, it is the cause for the exception to the general rule that [ignorance] covers everything at all times. Thus, the persistence of knowledge is the reason for the non-existence [of ignorance].
This is the state of affairs. It challenges the rule that "mere knowledge is the remover of ignorance. The phrase "if this were so" means:

if one accepts that by a single cognition there is the destruction of one ignorance and the suppression of others. The phrase "it would be futile" means that it would lack purposeful efficacy, such as the destruction of ignorance and so forth.
He says "the first" because that purpose is accomplished by the very first cognition.

On this point, they say: even ignorance that has been screened by a mental modification (vṛtti) covers [the object] again once that modification ceases, just as darkness that has been screened by a lamp returns when the lamp ceases. However, at the moment the modification ceases, if another modification arises, the ignorance that was screened remains in that very state, just as it was at the moment the lamp ceased.

Just as darkness [vanishes] upon the arising of another lamp, so too, when something exists at the moment of fire and is absent in its absence, that thing is produced by it; thus, in accordance with the definition common to the preservation of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), the status of being the effect of the second and subsequent mental modifications (*vṛtti*) is also secured for the removal of the veil.

Regarding that fruitlessness, the authors of the *Nyāyacandrikā* say: "The destruction of a particular ignorance by a particular knowledge is itself the suppression of other ignorances that veil that same reality."

Even for one who has attained the first knowledge, the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇa-tiraskāra*) can be accomplished by the second and subsequent knowledges, in accordance with the specific requirements of the nature of what is to be achieved (*sādhya-lakṣaṇa-viśeṣa*). Therefore, the second and subsequent knowledges are not fruitless; for even in the absence of a purpose consisting in the destruction of ignorance (*ajñāna-nāśa*), there exists the result characterized as the removal of that veil.

He refutes [the objection]. Regarding this, he says: "In this regard, they say. First, he demonstrates a point established in the case of continuous perception (*dhārāvāhana*), providing an illustration: "This is a jar. Indeed, a single perceptual cognition, while destroying one instance of ignorance, obscures all other instances of ignorance. And that...

Ignorance that was previously suppressed covers that [object] again at the moment the cognition of the jar ceases, or if it does so by virtue of a desire to know (ubhutsā) and the like. At the moment of the destruction of the first arisen cognition of the jar, another perception of the jar arises; then, the ignorance that was suppressed remains in that very same state.

This is the meaning. The definition of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: that which exists when something else exists at the subsequent moment, and which does not exist when that thing does not exist, is produced by it. This definition applies to both things with a beginning (*sādi*) and those without a beginning (*anādi*). For instance, when a staff or similar cause exists, the effect such as a jar exists in the subsequent moment; and when the staff or similar cause is absent, [the jar does not exist].

The effect, such as a jar, is non-existent [prior to its production]; therefore, the jar and so forth are produced by causes such as a staff. Likewise, when an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occurs, there is the existence of the prior non-existence of suffering (*duḥkhaprāgabhāva*) in the subsequent moment; whereas when the expiation is absent, because suffering itself arises, there is the non-existence of the prior non-existence of suffering. In this manner, even for beginningless suffering—

The non-existence prior to an action (*prāgabhāva*) is accepted as being accomplished by the performance of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), since it is that which is to be maintained through such expiation. Likewise, in the present case as well, he demonstrates its status as something to be accomplished [by the second cognition]. This is expressed by the words "And so" (*tathā ca*). When the second cognitive function arises, there exists in the subsequent moment the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇa-tiraskāra*) which was already established by the first cognition.
Furthermore, in the absence of the arising of the second modification (*vṛtti*) at the moment the first cognition perishes, the aforementioned concealment would be non-existent;
for even though that [concealment] is established at the very time of the first cognition, it is produced by the second modification.

The meaning is that one should apply the same principle to the third and subsequent cognitions as well: that their fruit is precisely the removal of the veil (*āvaraṇa*). Regarding the phrase "of non-veiling" (*anāvaraṇasya*), it means "of the removal of the veil.
Not every mere cognition is a transformer of ignorance (*ajñāna-vivartaka*), as is seen in the case of a continuous stream of second and subsequent cognitions.
Regarding the phrase "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*), the author of the *Nyāyacandrikā* states a refutation by means of another method: "But not...

One should not say: "If there were no obscuration of other cognitions, then even at the time of a single cognition, since the object would be covered by those non-obscured [cognitions], it would follow that there could be no experience of the object."

The meaning is that at the arising of the first cognition, there is only one ignorance that veils the object; as for the others, it is not even admitted that they veil the object at that time, and therefore there is no need for their removal.
And thus, even the second and subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (dhārāvāhika) possess efficacy by virtue of each destroying a single instance of ignorance;
nor does it follow that the object would fail to appear because an obscuration could still exist despite the arising of knowledge,
for ignorances exist in the form of distinct states (avasthā).
And the cognitions, which have as their nature the concealment [of reality] characterized by their respective times,
are destroyers of the ignorance that conceals the objects characterized by those same respective times; thus,
when a particular cognition arises, there is the destruction of the ignorance concealing the object of that specific time.
Since existing ignorances have perished, and since other [ignorances] belonging to different times do not obscure the object,

there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the manifestation of the object at that time; this is just as the rain resulting from the Kārīrī sacrifice occurs at a proximate time, so too with the jar or other objects that are the objects of ignorance.

Since that [specific] time is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) and does not enter into the category of the object itself, there is no inconsistency whatsoever even if ignorance is removed by successive cognitions— the second and subsequent ones in a continuous stream— which do not have the subtle distinctions of those respective times as their objects.

To this, they ask: "What follows from that? He refutes the doubt of one who does not understand the intention by stating, "And it is not so," and so forth. The meaning of the word "evam" (thus) is: when the first cognition does not obscure the other veiling ignorances. The phrase "at each respective time" [is used].

All the *avasthā-avidyās* (empirical ignorances) do not possess the quality of veiling the consciousness of the object at all times, like the *mūla-avidyā* (radical ignorance), because that would be purposeless. Rather, one particular *avidyā* veils the consciousness of a certain object for a certain period of time, while another veils it at a different time; it is in this manner [that they function].

The meaning is this: although cognitions are obscurers of the consciousness of their respective objects—since they are characterized by specific times—they nevertheless remove ignorance because they act as obscurers of their own respective objects at the very time of their own arising.
Having thus expressed this intention, he now dispels the objection regarding the non-manifestation of objects. "And so it is," he says.
The meaning is: "given that it has been established that other ignorances do not act as obscuring factors at the time of a single cognition.

Regarding the phrase "at that time" (*tatkālīna*): it means of that ignorance which is postulated as an obscuring factor for an object that arises simultaneously with some particular cognition. Regarding the phrase "not that" (*na tat*): it means [not] that which exists at the time of some particular cognition. Now, by those various...

Since it is precisely that karma which is qualified by specific times that possesses the nature of being an obscuration of such-and-such knowledge, why is it accepted that these specific times function as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*), rather than having them enter the category of the things to be obscured (*āvaraṇīya*) as qualifiers?

Anticipating this objection, [the author] states: if that were the case, then even for the second and subsequent mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which function to remove the ignorance (*ajñāna*) that has presented itself as an obscuration in the locus of the continuous stream (*dhārā*), it must be admitted that they possess as their object a subject qualified by its respective specific time.
This is because it is impossible for them to remove that ignorance without having the same object; yet such [simultaneity of object] is not possible.

Because the distinctions between moments are not perceptible, the resolution is that their status as indicators (upalakṣaṇatva) is accepted. Intending this solution, he states an example for the status of a particular time as an indicator:
"in the case of rain, which is the fruit of the Kārīrī [sacrifice]. Rain is the result produced by the sacrifice named Kārīrī.

It must be stated that [the rain] is to be protected immediately upon completion, and not at another time; for at that moment, since the crops are withering, rain occurring at a later time would be of no use. Thus, it is not logical for the rain to enter into the category of the result as a qualification of a proximate time, even in the absence of a specific sacrifice.
The meaning is that, although [ignorance] exists, it is accepted as being merely an *upalakṣaṇa* (a secondary indicator) because it serves to distinguish it from other moments in time.

However, some maintain that only the ignorance removed by the first cognition is the concealer of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), whereas those removed by the second and subsequent cognitions have as their objects subjects qualified by specific locations and times; for this very reason...

When the perception of Caitra—which consists of the ascertainment of his existence and which removes ignorance—is produced, one who is prone to forgetfulness does not experience the obscuration of the essential nature (svarūpāvaraṇa) in the form "I do not know Caitra"; rather, there occurs only an obscuration of specific attributes (viśiṣṭāvaraṇa), such as "Now, where is he? and so forth.

If it is observed that even when something is seen once, there is an obscuration of its true nature such that one says "I do not know," let it be so in that case; however, in other instances where [an object] is seen once, there are simply cognitions regarding the objects themselves and non-cognitions [regarding them].
This being the case, the second and subsequent cognitions in a continuous stream (*dhārāvāhika*) do not possess the capacity to remove ignorance.
It should not be argued that ignorance qualified by gross time is removed by the first cognition alone,

whereas ignorance qualified by subtle time— which is excluded from the preceding and succeeding cognitions— is removed by the second and subsequent cognitions which do not have that [subtle time] as their object.

In the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhana*), there would be no subduing of the veil by the second and subsequent cognitions; thus, he presents the refutation of this objection in three ways, beginning with "Some, however" (*kecit tu*). First, he states the actual state of affairs: "By the first cognition," etc. He cites experience as the proof for the aforementioned established principle.

He shows this with the words "for this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because of the acceptance of the aforementioned division. One might object: "The stated division is not established, since even when an object has been perceived once, there is an experience of the obscuration of its own nature as before"; anticipating this, he says: "of those characterized by forgetfulness. In that regard:

"Let it be so" means that even in the case of the experience of the veiling of the true nature (*svarūpa*), ignorance—which is to be removed by the second and subsequent cognitions—may still veil the true nature; such is the meaning. Thus, the intended sense is that the aforementioned division is the general rule (*autsargika*). "Elsewhere," however...

The meaning is: a state where there is no possibility of forgetfulness. Now, if ignorance were to have a qualified entity as its object, it would follow that it could never be removed; for even subsequent cognitions regarding an object already seen once would—like the first cognition—have only the thing-in-itself (svarūpa) as their object, and thus would lack the same object as the [first] ignorance.
He says "no" because it is untenable for that [non-existence] to be the sublater [of existence]. He says, "And cognitions," etc.

The point is that since even cognitions regarding an object perceived once—such as "Caitra is here now"—are admitted to have qualified objects as their content, the aforementioned fault does not apply. But [one might ask], how can cognitions have qualified objects as their content?

Indeed, [the qualification] beginning with "second" and so forth is postulated in the case of the locus of persistence (*dhārāsthala*) for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*). And thus, in that context, is it intended that cognitions have as their object a jar or the like qualified by a gross time consisting of half a *ghaṭikā*, a *ghaṭikā*, and so on; or rather, [a jar or the like] qualified by a subtle time consisting of moments (*kṣaṇa*)?

Anticipating the objection that "having [the first cognition] as its object" (viṣayakatva) is what is intended, he raises a doubt that in either case, the defect of deviation remains unavoidable in instances of continuous cognition (dhārāvāhika-jñāna), such as the second and subsequent cognitions. He says: "And this being so... [This means:
since the second and subsequent cognitions, as well as the ignorance to be removed by them, generally have a qualified entity as their object.
The meaning is "it exists. "By the first cognition alone" means, as the ellipsis suggests, by that which has a gross temporal qualification as its object.

Regarding "prior and posterior": in the case of a continuous stream [of cognitions], cognitions have a duration of only a single moment; therefore, there are subtle moments excluded from the time-points of the prior and posterior cognitions.
The meaning is: of that ignorance which resides in the object as qualified by those [moments] whose nature is momentary (*kṣaṇa*).
"By those which do not have that as their object" means by those which do not have [the object] as qualified by subtle time as their object.
In the case of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhana*), it is the very first cognition that persists for that duration of time.
Because, according to the doctrine of possibility (*saṃbhava*), a distinction between the functions [of the senses] is not admitted; and even if that were admitted,

a gross temporal state would still consist of five or six functions, since it is possible for it to have as its object the distinctions among qualifiers such as gross time, which are mutually excluded by way of possibility.

Even if it is accepted that [cognition] consists of a continuum of multiple functions arising at every moment, there is no loss [of the definition of perception], because subsequent functions lack validity— since they have as their object only what has already been apprehended— and thus do not remove obscurations. For indeed...

Validity consists merely in the non-sublation of the object; for otherwise, since there is no difference in the non-sublation of the objects of inference— the mountain and the fire residing upon it— there would follow the undesirable consequence that the validity of the inference applies equally to both cases, regardless of whether [the object] was previously known or not yet apprehended.

Nor is there any undesirable consequence [in our position], for although one might say "inference regarding fire is a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), we do not observe the conventional usage "inference is a means of valid cognition."

Where there is a continuous manifestation for a long duration in relation to a single object such as the Śrīmūrti, there is only one mental modification (*vṛtti*) having that Śrīmūrti as its object, because there is no evidence for its division [into multiple moments]. This is because, in our system (*siddhānta*), it is not accepted that a mental modification lasts for only a single moment. Thus, he states that there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case.

Regarding the phrase "the stage of continuous flow" (*dhārāvāhana-sthala*): Now, if there were oneness of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in that state, it would contradict the well-known usage of the term "continuous flow," because such a thing is impossible in a single [modification]. Furthermore, since meditation (*dhyāna*) and absorption (*samādhi*) would also result in being of the nature of a single modification according to the aforementioned reasoning, this would contradict the *Bhāṣya* and other texts which establish that these two consist of a succession of cognitions (*pratyaya-saṃtati*).

Anticipating the objection that this might lead to an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*), he avoids the charge of inconsistency by accepting that a continuous stream (*dhārā*) consists of multiple mental modifications (*vṛtti*). [He says: "Even if that is admitted. [The phrase] "by possibility" implies "of the stream.
[The phrase] "by way of reasoning" implies that there is no fault of the second and subsequent modifications failing to remove ignorance.

Even while accepting that continuous mental states (*dhārāvāhika-vṛtti*) have momentary duration—just as in the Nyāya school—the author avoids the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The phrase "arising at every moment" (*pratikṣaṇodyat*) means those mental states which arise anew at every moment;

the intended meaning refers to their continuum (*saṃtāna*). The phrase "even if [this] is accepted" implies "of the stream" (*dhārāyāḥ*), as is understood from the context. And "because of non-cessation" (*ahāneḥ*).
The meaning is that there is no loss in the form of a violation of the rule that "knowledge is the remover of ignorance.
He states the reason for the absence of such loss: "due to the absence of novelty" (*aprāptyabhāvena*). He provides the reason for that:
"merely concerning an object already apprehended" (*adhigatārthamātra*). The meaning of the word "merely" (*mātra*) is the absence of having as its object something not yet apprehended. Thus...

And the meaning is that there is no validity (*prāmāṇya*) for the second and subsequent cognitions, because, like memory, they have as their object only that which has already been apprehended. Now, one might object: validity does not consist in being an uncontradicted experience of an unapprehended object; rather, it is simply uncontradicted experience.
Just as in the case of the two [cognitions] of "ground" (*bhūmi*) and "recollection" (*smṛti*), there are no entities whose referents or exclusions have not yet been apprehended;

likewise, validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists merely in the experience of an object that is not sublated, and this remains intact in second and subsequent cognitions. Therefore, there would be no loss in the form of a violation of the rule regarding them. To this, he says: "No," and so forth.

Immediately after the word "validity" (*prāmāṇyam*), the phrase "that being so" (*tathā sati*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The Naiyāyika raises an objection: "And it is not a case of an undesired consequence" (*na ceṣṭāpattiḥ*). The connection is with the words "not" (*na*) and "undesired consequence" (*iṣṭāpattiḥ*). [The objection continues: "Because no such practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is observed. Thus, since the determination of validity and invalidity follows practical activity, [this would apply] to inference.

Since it has been established that the mountain-part (*parvatāṃśa*) is not a subject of definition (*alakṣya*) due to the absence of truth (*pramātva*) therein, the qualification "not previously apprehended" (*anadhigatatva*) must indeed be included in that definition in order to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) regarding the truth of the inference of the mountain-part. Consequently, the second and subsequent moments of a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) do not possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).
The state of being.

Furthermore, in the *Vivaraṇa*, it is stated that although ignorance—which is established by direct witness—may be the object of inference and other means of knowledge for the purpose of conveying its exclusion from non-existence, it is nonetheless not known through [ordinary] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, since subsequent mental modifications (*vṛtti*) lack the status of being valid cognitions, [they do not apply to Brahman]; thus, [there is only] meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth.

Even if [the means of knowledge] do not function as the remover of ignorance— just like other mental modifications (vṛtti)— there is no loss, because it is accepted that only those modifications which are themselves valid cognitions (prāmāṇa-vṛtti) are the removers thereof.
He states another reason for the inclusion of "being unknown" (*ajñātatva*) in the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*). [The phrase] "in the *Vivaraṇa*" connects as follows:
because it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not known by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Here, the word "inference" (*anumāna*) refers to inferential knowledge (*anumiti*), and the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) also refers to valid cognition (*pramiti*).

It should be understood that this is because the definition of valid cognition (*pramā*) is the subject at hand. Now, one might object: "If ignorance (*ajñāna*) is an object of mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—such as inference, verbal testimony, or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—how can it be said that it is not known by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

To this, he says: "Established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣisiddha*). This means that the nature of ignorance is established by the witness-consciousness in the form of the experience, "I am ignorant."

Considering that because it is already known, there is no "truth-status" (pramātva) defined by "being unknown" regarding the object—which is ignorance itself—in the case of the inference of ignorance and so forth, its "non-cognisability by a means of valid knowledge" (pramāṇāvedyatva) was stated. Nor should it be argued: "Since the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) itself is a means of valid knowledge, how can it be said that [ignorance] is generally uncognisable by a means of valid knowledge?"
This is because what is intended is precisely the state of not being known by any means of knowledge other than the witness (*sākṣin*).

Alternatively, since the witness is eternal and thus not produced by the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it—like the knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara*) which is accepted by others as such—is excluded from both valid and invalid cognitions; therefore, it is stated that [Brahman] is not known by it, as it lacks the status of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

[The opponent says: "But if ignorance (*ajñāna*) is established by the direct perception of a witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), for what purpose then are inference and other means of knowledge adduced in that regard? To this he replies: "For the sake of excluding [it from] non-existence" (*abhāvavyāvṛtti*).
The purpose is to convey the exclusion of ignorance from that which is considered by others to be ignorance, namely, that which is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*).
The meaning is that those [means of knowledge], such as inference and the rest, for which there is a specific purpose are "tathā" (of such a kind). This is what is being said:

"I am ignorant"—this ignorance, established by the experience of both [the self and the object], is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), according to the proponents of our own school (*siddhāntin*). At that time, it is not of the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), according to the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

Furthermore, since the difference of ignorance (ajñāna) from its counter-positive (pratiyogin), namely non-existence, is established through inference and other means, those [means] are not redundant. Nor should it be argued that nothing is gained by proving its positive nature;
for this is established by scriptures such as, "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti."

Because the status of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) for the transformation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is established, it follows that [the knowledge of Brahman] is the fruit of that means of proof. "Therefore" means:

because the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*), which consists in being previously unapprehended (*anadhigatatva*), is absent. "Like the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth" means: a modification in the form of meditation is not considered knowledge, because it is not produced by the causes [of knowledge], such as the mind.

Since the status of [knowledge] as an instrument has been refuted and will not be maintained, it is rather of the nature of an action, like going and so forth, because it is to be accomplished by human effort; therefore, it is not the remover of ignorance regarding the true nature of the object of meditation, nor do mental modifications such as desire and aversion [perform this function].

The meaning is as follows: [the first modification] does not remove ignorance regarding its own object because it lacks the nature of valid knowledge (*jñāna*). As for the second and subsequent modifications, although they possess the nature of recollection (*smṛti*), which is a form of knowledge, they are not accepted as removing ignorance because they lack the status of being valid knowledge (*pramā*).
Now, one might ask: even if they lack the status of valid knowledge, why is there no loss [of their function]?

Anticipating the objection that by accepting [the definition] as "being knowledge," it would necessarily follow that mere knowledge (jñānamātra) is the remover of ignorance—which would entail the loss of the [definition's] character of being non-deviant—the author says: "Only of the functions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavṛtti*)," meaning "but not even of those functions whose object is merely what has already been apprehended. And thus:
The sense is that no such restriction—that "mere knowledge alone is the remover of ignorance"—is accepted, by which the aforementioned fault would arise;
for after the word "abhyupagamāt" (because of acceptance), the words "ity āhuḥ" (so they say) are to be supplied as the ellipsis, since the passage begins with "kecit tu" (but some [say]).

If it is objected: "Is this not also a restrictive rule, since indirect cognition (*parokṣavṛtti*) does not necessarily remove ignorance (*ajñāna*)?"—to this some say: Ignorance that veils the object is of two kinds. One is located in the object itself, such as the rope [in the case of a snake], serving as the material cause (*upādāna*) for its various manifestations (*vikṣepa*), and is to be inferred from its effects. The other is located in the person.

The experience "I do not know the object" is impossible for that which resides in the person (the self), because it cannot be the material cause of a distraction mixed with the object; nor is it possible for that which resides in the object, because it cannot have contact with the light in the form of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

Because both [types of modification] are necessary; and likewise, because in the case of indirect perception (*parokṣa*), there is no emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*); and because, even when the size of a distant tree is understood through the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), one observes a discrepancy regarding its size that contradicts that [information].
Even when the ignorance residing in the object is removed by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), there is indeed the cessation of the ignorance residing in the person (*puruṣa*);
thus, he raises an objection regarding the violation of the rule that "mere valid cognition (*pramā*) alone is the remover of ignorance. He begins with "But surely...
(*nanu*) in order to state that there is no such violation, since even indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) possesses the capacity to remove that [ignorance]. Regarding this ignorance...
He states its twofold nature with the words beginning "it is of two kinds. Regarding the phrase "the rope and so forth":

this refers to the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the rope and so forth in the form of a snake and the like; the meaning is that it is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [manifestation]. Regarding the phrase "to be inferred from its effects":

the meaning is that it is to be inferred from the impossibility of the effect known as the manifestation, and is not established by direct experience. Now, [one might object]: "But the rope and so forth..."

Since it is established by experience that one who possesses ignorance [of an object] has the intuition, "I do not know the rope," how can it be argued that such ignorance is inferable solely from its effects?
Anticipating this objection, he states that the object of that experience is not the ignorance residing in the object itself, saying:
"It is other. Here, the ignorance that veils the object is of two kinds; one...

The connection is that one [kind of error] is based on the object (*viṣaya-āśrita*) and the other is based on the person (*puruṣa-āśrita*). Thus, having demonstrated that "that" [first kind of] valid cognition is based on the object, he demonstrates that "that" [second kind of] valid cognition is based on the person; this is how the introduction of the word "another" (*anyat*) should be understood. Now, [an objection may be raised]: surely the projection (*vikṣepa*) of a snake and so forth does not [arise] from a single ignorance alone?
And because the experience "I know" is established, what is the use of a twofold division of ignorance? To this he says:

"Of that which rests upon the Puruṣa. The meaning is: since it is impossible for [ignorance] to have as its limiting adjunct (upādhi) that distraction (vikṣepa) which is mixed with—that is, has attained identity with—the object, whose substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) is the rope and so forth. Not...
The meaning is that it is because of the impossibility of a connection with that light, which is of the nature of a witness (*sākṣin*) characterized by the form "I know.
Now, he avoids the charge of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*). "And thus" means: when there is a twofold nature of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
And thus, even in the case of indirect perception (*parokṣa*), although the ignorance residing in the object has not been removed...
The connection is that there is indeed the cessation of ignorance residing in the person (*puruṣagatājñānanivṛtti*). And thus, the sense is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [in the rule].

He states two reasons for the opponent's claim that knowledge lacks the capacity to remove ignorance residing in its object, beginning with the words "of the modification" (*vṛtteḥ*) and so forth, ending with "due to the absence of exit" (*nirgamanābhāvāt*).

The point is that since it will be explained later that only a mental modification (*vṛtti*) which is in contact with the consciousness of the object can remove the ignorance residing in that object-consciousness, the contact between the modification and the object-consciousness would not be established in the absence of [the modification's] going out [from the internal organ].
"Contrary to that" means: a tree seen at a distance [is perceived] as if it were a nearby tree.

The meaning is: because of the observation of a specific kind of distortion in the form of dimension that is the opposite of the specific dimension belonging to a distant tree, which is the object of a mediate cognition (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by the words of a great authoritative person (*āpta*). If mediate cognition were to remove [doubt] with respect to its object, [it would do so] by means of that [distortion].

The meaning is that, through the cessation of ignorance regarding specific dimensions by means of the comprehension arising from the words of a reliable authority, there occurs the removal of the mental distraction (*vikṣepa*) consisting of erroneous notions of dimension; for [in that state], there is an absence of material causes (*upādāna*).

This is because one experiences the cessation of that ignorance—previously experienced as "I do not know the meaning of the scripture"—immediately after its instruction. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvadīpana* that the purpose of the *Vivaraṇa*'s statement regarding the exclusion of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) from inferable objects and the like is the cessation of the ignorance concerning those objects. Others, however, [hold a different view].
