Just as a film on the eye belongs only to the person and is an ignorance that obscures the object, there is no evidence for an ignorance residing in the object itself apart from that [personal ignorance]. Nor is it impossible for that which resides in the person to undergo the transformation of projection toward the object; or, even if such a possibility were granted—

It must be stated that when the ignorance regarding the size of a distant tree is removed through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), the distraction (*vikṣepa*) consisting of a contrary perception of its size cannot occur.
He states the cause for the cessation of the knowledge residing in the person by means of indirect knowledge: "the meaning of the scripture.
By the expression "I do not know the meaning of the scripture," there is an experience of ignorance regarding the meaning of the scripture;
after the instruction on the meaning of the scripture, that ignorance regarding the meaning of the scripture is now ceased.
Cessation [of ignorance] is experienced. In that regard, the meaning of the scripture is twofold: consisting of *dharma* and consisting of *brahman*.

Regarding the scriptural meaning consisting of *dharma*, the knowledge produced by instruction is indeed mediate (*parokṣa*) and never immediate (*aparokṣa*), because it is incapable of direct realization; and thus, in that case, there is no cessation of ignorance residing in the object.

Since there is no possibility of [ignorance] residing in the person, it must be said that only the knowledge pertaining to the person ceases; otherwise, it would contradict the experience of its cessation and the scriptural teaching that the nature of Brahman is the object of the treatise. Knowledge produced by instruction is indeed indirect (*parokṣa*); nevertheless, by that much alone, the ignorance residing in the object—which veils the subject—ceases.

Because it would otherwise follow that injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and so forth are purposeless. Therefore, one must state that only the ignorance residing in the person (*puruṣa*) is removed;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the experience of its removal even in that case—this is the sense.
He states the consensus of the *Vivaraṇa* and other works regarding the fact that indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) removes ignorance, saying: "For this very reason."

The meaning is: "solely by the force of the aforementioned experience. Regarding the phrase *tad-viṣaya*, the word *tat* (that) refers to the inferable object (*anumeya*) and so forth; the word *suṣupti* (deep sleep) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*); and the word *vyāvṛtti* (exclusion) refers to cessation (*nivṛtti*).
This is explained in the *Tattvadīpana*. And thus, [it concerns] the absence of the cessation of ignorance residing in the object, such as the inferable, etc.

The meaning is that, because [the matter] will be explained later, it is understood that the intended sense therein is that the cessation of ignorance residing in the person occurs through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), such as inference and so forth; this remains the case even though there is no twofold division of ignorance.

He presents the view that there is no deviation from the rule that "mere valid cognition (pramā) is the remover of ignorance" by stating, "But others [say]... [The argument is as follows: Is the ignorance residing in the object, which depends on the ignorance residing in the person, accepted for the purpose of veiling the object? Or is it for the purpose of producing the illusory projection (vikṣepa), such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell? It cannot be the first.
Thus he says: "Like a film over the eye. This means like a cataract (kāca) or similar defect located in the eye. He says that the second [alternative] is not [tenable]:

"Not by way of anything additional to that. The sense is that even in the absence of ignorance residing in the object, the arising of *vikṣepa* (projective illusion) is possible according to the method to be explained later.
He raises an objection, claiming that the lack of evidence is unestablished: "And not... No.

"It is possible," he says. The sense is that there is no absence of existence (sattvābhāva) in the consciousness limited by the mother-of-pearl and so forth belonging to the ignorance residing in the person (puruṣa). He states the defect in the view that the ignorance residing in the person alone is the material cause (upādāna) for the projection (vikṣepa) residing in the object: "If that were possible," and so on. [The defect is that] the ignorance residing in the person [would have to be the cause of the projection] residing in the object.

The meaning of that word [“ignorance”] is its being transformed (*pariṇāmitva*). It is not possible, because ignorance residing in the object is not admitted, and ignorance residing in the person has already been removed by the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by the teacher’s instruction; this is the intended sense.

According to the view of Vācaspati, since the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman as it is objectified by ignorance residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), it follows that [illusory objects] such as nacre-silver are likewise illusory manifestations of Brahman as it is objectified by ignorance residing in the person [who perceives them].

They say that even when the single state [of the mind] ceases through its functioning in a hidden manner, a contrary expansion of size (parimāṇa) arises by means of another state. Others, however, maintain that because the transformation of mother-of-pearl into silver and so forth is logically consistent, it is the envelopment of the object [that occurs].
Ignorance residing within the object itself, like a cloth, is its obscuration.

He addresses the first objection with the words "according to the view of Vācaspati. On the position that an error such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it must be stated that ignorance resides in the consciousness of the object (*viṣayacaitanya*);
however, on the position where its being a transformation of ignorance is not accepted, its residing in the consciousness of the object [is not required].

The meaning is that it is not required. Regarding the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*), the word "Brahman" refers to Brahman in the form of consciousness delimited by mother-of-pearl and so forth, and not to the full, undivided Brahman;

for it is accepted that only consciousness delimited [by an adjunct] serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the silver in mother-of-pearl and the like—this is the intended sense. The distortion (*vikṣepa*) consists in the form of a contrary dimension.
The phrase "it is not possible" addresses the second objection. Regarding the expression "by means of indirect cognition":

just as the cessation of ignorance through indirect knowledge is experienced, so too, in the case cited, even when indirect knowledge exists, the arising of a contrary measurement is likewise experienced. Thus [it is said].

The sense is that, in accordance with the two types of experience, it is postulated that only the ignorance residing in the *puruṣa*— which veils the object— is such that one part of it is dispelled by immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) while another part persists; however, a twofold nature of ignorance itself is not accepted, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Regarding the phrase "by means of another state," the ellipsis is "of ignorance itself residing in the person. In reality,
even according to the view that indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is the remover [of ignorance], it is only indirect knowledge that is free from obstruction which removes ignorance.

And in the present context, due to the influence of error, qualities such as distance—which are dependent on location—even knowledge produced by the words of a reliable person does not remove the ignorance residing in the person. Therefore, there is no room for the suspicion that there is an inconsistency regarding a contrary measurement. Nor is it the fourth [alternative], because it follows immediately after the instruction of a reliable person.

It should not be argued that there would be the experience of specific dimensions residing in a tree situated at a distance; for even when ignorance exists, it is logically possible for indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) in the form of a certain conviction to act as an obstacle to that experience. Furthermore, it is not the case that every instance of valid cognition (*pramā*) necessarily removes ignorance.

It should not be said that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule regarding indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramā*), because it must be understood that "unobstructed" (*apratibaddha*) is intended as a qualification of valid cognition (*pramā*). Thus, following the rule that "any unobstructed valid cognition whatsoever is the remover of ignorance," [the definition] is stated so that there may be no deviation from it.

The capacity of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) to remove ignorance has been demonstrated; however, now [the author] introduces the view of others, who hold that such a rule does not exist, but rather that only obstructed direct knowledge (*prativaddhāparokṣajñāna*) removes ignorance, and therefore there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding indirect knowledge. This is introduced with the words: "But others... In the world, [the cause of] a jar and so forth is clay and so forth.

Since the nature of being a transformation (*pariṇāmatva*) is well-established [in the case of the world], it is likewise established for nacre-silver and the like. Furthermore, that which undergoes such transformation is determined—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) assisted by the method of elimination—to be none other than ignorance (*ajñāna*), and not the nacre or similar objects; for it is impossible for illusory silver and the like to be transformations of those material objects.
And [it is] like silver in the case of consciousness directed toward an object.

Nor should it be argued that, such being the case, there is the fault that the manifestation [of the truth] from the witness (sākṣin) conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) would be impossible due to its lack of contact with that [truth], and that indirect mental modification (parokṣavṛtti) could not remove [ignorance].

Even when there is contact, the witness-consciousness of the ignorance regarding the state-form (avasthārūpa) is the manifestation of that very root-ignorance conjoined with it— as in the experience "I do not know the mother-of-pearl"— because the mother-of-pearl and so forth are non-different from the consciousness that is the object of the root-ignorance.

Because there is no contradiction with the experience of that [ignorance] being its object; and because, in the *Vivaraṇa* and other works, during the demonstration of the proof for root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the perception "I do not know this" is presented as the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).

The state of being transformed by distraction is established with clarity in [the case of] that [which belongs to the intellect], but it is not so established in the case of that which resides in the *puruṣa*;
therefore, in accordance with the clarity of that establishment, one must accept that ignorance (*ajñāna*) in the form of a state exists only as residing in the object, and not [in the *puruṣa*].
The sense is that even ignorance residing in the Puruṣa cannot exist in a state [separate from the Puruṣa], because it would be purposeless and because there is no evidence for it.

Although ignorance, even when supported by the Puruṣa, does not abandon the Puruṣa but—by way of a modification (vṛtti)—goes outwards like a long ray of light and takes refuge in the object-consciousness, such as silver; [it is in this manner that the superimposition occurs].
Even if transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) were thus established, that establishment would not be straightforward;

for, like fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the ignorance of the states (*avasthājñāna*) is also devoid of activity, and thus the logic of light (*prabhānyāya*) does not apply to it. With this in mind, it was stated that [the objection] is "not straightforward" (*anaja*) regarding the establishment of transformation. Likewise:

"Satīti" means "given that the ignorance which veils the object resides in the object. "Tata iti" means "from the witness (sākṣin)," as indicated by the ablative case. "And [there is] impossibility" refers to the fact that indirect mental modification (*parokṣavṛtti*) does not go out to the location of the object; this is the intended meaning.

He dispels the first objection with the words "of the ignorance regarding the state" (*avasthārūpājñānasya*). The meaning is this: in the experience "I do not know the mother-of-pearl," the object is not the ignorance residing in the object (*viṣayagata*), but rather the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) itself, because only that is in contact with the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*). Now, [an objection]: as for the root-ignorance...
Since it has Brahman as its object, how is the experience of it having nacre as its object possible?

Or, how is the experience of the ignorance of the state (avasthājñāna) having nacre as its object possible? For that too has only the Consciousness delimited by nacre (śuktyavacchinnacaitanya) as its object. [This is because] the nacre is the Consciousness which is the object of the ignorance of the state...

If it is argued that the experience of having nacre as its object is not contradicted by way of identity (*tādātmya*), the reply is the same; with this intention, he says: "Of the nacre and so forth as well. Regarding the phrase "as non-different": since everything that is insentient (*jaḍa*) is superimposed upon the consciousness that is the object of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the nacre and so forth also possess the nature of identity with that [consciousness].

The intention is that there exists non-difference from that [the Self]. He cites the consensus of the *Vivaraṇa* and other works regarding the fact that the experience "I do not know the mother-of-pearl" has as its object the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). Regarding the phrase "in the *Vivaraṇa* and so forth":
[an objection is raised]—"But in the section establishing root ignorance, the experience 'I am ignorant' was shown to be the one presented."

Thus, it is the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) that is established. As for the experience "I do not know this," its object is indeed the ignorance pertaining to a particular state (*avasthājñāna*);

nor should a contradiction with the context be suspected, since the ignorance pertaining to a state must also be established in order to account for transformations characterized by such things as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Even in the section establishing primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), its proof arises as a necessary consequence (*prasaṅga*). Just as the experience "I do not know this [object]" has as its object the ignorance of the consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by that particular object, so too the experience "I am ignorant; I do not know reality" [has as its object the ignorance of the consciousness delimited by reality].
"The object of fundamental ignorance" is the method of illustration.

Even if one accepts the distinction that the general experience of ignorance, "I am ignorant," has as its object the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), whereas the experience of ignorance qualified by a specific object, such as "I do not know this mother-of-pearl," has as its object a state-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*), [the problem remains]. State-ignorance...

Since the states [of consciousness] are non-different from that which possesses them, and because either the root-ignorance is in contact with the witness (*sākṣin*) or there is a real identity between the witness-consciousness and the object-consciousness,

it is established that even the ignorance regarding an object residing in that state is an object of the witness; this remains so even though indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) does not remove ignorance.

Consequently, since the experience of that cessation is established as being a delusion caused by non-apprehension— due to the presence of an obstructing factor residing in the subject (*pakṣa*) which consists of the certainty of its existence— it follows that it is indeed a form of non-perceptual knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*).

They say that this is because it is accepted as a rule that knowledge is the remover [of ignorance]. But if it is objected: "Even this rule does not hold, for it is not accepted that the perception of ignorance, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), pleasure, pain, and their attributes is the remover of ignorance."

Ignorance and the like do not constitute an obscuration for direct perception, because it is impossible to deny the rule that [perception] in its form as immediate knowledge— which is of the nature of a witness— acts as a remover [of obscurations].

Furthermore, since it is possible to demonstrate the experience of ignorance as qualified by specific objects even in the context of establishing primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), there is no evidence that experiences such as "I do not know this" have primordial ignorance as their object; rather, they have only the state of ignorance (*avasthājñāna*) as their object.

And because that [ignorance] must be spoken of as having that [self] as its means of proof, once it is established that it resides in the object, the doubt—intending to show that the experience of that [ignorance] is impossible due to the absence of contact with the witness (sākṣin)—is restated as: "I am ignorant. [This refers to] the ignorance residing in the object being [perceived] by the witness.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that even though there is no direct relationship, there is no impossibility of experiencing it because an indirect (paraṃparā) relationship is possible: "of the state and the possessor of the state. "By non-difference" means identity (*tādātmya*). And thus:

The meaning is that because it is a state of the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna) which is in contact with the witness (sākṣin), there is a connection of the knowledge residing in the object with the witness by way of the root-ignorance. Regarding the term "witness" (sākṣī): in reality, there is a connection between the consciousness of the witness and the consciousness of the object, which is the locus of the state-ignorance.

The meaning is that because of the oneness [of consciousness], there is a connection between the witness (*sākṣin*)— which is supported by the non-differentiated consciousness residing in the hand— and the ignorance located in the object, along with that witness. As for what was stated regarding the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of indirect cognition (*parokṣavṛtti*), that is not so, because it is accepted that direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) is the remover of ignorance.

Likewise, there is no acceptance of a restrictive rule (*niyama*); for if such a rule were accepted, there would be the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the operation of [the means of knowledge] directed toward what is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*).
[Objection:
But then, this contradicts the experience of the cessation of that ignorance—which was previously experienced as "I do not know the meaning of the scripture"—immediately after its instruction.

Thus he says "no" [to the objection], stating "of indirect knowledge. The word "from that" means "from indirect knowledge. Regarding the phrase "because error is established": one should not argue, "How can error be postulated here, given the absence of any sublation?
This is because [error is established] in relation to the ignorance residing in the object.

The sense is that the postulation of an infinite number of intervening cognitions pertaining to the person involves the defect of theoretical complexity (*gaurava*), which serves as a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
How, then, can it be accepted that the operations of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) bring about their cessation? To this he replies:
"Of direct knowledge alone" (*aparokṣajñānasyaiva*); but not...

The intention of the particle *eva* is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), because the mere cognition that constitutes a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*) is common to indirect knowledge. Regarding the phrase "its property" (*taddharma*): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
[The reason for this] is "because it is not accepted," meaning that ignorance (*avidyā*), the ego-sense, and so forth, do not necessarily exist at the time of their own manifestation.
The meaning is that this is because those [three] veils are not admitted [in his case]. He offers a rebuttal by stating a restriction on the rule: "No.
Now, who is this "Witness" (sākṣin) who is spoken of as distinct from the individual soul (jīva)? Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*:
"The immutable consciousness (kūṭasthacaitanya), which serves as the substratum for the two bodies, [is the Witness] of its own limiter..."

It is called the "Witness" (sākṣin) because it directly perceives the two bodies and is itself changeless; for even in common worldly usage, witness-hood is well-known to consist precisely of neutrality and awareness. Although the modifications (vṛttis) of the individual soul (jīva) have the two bodies as their instruments, nevertheless—

By stating that the witness (*sākṣin*) is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which has pleasure and so forth as its attributes (*dharmin*), the witness is indicated as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). This is because, in common worldly usage, it is precisely the ego—the substratum of pleasure and so forth—that is well-known as the "living being. Thus, the witness is distinct from that which is the individual soul.

He raises an objection: "That which is conventionally designated does not exist, because there is a lack of means of valid cognition (*māna*). Regarding the word "atha" (now/then): the connection is "Who is this that is conventionally designated as distinct from the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)? The word "what" (*kim*) has the sense of an objection. And [it is so] "because of being changeless" (*nirvikāratvāt*). Now, one might object: "The state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtva*) consists in being the agent of the act of seeing, yet [the Self] is also said to be changeless."

If it is argued that there is a mutual contradiction between the state of being free from modifications such as agency and [the state of being a seer], we say no; for agency belongs to the immutable one who is the very nature of seeing—the witness (sākṣin) who is the direct seer—according to the rule of the Sūtra "In the case of a name, [it applies] to the direct seer" (V.S. 1.1.5). Thus, in the sun, which is of the nature of light, the term "light" (prakāśa) is used because it shines.

The meaning of the sūtra is that because it is merely a figurative designation (upacāra) like "agency" (kartṛtva), the suffix *iti* occurs after the word *sākṣin* when used in the sense of "one who sees directly," since the word *sākṣin* functions as a technical name (*saṃjñā*). Now, an objection is raised: from the word *sākṣin*, only the characteristic of being a witness—that is, mere consciousness—is understood, but not changelessness or neutrality; how then [can this be so]?
In the definition of a witness (*sākṣin*), even "changelessness" (*nirvikāratva*) is added. To this, he says: "For even in the world... (*lokepi hi*).

The word "even" (*api*) is explained as an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*); and that emphasis is for the purpose of excluding the doubt that neutrality (*audāsīnya*) and awareness (*boddhatva*) might each individually constitute the definition. The word "for" (*hi*) is explained as a term well-known in common usage (*loke*).
For when two people are disputing, one who is other than those two, who perceives their dispute directly and remains impartial, is called a witness; therefore—

The qualification "indifference" (udāsīnatva) is necessary; since mere indifference exists even in pillars and the like in the context of a dispute, the qualification "being a cognizer" (boddhatva) must be understood as intended to exclude those. [This refers to] the two bodies, gross and subtle, which delimit one's own two limiting adjuncts (ahaṃkāra).

As for what was stated—that the consciousness which illumines is the witness—that is not possible. For there is no evidence for such a consciousness inherent in the elements (*bhūta-caitanya*). Nor should it be argued that the manifestation of the two bodies would be unestablished in the absence of that [consciousness], because that is established by the very modifications (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is itself of the nature of light. Thinking thus, he raises an objection with the words "Even though... (*yadyapi*).

It should be understood that, according to the position which does not accept the existence of an eternal consciousness distinct from the insentient ego (ahaṃkāra), there is no living being (jīva) apart from the insentient ego; furthermore, this is because the view that mental states (vṛttis) are modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is established by such scriptural texts as "Desire, resolve," and so forth. Regarding these mental states:
Even though they possess the nature of illumination like a lamp and so forth, because they are insentient (jaḍa), it is not possible for them to manifest the two bodies;

however, if self-luminous, eternal consciousness (svaprakāśanityacaitanya) is admitted, then it is possible for those [faculties], being endowed with its reflection, to take the form of the experience of the two bodies. Therefore, such...
With the intention that consciousness is the goal to be attained, he says, "Nevertheless" (tathāpi).

This non-dual reality, which is always slightly illuminated by the immutable consciousness that is pervasive everywhere yet seemingly delimited by itself, becomes separated from the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which contains the reflection in the form of the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya).

The veil is illuminated by the rising cognitions as they sever [the obstruction]; however, during the intervals between them, it is illuminated solely by the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) in the absence of those cognitions. For this very reason, there is the constant manifestation of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and other such factors.
From association [with other categories], there is the state of not being an object of doubt and so forth.
Furthermore, it is established by experience that while the two bodies appear indistinctly during the interval between mental states (*vṛtti*),

at the time when those states have the two bodies as their object, the agent of the "I" appears distinctly in such forms as "I am fat. Therefore, for the sake of accounting for that indistinct appearance [of the body], [the following is proposed]:

With the intention that an eternal witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) distinct from the knowledge consisting of mental modifications (vṛttijñāna) must be accepted, he says: "pervading everywhere" (sarvataḥ prasṛtena).

This means "pervaded. The connection is as follows: the two bodies, which are already being slightly illumined by the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthacaitanya), are clearly manifested by the mental modifications (vṛttijñāna). [The subject] is of the nature of the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya).

"That which has a reflection" means that which is joined with a reflection within its interior. By this, the distinction between the individual self (*jīva*)—which is the reflection in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—and the witness (*sākṣin*), who is the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) that serves as the original image (*bimba*), is demonstrated.
Just as sparks flying out from an iron ball heated by fire emerge already possessing fire, so too does the witness exist as the original image.
In this way, even the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) arising from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is endowed with the reflection of consciousness,

arise as containing that very reflection; therefore, it is indicated [by the mention of the internal organ] that it is possible for these modifications to take the form of the experience of the body and so forth.

The state of containing a reflection has been described; in order to show the occasion when the consciousness that is the witness of the two bodies appears indistinctly during the waking state, it was said "repeatedly cutting off. He states that very occasion clearly with the words "but in the intermediate time," where the word "but" (tu) [serves to distinguish this from the previous state].

The particle *eva* provides the explanation; the connection is that the two bodies are manifested together with the absences of mental modifications (*vṛtti*). The phrase "by the absences of mental modifications" means by the destructions of those modifications. This is also an illustration;
the meaning is that they are manifested together with the arisings of mental modifications and with the various types of mental modifications. This is the intended sense.

If eternal consciousness were not admitted, the manifestation of the arising and destruction of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), as well as their distinctions and so forth, could not occur through direct perception;
for it is impossible for the arising and destruction of something to be perceived by that very thing itself,
and because there would remain no further direct modifications to take those modifications as their objects.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for those two [the self and the object] to be grasped by a third [cognition], one must therefore accept that eternal consciousness exists as a witness even to the destruction of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) and so forth. To show another argument for this very point, he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*).
The meaning is: precisely because of the existence of the witness whose nature is eternal consciousness. [This applies to] the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the body, and so forth...

Furthermore, it is established by experience that the capacity for pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and other such factors, always possess the status of being the recipient of the fruit characterized by the cessation of doubt and the like during their state of existence; for never at any time does one think,
"I did not exist," or "I do not exist," or "I do not breathe," or "I am not a Brahmin."
In this manner, beginning with "vetti" and so forth, he states that egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) is indeed free from doubt for someone;

and that [egoity] is not possible without a constant connection with light (*sadāprakāśa*). For it is observed that objects such as jars are never the objects of doubt and the like only during the state of their connection with light; therefore, [egoity must be] constantly luminous.
However, the state of being an associate (*saṃsargitva*) for the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth is not possible on the view that cognition is produced (*janyajñāna*),
because they are subject to arising and destruction,
and because they generally have external objects as their domain; therefore, [the association] of the ego-sense and so forth—

The point is that, in order to account for their never being objects of doubt and so forth, it must be stated that they are always in contact with the light whose nature is consciousness, which is self-evident.

Furthermore, there is the recollection during the interval between other cognitions, such as: "During all this time, I was indeed perceiving this. Nor should it be questioned how the empirical activities, memory, and so forth of the individual soul (jīva) occur when they are illumined by the immutable witness (kūṭastha), for [this is explained] through mutual superimposition (anyonyādhyāsa).

Because the immutable [consciousness] would become another individual soul (jīva) by falling into the state of being a single soul; nor should it be argued that the consciousness of the individual soul itself may be the witness, rendering the immutable one unnecessary.

In the presence of a witness (*sākṣin*), he states another supporting argument: "anyajñāne" and so forth. The mention of *ahaṃkāra* (the ego) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) occurring within the stream [of consciousness] as well. If one does not accept a witness whose nature is eternal experience, then regarding the continuity of the modification directed toward the divine and auspicious form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the *ahamartha* (the referent of "I") belonging to that time [would be unaccounted for].
Furthermore, at that time, because a produced experience (*anubhava*) is impossible for the mental modifications (*vṛtti*), impressions (*saṃskāra*) cannot arise;

consequently, there would be no subsequent recollection (*anusandhāna*). Indeed, during the state of a continuous flow (*dhārā*), neither an experience produced within the sphere of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) nor one produced within the sphere of each individual modification is possible, as that would entail an interruption of the flow.
Furthermore, because the continuity of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is maintained by the causal complex being conjoined with desire, its interruption is impossible;

therefore, the sense is that one must assert a permanent experience as the witness (*sākṣin*) of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) and so forth, occurring during the period of the stream of other cognitions. The phrase "and [the fact of] recollection" implies that it is logically consistent. Now, [an objection]:

How could the recollection "I saw this very thing" be possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) regarding those mental modifications (*vṛtti*s) experienced by the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which has the *aham-artha* as its object? This is because the witness, who is the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*) acting as the original prototype (*bimba*), is distinct from the individual soul, which is the reflection (*pratibimba*) of that *aham-artha*. Consequently, regarding an object experienced by one [the witness], [the other]...
He raises an objection, saying: "Because there is no possibility of one [consciousness] remembering what belongs to another. He replies: "And not [in the case] of the immutable [Self].

Since it is accepted that memory of an experienced object occurs for oneself either through identity with itself or through the proximity of identity with itself, there is no over-extension [of the principle]; for [memory does not occur] between the individual souls of Devadatta and Yajñadatta.

There is a mutual identity [between them], by virtue of which the fault would arise that Yajñadatta might have a memory of an object experienced by Devadatta; with this intention, he offers a rebuttal: "by means of mutual superimposition.
This means: by means of the superimposition of identity. Since the fact that the individual soul (jīva) is superimposed upon the immutable (kūṭastha) has already been established previously...

The intended meaning is that [the witness] is identical [to the self]. Nor does it follow from this that, because the witness is one in all bodies, Yajñadatta would experience the egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth experienced by Devadatta’s witness; for Yajñadatta and others are also present within Devadatta’s witness.

It should not be argued that [the two] become one because they are both sublated; for we accept a distinction between the two Sākṣins who have attained identity with their respective individual souls (jīvas) due to the difference in the limiting adjuncts (avacchedaka) consisting of the two bodies.
It is precisely in order to indicate this distinction of the Sākṣins based on the difference in their limiting adjuncts that [the author] says "of its own limiting adjunct."

It should be understood that the qualification was stated previously. Now, one might raise the objection: "Granted that there are two types of consciousness called the *jīva* and the *kūṭastha*, why could the *jīva* itself not be the witness (*sākṣin*)? This is expressed by the words "na ca" (and not). The phrase "kiṃ kūṭasthena" means "what is the use of the *kūṭastha*? or "what is the purpose of the *kūṭastha* being the witness? It does not mean...
The objection applies only to the immutable [Self], because that has been established.
Since it is impossible for that [Self] which performs worldly and Vedic activities to be a detached witness,

it cannot possess the witnesshood described in the Śruti as "the witness, the knower, solitary, and devoid of qualities" (sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca). Therefore, the fruit of action belongs to the one who eats the *pippala* while the other looks on without eating, as stated in [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6].
And because [the Self] is recorded in scripture as distinct from the enjoyer, the individual soul (jīva), who is the indifferent witness (sākṣin) whose nature is luminosity.
Furthermore, in the *Nāṭakadīpa*, the witness is distinguished from the individual soul by means of the illustration of a lamp situated in a dance hall.
For instance: "The lamp situated in the dance hall [illuminates] the master and the audience..."

The dancer: [He] would illuminate it without distinction, and even in its absence, it shines. Likewise, the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) qualified by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), is called a "dancer" because it possesses joy and dejection caused by the conceit of the completeness or deficiency of the enjoyment of sense objects.
Do not consider it equal to sovereignty.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that, because in this world it is well known that only one who is indifferent (*udāsīna*) possesses the status of a witness (*sākṣin*), and both in accordance with that worldly consensus and in accordance with scripture, the status of witness belongs only to the one situated in the "kūṭastha" (the immutable), and not to the individual soul (*jīva*). He states the definition of a witness in the scripture: "The knower, alone" (*cetā kevalaḥ*). This means the knower is alone, being neither an agent nor indifferent.

Thus, the Śruti itself refutes the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others that the Self possesses qualities such as knowledge, by stating, "He is devoid of qualities" (nirguṇaḥ). The word "and" (ca) is intended to refute the Digambara doctrine that the Self is of intermediate dimension and active; its meaning is that [the Self] is "inactive" (niṣkriyaḥ). Furthermore, regarding the distinction of the Witness from the individual soul (jīva), he cites the Śruti as well.

Regarding the phrase "of the two, the other": between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the immutable witness (*kūṭastha*), it is the *jīva*—the one other than the immutable witness—who consumes the "pippala," the fruit of action, as it is sweet. Since the body has been described as the *aśvattha* tree, it should be understood that the fruit of action is described as the "pippala" (fig) fruit; thus it is said to be "sweet."

The qualification refers to the intention of meritorious fruit: [the Self] is other than the individual soul (*jīva*), immutable (*kūṭastha*), and not eating—that is, not performing the enjoyment of the fruits of action; it "beholds" (*abhicākaśīti*), meaning it beholds directly and immediately as the witness of the intellect and so forth, that is to say, it shines forth. Here, by the phrase "not eating,"...

When the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) has been negated, the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) is also necessarily negated. Thus, by the two words "not eating" (*anaśnan*) and "beholding" (*abhicākaśīti*), it is shown that while remaining indifferent (*udāsīnatve*), the Self possesses the nature of a witness (*sākṣitva*) characterized as pure consciousness; this is the meaning. The witness (*sākṣī*) described in the *Kūṭasthadīpa* is also seen in other [scriptural] examples.
He states that deep sleep has been described as common [to all] by way of its specific characteristics, saying: "In the *Nāṭakadīpa* as well.

He recites the verse from that work which establishes the illustration: "Standing in the dance hall... [referring to] the Lord who possesses the conceit of being the dancer, while those situated in his vicinity [behold him] without distinction. For the lamp—

Having attained growth, it reveals the master; having attained a middling state, it reveals the refined assembly; and then, having attained an inferior state, it reveals the dancer. Thus, by undergoing modifications such as growth according to the degree of its manifestation, the lamp does not waver; rather, it remains in a single, uniform form.

The meaning is "he should reveal. And this qualification is to be understood as intended to demonstrate that the witness is changeless and immutable (*kūṭastha*) in the case of the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*). "Even in its absence" means even in the absence of a master, an assembly member, and so forth. The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is the master; the objects are the members of the assembly.

Keeping in mind the summary verse which states that "the dancer is the intellect (*mati*), the senses hold the rhythm (*tāla*) and so forth, and the lamp is the witness-illuminator," he says: "In the same way. He states the similarity that serves as the basis for the conceptualization of the individual soul (*jīva*) as being like the master who presides over the dance: "Regarding the objects..."

Even though it exists in the vicinity of that [intellect], because it lacks its qualities, it is like an object of enjoyment for the refined person; yet because it undergoes various transformations, it is like a dancer.
Thus, while illuminating the five senses, even in states such as deep sleep where the ego and other factors are absent, [the Self remains].

The Witness (sākṣī) is the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-caitanya), which is the substratum for the illusion of the individual soul (jīva)—the ego characterized by the luminous reflection of consciousness. Thus, this Witness is distinct from the individual soul; nor is it merely a category of Brahman, but rather it is said to be the consciousness in which the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord has not yet been manifested.
In the Kūṭasthadīpa (The Lamp of the Immutable Self).
The state of possessing joy and so forth, induced by the completeness or incompleteness of the dance and its accessories, is indicated for the Lord by the term "pride" (*abhimāna*).

Just as the members of the assembly (*sabhyāḥ*) are situated around the Lord, so too are the objects such as form and the rest situated around the individual soul (*jīva*); thus, because of the similarity between the objects and the members of the assembly, the status of being "members of the assembly" is metaphorically attributed to the objects.
With the intention that this is logical, he says: "Even though they exist in the vicinity of that. The word "that" (tat) refers to the individual soul (jīva). Now, one might object:
"Why not assume that even those objects existing in the vicinity of the individual soul possess sovereignty equal to that of the soul itself?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because of the absence of that [sovereignty]," with the intention that there is no cause for such sovereignty.

The meaning is that there is an absence of joy, dejection, and so forth, which would otherwise be imagined as being equal to [the intensity of] the Lord (*prabhu*). Alternatively, he states the similarity of the objects (*viṣaya*) to the members of an audience (*sabhyapuruṣa*): "due to the lack thereof. He states the similarity of the intellect (*buddhi*) to the dancer (*nartakī*):
"of various kinds. Just as men who hold the rhythm (*tāla*) and other instruments follow the dancer.

In this way, by the similarity that the sense organs also follow the intellect (dhī), the equality of the sense organs to the man who holds the rhythm-beat (tāla) and so forth is brought into the verse; the meaning of the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "the intellect and... is this. The meaning of the final quarter-verse—that the Witness (sākṣin), which illuminates the individual soul (jīva) and the rest, is like a lamp—is summarized as follows: [he] summarizes it.

By the words "illuminating," etc., the meaning is "making manifest. Before the word "illuminating" (*dīpayan*), the phrase "in the waking state, etc. (*jāgradādau*) is to be supplied as a remainder. With the intention that the witness (*sākṣī*) described in the *Nāṭakadīpa* is none other than the immutable one (*kūṭastha*) described in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*, he says:
"qualified by the reflection of consciousness" (*cidābhāsaviśiṣṭa*). This is stated in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*.

For it has been stated that the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-caitanya*), which serves as the substrate for the delusion of being a living soul (*jīva*), is the illuminator of the *jīva* and so forth.

And in the *Nāṭakatīpa*, having postulated the *jīva* as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) qualified by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), the consciousness that illuminates that [ego] is called the Witness (*sākṣin*). Consequently, it is understood from what is stated there that the Witness is indeed the immutable one.

Because of the equality established by [the Witness] being the substratum of the individual soul (jīva) in the form of its reflection within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), and because [the Witness] illuminates it; thus, in the previous work *Kūṭasthadīpa*, the distinction between the Witness and the individual soul was demonstrated through the analogy of a lamp situated in a dance hall. Therefore, [the Witness is shown] as distinct from the individual soul.

The sense is that the intended meaning is established because [the witness] is shown even in the *Nāṭakadīpa* as distinct from that [jīva]; for example, the witness does not belong to the category of the *jīva*, because the *jīva* lacks neutrality (*udāsīnatva*),
nor does it belong to the category of the Lord (*īśvara*), because he who performs activities such as the creation and governance of the world lacks neutrality.

Because God (Īśvara) exists as something remote (*parokṣa*) due to His being an entity, and because it is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be the witness (*sākṣin*) in the form of an eternal and immediate presence—since [the soul] is characterized by being awakened and so forth—with this intention he says: "Thus, from the individual soul... Here, the word *brahma* refers to Īśvara and not to the consciousness (*caitanya*) that is the seer. He then asks: "Who, then, is the witness?"

"But what? [is the question]. The answer is "untouched" (*aspṛṣṭa*). "It has been stated"—this refers to the verse in the Śaiva Purāṇas which concludes with the words: "Thus, the immutable Śiva has been clearly discerned as being devoid of the states of individual soul (*jīva*) and Lord (*īśvara*), absolute, and self-luminous. The phrase "having the form of the world" (*jagadrūpatva*) is the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) [in the compound *jīveśatvādi*]. Śiva is absolute, indifferent, and pure.
The meaning is "the Supreme Self."

In the *Tattvapradīpikā* as well, it is stated that while the Supreme Lord is variegated (*śabalita*) and possessed of attributes (*saguṇa*), He is "the absolute" (*kevala*) and "without attributes" (*nirguṇa*). Because such qualifications would otherwise be untenable, it is established that Brahman—which is the inner self of all and pure—is understood as the Witness (*sākṣin*) through its non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*). However, in the *Kaumudī*, it is said that there is one...
"The Lord is hidden in all beings, all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings, the supervisor of actions, the abode of all beings, the witness,
the conscious one, absolute, and devoid of qualities"— thus has the divinity and other attributes of the Supreme Lord alone been heard in the Śruti.
A certain differentiation of form, which is the witness (sākṣin) of the soul's engagement in and withdrawal from activity, while remaining itself indifferent, is called the Witness.
To provide corroboration for the statement that the conscious self (cidātman) alone—devoid of attributes such as lordship—is described elsewhere as the witness, he says:
"In the *Tattvapradīpikā* as well.
[This refers to] all individual souls (jīvas), which consist of reflections of consciousness within the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa).
The inner reality, which is the pure essence constituting the very nature [of Brahman], exists as the inward substrate;

it is devoid of the states of being an individual soul (jīvatva), a Lord (īśvaratva), or the form of the world (jagadrūpatva). Precisely because it is the substrate for each respective individual soul through its non-difference from Brahman, and by attaining identity with each such soul, it assumes differentiation in every body.

"It is understood that he is the witness of the existent (*satsākṣī*). The word "iti" indicates a manner; it expresses the state of being the witness of the existent, and thus one understands his witnesshood. A certain specific form of the Supreme Lord alone is the witness named [Sākṣin], because of scriptural texts such as "He is the deity," and not a witness distinct from the Lord, since [the witness] possesses deityhood and so forth.

The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is "because of contradiction with scripture" (*śrutivirodhāt*). By the phrase "godhood and so forth" (*devatvādīti*), attributes such as being the inner self of all beings (*sarvabhūtāntarātmatva*) are included. This is what is meant: attributes such as godhood and the like are well-known in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other sources as belonging to the Supreme Lord; therefore, they do not belong to anyone else.
Witnesshood, divinity, and so forth [belong to the Lord], because [otherwise] it would contradict the scriptural texts. Although divinity— such as that of Hiraṇyagarbha, Indra, and others—
is common to individual souls (jīvas), nevertheless, because the other attributes are unique to the Lord, divinity also must reside in the Lord alone.

The sense is that [He] is the object of apprehension. He refutes the duality attributed to the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara) by virtue of His manifestation as Śiva and Viśva. "One" (eka): the meaning is that although the Supreme Lord, who is the original prototype (bimba), possesses distinct names such as Śiva and Viṣṇu due to differences in form, there is no difference in His essential nature as Īśvara. And thus, another eternal Śruti says:

"Śiva is Acyuta. Since the word *acyuta* is conventionally established as a name for Viṣṇu, there is no difference between us two in terms of words or meanings in this world; hundreds of such Smṛti passages are to be seen here. In the Śruti, the phrase "in all beings" follows immediately after [the previous statement]—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. And likewise, the Smṛti says: "The Lord..."
"It dwells within the heart-region of all beings. If that is so, why is it not perceived by everyone?

To this he says: "hidden" (*gūḍha*). Likewise, the *Smṛti* states: "I am the light of all, veiled by my own *yogamāyā*. Here, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the referent of the word "I"; "light" (*prakāśa*) means that which is manifesting.

By accepting that the Supreme Self abides within all beings, there might arise a doubt that it too is divided due to the difference in its substrates; he wards this off by stating "all-pervading" (*vyāpī*). Even though it is all-pervading, like space, he wards off the notion that it is actually different from the individual souls (*jīva*) by stating "the inner self of all beings" (*sarvabhūtāntarātman*). [This refers to] all beings, from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass.

"The self situated within the aggregates is the nature of all living beings," and so forth. [An objection is raised: "If the Supreme Lord were non-different from the individual soul (jīva), who is both the agent and the object of action, then He too would possess that agency. To this he says: "The supervisor of actions" (*karmādhyakṣa*).

The meaning is that He is the witness of the actions performed by the individual soul, but He Himself is not their agent. [This distinction exists] due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul and the Supreme Self.

The sense is that the systematic arrangement of phenomena (*dharmavyavasthā*) is possible through differentiation. By the words "in all beings" and so forth, there is a designation of beings as non-different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

And that [Brahman], being beyond the locus of attributes such as causality and the like, is directly manifest; illuminating the ignorance and other states residing in the individual soul (jīva), it is the innermost essence of the jīva. Furthermore, during deep sleep and similar states when the effect and cause have merged, it manifests the mere ignorance residing in the jīva and is designated by the term "Prājña" (the Intelligent One).

Anticipating the objection that [the Self] might be accompanied by a second entity, he says: "The abode of all beings. "Abode" (*adhivāsa*) means that in which beings dwell above (*adhi*); it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"The abode of all beings" means the substratum of all beings. And there is nothing for those things placed upon it apart from their substratum.

The sense is that there is no contradiction with the state of non-duality (advitīyatva) on the grounds that a separate sentient being exists. With the intention of showing that He is not only the witness of the karmas residing in the individual souls (jīvas), but the witness of the souls themselves as well, he says: "the witness.
The remaining portion of the scripture has already been explained previously; [He is] the "approver" (anumantā) by way of constant proximity.
"Being himself the knower": although the individual soul (jīva) possesses activity, [the Self] is himself devoid of it;
being characterized as the witness (sākṣin) of specific forms, he employs the term "witness" in that context. Regarding the phrase "what is called the witness":
the word "name" (nāma) indicates its well-known status in the Śruti. Now, one might object: the witness is directly perceived by the individual soul.
This is because it is accepted that [the Self] consists of the experience of ignorance, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth. However, God (*Īśvara*) is eternally beyond perception;

since He is characterized by causality, omniscience, universal control, and so on—which are unperceivable by the individual soul (*jīva*)—God in His form as the reflected Consciousness (*bimba-caitanya*) qualified by those attributes is likewise unperceivable. If this is argued, we say: no.

With the intention that its direct perception (*aparokṣatva*) is established by accepting it as a particular form (*rūpaviśeṣa*), he says: "And that [is... Nor should it be suspected that there is a lack of evidence for such a distinction of forms in the Lord (*īśvara*), because the mantra "The one God" (*eko devaḥ*) and the portion of the mantra "Another, not aging, gazes on" (*anaśnan anyo abhicākaśīti*) refer to a distinct form of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) who is indifferent (*udāsīna*).

The sense is that because [the Lord] is the locus of attributes such as being the cause, all the scriptural passages concerning creation are authoritative with respect to the Lord. And He is both immediate to the individual soul (*jīva*) and its internal organ;
this is the connection. He states the reason for both cases: "illuminating the ignorance and so forth residing in the individual soul."
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its attributes such as pleasure and pain, and so forth.

Witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), by means of illuminating ignorance and the rest, becomes the sustainer of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) such as "I am ignorant" and "I am happy or miserable. Therefore, it is the Witness.

The meaning is that [the Self] is the "innermost" (*antaraṅga*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), because in the world it is well-known that a person who carries out the affairs of a king and so forth is the "innermost" of the king. Now, an objection is raised: since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), its modifications (*vṛtti*), and so forth—which constitute the objective field of the witness (*sākṣin*)—have ceased during deep sleep and other such states, the conscious Self (*cidātman*) cannot possess the nature of a witness at those times.

And if that were so, there would be a contradiction in the conventional usage of its status as a witness even during deep sleep and other such states—based on such [scriptural] passages as "I am Śiva, the eternally auspicious, pure consciousness, the witness distinct from them. To this he says: "And in deep sleep, etc. Regarding the phrase "distinct from them": the meaning is "distinct from the enjoyer and the rest. Even then, because the primal ignorance, which is the object of witnessing, exists, [there is no contradiction].

The intention is that there is no contradiction; for, with the view that both scriptural passages concerning deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and non-awakening (*akrānti*) are authoritative with respect to the Witness (*sākṣin*), who is a specific form of the Supreme Lord itself, he says:
"designated by the word Prājña."
The sense is that in both the passage concerning deep sleep and the passage concerning departure, it is precisely the aforementioned Witness who is established by the term "Prājña."
Just as one embraced by a beloved woman perceives no other sensation whatsoever from the outside, even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman),
perceives no other sensation from the outside; mounted upon the conscious Self, he departs.

Based on the two scriptural statements "He goes" and "He departs," it has been established in the *Suṣuptyutkrānty-adhikaraṇa* that the Supreme Lord is distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) during the states of deep sleep and departure; furthermore,
it has been described in the *Tattvaśuddhi* that this determination also concerns the witness (*sākṣin*), just as in the case of the [erroneous] cognition "this is silver."

In the case of an error, although the "this" aspect (idam-aṃśa) actually belongs to the category of the mother-of-pearl, it appears as belonging to the category of silver; likewise, although the Witness (sākṣin) belongs solely to the category of Brahman, he appears as belonging to the category of the individual soul (jīva). Having stated that the Witness is useful for the soul's worldly dealings such as pleasure and so forth, this very position is thus supported.

But surely, since it was stated in the section [sūtra 1.3.42] beginning with "nanu suṣuptyutkrāntyorbhedena" that the word *prājña* occurring in the scriptures concerning deep sleep and so forth refers to the Supreme Self characterized by being the Lord of all and the Sovereign of beings, how can the word *prājña* [refer to anything else]?

Therefore, he speaks of the state of being the Lord of the indifferent (udāsīneśvara-paratva). "As follows" (*tadyathā*): in the illustrative sentence, external objects such as chariots and so forth are the context; the "person" (*puruṣa*) is the individual soul (*jīva*), while the "wise one" (*prājña*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
Enveloped by that [Supreme Self] during deep sleep and other states, having attained oneness through the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he is external.
He cites a scriptural passage concerning departure (*utkrānti*) regarding the waking world:
"Mounted by the conscious self" (*prājñenātmanānvārūḍhaḥ*). "Mounted" means presided over; "uttering sounds" means making noise due to the force of pain; "he goes" means he departs from the body.

The meaning is "it departs. Regarding the phrase "of the two states," the locative case indicates that the word *prājña* (the wise one) is to be supplied immediately after; thus, the connection is as follows: by means of these two statements, the Supreme Lord—who is established as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*)—is determined to be the witness, as has been described in the *Kaumudī*.

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, the sixth chapter consists merely of a restatement (*anuvāda*) concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), and it is not intended to refer to a Lord (*īśvara*) distinct from that;

such being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: in the two passages beginning with "As with a beloved woman" (*tadyathā priyayā*), the term "person" (*puruṣa*) refers to [the Self] in the states of deep sleep and departure.

Because the Supreme Lord is designated by the word "Prājña" in the nominative case (third case-ending) in non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*), the sixth chapter is not merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the soul; rather, it is intent upon establishing the Lord who is distinct from that soul. And that establishment [is achieved] by restating the soul as established in common worldly experience and [then demonstrating] its non-difference from the Lord.

And likewise, a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) is seen for the purpose of establishing this: "This indeed is that great, unborn Self, which consists of consciousness" (*sa vā eṣa mahānaja ātmā yo 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ*).
The meaning is that this [Self] which consists of consciousness—the individual soul (*jīva*)—is the great Self, the full Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

The determination of that subject matter: Now, it might be argued that this determination is untenable because it refers to a witness (sākṣin) who is the indifferent Lord (udāsīneśvara), since immediately after the passage "He indeed is this great unborn Self," there follows the teaching of His collection of qualities such as being the Lord of all and the sovereign of beings, in the words "He is the Lord of all, He is the ruler of beings," and so forth. To this, we say: no.

The intended meaning is that statements such as "being the Lord of all" found in the *Jñeyabrahma-prakaraṇa* are intended solely as praise (*stuti*). To corroborate the view of the author of the *Kaumudī*, he introduces another opinion, stating:
"In the *Tattvaśuddhi* also... [regarding] the locus of the error "this is silver," by way of non-difference from silver...

Even though the silver aspect appears, it is not included within the other [real] silver, because—unlike real silver—it lacks sublation (*bādha*). Nor is it included within the mother-of-pearl, because that would entail the consequence that it, like the "this"-aspect of the mother-of-pearl, would be unknown.
Therefore, just as the "this"-aspect is in reality of the nature of mother-of-pearl but appears as silver...

Some, however, hold that the *jīva* itself, conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopādhika*), is the witness (*sākṣin*) because it is directly the seer. For even in the world, being a witness is well known to consist in being a seer while remaining a non-agent; and this is possible directly only in the *jīva*, whose nature is unattached, indifferent, and luminous. Thus, the *jīva* becomes an agent through its identification with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

Because [the Lord] remains himself indifferent even when superimposition occurs, the mantra "One God" (ekodeva) primarily establishes the witnesshood of Brahman with respect to its state as the individual soul (jīva). The mantra "Two birds" (dvā suparṇā),
however, according to the principle of the *guhādhikaraṇa*, refers to both the individual soul and the Lord.

Thus, there is no non-difference even for the Witness (*sākṣin*); in reality, the Witness—who is the substratum of the imagined individual soul (*jīva*) and the experiencer of pleasure and so forth—is non-different from the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*). However, due to the appearance "I experience pleasure," and so on, there is a sense of non-difference from that individual soul. Therefore, [the attributes] such as the pleasure of the individual soul...

The meaning is that its function (*upayoga*) pertains to that experiencer of pleasure and so forth within empirical discourse (*vyavahāra*), who has attained the state of being one with the individual soul (*jīva*).

The phrase "this very [soul]" implies that even from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*vastutaḥ*), there is no inclusion of the witness (*sākṣin*) within the category of the individual soul, because that would contradict the statement that it belongs to the category of Brahman.
The sense is that it is understood that the non-difference of that [witness] from the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*) is the view favored by the author of the *Tattvaśuddhi*.

Without presenting the position that there is a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the witness (*sākṣin*), he presents the position of their non-difference with the words "some say" (*kecit*) and so forth; the connection is that "the witness is the individual soul itself. The intention of the word "itself" (*eva*) is that the witness is not a distinct form of the Lord (*īśvara*), because there is no evidence for that. [This is said] upon the acceptance of the individual soul's status as the witness.

He states the reason: "because of being the direct witness" (*sākṣāddraṣṭṛtvāt*). By saying "having ignorance as its limiting adjunct" (*avidyopādhika*), he indicates its neutrality (*audāsīnya*). To elaborate on this very point—that this alone is the definition of a witness and nothing else—he recalls what was stated previously: "for even in the world... (*lokepi hi*). Having previously stated it in brief, he now elaborates upon the fact that the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is the witness: "And that... (*tacceti*).

"Directly" (*sākṣāt*) means that the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is possible for the *jīva* who is of the nature of a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā-pratibimba*) by its own nature. By this, it is indicated that since the status of being a witness is possible for the *jīva* already established [in scripture], one need not postulate a witness distinct from that [jīva], as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Now, [one might object]: regarding worldly and Vedic...

Anticipating the objection that neutrality is unestablished for one who engages in worldly activity (*vyavahāra*), it is stated that agency and so forth belong only to the Self through its identification with the intellect (*buddhi-tādātmya*); however, since its inherent nature is neutrality, its status as the Witness (*sākṣitva*) is maintained.

He says that it is possible: "of the individual soul (jīva), [it is] the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Now, if one accepts that the Lord (īśvara) is the witness (sākṣin), there would be a contradiction with the mantra; therefore, he says: "The one God... As for the mantra, it has been stated that the witness is indeed immediate (aparokṣa) to the individual soul, but for the Lord, who is indifferent (udāsīna), immediacy is not possible.

The sense is that since the Lord, who exists as the substrate (bimba), possesses a difference from the individual soul (jīva) due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it is impossible for the consciousness of another individual soul to be directly perceived by one individual soul; therefore, the portion of the mantra that establishes the Witness (sākṣin) intends Brahman as it has assumed the state of an individual soul.

It should be understood that the phrase "the mantra, however" (*maṃtrastu*) indicates, by means of the word *tu*, the impossibility of the difference in form of the Lord being directly perceived as a reason. Now, an objection may be raised: just as in the *Guhādhikaraṇa* it was stated in the commentary that the mantra "those two who have entered the cave" refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), so too the mantra "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) refers to both the individual soul and the Lord.

And likewise, in the mantra "Two birds," the statement "One of them eats the sweet pippala fruit" results in referring to the individual soul (jīva), while the statement "The other looks on without eating" results in referring to the Supreme Lord (parameśvara); consequently, this applies to the case where the individual soul is the witness, as it establishes the witnessing nature of the Lord.

Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction with the portion of the mantra stating "eating, one is not the other," he says: "The mantra 'dvā suparṇā'. Even when the mantra refers to both the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self (para), there is no contradiction whatsoever, just as in the case of the mantra "ekodeva" (the one God).
The meaning is: because of the acceptance of [the soul] as being the Supreme Self that has attained the state of a living being (jīva).

They say that there is no contradiction whatsoever because, as explained in the commentary on the *Guhādhikaraṇa* citing the *Paiṅgirahasyabrāhmaṇa*, [the term "seer"] refers to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Others, however, maintain that in reality, the witness (*sākṣin*) is indeed the individual soul itself, in its form as being all-pervasive and conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*).

Since even the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth belonging to one person are perceived by another person due to the non-distinction in their contact with the Witness (*sākṣin*), who illuminates that other person’s own internal organ, [the objection is invalid].
Now, in the commentary on the *Grahādhikaraṇa*, the *Paiṅgirahasya Brāhmaṇa* has been cited; and it is as follows:

"Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit"—this refers to the *sattva* (the intellect). "The other looks on without eating. "The other, being wise, looks on without eating"—by this Brāhmaṇa passage, the statement regarding eating has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its object; it does not refer to [the Self] that does not eat.

It has been explained that [the term] refers to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field). Nor should it be asked: "If the mantra is explained by the Brahmana itself as referring to the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña*, how can the Commentator state that it refers to the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)?
For that statement is merely a *kṛtvā-cintā* (a hypothetical discussion for the sake of argument), and thus there is no contradiction. Thus it is.

If the *kṣetrajña* favored by the Brāhmaṇas were to be that which possesses the reflection of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its form, then it would possess the status of a witness (*sākṣitva*) as stated in the scriptural passage "He is indeed the witness" (*sa eva sākṣī*), and not [the status of a witness] for the reflection in ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus, [this applies] to that which has the nature of a reflection in ignorance.

Fearing that the position of the individual soul (*jīva*) being the witness (*sākṣin*)—which possesses the nature of Brahman—would result in contradiction with the portion of the mantra "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) as determined by the *Paiṅgi Brāhmaṇa*, [the author] says: "as cited in the commentary on the *Guhādhikaraṇa*"; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
The *paingi* [Upaniṣad] intends by "the Knower of the Field" (*kṣetrajña*) the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the reflection of consciousness residing in the internal organ;

for it is impossible for such a being—which is asserted in that text to possess agency and enjoyership as its very nature—to be a witness (*sākṣin*). Rather, [the witness] is unattached and indifferent.
The *jīva* alone, which is a reflection of ignorance (avidyā) within the nature of light, is intended by the Brāhmaṇa as the *kṣetrajña*;

for it has been established that its status as a witness, as stated in the scriptural passage, is possible while remaining unchanging. Therefore, according to the position that the witnesshood belongs only to the *jīva* as a reflection of ignorance—
The meaning is that there is a contradiction with the mantras that follow the Brāhmaṇas regarding the secret doctrine of Paiṅgi.

Now, having accepted that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the reflection of consciousness within ignorance (*avidyā*), alone possesses the status of the witness (*sākṣin*), the author introduces another view to state a certain distinction, beginning with "But others [say]..."— meaning that [others do not hold that] the Lord (*īśvara*) is the reflection of consciousness within ignorance.

The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that it is impossible for that [Self] to be a witness (*sākṣin*) if it were not immediate (*aparokṣatva*). The phrase "by way of form" (*rūpeṇa*) is to be construed with "as a witness.

He states the reason why there can be no witnessing by way of a common form for one whose limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the ignorance (*avidyā*) common to all bodies: "In another person... [referring to] the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of Yajñadatta.
The meaning is "of their modifications"; "with respect to another person" means with respect to Devadatta. "His own" means his own, Devadatta’s;
the Witness is the illuminator of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). Together with that Witness, just as Devadatta’s internal organ [is perceived], so too are Yajñadatta’s internal organ and the rest.

The meaning is that, due to the lack of distinction in contact (*saṃsarga*), just as Devadatta’s own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is perceptible to him, so too would Yajñadatta’s internal organ and its modifications (*vṛtti*) be perceptible to Devadatta. In this context, it follows that for one person, the internal organs and so forth of other persons would also have to become objects of perception.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: the reason therein is "one's own internal organ" (*svāntaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth; such is the division. One might object: "Even though the Witness (*sākṣin*) is one in all bodies, there is no aforementioned defect because the cognizers (*pramātṛ*) differ for each body. To this, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*).
For if the internal organ and so forth belonging to Devadatta were perceptible to him, then [there would be] contact with Devadatta’s Witness.
Nor does it follow that [the status of being a witness] is not established because the cognizer differs according to the difference in internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), since,
while the witness remains non-different in all cases— including the internal organ which is manifested by the witness—
the difference in the cognizer is irrelevant. Therefore, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the witness by virtue of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ.

And thus, because there is a distinction of witnesses for each individual, and because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth belonging to one person cannot come into contact with the witness of another person, or because they are unfit [to do so], their non-manifestation is logically established. Furthermore, since the internal organ exists even in deep sleep in a subtle form, the witness conditioned by it certainly exists at that time as well.

It should not be argued that because the Self conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possesses the status of a knower (pramātṛ), it cannot be the witness (sākṣin); for even though the knower is absent during deep sleep (suṣupti), the witness exists, and therefore a distinction between the two must necessarily be asserted.

Aging is the causal factor; likewise, since there is no difference in the contact with the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)—which is the causal factor for the non-mediate nature (*aparokṣatva*) of Devadatta—then even for Yajñadatta’s body, sense-organs, and so forth, there would arise the defect of rendering them non-mediately perceived by him. Witness-consciousness is the causal factor for mediacy.

He refutes [the opponent] by stating that [the distinction] must be resolved solely through a difference in association (*saṃsarga-bheda*), and not through a difference in the cognizer (*pramātṛ-bheda*), because the latter is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*).
The phrase "manifested by the witness" (*sākṣi-bhāsya*) means "there being non-difference of the witness" (*sākṣy-abheda*), which implies that the witness is one. As for "because it is irrelevant":
with respect to Devadatta, only his own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

The phrase "nānyadīpāntaskaraṇādikam" (nor any other lamp, internal organ, etc. is to be understood as a restrictive rule (*vyavasthā*); the sense is that it is impossible for the individual soul (*jīva*), which has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), to be a witness (*sākṣin*) in a universal form. And the phrase "tathā ca" means: when there is the intention to distinguish between witnesses based on the distinction of their respective limiting adjuncts.

The meaning is that the absence of perceptibility is established either because of its unsuitability for that [object], or by postulating its unsuitability with respect to another person. Now, if the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of ignorance (*avidyā*),
acts as a witness (*sākṣin*) precisely in its form as having ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then its status as such is possible even during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), in every body.

If it is argued that for the sake of establishing the distinction of the witness (*sākṣin*), its being the witness consists in its having the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then its status as the witness would not be possible during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because scripture declares the dissolution of the internal organ in deep sleep;
anticipating this objection, he says: "Even in deep sleep... [and] he raises the doubt: "No."

"Of that which is conditioned by the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇopahitasya*) means "of the *jīva* who is the reflection [of consciousness] in ignorance"—this is the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "therefore":

the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) is not possible for the *jīva* conditioned by the internal organ, because that [conditioned *jīva*] is a knower (*pramātṛ*); otherwise, it would simply be the knower.
