The sense is that there would be no distinction between one who has attained the status of a witness (*sākṣitva*) and a mere non-witness (*asākṣin*).

Anticipating the objection that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "In deep sleep," and "even in the absence. This refers to the state characterized by oneness with the Supreme Self—designated by the word *prāṇa* at the time of deep sleep—in accordance with the scriptural text: "Then [all these become] one in this *prāṇa*" (*athāsmin prāṇa ekadhā bhavati*).

The sense is that [the self] is not dissolved because of the scriptural teaching regarding the dissolution of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). This is by virtue of the existence of the witness (*sākṣin*). At the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the existence of the witness must necessarily be asserted, because its existence at that time is established by many scriptural passages such as "In the three abodes" (*triṣu dhāmasu*). "Abodes" (*dhāmasu*) means states; at that time—
Furthermore, it is observed that one who has awakened from deep sleep—states experienced by the witness as ignorance and bliss—recalls:
"I did not know anything" and "I slept happily. Moreover, there is the observation of the recollection:
"I slept," wherein the "I"—the subject of cognition—is remembered as persisting through the time of deep sleep, just as it does during waking and dreaming.

It must be stated that for that [subject] as well, its non-existence at that time must be asserted; however, because this would contradict many Śrutis that establish the dissolution of the knower during deep sleep, one must assume that the recollection "I slept" and so forth is of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*) regarding the aspect of the "I-meaning" (*ahamartha*), and thus the knower does not cease to exist then.

Existence is necessary; thus, at the time of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), because a non-distinction between the witness (*sākṣin*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—who are respectively existent and non-existent—is impossible, the witness must be declared as indeed distinct from the knower. This is the meaning. On the view that the knower and the witness are non-different, the knower lacks neutrality (*udāsīnatva*), and consequently, the status of being a witness [would be lost].
It should be understood that the word "and" (ca) is used for the purpose of including the fault of the nature of origination.

They say that since the distinction between a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is accepted in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the distinction is thus established: the knower (*pramātṛ*) is qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whereas the witness (*sākṣin*) is merely conditioned (*upahita*) by it.
And he provides the reason for the statement "nor speech" by saying "qualified by the internal organ.

Since the internal organ is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), who is characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*), it functions as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) that brings about the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*), and as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that brings about the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*). Thus, there is a distinction between the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) and the limited (*upahita*).

The meaning is that although the qualified knower (*viśiṣṭapramātṛ*) possesses the nature of an agent and enjoyer, the superimposed [consciousness] (*upahita*) can still possess the status of a witness (*sākṣitva*) because it is indifferent (*udāsīnatva*). Now, one might object: since there is a difference between being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) and being a limiting adjunct (*upādhitva*), how can this be so even for the single internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)?

By postulating a distinction in the form of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, the systematic arrangement is established that the status of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) belongs to that which is qualified by it, while the status of being a witness (*sākṣitva*) belongs to that which is conditioned by it (*upahita*). To the question of how there can be a distinction between these two, he says: "Between the qualifier and the condition. Being a qualifier consists in being a differentiator while being connected with the effect [of the action], as for example—

In cases such as "Bring the blue lotus," the blueness—which is not the primary denotation—is the differentiator of red lotuses and the like, and because it is connected to the action of bringing via the medium of the lotus; furthermore, in the definition [of secondary indication], the word *kārya* (action/task) refers to that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Thus, in examples such as "Whatever has crows is Devadatta’s house," [the crow indicates the house].
The subordinate element, namely "Devadatta's house-ness," has a connection with the action through its function as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*);

however, it also possesses the quality of excluding other houses. Therefore, in order to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case, the term "subordinate" (*satyam*) is used [to specify that the connection must be through subordination].
Furthermore, to prevent over-extension in cases such as the blue lotus (*utpala*), the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is added [to specify that the connection must be through being a qualifier].

The definition of an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) is: being non-identical with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), being a differentiator (*vyāvartaka*), and existing at the time of the connection with the effect (*kāryānvaya*).
For example, in the case of "bring the red crystal," the hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*) situated near the crystal is an *upādhi*.

Its being an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) is due to its lack of connection with the effect characterized by bringing [the object], because it serves to differentiate it from other crystals, and because it exists at the time of the connection with the act of bringing. Among these, the first [reason] is true; [the second is stated] to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to [qualities such as] color (*nīlatva*) and so forth, which are qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Nor is...
It must be stated that even blueness and the like, which are intended as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), are themselves the objects to be defined (*lakṣya*) in this context;
for while there is a conventional usage of the term "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) in the case of the hibiscus flower and so forth, there is no such usage for blueness and the like.
Furthermore, in the case of the hibiscus flower and so forth, there is no conventional usage of the hibiscus as a qualifier of the crystal and the like. And thus:

Since a distinction between a qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*) and a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is necessarily required, it is indeed appropriate to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to such things as "blackness" (*nīlatva*), which are intended as qualifiers but are not the actual objects of definition (*alakṣya*); for instance, in the case of the command "Enter the house like a crow," if at the time of the connection with the action of entering— [The sentence continues: ...if [the crow] were present at that time, it would be included in the definition; however, since it is not, there is no fault. Thus, the exclusion of over-extension is logically sound.
By the turn of fate, when the crow that served as the indicator has gone elsewhere and another crow arrives at that house,
the crow that has arrived there lacks the quality of being a differentiator from the crow previously situated there;
thus, even though the crow that arrived there was not previously present, it remains devoid of the status of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

The second "truth" (satya) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension (*ativyāpti*); the qualificand portion (*viśeṣyadala*) is for the purpose of excluding over-extension in the very case mentioned above, namely with respect to the crow who serves as a mere secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇībhūta*). Now, one might object that where the crow serving as the secondary indicator happens to be present by chance even at the time of the effect, the entire definition exists in that crow serving as the secondary indicator, and thus there would be over-extension.

It must be said that pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in being present necessarily at the time of the effect; for even so, in the case of the statement "bring the red crystal," although the *japā* flower exists at some place at the time the word is heard, [it is not the cause].

If it is argued that, because it is possible for the *japā* flower to be absent by chance at the time of the crystal's perception, there is no rule that the flower must exist at the time of the effect [of the illusion], then let this definition be intended to apply to the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*)— which possesses the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being "auditory"— and to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as well.
It has a sound like that of a hibiscus flower or some other [wind-blown] object.

If it is objected: "Since the witness (sākṣin) of the nature already described is necessarily veiled by ignorance (ajñāna), which obscures pure consciousness (caitanyamātra), how can there be the manifestation of ignorance, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and so forth, when [the witness] is thus veiled? [The answer is: Ignorance is veiled within itself like Rāhu.

Some say, "It illuminates, it illuminates. In reality, however, there is no fault in the conceptualization that, according to experience, the ignorance veils the consciousness of the witness (*sākṣicaitanya*)— which illuminates the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its attributes— rather than [veiling] the consciousness itself.
Let it be that the well-known nature of being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consists in its being a delimiting factor (*saṃjakatva*). Nor is there a lack of universal application (*ananugama*),

because the definition of a limiting adjunct as "that which resides in itself" and so forth applies to well-known limiting adjuncts such as the earring in the case of the reflection and the reflected object,
or the mirror and the like in the case of the face and its reflection, or pleasure and the like as delimited by themselves.

Furthermore, since it is necessary to include that [specific instance] within another definition that subsumes it as a sublated object (*bādhita*), this is not a fault; for it is well known that a definition is faulty only when a universal definition is possible. And thus:
Since it is possible for the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— as the material cause— to possess both types of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),

if one accepts that the individual soul (*jīva*) conditioned by the internal organ is the witness (*sākṣin*) in accordance with the definition "that which is not involved in the effects [of the adjuncts]," etc., then the status of being a witness ultimately results as residing solely in the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*).

However, since pure conscious life (jīvacaitanya) is strictly indifferent (udāsīna), there is no impossibility of the conditioned self being the witness, nor is there any confusion between the knower and the witness; this is the summary. [The opponent] objects to the previously stated fact that ignorance, the ego-sense, and so forth are illumined by the witness, asking: "Is it only consciousness...? [The answer is: "It is the entirety... [of consciousness].

The meaning is: "by that which veils consciousness. If it is asked, "How so?"—it should not be argued that once the veil is removed by a direct modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the witness (*sākṣin*), the manifestation of ignorance and the like becomes possible through the witness whose veil has been removed;
for that would entail a contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that those [objects] are manifested solely by the witness. This is because... [the mind].
Since the status of [the ego] as an instrument will be refuted later,

and because an immediate mental modification (*aparokṣa-vṛtti*) directed toward the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*) is impossible, there is no absence of doubt and so forth regarding the existence of the ego and other [factors] at the time of their own existence; thus, there is no constant cessation of doubt concerning them.

Furthermore, since it must always be stated that [the objects] are in contact with light by virtue of being the instigators [of cognition], their constant manifestation cannot be possible through an occasional mental modification (*vṛtti*). Moreover, if one were to accept a continuous stream of modifications directed toward the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of the perception of external objects such as jars, because two simultaneous modifications are not admitted. Therefore:

It must be stated that ignorance (*avidyā*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth, are manifested solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*); yet that is not possible, because [the witness] is itself veiled. Nor can it be said that there is some other consciousness apart from the witness-consciousness that is veiled, because nescience (*ajñāna*) is the veiler of consciousness alone; otherwise, [it would follow that]...

The intention of the objection is that [if this were so], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the absence of concealment even for consciousness other than the witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya).

He refutes this by showing, through an example, that the witness, even when concealed, possesses the capacity to illuminate ignorance, stating "like Rāhu": just as the lunar orb and the like, though entirely concealed by Rāhu...
Even if it were to illuminate only its own substrate and the *ahaṃkāra*, since no illumination is observed beyond that, here too the witness (*sākṣin*), though veiled,
could somehow manifest only ignorance (*avidyā*) and not the *ahaṃkāra* and so forth.
Because there is a lack of conviction in the claim that [the self] is an illuminator, he says, "In reality," and "in accordance with experience.

This means: although, in the case of the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, knowledge cannot exist eternally due to the occasional nature of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) as described above, it is nonetheless in accordance with the existence of results—such as the cessation of doubt—which follow from the eternal connection with light (*prakāśa*).

For this very reason, because they are always in contact with unobstructed light, they are not objects of ignorance, erroneous cognition, or doubt; however, if the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) were unobstructed, it would follow that bliss—which is of the same nature as that consciousness—would also be manifest. This is not so, for such a consequence is acceptable.
This is because unconditioned love for the Self is observed to be prompted by the manifestation of the nature of bliss (*ānandarūpa-prakāśa*);
and furthermore, because the *Vivaraṇa* states: "Bliss, characterized as the locus of supreme love, indeed shines forth.
It might be argued that even now, there is liberation when bliss manifests.

The consequence of there being no distinction between the two states of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) demonstrates precisely the fruit of [this] experience. "For this very reason" means: because of the postulation that ignorance has the nature of being an obscuration even while excluding the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*). "Being beyond the range [of cognition]" means: [it is not an object].
Now, since ignorance is of the nature of a non-entity, since the ego-sense is not the Self,
and since the states of pleasure and pain are attributes of the non-Self, it is unproven that these— namely ignorance, contrary knowledge, and doubt— are never objects of doubt and the like.

If it is argued that [the definition] intends the absence of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth— characterized by the mode "existence of ignorance, etc."— at any time whatsoever during the period when ignorance and so forth exist,

then the sense is that there is no fault even if one admits ignorance, contrary cognition (*viparītajñāna*), and the like directed toward specific features (*viśeṣa*) contained within those [ignorance and so forth].

He raises an objection: "Of the witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*). Now, one cannot say that this is a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), no effect produced by the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is observed; therefore, he says:
"In the form of bliss. For in the world, it is established by experience that there is attachment toward whatever bliss is being experienced.

And thus, once it is established that affection (*prīti*) has as its object the manifest bliss (*ānanda*), then— since affection is observed even in all living beings toward their own selves during states of suffering— it follows that affection directed toward the self also has as its object the manifest bliss of the self. [This is true even of] affection directed toward sons and the like.

To that extent, [the love for others] is conditional (*aupādhikī*), and the condition (*upādhi*) is the fact of being a means for the manifestation of the Self's own happiness; for no affection is observed toward those [objects] when they are in a state of absence from their status as conditions, whereas affection for the Self is unconditional (*nirupādhikī*), because, unlike in the case of sons and so forth, affection for the Self does not exist for the sake of anything else. And thus:

The Śruti says: "But for the sake of the Self, everything becomes dear. Likewise: "This [Self] is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else, because it is more internal. By the term "more internal," that which is most internal to all is expressed. And thus, that which is the consciousness of the Self, being most internal to all, is this very thing which is immediate (*aparokṣa*).

The meaning of the second scriptural passage is that [the Self] is more beloved than everything else, including one's son and so forth, with whom one converses as objects of affection. Thus, if the bliss of the Self were not manifest, then the unconditional love for the Self established by both scripture and experience would not exist; for love consists in the manifestation of bliss.

Therefore, because of the rule that [the witness-consciousness] has [bliss] as its object, it is entirely appropriate to state that there is no undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) regarding the manifestation of the bliss of the witness. Regarding this point, he also cites the consensus of the elders: "It indeed shines," meaning that bliss is characterized by being the object of supreme love and being the locus of supreme love.

Thus, it is indeed spoken of as "bliss" precisely because it is the supreme object of love; otherwise, that [designation] would not apply—this is the intended meaning of the word "only" (eva). Furthermore, since that bliss is non-different from the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), there is indeed consensus regarding the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature (svarūpānanda) even during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra).

He raises an objection regarding the admission of the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*), beginning with the words "It might be so" (*syādetat*) and ending with "Therefore, it is improper to imagine that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) is unobscured. [The objection continues:
"But even if the bliss of the witness, which is differentiated by imagination, were to manifest, how could that which is undivided..."
If it is argued that there is a distinction because Brahman-bliss, while veiled during the state of transmigratory existence, does not manifest, we say no;
for the aspect of non-limitation in bliss is not a human goal (puruṣārtha), and because the mere direct perception of bliss exists even now. [Objection: But [the bliss] is limited...

Witness-bliss (*sākṣyānanda*) is surpassable (*sātiśaya*), because one experiences a degree of excellence among the various worldly pleasures derived from the Vedas, which are themselves less distinct than the bliss common to deep sleep (*suṣupti*). However, the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*) is unlimited and unsurpassable (*niratiśaya*).

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) raises a specific objection with the words "But surely" (nanu). In ignorance (avidyā), there is the reflection of bliss which is the bliss of the witness (sākṣyānanda); its difference from the bliss that constitutes the original object (bimba) is merely imagined (kalpita).

Thus, even though during the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) there is the manifestation of the reflected bliss—which is non-different from the unobscured witness—[the following objection arises].

The bliss of Brahman, which exists as the archetype (bimba), does not manifest. Likewise, although the bliss of the witness (sākṣyānanda) does manifest, it manifests as distinct in every individual body and not as undivided;
this is the meaning of the distinction. The reason for the non-manifestation of the bliss of Brahman as the archetype is stated: "of that which is veiled" (āvṛtasya). Here...

Although primordial ignorance (mūlājñāna) has pure consciousness alone as its locus and that [consciousness] as its object—and not the Lord who exists as the archetype (bimba)—even though the latter is unobscured, it appears as if obscured to the individual soul (jīva) because of the imagined difference from the perspective of the jīva.
Thus, its non-manifestation to the jīva is possible. Likewise, in liberation, the archetypal...
Even the manifestation of the bliss of Brahman (brahmānanda) is unestablished, because upon the cessation of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna),
the state of being a reflection— which is produced by it— must necessarily cease, and with it, the state of being the original object (bimba) must also necessarily cease. Nevertheless,
it should be understood that the intention of the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) is merely to silence the opponent's position.

The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) states that whether the distinction in liberation consists in the manifestation of unconditioned bliss or merely the manifestation of bliss, in either case it is impossible to state such a distinction. He says "not" (*na*), because limitation (*avaccheda*) is indeed duality (*bheda*), and that [duality] is superimposed upon the Self (*ātman*). Thus, he points out the flaw [in the opponent's position] by considering the case where the absence of limitation is something distinct from bliss.

Regarding the phrase "of the part that is non-distinct": if bliss itself is the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) for the imagined absence, then one might think it is included within the second category; considering this, he refutes that category with the words "and of the mere immediacy of bliss. And thus, it is not [the case].

The sense is that there is a distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection regarding this distinction by another method: "But [is it not] undivided? The witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*), manifesting as divided with respect to each body, is bliss (*ānanda*) that possesses excellence—that is, it possesses excellence in the form of degrees of superiority and inferiority.
He states the reason for the excellence of the bliss of the witness, which is the meaning of "eternal": "because it is common to deep sleep.

Clarity is excellence; extreme clarity is supreme excellence. The bliss of the witness manifesting during the time of deep sleep is indeed clear; otherwise, there would be no such recollection as, "I slept happily."

Because it would follow that [the bliss of deep sleep] could not be an object of reflective awareness (*parāmarśanīya*). For it is well known in the world that only that pleasure which has been clearly experienced can subsequently be an object of reflective awareness, and not mere unexperienced pleasure.
And thus, compared to that, the witness-bliss (*sākṣyānanda*) lacks clarity during deep sleep. [This is unlike] sandalwood-paste and so forth...
The meaning is: because of the experience of a specific excellence within the pleasures associated with sense objects. Regarding the term "unlimited" (*anavacchinna*):

the literal meaning is that the bliss of Brahman, which consists in the absence of any imagined limitations, manifests at the time of liberation as being entirely devoid of any general excellence (*atiśaya-sāmānya*). In liberation, the bliss of Brahman exists in a single form as fullness.
And it shines forth. Now, such a manifestation of the bliss of Brahman does not exist; rather, there is only the manifestation of a bliss possessed of both excellence and deficiency.

Therefore, even when the bliss of one's own true nature (*svarūpānanda*) flashes forth, no one attains peace, because they are seized by the demoness in the form of the longing for a bliss superior to that.
The meaning is that there is a distinction between cyclic existence and liberation.

If it is argued that this is because the *Ānandavallī* concludes with the bliss of Brahman after describing a progressive increase by factors of a hundred, beginning from human bliss; [we reply: No, for in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), there is no such increase, since the bliss of the witness (*sākṣi-ānanda*), the bliss of the object (*viṣaya-ānanda*), and the bliss of Brahman (*brahma-ānanda*) are in reality one and the same.

Because it is possible. If you argue that the Śruti declares an ever-increasing excellence in human bliss and so forth, who indeed says that the Śruti does not declare it? However, it is said that its demonstration is impossible within the doctrine of non-duality (advaitavāda). But surely, of a single solar light...

If it is argued that, just as a difference in the degree of manifestation is observed due to the proximity of specific manifestors such as the palm of the hand or a crystal mirror, it is logical for bliss (*ānanda*)— though it is one— to possess degrees of excellence and deficiency in its manifestation through the mediation of different states of happiness (*sukha-vṛtti*) which act as its manifestors;

He cites scripture as authority for the fact that the bliss of the witness—which is of the nature of a reflection of ignorance—is perceived in the world as the bliss of sense objects and is therefore subject to degrees of excellence, whereas the bliss of Brahman is of a single, uniform nature.
This is stated in the *Ānandavallī*: "The human bliss, the bliss of a sovereign ruler of the whole earth, and that [bliss] multiplied a hundredfold..."

The joy of human *gandharvas* arises; that same joy, multiplied a hundredfold, becomes the joy of divine *gandharvas*. In this very manner, among the joys of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and so forth, that which is called "the one bliss of Brahman" refers to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha.

The description of their increase and decrease is to be applied up to the conclusion, according to the sentence "He who is here in a person and he who is there in the sun are one"—this is the remainder [of the argument]. "Person" (*puruṣa*) means a human being;
the first "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of including animals and so forth. The word "sun" (*āditya*) refers to the deity presiding over the solar orb.

The second "ca" (and) has the purpose of including all other deities besides that one; thus, the meaning of the Śruti is that the bliss of Brahman existing everywhere—among gods, humans, and animals—is one and of a single form, and not something subject to gradation like the bliss of the witness (*sākṣyānanda*). [This refers to] the bliss of the witness and the bliss of the object.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) objects: "If there were a difference among the blisses of Brahman, then a distinction between liberation and transmigratory existence could be stated according to the manner described; however, that very [distinction] is unestablished for you. He refutes this by saying, "No, because it is impossible.
The meaning is that it is impossible for excellence and deficiency—characterized as specific species—to coexist within a single individual instance.

The proponent of the established view (siddhāntin), intending that although bliss in its ultimate reality is one, distinctions such as superiority and so forth are possible within it when it is characterized by imagined differences, raises an objection:
"Of human bliss and the rest," in accordance with experience.
The meaning is that it is improper for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) to deny the excellence of bliss and so forth established by the *śruti*.

As if unaware of the [opponent’s] intention, the proponent of the prima facie view offers a refutation: "What [is the harm]? The proponent of the final view (*siddhāntī*) raises an objection: "What kind of impossibility [is there]? He states that [objection] with the words "But what... and "In the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*)," referring to the position that bliss is one.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "it is impossible": even in the case of a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), the proof of that [identity] is impossible due to the absence of a corresponding illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
such is the intention of the opponent as well. Even within a single manifestation of bliss (*ānanda-vyaktyām*), by means of the difference of limiting adjuncts...

Revealing his own intention—that it is possible to establish the excellence of bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth as proven by scripture and experience—the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) raises an objection: "But [if] of one and the same...
[He continues: For, compared to that manifestation of light which is devoid of contact with the palm of the hand and so forth, [there is a manifestation] upon the palm of the hand...

A slightly greater manifestation [is seen] compared to that; a greater manifestation than that is seen in a crystal; and a still greater manifestation than even that is established by experience in a mirror and so forth.

Similarly, in the present case as well, [the Self is manifested] through various mental states (*vṛtti*) that manifest the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*), according to the degree of intensity of those respective states.
The meaning is that the excellence and other qualities of the witness are logically established;

for there is no lack of agreement regarding the illustration: the sunlight, spreading everywhere, appears indistinctly upon the surface of the sky or a low-lying ground even without contact with the palms of the hands or similar objects.
Just as flowing water, when its movement is obstructed by contact with the palm of the hand,

becomes more intense due to its thickening, so too, when its movement is obstructed by contact with a bright mirror or similar object, it becomes even more intense due to its thickening and the blending of its own radiance with that of the object.

Regarding the term "illumination" (*prakāśa*): in that case, because one does not admit a gradation in manifestation based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that serve as manifestors; and since the illustrative example is accepted—just like the solar light spreading through the sky—the lack of clarity belongs to the unconditioned bliss (*anavacchinnānanda*).

[The opponent argues: "It is merely an increased manifestation of bliss delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of pleasure, like the light of the sun as it is not obstructed by the palm of the hand. [This is incorrect], because it would follow that worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) itself is more desirable than liberation. By this, [the state] during the period of worldly existence...

Even though bliss is fully present, it does not shine forth clearly— like the light of a lamp tossed by a violent wind— due to being distracted by false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); however, because these are absent in liberation, it shines forth as it truly is, and thus [the objection] is refuted.

If light were a single individual entity and of a uniform nature by itself, then it could serve as an illustration for such a bliss of one's own essential nature; however, light does not possess the state of being a single individual entity, because it consists of a multitude of various rays,
nor does it possess uniformity, since the solar rays vary in intensity here and there.
The proponent [of the previous view], revealing his underlying intention, refutes [the argument] by stating, "because of the perception of various forms in the form of abundance.

He explains: "Because of non-agreement" means "because it is not accepted by me. "Of that which is spreading forth" means "of that which has the nature of moving. "When movement is obstructed" refers to the obstruction of the movement of the sun's rays.

The meaning is "it exists. For this very reason, on that portion of the ground where the rays of the sun do not spread due to the obstruction created by the palm of the hand or similar objects, a shadow in the form of darkness is perceived.
He provides an illustration for the thickening [of darkness] resulting from the obstruction of the movement of light: "on a low-lying surface," as in the case of a low-lying surface.

The meaning is that when the flow of spreading water is obstructed by contact with the palm of the hand, the water becomes thickened; it is "more" (adhika) in this sense. Regarding "excessive" (adhika): compared to the light in the sky which is free from contact with the palm of the hand and so forth and is thus clearly unmanifest, [the light here] is more intense; such is the brilliance of that lamp.
"Because of the addition of fuel" (*saṃbalanāt*) means: the radiance of a mirror or the like which I call "light" (*prabhā*). "Even from that" means:

even from the light residing in the palm of the hand. "In that case" means: since it is not admitted that there is a gradation in the manifestation of light—which is uniform in nature—caused by the gradations in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), that [example] cannot serve as an illustration.

The meaning is that it is possible. Having accepted the stated example, he states a further objection for the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*): "And if there were agreement regarding the example, [there would be no activity] toward liberation. Thus, the implication is that in the established doctrine, no one would ever engage in the means for its attainment with liberation as the goal. Regarding liberation and saṃsāra...

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) states that even the specific manner of resolving the objection regarding the consequence of a distinction has been refuted by the reason to be stated hereafter, saying: "By this [it is shown]... The cognition of the body as the self when it is not the self, and the cognition of the body as belonging to the self when it is in reality devoid of any connection with the self—both of these are false cognitions (mithyājñāna).

Furthermore, during the states of waking and so forth, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by false knowledge cause a distraction and produce an indistinctness even while the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is manifest; and in deep sleep,
those same impressions distract the bliss that is manifest even then, thereby obstructing its realization as the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
For indeed, it is solely by the power of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of false knowledge, awakened by specific karmic residues that determine future births,

that every living being abandons the experience of bliss during deep sleep; consequently, because the manifestation of the bliss of deep sleep is unstable and lacks the quality of being desired as an ultimate goal, it is not the supreme human end (*apuruṣārtha*).
The meaning is "you."

Since the bliss of one's own nature shines forth without distinction, and because it is impossible for that which does not shine forth due to the defect of distraction to be subject to the attainment of liberation even at the time of death,
it is therefore improper to imagine that the bliss of the witness is unobscured.

Regarding this, the masters of Advaita-vidyā say: just as when the reflection of a single, most excellent white form appears in many mirrors possessing varying degrees of tarnish, there arises in each instance a variation [in the reflection] corresponding to the degree of tarnish in that particular limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
The intensity of the reflection [of bliss] is superimposed according to its degree of excellence. Thus,

although the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is in reality beyond all gradation, when it exists as the bliss of the witness (*sākṣyānanda*) through being reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [it appears limited] by means of specific objects dependent upon the abundance of one's ordinary merits.

And when there is the state of objective bliss, [this occurs] because it is reflected in a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) which consists of pleasure and is characterized by degrees of purity in the form of the excellence or deficiency of sentient beings resulting from contact.

In the illustrative example, even though light continues to shine, there occurs either the destruction of some of its parts due to its having constituent parts and being struck by a violent wind, or a dispersal consisting of the obstruction of the luminosity inherent in the form of the light.
It is possible for the light of a lamp to possess an indistinct luminosity;

however, in the case of the bliss of Brahman, which is devoid of specific qualities such as parts and attributes, no such distinction is possible—this he states with the words "nirviśeṣa" (without distinction) and "prakāśamāna" (shining). [The word] "sati" is used in the locative absolute sense; "tatra" is used in the locative sense of location.
"Even in liberation, it is not so. This means: "of that which is manifest in the state of liberation. "Excellence" (atiśaya) means:

as in the case of the example, whether it consists of the nature of the parts or the nature of a specific genus. "Therefore" means: because of the consequence that there would be no distinction between liberation and saṃsāra. What was reached by the passage beginning with "It might be argued" (syādetat) [is now addressed].
He refutes the prima facie position with the words "here they say," and so forth.
By stating an illustration corresponding to the gradations in the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*),
he establishes that this bliss of one's own nature is proven by both scripture and experience.
He establishes the state of possessing excellence and deficiency expressed by the term *tāratamya* (gradation). [He says] "as follows" (*yathā*). Regarding "of that which is most excellent":

the meaning is "among white forms, of that which is the very best. By the word "of one" (*ekasya*), it is indicated that the excellence and deficiency to be described later do not exist there by their own nature. The words "in this and that reflection" (*pratibimbe*) refer to these respective instances.

Regarding the term "grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): it refers to the "diminution of whiteness. In the reflection in a slightly soiled mirror, a diminution is superimposed; in the reflection in a moderately soiled mirror, a greater diminution is superimposed relative to that [former];
and in the reflection in an extremely soiled mirror...

And an extreme reduction is superimposed upon it; consequently, the white form reflected in such mirrors is manifested according to its degree of intensity. The meaning is that although it is, in reality, of a single form and shining by its own nature, [it appears otherwise]. Regarding the phrase "the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa): even in deep sleep, the internal organ...
It should be understood that the witness-bliss (sākṣyānanda) is common to deep sleep because it exists in a subtle form;
however, according to other schools of thought, the state of witness-bliss is to be seen as being due to its reflection in ignorance (avidyā).
The phrase "the state of bliss" (ānandabhāva) implies the sense of "when [this] has been attained."

"Accomplishment" (*saṃpatti*) means ripening, that is to say, the state of being ready to produce a fruit. It refers to one who possesses a gradation of purity characterized by the excellence or deficiency of the *sattva* element, which is caused by contact with specific objects that depend upon the accomplishment of past meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*). Such a person is [the one described].

The meaning is: when the experience of the bliss of objects occurs by virtue of being reflected in the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which are themselves of the nature of happiness. It is stated that the mental modifications are of the nature of happiness because they manifest the happiness that is their own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
This is what is meant: [it is the result] of having been well-accomplished in previous births...

By the power of the ripening of meritorious karma, when the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) comes into contact with specific objects through the medium of mental states directed toward particular objects of form such as garlands and sandalwood paste, there arises an excellence of the quality of purity (sattva-guṇa) residing therein due to its connection with those superior objects.
From association with inferior objects, a state of degradation occurs.

Consequently, the mental modifications (*vṛttis*), which are transformations of the *sattva* aspect residing within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), arise having the bliss of one's own true nature as their object; yet even as they arise, they are themselves possessed of degrees of excellence and deficiency.
The reflection of bliss that arises within these is called the bliss of sense objects (viṣayānanda).

Due to the defect of gradation in the impurity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the quality of tamas, a gradation of inferiority is superimposed; thus, even though bliss is manifest during the state of saṃsāra,
a gradation of inferiority is superimposed upon it.

There is no lack of satisfaction because of its excellence; for upon the dawn of knowledge, all superimpositions of inferiority cease, and thus the superimposed state of being "excellent" (sātiśaya) is removed. The qualification "having accomplished all that was to be done" is appropriate because [the Self] is the object of unconditional love.
Being manifest, the witness is indeed bliss and remains entirely unobscured.

Now, it must be said that due to the deficiency residing in the mental state (*vṛtti*) which has the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*) as its object, a superimposition of deficiency occurs upon the bliss of objects, which is of the nature of a reflection;
for just as a superimposition of deficiency occurs upon a reflection due to the deficiency residing in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a mirror caused by a soiled substance.

Because of this observation: likewise, in the case of the states of deep sleep (*suvṛtti*), which have the bliss of one's own nature as their object and consist of a transformation of the *sattva* quality, some impure substance that acts as the cause of deterioration must necessarily be postulated;
for it is only an impure substance in direct contact with a mirror [that causes its tarnishing].
Because it is observed that [the mirror] acts as a cause for the removal [of the reflection], he says: "consisting of the quality of *tamas*.

Since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is composed of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the quality of *tamas* persists even in its modifications (*vṛtti*). The defect consisting in the gradation of turbidity produced by that [adjunct] is the "deterioration" (*apakarṣa*).

This means that the defect residing in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consists of gradation (*tāratamya*). Therefore, due to that defect, a diminution (*apakarṣa*) is superimposed upon the joy of the object, which exists in the form of a reflection within the sattvic modification; this is the meaning. Previously, contact with an object was indicated as the cause for a modification consisting of pleasure; in that context, the word "particular" (*viśeṣa*) in the phrase "particular object" (*viṣaya-viśeṣa*) [is intended to exclude the general].

The gradation of those [objects] was previously indicated as being caused by the gradation of excellence in the modifications (*vṛtti*) consisting of pleasure that have reached their respective objects; however, here, it is characterized by gradation as the cause of the decrease in modifications consisting of pleasure, and as the cause of the gradation of that decrease.
It should be understood that the distinction is that a substance consisting of the quality of *tamas* is designated as "impure. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"Thus, in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). Even though bliss is manifesting, there is a gradation of inferiority superimposed upon it; therefore, because it possesses degrees of excellence, this refers to the bliss derived from sense objects.
And thus, for one who experiences inferior bliss, who is overcome by a thirst for superior bliss,

and who strives to achieve it— acting even toward things that result in suffering due to the delusion that they are its means— the characteristic state of falling into the wombs of gods, humans, animals, and so forth [arises].

"It becomes a misfortune" means that there is no liberation (*nirvṛti*). Regarding "from cessation": the meaning is that when fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) ceases, the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are its effects cease, and thereby the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of deficiencies and so forth produced by them ceases. Regarding "the state of having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtyatā*):

one who has performed (*kṛta*) the entire collection of duties (*kartavyajāta*) is "one who has accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*); the state of such a person is "the state of having accomplished what was to be done. This is indeed [the case] for a *puruṣa*.

Because of the dawning of knowledge (*vidyodayāt*). Previously, there was a multitude of duties to be performed for the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness; but when knowledge has dawned, since suffering alone has ceased, and because of the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature—which is supremely exalted, pure, and like a stainless mirror—there is no longer [need] for its cessation or its attainment.
The sense is that there is nothing further to be done, which constitutes the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*). Thus the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled his purpose.
By understanding this through the direct realization (*aparokṣa*) of Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, one becomes truly wise.

One becomes wise and one has accomplished what was to be done. O Arjuna, descendant of Bharata, since scholarship and the like cannot be attained without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the sense is that you should therefore accomplish that very thing and abandon everything else. Regarding the phrase "due to the specific attainment," the words "of liberation and saṃsāra" are to be supplied as the remainder. Now, [an objection]:
One might argue that the bliss of the witness (*sākṣyananda*), like the bliss of Brahman, must also be veiled;
and if that were so, there would be no distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). To this, he says: "Unconditioned" (*nirupādhika*).

Such love is possible only because it exists while the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) remains veiled; for in the world, it is only toward a happiness that is manifest [that such love arises].
The meaning is that this is because the experience of joy is established through direct perception.

Others, however, hold that even though bliss is manifest, because one experiences its concealment— thinking "it does not exist" or "it is not manifest"— it is indeed concealed; for even within a single witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),
since a distinction of forms imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*) is possible, there is a concealment of that which is of the nature of consciousness in its aspect as bliss.
And because there is no contradiction; for since the manifestation of the essential nature does not remove the veil, the veil is not in contradiction with that which is manifesting.

When the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position is reached— that if the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) were unobscured, its non-different bliss (*ānanda*) would also necessarily be unobscured, resulting in the undesirable consequence that there would be no distinction between liberation (*mukti*) and worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)—
the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is shown: even though the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) is unobscured, a distinction between those two states is indeed possible.
Now, having accepted its state of being veiled, he presents the established conclusion (siddhānta) by stating the distinction between liberation and saṃsāra:

"But others [say]... Having established the Vedānta position, [he argues that] because one observes the worldly usage [of statements] such as "I have no bliss of my own essential nature" or "it does not manifest," there must indeed exist an obscuration (āvaraṇa) which is the cause of that [usage].

The meaning is that there is no consequence of non-distinction between the two states, because in the state of saṃsāra bliss is obscured, whereas in liberation, due to the destruction of those veils, there is the manifestation of the bliss of one's own nature. Here, the connection is that "even though bliss is manifesting, it is indeed veiled," and not unveiled; for if it were unveiled, [the aforementioned objection] would apply.

The intention of the word "only" (*eva*) is that it would result in a contradiction with empirical usage. Now, one might object: "In this way, there would always be a lack of unconditioned love for the Self, because the manifestation of the bliss of its own nature is not present [in ordinary experience], and the manifestation of the bliss produced by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is only occasional. To this we say: no, for by the force of the resulting fruit, even that which is veiled [is established].

Because it is postulated that the manifestation of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*) is the cause of unconditional love, and because the intent of the *Vivaraṇa*— which states that "bliss, characterized as the object of supreme love, indeed shines forth"— is also appropriately understood here in this very sense; it is with this same intention [that the following is said].

It should be understood that it was stated "even while being manifest" because otherwise, if one were to assume that the bliss of the witnessed object (*sākṣyānanda*)— which is non-different from the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*)— is concealed, the qualification "being manifest" would be useless due to its lack of utility, resulting in the consequence of redundancy; for if the bliss of the witnessed object, which is one with the witness-consciousness, were concealed, then the witness-consciousness itself would also have to be concealed in that same locus.

Because being veiled and being unveiled are contradictory at the same time, he says: "Even in one [consciousness]. Just as, in reality, within the single consciousness itself, two distinct forms called "jīva" and "Īśvara" are conceptually constructed by the force of conventional usage—such that one thinks, "I am the Lord, but [the other] is a transmigrating being"—so too [is it said]: "I am happy; knowledge is bliss. It is not [the case that]...

Because we observe the empirical usage of difference arising from the bliss [of Brahman] due to the non-dissolution of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth in the form of "I am," etc., two distinct forms called consciousness (*cit*) and bliss (*ānanda*) are postulated as established from beginningless time in accordance with that [usage]. And just as in a single consciousness...
Ignorance and so forth are postulated as delimited by the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), while their absence is postulated as delimited by the state of being the Lord (īśvaratva).

Similarly, concealment is postulated as delimited by bliss (ānandatva), while its absence is postulated within the consciousness that manifests the ego and other factors, as delimited by consciousness (citva); this is done on the strength of the resulting evidence (phalabala), and thus there is no contradiction.

The meaning is that there is no contradiction with non-duality (advaita), because even the distinction consisting of the forms of "living" and so forth is admitted to be imagined by ignorance (avidyā). Now, one might object: although there is no contradiction between concealment and its absence through different forms within a single witness (sākṣin), bliss—
To the objection that it is contradictory for something to be manifest yet veiled—since manifestation is opposed to concealment—the author replies "no," stating:

"of the manifestation of its own nature. This is because the assumption that concealment is opposed to manifestation applies only to adventitious modifications (*āgantuka-vṛtti-rūpa*), and not to the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-prakāśa*); therefore, that [essential nature] is not opposed to concealment.

The meaning is "because it is the means of accomplishment. Now, one might object: since the text states that "even though bliss is manifest, it is veiled," the qualification "being manifest" must be intended to indicate that the manifestation of the essential nature (svarūpa) does not contradict its being veiled; thus, such a purpose for that qualification is possible.

If it is argued that what was stated— that the qualification [of the Self] serves the purpose of making known the possibility of unconditional love toward the Self— is indeed possible, then, in the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*),
let it be that the qualification serves both purposes in the manifestation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-prakāśa*).

For it must necessarily be made known that, just as [the self] is not opposed to its own obscuration, so too in the view that bliss is an obscuration, unconditioned love for the Self in its nature as bliss must also be possible.

For it is observed that even while [the object] is manifesting as "I do not know the meaning spoken by you," there is still an obscuration. Nor should it be argued that in that case one experiences only the obscuration of the particular (viśeṣa) through the delimitation of the unobscured universal form (sāmānyākāra); for if one obscuration were to appear through the delimitation of another, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Nor...
It should not be argued that the relation of generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣabhāva*) is the regulator [of the scope of ignorance], and thus there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);

for since there exists no relation of generality and particularity distinct from the relation of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), it would follow that one could experience the ignorance that conceals smoke by saying, "I do not know fire."
Therefore, that portion of ignorance which manifests as delimited is what is said to be "veiled"; thus, it is logical that ignorance persists even while [the object] is manifesting.
And just as ignorance veils consciousness (caitanya) by setting aside the witness-self (sākṣin), so too does it function.
In this way, even bliss (ānanda) is swallowed by the form of those various pleasures and those various states of pleasure.
He states another reason for the fact that the manifestation of one's own nature (*svarūpa-prakāśa*) does not contradict its concealment: "What has been said by you," etc.

After the word "only" (*eva*), the phrase "the meaning taught by the authoritative teacher" is to be supplied as the remainder. Following the instruction of an authoritative teacher (*āpta-upadeśa*)—namely, that Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) known through the Vedāntas, and that he is difficult to be known by those of unrefined self—a person of dull intellect...

It is well known in the world that when there is no comprehension of the meaning of a sentence, a person who is dull-witted experiences the ignorance [of thinking], "I do not understand the meaning spoken by you. In such a case, one understands from the observation of worldly usage: "I know that there is some meaning in your statement because it is the word of a reliable authority (āpta), yet I do not know its specific detail. This is how it is understood.

That universal form which constitutes the meaning of your statement, characterized by "you," shines forth as the object of the ignorance that veils the particular; and thus, in the experience "I do not know the meaning spoken by you," it shines forth as the qualifier of that ignorance.

Because the general form is not an object of obscuration, and because the particular, which is the object of obscuration, does not manifest; for that which is manifest cannot be experienced as being obscured.
Because the form of the horn is not an object of obscuration, [and] because the particular, which is the object of obscuration...

Because there is an absence of manifestation [of that object], he raises the objection that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He refutes this with the words "And not there," meaning that if one were to admit the manifestation of the ignorance that veils one object by way of delimiting another, there would follow the absurd consequence that the ignorance experienced in the form "I do not know Caitra" would have Viṣṇumitra as its object.

He refutes [the objection]: "Of another obscuration," etc. Now, the form characterized as the meaning of your own statement is indeed of a general nature; for just as it exists in Śrī Kṛṣṇa as taught by an authoritative person (āpta), so too it exists in the means for realizing Śrī Kṛṣṇa taught by you, since the status of being the meaning of your statement applies to them as well.

However, the specific form characterized by such attributes as "being knowable through Vedānta" and so forth resides exclusively in the essential nature of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus, by accepting that the ignorance concealing the specific [nature] is manifested through the delimitation of the general form, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. [This applies to] Caitratva...
Viṣṇumitra objects that there is no relationship of generality and particularity between the two, stating: "And it is not the case that [there is] a generality...

Does this mean that the states of being a Śrīkṛṣṇa-form and being a Viṣṇu-form possess a relationship of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva), like a generality and its particulars? Or is it something other than that? It is not.
With the intention that the second [alternative] is untenable because it cannot be established, he says: "Pervaded... He states the fault in the first [alternative]: "Fire...
Therefore, one must say that in the experience of ignorance, that which appears as the qualifier of ignorance is itself the object of the veil; it is not as you have stated, namely, "I do not know."
If it is accepted that a cognition has the property of having the object as stated by you as its qualifier (prakāra) while taking "ignorance" (ajñāna) as its qualificand (viśeṣya)—
such that the object stated by you exists only as a qualifier— then,
due to the absence of the cause consisting of the cognition of that qualifier, there could be no experience of that [object] as qualified by ignorance.

It should not be argued that because the experience of ignorance is admitted to be of the nature of the eternal witness (*sākṣin*), it does not require a further cognition as its qualifier; nor should it be argued that being manifest and being veiled are contradictory,
since manifestation is opposed to concealment— for such a contradiction has already been addressed.
With the intention that [ignorance] has already been refuted, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
This means that it is impossible for the ignorance that veils one thing to appear as delimited by another thing.
Regarding the phrase "delimited by which" (*yadavacchinnam*), it means "qualified by which object."

Now, one might object: "If bliss (*ānanda*) were indeed veiled, it would not manifest specifically during states of contact with sense objects. To this, he says: "And ignorance (*ajñāna*)," etc.; that is, it veils [bliss] by completely swallowing it up.

This indeed is the subduing of the veil over objective pleasure; and that subduing of the veil occurs in varying degrees—like the subduing of external veils at the time of dawn—by virtue of specific modifications (vṛtti) induced by specific causes. Therefore:

They state that the mutual distinction between the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*), the bliss consisting of objects (*viṣayānanda*), and the various forms of objective bliss is thus established. In every respect,
because the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is unobscured, there is no dependence upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*) for the purpose of overcoming an obscuration.

Therefore, the manifestation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth is exactly the same [in both cases]. Now, one might object: "In this way, how can there be a synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) of the ego-sense and so on? For it is impossible for impressions (*saṃskāra*), which consist of the subtle state of cognition, to be deposited by the eternal Witness (*sākṣin*), since that is not possible while cognition itself exists."

[Objection: Since it is admitted that a mental modification (*vṛtti*) has the nature of overcoming an obscuration, how can it be said that ignorance does not obscure the bliss when it is made an object of a modification of bliss? To this, he says: "This very [bliss]," etc.

The very nature of bliss—which, by virtue of being the object of a modification of bliss, is not subject to obscuration—is what constitutes the overcoming of the obscuration produced by the modification.

This is the meaning. Now, an objection is raised: since the modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of bliss is of a single uniform nature, the subduing of the veil (*āvaraṇa*) produced by it must also be of a single uniform nature. Consequently, at the time of contact with an object, bliss would manifest only in a single uniform manner, and not in varying degrees of intensity such as superior or inferior. To this, he says: "And that... Just as at the time of dawn...

According to the gradation of light, there occurs a corresponding gradation in the overcoming of external darkness; consequently, there arises a manifestation of objects shrouded by various degrees of that darkness characterized by such gradations.
In this way, whatever distinction exists among the mental modifications (vṛttis) is brought about by the specific nature of the particular object, which serves as the specific cause.

The suppression of the veils occurs precisely through the influence of the gradations of excellence; consequently, bliss also manifests as being endowed with degrees of intensity. Even so, since bliss is admitted to be one, how can its manifestation as differentiated be established?

To this he replies: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is that, although in reality there is only one bliss (*ānanda*), a distinction is admitted due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Thus, when the veil has been removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), the bliss that shines forth is the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*); whereas in the state where that [veil] has not been removed, [the bliss is experienced] through its connection with mental modifications (*vṛtti*).

The meaning is that the distinction between the bliss of one's own nature (*svarūpānanda*) and the bliss derived from objects (*viṣayānanda*)—wherein the latter is the bliss manifesting as an object—must be understood; for, since the difference in bliss is admitted through the difference in mental modifications (*vṛtti*), the well-known mutual distinction among various objective pleasures is thereby logically established. [This applies] to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth alone...
With the intention that the state of being manifested by the witness (sākṣin) is established as the primary subject under discussion, he says: "In every way" (sarvathāpi). This means:

whether in the view that the bliss of one's own nature (svarūpānanda) is unobscured, or in the view that it is obscured. By the word "by that" (tena), he means: by the consciousness of the witness (sākṣicaitanya). Now, [an objection]: in the Siddhānta, since it is accepted that a mental impression (saṃskāra) has the same form as the experience (anubhava)...

He raises an objection, suggesting that for the purpose of mental construction (*saṃskāra*), the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) indeed requires a modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth. This is expressed by the words "But if it were thus" (*nanvevam*).
The meaning is: provided that the witness-consciousness does not require a modification regarding the ego-sense and so forth. "Recollection" (*anusaṃdhāna*) refers to memory (*smṛti*).

"Producing that substratum" means producing a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). He states the reason for the impossibility of producing that substratum with the words "of that which consists of the subtle state of knowledge," and so forth. Now, if there is a connection with another [object] in the form of a mental impression consisting of its subtle state during the period when the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) persists, then what of that state?
He says "let there be no arising from that" with the words "by the eternal. Thus,
although the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) delimited by the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth does not require a mental modification (vṛtti) because it is unobscured,
there is still a dependence on it for the sake of producing a latent impression (saṃskāra).
The sense is that because [the self] exists, the established doctrine— that the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth are manifested solely by the witness-consciousness— would be contradicted.

On this point, some say: the *ahaṃkāra*, which is always being illumined by the witness (*sākṣin*) with whom it is conjoined, is also illumined by that same witness—even though it is delimited by itself—when it undergoes transformation into the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward various objects such as a jar. Because that [ahaṃkāra] is non-eternal, its [illumination] is possible.

The deposition of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in a pot or other object does not occur in the same manner as [the impression] in the case of an object [of cognition]; for there is no rule that the deposition of a latent impression regarding its own object occurs solely through the Witness (*sākṣin*) as delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having its own form. If that were the case, since a latent impression regarding the modification itself would be impossible, it would follow that the modification could never be remembered.

This is because [the objection] has already been refuted by the rejection of *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent cognition) through the removal of the infinite regress (*anavasthā*) resulting from the operation of another mental modification (*vṛttyantara*) upon that which is the object of the [original] modification.

Rather, the rule is simply this: when something is manifested in the consciousness delimited by a particular mental modification (*vṛtti*), that modification deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding that object.

He provides the resolution that there is no contradiction with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the formation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) occurs even without the functioning of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth. Regarding this, some say [the following], using the passage beginning with "The non-dual Self itself" and ending with "is manifested by the ego-sense as conjoined with its own [objects]," concerning the ego-sense.

It has been shown that just as there is manifestation by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) as delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), so too there is manifestation by the witness-consciousness as delimited by a mental modification (vṛtti) whose object is things such as a jar or a cloth. To this he asks: "What follows from that?
and answers: "Of that," meaning because the witness-consciousness as delimited by a mental modification having a jar or similar object is non-eternal. By that...

Just as the deposition of an impression (*saṃskāra*) is possible in an object such as a jar, so too is the deposition of an impression possible in the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and other such things by that very same witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) as delimited by its own mental modification (*vṛtti*); thus, the meaning is that there is no requirement for a mental modification directed toward the ego-sense as its object. Now, [one might object]: in the case of objects like jars, which are distinct from the ego-sense...

Since it is observed that the impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding an object such as a jar is deposited solely by consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose form is that very object, the rule is established that the deposition of an impression regarding its own object occurs only through a mental modification having that same object. Thus, having raised the doubt— namely, how there could be the deposition of an impression regarding something else within the mere ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) by means of a mental modification having a different object— he says:
"No," he says. The sense is that there is no evidence for such a restriction, and it would be logically irrelevant (*aprayojaka*).

He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against accepting such a restriction with the words, "If that were the case. Now, one might object: "Let there be yet another modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the modification consisting of cognition, in order to obtain the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and so forth"; to this he replies, "Because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)."
If, for the sake of establishing the recollection of a mental modification (vṛtti) whose object is a jar or the like, one must admit another mental modification having that [first] as its object,
then a third modification having that [second] as its object must likewise be admitted for the sake of recollecting the second modification; and so on, for each successive modification.

It would follow that there is an infinite regress of successive occurrences (*vṛtti*). Nor can it be argued that there is no risk of an infinite regress because one may assume the destruction of some among the second, third, and subsequent occurrences even while they are still unperceived; for [once] an occurrence has arisen...
Because the mental modification (*vṛtti*) must necessarily be known— otherwise, even while a modification in the form of a jar or the like exists,

there would arise the possibility of doubt as to whether "this is known by me" or "not," or whether after the destruction of the modification, "this was known by me" or "not"— therefore, the mental modification must necessarily be known.

In the view that a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is known by another modification, one would fall into an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) by this very logic; thus, by this same reasoning, the subsequent cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) is refuted in the case of the commentaries (*nibandhana*).

Consequently, there is no rule that a modification deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding its own object solely through itself, because such [self-apprehension] is impossible in the case of modifications—this is the meaning.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is admitted that a mental state directed toward one object deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in another object, then it would follow as an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that a mental state directed toward a jar would deposit such a print even in a cloth. To this, he says "But...

and states the determining factor (*prayojaka*) to avoid this over-extension: "by the mental state delimited by the object of which thing... That is, [the mental state] delimited by the object of whichever thing...

According to the rule that as many objects as manifest in consciousness (caitanya) through a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward those very things, so many impressions (saṃskāra) are deposited in those objects—there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga), because in the case of consciousness delimited by a modification directed toward a jar, cloth and other things do not manifest. [Objection: But surely, only by means of a modification directed toward itself...
The meaning of the particle "eva" (only/just) is that there is a restriction [to the effect] that [the sense organ] deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within its own sphere of operation.

And thus, it is logical that even cognitions, pleasures, and the like— which are modifications of the internal organ— though they emerge from it like sparks from a heated iron ball, are manifested by their respective individual, non-eternal witness-consciousness, just as fire is manifested by its own delimited fire. This applies to them as well.
As for the infusion of a mental impression (*saṃskārādhāna*), that consciousness which resides in a cognition having the single form of a jar would manifest the jar itself.
Thus, as stated by the author of the *Kūṭasthadīpa*, the "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) of the jar is manifested by the Brahman-consciousness;
this refers to the knowledge—which is a qualification of the object—as being delimited by the object.
The position that [objects] are illumined by the Brahman-consciousness, as well as the position stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*—
namely, that knowledge, desire, and so forth are manifested by the eternal witness (sākṣin) whose nature is unconditioned, pure consciousness.
Now, it is indeed undisputed that the manifestation of a jar or other object occurs within the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the jar and so forth;

and in that case, the manifestation of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) within that consciousness is also shown in the preceding text to be illumined by the Witness (*sākṣin*), which is itself delimited by the very same [consciousness] transformed into the form of the mental modification directed toward objects such as the jar. And thus:

Granted that there is the depositing of a residual impression (*saṃskāra*) even in the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of a jar or the like; nevertheless, because it is unestablished that the modification in the form of the cognition of a jar or the like has its manifestation in the consciousness delimited by itself (*svāvacchinna-caitanya*), such a modification would not produce a residual impression whose object is itself. It is just so.

Since there would be no manifestation of pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and so forth— which are attributes of the ego (ahaṃkāra)— within the consciousness delimited by the mental modifications (vṛtti) of jars and the like, no latent impressions (saṃskāra) could be deposited in them; nor,
even if no impressions were deposited in the modifications consisting of pleasure and so forth due to the modification of a jar, would pleasure [be experienced].

It should not be argued that there is no risk of infinite regress— on the grounds that the superimposition [of consciousness] upon those mental modifications (vṛtti) such as those concerning a jar, which are themselves of the nature of cognition, occurs through the very internal-organ modifications whose objects are suffering and so forth, just as one might resort to another modification for the sake of superimposing it upon them; for a modification whose object is pleasure, pain, and so forth, must indeed be admitted.
Is it of the nature of knowledge, or is it of the nature of an activity like the modifications of desire and so forth?

It cannot be the first, because of the absence of an instrument (karaṇa) that produces it, since the status of the self as an instrument has not yet been established. Nor can it be the second, because if another modification directed toward that [object] were admitted in order to deposit a latent impression (saṃskāra) for that [first] modification, [an infinite regress would follow].

That same infinite regress results; therefore, raising the objection as to how an impression (*saṃskāra*) can be deposited in modifications (*vṛtti*) consisting of objects such as jars—which are not of the nature of cognition—and in modifications consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are distinct from cognition—the author says: "If this is so" (*evaṃ ceti*). This means: provided that the stated rule holds true.

The various modifications (*vṛttis*) that arise within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), whether they be of the nature of knowledge or otherwise, are all indeed illuminated by the eternal consciousness delimited by each respective [modification]. Thus, although consciousness is eternal,
it is [perceived] as being delimited by those [modifications] through the process of being their illuminator.

The meaning is this: since the mental states (dharmas) of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arise and are impermanent, it is possible for there to be a latent impression (*saṃskāra*)—which consists in their destruction and has those very states as its object—belonging to that consciousness which is qualified by those states and which manifests them; thus, there is no impossibility of latent impressions in the case of cognition, pleasure, and so forth. This is the point illustrated by the example.

One's own state is like a spark; it is like the form of a single jar, having the nature of being the form of that [jar]. That which is both that [form] and the Lord (the Self) is the Consciousness (cit) situated therein—the reflection in the mental modification (vṛtti) shaped like a jar, which is to say, the cognition of the jar. It is the jar itself, not [a property] of the jar.
