The particle *api* (also) signifies the meaning of *eva* (indeed/exactly). The meaning is that "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) consists in being the object of non-cognition;

[in other words], cognition residing in the object by way of the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*). And that cognition is a qualifier of the object, because of the experience "the pot is cognized" (*jñāto ghaṭaḥ*); this is the point. Now, regarding these two...

Since the consciousness that illumines knowledge, desire, and so forth is eternal, how can there be a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding knowledge, desire, and the like? Nor [is it the case] that,

according to the method previously stated, the modifications (*vṛtti*) such as knowledge and desire [are related] to the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) as delimited by each respective [modification].
It must be stated that the production of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) occurs in both positions by taking the state of being manifest (*prakāśyatva*) as the basis.

For the cognition in the form of a reflection whose object is a jar or the like, there exists a "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*)— termed such— which is not delimited by anything other than that [reflection] residing within it.

Furthermore, since consciousness (*caitanya*) must necessarily be admitted to have a form that is immediate (*aparokṣa*) with respect to that which it is in contact with, its contact with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) must certainly be asserted; thus, because there exists an impermanent form in contact with that [consciousness], there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the production of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) within them. Others, however, [hold as follows]:

They establish the existence of latent impressions (saṃskāra) in the substrate of the "I" by accepting an imagined veil of ignorance in the form of the "I," which persists even during deep sleep to account for the continuity of ignorance and other factors.

Because it would contradict the statement that objects are illumined by the Brahman-consciousness which has them as its locus, and because in the second view it would entail the contradiction of stating that mental modifications such as knowledge and desire are illumined by the unconditioned witness (sākṣin), how then can those two [views] be established? To this he says: "Of those two also... [referring to] the object-conditioned...

In the view that the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacaitanya*) is the illuminator of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), that consciousness of Brahman is accepted as being of the very nature of immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*) regarding cognizedness, because there is the experience of the immediacy of cognizedness in such instances as "this jar is known. [This is] undivided (*anavacchinna*).

Pure consciousness (*śuddha-caitanya*) is also accepted as being of the nature of immediate cognition (*aparokṣa-jñāna*) with respect to desire, knowledge, and so forth; for even mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as desire are experienced as immediate. Thus, there are two kinds of consciousness, both of which are of the nature of immediate cognition.

A connection with its own objects, such as knowledge, desire, and so forth, is necessarily inevitable for immediate cognition (*aparokṣajñāna*), because it is governed by the rule that immediate cognition consists in the experience of an object that has attained identity with itself;
consequently, at the moment of the destruction of the knowledge, desire, and so forth that constitute its own objects, [the cognition exists] in a form qualified by that knowledge and so forth.

The meaning is that the formation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by destruction is possible even for the two kinds of consciousness. In the phrase "of those two as well," the locative case [is used] with the words "of consciousness" and "of the two kinds"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. The word *tat* refers to the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of knowledge, desire, and so forth; and if it must necessarily be stated that the depositing of its own latent impression occurs only through a modification whose object is itself, then even in that case—

There is no logical inconsistency, because it is possible for latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) to be deposited in the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth by means of the veils of ignorance (*avidyāvṛti*), which have as their object the ego-sense and its attributes. Nor should it be argued that if one accepts a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is another modification, the aforementioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would follow;
for the veils of ignorance are not amenable to direct experience, and thus there is no need for knowledge regarding them.

Alternatively, at the time of experiencing knowledge, desire, and so forth, no other modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) arises for the sake of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Nor should it be argued that there is unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the production of a latent impression for modifications of ignorance that have not been previously established; for it has already been established that such modifications produce that [latent] knowledge during deep sleep. With this intention, he states another view: "But others say... (*anye tu*).

The sentence should be construed as follows: "Having accepted an ignorance-modification (*avidyā-vṛtti*) in the form of 'I'—which, though imagined during deep sleep, has as its object ignorance and the like, just like other modifications such as ignorance—in order to establish the continuity (*anusaṃdhāna*) of ignorance and so forth for one who has arisen from sleep.
This is because, according to the literal sense [of the opponent's view], the continuity of ignorance and the like that occurs upon waking must be established [as having existed] during deep sleep.

It would be an error. One should understand that it would be an error [to claim] that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the "I-form" belongs to the very same imagined veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvṛti*) due to its proximity;
this is because the phrase "ignorance and so forth" (*avidyādi*) is intended to include both pleasure and deep sleep, as in "I slept happily."

Because we observe the subsequent recollection— after waking up— of the pleasure, deep sleep, ignorance, and so forth existing at the time of deep sleep, expressed as "I slept and knew nothing," it is not necessary to postulate a limitation in the form of a veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) for the experience of ignorance and other factors during that time, since such experience exists in the form of the eternal witness (*sākṣin*).
Because, due to the impossibility of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it would follow that there is no subsequent recollection (*anusandhāna*) as previously described.

If it is objected: "But if one accepts a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) whose objects are nescience (*ajñāna*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth, then the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that these are known solely by the witness-consciousness (*kevalasākṣivedyatva*) would be contradicted," we reply: No, because the modifications of ignorance do not require the causes of knowledge already postulated [for ordinary cognition].

The meaning is that because it lacks the nature of being produced, it lacks the status of existing as a modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of knowledge; for it is accepted that the term "pure witness" (*kevala-sākṣin*) refers exclusively to the witness itself when it is not conditioned by a modification consisting of knowledge. The mention of the "referent of 'I'" (*ahamartha*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its attributes, since the same logic applies and there is no subverting evidence to the contrary.
It should be understood that this is because even regarding those phenomena, the formation [of karma] is established by means of the veil of ignorance.
And on this view, there is no impossibility of the synthesis of the referent "I" occurring during the flow of other cognitions— such as "for all this time, I was indeed seeing this"— because,
due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*), two states can coexist just as pleasure and pain do simultaneously.

Others, however, maintain that the manifestation in the form of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) is indeed a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), but unlike other modifications such as meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth, it is not incompatible with [other cognitions] even during the time of a continuous stream of other cognitions; thus,
a continuity of this "I"-manifestation is possible.

Knowledge is established as being produced by that [cause], because it is something that is produced. For in that case, the definition of perception—such as the eye and so forth—is not possible; nor is there any [need for] a mark (*liṅga*) and so on, since we observe the persistence of the notion of "I" even in one who is devoid of the recollection of marks and the like. Nor, moreover...
The mind is not the instrument for that [recognition], because it is never postulated as an instrument for anything that serves as its material cause (*upādāna*).

If it is argued that, in that case, the recognition of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) would also not be a cognition, we say no; for although the "I"-portion lacks the nature of cognition, the "that"-portion possesses it by virtue of being the instrument of memory.

They say that because it is produced by a constructed mental impression (*saṃskāra*), it is non-cognition (*ajñāna*); for there is no contradiction between being cognition and being non-cognition, just as there is no contradiction between being mediated (*parokṣa*) and being immediate (*aparokṣa*) within a single cognition according to its different aspects, nor between being valid (*pramā*) and being invalid (*apramā*).

Now, in this view, since an ignorance-modification (*avidyāvṛtti*) having the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) and so forth as its object cannot occur during the time of a continuous stream of non-discriminative knowledge (*anyajñānadhārā*), the depositing of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) would be impossible; for if an ignorance-modification were admitted at the time of that stream, it would entail the occurrence of two simultaneous modifications.
He refutes the doubt by means of an illustration, stating: "And not in this case...

This refers to the position that impressions (*saṃskāra*) are deposited by the veils of ignorance (*avidyāvṛti*). The phrase "by means of a difference in delimiters" (*avacchedakabheda*) means that we observe such experiences as "there is pain in my head" or "there is pleasure in my foot. [The phrase] "two veils" (*vṛtidvaya*)...

The meaning is that even at the time of the flow of one cognition, another mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) having another object as its domain, and a modification of nescience (*avidyāvṛtti*) having the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) as its domain, do not contradict each other within the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) due to the difference in their limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*).
Regarding the word "stream" (*saṃtāna*): [the objection] "But surely, another... [is raised].

If it is argued that at the time of the stream of knowledge (jñānadhārā), it can be said that there is only a single veil of ignorance (avidyāvṛtti)— because there is no evidence for its multiplicity and because of parsimony (lāghava)— this is true; nevertheless, since the stream [of knowledge] consists of a succession of modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), it is possible that the veil of ignorance existing at that time also takes the form of a succession.
It was stated thus merely for the sake of formal consistency; therefore, he says: "because of the possibility within the continuum" (*saṃtānasaṃbhavāt*).
Regarding the aspect of the "I-sense," the depositing of impressions (*saṃskāra*) is possible through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone.
Thus, even in that aspect, a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) need not be postulated, because when the mental modification is possible, it is illogical to postulate another. Not so.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that at the time of the flow of another cognition, a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) having the sense of "I" (*ahamartha*) as its object cannot occur, because two cognitions cannot coexist simultaneously—just as pleasure and pain cannot coexist. This is because, according to his view, he does not admit that the "I"-modification exists for the sake of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) and is of the nature of a cognition. He states this view with the words: "But others... (*apare tu*).

In that case, this mental modification (*vṛtti*), like a jar or other objects, would also be of the nature of cognition; and consequently, because it would follow that the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) as qualified by a cognitive modification, the established doctrine—that the "I-sense" is manifested solely by the witness—would be abandoned. With this intention, he raises an objection with the words "But [what about]... He refutes it with the words "In meditation, etc. [and] "desire, etc."

The first word [of the verse] is for the purpose of inclusion. "In some instance" refers to the connection with experience; that is to say, it means that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the modification (*vṛtti*) of knowledge, cannot be postulated as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for any modification other than the modification in the form of "I" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*). "Then" [refers to]: "I who, in a dream..."

The meaning is that if there were no knowledge regarding the "I-component" (*ahamarthāṃśa*) in the recognition— "I, who directly experienced the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa, now remember him"— then such recognition would not exist, because it is produced by the causes of knowledge. [The opponent] rejects this with the phrase "No," [arguing that] recognition exists even in its entirety.

It might be argued that cognition could not exist in a single act of recognition, because it is impossible for the nature of cognition and its absence to coexist due to their mutual contradiction; therefore, he says: "of that. This means "of the recognition.
Regarding the phrase "by way of a distinction of parts": here, a "part" refers to a portion of the object, and this has already been demonstrated previously.

Regarding the phrases "the aspect of 'I'" (*ahamaṃśa*) and "that aspect" (*tadaṃśa*): concerning the phrase "in its being indirect" (*parokṣatve*), in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is accepted that in the inference "the mountain possesses fire," the aspect of fire is indirect (*parokṣa*), whereas the aspect of the proximate mountain is direct (*aparokṣa*). He states an example agreed upon by both schools: "But as for validity... (*pramātva tu*).
But others [hold] that even the mental state (*vṛtti*) in the form of "I" is indeed cognition, because of the experience: "I know myself.

Nor is there an impossibility of an instrument (*karaṇa*), for in accordance with such experience, one may postulate that the internal sense-organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), namely the mind (*manas*), is indeed the instrument; thus he says. This being so:

The rule is thus established: that only those mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which are immediate (*aparokṣa*) regarding external objects have the power to overcome the veil (*āvaraṇa*). But is this not even a rule? For in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the modification in the form of "this" (*idamākāra-vṛtti*) does not overcome ignorance (*ajñāna*); otherwise, in the absence of a material cause (*upādāna*), [the appearance of silver] would not occur.

If it is argued that this is because silver cannot arise [from the substrate], they reply here: even when the ignorance regarding the "this" portion is removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of "this,"...

One must accept that even the "I-means" (ahamartha) portion of the recognition (pratyabhijñā) previously demonstrated possesses the nature of knowledge; otherwise, the proof of the permanence of the individual soul (jīva)— which is the "I-means" consisting of consciousness conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)— as seen in the Sūtras and the Bhāṣya, could not be established through the authority of that recognition.
And thus it would contradict both the Sūtra and the Anusmṛti. "Anusmṛti" means recognition; and accordingly, the Bhāṣya on that Sūtra states:
"He who saw yesterday is the very same 'I' who remembers today. And likewise:

He states the view of those who consider it incorrect to assert that there is an absence of "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) in the "I"-portion (*ahamaṃśa*) of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), beginning with the words "But others... (*itare tu*). The phrase "from experience" (*anubhavāt*) means: because cognition-ness is experienced in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which has the referent "I" as its object. The phrase "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*) refers to the *Bhāṣya* on [the Sūtra] *viyadādi*, which concerns the intellect (*buddhi*).
"Because [the self] is admitted to be the cause. For this very reason, although qualities of the *ahaṃkāra* such as knowledge (*jñāna*),

pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth are manifested solely by the witness (*sākṣin*), the "I-object" (*ahamartha*)— which is the unique object of the mind (*manas*) and consists of the *satva* element— is established as a sense-organ (*indriya*) in the *Prāṇapāda*.
It should be understood that this has been established by the commentators themselves, beginning with the author of the *Bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the object being manifest solely to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsyatva*) pertains exclusively to objects such as ignorance (*ajñāna*), pleasure (*sukha*), and so forth, which are distinct from the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*). Now, [if one asks] regarding the mind...

If it is argued that, in the view that [the self] is of the nature of an indriya (sense organ), its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*)—just as the eye and other organs are toward form and so forth—must be asserted;

and that this is not possible because the "I-sense," being superimposed upon the unobstructed witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), lacks the state of being unknown, and thus the mind lacks the capacity to make known what was previously unknown, we say: no, because of that mental modification (*tadvṛtti*).
The meaning is as follows: validity (*pramātva*) consists in either being an experience of that specific mode or being an uncontradicted experience.

Thus, according to this view, since it is possible for a cognition having the form of "I" (*ahamākāra*) to possess validity, its cause—the mind (*manas*)—can also be considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the eyes and other senses. [Objection: But in that case...

Fearing that the rule regarding the subduing of veils by cognitions (*vṛtti*) directed toward objects beyond the senses might be contradicted in the case of a cognition of the "I-form" (*aham-ākāra*) which is immediate (*aparokṣa*), he demonstrates a restriction of that rule [with the words] "this being so.
This means: when the admission of a cognition of the "I-form" as immediate is accepted.

He raises an objection even to the stated rule with the words "Now, [is it not the case]...": "This is silver. In a case of error, first there arises a direct cognitive state (*aparokṣa-vṛtti*) in the form of "this" (*idam*); subsequently, the error "this is silver" occurs.
In that situation, does the first-arisen cognitive state in the form of "this" lack the capacity to remove ignorance (*ajñāna*), or does it possess it?

Regarding the first [proposition], he states the deviation from the rule: "This too is not [the case]," meaning that there is no such rule as "only a mediate (parokṣa) mental modification (vṛtti) removes ignorance," because there is a deviation in the case of a mental modification in the form of effort (alam). Likewise, there is no such rule as "only a non-mediately perceived (aparokṣa) mental modification directed toward external objects removes ignorance."

There is no restrictive rule either; the meaning is that this is because there is a deviation in the case of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form "this" (*idam*). Regarding the second [alternative], he states the subverting argument: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: if the mental modification having the form "this" were not capable of suppressing ignorance (*ajñāna*).

In that case, the ignorance to be removed by the mental modification having the form "this" would be one thing, and the ignorance that serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver would be another. And thus...
"There is no deviation, nor is there any impossibility of the production of silver"—thus he resolves [the objection] with the words "here they say."
Because the ignorance regarding specific features such as "being mother-of-pearl" has not been removed, that very [ignorance] is the material cause of the silver;
for it is experienced that the superimposition of silver occurs when there is ignorance of "being mother-of-pearl," and its absence occurs when that ignorance is gone.

For it is stated in the *Vivaraṇa* commentary on the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya* that ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is established through both positive and negative concomitance, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and the like; for this very reason,
the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) is the substrate (*ādhāra*), while the "shell-portion" (*śuktyaṃśa*) is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the object of playful ignorance; it is the substratum that, though not possessing that form, appears in the intellect as being superimposed with that form—this is the analysis in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*.
Others, however, [hold that] it is the substrate of that which is perceived as merged with the "this" portion in the cognition "this is silver."
The very ignorance regarding the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) of the silver is its material cause (upādāna);

and since that ignorance persists along with its power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti), even though its power of concealment (āvaraṇa-śakti) alone has been removed by the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of "this," there is no impossibility of its being the material cause.
He states the proof for the claim that the very ignorance which obscures specific features such as "being mother-of-pearl" (*śuktitva*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the silver:

"The ignorance of being mother-of-pearl, etc. The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to qualities such as having a blue back. "Only silver is superimposed" means that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*). The first instance of the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the specific feature, while the second...

That word refers to superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Regarding this, he provides the consensus [of the commentators] with the words "superimposition," etc.; the *Pañcapādikā* commentary explains the compound as having the analysis:

"that which possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) being experienced. Now, [one might object]: it is only when the substance present before one is known as qualified by its specific form, such as "mother-of-pearl-ness" (*śuktitva*), that [the absence of that knowledge acts as] the cause of error.

If it were admitted that [the substrate] is concealed, then that [concealed substrate] alone would be the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*). However, this is not the case, because the locus is precisely this "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) as qualified by its own form, which is the object of the ignorance that is its manifestation.
And thus, according to the rule that the locus and the superimposed object must be objects of a single cognition, [it is established that] "this is silver."

It would have the form of an error. If it were not so, it would not have the form of the cognition "this is silver," because the "this" (idam) portion would lack the status of being the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). To this he says: "For this very reason. The meaning is:

precisely because it is the object of the ignorance that serves as the material cause (upādāna) of the superimposition. [He adds: "the 'shell' portion"; that is, the nature of being a shell (śuktitva).
The meaning is that, in its specific form, it is consciousness delimited by that which stands before one.
With the intention of showing that the absence of the "this" (idam-aṃśa) being the substratum is desired, he says: "the 'this' part.
Now, if it were its locus, then its status as the substratum would necessarily follow, because there is no difference between the two.
"No," he says, "that [is] *vilāsa*. *Vilāsa* is the projection (*vikṣepa*) of silver and so forth; it is the state of being an object and the state of being concealed.

Regarding the phrase "though not having that nature": the word "that" refers to the superimposed silver and so forth; thus, the meaning is that although [the substrate] is devoid of identity with the superimposed silver and so forth, it nevertheless manifests as non-different from it. This is because the superimposed [silver] belongs to the substrate itself.
In this view, it should be understood that although the "this" (idam) portion [of the object] is in reality not of that nature, it appears so due to its identity with silver.

In this theory, there is no single cognition whose object is both the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the superimposed (*āropya*); rather, it is only the locus (*ādhāra*) and the superimposed that share that status.

Thus, the implication is that there is no contingency of the erroneous cognition (*bhrama*) referring to the "portion of the mother-of-pearl" (*śuktyaṃśa*). Now, [an objection]: if the substrate and the superimposed [are related] in the superimposition...

Since the possibility of luminosity (*prakāśamānatva*) has been established in the *Bhāṣya*, the *Ṭīkā*, the *Vivaraṇa*, and so forth, one might fear that [the following view] contradicts them; therefore, he states another opinion that is not in contradiction with those: "But others...
The term "intermingledness" (*saṃbhinna-tva*) means identity (*tādātmya*). "Ignorance alone" means—and not...

The meaning of the particle *eva* is "ignorance of the specific aspect. The intended sense is that since the specific aspect cannot serve as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) because it does not manifest during superimposition (*āropa*), [the substrate must be the ignorance of it]. Since the perception of the specific feature, such as "shell-ness," acts as an obstacle to superimposition, the previously mentioned positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has as its object the absence of that [perception].

The sense is that there is a distinction [between the two]. Now, one might object: since the ignorance regarding the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*) has been removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this," how can the "this" portion serve as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)? To this, he says: "And of that... This means: of the ignorance regarding the "this" portion.
In the case of the superimposition of a tree's downward reflection in water,

and in the case of the superimposition of the phenomenal world that persists even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), although the obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is removed immediately after the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the substrate as the Self of all, it remains accompanied by the momentum of the tendency toward projection (*vikṣepaśakti*).

They say this because the cognition of silver is accepted as the material cause [of the illusory object]. However, Kavi-Tārkika-Cakravartin Nṛsiṃhabhaṭṭopādhyāya maintains that there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" prior to the production of the silver, since the silver arises apart from the erroneous mental state in the form of "this is silver. Therefore, of that [silver]...
They consider the investigation into the existence of that which removes ignorance to be without foundation; for,
apart from the two-fold modification in the form of error, no modification in the form of "this" (idam-ākāra) is established by experience,
since there is no occurrence of a duality of cognitions.

Nor is the knowledge of the generality of the substratum the cause of superimposition, because there is no evidence for its being the cause of that [superimposition] when it is to be inferred from the effect.

[Objection: But surely, nowhere has it been observed that there is a cessation of only the portion of knowledge that constitutes an obscuration, while its power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) continues to persist. To this, he says: "Reflected in water," and "the world-appearance" (*prapañca*). The sense is that even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), there is the continued perception of the world-appearance consisting of the internal organ and so forth. [He says] "in its entirety": for in cases such as the error of silver, etc.,...

There is no direct realization of the substrate in its entirety as its own nature, because there is an absence of direct realization of the mother-of-pearl in its specific form as "mother-of-pearl-ness" and so forth; therefore, even though the ignorance regarding the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) has been removed there,
since the ignorance regarding the "specific-aspect" (viśeṣāṃśa) has not been removed, there is no possibility of the non-arising of superimposition upon that substrate.

However, regarding the delusion of a reflection in water, the tree does not exist [there at all]; since there is a perception of its specific qualities in every respect— such as "this tree indeed has its top upwards"— the ignorance concerning the general aspect is removed,
while the ignorance concerning the specific aspect remains unremoved.
Since it is impossible to distinguish [the parts], it cannot be said that knowledge is the material cause (upādāna) of the specific [manifestation];

therefore, in this case, even when the portion of concealment of a single ignorance is removed in accordance with the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the downward-pointing nature of the tree and so forth—

In the same way, it must be stated that even in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), although the veil [of ignorance] has been removed through the direct realization of the reality of Brahman, there remains a persistence of that portion of ignorance which possesses the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti). Thus it is.
The point is that even in the case of the superimposition of silver, it is possible for the nescience (ajñāna) regarding the "this" (idamaṃśa) portion to serve as the material cause (upādānatva).

Thus, there is also the suspicion of an exception to the rule— that all immediate (aparokṣa) mental modifications (vṛtti) directed toward external objects necessarily dispel the veil (āvaraṇa)— in the case of the mental modification in the form of "this" occurring at the locus of error.

Having refuted [the objection] by demonstrating that there is no absence of either the removal of ignorance regarding the "this" portion (*idamaṃśa*) or the removal of the mere veil over the "this" portion, [the author now states: first of all, in the case of an error, even the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of "this" does not exist; therefore, there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and the resolution thereof is far from being necessary.

He says "refuted" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by the poet-logician," he says "an erroneous mental modification. In the two previous views, because there exists a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this," the cognition of shell-silver and the like is understood to be of the nature of consciousness manifested by that [modification], and not of the nature of the modification itself.
However, in this view, since that [prior modification] is absent, it should be understood that such cognition is indeed of the nature of a mental modification.

This will become clear later. With the words "tathā hi" and so forth, he refutes this [position] that consists of a modification (*vṛtti*) possessing a form (*ākāra*), which is of the nature of knowledge of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*). He asks: is that [modification] established by experience, or is it to be postulated as an effect, or is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) to be postulated? Regarding the first [option], he says: "Not at all," [meaning] "not insofar as there is a duality of cognitions. [The phrase] "this" refers to one cognition.
The meaning is that [the opponent claims] "inferior knowledge" arises from direct experience. He refutes the second [alternative] with the words, "Nor by means of the substrate.
An effect in the form of superimposition, being untenable without a general cognition whose object is the substrate—the cause of that [superimposition]—leads to the postulation of such a cognition.
Furthermore, one should not think that the veil in the form of the appearance "this" is established as being of the nature of a cognition of the substrate's general features;
for the meaning is that there is no evidence for the cognition of the substrate's general features being the cause of superimposition.
Furthermore, the non-arising of silver and so forth in the absence of contact with a substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not the proof [for your position];

for it follows that the cause of superimposition is simply the contact with a defective sense organ. Nor is it the case that contact does not pervade all errors, since the manifestation of the substrate occurs spontaneously.

It must be stated that [this ignorance] also pervades the superimposition of the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth upon the self-luminous inner self (pratyagātman), because that [ignorance] likewise does not pervade the superimposition of jars and other objects; for prior to the perception of a jar or the like, it has as its object only Brahman, which is formless and serves as the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna).

Because a visual function is impossible [in that case], and because the manifestation of its own nature is veiled; for if the mere manifestation of the substrate were the cause of superimposition by virtue of being common to both the veiled and the unveiled states,
then even prior to the contact with the "this" portion of the mother-of-pearl, that [substrate] delimited by it...

[The opponent] objects that [the existence of] the unmanifested light of the nature of consciousness is established even then, because superimposition would consequently follow. He raises the doubt that there is a lack of evidence [for this], saying "But not... It is established by experience that the superimposition of the form of silver and so forth occurs only when there is contact between the eye and the object "this," and not otherwise; thus, the stated positive concomitance (anvaya) is established.

Through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the cognition of the commonality of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānyajñāna*) is the cause for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and so forth. Nor does the aforementioned positive concomitance and so on establish that non-contact (*asaṃprayoga*) alone is the cause of superimposition.

It should be stated as "of the knowledge of the substratum" (*dharmijñāna*). If that were the case, since there would be no possibility of sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*) in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would result;
therefore, by means of those very positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which establish that sensory contact is the cause of superimposition—
In cases such as the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl, it is postulated that the cognition of the substratum itself—brought about by sensory contact—is the cause;

thus, the stated positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) serve as proof for the fact that the general cognition of the locus is the cause of superimposition. This is the hidden intention (gūḍhābhisaṃdhi).
He criticizes [the position] without understanding the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*). "From that" means from what has been stated, namely from the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.

It is said "is not seen" because mere contact (*saṃprayoga*) is common to both valid cognition and error. The proponent of the view that the substratum (*dharmin*) is the cause of knowledge reveals his own intention with the words: "And not the contact," [referring to] the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
He states that there is no deviation [of the cause] from general cognition, just as there is none from sensory contact:
"But the manifestation of the substrate... The word "but" (tu) is intended to distinguish it from sensory contact.

The meaning is that the manifestation of the substrate, acting as the agent, pervades not only the superimposition of mother-of-pearl as silver and the like, but also the superimposition of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth.

The meaning of "from itself" (*svataḥ*) is as follows: because external consciousness is veiled, the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) therein is produced by a mental modification (*vṛtti*); however, because the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*) is unveiled, it is established by itself (*svatas-siddha*) in the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, as well as in the superimposition of the dream-world and so forth. He also states an exception even regarding the general knowledge of the substrate.

Regarding the phrase "of that too": the meaning of the word "that" refers to the aforementioned cognition; the sense is that it lacks pervasion over the superimposition of jars and so forth. Thus, the underlying point is that the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*) is not the cause of superimposition. He demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) indicated by the term "non-pervasion" with the words beginning "jars and so forth."

In the case of the superimposition of a jar and so forth, is there an illumination of the substrate produced by a mental mode (*vṛtti*), as in the case of the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl, or is it self-established, as in the case of the superimposition of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth? It is not the first; thus he says:
"from the perception of the jar and so forth. The word "that" refers to the jar and so forth. It is not the second; thus he says: "by its own nature."

Is it not the case that the mere manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and not the manifestation of a substrate that is already [previously] revealed? Thus, in superimpositions such as "the pot exists" or "the cloth exists," the substrate—
the pot and so forth— is of the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*).

Anticipating the objection that because Brahman is self-luminous, the mere manifestation of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) exists even there, and thus there is no deviation [of the definition], he says: "Whether veiled or unveiled. Regarding the phrase "even then":
the meaning is "even at the time prior to the contact [with the sense organ]."
In the case of superimposition in general, the manifestation of the locus in general is the cause.

In the case of illusory superimposition, it is the manifestation of the manifested locus; thus, there is no over-extension, as the general serves as the cause for the general, and the particular for the particular.

It should be stated that [this applies] starting from the city; for even so, because there is no sublation of illusory superimpositions such as the yellowness of a conch-shell, the water in a well, or the smallness [of objects], visual cognition does not occur without being conditioned by color (rūpa).

Because at that time, due to the absence of the perception of whiteness residing in the conch and so forth, and because prior to superimposition there is no possibility of a mental modification (vṛtti) having as its object the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), which is the colorless conch and so forth.

The proponent of the view that the substrate-knowledge (*dharmijñāna*) is the cause [of superimposition] raises an objection: "And superimposition is not [possible] in the case of a universal. [The author replies: "In the case of illusory (*prātibhāsika*) [superimpositions]. The manifestation of the substrate is intended by the Teachers as the cause only in the case of illusory superimpositions; it is [the cause] in those cases alone.

The meaning is that since it has been established in works such as the *Adhyāsabhāṣya-ṭīkā-vivaraṇa* that superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is produced by three causes— defect (*doṣa*), contact (*saṃprayoga*), and the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)— the status of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as a cause is established within those very [three], being obtained through the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends contact as a cause.

The word "cause" (*hetu*) is to be supplied immediately after the word "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), so as to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The meaning is that there is no possibility of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and the like prior to their contact [with the senses]. Since the superimposition of silver and the like is of a phenomenal nature (*prātibhāsika*), for its substrate to be directly perceived—

The meaning is that [the cause] must depend on an operation contingent upon conjunction (*saṃprayoga*); this is because of propriety (*aucitya*). And thus, if the cognition of the substratum (*dharmin*) were the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), there would be no sublation, since there exists proof—such as positive concomitance—that establishes conjunction as the cause.
The sense is that once its status as the cause of superimposition is established, the concealment of the "this" (idam) aspect is thereby established.

[The opponent objects: "Even in the case of all illusory superimpositions (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*), there is no universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the manifestation of the substrate and the light [of consciousness]. [The author replies: What does this poetic fancy follow? It refutes [the position] by saying, "even so."
The meaning is: even if it is accepted that the immediate perception of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the sole cause for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the phenomenal appearance;

nevertheless, first there arises a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" with respect to the substrate (*dharmin*), and by that modification, [the consciousness] delimited by the conch, water, and so forth, is manifested within the consciousness.

The process is that there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of blue color and so forth; and thus, in that case, does this mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form "this" take as its object merely the substance such as a conch-shell, or the substance qualified by color? It is not the first [option], as he says: "not unqualified by color. A visual modification whose object is a substance unqualified by color is not possible.

The point is that otherwise, even speech and other such things would result in being objects of visual perception. Regarding the second [alternative] as well, does it take as its object a substance qualified by a white color, or one qualified by a superimposed color? It cannot be the second, because a cognition whose very nature consists in residing in a conch-shell or similar object qualified by a superimposed color is, by definition, an error.

Because there is an absence of the cognition of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*). He says "not the first" [referring to the initial alternative], meaning "at that time. The sense is: at the time prior to superimposition (*adhyāsa*). The underlying idea is that if whiteness were perceived at that time, it would follow that superimposition is absent.
Regarding the phrase "due to impossibility": thus, there is no manifestation of the substrate's luminosity.
The point is that, because it is impossible [for the cognition of the substrate to exist] otherwise, the cognition of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*) cannot be the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

Now, one might object: "Even prior to superimposition, a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) directed toward the conch-shell and so forth necessarily arises in the form of a mere substance; for there is a rule that a visual modification directed toward a substance must have color (*rūpa*) as its object."
And because [the conjunction] is the instrumental cause (*prayojaka*), there is no such consequence that air (*vāyu*) and so forth would also be visible; for in the perception of a substance,

the manifested color residing in the substance (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the determinant, and since the substance is apprehended prior to the superimposition, it is possible— even under the influence of a defect— that only the white color, though in close proximity, is not apprehended, just as the "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*) is not apprehended.
This has been stated in the Bhāmatī:

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of illusory appearances, let the aforementioned specific cause suffice for the mere superimposition of silver; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (aprasaṅga) of the superimposition of a yellow conch and the like occurring even before sensory contact, whereas in the case of such a superimposition, contact with a defective sense organ [is required].

Since it must necessarily be stated that there is a cause, and since simplicity (lāghava) establishes its causality in general for all illusory superimpositions (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*), the occasional nature of the superimposition of silver is also accounted for by that very [cause], namely, the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because the status of being a cause of superimposition is unestablished, whether in a general or specific sense.

And regarding the conch, whose whiteness is obscured by a defect, one grasps it as having the nature of a mere substance; the meaning is that "whiteness" refers to the quality of white color. Or, even if there were a perception of the conch and so forth as qualified by the quality of white color, there would still be no impossibility of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because [the error] arises through the power of the defect (*doṣa*) acting upon the color.

Since that [superimposition] is possible even by means of the mere apprehension of the genus "whiteness" (śuklatva), and since there is no deviation in the case of illusory superimpositions (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*) regarding the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it is established that the modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" (*idam-ākāra*) consists in the knowledge of the locus (*dharmin*).

If it is argued that once that [knowledge] is established, the teachers' investigation into whether or not it possesses the capacity to remove obstructions is indeed supported by a basis and is not baseless— this is true; however, this very lack of satisfaction (asvarasa) in this view is indicated by the statement, "the Upādhyāyas think otherwise."

In cases such as the illusion of a yellow conch, although there is in reality no deviation (vyabhicāra), the proponent of the view that the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is a necessary cause [of error] raises an objection, assuming such deviation for the sake of argument: "And not even in the case of those which are merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*)," etc.

The term "defined" (*nirukta*) means the manifestation of a manifest substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "That being so" (*tathā sati*)... [means:]... [refers to the following:]... [the rest of the sentence follows].

The meaning is that, in cases of superimpositions such as a yellow conch, one does not admit that the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause. If, like the immediacy of the substrate,

sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*) were also not admitted as a cause for superimpositions such as a yellow conch, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the superimposition of a yellow conch occurring even before sensory contact.
Therefore, the meaning is that in order to avoid that [objection], the causality of "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*) must necessarily be asserted in that context.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of that very [conjunction]" (*tasyaiva*). This means: of the conjunction with a defective sense-organ (*duṣṭendriya-saṃprayoga*) alone. Having stated "in general" (*sāmānyataḥ*), he demonstrates what that generality is: "In the case of mere illusory superimposition" (*prātibhāsikādhyāsamātre*).

The meaning is that, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is precisely the nature of being an illusory superimposition (*prātibhāsikādhyāsatva*) that serves as the delimiting condition for the effect of contact with a defective sense organ, and not the nature of being a superimposition such as "yellow conch," because of its complexity (*gaurava*). He asks what follows from that, and replies:

"From that very [contact]" (*tata eva*). Regarding the contact: in order to avoid the previously mentioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the superimposition of a yellow conch and so forth, in that case—
The meaning is: "from the contact with a defective sense organ alone," as established in general.

Regarding the phrase "even of its occasional nature": in order to avoid the constant superimposition of silver and so forth, it must be stated that the manifestation of the light of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the cause of the superimposition of silver and so forth. This being the case, [the following applies].

For your intention, as one who maintains that the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*) is the cause [of superimposition], is that since the light of the substratum—which consists of consciousness delimited by the mother-of-pearl—is veiled, its manifestation does not occur at all times; thus, the contingency of the constant superimposition of silver and the like is avoided. And this avoidance of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)— [The opponent objects: But how can there be a veil (*āvaraṇa*) for that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*)? For it is a contradiction that something self-luminous should be veiled. Furthermore, even if it were veiled, since the substrate-consciousness (*adhiṣṭhānacaitanya*) is eternal, how could its manifestation ever be absent? If you say that the absence of manifestation is due to the non-manifestation of the objective aspect (*viṣayāṃśa*), then we reply: no, because the object is not distinct from the substrate-consciousness. If you say that the object is indeed distinct, then the substrate-consciousness would be manifold, and the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) would be abandoned. Moreover, if the substrate-consciousness were eternal, the superimposition of silver and the like would always occur. Therefore, your position is untenable. [The proponent replies: This is not so. Even though the substrate-consciousness is self-luminous, its manifestation is obstructed by the beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). Consequently, the superimposition of silver and the like occurs only when that obstruction is removed by the contact of the sense organs with the object. Thus, there is no over-extension. Furthermore, the manifestation of the substrate-consciousness is not eternal, because it is dependent upon the removal of the obstruction. Nor is the substrate-consciousness manifold, because the difference between the object and the substrate is merely apparent (*kalpita*). As for the objection regarding the constant occurrence of superimposition, that too is resolved by the fact that the removal of the obstruction depends upon specific conditions such as the functioning of the senses. Therefore, your view is consistent.
The meaning is that in cases such as the superimposition of a yellow conch, [the error] is obtained from the very sense-contact (*saṃprayoga*) already established. Regarding the phrase "in general":

the mere manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-prakāśa-mātra*) is the cause for any superimposition whatsoever; however, the manifestation of the substrate must be fully evident (*abhivyakta-adhiṣṭhāna-prakāśa*).

"Because it is the sole cause of illusory superimposition (*prātibhāsikādhyāsa*). This means that even the two previously mentioned types of causal relationships cannot be established. [Objection: But surely, since simplicity (*lāghava*) establishes its causality in general for all illusory superimpositions, [it follows that it is the cause]. [Response: This is incorrect, because in the case of the superimposition of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth upon the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), [the witnessing consciousness itself is required as the substrate].
Furthermore, because there is no possibility of sensory contact in the superimposition of dreams, there is no deviation [from the rule]; nor does this apply to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth.

Now, even if similarity is not a cause for other types of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) that do not depend upon it, in the case of superimpositions such as silver that do depend upon it, there exists a cognition of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*)— which consists of the cognition of the general features of the object qualified by specific attributes such as color— that takes the form of the similarity of the silver and so forth.

A further cause must necessarily be stated; for if mere contact with a defective sense organ were the sole cause, it would follow that silver is superimposed upon a piece of coal just as it is upon a mother-of-pearl shell. Nor should it be argued that similarity is also a cause by way of being a defect in the object, since a delusion of similarity occurs even toward things that are dissimilar.
Because of the existence of superimposition upon reality; for instance, from afar, one perceives the mass of water in the ocean as being a blue rock.

It should be said that, according to the view that the practice [of meditation] is empirical (*vyāvahārika*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*) therein is not a defect; nevertheless, even so, since it is impossible to avoid the defect according to the view that it is illusory (*prātibhāsika*), [the defect remains] in the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) regarding the superimposition of a dream, which is illusory.
This is because the deviation mentioned therein is established by common consensus and is firmly rooted.

Furthermore, in the case of the superimposition of a dream, the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as it is revealed is not the cause; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the dream-phenomenon would lack immediacy (*aparokṣya*). However, in the case of external illusory superimpositions...
It should not be argued that the contact with a defective sense organ (*duṣṭendriya-saṃprayoga*) is the cause [of error] and thus there is no deviation [in the causal rule];

for, by the parsimony (*lāghava*) you have stated regarding mere illusory superimposition (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*), it is more appropriate that the manifestation of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-prakāśa*) is the cause. In the case of external superimpositions, the contact [with the object] is the substrate...

If it is argued that [the reflection of consciousness is possible] because the capacity for such reflection exists through the production of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that manifests consciousness, and because it has been shown that even in cases such as the repeated perception of a yellow conch, a modification manifesting the consciousness of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is possible— this is true; when examined with subtle vision, it is exactly so.
However, it should be understood that from a gross perspective, the cause for mere illusory superimposition (prātibhāsikādhyāsa) is stated to be the rapidity of the contact;
this is because prior to the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl and the like, the functioning of the "this" (idam) term is established through another means.

He raises an objection regarding the causality of the knowledge of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*). [The opponent asks: "But surely, by means of similarity..."—the phrase "another superimposition" refers to the superimposition of a yellow conch and so forth. The sense is that there is an absence of similarity between the conch and its yellow color, etc. The word *tat* (that) refers to similarity, [as in the case] of mother-of-pearl and the like with respect to silver and the like.

The meaning is: "a subject characterized by that specific form and so forth which constitutes similarity. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to such qualities as having a head, which are required for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a person upon a post and the like.
Regarding the phrase "of mere contact" (*saṃprayogamātrasya*), the meaning of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is "in the absence of dependence on similarity."

The meaning of the word "charcoal" (*kāpṛmiṅgāla*) is that which has been burnt by fire and possesses a blue appearance. Now, even though similarity is required, it is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) by its very existence as an objective reality (*svarūpa-sat*); for by that much alone, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is avoided, and it need not be known.

Considering that its cause is likewise not established as the cause of the cognition of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*), he raises an objection: "Nor is it similarity. If that [substrate] were the cause by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), there would be no superimposition (*adhyāsa*) due to the error of similarity;
for in cases of the error of similarity, that similarity [of the substrate] is absent. Therefore, it is the cognition of similarity [that is the cause].

The proponent of the theory that knowledge of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*) is a cause [of superimposition] offers a rebuttal, stating that one must state a cause for superimposition that is common to both error and valid cognition; thus, the existence of a substrate qualified by those [attributes] is established. He says, "Even in the case of dissimilar things," and provides an example therein: "the flood of the ocean's waters. Here, the word *pūra* means a current, [referring to] the water of the ocean.

In reality, because its nature is white, there is no actual similarity to a blue stone surface; therefore, the sense is that the attribution of being a blue stone surface arises from the delusion of perceived similarity.

Nor is it logical to argue that, according to the principle "it is not from those very causes," the causal complex for the cognition of similarity itself might be the cause of superimposition; for the causal complex of a cognition is never observed to be the cause of an object, and furthermore, the status of being a cognition of similarity is itself simpler [and thus more parsimonious]. Nor...

Just as there is no fixed rule that the superimposition of blueness occurs only upon water due to the proximity of the sky— even when the water is inherently pure, contained in a bright golden pitcher, and transparent—

nor is there a fixed rule that it occurs only on mother-of-pearl and not on coal and the like, simply because of the nature of the object itself; so too [is the case with the superimposition of silver].

It should be stated that [superimposition] depends upon the cognition of similarity; for even though there is no superimposition of the form of a lotus bud upon a piece of cloth by its own nature, one observes the superimposition of that very form upon it when it has been fashioned into that shape through cutting and other processes. Thus, the superimposition of that [form] is not [dependent on similarity].

This is because it is determined that [the superimposition] depends on the presence or absence of a cognition of similarity, rather than following from the intrinsic nature [of the object]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of that superimposition occurring there at other times as well. Now, even in the view that the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is the cause, the contact with a defective sense organ (*duṣṭendriyasaṃprayoga*) [is required] by virtue of being part of its causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

It must be said as follows: since it is necessary, the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the causality of a specific superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is precisely the state of being a causal complex for the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśyajñānasāmagrītvam*), and not the state of being a cognition of similarity (*sādṛśyajñānatvam*). Consequently, there is no establishment of the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*); with this intention, [the author] presents the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the superimposition of silver upon a coal.

He suspects that [the opponent] has forgotten [this], thinking: "And it is not from that alone. The meaning is: "Let that very cause be the cause of that; what is the use of an intermediate one?"—according to this maxim. He brings forward the objection of the proponent of the knowledge of the substratum (*dharmijñānavādin*): "By the causal complex of cognition" (*jñānasāmagryāḥ*), for when the property (*dharma*) is held to be the cause of cognition, there is the knowledge of the substratum.

The cause is held to be that which brings about the manifestation of an object such as silver; and thus, by the maxim "from that very cause," the causality attributed to the sensory contact— which constitutes the causal complex for the cognition of the substratum—
would apply only to the manifestation of the object such as silver, and that is not possible, just as [contact] is not the cause in the case of the cognition itself.
The meaning is that the causality of the production of an object [of cognition] has not been established anywhere [else]. "From that" means:

because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking the nature of the cognition of similarity itself as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of causality, rather than the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of similarity. And thus:

The meaning is that the knowledge of the substratum (dharmijñāna) is established. Thinking that the knowledge of the substratum is not established because the cognition of similarity, even if it lacks causality for a specific type of superimposition (adhyāsa), still allows for a systematic distinction (vyavasthā), he raises an objection again:
"Nor [is it] by itself," etc. [This refers to] the blueness of water and the pearl.

Even when similarity is equal [in both cases], the reason for the restriction—that the superimposition of blueness is observed only in water and not in a pearl—is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the object such as water, and nothing else; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the proximity of the blueness residing in a leaf is the regulating factor for that superimposition in water, rather than its nature? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase *śubhrakaladhauta*: it means "even when situated in a particular vessel made of stainless gold. Now, one might object: "Even so, just like the blue color appearing in water, this superimposition occurs here precisely because of contact with a substance"; to this he says "no," with the words *svataḥ śubhre'pi*. This qualifies the water; the word *svaccha* is the explanation of the term *svataḥ śubhra*.
Thus, having established that in some cases the very nature of the object itself (*svabhāva*) serves as the cause for superimposition (*adhyāsa*), he states the resulting conclusion:

"From the very nature of the thing" (*vastu-svabhāvāt eva*). This is just like the aforementioned superimposition of yellowness on a conch shell; even in the case of the superimposition of blueness on water contained in a golden vessel (*bhṛṅgāra*) and the like, there is no requirement for the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśya-jñāna*).

Because the requirement for the superimposition of a lotus bud is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the determination regarding the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl is likewise based solely on the presence or absence of the manifestation of similarity;
it does not depend on the intrinsic nature of the object, since resorting to the intrinsic nature of an object is a recourse taken only when no other way out exists. And thus:
Considering that the proof for the status of the substrate-cognition (*dharmijñāna*) as a cause is unimpeded, he refutes [the opponent] with the words "a piece of cloth from itself.
The meaning is: even in the absence of superimposition upon that state of the lotus (*puṇḍarīka*) being a water-lily (*utpala*).
In this very context—namely, in the case of the piece of cloth itself—that form which has been produced or brought about through cutting and so forth.
The meaning is: "that [piece of cloth] which has the form of a lotus bud"—that is, that [piece of cloth] which possesses the appearance of a lotus bud.
"Superimposing that" means superimposing the state of being a lotus bud.
The connection is: "because of the certainty that it conforms to that superimposition. "Otherwise" refers to the very nature of the thing itself.

The meaning is: "in its being the cause of superimposition upon that. "Even at other times" means even prior [to the actual superimposition], because its form is produced through cutting and so forth.

It is said: Even on the view that the cognition of similarity is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), its status as a cause must be asserted only in the case of superimpositions such as [the perception of] silver, which are obstructed by the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*);
it is not, however, so in the case of superimpositions such as a yellow conch, which are not so obstructed.
Because it is impossible [for doubt to arise], and because there is a rule that among those [cognitions] which are obstructed by the perception of a distinguishing feature (*viśeṣadarśana*),
the causal complex of the obstructing cognition (*pratibandhakajñānasāmagrī*) must necessarily be the obstructor,
it must be stated that the causal complex of the perception of a distinguishing feature is necessarily the obstructor. For this very reason...
Since all established conventions are thereby accounted for, what is the use of postulating similarity as the cause [of error]?

For instance, when the eye is in contact with charcoal and so forth, because the causal complex for perceiving specific features such as its blackness is present, there is no superimposition of silver.

Even in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, the visual organ does not come into contact with the entire object; since the object exists [in its entirety] during such contact, there is no superimposition of it [as a real shell].
However, when contact occurs only with a portion that resembles [the silver], because the object as a whole is absent, superimposition occurs.

Now, [the author] refutes the prima facie view— held by one following the position of certain Naiyāyikas— which maintains that although similarity may not be the cause for other types of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the knowledge of the substrate (*dharmin*) must necessarily be a cause, by way of establishing that the knowledge of similarity is the cause for a specific type of superimposition, as suggested by the passage beginning with "nanu sādṛśyanirapekṣe 'dhyāsāntare akāraṇatve'pi."

It is said, starting with "ucyate" and so forth. The phrase "not however" (*na tu*) means [not] in those cases which are not obstructed by the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*), such as the form: "This [conch] possesses the property of being a conch, which is pervaded by the absence of yellowness," or "This [water] possesses the property of being water, which is pervaded by the absence of blueness. Even when the aforementioned perception of specific features is present, [the erroneous cognition that] "the conch is yellow" or "this is blue... [persists].
The meaning is that [it is] water because of the perception of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).
Regarding "due to impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*): it means that, in reality, the object of sight cannot possibly exist there;
furthermore, it means that it does not conform to the cognition of similarity, just as one might have the delusion that a lotus is a bud. Therefore...

What is said in that regard? "And [in the case] of those things which are sublated by the perception of a specific quality. If the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) were the sublater, then upon stating that singularity is the sublater of burning, it would follow as a consequence that the sensory contact—which constitutes the causal complex for the knowledge of the substrate—is itself the sublater of superimposition. To avoid this, [the author says...]

The term "obstructing" (*pratibandhaka*) is an adjective qualifying "cognition. Since the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) is conducive to superimposition (*adhyāsa*), it would follow that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for obstructing [the production of a cognition] would itself be an obstruction to burning; to prevent this, the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) is included. This does not over-extend to gems and the like, because they lack the nature of being obstructing cognitions.
There is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because the absence of the knowledge of the obstruction-breaker is not part of the causal complex for knowledge;

thus, in that case, the cognition of the absence of the probandum in the subject (pakṣa) is a direct inhibitor of inference because it apprehends the absence of the object to be grasped (grāhya). In that regard:

The meaning is that it is well-established as a rule that the cognition of that which possesses the pervader of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavyāpyavatājñāna*) is an obstacle to inference because it constitutes the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the obstructing cognition. "From that very [fact]" means:
precisely because the causal complex of the obstructing cognition is accepted as being itself an obstruction. "Why? [is the question].
And thus, the point is that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this," which consists of the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*), is not established.

He avoids the previously mentioned undesirable consequence regarding the non-causality of the cognition of similarity by stating, "in the case of charcoal, etc. Here, the specific quality such as blueness residing in the charcoal is the object, and the causal complex for its perception is the eye.
It should be understood that because of its existence, there is no identity with the charcoal in conjunction [with it]. Regarding the phrase "the blue part, etc.": the word "etc.

is for the purpose of including the triangular part. Regarding the phrase "because of its existence": the meaning is "because of the existence of the causal complex for the perception of the specific feature. Regarding the phrase "not that": the word "that" refers to silver and so forth. Now, if at the time of contact with the mother-of-pearl...

If it is argued that in the absence of the superimposition of silver, even sensory contact would not be a cause of superimposition, he says "no": "only so far as there is a similar part. The meaning of "due to its absence" is:
due to the absence of the causal complex for perceiving blueness and so forth.

[Objection: Even then, because the causal complex for perceiving the specific feature of "mother-of-pearl-ness" (*śuktitva*) is present, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that no superimposition occurs. [Response: No; for you too must admit that at the time of superimposition there is an absence of the perception of "mother-of-pearl-ness," and therefore, prior to that, the causal complex for it is absent. This is my position.

If you argue that the non-recognition of the nacre-ness at that time is due to the acceptance of an absence of the causal complex for perceiving it—because of the obstruction caused by the defect consisting in the superimposition in the form of a cognition of similarity—then, in accepting that, you fall into the "dawn at the very threshing-floor" (ghaṭṭakuṭṭīprabhāta) maxim; [we reply: no, because immediately after approaching [the object],...

Even while the glittering appearance (cākacikya) in the form of a resemblance to silver is being perceived, the causal complex for that [appearance] is not established as an obstacle to the perception of the nature of mother-of-pearl (śuktitva), either because it is obstructed by defects such as distance and so forth.
He raises an objection with the words "even then" (*tadāpi*). This means: even at the time of contact with a mere similar portion.

Regarding the phrase "the consequence of non-superimposition" (*anadhyāsa-prasaṅga*): thus, in order to avoid the consequence of the absence of superimposition, the cognition of similarity must be accepted as a cause of superimposition by way of being a defect (*doṣa*). And from that, this aforementioned fault [remains].

The intention of those who maintain that the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*) is the cause [of superimposition] is this: because an obstructing factor is present, the causal complex for the unobstructed perception of "shell-ness" does not exist; therefore, the superimposition of silver is logically established.
To avoid the consequence of there being no superimposition at all, [the author] states an object agreed upon by both parties.

The proponent of the denial of the knowledge of the substratum (dharmijñāna) demonstrates this with the words "no," and so forth. "By you as well" means even by one who maintains that similarity is the cause of [recognition]. "Because it must be expressed" means that at the time of contact with only the similar portion, when the causal complex for perceiving the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*) is present...

It is true that, since superimposition is observed even when there is the relation of identity characterized by visual contact, one must necessarily postulate a defect as an obstacle to the causal complex for perceiving the specific feature of "shell-ness" (śuktitva) in accordance with that observation; however, that defect is not the cognition of similarity, but rather—

Therefore, since factors such as distance are themselves defects, the cognition of similarity cannot be the cause of superimposition (adhyāsa). Thus, the intention of even those who deny [the existence of] the substrate (dharmī) is that the cognition of the substrate is not established. The proponent of the cognition of the substrate, exposing their own underlying intention, raises an objection: "It is mine," "it is yours."
The meaning is: "of one who follows the views of the poet-logician (kavitārkika) and is intent on denying the cognition of the substratum (dharmin).

The sense is that even for you, who have gone far [from our position], the undesirable consequence would follow that the cognition of similarity (*sādṛśyajñāna*) is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). The proponent of the denial of the cognition of the substratum, revealing his own intention, says:
He dispels the objection regarding the consequence of non-superimposition with the words beginning with "tat" (that), etc.; "tasya" means of that perception of similarity.
"Tatsāmagrī" means the causal complex for the perception of the nature of mother-of-pearl.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) is used to include defects such as attachment to silver. [Objection: But even for a person standing at a distance...
Sometimes, even in the case of a mother-of-pearl shell, there is an equal deviation [of the cognition] due to the perception of it as a shell, despite its distance;

just as with the cognition of similarity, so too, in the case of silver, there is an equal deviation for one who has passion [for it] after approaching nearby upon seeing the shell. Thus, distance and the like are not defects either.

It might be so. And if, in some cases of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), a certain defect (*doṣa*) such as remoteness and the like is established as the cause of superimposition by virtue of its being a defect, then in the case of a flame and the like,
the error "this is that same lamp-flame" and so forth would [arise] through the defect consisting precisely in the cognition of similarity.

Since it is established by universal experience, its causality as a defect (doṣa) in certain cases, such as the superimposition (adhyāsa) of silver, is unavoidable; furthermore, the status of the cognition of similarity as a defect is approved by the Bhāṣya, as seen in the Devatādhikaraṇa Bhāṣya: "From similarity arises recognition."

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of hair and so forth": likewise, even in the Buddhist section (*bauddhādhikaraṇa*), it is stated that the synthesis [of cognitions] is based on similarity. If it is argued that this is incorrect—that since synthesis means recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and thus the cognition of similarity functions as a defect (*doṣa*) which is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the refutation [of such a view] is improper—this is true; nevertheless...
This should be meditated upon by relying on a coarse understanding.

The manifestation of the blue surface and so forth is due either to the non-occurrence of the perceiver or to the absence of its causal complex; likewise, the whiteness [of a conch] is not perceived because of the defect that causes the superimposition of a fixed blue color upon the ocean water,
and because of the non-occurrence of the perceiver of the waves and other factors that manifest blueness at a distance.
The superimposition of "stone-surface-ness" and so forth upon a mass of water occurs due to the absence of the causal complex for perceiving specific features such as solidity;

whereas, on a wide cloth, because the causal complex for perceiving specific features such as its expansive form exists, there is no superimposition of "white-lotus-bud-ness," but rather, when it has been fashioned into that shape through cutting and so forth, the absence of that [original] causal complex results in the superimposition of that [new] form.

He states the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagryabhāva*) due to the absence of its auxiliary factors (*sahakāryabhāva*). [The word] "manifesting" (*vyañjaka*) means "that which manifests the nature of mother-of-pearl.
