The term "perceiver" (*grāhaka*) refers to the contact of the eye with the blue portion [of the object]. [The phrase] "that causal complex" means that the absence of the causal complex for the perception of the specific feature of mother-of-pearl must be stated by both [parties].

He applies the principle stated regarding the error of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell to other cases as well. Thus, the defect consisting of the cognition of similarity, as well as the perception of specific features such as the mass of water being [actually] dry land, act as obstructions;
likewise, even the causal complex for perceiving white color and so forth serves as an obstruction there.

And the superimposition of the quality of being a blue stone-slab occurs there precisely because of the absence of the causal complex for obstructing cognition; it does not occur through the production of a knowledge of similarity based on the prior illusory attribution of blueness to the water.

The meaning is that, given the presence of those defects, there is a superimposition (adhyāsa) of the nature of a blue stone surface. Now, one might object: in the case of a flood of water from the ocean, the absence of the causal complex for perceiving the specific quality consisting of white color is unestablished; for at the time prior to the superimposition of the nature of a blue stone surface, the white color exists in the water conjoined with the eye.

By accepting identity (*tādātmya*), the visual contact consisting of identity with that which is conjoined with the eye exists, as does [the contact] with light and so forth; likewise, the absence of the causal complex for perceiving specific forms such as "being a mass of water" is also unestablished, because [factors such as] waves, which manifest "being a mass of water," are present.

Since perception also exists there, he says: "restricted" (*niyata*). The water of the ocean appears as blue due to superimposition even after one has approached it from nearby; therefore, its [superimposition] is restricted. This is what is meant: like the superimposition of silver upon that which is essentially white in form.

The meaning is that the superimposition of the nature of a blue stone surface and so forth is possible. For, when there is the superimposition of the nature of a blue stone surface upon water, the causal complex for the perception of the specific [white] color—which consists of the perception of the white color itself—is obstructed by the defect that serves as the cause for the superimposition of the form of the blue stone; therefore, that [causal complex] is not unobstructed.

Due to the defect of distance, there is no proximity with a manifesting wave or the like of the mass of water; consequently, both the causal complex for perceiving the specific form of the mass of water and the causal complex for the cognition of the two types of obstructions are absent. Thus, through the absence of these two types of obstructive causal complexes, there occurs the superimposition of qualities such as "being a surface of blue stone" upon the waters of the ocean.

Regarding the phrase "it occurs": here it should be understood that, although the absence of the causal complex for perceiving the specific difference (as described above) is required when superimposing the nature of a blue stone surface upon the flood of water in the ocean, the superimposition does not arise from that alone; rather, it occurs through the superimposition of the color blue upon the water.

Immediately following the perfection of the resemblance to the surface of a blue stone, there is the superimposition upon it; thus, just as there is a superimposition of the nature of a blue stone-surface at a distance, so too, after approaching the flood of the ocean's waters,
there is the practical usage [of the term "ocean"] based on the similarity of blueness and immobility in this flood of ocean water at a distance from me.

There was the delusion that it was a surface of blue stone; now, with that [delusion] ceased, it is understood as gold. Thus, in various instances, due to the defect of similarity (*sādṛśya*), my previous delusion was otherwise, and now it has ceased.
It is precisely this worldly convention that establishes the cognition of similarity as a defect in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*).

It should be understood that this establishes [the lotus] as a specific cause; furthermore, it modifies another example of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which grasps similarity as the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). "Extended" (*vistṛta*) means its circumference or width; the perception of that [width] is the obstacle to the superimposition of the state of being a lotus bud.
The meaning is: because that causal complex exists.

If it is argued: "In that case, why would there not be a superimposition of silver upon a piece of iron touched by the hand, since there is no requirement for the cognition of similarity [to silver] and because the causal complex for perceiving its specific blue color is absent?
[The reply is: It indeed occurs, but it is [the superimposition of] copper or the like.
Since there is also an absence of the causal complex for perceiving a distinguishing feature (*vyāvartaka-viśeṣa*), there must also be a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of that [feature];

thus, in some cases where multiple things are superimposed, it becomes an object of doubt. In other cases, such as when a sword-hilt (*kośagraha*) is mistaken for silver, there occurs only the superimposition of silver upon what is mostly non-silver.

In some cases, even when there is knowledge of similarity—as in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like—there may be no occurrence of superimposition due to the absence of defects in the instruments and so forth; and even in the absence of such superimposition, there is no deficiency.
Therefore, this modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" is not to be inferred from its effect, nor is the object "this" unperceived.
It is to be conceived as the cause of association.

According to the view that the cognition of similarity is the cause [of error], in the case of visual contact, the visual cognition of similarity is the cause for the production of the superimposition of silver and so forth, by virtue of being both a cognition of the substrate (dharmijñāna) and a defect;
and in the case of contact with the sense of touch, the tactile cognition of similarity is likewise [the cause] in the manner described.
In the view of certain poets and logicians, regarding the arising of superimpositions such as [the perception of] silver, it is established that—

out of fear of the undesirable consequence of requiring knowledge of the substratum (dharmijñāna)— knowledge of similarity is not accepted as a cause for any superimposition whatsoever; and thus, in a case involving the contact of the sense-organ of touch with this object (idamartha), [this principle holds].
He raises the objection: "But would it not be so?"—that is, since the cause of superimposition (adhyāsa) as you define it exists, why should it not occur?
The meaning is that even without the cognition of similarity, superimposition is admitted merely through the absence of the causal complex for perceiving a specific feature that would prevent it.

Is it that the superimposition of silver is being established there? Or is it that the superimposition of silver itself is being established? Regarding the first case, he says "it indeed occurs," meaning that this is an instance of what is already accepted (*iṣṭāpatti*). He raises the second alternative with "but what [if]...
In that regard, there is the absence of the causal complex for the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*) regarding the superimposition of copper and so forth.

Thinking that there is no basis for the objection that "because it is common [to both], there would only be a superimposition of silver and so forth," he refutes it with the words "tāmra-ādi" (copper, etc.). The word "ādi" (etc. is for the purpose of including fragments of tin, gold, and so on. The phrase "in some cases" (*kvacit*) means even in a case where a fragment of iron has been touched by the palm of the hand. The term "gocara" (object) [is used].

The meaning is that this object, in the form of a piece of metal, becomes an object of doubt, such as: "Is this silver, or is it copper, or is it gold, and so forth? However, in a situation where there is the perception of specific distinguishing features that exclude copper and the like, there is indeed only the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver.
He says, "It happens," and explains: "In some cases.

In a place such as a treasury where, for the most part, only fragments of silver are situated, when someone enters there and by chance touches a fragment with the palm of his hand, there occurs only the superimposition (adhyāsa) of silver upon it. This is because his cognition is that of "a treasury of silver."

The meaning is "because it exists. Now, an objection is raised: in some cases, such as a piece of iron touched by the palm of the hand, the non-occurrence of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver is observed;

yet that would not be possible according to your view. This is because, since the absence of the causal complex for the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*) is present there as well, the occurrence of the superimposition of silver would necessarily follow [for you]. For me, however...
Because the cause, which consists of the cognition of similarity, is absent, it can be said that [superimposition] does not occur; therefore, he says:

"Even when [it exists] in some cases. Just as, even when the cognition of similarity exists immediately after approaching [the object], the absence of the superimposition of silver is accepted in your own view, so too it is in my view.

The meaning is that the absence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in certain cases does not entail any fault. "Therefore" (*tasmāt*): the meaning is that the cognition of the substrate (*dharmin*) and the attributes (*dharma*) cannot be established as the cause of superimposition by any means. Regarding the threefold alternative: is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form "this" (*idamākāra*) established through direct experience, or is it to be inferred from its effect, or is it to be inferred from its cause?

Having set aside the first two [alternatives], he refutes the third: "Nor is it unobstructed. This qualification—"unobstructed"—is applied because, at the time of the eye's contact with this object, when there is a distraction elsewhere, no cognition having this object as its domain arises.

For it is precisely because of this [woman's] state that we also maintain that the silver, which is a transformation of ignorance agitated by the contact of the defiled sense-faculties, has as its object something existing at the same time as itself. And in that case:

Because it arises at the same time as the cognition, consists of a mere appearance, and is devoid of external reality, there is an absence of prior sensory contact with it; nevertheless, by relying on its identity [with the object], this [cognition] is established as being produced from sensory contact with that very object,
and thus the perception "I see silver with my eyes" is logically justified.

For even in the absence of its own sensory contact (*svasaṃprayoga*), there is the experience of the illusory silver as being visual (*cākṣuṣa*). Nor can it be argued that it is not visual because of the absence of sensory contact—since that would constitute a sublation (of the experience)—nor that it is produced by a defective sense-organ contact at the same time as this mental modification (*vṛtti*); for the sense-organ is the cause of the cognition.
Because it is not postulated that association (saṃprayoga) is the cause of the object.

With the intention that the obscuration arising by virtue of the aforementioned association is produced as nothing other than an error (*bhrānti*), and not as a valid cognition (*pramā*) of the nature of the mere object "this" existing prior to the error— since there is no evidence for that— he says: "From that," meaning existing within the consciousness delimited by the object "this."

The nescience (*avidyā*) that undergoes transformation into silver attains a state of agitation— meaning it becomes oriented toward its effect— due to the cause of superimposition consisting in the contact with a defective sense organ;
and in the subsequent moment, it transforms into the form of silver through the defective sense organ.

The modification (*vṛtti*) also arises at that very same time through conjunction. Thus, the meaning is that the modification—which arises from a defective sense-organ in conjunction with an object—takes as its object this "this-object" (*idamartha*) as qualified by silver produced at its own time. The word "its own" (*sva*) refers to the modification.

It being established that there is a distinction between the two positions: in the position where there is knowledge of the substrate (*dharmijñāna*), the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form "this" (*idamākāra*) is what disturbs ignorance; whereas in the position where that [knowledge of the substrate] is absent, the contact (*saṃprayoga*) which is the cause of the knowledge of the substrate is what disturbs knowledge (*vidyā*).
Among these, the latter position is not tenable, because of the contact with the object "this."
Because this [cognition] lacks the causal conditions for a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is silver,

and because there is no sensory contact with the eye prior to the cognition regarding silver at the time the cognition arises; thus, due to the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for a mental modification having silver as its object, the mental modification "this" has as its object the substrate alone.
Anticipating the objection that [the object] is established [as real], he says: "And there" means in the case of an error.

That which exists only as revolving at the time of its appearance—that is, that which revolves merely through its appearance—in that [object], what is it that is pervaded by the cognition? This refers to the contact with the object "this."

Even though it arises as a modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is silver, its causality [in producing that modification] is possible. Nor should it be argued that if a modification having another thing as its object were admitted due to contact with something else, then from the contact of the sense organ with a jar, there would follow a modification having a cloth as its object; for [in the case of valid perception], regarding a modification whose object is itself, the self—which is the substratum of identity with itself—is the cause.

With the intention that the postulation that "simultaneous conjunction with the sense organ" is the cause is sufficient to avoid the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "tatprācīna" (preceding that).
This means "preceding the appearance of silver. "Tādātmya" (identity) refers to [the identity] of the silver with the object denoted by "this" (*idamartha*).

The sense is that because it is imagined (*kalpita*), the object "this" (*idamartha*) is the locus of identity with silver; however, the pot is not the locus of identity with the cloth because the pot is not superimposed upon the cloth. He states the reason for postulating that silver—which is not the locus of contact with the eye—is nonetheless the object of a visual mental modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*).

Regarding the phrase "by the eye": the proponent of the theory that [the content] is the knowledge of the substrate (*dharmijñānavādī*), while asserting an alternative explanation for the experience of being seen by the eye, raises an objection with the thought that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the contact of the sense organ with the substrate has as its object the substrate alone. He says: "And not...
That silver, at the same time as this [substrate-]modification, is not [perceived], even though it is produced by the contact of the defective sense organ.

He states the reason for this [claim] that "it exists" as follows: "of the cause of cognition. Thus, on the view that illusory silver is perceptible by the senses, one must postulate that the contact with another object (the shell) produces a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward another object (silver); likewise, one must further postulate that the sensory contact, which is the cause of cognition, serves as the cause for the production of the object, such as the silver.
The sense is that it would be a cumbersome burden to assume [this].

But rather, this [object] is produced immediately after the mental modification (*vṛtti*); it is manifested through superimposition upon the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) revealed by that [modification].

As for the experience of its being visual, that is due to the indirect [causality] of the object's being the generator of the mental modification which manifests the consciousness that illuminates itself.

"By mere dependence on the eye. If that were the case, it would follow that there is no dependence on the eye even in the error of a yellow conch-shell. For in that instance, there is indeed dependence on the eye for the apprehension of the conch-shell, since it is impossible for the conch-shell alone to be perceived by the eye without its color (rūpa). Nor...
Because it is not admitted that the yellow color is perceived through the sense organ when it is superimposed;
nor is the yellow color itself superimposed in its own form, but rather [it is superimposed] upon the conch by one who is experiencing the yellow bile located in the eye.
Since it must be admitted that mere conjunction is superimposed, it should be stated that the eye is required precisely for the sake of direct experience.
It may be objected: "If association (*parisaṃprayoga*) is not the cause for objects such as silver, then what is the cause there?

For since ignorance alone is always present, it cannot logically be the motivator for the occasional appearance of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and so forth. To this, he states the answer: "But what... and so on.

This [modification] occurs immediately after the mental function (*vṛtti*). From the contact of the sense organ and so forth, a modification arises whose object is merely this "this-ness" (*idamartha*).

Being agitated by that [modification], which serves as the instrumental cause for superimposition, ignorance (*avidyā*) transforms itself into the form of silver. And of that silver, [the property of being] delimited by the object "this," which is manifested by the modification in the form of "this"—

Consciousness (caitanya) is the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna). Thus, the meaning is that silver, like the ego (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, is manifested by consciousness even without a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward itself as its object. In the phrases "produced by that" (tajjanya) and "manifested by that" (tadabhivyakta), the word "that" (tat) refers to this mental modification; for such a modification occurs only occasionally (kādācitkatva). This applies to the superimposition (adhyāsa) of silver and the like.
The meaning is that it is occasional (*kādācitkatva*). "Manifested by that" means manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*). Nor should it be argued:

"How can things like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, which are manifested by external consciousness, be manifested by the witness-consciousness in the same way as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth? [For they are] unconditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a cognition whose object is themselves.
Because that which is illumined by consciousness alone— that is, that which is illumined by the witness— is the meaning of the word [in this context]. And thus,

just as the consciousness that illumines ignorance (*avidyā*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and their attributes does not become conditioned (*upahita*) by a cognitive modification (*jñānātmakavṛtti*) whose object is ignorance and so forth, so too is it with the case of mother-of-pearl, silver, and the like.

It should be understood that the luminous consciousness (*bhāsaka-caitanya*) itself is said to be manifest by the witness (*sākṣi-bhāsya*) because it is not conditioned by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is the silver in the mother-of-pearl and so forth. Now, an objection is raised: "If the silver in the mother-of-pearl were manifest by the witness, would this not contradict the experience of its being visual? To this he replies: "But the experience of its being visual..."

The silver in one's own mother-of-pearl shell depends upon the eye for its manifestation; this is because the visual organ acts as the cause (*janaka*) for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) delimited by the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*), which serves as the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of that [silver].

Furthermore, that dependence exists only through a secondary succession (*paramparā*), since it is required for the sake of the mental modification whose object is its own substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). It is not, however, [directly required].

The literal meaning is that because [the cognition] does not depend on anything else for the purpose of functioning directly upon its own object, the experience of it being visual (*cākṣuṣatva*) is established there merely by some kind of dependence on the eye. Now, one might object: "But surely the experience 'I see silver with my eyes' refers to [the quality of being seen] residing in the silver..."

The actual state of affairs is that [the cognition] apprehends the status of being an object of visual function (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*), but not the status of being an object of consciousness manifested by visual function as it pertains to the silver in the mother-of-pearl; and thus, by the passage beginning with "merely through the indirect dependence on the eye," [it is explained] regarding the experience of its being visual (*cākṣuṣatva*).

If it is argued that the status of the silver as an object is its being the object of consciousness manifested through the operation of the visual organ, and thus the nature of the experience of that [silver] is merely imagined (*kalpita*), that is incorrect; for, like the case of words, an experience cannot be explained away [as mere imagination]. This is because, in reality, the "this-ness" (*idantva*) residing in the object "this" (*idam-artha*)— [...is not sublated by the subsequent cognition of the substrate. (Note: The provided fragment ends here.)

In this context, just as there is a superimposition of a relation upon the silver in the mother-of-pearl, so too there is a superimposition of the visual quality—which belongs to the object "this" and is being experienced therein—upon the silver in the mother-of-pearl;
for this is the meaning intended in the present case. And thus, that which is to be superimposed is upon itself.

The meaning of the text should be understood as follows: in order to attain that status of being an object of visual activity which belongs to the thing "this" (the nacre), there is a requirement for the eyes regarding the silver in the mother-of-pearl; this is merely a requirement for the eyes through a mediated succession (*paraṃparayā*), and thus there is no fault whatsoever.
If that were so, it would follow that both the conch-shell and its contact [with whiteness] would be non-perceptible;

for those two would lack the status of being manifested by the witness-consciousness through a connection with the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "yellow" located in the region of the eye.
Furthermore, it is because we do not accept that there is a single mental modification (*ekavṛtti*) involving the conjoined yellow color and the conch shell.
Nor is it maintained that the superimposition of conjunction occurs in the conch shell due to the defect of the yellow tint located in the region of the eye;
rather, [it occurs] in that [conch shell] by means of that [yellow color] which has gone out together with the rays of the eye and pervades the object.
It is possible that superimposition through contact is like safflower dyeing a cloth red;
for it must be stated that this is the contact with the Witness (sākṣin) manifested by a mental modification (vṛtti) assuming that [object's] form.

He refutes the view that illusory silver and the like are manifested solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) and not through the senses. "If that were the case" means: the dependence on the senses is for the sake of obtaining sensory perception of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) alone, and not for the sake of the superimposed object (*āropya*). The meaning is: if one accepts that the dependence on the senses is for that purpose [of perceiving the substrate], then [the following applies]. "For indeed... refers to this:

It should be understood that even in the case of a yellow conch-shell illusion arising from distance, superimposition on a substrate is established prior to the visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) directed toward the previously perceived substratum;

it is not, however, the case that there is a perception of yellowness [without a substrate]. The phrase "dependent on the eye" (*cakṣurapekṣā*) is to be supplied [to the following]: without color (*rūpa*), there is no mere conch-shell [perception].

Having accepted that the eye is incapable of grasping [the object], the proponent of the view that the superimposed is revealed by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) objects: "And yet one does not experience pleasure. This means "yellow color. The meaning is: just as silver is superimposed upon a mother-of-pearl shell in its own form, yellow color is not likewise superimposed upon the conch-shell. [This refers to] the yellow [color] residing in the eye.

A particular substance endowed with a yellow form— specifically that yellowness which is being experienced as belonging to the yellow substance— is superimposed upon the conch shell itself; just as the redness experienced in a flower and so forth is [superimposed] upon a crystal gem and the like.
The superimposition of relation is likewise.
Nor should it be argued that if one admits the superimposition of what belongs to one thing onto another, it would entail the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension of something as otherwise);
for we do not accept *anyathākhyāti*, since we admit the production of an indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) relation that is being superimposed.

The meaning is that there is a difference [from the previous case], such as the presence of the quality of *sattva* (whiteness) and so forth. "For the sake of the experience of yellow" means for the sake of that prior experience of the color yellow in a yellow substance which arose from the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a connection with the color yellow onto the conch shell. In that regard, is it [the cognition] located precisely in the region of the eye?

"Is the experience of yellowness [of the substance] in the conch itself, or is it the experience of yellowness in the substance in the conch after it has reached the location of the conch? He refutes the first alternative with the words "If that were so. This means that one would have to admit the experience of the yellow color occurs in the substance in the conch while it is still located within the eye. [He then addresses the second alternative: "In the case of the conch and its conjunction..."
The meaning is: [the manifestation] of the conch and of the conjunction between the conch and its yellow color.

Does the appearance of the conch and that conjunction occur through the witness (sākṣin) as manifested by a mental modification (vṛtti) whose object is not yellow, or rather through the witness as manifested by a mental modification whose object is the conch together with its conjunction? It is not the first; thus he says:

Regarding the phrase "the region of the eye": by means of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of yellow that has reached the region of the eye, the consciousness delimited by the yellowness situated in that region is manifested.
And together with that witness characterized by the manifested consciousness, the superimposition of the conch occurs upon the conch.

The meaning is that because there is no connection between the yellow color and its conjunction [with the conch], there would be no direct perception (*āparokṣya*) of either the conch or that conjunction. He says "not the second" [alternative] with the words "yellow-colored-conjoined," etc. [He adds] "and because it is not admitted";

the remainder is "by the proponent of the theory that [objects] are manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Even when the substance has reached the location of the conch, there is the experience of yellowness.

Thus he raises the second objection. "Not so, because of that which pervades the object" means that the substrate in the form of the conch-shell is pervaded by that substance (the yellow color). And thus, since consciousness located precisely in the region of the conch-shell is manifested by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of the yellow color of the substance, [the error occurs] in the conch-shell.
The sense is that direct perception (*āparokṣya*) of both [the cloth and the color] is possible through their conjunction. As for safflower (*kusumbha*), it is a specific substance;
just as when a cloth is pervaded by it, the red form experienced in the safflower [is perceived in the cloth].
The meaning is that it is likewise a superimposition of association.

If that were the case, then when a conch shell is viewed by one whose eyes are affected by jaundice—as if it were coated with gold—there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasanga) of others perceiving it as yellow. Nor can it be argued that [the cognition] is grasped near the object and then, like a bird flying over the sky, is capable of being grasped at a distance; for this is not possible for others who are not in close proximity.

It must be stated that [the object] is apprehended; for even in the case of others whose eyes are placed near that eye, since proximity (*sāmīpya*) exists, the apprehension of that [color] would be unavoidable.
Even so, there remains the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of blueness upon the sands of the riverbed flowing with the water of the Achana River.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to speak of a superimposition being experienced when there is a superimposition of blueness upon the sky, or a superimposition of blueness upon red garments at night under moonlight,
one cannot avoid admitting a visual modification (*cākṣuṣa-vṛtti*) whose object is the locus as conjoined with that blueness.
And because the non-employment of the eye is difficult to avoid, the *Pacapadika* passage— which establishes that for a child who has not tasted a bitter flavor,

the appearance of bitterness in what is sweet is caused by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from experiences in a previous birth— demonstrates that this [superimposition] exists in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).
And because this very bitter taste is clearly demonstrated to be sensory.

He states the objection to the view that the yellow substance contained within the eye, which is experienced by everyone when the eye is functioning, exits through the rays of the eye and pervades the conch shell: "If that were so," and so forth. When a person whose vision is impaired by jaundice sees a conch shell, then for others besides him as well, it would be yellow.
The meaning is that [the objection] follows from the experience of [seeing] a conch shell. Now, one might argue:

when the substance of the yellow pigment travels from the region of the eye to the location of the object, the yellowness is apprehended by the person whose eyes have been affected by the pigment, starting from the region of the eye up to the extent of the object's pervasion; and so it would be for others as well.

If it is grasped near the eyes and in the middle, it can also be grasped at the region of the temple, and not otherwise; regarding this, he states an illustration: "In the sky," etc. Just as a bird (*vihaga*) flying up again and again in the sky is perceived by the very same person from whom it started its flight on the ground.
The meaning is that just as even one who has gone far up into the upper reaches of the sky can be perceived by others, so it is in the case at hand.
He states the disparity with the example: "of others also. For in the example, someone seeing a bird far up in the sky directs another person, saying, "My..."

If your eye were placed near his eye, then even you would be able to see that bird; thus, having done so, he sees it, whereas such a thing is not possible in the case at hand—this is the meaning. Or, let it be granted that there is superimposition (adhyāsa) upon what is being experienced.
He says, "Even so," because in cases where there is a superimposition of blue color and so forth upon something being perceived while depending on the eye,
it is impossible to say that such dependence exists in its entirety. If, however,
a blue form exists in the serpent serving as the substratum for the water, or in some particular substance mixed with water, then [the blue] is experienced right there.

To dispel the doubt that the reflection of the nail might be in the water, the qualities of "excessive whiteness" for the sandy ground and "transparency" for the river water are employed as qualifiers. Transparency means purity; and regarding the phrase "in the moonlight at night," its purpose is exactly the same as previously stated.

It must be seen that [the role of the sense organ] is unavoidable because it is difficult to refute. In this regard, even in cases of superimposition such as the yellowness of a conch-shell or the blueness of water, although there is no admission of a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) whose object is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) as conjoined with the superimposed qualities of yellowness or blueness,
the non-utilization of the eye— which has as its object only the substratum (*dharmin*) such as the conch-shell— is not difficult to refute.

It should be understood that this is because the possibility of the occurrence of a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) has already been demonstrated. He states an authoritative opinion (*samatim*) regarding the fact that the superimposed object (*āropya*) is the object of a modification produced by the sense organ: "anāsvādita... [etc.].

Otherwise, the dependence upon the operation of the sense of taste in that case would be untenable; therefore, in the instances of superimposition such as the cited blueness, [the cognition arises] solely from the contact with the substrate.

The meaning is: "by that boy who has not tasted"—that is, who has not experienced—the bitter taste with the sense organ of the tongue in this life; the appearance of bitterness, the direct perception of bitterness, in sweet breast-milk and the like, is produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) generated by the experience of a bitter taste in a previous birth. Regarding superimposition (*āropa*), [the object] to be superimposed...

The literal meaning is that [the appearance] has as its cause the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born from a previous experience of a similar kind. In this text, it appears that the manifestation of bitterness is produced by the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*) assisted by a latent impression;
for if it were produced by the latent impression alone, it would follow that it is a memory (*smṛti*). And thus:
Since the sweet substance, which is the locus for the superimposition of bitterness, is unfit for the gustatory sense-organ,

it follows by process of elimination that it is the bitter taste itself— which is superimposed in its own essential form— that becomes the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the gustatory sense-organ; thus it is made clear.

The sense is that this text is intended as an agreement regarding the fact that the object of superimposition (*āropya*) is perceptible by the senses. "Otherwise" means that if one does not accept the bitter taste (*tiktarasa*) as being perceptible by the senses, then in a case where a child perceives bitterness there,
there would be no operation of the gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*), because a sweet substance is unfit for that [perception].

In reality, however, in the expression "the appearance of bitterness" (*tiktatāvabhāsa*), there is a *karmadhāraya* compound between the words *tiktatā* and *avabhāsa*; furthermore, the word *avabhāsa*— derived from the etymology "that which is made to appear" (*avabhāsyate*)— refers to the superimposed bitter taste, as is likewise shown in the *Pañcapādikā* by the use of the term *avabhāsamānatā*.
Because it has already been explained: even the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births are a cause for the production of the superimposed bitter taste.

In cases of illusory superimposition (*prātibhāsika-adhyāsa*), there is the triad of causes consisting of the defect (*doṣa*), the impression (*saṃskāra*), and the knowledge of the general form of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānya-jñāna*). Regarding the superimposed...

Since the fact that [the substance] is the cause for the production of the object of cognition (māna) is clearly stated in the *Ṭīkā*, the *Vivaraṇa*, and other works, how then does this text clarify that this very cognition (*māna*) has, by its own nature, the quality of being perceptible (*aindriyakatva*), like a bitter taste? And if there were an absence of perceptibility in the bitter taste...

It should not be argued that the operation of the gustatory faculty is untenable; for there is no evidence that the gustatory faculty is active at the time when bitterness is superimposed upon other things by a child or others. Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the non-appearance of bitterness would follow as a logical consequence.

For it is possible for bitterness to be manifested by the consciousness limited by the sweet substance—[consciousness] which is itself manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that sweet substance produced by the sense of touch—by accepting the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of bitterness [upon that consciousness]; thus, bitterness can be illumined by the consciousness that is its own substrate even without a mental modification directed toward itself. Or, let it be so.

In the case of the superimposition of bitterness, there is a dependence upon the gustatory sense organ (*rasanendriya*). Nevertheless, the sensory nature of the bitter taste being superimposed is established by its relation to the sweetness residing in the substance that serves as the locus of the superimposition.

Since it is possible for the sweet taste (*madhurarasasya*) to be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhānatva*), its dependence [on the sense organ] is justified when there is the apprehension of that sweet taste which serves as the substratum. Furthermore, because the word "sweet" (*madhura*) occurring in the *Pañcapādikā* is common to the category of sweet tastes (*madhurarasasādhāraṇatvena*), there is no contradiction with that [text]. Nor, in the apprehension of the sweet taste...

It must be stated that the impossibility of the superimposition of bitterness [on sugar] is not a valid objection; for even when there is perception of taste, if the direct perception of the universal "sweetness" (madhura-rasatva-jāti) is obstructed by a specific defect, the superimposition of bitterness is possible.
Therefore, the object of superimposition is manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) alone.
It should be understood that this is the faultless, universally established practice of the ancient noble ones;

henceforth, following the commentary on the *Pañcapādikā* text composed by Kavi according to his own tradition, that very work is being followed. Therefore: [regarding] the object being superimposed...

The meaning is that even on the view that [error] is manifested by a witness-consciousness, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the eye is of no use in cases of superimposition such as a yellow conch-shell.

Since superimposition arises simultaneously with the visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*) which has that [object] as its sphere, and since it is the object of that modification, its visibility must be admitted; for in the absence of color-form (*rūpa*),
there is no modification whose sphere is the substrate alone, and consequently, there would be no manifestation of consciousness as the object.
For it is impossible for the blueness and other qualities superimposed upon water to be objects of that [visual] perception; however, in the case of the superimposition of a bitter taste,
since there is an absence of being perceivable by a single sense organ for both the substratum and the superimposed object,
[the cognition arises] through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the substratum produced by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*).
In the manifestation of limited consciousness, it arises precisely from the contact with the sense of taste which has been impaired by bile; therein,

the superimposition of the bitter taste and the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that object arise simultaneously, and thus the bitterness must also be admitted as being perceived through the sense of taste.

For, since there is no utility for the sense of taste even indirectly with respect to a bitter taste— which is manifested by consciousness made manifest through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward its substrate by means of the sense of touch— it is impossible to justify the experience of it as being tasted (*rāsanatva*) in any other way whatsoever; and the same applies to the silver as well.
Since its visibility is logically established, the experience "I see" is not to be sublated.

"Having that as its object" (tadgocara) means having the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) as its object. "That whose arising is simultaneous with the mental modification" (vṛtti-samakāla-udaya) refers to superimposition (adhyāsa) such as the yellow color and so forth; this is the meaning. [This is said] provided that it is accepted that the mental modification produced by the contact with the substratum has as its object the conch-shell and so forth as qualified by the superimposed color and other attributes.

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-appearance of the superimposed form and so forth. The phrase "and in the absence of a mental state (*vṛtti*) whose object is the locus alone, without the form" means: and "the superimposed [object] also"—that is, if one does not admit a mental state whose object is a conch-shell or the like as conjoined with blueness and so forth; this is the sense of the word "and" (*ca*). The word "that" (*tat*)— [End of excerpt]

Regarding the statement in the *Pañcapādikā* that consciousness is the substrate for the superimposition of the bitter taste— which is an object of the senses— this occurs, as in the case of visual superimposition,
by virtue of both the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the object of superimposition (*āropya*) being objects of a single mental modification (*vṛtti*). However, [in the case of the internal organs]:
He establishes this by means of the function of the gustatory organ whose object is exclusively the bitter taste, [stating]: "But in the case of the superimposition of the bitter taste...

[and] "...delimited by that. This means: delimited by the substrate in the form of a substance such as sugar and so forth. Together with that gustatory organ which has been impaired by the defect known as *pitta*...

The meaning is this: due to the contact with the substrate in the form of a sweet substance, there arises therein—within the consciousness delimited by that substrate—the superimposition of a bitter taste; at that very moment, there also arises a gustatory mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose sole object is the bitter taste being superimposed. Now, [an objection may be raised]: is the manifestation of the substrate of the superimposition of the bitter taste a matter of gustation?
Why is the view that the bitter taste is merely of the nature of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) not respected? To this he says:
"By the sense-organ of the skin," etc. [The phrase] "the bitter taste is illumined by consciousness" implies the ellipsis "if it were accepted.
[The phrase] "even through a succession" means as in the case of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and so forth.

The meaning is: "also by way of producing a mental state whose range of operation is restricted to the substrate (*dharmimātra*) alone. The underlying intention is that the substrate—such as a sweet substance—is not an object of the gustatory faculty. In that context, regarding the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in the form of bitterness, the explanation of the phrase "in some way" (*katham api*) is "by another method. This is because, although during the time of dreaming [objects] are manifested solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*),...

Since it will be explained later that the experience of tastes, forms, and so forth— as well as their being present on the tongue or being visible— is of the nature of superimposition, such a justification is possible in the present case as well;
for even a bitter taste and the like, though merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), are not in sensory contact [with the senses], just like the objects of a dream.

It should be understood that although the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is equal [in both cases], nevertheless, by one who does not know that specific manner, it was stated there that "in some way" and so forth. "In the same way" means: just as the experience of being tasted was established by taking the state of being an object of a gustatory modification (*rāsanavṛtti*), so too [the experience of being seen] is established precisely by taking the state of being an object of a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*).
The meaning is that since the experience of visibility is possible, it is improper to conceive of that experience as being of the nature of a superimposition.
Furthermore, it is not the case that for a non-associated silver to be visual,
the contact between object and sense-organ is the cause in every instance of perception; rather, in the perception of a substance,
its conjunction [with the sense-organ] is the cause, and in the perception of silver, the conjunction with silver is the cause.
It should not be argued that this would result in the destruction of the established rules regarding the relationship between cause and effect;
for the first rule is unestablished because there is no single, common property of "contact-ness" (sannikarṣatva) that pervades conjunction (saṃyoga) and the other types of contact.
As for the second rule, even according to the Nyāya method, it applies to certain substances that are unfit for conjunction, such as darkness.

Because the superimposition of substantiality (*dravyatva*) is possible from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), there is no contradiction with the second rule; for it is accepted that in the case of illusory silver, substantiality— which actually belongs to the substratum— is perceived through superimposition upon that which is the locus of substantiality according to empirical view, just as "this-ness" (*idantva*) is [superimposed].

It is incorrect to claim that [the causal relation] should not be sublated because the third rule is unestablished— due to the fact that even when specified, the postulation of a causal relation apart from the general nature of the second rule (niyama) is struck down by the fallacy of complexity (gaurava);
for when a sublater exists, its sublation is necessary.

Having considered this, he entertains a doubt with the words "na ca" (nor). He dispels the suspected objection with the passage beginning "sannikarṣatvasya" (of the nature of contact), etc. The phrase "due to the non-establishment of the first rule" means that the rule—that sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) is the cause in all produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*)—is not established. The word "produced" (*janya*) [is used] to exclude the eternal witness-consciousness (*nityasākṣirūpa*).

This is for the purpose of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*). According to the view that verbal cognition can be immediate (*śābdāparokṣa*), it should be understood that "being distinct from verbal cognition" (*śābdabhinnatva*) must also be included as a qualification of perception. Here, this should be noted: in the Nyāya system, there exists a commonality (*anugata*) consisting in being any one of [the relations] such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth; alternatively, like "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) and the like, it may be an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).
Since the possibility of [other types of] proximity (*sannikarṣatva*) exists, the contradiction with the first rule is unavoidable.

Having stated that the first rule is unestablished (*asiddhatva*), he states that there is no contradiction with the subject at hand by accepting the second rule—that for the perception of a substance not produced [by other causes], sense-organ conjunction (*indriyasaṃyoga*) is the cause. [He says: "of the second rule. Of the second rule...

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), that which is the locus of substanceness (*dravyatva*) is the object [of the cognition]; thus, there is no contradiction with the second rule. He states the restrictive reason for postulating that this rule has conventional substance as its object: "in that which is unfit for conjunction" (*saṃyogāyogye*).

"Somewhere" means in cases such as unity, duality, and so forth. The meaning is that even there, because it is possible for the superimposition of substantiality (*dravyatva*) to occur through the delusion that these are the substrata of number— in the manner of "unity is one," and so on—
there is thus a violation of the rule that conjunction with a sense organ is the cause for the perception of substance in general, [if that were restricted] to unity and the like.

The meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of that [darkness] at the time of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of substantiality (*dravyatva*). He provides an example for the superimposition of substantiality upon what is not a substance with the words "as in darkness. Since, according to the Siddhānta, its status as a substance is accepted, he specifies "according to the Naiyāyika method. This means according to the method stated by the Naiyāyikas that "darkness is the absence of intense light."

The meaning is that for those who know that "being the substratum of qualities" (*guṇāśrayatva*) is the definition of substance (*dravya*), the misconception of substantiality can arise through the delusion that [the shell] possesses the nature of silver. Now, one might object: "In cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, substantiality exists by its very nature, just as it does in jars and the like; otherwise, even the universal (*jāti*) 'silverness' would not exist there."
Because the genus "silver-ness" and so forth in the case of silver seen in a dream and similar instances is yet to be established [as real],

even nacre-silver and the like become substrata for substanceness from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). For, within the sphere of empirical experience, just as there is a sublation of "silver-ness" in the case of nacre, so too do "substanceness," "silver-ness," and other properties [persist] in nacre-silver.

If it is argued that because no contradiction with the [first] rule is observed, and likewise, if one accepts that even silver in a mother-of-pearl shell (śuktirajata) and the like—which are not in contact with the sense organs—are objects of sensory mental modifications (vṛtti), then the contradiction with the second rule is also unavoidable; [the reply is: true, but in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, there is [the appearance of] silverness, substanceness, and so on.
Following the view that "there is no birth" (*jāti*), he establishes the cognition of substantiality (*dravyatva*) therein. Regarding the phrase "illusory silver" (*prātibhāsikarajata*):
the meaning is that, just as the quality of "this-ness" (*idantva*) residing in the object "this" is superimposed there, so too is the substantiality residing in that [silver] superimposed upon it.
And thus, from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), illusory silver is not a locus of substantiality.
The term *bhāva* means "that which comes into being.

Furthermore, according to the principle that "whatever is the cause for a general category is also the cause for its specific instance," this applies even in cases such as seeds and sprouts, where one accepts a general causal relationship.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that one sprout could arise from another seed, and so forth; for,

since the specific causal relationship between cause and effect is not established— being as non-existent as a camel’s udder— it cannot be maintained here either that the conjunction of substances is the cause for the perception of a substance.

It should be stated that if one accepts a general rule [that a substance is perceived through conjunction with a sense organ], there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that another substance would be perceived through conjunction with something else. This is because we accept the specific rule that for the perception of a particular substance, conjunction with that very substance is the cause. Otherwise, even under a third rule, it would be impossible to avoid such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, there is no violation of an established rule; moreover, even if a previously established rule were violated here,

there would be no fault, because there is the experience— unestablished by any other means— of such cognitions as "I see this silver" and "I see blue water," which occurs even in the case of those things first grasped in mere perception.
This is because it is impossible to establish such rules as "the contact of the sense-object is the cause" and so forth, without assuming a limitation of their scope to the conventional realm.

But surely, if it is accepted that sensory conjunction (*indriya-saṃyoga*) is the cause for the perception of a substance, then a third rule would also be unavoidable: that for the visual perception of silver, the conjunction of the eye with silver is the cause, since silver is a specific kind of substance. [This is so] because of the conjunction of the eye with silver.

He dispels the doubt that "because a specific sense-object contact is the cause for the perception of a specific substance, this principle is established by general logic" by stating "yatsāmānya" (that which is general).
This refers to the general relationship between cause and effect; where [it applies]...
The meaning is that this logical principle applies only in that specific case and not elsewhere. The connection is with the phrase "by virtue of the logical principle having that as its object.

The word "tat" (that) means "from the logical principle. Now, [an objection is raised]: if one accepts a causal relationship between the generality of seeds and the generality of sprouts, then from another seed, another sprout would arise...

He raises an objection, suggesting that here too there is indeed the application of the stated principle because of the existence of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of one who speaks of such an over-extension: "And not even here... To avoid the aforementioned over-extension, just as for each specific instance of a sprout the causality of each specific instance of its seed is postulated according to the stated principle, so too in the present case, regarding the perception of each specific substance...

By that same reasoning, it is established that the conjunction with each respective substance is the cause; however, by that reasoning, a third causal relationship is not established—this is the intention behind saying "that substance," etc. Now, one might ask: why is a third restrictive rule not postulated by that reasoning in order to avoid over-extension? To this, he says:
"Otherwise" means: in the case of postulating a third restriction. "Of an over-extension" (atiprasaṅgasya) means:

of that which takes the form of the visual perception of another's silver resulting from the eye's contact with another's silver. Nor should it be argued that there should also be a third restriction, just as there is a restriction regarding the individual [substratum].

The sense is that it has been stated that such a thing—which is useless for avoiding an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and is like the teat on the back of a goat (*ajāgalastana*)—is not to be postulated. "Therefore" means: because the first and third rules are unestablished, and because the second rule is not contradictory. [Objection: But what about the contradiction between the first and second rules?

Since the difficulty of avoiding [the objection] has been stated previously, and since the contradiction regarding the restriction of manifestation—which falls within that same category—is likewise unavoidable, the claim that "there is no violation of the established restriction" is incorrect; therefore, he says: "Furthermore, here... This means in the case of shell-silver and the like. [He adds: "Of that which is not otherwise established," [meaning] at the time of a dream.

For, just as there is the experience of visual perception and so forth regarding silver and other objects that are manifested solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), here too it is possible to conceive of [the experience] as being of the nature of a superimposition (*āropa*). Since its non-otherwise-establishment (*ananyathāsiddhatva*) is established, the absence of a postulated causal complex (*kḷptasāmagrī*) is equal here as well as in dreams; otherwise, even in dreams, [one would have to admit] the sense organs...

The connection [of the phrase] is: "because it is impossible to justify the experience. One should here reflect on such points as: since there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating an activity [of the self], and since that experience contradicts perception, it is reasonable to interpret the scriptural statement regarding its cessation at that time in another way.

And this being the case, since there is no possibility of formulating a restrictive rule that "in valid cognition contact is the cause, but not in error," it follows that there must be the superimposition of silver located elsewhere— which is indeed uncontacted— right here; thus,
the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (the apprehension of something as otherwise) is as easy as a stretching out of the legs.
Furthermore, because it is impossible for silver located in another place to be perceived directly by one whose consciousness is unconfined [to that location] due to its manifestation,

and because the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the object of error is established through arguments such as the impossibility of explaining both its appearance and its sublation, [the illusory object is proven to be indeterminable].
Nor should it be argued that if one accepts the perceptibility of a phenomenal object merely through its conjunction with its substrate,

then why— at the very time of the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl— there should not also be visual perception of the red color (of the lac) which is to be superimposed there at a later time?

He raises the objection that if one assumes a contraction of the established rules [of perception], then the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of nacre-silver and the like would not be established. He says, "And this being so... [referring to] the Nyāya position that silver and so forth located in another place are the objects of error; in that case, how can there be contact with what is not proximate?
When the proponents of the theory of the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*) raise the objection regarding the nature of perception,

[they respond] that "contact is the cause of perception," and so forth; whereas in your own system this [definition] is restricted by being limited to the objects of empirical perception (*vyāvahārika*), in my view as well, it applies to perceptual valid knowledge (*pratyakṣapramā*).

The meaning is that the opponents' rebuttal— that there is no refutation of the theory of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension)— is well-stated, because it is logical to assume a restriction [of the definition] by taking "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*) as the cause on the grounds that it is the object of valid perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapramā*). This remains so even if proximity is not a cause for perception in the form of an error (*bhrama*).

He refutes the objection that this leads to the doctrine of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) by stating "manifested" (*abhivyakta*). He will explain that for an object to be perceptually immediate (*aparokṣatā*), its contact with the sense organs is not the determining factor; rather, it is its non-difference from manifested consciousness (*abhivyakta-caitanya*). Consequently, even if the silver and so forth that are the objects of an error exist in another location, they possess perceptual immediacy.

"It arises" means that silver, having attained identity with the mother-of-pearl, is established. [Objection: "But even so, this 'silver-in-mother-of-pearl' would be real, like the mother-of-pearl itself, and not indeterminable (anirvacanīya), because there is a lack of evidence. To this, he says:

"It is known" (*khyāti*) means it is perceived directly (*aparokṣapratīti*); thus, the existence of the object of error in another place and its non-existence (*asattva*) are both refuted. [Otherwise] there would be cognition of the non-existent, because direct perception is impossible for that which lacks identity (*tādātmya*). [For example,] "silver does not exist in the mother-of-pearl even at the three times..."
By the force of the perception that sublates what has been sublated, the absence of silver in the mother-of-pearl is established even at the time when the silver appears;

for if there were no silver in the mother-of-pearl, then the [illusory] manifestation would be inexplicable, and if it were truly present there, then—just as the "mother-of-pearl-ness" in the mother-of-pearl—it would not be sublated. Thus, [the absence is established] through the inexplicability of both the manifestation and the sublation.

Its indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva) is established. Because the silver in the mother-of-pearl possesses both origination and destruction, its indeterminability is proven; this has been explained in detail during the discussion on the definition of illusory manifestation (vivarta), and thus it is not elaborated upon here. The phrase "the argument of possessing origination, etc. is the meaning of the word "ādi" (and so forth).

The proponent of the view that nacre-silver and the like are manifested by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) raises the objection: "Is it not the case [that there would be] the same contingency?"—meaning that because nacre-silver has the object "this" (idamartha), which is the locus of its identity with itself, as its object through visual contact, it would follow that it is the object of a visual modification (cākṣuṣavṛtti). To this he replies, "In that very place," meaning:
of that very thing which is to be superimposed at another time upon the nacre itself. Why? Because [it is so] for every modification.

That very vṛtti which takes the silver in the mother-of-pearl as its object—why does it not also take the silver existing at another time as its object? For that vṛtti has as its cause the contact with this object (the mother-of-pearl) which serves as the locus for identity with silver; [it lacks] the cause consisting in contact with this object which serves as the locus for identity with silver existing at another time.

The meaning is that there is no distinction even regarding being produced by sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*). Thus, sensory contact is not the cause of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is silver; rather, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is the cause specifically for the cognition of the qualified substratum (*viśiṣṭadharmijñāna*).
Furthermore, the cognition of similarity, acting as a defect (*doṣa*) and as the cognition of the substratum, is the cause for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and so forth.
The sense is that one must accept the view that silver and the like are manifested by consciousness even without the operation of a mental mode (*vṛtti*) directed toward them.
This is because, although at the time of the superimposition of silver there is no difference in the perception of the glittering quality common to both the mother-of-pearl and the silver,
due to the absence of personal defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, there is no superimposition of the mother-of-pearl at that time.

Thus, since I also accept that there is no arising of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that [silver], it follows that there is only one single sense-produced modification whose object is silver as conjoined with the "this" portion;
there is no prior modification having the form of "this. Therefore, the presence or absence of the capacity to remove ignorance does not reside in this [single modification] alone.
Others,

however, hold that the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is the cause of superimposition; thus, having accepted this modification (*vṛtti*) in the form "this," [the object is perceived] by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) manifested precisely by that [modification].

In the view that there are two cognitions, it is held that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of silver is useless; for since the manifestation of the silver superimposed upon that [substratum] is possible, and since the depositing of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding the object— silver— is established by that very mental modification which manifests the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣin*) that illumines it, [the separate modification is redundant].

The first cognition, "this," serves as the cause for superimposition; the second cognition, "this is silver," has as its object the silver that is superimposed, but it does not have the "this" portion as its object apart from that which is merely superimposed.
Even in your own view, why could the superimposition of redness upon a conch shell not occur at the very same time as the superimposition of silver?
Since both the substrate and the cognition of similarity are common to the superimpositions of both silver and redness, this indicates an equality of fault [in your position].
Regarding the phrase "at the time of the superimposition of silver":
even though there is no difference in the defects of the object— namely, the perceived similarity— at the time of the superimposition of silver,
it is not [the case that the cognition does not arise] because of the absence of the personal defect consisting of passion directed toward copper and because of the presence of passion for silver.
The rebuttal is accepted as being "the superimposition of color. With the intention that "then my answer is likewise equal," he says: "Since...
This means: from the human defect consisting of passion (*rāga*) and so forth, or from the absence thereof.
By the word "passion and so forth" (*rāgādi*), the revolving of the color within the intellect (*buddhi*) is included.

By the phrase "due to the absence of defects" (*doṣābhāvāt*) and so forth, the passion for silver (*rajatarāga*) is included. "Precisely from that" means: because of the absence of passion directed toward the substrate (*raṅga*), because of the presence of passion for silver, and because of no other cause, the production of silver itself occurs there, and the arising of a cognitive state (*vṛtti*) whose object is a substratum qualified by silver at that time is admitted.

This is the meaning. He concludes the critique of the Kavitārtika’s view with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that there is no evidence for the cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*) being a cause [of valid knowledge]. "Not here" (*nātra*) means "not in the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of 'this'. That the statement regarding the lack of evidence for the cognition of the substratum being a cause was made because of that [lack of evidence] has been established in various places.

This very point expresses the view that [the cognition] has that [silver] as its cause for one who intends it; others, however, say "the knowledge of the substrate" (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Regarding this, some maintain that even in the position of the *ākāra-vṛtti* (cognition with form), a vṛtti directed toward the silver must be admitted; he refutes that view with the words "having the form of 'this'" (*idam-ākārām*). Others, however, [hold that it is] having the form of "this"...

The connection is that the modification (*vṛtti*) assuming the form of silver is useless once the modification assuming the form of "this" (*idam-ākāra-vṛtti*) has occurred. The phrase "because the knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*) is the cause of superimposition (*adhyāsa*)" is the reason for accepting the modification in the form of "this. The word "iti" signifies a reason. The meaning is: because the knowledge of the substrate is the cause of superimposition. [This refers to] the modification in the form of "this."

Is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of silver—which is distinct [from the substrate]—for the purpose of manifesting the silver, or for the purpose of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*)? Regarding the first [option], he says: "By that very manifestation. This means: by that which is manifested by the modification having the form of "this" (*idam*). He refutes the second [option] with: "The illuminator of that," etc. It is not [so].

And it must be explained how, through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward one object, an impression (*saṃskāra*) can be deposited in another object. The point is that the impressions are deposited in as many objects as are manifested within the consciousness delimited by that very modification; this has been stated previously. As for those who... [text ends]

They maintain that the impression (*saṃskāra*) of its own object is deposited solely by the functioning (*vṛtti*) upon its own object. According to their view, there is indeed a functioning whose object is the superimposed silver. Regarding the doubt as to whether that second functioning has as its object the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by the superimposed silver, or whether its object is the silver alone, he demonstrates the resolution through two views.

Regarding the phrase "the position of two cognitions" and so forth: the connection is that the second cognition, which has the form "this is silver," though non-existent [as such], has the superimposed silver as its object. He states the purpose of specifying this particular form with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely).

Some maintain that the meaning of the cognition "I know this silver" is the experience of having as its object silver that has attained identity (*tādātmya*) with this [substratum]. Others, however, hold that ignorance residing in consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect evolves (*vivartate*) in the form of silver.

Thus, this silver-cognition, which is a mere appearance (ābhāsa) of ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the "this" portion, undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into that form;
however, unlike the mental modification directed toward the "this" portion, there is no such thing as a non-superimposed cognition of silver. And so it is said:
In the case of silver, this is because there is the manifestation of the non-relation of "this-ness" residing in the substrate; however,
for cognition as well, since the manifestation of the relation of "this-ness" as its object residing in the substrate is possible, that [cognition] is not [non-apprehension either].

It must be stated that its being the object of that [knowledge] is what needs to be explained; for since this [silver] is not the object of the knowledge whose locus is its own identity, there is no possibility of the consequence that it would be the object of the relation with that [identity]. Nor is it possible for the substratum and the superimposed object to be necessarily manifested together in a single cognition.
Because this is established in the *Bhāṣyavivaraṇa*, it must be stated that they have a single locus of occurrence (*ekavṛttiviṣayatvam*).

Even though there is a difference in their respective mental modifications (*vṛtti*), they say that these two are similar to the sun in their illumination within a single witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) manifested by a mental modification in the form of "this" (*idam-ākāra-vṛtti*).
He provides experience as the proof for the second mental modification (*vṛtti*) having a qualified object, namely: "I know this is silver.
He states the view that the second *vṛtti* has only the superimposed (*adhyasta*) as its object, beginning with the words "But others," etc.
In the theory of two cognitions, he demonstrates that the second *vṛtti* is a modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*), starting with "Just as," etc. It evolves (*vivartate*).

The meaning is "it transforms. Regarding the word "thus" (*evam*): the meaning is that [ignorance] is delimited by that *vṛtti*-cognition which has the "this" (*idam*) portion as its object. Ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the *vṛtti* having the form of "this" transforms into the form of a *vṛtti* whose scope is solely the superimposed silver; and that *vṛtti* is the appearance of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*).
The meaning is: "because it is not produced by a cause that generates a [valid] cognition. Regarding the term "unpracticed" (*anabhyasta*):

the cognition of silver, which is of the nature of a false appearance of cognition, is merely *prātibhāsika* (illusory), and not *vyāvahārika* (empirical) like the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "this" (*idam*).
Even this false appearance of cognition, like the silver in the mother-of-pearl, is directly perceived as the sublater of the ignorance regarding the mother-of-pearl.

The meaning is "because it is sublatable. One might object that if the appearance of cognition had as its object only the silver, it would not take the form "this is silver"; however, even though the appearance of ignorance lacks the "this" (idam) portion as its object...
With the intention that such a form is possible for it, he says, "And thus" (*tathā ca*). Regarding the appearance of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*), the meaning is:

provided that the consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having this as its object is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). In the cognition of the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*), which serves as the substrate for the appearance of cognition, there exists that very state of not having "this" as its object.
The conjunction with that [silver] appears as the cognition whose object is silver; regarding this, he states an illustration: "of silver," etc.
The meaning is: just as the conjunction with "this-ness" (*idantva*), which resides in the substrate of the silver, appears in the silver, so it is here.
Now, if the conjunction with "this-ness" is grasped when the silver is being grasped by the appearance of cognition, then [it would follow that] this...
You too must necessarily accept this [notion of] "this-ness" (*idam*), because without the apprehension of that [substratum], the apprehension of its relation [to silver] is impossible.
Thus, he raises the objection that the appearance of cognition is established as having for its object the portion of "this" qualified by silver. [He says:
"If not... [meaning: if the aspect of the relation were within the scope of the appearance of the cognition of silver...

The phrase "of that which is situated within the qualification of the cause" (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇamadhyastasya*) must be stated. The underlying intention is that otherwise, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that a perceptual cognition of a relation as determined by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth would not have "pot-ness" as its object. [This applies to] the appearance of knowledge (*jñānābhāsa*) in the form of "this-ness" (*idaṃtva*).

Even in the absence of having the counter-positive as its object, the cognition of the "this" aspect—which has attained identity with the illusory cognition (jñānābhāsa) by virtue of being its substratum—does have the counter-positive as its object;
for the illusory cognition has the relation as its object. [This applies] to the illusory cognition...

He offers the following rebuttal: "The state of having a relation as its object is possible; by that much alone, the avoidance of the aforementioned over-extension (atiprasaṅga) is established. Regarding the phrase "of that which is the locus of identity with itself," the word *sva* (self) refers to the appearance of cognition (*jñānābhāsa*). As for the phrase "even though there is a difference in the mental modification (*vṛtti*)," this is because the Vivaraṇa authors themselves accept that the mental modification of ignorance has as its sole domain that which is superimposed (*adhyasta*). Thus, the rule stated [by them] is as follows:
The sense is that the intention of the authors of the Vivaraṇa appears to be that the supreme forest-enclosure is the witness, which is the state of knowledge (jñānapada).

Now, since the manifestation of all objects is possible through the grace of the Witness alone, what is the purpose of the mental modification (*vṛtti*)? For even if it is admitted that the *vṛtti* is required for the sake of depositing impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding objects such as a jar, the assumption that it must go outside [the body] is useless; for, as in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*), [manifestation occurs] by means of a *vṛtti* that has not gone outside.

Since the manifestation of even objects such as jars is possible through the witness-consciousness alone, there is no lack of consistency in the distinction between the indirect (parokṣa) and direct (aparokṣa) cognitions;

for that distinction is established precisely by the difference in the types of mental modifications (vṛtti), which are prompted by specific instruments, just as in the case of verbal cognition and inference.
