On this point, some say: in the case of perception, it is consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by the object—by virtue of the object being its locus—that constitutes the manifestation of the object; for since a relation in the form of direct identity (sākṣāt-tādātmya) is possible, it is improper to postulate any other relation, such as the relation of essential nature (svarūpa-sambandha). Therefore, for the sake of manifesting that [consciousness]:
In cases where [the object] is imperceptible, it is logical to accept that the manifestation lacks an external basis.

Thus, when there is a suspicion of deviation from the rule that "only those mental modifications (*vṛtti*) which have external objects as their immediate content possess the power to overcome the veil," this suspicion cannot be resolved by either accepting or rejecting the existence of such a modification (*vṛtti*) in the case of the mental modification having the form of "this" (*idamākāra-vṛtti*), which occurs in instances of error.

Having reflected somewhat on the position of the two-fold knowledge, [the author] raises an objection regarding the previously mentioned emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*). He begins with "But surely" (*nanu*). The question "What by the modification?

implies the following intention: "Let the modification be as described; however, its emergence is utterly remote. [The opponent objects: "If the mere witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) itself consists in the experience of the object, then how can there be a recollection of that object at a later time?"

If there were no mental impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the destruction of the experience, such [recollection] would not occur; likewise, if an adventitious modification (*vṛtti*) is not admitted, there would be no conformity with the eyes and other senses, because the eyes and so forth would be of no use to the eternal witness (*sākṣin*). Therefore, suspecting that a modification must be accepted, he acknowledges it [by saying]: "the pot, etc. (*ghaṭādi*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that the very illumination of the object is the fruit of its [the mind's] emergence? [Reply: No; he says, "as in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣa*). [Objection:

The distinction between perceptual and non-perceptual cognitions is established by experience, and that distinction is accounted for only if one accepts the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the case of perception.

He says "no" to the claim that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) is consciousness delimited by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that has gone outside [the body], while mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) is consciousness delimited by a mental modification that has not gone outside. This he states with the words "And it being so," etc.
The meaning is: "in the absence of the mental modification going outside. Knowledge produced by the senses is perception; that which is other than that is [mediate].
The meaning is that this is because a distinction [between types of knowledge] is logically established by the fact that [inference] is indirect (parokṣa) knowledge.

Just as in verbal cognition there is a specific universal called "verbal-ness" (śābdatva) produced by the specific instrument consisting of the word, or just as in inference there is "inferential-ness" (anumititva), so it is here. [This refers to] the specific instrument.

The sense organ (*indriya*) and inference (*anumāna*), etc., are also [included]. The meaning is that the generic nature (*jātya*) residing in the modifications (*vṛtti*)—which is of the form of perception (*pratyakṣatva*) or otherwise—is either of the nature of a limiting adjunct (*upādhirūpa*) or has that very [organ] as its cause. He establishes the emergence of the modification (*vṛtinirgama*) by saying, "On this point, some say," [referring to it] as having the object as its locus (*viṣayādhiṣṭhānatayā*).

The meaning is that consciousness delimited by an object (*viṣayāvacchinna-caitanya*) alone is the manifestation of the object, and not the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīva-caitanya*), because the latter lacks a direct relation of identity (*tādātmya*) with respect to the object due to its lack of being the material cause (*upādānatva*) of that object. "Of another" means: of a mediated relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*).

The distinction is as follows: since a relation in the form of identity (*tādātmya*) is possible, it is not logical to postulate a relation of essential nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*); and since a direct relation is possible, it is not logical to postulate any other relation. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In order to manifest that [identity]."

The meaning is that since it is the Brahman-consciousness itself, as delimited by the object, that illumines the object, and because that [consciousness] is veiled, this [manifestation] is for the sake of achieving its manifestation in the form of the removal of the veil. Now, an objection is raised: according to the reasoning already stated, even in the case of immediate perception (*aparokṣa*), it is indeed the Brahman-consciousness delimited by the object that is the illuminator of the object.
And consequently, it would follow that its emergence occurs even there [in the intermediate state]; therefore, he says "no," specifying "in the case of an object situated beyond one's perception."

Others maintain that since it is impossible for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) to have a contact with a fire or other object that is spatially remote, and because no exit-door for the modification is perceived— despite such a door being required by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as in the case of the sense organs— it must be admitted, out of necessity, that the consciousness delimited by the non-emerged modification itself becomes the cognizer of the object through its own essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

However, since the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is established as the cause of immediacy (*āparokṣya*) with respect to pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are directly connected with consciousness—they maintain that even in the case of objects such as a jar, it is consciousness itself as connected with the object that is the cause of immediacy;
thus, they justify the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) for the purpose of manifesting that [consciousness]. Others, however, [hold a different view].
The clarity perceived in what is directly experienced is not found in what is understood through verbal testimony or inference;

for even if the specific qualities of a mango tree have been taught by a reliable person a hundred times, there is no such clarity as that which exists when it is directly perceived, since even thereafter the inquiry "What is that? persists. Nor is this the case [in the latter instances].

Even when there is a comprehension of sweetness and so forth from a word, because there is no word expressive of a specific subordinate genus residing in the sweetness of a mango, or even if such a word exists, because its relation [to that object] has not been grasped due to it being unheard of,
there is no comprehension of sweetness as qualified by an uncommon specific genus from that word.

It should not be suspected that the persistence of the inquiry "it does not exist" is logical, because from this word [it is known] that there exists in the mango-tree a specific sweetness that surpasses all others.

With the intention that there is an absence of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) as the cause for the emergence of the mental mode (*vṛtti*), he says: "obstructed" (*vyavahita*). He states another justification for the emergence of the mental mode: "But others [say]... regarding the phrase "established among those things in contact" (*saṃsargiṣu kḷptamiti*). "Contact" (*saṃsarga*) here means identity (*tādātmya*);
since in some cases of the direct perception of an object, it is established that contact is the causal factor, it is possible that the very same contact is the factor in other cases as well.

The meaning is that its abandonment is impossible. The sense of the particle *eva* (only) is that [the consciousness] is indeed conjoined with the object, and not the individual soul-consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) unconnected with it. "That" refers to the manifestations of the Brahman-consciousness delimited by the objects. In the case of a perceptible object, the sublation of the veil is necessary.
He explains that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is for the purpose of overcoming [the object] by means of its presentation. Regarding the phrase "but others":
one might ask, "Even when an object such as sound is cognized, why would there not be clarity? He says "no," with the words "for not...
*Parimala* means fragrance; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include the taste contained within the mango fruit.

Even if the authoritative statement "there is a sweet taste, etc. is repeated a hundred times, the resulting cognition of the taste and so forth is only as qualified by the generality (sāmānya) of sweetness;
it is not a cognition of the taste as qualified by a specific sub-genus (jāti) pervaded by sweetness. And thus, regarding the taste and so forth...

With the intention that the desire to know the specific genus (*jāti-viśeṣa-jijñāsā*) is justified precisely because of the absence of knowledge regarding the specific genus, and not because of a lack of clarity even when [the object] is understood through verbal testimony, he raises an objection with the words: "Nor from verbal testimony" (*na ca śabdāt*).
Even when there is an apprehension of mere sweetness (*mādhuryam*), which is the sweet taste (*madhura-rasa*), [there remains a desire to know more].
The connection is that there is no apprehension of sweetness delimited by a specific uncommon genus from the word;
the meaning is that there is no apprehension of sweetness as being delimited by that which is a specific uncommon genus.
He states the reason for the absence of a means [to cognition] when there is an absence of understanding the specific sub-class (*jāti-viśeṣa*), beginning with the words "rasāla" and so forth;
the meaning is that because there is no word to denote that specific sub-class residing within the sweetness and other qualities of the mango tree (*rasāla*).

He states that even by accepting a word that denotes it, its comprehension is not possible due to the absence of the apprehension of its expressive power (*śaktigraha*); this is expressed by the phrase "even though that exists. Regarding the phrase "of that":
it means "of the word denoting a specific intermediate genus. This is to be connected with the words "and it cannot be doubted."

Even in the absence of a word that directly denotes it, there exists a sentence-form of speech that conveys it, and through that, there is also the comprehension of a specific universal (jāti). Thus, because there is a lack of clarity regarding the specific universal once it has been comprehended,
he says "rasāste" and so forth, with the intention that there is a desire to know (jijñāsā).

This is because there is also the comprehension of a specific intermediate genus residing therein; for this word denoting a particular does not, setting aside the particularity residing in that [object], convey a particularity residing in something else, as that would result in invalidity. Nor does it [convey] the particularity residing in that very object merely as a "particularity" in its general sense.
It must be stated that one does not desire to know [the object] by means of its form (*rūpa*) as something distinct; for even in the case of perception,

since a specific sweetness or a specific genus is apprehended only in its own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and because no further distinctions residing within that specific genus are apprehended, it would follow that the desire to know would persist.

Therefore, one must accept the following distinction: clarity—which is capable of terminating inquiry—arises because [an object] is enveloped by the consciousness whose single flavor is immediate and which is manifested as graspable by perception; whereas in that which is known through words and other means, such clarity is absent, and thus it is indistinct. For this very reason, pleasure and the like, being cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), possess clarity.

Does this word [“this”] convey a specific universal residing in that [object], or one residing elsewhere? He accepts the first alternative: “residing in that, it is a sub-universal. He refutes the second: “for it is not ‘this’,” meaning “in that case,” i.e., regarding the sweetness of a mango and so forth; for the object of the word’s intended meaning (tātparya) alone is its [referent].

The sense is that [this is so] because of the acceptance of its being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be argued that there is no undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) regarding its lack of validity; for the sense is that it is impossible to accept such a thing in the case of the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*).
Having accepted the existence of a specific genus residing in sweetness, he raises an objection: "Nor is it only that which resides in it."

Regarding the term "in general" (*sāmānyena*): the meaning is that "particularity" (*viśeṣatva*) is a universal form (*sāmānyarūpa*), because it exists not only in the specific types of sweetness found in the mango, but also in the specific types of sweetness found in other fruits. Regarding the phrase "not as a particular" (*na viśeṣya*): it does not cause the cognition of a specific type [of sweetness] as being qualified by a particularity residing within that specific type. And thus:

The point is this: although the specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) residing in the sweetness of the *rasāla* fruit is understood from the word in its general form, it remains an object of inquiry precisely because it has not been understood as qualified by the unique, uncommon attributes belonging to that specific universal.
Is the uncommon attribute residing in that specific universal of the nature of a universal (*jāti-rūpa*), or rather...?

Alternatively, [the definition] might be the *upādhi* consisting in "subsisting in that which possesses a specific universal while not subsisting in that which does not possess it. Neither the first [alternative] holds, because the existence of a universal (*jāti*) is not admitted. Nor does the second hold, because even by perception [one can apprehend] a specific universal residing in the sweetness of a mango.

Because, if that [particular] were not grasped, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the persistence of the desire to know the specific universal even when it has been apprehended through perception. Therefore, it must be stated that even by perception, that specific universal is grasped precisely in its own form (svarūpeṇa).
And since such an apprehension in its own form exists even from the aforementioned word, then regarding that which is apprehended through a word, insofar as it is clear, [the same applies].
With the intention that there would be no persistence of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*), he says: "Even by perception" (*pratyakṣeṇāpi*). Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*):
the meaning is that, as in an object understood through perception, there is a lack of clarity in an object known through words and so forth.
He states the cause for this clarity, which is established by experience, saying: "manifested" (*abhivyakta*). This refers to immediacy (*aparokṣatva*).

Self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) consists in being of a single essence and a single form. That which is manifested as immediate, unitary, and of a single flavor—consciousness (*caitanya*)—is, through identity (*tādātmya*) with it, the state of clarity (*spaṣṭatā*) and the specific nature of objectivity (*viṣayatā*) in that which is grasped by perception; this is the meaning. By this, the consciousness of the object, which serves as the cause for the clarity residing in the object, is indicated.
It has been indicated that for the sake of achieving the removal of that obscuration (*āvaraṇa-nivṛtti*), the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛti*) is required.

By the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) and so forth, he demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the role of the removal of obscuration as the cause of clarity.
The meaning is: "precisely because of the contact with the manifested consciousness" (*abhivyakta-caitanya-saṃsarga*).

They justify the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) by arguing that even though Brahman is known through verbal cognition, it remains indistinct as long as ignorance has not been removed prior to reflection (*manana*) and so forth; once that [ignorance] is removed thereafter, it becomes distinct. But even with this much—
It has been stated that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is for the purpose of removing the ignorance that veils the object; however, that is incorrect.

For even if one accepts that the ignorance veiling the consciousness delimited by the object is not removed unless the modification emerges, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of this principle. Nor is it the case that...
If that were the case, it would follow that Devadatta’s knowledge of a jar would result in the cessation of Yajñadatta’s ignorance regarding that same jar, because they possess the same object.
This is because knowledge and ignorance residing in the consciousness whose locus is the "I-sense" (ahamartha) have distinct substrates.
It should not be argued that, in the case of a contradiction between these two, the factor of having a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) is irrelevant;

for even if one accepts the emergence of mental modifications (*vṛtti-nirgama*), it is the state of having a common locus and object (*samānāśraya-viṣayatva*) that constitutes the cause of the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance.

Furthermore, because Devadatta’s cognition of a jar and Yajñadatta’s ignorance of a jar would both result in having the same locus and object— namely, consciousness delimited by the jar— an unavoidable over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would ensue.

Regarding the phrase "verbal function" (*śābdavṛtti*): the meaning is that the verbal function produced by words does not remove ignorance prior to the performance of reflection (*manana*) and so forth, because it is obstructed by non-conviction (*asaṃbhāvanā*) and contrary conviction (*viparītabhāvanā*); however, subsequent to that performance, it does remove ignorance because it is no longer obstructed.

"Even by this much" means even by the passage beginning with "here some say," which consists of the presentation of the three names. This refers to the view that ignorance, which veils the object, resides in the person (*puruṣagata*);

for even if there is the possibility of its cessation through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that has not yet emerged [from the heart], in the alternative position where that [ignorance] resides in the consciousness delimited by the object (*viṣayāvacchinna-caitanya*), [the following applies].

Anticipating the objection that there would be a requirement for its [the vṛtti’s] exit, [the author] qualifies ignorance with the phrase “residing in the consciousness delimited by the object,” with the intention that there is no obstacle to the cessation of ignorance regarding the object even by means of a vṛtti that has not itself gone outside. Now, [an objection]:

The opposition between knowledge and ignorance, characterized by the relationship of the sublated and the sublator, consists in having the same object while residing in the same locus. And that common locus is possible only when there is an emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*). [This occurs] in the locus of ignorance...

Since even knowledge in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) attains its existence within the consciousness of the object, if there were no emergence [of that modification], it would be impossible for the two to have a common substratum. Consequently, the mere fact of having the same object would result in a contradiction arising from their coexistence; thus, he raises the objection that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And it is not so.

"Satīti" means "provided that there is no emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti). "Satvāditi" implies the remainder of the sentence: "because of the existence [of the difference] between Devadatta’s cognition of a jar and Yajñadatta’s non-cognition of a jar. "Ahamartheti":
provided that there is no emergence of the mental modification, cognition resides solely in the *aham-artha* (the self as the locus of "I"), and not in the consciousness of the object.
Furthermore, the ignorance that veils the object resides only in the consciousness of that object (*viṣayacaitanya*), not in the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*).
Thus, the meaning is that even the condition of having a common substratum (*samānāśrayatva*) does not enter into the category of factors that cause [the contradiction].
Regarding the phrase "having a common substratum and a common object": when there is a contradiction between knowledge and ignorance, provided they have a common substratum—

Even if one postulates that having the same object (*samānaviṣayakatva*) is the determining factor and accepts the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in order to maintain that, the aforementioned defect remains as it was; for when there is a contradiction between those two, a different determining factor must be postulated than the one stated, and that [different factor] is established even without the emergence of the mental modification. Therefore...
The collective meaning is that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is not established even by way of providing a justification for the contradiction.

Regarding the phrase "belonging to Devadatta": when there is a connection—by means of the emergence of the mental modification consisting of Devadatta’s cognition of the jar—with the consciousness delimited by the jar which is the locus of Yajñadatta’s ignorance of the jar, [then] Devadatta’s...

The meaning is that, while it is obtained that Devadatta’s knowledge of a jar and Yajñadatta’s ignorance of a jar share the same locus and have the same object, there is no cessation of Yajñadatta’s ignorance of the jar through Devadatta’s cognition of the jar; thus, the aforementioned defect remains as it was.

Since it must be stated that ignorance which obscures a particular object for a particular person is removable by the knowledge of that same object belonging to that same person— because the factor of contradiction must be specified individually and common substratum (*sāmānāśrayatva*) is not required— it follows that [the theory of] the non-acceptance of the emergence of mental modes (*vṛtti-nirgama*) is untenable. Regarding this, they say:

If it is argued that the very factor which causes the contradiction between knowledge and ignorance—that ignorance which is directed toward a particular person—is difficult to define, we say no; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even indirect (parokṣa) knowledge could remove the ignorance residing in the object. Furthermore, [the opponent claims] that the knowledge which removes [ignorance] must be immediate (aparokṣa).

If it is argued that this is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), what is that "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*)? It cannot be a universal (*jāti*), for in the case of a visual cognition whose object is a person qualified by a staff— as brought forth by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form "this man had a staff"—
if that [immediacy] were present even in the portion consisting of the staff, it would follow that the ignorance residing in the object regarding that staff would also be removed.

Furthermore, because there would result the experience of immediacy even with respect to that portion [of the object] in the thought "I directly perceive the staff," even if such an experience does not occur,

one would have to postulate a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as a means of contact (*sannikarṣa*) and thereby accept a conceptual immediacy (*kālpānikāparokṣya*) therein due to its being produced by sensory contact; and this would apply to inference and other forms of cognition as well.

Otherwise, one would have to postulate a sense-object contact (*sannikarṣa*) such as the cognition of a mark (*liṅgajñāna*), which leads to the undesirable consequence of accepting that [the cognition of the universal] is indirect.
Furthermore, if there were direct perception (*aparokṣa*) regarding the aspect of the staff,
it could not be a universal (*jāti*), because a universal is necessarily characterized by pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

If this [ignorance] is not the motivator, then what is that which you, the proponent, intend to be the motivator, independent of the emergence of a modification (*vṛtti*)? To this he says: "That which is ignorance. Regarding the word "that": the meaning is that such ignorance is to be removed by a cognition belonging to that person and having that [object] as its content. And thus, in the body of the motivator, that which—

By the phrases "depending on the person" (*puruṣaṃ pratītya*) and "belonging to him" (*tadīya*), it is indicated that there is no over-extension of the argument (*atiprasaṅga*), because a restriction is obtained: that the ignorance which obscures the object for Yajñadatta is removed only by Yajñadatta’s own knowledge, and not by Devadatta’s knowledge. [The author] now begins to establish the emergence of the function (*vṛtti-nirgama*) with the words "here they say," and so forth.

"What is that? [The opponent asks: "Does the meaning of the word 'directness' (*aparokṣatva*) refer to a universal (*jāti*) or an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*)? He refutes the first [option] with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvat*). [He explains: When Viṣṇumitra was previously perceived as qualified by a staff, there occurs at the present time a perceptual recognition (*pratyakṣa-pratyabhijñāna*) of him even when he is devoid of the staff.
[The cognition] "This Viṣṇumitra was to be punished" arises from the sense organ together with the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) that brings the form [of the object] forward.
In that regard, does perceptuality exist in the aspect of "punishment" (*daṇḍa*), or not? Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "Even in the aspect of punishment," etc.

This is because it would result in the undesirable consequence (*nivṛttyāpāta*). Nor can one say here that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for [one might ask]: "What kind of punishment is he being punished with now?"

The meaning is that there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the desire to know (jijñāsā) would never arise. Now, even in the absence of the experience of the cessation of ignorance, you postulate perception with respect to the portion consisting of the staff; and as for the ground for such a postulation, you follow the view that it is "being produced by sense-object contact" (indriya-sannikarṣa-janyatva), and that "contact" is a relation (pratyāsatti) between the cognition and its object—thus, you postulate a latent impression (saṃskāra).
Anticipating this objection, he states the over-extension [of the definition] with the words "even in the absence of direct experience," and so forth:
in inference, the cognition of the logical mark (*liṅga*) is the contact; in comparison, the cognition of similarity is the contact;
and in verbal cognition, the presentation of the word-meaning is the contact.

The sense is that, by the assumption that in presumption (*arthāpatti*) the cognition of an incompatible object-constituent is the contact (*sannikarṣa*), and in the cognition of absence (*abhāva*) the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the contact, it would follow that [presumption] is reduced to the means of valid cognition of perception (*pratyakṣa*). "By accepting that" refers to this.

The meaning is that it would entail the admission of [the cognition's] being non-mediately perceived (*aparokṣatva*). [The author states: "Even with respect to the part consisting of the staff, there is no perceptuality.

He refutes the second alternative: "With respect to the part consisting of the staff," because of the rule regarding its being a pervading occurrence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*). Otherwise, within a single act of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the part consisting of "that-ness" would result in being a memory (*smṛti*) due to being produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).
The sense is that it would result in the confusion of castes (jāti-saṃkara).

Even if there were no such restriction, it would be impossible for that [cognition] to be a non-pervasive class-property (*jāti*), because the distinction between its delimiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) cannot be established. Nor can it be an adjunct, because such an adjunct cannot be defined.

If it is argued that it is "being produced by the sense organs" (*indriyajanyatva*), we say no; for this fails to encompass the direct perception of the Witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*). [The same applies to] inference...

Furthermore, there would be over-extension [of the definition] to the perception of a jar qualified by weight and so forth as presented by verbal cognition; for even though that aspect is non-perceptual due to the absence of other causes,
it is the sense organ itself that functions through the power of the auxiliary factor of "presentation" (upanaya).

Because it is the cause [of cognition], and because the property of being produced by the sense-faculties (*indriyajanyatva*) is difficult to apprehend among many [objects] due to the non-apprehension of a pervasive delimitor of producedness (*anugata-janyatāvacchedaka*); and when that [property] is apprehended,
since that very [cognition] which is first perceived can be established as having a direct (*aparokṣa*) nature, it is a perceptual experience (*pratyakṣānubhava*).
Because it is impossible to conceive that being produced by the senses for a fit object consists in its having the nature of a direct perception (aparokṣa) suitable to that [object].

Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of that restriction": even if there is no rule that a universal (jāti) must be omnipresent (vyāpyavṛtti), it must be stated that in the present case of recognition, there is perceptuality with respect to the portion consisting of Viṣṇumitra, while there is perceptuality with respect to the portion consisting of the staff, and its absence with respect to the portion consisting of the staff. Consequently, without a difference in the delimitors (avacchedaka), [there can be no] counter-positive...

Since it is impossible for the absence of those two to coexist in a single locus, a distinction between limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) must be asserted; however, that is difficult to define. Therefore, because it is impossible for the genus "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva-jāti*) to be non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*)—defined as being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-locative with itself—it must be admitted that it is indeed a pervasive genus (*vyāpyavṛtti-jāti*). And in that case:

The sense is that the refutation has already been stated. Now, an objection is raised: in the present case, the failure to establish a distinction between the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is unproven;

for there exists a distinction based on whether [the cognition] is produced by ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*), or whether it consists in being a cognition not produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), or whether it consists in having Viṣṇumitra as its object, or whether it consists in being immediate (*aparokṣatva*).

If it is argued that this is because both [existence and non-existence] can serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for that [perceptibility], we say no; for even the aforementioned adjuncts consist of existence and non-existence, and if one were to require further adjuncts for their sake, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is the intended meaning. He refutes the position that "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) is the adjunct with the words "Nor... (*nāpi*).

If it is argued that [the definition] is unproven because it is indefinable, that is not so; for one must state what is intended by the opponent as "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*): is it being produced by the sense organs, or being produced by their contact with the object, or something else? Regarding these, he first restates and then refutes the first alternative, beginning with the words "indriya... (by the sense organs). He points out both the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)—since it does not extend to the eternal witness (*sākṣin*) which is of the nature of the perception of pleasure and so forth—and also over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*).

Regarding the term "inference" (anumiti): when a jar whose heaviness has been experienced through either inference or verbal testimony comes into sensory contact, there arises the perceptual cognition, "This jar is heavy. In that case, the meaning is that there is a pervasion (vyāpti) regarding the aspect of heaviness which serves as the qualifier.

[Objection: But surely, since gravity is imperceptible due to its being unfit for the senses, the fact that [the cognition] produced by it [is perceptual] is unestablished in the case of a direct cognition of that part; to this he says: "By another cause. The sense is that just as, in the view of Rucidatta, the mind (*manas*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) in inference, so it is here. Not [otherwise].

It should not be argued that "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) consists in being produced by a sense organ (*indriyajanyatva*), and since there is no such production by a sense organ in the cognition of a portion of gravity, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For even so, the objection remains that the definition does not exclude the direct perception (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) of the Witness-consciousness. Furthermore, [the definition fails] because it does not apply to the multiple direct perceptions of color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities, which are not produced by the senses.

He says "anugatā" (inherent), because without a knowledge of that [inherence], there can be no knowledge of being produced (*janyatva*), since the inclusive determinant of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*) is difficult to grasp. Now, one might object: "Is there not some indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), established by the experience 'I perceive directly,' which serves as the determinant of being produced? Anticipating this doubt, he says...

In that case, he says that only that [specific cognition] would constitute immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) and nothing else: "And upon the apprehension of that" (*tadgrahe ca*). This is because the apprehension of the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) must necessarily occur prior to the apprehension of the producedness of the object to be delimited (*avacchedya*); therefore, immediacy—which is fit for the experience "I perceive directly"—is not applicable to that [other cognition].
The meaning is that it is because [the self] cannot logically possess the nature of a dharma.

By this, it is established that immediacy (*āparokṣya*) consists in being produced by sense-object contact; furthermore, in the case of the inferred portion produced by a sense organ aided by mental presentation (*upanaya*),
there is no production by sense-contact, since even in inference there is the manifestation of what is presented.

The doubt that the application (upanaya) is not a means of contact because it is common to other instruments of valid cognition is also refuted, since there is no lack of consistency [in its status as a cause] despite the lack of a commonality among the contacts such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and the rest.
If it is argued, "Let that very immediacy which you accept be mine as well," we say no;
for that [immediacy] must be demonstrated in the very context where the immediacy of verbal knowledge is being investigated, and its refutation will be shown right there.
In that case, is directness (*aparokṣatvam*) simply the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) stated [as such]?

Is it pervading (*vyāpyavṛtti*) or non-pervading (*avyāpyavṛtti*)? Not the first, because there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the portion of the staff in the perception "This man possessed a staff. Not the second, because no distinct limiting adjunct can be determined. Nor is it the case that...

It must be stated that, while the limiting condition (*upādhi*) consisting in the nature of being immediate (*aparokṣatva*) exists therein with respect to the delimitation of having Viṣṇumitra as its object,
the absence of that same [condition] also exists in that very same [cognition] with respect to the delimitation of having a staff as its object. This being the case,

since the absence of the property of having Viṣṇumitra as its object must be asserted in respect to the portion consisting of the staff within that perception— [it follows that the cognition is not a valid perception].

The sense is that the aforementioned position regarding the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is untenable; for if one requires another delimiting factor to avoid the contradiction between the property of being related to Viṣṇumitra and its absence, there would result the previously mentioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, if one were to accept an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), it would follow that all universals (*jāti*) would vanish. Thus, the proposed view of the adjunct is not possible.
He refutes the second alternative regarding the category of "accessory conditions" (*upādhi*) with the words "by this.

This means: by way of the consequence of defects such as under-extension (*avyāpti*). Śaṅkika states that the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) which was mentioned in the position that "immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) consists in being produced by the sense organs" does not apply to the position that it consists in "being produced by contact with those [objects]."

"Bring it near. The point is that, due to the absence of any other cause, even though there is the state of being produced by a sense organ (*indriyajanyatva*), there is no state of being produced by its [the object's] contact (*tatsannikarṣajanyatva*), because the application (*upanaya*) lacks the nature of a contact (*sannikarṣatva*), and because there is an absence of any other contact.
He states another refutation: "Conjunction, etc."—namely, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), and so forth.

"Due to the non-universality of the contacts" means that there is an absence of a single, recurring property of "contact-ness" (sannikarṣatva) across conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the other types of contact.

"And due to the non-universality" refers to the fact that [the property of] being produced by sense-object contact is not uniform; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. And thus, in the case of direct perceptions (*sākṣātkāra*) whose objects are a jar, its color, the nature of color, sound, the nature of sound, pleasure, and so forth—

The sense is that there would be no corresponding perceptual cognition such as "I am directly perceiving. Regarding the position of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), he anticipates a third alternative: "Or else, that which is intended by you... That very non-mediate character (*aparokṣatva*) residing in the cognition which is accepted by you, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), exists in my view as well. Thus...

The sense is that since immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) can serve as a qualification of the knowledge that removes ignorance, there is no possibility of its removal by indirect (*parokṣa*) knowledge. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) refutes this, stating "not of that," on the grounds that the immediacy favored by me cannot possibly be the cause for the removal of that [ignorance] when it resides in knowledge.

The meaning is: "of that which is directly perceived according to my own view. The introduction refers to the context, which should be seen at the conclusion of the third chapter. It is precisely there that it should be shown: for the directness (*aparokṣatva*) of knowledge is not caused by a specific instrument, but rather consists in its non-difference from the directly perceived object; and this is what constitutes directness.

Therefore, because it resides in knowledge whose nature is consciousness that illumines the object, the pervasion [of the definition] is not absent from the direct perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*);
and the immediacy of an object consists in its being conjoined with the consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage.

Because [ignorance] cannot serve as a qualifying attribute that causes its own cessation, since it is that which is to be ceased; therefore, the knowledge of the Self taught in the scripture, "The knower of the Self overcomes grief," is the knowledge of Brahman—
which is necessarily conjoined with Brahman, the material cause of all things and the substrate of root-ignorance.
The functions of the senses do not remove fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna).

Non-difference consists in the identity [of the object] with the consciousness that is its own substrate— that consciousness which is directed toward the object, conducive to its empirical usage, and whose veil has been removed— just as the pot and other objects are non-different from the consciousness of their own substrate, which is manifested by a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward them and conducive to their own empirical usage.
Because of this, the state of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), defined as non-difference from consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage, is established.

Likewise, in the case of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, there is the direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*) of the pure Witness (*sākṣin*) who is their substrate; whereas in external objects such as jars, there is the direct perception of the Witness conditioned by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) assuming the respective forms of those objects, such as "the jar," and so on.

The method to be shown there is as follows: since the consciousness that serves as the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) of the jar and so forth—which is of the nature of immediate cognition—is identical with each respective object, its status as "immediacy" is established as having a form non-different from the immediate object. Regarding the phrase "as that which is to be employed": this refers to the state when the ignorance residing in the consciousness of the object has been removed.

The object, such as a jar, attains immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) in the form of non-difference from the consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage. When that [immediacy] is attained by the object, the cognition of it attains immediacy in the form of non-difference from the object that is immediate. And thus, [this immediacy] resides in the consciousness pertaining to the object.

The meaning is that prior to the cessation of ignorance, since knowledge has not yet attained immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), it is impossible for the immediacy residing in knowledge— which the proponent maintains is brought about by the cessation of ignorance regarding the object-consciousness— to serve as the causal factor (*prayojaka*) for that very cessation of ignorance.

The literal meaning is that its cessation cannot serve as a qualifier for the specific knowledge that brings about that cessation, because it acts as a causal factor (*prayojaka*) for the cessation itself. Therefore— referring to the previously stated definition of the contradiction-causing factor, namely that ignorance which relates to a particular person— the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) [of the object] pertains to the knowledge that brings about the cessation.
The meaning is that [the definition] is impossible because it cannot function as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the connection is that the qualification of the sublating knowledge (*nivartaka-jñāna*) must be stated as being "necessarily associated with the consciousness that is the substratum of ignorance. This refers to the capacity of even indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) to remove ignorance.

The phrase "to prevent an over-extension" (*prasaṅgavāraṇāya*) is the ellipsis. Now, one might object: "It has never been established anywhere that a cognitive modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) conjoined with an object can remove ignorance residing in that very object. Anticipating this, and with the intention of showing that this is indeed established in the case of a cognitive modification whose object is Brahman, he says: "of the knowledge of Brahman" (*brahmajñānasya*). [This refers to] the locus of the root-ignorance.

The meaning is: "in Brahman, which is the material cause of all beings, [the cognition] is necessarily connected. When a cognitive state (*vṛtti-jñāna*) whose object is Brahman arises, it necessarily arises as being connected with Brahman; it is for this reason that its being the material cause of everything is cited as the logical ground (*hetu*) for every effect whatsoever.

The sense is that, given the rule of association with Brahman— which has been the material cause since beginningless birth— the rule of association is also established as a matter of fact for the knowledge whose object is Brahman (*brahmaviṣayaka-jñāna*) with respect to Brahman itself, which is the locus of the primal ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) to be removed by that very knowledge. This is so regarding the capacity of the knowledge of Brahman to remove ignorance.

He states the proof for this [removal of ignorance]: "He crosses over sorrow. Here, the word *śoka* (sorrow) refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), while the word *ātman* refers to Brahman, which is non-different from the inner self (*pratyag-abhinna*).
The phrase "of what has been heard" (*śrutasya*) is understood to mean "by way of being the remover of ignorance" prior to that word.

Accepting the rule that [cognitions] arise as being conjoined with consciousness delimited by their respective objects precisely through the power of the contact between those specific sense organs and their objects, one must state that the defining characteristic of the subverting cognition is its necessity of being conjoined with the consciousness that is the substratum of ignorance. And thus, the cognition of a word which—

It has thus been established that the factor which determines the opposition between knowledge and ignorance is this: whatever serves as an obscuration regarding a particular object for a person, that [obscuration] is necessarily removed by a knowledge whose own existence is contingent upon its connection with the consciousness that is the locus of that ignorance regarding that very object. And this being so—
It would follow that even verbal knowledge whose object is the nature of the channels and the heart would have the power to remove ignorance.

Since there is no contact between the consciousness of the object and the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) that function indirectly (*parokṣavṛtti*), what is the cause for such contact in the case of sensory modifications (*aindriyakavṛtti*)? To this he says: "By virtue of the capacity for contact with the respective sense organs.
By this, it is established that indirect modifications are necessarily characterized by contact with the consciousness of the object, which is the substrate of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

It has been indicated that because there is an absence of the qualification of form (*rūpaviśeṣaṇa*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in a case where, although the first part exists in dependence upon something, there is ignorance regarding it. He shows the final determining factor (*prayojaka*): "And so" (*tathā ca*). This means: when the aforementioned qualification is present. There are many ignorances (*ajñāna*) that veil the consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by a jar.

They exist. Among them, some are obscuring factors with respect to Devadatta, while others are obscuring factors with respect to Yajñadatta and so forth; thus, for each respective object, there are many instances of ignorance according to the distinction between individuals. And so it is with the ignorances that obscure the objects.

The ignorance that exists in the middle, which pertains to a person such as Devadatta, which is the veiler of a specific object— namely, the veiler of the object that is the jar— is [removed] by that [knowledge] belonging to Devadatta, which has that same object, namely,
the knowledge whose nature is necessarily acquired through the contact with the consciousness that is the substratum of that ignorance, and which has that jar as its object.

The meaning is "that which is to be turned back. Regarding the phrase "that ignorance" (*tadajñāna*): it refers to that ignorance which was previously mentioned as being the concealer of the jar. The consciousness that is the locus of that ignorance is the consciousness delimited by the jar (*ghaṭāvacchinnacaitanya*). The acquisition of its own existence (*ātmalābha*) is restricted to—that is, pervaded by—the relation that exists therein.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: that knowledge which has the jar as its object (the *vṛtti-jñāna*) acquires its own existence (*ātmalābha*)—which is its origination (*utpatti*)—only when it is in contact with the consciousness (*caitanya*) that is the substratum of the ignorance (*ajñāna*) regarding that [jar]. And that [consciousness] is that very knowledge. As for the restriction (*niyama*): whenever there is the knowledge consisting of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the jar, [it occurs] when the sense-organ [is in contact] with the jar.

The acquisition of its own existence by that [knowledge] which is produced through sensory contact consists in its relation (*saṃsarga*) with the consciousness delimited by the jar within that very jar; such is its nature. As it has been stated previously: "The sensory modifications (*vṛtti*) arise only as being in relation with the consciousness delimited by their respective objects."

Regarding the phrase "having entered into the rule" (*niyamam upetya*): here, the rule clearly appears that whenever the modifications (*vṛtti*) of the senses arise, at those very times there is a conjunction of them with the consciousness of the object (*viṣaya-caitanya*).
This same principle applies to other objects, to other persons, and to other forms of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

This should be applied specifically to each case. Now, it might be argued that the objection—that there is no risk of inferential (parokṣa) mental modifications removing ignorance because they lack contact with the consciousness of the object, and thus are not subject to the aforementioned causal factors—is incorrect; for even an inferential modification sometimes possesses contact with its object.

For instance, regarding the doubt arising from the statement that "the channels (nāḍīs) exist in the heart-lotus" (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), when a cognition is produced in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) located in the heart-lotus,
it occurs by delimiting either the channels or the heart as the substratum.
Since that [consciousness] is veiled, and because there is a connection with the consciousness delimited by either one of those two objects, it possesses the capacity to remove that veil.

For it may happen that, even when there is contact with an object—whether through the sense-channel (*nāḍī*), the heart, or one of the other [means]—verbal knowledge can arise even without contact with the external object;
therefore, it does not acquire its own existence as being necessarily dependent on such contact. Consequently, it is ignorance...

Some say that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) must be postulated in order to account for the removal of the contradiction with knowledge. Others, however, state that because it is simpler to establish that ignorance residing in the object is removed by a knowledge that has the same locus as itself, the emergence of the *vṛtti* follows as a necessary consequence. Still others [hold that] regarding external light...

They say that the emergence of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is established because the removal of external darkness is observed only when there is a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); this is in accordance with what is observed. Furthermore, there is no undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), for otherwise it would follow that no desire to know either of those two objects could arise.

He states that [this objection] is refuted by the phrase "by the term 'indefinite' (*aniyata-pada*)": "And this being so... The connection is as follows: when the cause of contradiction contains an element of necessity (*niyata-garbhatva*), there is no consequence that verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*) would also fail to remove ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Whenever [the heart and so forth]...

He states the reason why there is no fixed rule that the emergence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding the object of a word occurs at that very time through its connection with the consciousness delimited by some object, such as the heart, etc., because of the non-exclusion [of other possibilities]. He says "of that" (*tasya*); the meaning is "of such verbal cognition. For, in the case of sensory modifications...

A rule regarding the arising [of mental modifications] in specific locations within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), delimited by the physical seats of the respective sense organs, is thus conceivable. However, for those modifications of the internal organ that arise independently of the sense organs—such as the verbal modification whose object is the heart and so forth—there is no cause for a restriction to a specific location. Therefore, [the rule does not apply].

The meaning is that there is no fixed rule such that [the experience] sometimes arises in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) delimited by the region of the heart and so forth due to the force of destiny, while at other times it arises in a different region, having abandoned the region of the heart and so forth. In this context, the genitive case in "tasya" (of that) is connected with the locative and the ablative cases.

"Therefore" means that it is impossible for the modification-knowledge (*vṛtti-jñāna*) to remove ignorance without a contact with the consciousness that is the substrate and object of that ignorance. Thus,
the emergence of the modification is established as the means for effecting the opposition between knowledge and ignorance.
He states other reasons for establishing this very point according to different views, beginning with the words "others, however" (*anye tu*). Regarding the phrase "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*):

at the time when, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one grasps that ignorance residing in the object is removable by knowledge, one grasps—on account of parsimony—that it is removable by a knowledge that is co-located (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with it, and not otherwise.

The meaning is "being removable by a cognition that has a different locus. This is what is intended: since ignorance resides in the consciousness that constitutes its object, the effect of knowledge—characterized as the removal of that ignorance—must likewise reside in that same [consciousness];
and thus, regarding the effect in the form of the cessation of ignorance...

Because of the capacity for sense-object contact together with the cognition that constitutes its own cause, a relationship characterized by co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible; thus, its abandonment is untenable. This is because the co-referentiality of cause and effect is a general rule (*autsargika*). [The term] "most external" refers to this.

The meaning is "in darkness. Regarding the word "only" (*eva*): its sense is that the destruction of darkness elsewhere has never been observed to occur through light existing in a different location. Since ignorance (*ajñāna*) also obscures its object, it is similar to external darkness; therefore, [the destruction occurs] either by means of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a support, or by consciousness as it ascends upon that modification.
Since light, by virtue of its function of removing obstructions, is similar to illumination,

the relationship between knowledge and ignorance— like that between darkness and light— is conceived as one of sublation and being sublated only when they possess a common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). And that [is postulated].

The meaning is that co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists in the relation of the cognitive modification (*vṛtti-jñāna*) with the consciousness that is the locus and object of ignorance; and that relation is dependent upon the emergence of the modification.
Some, however, [hold that] even when there is no need for the emergence of the modification for the purpose of overcoming the veil (*āvaraṇa-abhibhava*), [the relation is established].

They say that its dependence [on the senses] is for the sake of the coloring of consciousness (*cid-uparāga*), or rather, for the sake of manifesting the non-difference between the consciousness of the knower and the Brahman-consciousness which illumines objects. Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman? That which...
It is the ringing proclamation that [Brahman] is manifested through its function and has the Vedāntas as its means of valid cognition;
for all the Vedāntas, when scrutinized by the marks of purport— such as the uniformity of their opening and concluding passages— are seen to be in agreement regarding the non-dual Self.

They establish the systematic unity [of all scriptures] in Brahman, which is non-dual. And how this meaning is so has been explained in detail in the chapter on the "Systematic Unity of the Meaning of the Scriptures" (*Śāstrārtha-samanvayādhyāya*); it is not presented here for fear of prolixity.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrī-Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha* composed by Apyadīkṣita.]
May there be auspiciousness!

Thus, when the objection is raised that the removal of ignorance regarding an object can occur even through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that has not gone out [of the mind], making the acceptance of the modification's exit superfluous, the following response is shown: the acceptance of its exit is purposeful because the removal of that ignorance is not possible without it. Now, [the argument continues]:

Having accepted the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument that the emergence of the mental modification (vṛtti) is not required for the purpose of removing ignorance residing in the consciousness of the object, [the author] nevertheless establishes the emergence of the vṛtti by saying, "However, some...". It should be understood that these two methods have already been explained in detail previously, and thus they are not elaborated upon here.

He raises an objection, saying "Now" (*atha*), [arguing] that there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of the individual soul—designated as the consciousness of the knower—from Brahman.
Is this non-difference established by the Vedāntas as its means of valid knowledge, or by some other means of valid knowledge?
In this regard, the first alternative is not possible, because the Vedāntas are perceived to be intent upon matters such as meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

The second [position] holds that the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not based on the Upaniṣads, because it contradicts the Śruti; this is the intended meaning. Regarding that, he adopts the first alternative and provides a resolution with the words "vedānta... and so forth. He refutes their claim regarding the supremacy [of the Upaniṣads] by stating "sarvepi... and so forth. When one investigates where the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedāntas lies...

All the Vedāntas are in harmony with, that is, they attain their intended meaning (tātparya), regarding the non-dual Brahman who is non-distinct from the individual soul (jīva). He states the marks (liṅgas) that indicate this intended meaning: "Upakrama," etc.; the word "etc.
is for the purpose of including repetition (abhyāsa) and so forth. What are those Vedāntas? Or how [are they]?

In response to the inquiry as to how there can be the existence of the aforementioned marks (*liṅga*) in those [texts], and what the manner of understanding the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through those marks is, he says: "And just as... The meaning is that this alone is the object of the supreme intended meaning of all the Vedāntas, and not [the subject matter of] meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth; this has been explained in detail. Here too—
To the question "Why does he not elaborate further? he replies: "For fear of prolixity," meaning for fear of expanding the text.
[Thus ends the work] of one who has become like the pollen clinging to the lotus-feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrīmat Svayaṃprakāśānanda Sarasvatī.
In the commentary on the *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha* composed by Acyuta-Kṛṣṇānandatīrtha,
[the work] of Śrī Viśvanāthatīrtha, the venerable disciple of the worshipful feet of Śrī Bālamukundānandatīrtha.
The first chapter, "The Restoration of the Book," is completed.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.

Now, how can there be a systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with Brahman, which is non-dual? If it is argued that this is not so because of contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, we say no. For, by means of the scriptural texts and logical arguments cited in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which is apprehended through perception—is shown to be false, insofar as it is of the nature of a superimposition (*vivarta*) upon Brahman.

[This follows] from the understanding of "you" (tvam). Now, it may be objected that the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) cannot be established through scripture (*śruti*) or reasoning (*yukti*), because it contradicts perception (*pratyakṣa*) and other means of knowledge that apprehend the existence of jars and so forth, such as the cognition "the jar exists. On this point, the authors of the *Tattvaśuddhi* have stated: "Perception [does not contradict it]."
It does not perceive the jar, the cloth, or their existence as such; rather, it perceives pure Being (*sanmātra*) which inheres in the jar and so forth by way of being their substrate.
Thus, even perception is indeed concordant with the established doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman as the nature of existence.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Mahāgaṇapati.
Oṃ. I worship that Lord of All (Viśveśvara), who himself dwells in my field (kṣetra) as a Guru equal to Viśveśvara, known by the name Vāṇī;

[that is to say,] he is the self-luminous one known by the name Sarasvatī. Remembering the pair of feet of the Teacher (Ācārya), he composes this commentary, having made me his very form as the scribe.

"I am not the master in this matter," for "master" here means "capable. This is because, in the first chapter, during the investigation into the definition of Brahman, it was established through the various opinions of the teachers that the definition must reside in the Brahman that is to be known.

By defining the state of being established in Brahman, which is the nature of the Lord, both the denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word "That" (*tat-pada*) have been defined; likewise, following that, by defining the individual soul (*jīva*) and its witness (*sākṣin*), both the denoted meaning and the indicated meaning of the word "Thou" (*tvam-pada*) have been defined; and thus, by implication, non-difference in the form of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) has also been established.

The reality of the meaning of the sentence is established, because it does not exceed the intended meanings (lakṣyārtha) of the words. Thus, the subject matter of the first chapter—the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas with respect to Brahman, which is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*) and devoid of attributes—is established in substance within the preceding section. Now, [the second chapter...]

He begins another section in order to establish that the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas—the subject matter of the second chapter—is not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [The question is: "Now, how so? Concordance (*samanvaya*) means intended purport (*tātparya*).
Regarding the phrase "by perception" (*pratyakṣa*), etc.: [this refers to] the world-appearance (*prapañca*), which is a second [entity] in relation to Brahman.

The sense is this: because it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), its non-duality (*advitīyatva*) is sublated; and thus, how could the Śruti have its purport (*tātparya*) in a sublated object? For that would result in the scripture being invalid (*aprāmāṇya*). He provides the resolution: "No," because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is superimposed upon Brahman like a snake on a rope, and therefore non-duality is real and remains unsublated.

Regarding the phrase "by means of scripture and reasoning": these scriptural citations and arguments have already been presented by us on the occasion of defining the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*); therefore, they are not shown here.

Anticipating the objection that it is more logical for scripture and reasoning themselves to be sublated when they contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he raises the following challenge: "But surely..."
The meaning is that there is no [contradiction], because there is no conflict between the perception grasping the existence of jars and so forth— such as "the jar exists"—
and the scriptural statements and logical arguments that convey the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).
Existence, which would contradict the falsity known through scripture and the like, is simply not something graspable by perception.

Therefore, the very suspicion of contradiction with that [scriptural authority] is groundless; this he demonstrates through five viewpoints, beginning with "Here they say" (*atrāhuḥ*). He raises the objection: "If perception does not apprehend the jar and so forth, or if it does not apprehend the existence of the jar and so forth, then it would follow that it is objectless (*nirviṣaya*). To this, he provides the answer: "But rather... (*kiṃ tu*).
Regarding the term "substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna*): "mere existence" (*sanmātra*) means that Brahman, whose nature is Being (*sadrūpa*), alone is the object of perception.
Such being the case, there is not only an absence of contradiction with perception, but rather there is also a gain;
thus he says: "And so it is."

If that were the case, the perception would be merely "existent, existent" (*sat-sat*), and not the perception "the jar is existent" (*ghaṭaḥ san*) and so forth, which conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs. To this we say: no; just as in errors, there is the perceptual apprehension of the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*), which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The positive and negative concomitance of the sense organs is exhausted in that very [perception] alone. Just as the silver portion superimposed [upon the shell] appears through delusion, so too in all cases there is the apprehension of pure Being (sanmātra) by perception;
therein alone lies the operation of the sense organs, while the appearance of distinct objects such as jars and the like [is due to mental construction].

This is because it is accepted [as being] due to delusion. If it is argued that such an acceptance here is without foundation because no sublation (bādha) is observed—unlike in the case [of the dream example]—we say no; for even when no sublation is observed, [the status of an object] is like that of an entity separated by space and time.
Because the very unfitness of objects such as jars for perception is the root cause in that case. To explain:
a jar or the like, being perceived immediately after the operation of the sense organs, is perceived as indeed distinct from everything else;
for at that time, no doubt or error regarding the distinction of the jar and so forth is observed. Even in cases where...

Even in cases such as a post, where there is doubt regarding its being a person or something else, the distinction from things other than those [two] is indeed manifested, because it is neither doubted nor mistaken.
The proponent of the view that [perception] has jars and so forth as its objects raises an objection: "If that were the case. This means: if it had being-in-general (*sanmātra*) as its object.

"By the sense organs," etc.: it might be argued that even if perception had being-in-general as its object, the conformity with the presence and absence of the sense organs would still be established; however, this is not so, because perception would then lack jars and other such things as its objects.

It should not be said that this qualifying attribute is inappropriate because it would entail the non-existence of the injunction regarding the three states (waking, dreaming, and deep sleep), for the point is that there is no logical possibility of requiring the senses for the manifestation of pure Being (*sanmātra*), which is self-luminous.
Here, is the objector a partisan of the Siddhāntin or a proponent of Duality (*bhedavādī*)? In the first case, [the objection] is accepted by him.

By the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭam*), he states that pure Being (*sanmātra*) is not an object of perception (*pratyakṣaprameya*). [He says] "as follows" (*yathā*). "In that very case" (*tatraiva*) means: precisely at the time of the apprehension of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). "By error" (*bhrāntyā*) means: by the nature of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). Regarding "pure Being":
although it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), because it is veiled, there is a requirement for the sense organs in order to produce a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that removes that veil.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the phrase "of the jar, etc.," it is accepted that the manifestation of the jar and so forth, as well as of the entity consisting of its particular differences, occurs through delusion by means of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) characterized as pure Being (sanmātra), which is manifested by the sensory modification (vṛtti). By this, [it is shown that] "Being, Being" alone...

The objector who claims that [the universal] would be perceptible is also refuted by the proponent; for even if the validity of perception is not admitted regarding the existence of that [universal] in things such as a jar,
[the jar itself] remains present in perceptual cognition.
Because it is accepted that [objects] appear in the form of the witness (*sākṣin*). The proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*) raises an objection: "But surely...
Since sublation (*bādha*) is observed in the case of shell-silver and the like, it is appropriate to accept that they appear through delusion (*bhrānti*);
however, since no such sublation is observed for the duality of jars and so forth, for that...

The meaning is that it is untenable for [the world] to be established as mere illusion. Is it intended that no sublation by scripture (*śruti*) is observed, or is it the non-observation of sublation by perception (*pratyakṣa*), or the non-observation of sublation by common worldly experience (*yauktika*)?
The first [alternative] is unproven (*asiddha*), because all that is visible is [sublated] within Brahman by such [scriptural passages] as "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānāsti*).

With the intention of showing that [the opponent's view] is sublated by scripture (*śruti*), he says "No. He accepts the second [alternative] with the words "even in the absence of sublation. He refutes the third [alternative] as being unestablished (*asiddhi*) with the words "space, time," and "pot, etc.
The meaning is: of the pot and so forth, and of the entity consisting of the difference residing in them; [their] very unsuitability for perception [is the point].
To demonstrate the intended meaning first, he shows it with the words "indriya" (sense organ) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*):

the explanation of the term is that "the difference from jars and so forth" means the difference of the substrata (*dharmin*) such as jars and so forth. It is incorrect to say that [an object] is perceived as being divided from everything; for instance, in the case of a post (*sthāṇu*) or similar object in contact with the sense organs, [it may be mistaken for] a person (*puruṣa*) or the like in some instances.

Because a difference characterized by a counter-correlate (*pratiyogika-bheda*) is not perceived; or, if it were perceived, there would follow the impossibility of doubt. Therefore, he says: "Even where...

Furthermore, it is not possible for a difference—which necessarily involves the simultaneous perception of its counter-correlate—to be grasped through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because there are counter-correlates that are not in contact [with the senses] due to separation by space or time.

[Objection: Since [the cognition] arises from the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), let the knowledge of difference be of the nature of memory, just as the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that [object] is. [Reply: Even so, regarding the counter-correlate residing in the difference...

Because that [distinction] is absent in the aspect of the specific property (*vaiśiṣṭya*). Nor can there be the possibility of such an impression (*saṃskāra*) through an inference whose object is the distinction and its specific property—namely, "gold is distinct from a lump of earth because it is a substance"—since an inference cannot occur without the knowledge of the distinction, which would result in the fallacy of circularity (*ātmāśraya*). [This applies to] the subject (*pakṣa*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).

When there is the delusion of non-difference regarding the identity of the reason (*hetu*) with its locus (*pakṣa*) and so forth, inference cannot proceed due to the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and other such faults;
therefore, there is a requirement for the knowledge of their difference, which serves to dismantle that knowledge of non-difference. If it is argued:

"In that case, let there be perceptuality (*pratyakṣatva*) regarding the aspect of difference just as there is regarding the aspect of the qualification by the counter-correlate (*pratiyogivaiśiṣṭya*)," we say: no.

Because when the counter-positive (pratiyogin) is not perceptible, its qualification (vaiśiṣṭya) cannot be perceived; for the perception of a relation is impossible without the perception of both relata. Therefore, when the counter-positive is incapable of being perceived, it is merely of the nature of an illusion.

Regarding the term "appearance" (*pratibhāsa*): since the object of a single cognition is restricted to a specific difference, and objects such as a jar— which are restricted to being the object of a single cognition— are restricted to being the object of error alone, perception grasps only undifferentiated pure Being (*sanmātra*), which is conducive to the establishment of non-duality (*advaita*).

To this he replies: "And of difference" (*bhedasya ca*). The phrase "possessing the rule of being perceived together with its counter-correlate" (*pratiyogi-sahopalambhaniyamavataḥ*) means that, since it has been established in the case of the perception of conjunction and so forth that, for the perception of a relational entity, there must be a cognitive content encompassing all its relata and that such perception is produced by the perception of all its relata, [the same applies to] difference.
Even in the case of perception, it must be stated that [perception] consists either in having the counter-positive as its object or being produced by the perception of the counter-positive;

for the perception of difference is also a perception of a relational entity. And thus, since it is impossible to perceive all those counter-positives that exist, [the required condition] is not established.

Because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), difference is not fit to be an object of perceptual valid cognition; therefore, it is logical that its establishment is based on mere delusion. In our own system (*siddhānta*), however, the meaning is that since the perception of difference is of the nature of the eternal witness (*nityasākṣin*), it does not depend upon causes. [This refers to] the mere rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha*).
Regarding the view that difference is real (*bhedasatyatvavāda*), he raises a possible defense: "The cognition of difference," etc.

"Because it depends on residual impressions" (*saṃskārāpekṣaṇāt*) means because its production from those [impressions] is possible. For, according to others, in the cognition of difference, the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) appear only in their form as the delimiters of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakarūpa*); it is by that form [that they appear].

Since a prior experience encompassing all possible counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) is impossible, there can be no latent impression (*saṃskāra*); therefore, even the status of being a memory (*smṛti*) regarding the aspect of a non-proximate counter-correlate is not possible.
Even while conceding this point, the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) says: "Even so, it is not [the case that... regarding objects such as the Golden Mountain (*kanakācala*).

The meaning is that [the object] has not been previously experienced as the counter-correlate of a difference residing in a proximate jar. He raises the possibility of a prior experience regarding the aspect of "qualifiedness" (vaiśiṣṭya) with the words "the Golden Mountain" (kanakācala).
The meaning is that one should likewise observe such an inference regarding other objects. [This is rejected] because it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya).

The sense is that since the cognition of difference depends upon another cognition of difference, no cognition of difference whatsoever would be established. Regarding the phrase "by non-occurrence": the sense is that, since the cognition of non-difference regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth acts as an obstacle to inference, a cognition of difference regarding the subject and so forth—which serves to remove that obstacle—is necessary.
"Then" (*tarhi*) means: provided that it is impossible for the cognition of the relation with the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to be of the nature of memory.
