In the phrase "of that" (*tadeka-*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the counter-correlate; the meaning is: "of that which is necessarily the object of the cognition of the counter-correlate. The word "cognition" (*vitti*) refers to perception; [this refers to] the cognition of difference produced by the word "difference."
It should be understood that [the term "only"] is used because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not observed as an object. Regarding the phrase "because it is the object of error alone":

the word "alone" (*eka*) is included to prevent the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) would also be imagined (*kalpita*), since the substratum is indeed an object even with respect to right knowledge (*samyagdarśana*). Thus, the substratum is distinguished from the superimposed object.

The state of having error as its sole object is unestablished; thus, the meaning is that perception is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) only with respect to an existent entity, and it is in accordance with the sacred scripture (śruti) which speaks of existence.

The author of the *Nyāyasudhā*, however, says: "Even though jars and the like are perceptible by the senses, [the cognition] 'the jar exists' (*san ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth is merely the permeation (*anuvedha*) of the existence (*sattva*) of the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); thus there is no contradiction. Likewise, [the cognition] 'the jar is blue' (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth is the permeation of the blueness and other qualities of the substrate. If you ask, 'Why should this not be the case?'—it is not so, because of scripture (*śruti*)."

It has been stated that a reality whose nature is *sat* (Being) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, as this is not contradictory. Since this is accepted by all, and since the appearance "the jar is existent" (*san ghaṭaḥ*) and so forth is possible through its very permeation (*anuvedha*), it is cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate existence (*sattā*) in the jar and other such things. Because that [existence] lacks color and other qualities, [attributes] such as blueness reside in the jar and so forth alone.
"It must be postulated because of the disparity"— thus say the teachers of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*.
For although perception grasps the existence of jars and the like, it is [nonetheless] external in its object, such as perception and so forth.

Since it lacks the validity characterized by the revelation of reality (*tattvāvedakatva*), there is no fear that the non-dual Śruti and other texts would be sublated by its contradiction; for a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that which makes known what was previously unknown,
and in the case of insentient objects such as jars, there is no state of being unknown (*ajñātatva*) regarding their objects, namely perception and the like.

Since it cannot be admitted that Brahman is an object of ignorance due to the absence of any function of obscuration, Brahman— which is inherently luminous and thus possesses a manifestation that is naturally present— is itself the object of ignorance; therefore, only that which makes it known is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that reveals reality, and that alone is the object of the resulting valid knowledge (*pramiti*).
Or, let it be granted that objects such as jars are cognizable by the eyes and other senses in accordance with the experience of their being visible and so forth;

nevertheless, there is no contradiction with perception for the scriptures and arguments that establish the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca), because even perception does not apprehend the separate existence of jars and the like [as ultimately real]. Thus he says.

"But the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* says... [The meaning is as follows: In such cognitions as "the jar exists," the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the appearance of the jar's existence is not merely an object characterized by a relation to existence; therefore, there is no contradiction. He raises an objection regarding the consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the existence perceived in the jar must be admitted as residing in its locus, using the word "thus" (*evam*).

The meaning is: why should the appearance of blueness in a jar, such as in the cognition "the jar is blue," not also have as its object the relation of the substrate with blueness? And thus, [the jar] would be like the nature of Brahman; this is the sense. He refutes this by stating "no," on the grounds of the difference between blueness and so forth and [the attributes of] existing things. [He cites] "by scripture."
The phrase "sadeva" and so forth means "according to the Śruti. "Agreed upon by all" means that it must be accepted by everyone;

however, it is not as it is literally heard [in the Vaiśeṣika and other systems], because those [schools] do not accept it, and because there is no contradiction [with our position], just as a rope and the like are the material cause (upādāna) of a snake and the like, so too is the immutable [Brahman].

The meaning is that there is no contradiction in Brahman being the material cause (*upādāna*). Regarding the phrase "tadanu" (following that): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the substrate, which is Being (*sat*). Regarding the phrase "of that" (*tasya*): it means of Brahman, who is the substrate of the world. Regarding the phrase "only in the case of a jar, etc.":
the sense is that it is not possible to postulate that [superimposition] in the case of Brahman, because it would contradict the scriptures (*śruti*). As for perception...

He says, "But the teachers of the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka* [state]... because even though [the cognition] apprehends a separate existence in the case of a jar and so forth, there is no possibility of sublation of the Śruti by that [cognition], since it is a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
The phrase "of that which has an external object" means "of that which has as its object mere insentient matter. The word "tatva" means "in the state of being unapprehended."

The definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) agreed upon by many scholars is that it is a reality not sublated by truth, which is both the knower and the indicator of that [reality]. Since this [definition] does not apply to perception (*pratyakṣa*), the implication is that perception is merely a semblance of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*). Regarding the phrase "of a jar, etc.": although it is not sublated, it lacks the quality of being previously unknown (*ajñātatva*).

The intended meaning is that [the object] does not exist. Otherwise, since it would be possible to demonstrate the status of a pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsatva*) even for a single perceptible jar due to its non-existence, it would be impossible to demonstrate merely the absence of "not being known. Therefore, having accepted that [the cognition] is sublated and impossible, its status as a pseudo-means of knowledge [is established].
It should be understood that what is intended here is "establishment" (pratipādana), meaning the function, the task, or the result.

For this very reason, the Śruti also establishes that the Self alone is the object of knowledge in the passage, "The Self is to be seen," by stating that the Self is the very thing to be known (*prameya*). Indeed, by the phrase "is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*), the act of seeing is not being enjoined;
for that [act], being dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does not fall within the scope of an injunction. Rather, [it indicates] that the Self is worthy of being seen.

Thus, some maintain that because the Self alone is unknown, it is appropriate that it alone is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and this is thereby restricted; however, others hold that although the validity of perception— which grasps the existence (*sattva*) of jars and so forth— is established,

and although one understands that the means of knowing Brahman is not inferior [to that perception], the existence grasped by that [perception] is derived from the notion of a commonality (*anugata-pratyaya*).

Whether it be the form of existence (*satā-jātirūpa*)— as in the cognition of the connection with a specific place and time, "The jar exists here now"— or the form of the connection with those respective places and times— as in the cognition of the negation of its own nature, "The jar does not exist"— it results in either the form of the jar itself or the negation of that very nature. And that...

It is not contradicted by the doctrine of falsity (mithyātva). For even by one who maintains the doctrine of falsity, the intrinsic nature of a jar or the like, its relation to space and time, or the genus and so forth residing therein, are not denied.
Rather, what is denied is their non-sublatability; and non-sublatability alone is not what constitutes reality.

They say that one cannot argue, "Let it be perceivable by direct perception," because even across the three periods of time there is no sublation [of its existence], yet it is impossible for direct perception—which grasps only the present—to apprehend it.

He cites scripture as well as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that the self is self-luminous and is itself the object of knowledge (*prameya*). This is why he says, "For this very reason."

The meaning is: "precisely because it is unknown. Now, [an objection is raised]: does not the scriptural text "it is to be seen" enjoin the vision of the Self? To this he says, "No," for [he states] "not so. The reason is "because it is beyond the range [of the senses]. The sense is that only an action achievable through human effort is fit for injunction.
He asks about the application of the injunctive suffix: "But what [is its function]? He replies: "The suffix -tavya has the sense of 'fitness' (arha)," as in "the Self... [and so forth].
Even if one admits that an insentient object is unknown and accepts that perception, which reveals the insentient,
possesses a degree of validity equal to scripture (*śruti*), this does not contradict the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the existence of jars and other objects grasped by perception.

He states the apprehension of a contradiction with perception regarding the Vedic scriptures (*śruti*) and other sources that indicate falsity (*mithyātva*), beginning with the words "Some, however" (*kecit tu*).

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: existence (*sattva*), which is grasped by perception, results in being either the universal (*jāti*) form, or the form of relation to specific places and times, or the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar and so forth. He states the proof for its being of the nature of a universal (*jāti*).
"Anugata" (inherent) means in the form of "the pot exists," "the cloth exists," and so forth. Regarding the second [point], he states the proof: "iha" (here).

The meaning is that the cognition "the pot is here now" takes as its object, in the form of existence (*sattā*), precisely the relation between the pot and the space and time being perceived. Regarding the third [point], he states the proof: "the pot does not exist."

The meaning is that in the statement "the jar does not exist," because one experiences the negation of the jar's own nature in the form of a negation of its existence, the existence of the jar results in being the very nature of the jar. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that [is] not... [referring to] the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is distinct from the void (*tuccha*).

The sense is that its own nature (*svarūpa*) is accepted. The connection with "no" (*na hi*) is as follows: it is not the case that the nature of the jar and so forth is not admitted; likewise, the connection with "no" is as follows: it is not the case that its relation to space and time is not admitted;
and in that regard, the connection with "no" is as follows: it is not the case that the genus (*jāti*) and so forth are not admitted.

The connection [of the text] is as follows: the meaning is that all of this is indeed accepted by the proponent of the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world, because there is no contradiction. Then, he asks: "What kind of reality (*sattva*), which is opposed to falsity, do you not accept in the world?"—this is the question, "But what? The answer is: *saṃbandhaḥ | etatsarvaṃ jaganmithyātvavādinābhyupagamyata eva virodhābhāvāditibhāvaḥ | tarhi kīdṛśaṃ sattvaṃ mithyātvavirodhi yat tvayā nābhyupeyate jagatīti pṛcchati | kiṃ tviti | uttaram ||* [Connection: The meaning is that all of this is indeed accepted by the proponent of the falsity of the world, because there is no contradiction. Then, he asks: "What kind of reality (*sattva*), which is opposed to falsity, do you not accept in the world?"—this is the question, "But what? The answer is:

"Of them" means "of jars and so forth. However, the connection is that it must be admitted whether they are sublatable (*bādhya*) or not. Since falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being sublatable, its opposite—reality (*satyatva*)—must necessarily consist in being non-sublatable; if this is the case, then let this very [reality] be the object of a true perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus.

Anticipating the concern that there might indeed be a suspicion of contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*), he raises and then refutes that doubt with the words beginning "And not" (*na ca*). The phrase "of this" (*asya*) means "of the world" (*jagataḥ*).

Others, however, maintain that although truth in the form of non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) is indeed graspable by perception, there is nevertheless the perception of a difference in the degree of truth between Brahman and the entire phenomenal world—characterized by the mention of the subordinate vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the Śruti passage, "The vital breaths are truth; of them, this [Brahman] is the Truth"—wherein the truth of the phenomenal world and of Brahman respectively appear to be inferior and superior. Regarding this truth...

O King of kings, O Destroyer of the Destroyer of Love, [this applies] to the nature of being unassailable; for there is no such distinction of superiority or inferiority as "unassailability at all times" versus "unassailability for only a certain time."

Even if one were to accept that the object of perception is existence in the form of non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*), because there is no possibility of superiority or inferiority— such as having more or fewer objects— in qualities like sovereignty and beauty, which are the intended referents of words such as "and so forth" (*ityādi*).

He states the absence of contradiction with perception [in the words] "But others... The connection is as follows: even though existence in the form of non-sublatability (*abādhyatva*) is apprehended by perception, there is no contradiction with the scripture regarding falsity (*mithyātva*). Existence in the form of non-sublatability throughout the three periods of time is opposed to falsity, and that belongs to Brahman alone, whereas for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), however—

In order to state that there is no contradiction with perception—on the grounds that reality (*satva*) consists in being uncontradicted by ultimate knowledge (*tattvajñāna*), and this [reality] is not incompatible with falsity (*mithyātva*) regarding the world (*prapañca*) and Brahman—he states the proof for the difference in reality between them: "The vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). The mention of "vital breaths" is intended as an illustration for the entire phenomenal world.

This Supreme Self is the "truth of truths" for them; that is to say, He is the ultimate reality. Thus, in the Śruti, it is stated that while the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is inferior, the reality of Brahman is superior. In this context, he states the restrictive factor (*niyāmaka*) for using the term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the phenomenal world: "because it is the primary constituent."

The preeminence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which has the form of the thread-self (*sūtrātman*), should be understood as arising from its role as the sustainer of the universe. Nor should it be suspected that this is merely a figurative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); for in a sentence whose primary intent is to establish the true nature of Brahman, the mention of the vital breath—which is but a single part of the phenomenal world—is appropriate.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no purpose in indicating the whole [universe] as such, Brahman alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) by virtue of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is well-known as "real" [in a conventional sense]; however, the phenomenal world is not so, because it cannot be the ultimate reality due to its sublation by scripture (*śruti*). Thus, there exists a purpose consisting in the realization (*pramiti*) of Brahman. To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "and in the case of truth": "king" (*rāja*) refers to kingship (*rājatva*), which consists of the nature of a protector (*pālaka*) or a ruler (*niyantṛ*). This, moreover, is dependent upon a territory to be protected. Thus, in the expression "Viṣṇuśarman, king of kings," the superiority of Viṣṇuśarman is perceived in comparison to other kings; and these two [superiority and inferiority] belong to the act of protection.

Furthermore, regarding the nature of having a universal domain versus a limited domain, Manmatha is indeed renowned as the son of Nārāyaṇa and is exceedingly beautiful; thus, in the Purāṇas, there is the usage "Śrī Rāma, the destroyer of Manmatha," with the intended meaning that he is even more beautiful than him. In that regard:

"Beauty" (sauṃdarya) means possessing an excellence of form and so forth; it should be understood that "supreme beauty" means possessing a form and so forth even more excellent than that. Regarding the phrase "due to impossibility": [this refers to] the state of being a controller, which is distinct from beauty and the like, and consists in the absence of sublation (bādhābhāva). Furthermore...

The meaning is that [the distinction between them] is impossible because there can be no superiority or inferiority consisting of having a greater or lesser range of objects, nor can there be such superiority or inferiority consisting of specific types of existence (*jāti-viśeṣa*).
Now, even if existence is defined as being uncontradicted (*abādhitatva*), superiority cannot be established through another mode;
for instance, regarding the existence of both the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman in the sense of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time:

Even though both are equally related to Brahman, that which is accessible through the Veda is superior, while the other is inferior because it is accessible through worldly means of knowledge; such is the meaning of the scripture.

Even though that [existence] may be possible through another mode, because it must accord with other scriptural passages stating that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, and because it ultimately results in the aforementioned excellence and deficiency, the reality of jars and the like apprehended by perception consists in their non-sublation until the knowledge of Brahman is attained. Thus, it is not [the case that they are real in an absolute sense].

Some say that there is a contradiction with the scripture regarding falsity (*mithyātva*). Others, however, maintain that even though there is a conflict between the scripture— which grasps the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)— and perception— which grasps its reality, [the scripture prevails] because perception is tainted by the suspicion of defects,
whereas the scripture is free from defects, according to the maxim of the "cutting away" (*apacchedanyāya*) based on the priority of the former.

Furthermore, scripture (*śruti*) alone is more authoritative because of its priority; for it is recorded in the *Smṛti* that "the authority of the *Āgama* [scripture] itself is traditionally remembered as superior among those three. Nor is this *Smṛti* restricted to matters cognizable solely through the Veda, since there is no possibility of a conflict with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding such matters, and thus no suspicion [of invalidity] arises.
For it is only in the case of a contradiction with direct perception that it is appropriate to state the superiority of the Veda regarding the meaning of the Veda.

Since it arises from a fallacious origin, there might indeed be a suspicion of contradiction with worldly means of valid cognition (*laukikapramāṇa*) which apprehend existence as opposed to falsity; therefore, he says "not so" by way of another method: "In the scriptural passage 'The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed truth,' if the word 'truth' [refers to] the world's (*prapañcasya*) state of being unsublated throughout the three periods of time..."

If one were to establish [the world] as real, there would be a contradiction with another scriptural passage which establishes that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman— namely, the text "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed reality" (*satyam*). Since it is possible for both scriptural passages to be authoritative through non-contradiction, it is not [justified] through contradiction.

Therefore, validity must be abandoned; hence, the meaning is that since there is no sublation throughout the three periods of time regarding the excellence of being and the objects mentioned in the Śruti, one must conclude that [the authority] terminates right there and not elsewhere. Thus, by the passage beginning with "In this way, they say," the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) [is established].
It has been established that perception does not contradict the means of knowledge consisting of scripture and reasoning; however, it is now stated [by the author] with the words "But others...

that even if perception were to contradict scripture—since perception grasps existence as being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—it does not follow that the proof of falsity (mithyātva) is untenable, because the sublation of perception by scripture is indeed possible. Thus he says: "But others..."
The connection is that *śruti* alone is more powerful than perception (*pratyakṣa*). He states two reasons for the superiority of *śruti*:

"because it is free from defects" (*nirdoṣatvāt*). He raises the doubt that the principle of "absence of interruption" (*apacchedanyāya*) will be explained later, and that the same freedom from defects applies equally to perception as well, by saying "defect" (*doṣa*). This will become clear further on. Of *śruti*...
He states that Manu’s statement also serves as a restrictive authority regarding pre-eminence (*prāvalya*). Regarding the word "pre-eminence":

the meaning is that among those [means of knowledge] under discussion—namely perception, inference, and scripture—it is traditionally known (*smṛtam*) and well-established (*prasiddham*) among Vedic scholars that scripture alone possesses pre-eminence by virtue of its very nature as scripture.

Now, one might object: [is this not a rule] intended to establish the pre-eminence of the Veda regarding matters such as the fact that heaven is the result of [ritual action], which are cognizable solely through the Veda?

However, that statement [of the opponent] regarding falsity (*mithyātva*) is not something cognizable solely through the Veda; nor is it established by inference and so forth, because such means are admitted [to apply there]. Therefore, considering that if the Veda possesses superior authority (*prābalya*) in that regard, that statement is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), he raises an objection with the words "If not" (*na cet*). He refutes it with the word "In truth" (*tatra*). The meaning is: "in a matter cognizable solely through the Veda. And thus:
The sense is that if the statement were to have that [perception] as its object, it would be purposeless.

However, he states that it is meaningful if the statement is intended to establish the superiority of the scripture (*śruti*) which demonstrates the falsity [of perception]. He says: "Of the suspected...
That [statement] refers to the Vedic meaning in the form of falsity, for which a contradiction with perception has been suspected.

This is what is meant: when a conflict between the Veda and another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) arises regarding a certain matter, since it is impossible for both to possess validity in that matter, one must be sublated. When it is established that the weaker is sublated by the stronger, a further inquiry arises as to which possesses the greater strength; and thus it is said:
The meaningfulness of a statement arises from its capacity to convey a required sense. For example:

"A surface is seen in the sky like a firefly, like a fire. Yet no surface exists in the sky, nor does a firefly exist there as a consuming fire. Therefore, even regarding an object perceived through direct perception, it is proper to investigate it.
Furthermore, in the section on witnesses (*sākṣin-prakaraṇa*) in the *Nārada-smṛti*, it is stated: "One who explains matters after having investigated them does not fall away from dharma.

This is because it establishes that even what has been directly perceived must be scrutinized through the instruction of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, rather than placing blind trust in that direct perception. For indeed, [it is not as if] the sky...

The direct perception of the sky as possessing color cannot be refuted by means of perception or other instruments, without the instruction of the authoritative scripture (āgama) which establishes that among the five qualities such as sound, the sky possesses sound alone as its quality; nor can it be [refuted] regarding the sky in proximity.
Because nails are not perceived.

Now, it may be argued that when the invalidity of perception is observed in some instances, there might arise for those who contemplate the alternative opposed to falsity even regarding the perception grasping the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) a suspicion of defects in the form of invalidity;
and consequently, that perception suspected of defects would be set aside by the scripture on falsity, which is stronger due to its being free from defects.

It must be said that [the means of knowledge] is sublated; however, that is not possible anywhere, because no invalidity of perception is observed—this is the view of the proponent of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) being real. [The opponent raises] a doubt, illustrated by the citation of Nārada’s words.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "like a surface" (*talavat*). "Surface" refers to the appearance of a basin made of sapphire.

"Therefore" means that even though a surface and so forth are perceived in space and other such things—which are well-known to all people—such perception is shown to be invalid. "In the case of an object" (*arthe*) means even in the case of an object perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Making known" (*jñāpayan*)...

The meaning is that the teacher, by awakening his disciples to the meanings of the scriptures, does not fall away from *dharma*, which is the means for achieving the highest good (*śreyas*). It is argued that the witnesshood of the self as stated in the Śruti is untenable; for even if it were the knower, it would lack neutrality due to its being an agent.

Regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), one should not hastily place trust in the notion that agency in the self is real merely because of the perception "I act," for even in the world, we observe the sublation of things perceived through direct perception;
therefore, even though agency is seen in the self through direct perception, what [is its true nature]?

Having thoroughly investigated whether consciousness is real like the Self or merely imagined, [the teacher]—by means of scripture and reasoning—concludes that it is indeed imagined; thus, there is no logical inconsistency regarding its status as a witness.
Indicating this to his disciples, he shows that the teacher does not fall away from his duty; this is what is signified by the two statements of Nārada on this subject.

Regarding the section on witnesses (*sākṣiprakaraṇa*): with the intention that even though the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañcasattva*) is thus perceived directly, it is necessary to investigate whether that reality is real or merely conceptual, he states the general purport of Nārada’s statement as it applies to the present context: "Even of that which is perceived through direct perception... and so forth.

The term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) includes scripture (*āgama*), inference (*anumāna*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and so forth, as indicated by the word "etcetera. The connection [of the sentence] is that scripture is more powerful than perception because it provides a demonstration [of the truth]. Having shown that perception is stained by the suspicion of defects, its sublation by scripture is presented for its relevance to the present subject.

He explains [this] with the words beginning "nahi" (not). The connection is as follows: the perception of the blueness of the sky cannot be sublated by perception or other means of knowledge. He raises an objection, suggesting that even without scripture (*āgama*), there exists a sublator of the perception that "the sky is blue," namely, the non-perception of form (*rūpa*) in the vicinity of the sky. [The response begins with] "na ca" (and not). In the vicinity...

The meaning is that when there is the ascertainment of the absence of form, it is determined that "there is no form there," even at a distance; for, by the rule that form must exist pervasively [in its locus], it is impossible for it to exist in only one part of it.

The cognition of that [blueness] is at a distance because it is produced by the defect of distance; this is certain. Since blueness is perceived from afar, its non-perception nearby is possible—just as the non-perception of frost or hail [is due to their subtlety]—on the grounds that proximity itself is produced by a defect. This is established by the force of experience regarding the sky.

Furthermore, it is established that blueness is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). Nor is there sublation by perception on the grounds that for a person standing at a distance, there is a cognition of blueness in a region of space close to the earth, whereas for that same person who has gone near, there is an absence of the cognition of blueness in that very place; for [the cognition of blueness] belongs only to one situated above.

It is logical that the appearance of proximity to the earth [in the case of the blue color] is due to the defect of distance, just as [the blue color] appears in a cloud or a star; for if one perceives odor— which is perceived as being mixed with earth and other elements— in water and in air, [then the same principle applies].

Some are experts in the Purāṇas; for they maintain that the determination [of the location] must be stated solely on the basis of such scriptural authorities as, "One should know that [the fire] is situated in the earth itself," and "The wind is supported by [the fire]," and because the superiority of scripture over perception is beyond doubt.

To the question, "How then is there the cognition that the sky is blue at a great distance? he replies: "The cognition of it as such [is due to] its being at a distance. Regarding the phrase "its sublation," this means sublation by a definitive certainty—that is, of the direct perception of the blueness of the sky. He provides the reason for the phrase "and not [so perceived]" with: "because of seeing blueness at a distance. "Enveloping with frost" refers to a covering in the form of snow; that is near [to the observer].

Even though it exists, it is not seen; rather, it is seen from afar as having the nature of an obstruction such as a tree, and so forth. The meaning is that although form exists everywhere in space, it is seen when near. "Produced by defects" means its existence is dependent upon defects. And as for the non-perception in this case...

It might be argued that because the nature of the prior non-existence of perception is unproduced (*ajanya*), it lacks the quality of being produced (*janyatva*), and thus [the claim of its destruction] would be inconsistent;

however, one should consider that there is no inconsistency, since when the perception of that [object] is obstructed by the defect of proximity, the prior non-existence of that perception does not perish, and thus it possesses a duration dependent upon the defect. This applies to the form (*rūpa*).

Having accepted the rule that [the quality of blue] must be all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), the way in which it is not perceived nearby was explained; now, he states the non-establishment of that rule of pervasiveness, saying: "By the force of experience" (*anubhavabalāt*).

Having refuted the idea that the perceptual cognition of the blueness of the sky is sublated by logical certainty (*yauktikaniścaya*), he now raises and refutes the possibility of its being sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhyatva*).
By the words "nor indeed," etc., [the author] states that there is no blueness whatsoever in any part of the sky situated upon the earth;

rather, the perception of it there occurs due to the defect of distance. By saying "of that which is situated above," he shows that the direct perception of the blueness of the sky is sublated solely by scripture (*āgama*).
[The point] stands. He states another example for the sublation of perception by scripture: "In earth and so forth.

Having perceived fragrance in water and air just as in earth, some who lack proficiency might say that fragrance is also inherent in those two; however, it should be understood there that [the fragrance] has resorted to the water and the air.

The meaning of the statement "one should know that odor resides only in the earth contained therein" is as follows. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": by the word "etcetera," it is implied that taste is the quality of water alone, form is the quality of fire alone, touch is the quality of air alone, and sound is the quality of space alone; furthermore, the perception of taste and the other qualities occurs within earth and the other elements.

The Puranic statements establishing the systematic arrangement— that [the sense organs] have as their objects taste and so forth, which reside in water and other elements contained within earth and the rest— should be accepted.

For it is not possible for people like us to distinguish, through direct perception, that the fragrance and so forth residing in water and other substances— which are supported by [the presence of] earth established from birth— is a quality of earth alone and not a quality of water and so forth;
this is because earth and the other elements are generally intermingled with one another.
If it is argued that, since the manifestation of a quality belonging to one thing in another is possible, perception— which is suspected of error— is corrected there by scripture; then here too,
because of the relationship between material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeyabhāva*) between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), [the same applies].
Due to their mutual intermingling, the appearance of the attributes of one thing in another is possible; thus, perception—
which is suspected of this defect— consists of the fivefold aspects of "is," "shines," "is dear," "form," and "name."

"The first three are of the nature of Brahman, and the latter two are of the nature of the world"—let this be established by scripture according to the method stated by the elders; thus it is equal [to our position], and there is no contradiction with that which is to be relied upon.

[Objection: But surely, since the perception of odor occurs when there is contact with the earth-element portion in the form of flowers and so forth in water, and does not occur otherwise, it is possible to determine through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone that odor is a quality belonging exclusively to earth; why then is scripture (*āgama*) required? [Reply: No, he says "not so" (*na hi*).
The meaning is that it resides in a specific type of earth-substance (*pārthivadravyaviśeṣa*) which is naturally endowed with water as its support (*jalopaṣṭambha*).
The underlying intention is that the conceptualization—that odor exists in water itself, being sometimes natural (*svābhāvika*) and sometimes adventitious (*aupādhika*)—is logically consistent.
Now, one might object that the perception of odor and so forth in water and other such substances is subject to the suspicion of being invalid due to some defect.

It is reasonable that one is instructed by scripture because of its being subject to doubt; however, since perception grasps the reality of the world (*prapañca*) and is thus free from such doubt, how can it be sublated by scripture? With this intention, he raises an objection:
"Of earth and so forth. [The response is: Its freedom from doubt is unestablished.
He states that it is logical for that [position] to be sublated by scripture: "In that case," etc.; "as being conjoined," etc.

Here, "conjunction" means identity (*tādātmya*). Regarding "the property of another": since the real entity (*sad-vastu*)—established by scripture as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world—is the possessor of the property, its manifestation as "Being" (*sat*) within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is possible. Therefore...

The meaning is that [perception] is tainted by doubt as to whether it is of the nature of an error— because it apprehends the world of manifestation (*prapañca*) as having an existence that is otherwise non-existent— or whether it is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), because it apprehends the world of manifestation as having an inherent non-existence. He demonstrates the manner in which perception is sublated by means of the words of the elders, beginning with "it exists."
"The pot exists," "the pot shines," and "the pot is dear"—in these instances, existence (*sat*), consciousness (*cit*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are experienced within the pot.
Since the word "dear" (*priya*) has its primary meaning in bliss, the perception of the pot's identity with bliss is thus established. This is likewise the case for cloth and other objects.
It should be observed: names, jars, sounds, and so forth, which consist of features such as the conch-shaped neck, are experienced as the fivefold parts (*pañcāṃśaka*) of the nature of things;
that is, they are experienced as the fivefold parts of the world. And yet, even throughout the entire world, there is no experience of it being composed of exactly five [elements].

It cannot be said that there is no experience of the perception "suffering is dear," for in some cases, there is indeed an experience of suffering belonging to another; thus, the reality that pervades everything is Brahman alone, whose nature consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), since Brahman possesses that very form.

Because the state of being composed of name and form is established by scripture— through such scriptural passages as "The wise one, having reflected upon all forms"— perception, which grasps the existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
does not have the world's intrinsic reality as its object; rather, it has it as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The meaning is that the Śruti establishes that [the cognition] has as its object only the existence of Brahman as it follows through the world. Thus, having refuted the inherent superiority of perception over scripture, he now refutes the superiority based on its being a necessary presupposition (*upajīvyatva*). "And not thus" means that there is no acceptance of the sublation of perception by scripture.

For the perception of sound consisting of phonemes, words, and sentences is the very cognition of sound upon which the realization of falsity produced by the Śruti depends; since verbal comprehension does not arise without the knowledge of the sound, if the Śruti were to sublate mere perception, it would follow that the perception of sound itself would also be sublated. And so it is.
The meaning is that there would be an injury to those upon whom one depends for livelihood.

They say that by means of the authority of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*), the aspect of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-aṃśa*)—consisting of phonemes, words, sentences, and so forth—is dependent upon perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas the aspect of its existence (*sattva-aṃśa*) is not; thus, [scripture] sublates [perception] in that latter respect. Now, if scripture is more powerful than perception, then [in the case of the injunction] "the sacrificer [is the sacrificial post]..."

In the case of the statement "the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*)," one need not assume a figurative application (*gauṇī vṛtti*) of the word "sacrificer" to the grass-bundle in order to avoid contradicting direct perception. Likewise, in the case of "one should sacrifice with *soma*," when there is a syntactic connection through grammatical coordination (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*), the status of being a means to the desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) applies to the sacrifice, while [the instrumental case ending] applies to the *soma* creeper.
Furthermore, since it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to a difference in operations— namely, that the status of being a means to the sacrifice must also be made known—

it is necessary to explain the connection through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In doing so, rather than postulating a possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) such as "by means of a sacrifice possessing Soma" in order to avoid contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one should accept the other alternative, even though it contradicts the established position (*satpakṣavirodha*) in both cases.

If it is argued that this is because the identity of the sacrificer with the sacrificial grass and the identity of the Soma with the sacrifice can be established through scripture (*āgama*), which is more powerful than [mere] perception, it has been stated in the *Bhāmatī* commentary:
"Scripture possessing a specific intended meaning (*tātparya*) is stronger than perception, not merely scripture in general."

In the case of mantras, there is no intended meaning (tātparya) regarding the object that serves as the door to praise, just as there is none regarding the word-meaning that serves as the door to the sentence-meaning.

The perception arising through the auditory sense organ takes as its object both the nature of sound and its existence; however, by means of scripture (*śruti*), the aspect of its existence is sublated precisely by that perception. Furthermore, that [perception] does not serve as the basis for the form of the scripture, because it is possible for even a fabricated word to convey meaning, and thus for the sake of verbal comprehension...

He offers a rebuttal, stating that because that sentient being is not required [as a condition], and because that portion of the word’s own nature which is the perceptual basis (*upajīvya*) is not sublated—since there is no contradiction—there is thus no conflict with the *upajīvya*. He says, "By means of the authority of scripture" (*āgamapramāṇena*).
He anticipates an objection to the claim that scripture alone possesses greater force than perception, saying: "Now, as for the scripture... (*nanvāgamasya*).

In the Siddhānta, it is established that "guṇa" refers to a quality that accomplishes the sacrifice; thus, the meaning of the injunctive suffix (vidhi) is "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Consequently, when the terms *soma* and *yajati* are accepted as being construed in a non-co-referential relationship (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), the sacrifice is [established as] a means to the desired end.

Since the injunctional suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), heard only once, would result in a plurality of functions by [establishing both] that "Soma is the means for the sacrifice" and that "the sacrifice is the means for the desired object," the sentence containing it would likewise result in a plurality of functions; therefore, to avoid this, their coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) must be asserted.

The meaning is: "given that the established conclusion (siddhānta) stands. Regarding the phrase "to avoid contradiction with perception": under the view of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), the non-difference between the Soma and the sacrifice must be asserted. This is because, in instances such as "this is that" (*so 'yam*), it is well-established that two coreferential terms have the sense of the non-difference between their two referents; and that [non-difference] is contradicted by perception.

The meaning is "for the sake of avoiding that. Regarding the term *somavataḥ*, there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the possessive sense (*matvarthe*) for the word *soma*; thus, according to the Mīmāṃsā method, the sentence-meaning is: "One should effect the desired result by means of a sacrifice possessing Soma.

However, according to the Siddhānta (established conclusion) method, the sentence-meaning should be understood as: "A sacrifice non-different from that which possesses Soma is a means to the desired end."

The instrumental case in the word *somena* is for the purpose of making known that, in reality, the connection between the sacrifice and the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is characterized by the relationship of action and instrument (*kriyākārakabhāva*). This is what was stated by Vācaspatimiśra in the work titled *Bhāmatī*. "Not merely based on the scriptural statement" (*na śrutimātram*); and thus...

In the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*), since the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) has no intended meaning (*tātparya*) regarding the connection between the Soma and the sacrifice, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is stronger than revelation; therefore, it is appropriate to assume a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that avoids contradiction with that perception. Likewise, this applies to explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) such as "The sacrificer is the grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), because they too lack an intended meaning regarding their own literal sense.

Regarding the argument that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses superior authority, it is appropriate to assume figurative senses (*gauṇī*) and so forth even in those [scriptural passages] in order to avoid contradiction with perception; however,

since the scriptures that teach the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*) possess a definitive purport (*tātparya*), they have greater authority than perception, and thus their capacity to sublate it is established— this is the meaning of the passage in the *Samādhāna* (the section on the resolution).
Now, one might ask: "Why should even mantras and arthavādas not have a primary purport (tātparya) regarding their own literal meaning? To this, he says: "Mantra...

The sense is that because there is no fruit in their own literal meanings and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (gaurava), a primary purport is not postulated for them. By means of mantras such as "devasya tvā" and by arthavādas such as "the sacrificer is the prastara," the injunction...
The praise of the sacrifice is to be indicated by means of the meaning of the sentences consisting of mantras and so forth.

If there is an absence of *tātparya* (intentional meaning), how could the form of the deity and so forth—matters not contradicted by other means of knowledge—be established from those [scriptural passages]? If you argue that this is because a word possesses authority (*prāmāṇya*) only when it has *tātparya*, we say no; for [the scripture] states: "One desiring cattle, having performed the *vāravaṃtīya* as the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* upon the *revatī* verses... [and so on].

The aforementioned rule is not established, because we observe that a qualified injunction—such as "one should sacrifice"—possesses authority regarding the nature of its qualifiers, even though that nature lies beyond the primary purport of the injunction. For in this case, the *vāravaṃtīya* sāman, which has the *revatī* verses as its basis, is a qualifier; and unlike qualifiers such as *soma* and the like, this is not something already established in common worldly experience.
Otherwise, if the sentence were to possess authority only for the injunction of that specific sacrifice,

then a relationship with the substance, deity, and so forth— which are indicated [by the mantra]— would have to be stated; for otherwise, mantras and the like would lack a connection with that which they themselves signify.
Since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is connected with praise as its indirect indicator (*lakṣaka*), when praise is to be indicated, the meaning of the sentence— such as a mantra— serves as the means,
just as the current serves as the means when the bank is to be indicated by the word "Ganges. Therefore, they do not have their primary purport (*tātparya*) there [in the literal sense].
With the intention that there is no observation of a speaker’s intent (tātparya) regarding a secondary meaning (lakṣaṇā) in a case where it serves as a means [to another], he says:
"serving as a means for praise. In that regard, he himself provides an example: "serving as a means for the sentence-meaning," referring to words employed with intent toward the sentence-meaning.

The meaning is as follows: just as there is no *tātparya* (intentional focus) regarding the recalled word-meanings that serve as the means for understanding the sentence-meaning, so too is it with those [passages] such as "Vajrahasta," "Puraṃdara," and so forth, which set forth the embodied form of deities and the like, since injunctions (*vidhi*), mantras, and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) lack *tātparya* toward their own literal sense.

Since there would be an absence of *tātparya* (intentional focus) regarding the literal meaning in cases such as the corporeal form of a deity, those [scriptures] would not produce valid cognition (*pramiti*) concerning the deity’s form and so forth; for being the object of the Veda’s *tātparya* is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of being the object of the valid cognition produced by the Veda, and when the pervader is absent, the pervaded must necessarily be absent. As they say: "That which is the [intended] purpose..."

If it is argued that "the word [denotes] its meaning along with [its secondary attributes]," then there would be a contradiction with the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section on deities), because in that section it is established that even from mantras and other sources whose primary intent lies elsewhere, the possession of a physical form and so forth by the deity is proven. With this intention, he raises the objection:

"There is an absence of [primary] purport. To this, the qualification "not contradicted by other means of knowledge" is added; [as in the case of the passage]: "The sacrificer is the *prastara* (grass-bundle)."

This is for the purpose of excluding [statements] such as these. This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of excluding qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that are not established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), such as "Fire is the remedy for cold" and so forth; because the quality of being a remedy for cold is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no need for its establishment through an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). And thus...

The meaning understood even from mantras and other sources that are primarily intended for something else is indeed established, provided there is no contradiction with or sublation by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and since the form and so forth of the deity are of such a nature, their establishment is unimpeded—this is what was demonstrated in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. This is the underlying sense. [The author] refutes this, saying: "No."

The sense is that this very point has been established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section on the Deity), where it was demonstrated that the form and other attributes of the deity are of such a nature that their establishment is free from obstacles. He [the author] refutes this by stating that,
likewise, there is the extension (*atideśa*) of the properties of the *agniṣṭut*, which is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).

The meaning of the Vedic text is: "Having made the *vāravantīya* sāman—which has the *revatī* verses as its substratum—the *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, one should bring about cattle by means of this sacrifice, which possesses the characteristics of the archetypal *agniṣṭut*.
This is because it is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), wherein the sacrifice is qualified by specific attributes such as the *vāravantīya* sāman having the *revatī* verses as its substratum.
The meaning is "of the method of cultivation" (*bhāvanāvidhi*). Regarding the phrase "it has been stated":

the meaning is that there is no established necessity (*niyama*)—in the form of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*)—between being the object of the purport of a word and being the object of verbal valid cognition (*śābdapramiti*).
He explains the aforementioned point with the words "for here... (*atra hi*). And regarding the phrase "nor this...": if [the injunction] were *vāra-cantiya*...

If that [Vāravaṃtīya] were already established through the study of the Veda among those possessing the Sāman and Revatī verses, then—since that qualification would be understood from common experience alone, like curds and so forth—the authority of the sentence would consist solely in its capacity to produce a cognition regarding something distinct from that [qualification]; however, this is not the case. [Regarding] the Vāravaṃtīya...

The meaning is that since the study of the *sāman* occurs only within the *ṛgantara*s, the cognition of the specific qualification known as the *vāravaṃtīya*, which has the *revatī*s as its substratum, must be stated to arise from this very sentence.

Nor can there be an implication of the qualifier by means of an injunction regarding the qualified; for if the qualifier were understood through implication, the injunction would have the qualified as its object, and if that injunction existed, it would imply the qualifier—thus resulting in the fallacy of mutual dependence. Therefore, [the meaning] belongs only to a sentence whose primary purpose is the injunction of the qualified.

Validity must also be stated regarding the nature of the qualifier; yet there is no intention (tātparya) directed toward that [nature], for if there were intention toward both, it would result in a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda). Likewise, even in the case of explanatory passages (arthavādas), which are intent upon praising what is to be enjoined, [validity is established] by means of the objects that serve as the instruments of praise.
The intended meaning is this: since perception is more authoritative than those [other means of knowledge], one must assume other functions (vṛtti) for them so as not to contradict it.

For instance, in the sentence "one should sacrifice with soma," which is intent upon enjoining a qualified entity, if one accepts that the qualified object—the form of the sacrifice—is what is enjoined as non-different from the substance *soma*, then [the following applies] to that...
Just as in cases such as "one should offer with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where the enjoined element— curd and the like—
is not established by worldly convention,
[the specific details] such as the *vāravaṃtīya* chant based on the *revatī* verses arise solely from the sentence intended as a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Just as in the case of a qualifier; for even without [explicit] intention (*tātparya*), the establishment [of a meaning] is to be understood from scripture (*āgama*). This is because a scriptural statement devoid of intention cannot establish a meaning that contradicts perception—such as the perception that grasps the distinction between the *yāga* sacrifice and the *soma* creeper. In that case as well:
Therefore, this recourse to *atvartha-lakṣaṇā* (indication not based on the word's own meaning) is for the sake of avoiding contradiction with that [scriptural injunction].

[Objection: But surely an injunction whose object is a qualified entity implies an injunction regarding the qualifier—such as "one should perform the *vāravaṃtīya* *sāman* on the *revatī* verses"—which produces the cognition of the nature of a qualifier that was previously unknown; and thus, that qualifier is not something to be known through this [injunction] alone. [Response: No, he says "nor even... (*nāpi*).

Because of the postulation of a rule regarding the scope of the qualification: was the nature of the qualification previously established by a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) or not? In the first case, its postulation is redundant; in the second case, the implication of the injunction (*vidhyākṣepa*) is not established, since it is precisely the relationship between the substance and the deity that has already been established [by other means].

Since it is observed that [the injunction] implies the injunction for the sacrifice (*yāga*), so too, by one who asserts that the injunction of the qualified implies the injunction of the qualifier, it must be stated that the qualifier is already established prior to the implication;

and what is the specific injunction that establishes it? Therefore, it must be said that once the nature of the qualifier has been established by the implied injunction, [the qualified injunction follows].

The original injunction (*prakṛtavidhi*) is established as having a qualified object. And when that original injunction has a qualified object, there would be an implication of the injunction for the qualifier by means of that [injunction] for the qualified;

however, this is not the case because the implication of the injunction for the qualifier cannot be established due to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*). This is the meaning. Therefore...

The meaning is that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramiti*) for the specific designation "belonging to Revatī, Ādhāra, and Vāravatī" other than from the present sentence itself. [Objection: "In that case, let there be *tātparya* (intentional focus) even in that regard. [Response: No; he says "atha ca" (and if), the sense being that it would be overly cumbersome (*gaurava*). Nor should one suspect a contradiction with the maxim: "Whatever a word is intended for, that is its meaning. This is because [the present case] is not subject to such suspicion.

Because its general applicability (*autsargikatva*) is logically established, and because in the present case there exists a sublation (*bādhaka*) characterized by prolixity (*gaurava*), it does not apply here.
The phrase "in this manner" (*evam*) means as if in the form of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) within a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*). "There is no intended meaning" (*na tātparyam*):

thus, even though the specific forms of the qualifiers—Revatī and the Vāravantīya—are heard, they are not the object of the [text's] intention (*tātparya*). Consequently, there is no valid cognition (*pramiti*) regarding them.

The point is that, just as [the Veda] possesses the capacity to produce knowledge, it is also possible for other means such as mantras to produce valid cognition regarding the form and attributes of the deities;

thus, there is no contradiction with the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. He states the subject at hand: "From them," meaning from the mantras and arthavādas—specifically, from those scriptural statements which lack an intended purport (tātparya). By means of Soma...

Regarding the question—how there can be no contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa) in the Siddhānta view that the connection in the word "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) is through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), or how one might postulate figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) to avoid such contradiction—the author says: "By means of Soma... and so on. Regarding the phrase "there too": [it refers to] the sacrificer who is...

The meaning of the word "iti" here is "in this very [case]. It should be understood that the illustration refers merely to the postulation of another function (*vṛtti*) in order to avoid contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and not even to the portion concerning the metaphorical indication of possessive meaning (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*).

However, the Śruti concerning non-duality (advaita)—whose intended purport is non-duality as determined by the six marks such as the uniformity of the opening and concluding sections—is more powerful than perception; therefore, it is perception itself that is sublated. It is not the case that the Śruti must be interpreted otherwise to avoid contradicting perception. This has been established in the *Vivaraṇavārtika*.
Scripture does not possess greater authority than perception merely by virtue of having a specific purport;

for even though the injunction "one should cook the *kṛṣṇala* grain" has the purport of establishing that the cooking is for the sake of the *kṛṣṇala*, there is no primary connection with the act of cooking until the transformation and manifestation of its color and taste have occurred in the *kṛṣṇala*.

Regarding the objection that [the scriptural statement] contradicts perception, it is held that in order to avoid such contradiction, the word *śrayaṇa* is accepted as having a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) restricted solely to the act of heating. Similarly, although the sentence *tat tvam asi* has as its purport the establishment of the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman,
the non-difference between the denoted object of the term *tvam* and the denoted object of the term *tat* is contradicted by perception.
Furthermore, because [the Advaitins] accept the definition of consciousness as being abstracted [from its attributes] in order to avoid contradiction with that [perception],

surely even the non-dualistic Śruti, which teaches the falsity of duality, does not intend its own meaning— namely, its own falsity— for there is no evidence for such a thing; and thus, perception, which grasps the reality of duality, [remains authoritative].

"To avoid contradiction, it is more reasonable to interpret even the scripture concerning non-duality (*advaita*) in another way. To this he says: "But the scripture concerning non-duality... The phrase "from that" means from the scripture concerning non-duality; the signs of its intended meaning (*tātparya*) are clearly stated in the scriptures. He refutes the previously stated view that the strength of the intended meaning is the determining factor for its authority.

Regarding the phrase "In the Vivaraṇavārtika, however": the meaning is that it is established by the scripture (*śruti*) that the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the text is that the boiling (*śrapaṇa*) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*śeṣatvena*) to the *kṛṣṇalas*—which are *māṣas* made from gold (*suvarṇa*)—and thus the transformation of form and color is established therein.
The transformation of form and color (*rūparasaparāvṛtti*) consists in the prior destruction of the original form, color, and so forth, followed by the emergence of a new state.

The primary meaning of the word "placing on the fire" (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is that very operation consisting of placing [the substance] on the fire and so forth, which begins with the internal transformation of color, taste, and the like, and ends with that [transformation]; the meaning is its connection [with that process]. Even though the cooking of *kṛṣṇala* grains—consisting of the production of heat from the flames and so forth—is performed, [it is not the primary act].
The sense is that it is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that there is no manifestation of a transformation of color, taste, and so forth [in the fuel]. Now, one might object:

"In this case, placing [the pot] on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) is enjoined; and that is not sublated by perception, because the meaning of the word 'placing' is simply the act of cooking—which consists of actions such as placing the flame [upon the vessel]—and since that is possible even in that [case of the fuel]."

Furthermore, the manifestation of a transformation of color, taste, and so forth is not the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), because that result of cooking, which takes the form of an object (*karman*), is the meaning of the accusative case; and because, by virtue of its proximity to the result, it cannot logically constitute the act of cooking (*śrapaṇa*) which is to be enjoined. Thus, regarding the cooking that is to be enjoined...

Since there is no visible purpose [for the act], it is concluded that this is an injunction for an invisible (transcendental) result; thus, because there is no perceptible sublation of the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) which is the intended meaning (*tātparya-viṣaya*), the figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "cooking" as merely making something warm is not established—this is stated as an objection based on a lack of internal consistency. This refers to the statement, "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

"Extracted" (*niṣkṛṣṭa*) means extracted from the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*), which is the qualified form; the sense is "in that [consciousness] which remains as the mere substantive once separated. Here, this should be understood: the purport (*tātparya*) of the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) is solely to convey the reality that is consciousness (*caitanya*) of an undivided, single flavor. Why? [Because of the text: "Him alone... (*tamevaikam*).

"Know the Self; having known that very [Self], one transcends death. Through thousands of such scriptural passages, beginning with "It is to be seen as one alone," there is a restriction that the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sayings—which serves as the means to liberation—has as its object only such a reality (vastu) alone. This is the meaning of the scriptures: in which...
O seekers of liberation, know that this entire world is superimposed upon that Self; for here, the entire world, which is the object to be contained, [rests] within the Knower.
Even explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), like the injunctive sentences prescribing subsidiary elements such as the *prayāja* offerings,
have no other purpose than the cognition of their own literal meaning; it is only after those meanings have been cognized that they serve another purpose by virtue of their utility.

Just as in the case of the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, these [sentences] also possess an intention regarding their own internal connection, because they constitute a single syntactical unit (*vākyaikavākyatva*).

The restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is for the purpose of negation, and the single word (*ekapada*) is intended to establish the state of having a single flavor (*ekarasa*). If the Self, which is to be known by those seeking liberation, were of manifold flavors, the single word would be meaningless; for the oneness of the Self, being capable of the number one, is already established by the singular suffix itself. This is the purport of this scripture.

The meaning of the particle *eva* is that [one knows] that very same subject under discussion—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—and not even an atom distinct from it; this has been clearly demonstrated in the commentary on the *dyubhv-ādy-adhikaraṇa*. Having known—that is, having directly realized—it, one transcends transmigratory existence, which is denoted by the word "death," in a single way, that is, in a uniform manner.

The instruction of the scriptures and the teacher is to be observed as follows: since the purport of the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" does not reach its fulfillment without the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the words *tat*, *tvam*, and so forth, in order to convey merely the reality that is an undivided single essence,
one must proceed strictly according to their intended purport.
The acceptance of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not merely for the sake of avoiding contradiction with direct perception; rather,

it is because by accepting figurative indication in the sense of pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) for both the words *tat* and *tvam*, and thereby accepting the comprehension of the sentence-meaning,
the contradiction with direct perception is also resolved— it is for this much alone that the contradiction with direct perception is avoided.

The term "indication" (lakṣaṇā) is a conventional usage found in the treatises regarding the Great Sayings (mahāvākya). Thus, even though the intended meaning (tātparya) exists, the acceptance of indication in the Great Sayings—disregarding that very intention solely for the sake of avoiding contradiction with direct perception—is a weak argument for establishing that the intended meaning does not possess the quality of being the primary determinant [of meaning]. As for that which...
It has been stated that for the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), there is no intentionality regarding their own literal meaning since they serve as a means to praise;
he now refutes that. The phrase "of the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) also" means that they possess their own meaning as their primary purpose, rather than having another purpose.
Anticipating the objection that, in that case, the explanatory passages would not be subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*), he says: "only of those [meanings] already established by valid cognition."
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by means of arthavādas (declaratory passages) that lack contradiction with other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," and so forth.

The meaning is that since these [arthavādas] have no fruit by merely producing a cognition of their own literal sense, they are assumed to form a single syntactical unit with the injunction (*vidhi*) as commendations (*stuti*) of what is enjoined. This is just as, for instance, ritual acts such as the *prayāja* offerings have a requirement for a purpose (*prayojana*).

The meaning is that the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth possess syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) with the injunctions for the fruit-bearing *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in the same manner. Regarding the phrase "intermediate connection" (*avāntarasaṃsarga*): it refers to the connection—such as the corporeal form of the deity—which is naturally perceived from the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) prior to their connection with the injunction.

The meaning is that there exists an intermediate intention (*avāntaratātparya*). He states the reason why the sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and the sentences consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have an intention toward the cognition of their own literal meaning: "because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sentences" (*vākyaika-vākyatvāt*).
This is because it is accepted that these very sentences, while remaining as distinct sentences, constitute a single syntactical unit with the injunctive sentences.
The meaning is that the intention (*tātparya*) of sentences toward their sentence-meaning is established in a general sense.

This is because the Vivaraṇācāryas, in their *Nyāyanirṇaya*, have established that even when there is a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*), one does not admit a supreme intermediate intention (*paramāvāntaratātparya*). This applies even in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), where there would otherwise be the contingency of taking the primary meaning as the intended sense.

Furthermore, because this very definition [of perception] is accepted precisely so as not to contradict perception. How then is the superiority of scripture (śruti) stated? It is the general rule that scripture alone is superior to perception due to its being free from defects and its being posterior [in the order of cognition]. However, even perception that is sublated by scripture—
In some way, it must be honored by an offering of its own appropriate objects,
because knowledge devoid of objects is impossible; for this very reason, it has been displaced from the revelation of reality due to its contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita*).
Perception is established by presenting empirical objects that are capable of purposeful action.

As for the demonstration of the example regarding the absence of *tātparya* (intentional focus) upon a meaning that serves as a means to praise—just as in the case of word-meanings (*padārtha*) which serve as a means to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—that [example] is refuted by the statement: "only in the case of syntactic unity of words" (*padaikavākyatāyām eva*).
The meaning is this: when words exist in a state of syntactic unity through the communication of a single sentence-meaning; therein, of the word-meanings...

The meaning is that, because the sentence-meaning lacks the quality of being unprecedented (*apūrva*) in the same way [as the word-meanings], it is not accepted that there is also a distinct intermediate intention (*tātparya*) for them.

By this, the intention regarding the specific qualifier—the *Vāravaṃtīya* sacrifice based on the *Revatī* verses—is also explained. For, as a general rule, the intention of a sentence resides in the sentence-meaning.

Since an injunction of a qualified [object] (viśiṣṭavidhi) has its purport (tātparya) toward a qualified productive operation (bhāvanā) because it is established from the Siddhānta, does it not follow that its purport extends to the qualifiers? For if the status of being the object of the purport of an injunction of a qualified [object] were to reside in the qualificand alone, it would be untenable for that purport to have the qualified [object] as its domain.

For the logicians (*sīmāṃsakānām*), the conventional usage that a qualified injunction lacks intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding its qualifiers is intended to mean that there is no intentionality directed toward each qualifier individually; therefore, this is a logical rule (*nyāyaniyama*) that the capacity to produce valid cognition belongs to a statement only with respect to what is the object of its intentionality.
The meaning is that [the relationship] has been established by the teachers of the *Nyāyanirṇaya* and other [works]. To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"of such [statements] as 'The sacrificer is the *prastara* [grass-bundle]'. However, according to the method stated above, there would indeed be an intention (*tātparya*) regarding the non-difference of the sacrificer and the *prastara*, and so forth; yet that is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The meaning is that the fact that a scriptural passage possesses a secondary purport (*tātparya*) regarding what is stated does not constitute a ground for its superiority [in authority]. In this regard,

even though it is necessary to assume a subordinate purport for mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavādas*)— just as one does for sentences concerning the *prayāja* offerings and so forth— with respect to their respective meanings such as praise or the establishment of a basis, nevertheless, a lack of such a purport does not result in a loss of superior authority.

There is no loss of the status of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*). Since it is possible for the "great purport" (*mahātātparya*) to be that motivator, and because we accept that the great purport of the non-dualistic scriptures lies in the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
the falsity of the perception that grasps the reality of the phenomenal world therein is established.

One should consider such points as "because there is no sublation by Śruti" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in that case": it means provided that the intention (*tātparya*) is not the factor that determines predominance (*prāvalya*). Now, if it is argued that once the predominance of Śruti alone is established, its status as the general rule (*autsargikatva*) must be stated, and if one asks why that is so, [the answer is] because even other things [possess] predominance.
He shows two reasons: "because of its being hatred and because of its being external. Regarding the term *utsarga*:

when there is a conflict between scripture (*śruti*) and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), scripture alone is the sublater. And where scripture sublates perception and the like, those [latter] become devoid of scope (*niravakāśa*).

It occurs as follows: you [must admit] that in such a case, the Śruti itself is sublated by that [perception, etc. which has no other scope (*niravakāśa*). This is because of the logical principle that between that which has scope (*sāvakāśa*) and that which has no scope (*niravakāśa*), the one without scope is stronger. Now, one might object:
"In a situation where perception and the like—which have been sublated by Śruti—are themselves without scope, why is it accepted that they sublate the Śruti? To this, he says:
By the words "But what... and so forth, the meaning is that it must be rendered probable or established.

By the phrase "atadavat," the meaning is precisely because of the impossibility of a perception that lacks an object. By the word "pracyāvitam" (dislodged), it is meant that duality, being sublated by scripture, cannot possess the nature of reality; for a perception that contradicts non-duality cannot have the character of revealing the ultimate truth.

The fact that [the opponent's position] has been displaced from its status as a valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇya) is to be understood; it is established in the Bhāṣya and other works—this is the remainder [of the sentence].

In short, although the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated by the universally established perception that "this is not silver," it is nevertheless accounted for— out of deference to experience—
by the admission of silver as conjoined with the mother-of-pearl in the locus of the chest, and not in contradiction to that [sublation].
It is postulated that the object is silver, which is internal, mediated, and indeed non-existent. And thus,

[there is] the perception grasping the difference between the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass (prastara), which persists until the realization of Brahman through its correspondence with purposeful action (arthakriyā).

Since it is impossible to establish [the identity] by accepting that the object is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), the Vedic text "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) would otherwise be subject to sublation and thus become entirely devoid of an object; therefore,
