to avoid this, the Vedic text itself sets aside the general rule (*utsarga*).

Since, in our system (siddhānta), perception and other means of knowledge sublated by Śruti are admitted to possess only a conventional validity (vyāvahārikaprāmāṇya), it is established that the charge of being "without scope" (niravakāśatva)—in the sense of being devoid of an object—does not apply to perceptual cognition as it stands in the final doctrine. To demonstrate this, he states the *kaimutika* (how much more so) argument with the words, "What need is there for much [explanation]? [This applies even to perception], which is sublated by the Śruti of non-duality.

While there exists a subverting argument against the acceptance of the perception of jars and the like as being without an object— namely, the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)— no such subverting argument exists for the acceptance of the perception of mother-of-pearl-silver and the like as being without an object, even by those who maintain that [the object] is non-existent.

Nevertheless, because silver and so forth appear [in that cognition], the fact that it has silver and so forth as its object at that time is accepted in the Siddhānta, since it is impossible for an experience to be without an object. Therefore, where it follows that a perception sublated by Śruti would otherwise have no scope, it is proper to set aside the Śruti by means of that perception.

The meaning is that it is established that the primacy [of direct perception] is the general rule (*autsargika*), because of the scriptural statement: "And it is accepted by the final doctrine (*siddhānta*).
"Interspersed with mother-of-pearl" means having attained identity (*tādātmya*) with mother-of-pearl.
"Remote" means situated in another external location. "Internal" means having the form of the mental representation (*jñānākāra*). Not...

And regarding the phrase "it is imagined (*kalpyate*)," the word "for" (*hi*) indicates that this is due to contradiction with that [perception]. The meaning is: because it contradicts the experience of the distinctness between the "this-ness" (*idamartha*) and silver. The underlying point is that it is impossible for remote silver and the like to possess identity (*tādātmya*) with the "this-ness. The phrase "and thus" (*evam ca*) refers to the case of contradiction.

The meaning is: when it is logical that the Vedic scripture (śruti) sublates [the perception] because there is no room for anything else in between. Now, one might object: "Since the difference between the grass-bundle (prastara) and the sacrificer, which is sublated by the scriptural statement of their non-difference, has a merely apparent (prātibhāsika) object—just like the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—it is not necessary to assume a sublation of that perception by the scripture. To this he says "no."

"By accepting [the object] as having a merely apparent (prātibhāsika) nature. This indicates the reasoning for why it is impossible for the difference between the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass-stalk—the object of perception—to be merely apparent. "As long as... [is used] as in the case of nacre-silver.

Just as the sublation of the perception "this is silver" by the knowledge of Brahman results in the cessation of that perception and the absence of its appropriate causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), so too, prior to the knowledge of Brahman, there is the sublation of the difference between the sacrificial stone and the sacrificer,
as well as the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency.

The meaning is that there exists a reason for its being merely apparent (*prātibhāsikatva*). The phrase "of that which persists until the knowledge of Brahman" means "that which is free from sublation prior to the knowledge of Brahman. The phrase "by correspondence with causal efficiency" means "by virtue of having as its object a distinction capable of causal efficiency. Regarding "sublatability," it refers to the [false] identification of the sacrificer with the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*).
The phrase "of the apprehending perception" is to be supplied; "in every respect" has this meaning:

it has already been stated that it is impossible for that perception to have phenomenal difference as its object, and it will be stated immediately hereafter that it is likewise impossible for it to have empirical difference as its object.
Furthermore, an ultimate distinction cannot be accepted because it would contradict the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*).
Consequently, since that [distinction] would necessarily be rendered devoid of an object and thus lack any scope, the connection is that the scripture itself must be interpreted otherwise.
The [objection] regarding the locus of that proof and so forth is answered otherwise according to the method established [in the *Tatsiddhyadhikaraṇa*];

nor is perception justified here by accepting a distinction between a real and a conventional object for scripture and perception, as is done in the case of non-duality (*advaita*) scripture and perception.

It is impossible to establish the reality of the identity between the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) and the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) on the basis of a single *arthavāda*, because such a claim contradicts numerous scriptural passages supported by the sixfold marks of interpretive intent (*tātparya-liṅga*), which demonstrate that everything other than Brahman is false.

He states another method of interpretation [in the words] "tatsiddhi" (for the sake of its establishment). Since the primary meaning—namely, non-difference—is impossible due to contradiction with perception, the author of the Sūtras has shown the relevant quality (*guṇa*) in response to the inquiry: "What quality is to be assumed when the word 'sacrificer' is applied to the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) through secondary figurative usage (*gauṇavṛtti*)?"

Regarding the phrase "its accomplishment" (*tatsiddhi*): the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of that sacrifice (*kratu*) is its benefit (*upakāra*), which is a quality (*guṇa*) to be effected by the sacrificer and the *prastara* grass-bundle; the similarity between those two, consisting in their being the means of accomplishing the sacrifice, is what is meant by "quality.
In this same way, for other explanatory passages (*arthavādas*) as well, [the meaning is established] in order to avoid contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*).

The meaning is that these [reasons] have been formulated by the venerable Jaimini in other topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) as supporting grounds for their respective positions. Now, one might object: in cases where there is a conflict between non-duality (*advaita*) as taught in scripture and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), is it not the case that absolute non-duality is the subject matter of scripture, while conventional duality (*vyāvahārika dvaita*) is the subject matter of perception?

Just as a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is postulated [in other cases], so too here one might propose that the real non-difference between the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) and the grass-bundle (*prastara*) is the object of scripture (*śruti*), while the imagined difference is the object of perception; to this he says "no," beginning with "not" (*na*) and "here" (*iha*). "Here" means in the context of the statement "the sacrificer is the grass-bundle. [The opponent claims: "The sacrificer is the grass-bundle..."

Thus, it cannot be established by means of an *arthavāda* that there is an ultimate identity between those two, because this would contradict the scriptural texts on the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita-śruti*). Nor should it be argued that, since the non-duality scriptures also lack the nature of an injunction (*vidhi-rūpatva*) and are therefore no different from an *arthavāda*, there is an absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) [as to which set of texts is authoritative]. For even so, those [non-duality scriptures] are numerous.

With the intention that [the distinction] cannot be established due to the absence of any decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*), he says: "anaikety" (not one). Furthermore, if there were non-difference between the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*), that explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) would have no intended meaning (*tātparya*), because there is an absence of any indicative mark (*liṅga*) to grasp such a meaning; whereas for the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*), there exist six kinds of indicative marks that grasp their own intended meaning.
For instance, in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, beginning with "In the beginning,
my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," the Śruti concludes by stating "All this has that as its self," thereby presenting the reality as non-dual and comprising the self of all.

By the mark of uniformity between the opening and the conclusion, it is determined that the purport of this chapter lies in the reality of non-duality. "O dear one, before creation, this perceived world was indeed Brahman alone, without a second and of a single nature"— thus [the father spoke] to his son in order to instruct him.
This entire statement of Uddālaka means: "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam*);
that is to say, it has the nature of the existent reality (*sadvastu*) under discussion. The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not intended to be emphasized here.
Thus, there is repetition (*abhyāsa*) of the sentence "All this has that as its self" more than once.

The establishment of the non-dual reality is the proof of its unprecedented nature (*apūrvatva*), because it is not accessible through other means of knowledge. This is because the statement "A person who has a teacher knows" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.14.2] introduces the knowledge of the existent non-dual reality under discussion, and the subsequent statement regarding the lack of connection with the phenomenal world (*prakṛtyasaṃpatti*) declares that liberation is the fruit thereof. Furthermore, the fruit itself serves as an indicator of the text's primary purport (*tātparya*).

Furthermore, there are explanatory passages (arthavādas) such as those concerning the father and son, which serve to grasp the intended meaning; therein, by means of illustrations such as clay and so forth, there is the demonstration that the phenomenal world is non-different from Brahman, preceded by the demonstration that it is an effect of Brahman. Thus, by the sixfold marks of intentionality, the non-dual reality [is established].
Thus, the subsequent nature of that chapter is established; and so it is for the chapters as well.

Thus, when the sentence *tat tvam asi* conveys that the referent of the term *tvam* (the "you")— characterized by non-omniscience, the state of being an enjoyer, and so forth— is in fact Brahman characterized by omniscience, the state of being a non-omniscient enjoyer and so forth perceived therein is entirely without foundation.

To avoid that [objection], it is said: by adopting the established distinction that the state of being an enjoyer and so forth belongs to the Self when conjoined with the ego (ahaṃkāra), whereas the pure Self, when extracted from that, is of the nature of the indifferent Brahman, the figurative method known as *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (the abandonment of parts) is resorted to. Thus, regarding the *kṛṣṇala*...
In passages such as "one should take refuge," since there would otherwise follow the consequence that perception is entirely devoid of an object,
figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is employed in the scripture to avoid that result.
The signs of the intended meaning (*tātparyaliṅga*) should be observed in other *Tara* mantras and in other scriptural passages (*śruti*).

Thus, with the intention that the non-dualistic scriptures possess superior authority because they are endowed with these aforementioned signs of intended meaning, he says: "of six kinds" (*ṣaḍvidhā*).

[Objection: In that case, would the non-difference between the sacrificer and the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*) be merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), while the meaning of the scripture [would remain literal]? And therefore—
If it is argued that the perception of difference between the two [the Self and Brahman], though contradicted by scripture which establishes their non-difference on the conventional level,
may nonetheless have conventional difference as its object; and thus, since perception lacks any scope [for ultimate reality],
it cannot sublate scripture— this is not so, for the case is the same.

Because difference and non-difference cannot coexist in one and the same thing, such a conceptualization is untenable; therefore, let it be that their non-difference is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). The sense is that the meaning of the scripture is not the non-difference of silver in mother-of-pearl, because there is no perceptual appearance of the non-difference of the sacrificer in the sacrificial grass-bundle (*prastara*). Regarding the scripture...

Having shown that "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) is an instance of an exception (*apavāda*) to the general rule (*utsarga*) that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) possesses greater authority, he states another instance of an exception: "In the same way, 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*). For by the sentence "That thou art," the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is consciousness qualified by agency, enjoyership, and so forth, [is understood] according to its own natural sense as being something distinct.

By means of that which is the opposite of this— namely, through Brahman whose nature is consciousness characterized by omniscience, the state of being the enjoyer, the non-enjoyer, the agent, and so forth— an eternal non-difference is established. In accordance with that [non-difference],
if one were to admit attributes such as constant non-omniscience in the individual soul (jīva), then [the existence of] omniscience, which is its opposite, [would be contradicted].

Perception that apprehends transmigratory existence in the form of agency and so forth would be without a real objective basis; therefore, the sublation of the Śruti by perception—of which no other scope remains—must be accepted. And that sublation occurs only in the sense that the Śruti teaches the non-difference of the pure consciousness aspect of the substantive [the Self], and not as a sublation consisting in the contraction [of its meaning].

The meaning is that the distinction [between this case and others] is that, as in the phrase "the sacrificer is the *prastotṛ*," one abandons the primary sense in its entirety and conceives of a secondary (metaphorical) sense. "Of that which is colored by the *ahaṃkāra*" means: of the consciousness qualified by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "By the abandonment of a portion" refers to [the abandonment of a portion] of that which is denoted by the term *tvaṃ*.

It has two parts: the qualifying part (*viśeṣaṇa-bhāga*) and the qualified part (*viśeṣya-bhāga*). Therein, by means of abandoning the qualifying part, the *lakṣaṇā* (indirect indication) of the term "thou" (*tvaṃ-pada*) is accepted in the pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) which constitutes the qualified part.
The same should be understood regarding the referent of the term "that" (*tat-pada*). He states another instance of such exception (*apavāda*): thus...

Regarding the term *kṛṣṇala*: "In the case of application. This means that if, by the force of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*), one were to accept the cooking (*paryāśrapaṇa*) of *kṛṣṇala* seeds—extending up to the point where their color and taste are transformed—one would find no object for the perceptual observation of the absence of cooking in them; this is because it would contradict the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita*).

Because an absolute absence of cooking is impossible in those [worlds]; since one must state that the cooking mentioned in scripture exists in them only in a conventional sense, an absolute absence of it in them is likewise impossible in a conventional sense;
for there is no absence of cooking that remains uncontradicted during the time of conventional experience.
And because appearance-like status (prātibhāsikatva) is impossible, the meaning is that, consequently, the examination would be without an object. Likewise,

even in the case of "one should not sacrifice with soma," once the sentence-meaning is established as "one should effect the desired end by means of a sacrifice with soma," if one were to accept the non-difference between soma and the sacrifice on the strength of the direct scriptural statement (śruti), [it would lead to the aforementioned absurdity].

It should be understood that, lest perception apprehending a difference between the two find no scope, the possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) for the word *soma* is accepted in order to avoid contradiction with that perception.

In the passage "There is no diversity whatsoever here," since it is possible to somehow establish a subject matter, there is no need for the subordination of the more powerful Śruti; thus, there is no possibility of any lack of systematic consistency. Alternatively, this is not the case in instances such as "One should cook a kṛṣṇala" or "One should sacrifice with Soma."
The recourse to figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) is not based on direct perception, but rather on the impossibility of performance; for,

just as heating alone is performed in the case of the *kṛṣṇala* gold grain, the primary act of cooking cannot be performed [in its literal sense], nor can a sacrifice identical with the Soma substance and its instruments be performed by anyone, just as a sacrifice is not [identical] to those means.

It is possible [to say this]. Nor should it be argued that what is intended as something to be performed is merely being expressed by another word as "incapacity for performance" due to contradiction with perception—
as in the case of the statement, "One should make the lunar orb radiant."

Because even though the luminosity of the moon’s orb—which is intended as something to be performed—is not contradicted by perception, one observes an inability to perform it; therefore, that [luminosity] is distinct from that [moon].
Thus, for that very reason, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to in that case. Consequently, this follows the logic of the "cutting" (*apaccheda*).

Furthermore, there is no sublation whatsoever of the established scriptural authority regarding its greater force. Now, how is it that the principle of the "subsequent annulment" (*apacchedanyāya*) applies here? It is said in reply:

Thus, having shown that perception, being without scope, constitutes an exception (*apavāda*) that sublates the general rule (*utsarga*)—namely, the Vedic revelation—he demonstrates, with reference to the subject at hand, the inherent superiority of the Veda over perception. He does so by the phrase "in some way":
in cases where there is a conflict between the Vedic texts asserting the falsity of duality and the perception grasping that [duality] as real, [the Veda prevails].

Even that which is sublated by scripture is not entirely without scope; for [scripture] has its scope in reference to imagined duality and the existence of universals (jāti) and so forth residing therein. Therefore, the sense is that here it is perception alone that is sublated by scripture.
The meaning of the phrase "in some way" (kathaṃcit) is "by means of presenting imagined duality and so forth."

In some way, the word "prior" [in the compound] has "perception" as its understood remainder. "Not at all" means that under the view that *tātparya* (intentional meaning) is the determinant of strength, there arises the contingency of instability—namely, the observation of sublation even in the case of *śravaṇa* (hearing) and so forth, which are themselves the objects of that *tātparya*; however, this is not the case under the view that the primacy of *śruti* (direct statement) is the general rule.

The meaning is that it does not follow [as a valid objection], because of non-perception. Now, while many examples have been shown where direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is sublated by scripture (*śruti*), only one example has been shown where scripture sublates direct perception;
therefore, it must be said that, as a general rule (*utsarga*), direct perception possesses greater authority than scripture, and not otherwise.

Because the opposite view is unsatisfactory, he says, "Alternatively" (*athavā*). "Non-different from that" (*tad-abhinna*) means non-different from Soma. "Of her" (*tasyāḥ*) means due to the incapacity for performance. "From that" (*tataḥ*) means due to contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Precisely from that" (*tata eva*) means precisely from the incapacity for performance, and not from contradiction with direct perception; therefore, it is not [the case].

The meaning is that the primacy of perception (*pratyakṣaprāvalya*) is the general rule (*autsargikatva*), because it has been shown previously that there are many instances—such as the perception of the blueness of the sky—which are sublated by scripture (*āgama*). "Therefore" means: because the possibility of the primacy of scripture exists as the general rule. "There is no contradiction whatsoever" refers to [the contradiction of] scripture.

The meaning is that the sublation previously suspected— namely, that even in cases such as "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ), there would follow the establishment of the identity between the sacrificer and the grass-bundle—
is not present, because it has been refuted in many ways.

He raises an objection in order to apply the logic of "removal" (*apacchedanyāya*) to the present case: "Now, how [is this]? The explanation of the objection indicated by the word "how," as well as its refutation, will occur later with the words beginning "yat tu" and so forth;
for now, he first applies that logic to the present case: "It is said. (*ucyate*).

Just as in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, when there is an interruption (*apaccheda*) of the Bahiṣpavamāna chant by one who knows [the ritual], if it should happen that the knower is interrupted, the scriptural injunction— "having performed the sacrifice without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*), he should sacrifice again with it"— gives rise to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the interruption of the Bahiṣpavamāna by the knower.

The cognition that [the expiation] must be performed arises subsequently when there is a disconnection of the *pratihartṛ* priest, produced by the observation of the Vedic injunction stating, "If the *pratihartṛ* should be disconnected, one should give away all one's possessions," which conflicts with the prior cognition that the disconnection of the *pratihartṛ* does not necessitate the performance of the expiation.

It is sublated. In this same way, the perception of the reality of jars and so forth is sublated by the cognition produced by the subsequent scripture concerning their falsity. Nor is there a contradiction in the cited instance of the prior cognition of the duty of one occasional rite being [sublated] by the subsequent cognition of the duty of another occasional rite.

Even when there is a contradiction, the scripture that generates the cognition of duty based on a prior cause has its scope in cases where there is a simultaneous excision (apaccheda) of both [the Udgātṛ and the Prastotṛ], or where there is an excision of the Udgātṛ alone,
or where the excision of the Udgātṛ occurs later; however, non-duality is directly perceived.
One should not suspect an inconsistency by arguing that, since the Veda is sublated and there is no other object [of cognition], it would therefore be without a basis.
When, among the officiating priests who have approached while maintaining physical contact for the sake of the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant,

the *udgātṛ* priest is deprived [of his office], the sacrifice that has been commenced must be completed without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇā*), and then that same sacrifice is to be performed again; thus,
the completion of the commenced sacrifice without a fee is caused by that deprivation.

It is prescribed as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Likewise, for the *pratihartr* priest, an expiation consisting of the completion of the very sacrifice already commenced—characterized by the giving of a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the form of the gift of one's entire property—is prescribed on account of his severance. And thus, in a single performance, by chance...

When both [causes] have occurred in succession, since it is impossible to perform two contradictory penances that have been prescribed, and it being established that one or the other must be performed, the question arises as to whether the penance occasioned by the prior cause should be performed, or rather that occasioned by the subsequent cause.

He states the settled conclusion (*niṇaiya*) with the words "the disconnection of the Udgātṛ," and so forth. This text refers to that performance in which the disconnection of the Udgātṛ occurs first.
Regarding the phrase "by observing the Śruti": immediately after the occasion (*nimitta*) has arisen, the occasional injunction (*naimittika-śāstra*) [is to be applied].

The intended meaning is "because it is established by the Buddha. Regarding the phrase "the cognition of the duty occasioned by the disconnection": that expiation for which the disconnection of the *udgātṛ* is the occasioning cause is "occasioned by the disconnection of the *udgātṛ*";

the meaning is the cognition of the duty to perform that [expiation]. The word "contrary to that" refers to the duty occasioned by the disconnection of the *udgātṛ*, which is the referent of the pronoun "that."

And "being contradictory to that" is a qualification of "that which ought to be done" (kartavyatā). The sense is this: just as in a single ritual performance (*prayoga*) there is a contradiction between the state of being without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇatva*) and the state of giving away one's entire property (*sarvasvadakṣiṇākatva*), so too, within a single locus such as a jar or other phenomena, there is a contradiction between reality (*satyatva*) and falsity (*mithyātva*).
Consequently, the cognitions of these two stand in a relationship of the sublated (*bādhyatva*) and the sublator (*bādhakatva*). Nor is it [the case] as in the example cited...

Regarding the term *sthala*: it means "in that case where there is first an excision (*apaccheda*) of the Udgātṛ. Regarding the term *śāstra*: it means "the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) stating, 'If the Udgātṛ should be excised... Regarding the term *yugapat*: it refers to the situation of simultaneity between the excisions of the Udgātṛ and the Pratihartṛ; in such a case, [the rule applies] solely on account of the excision of the Udgātṛ.
The sense is that an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed because it has been so stated by the teachers.

"But [it is] perceptible" means that the reality of duality is perceived. "By the Śruti on non-duality" means by the Śruti on the falsity of duality. "Because there is no other object" refers to the reality perceived within the phenomenal world of duality.
The point is this: if, upon hearing [the word], there were no other sentient beings present there, then the cognition of a sentient being would be objectless;
yet this is not tenable, because a perceptual cognition is never seen to be objectless, and such a thing is not admitted.
In cases such as a jar where perception functions in a manner sublated by scripture, that perception—
having attained its empirical object and thus fulfilled its purpose—
is completely set aside once it is contradicted by the subsequent [scriptural] knowledge, just like a prior grammatical rule is superseded by a subsequent one.

Furthermore, because there is no search for another object, it can be asserted here as well that perception has scope regarding the existence of Brahman, which is known through all cognitions; for even in a single ritual performance, when two successive causes arise, there is a corresponding sequence of the duties to be performed contingent upon those causes.

Just as the two cognitions of "this is a jujube fruit" and "this is red-colored" arise sequentially, so too the two cognitions regarding what ought to be done are both valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, there is no sublation of the preceding cognition by the subsequent one, nor is there any annihilation [of its validity].

An example: for this very reason, according to the section on disconnection (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*), the meaning of the scriptural injunction regarding the ritual procedure is as stated in the *Śāstradīpikā*: "Even though a sacrifice must be performed in one way prior to the occurrence of a contingency (*nimitta*), when that contingency has arisen, it must be performed in another way. Thus says the *Śāstradīpikā*.

He offers this rebuttal: "In that case," [meaning] even though the absolute reality (*pāramārthika-sattva*) has been negated by the Śruti within the dualistic phenomenal world (*dvaita-prapañca*), the empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-sattva*) is not negated by it; therefore, the perception of reality (*sattva-pratyakṣa*) is not without scope. The word "object" (*viṣaya*) implies "in the form of reality" (*sattva-rūpa*). Now, one might object: "Is not reality in Brahman absolute?"

In the view that there are three levels of existence— wherein the existence of the phenomenal world (prapañca) such as jars and the like is empirical (vyāvahārika), and the existence of illusory silver in mother-of-pearl and the like is apparent (prātibhāsika)— no separate object need be sought for the category of the existence of jars and so forth; for the very object existing in the jar and such is its empirical existence.

Anticipating the objection that in a case where there is a contradiction between two coverings (apacchada), the scripture based on the prior cutting-off (pūrvāpacchedanimittaka) is entirely sublated, he says: "In this case too," meaning that even though the perception of the reality of duality— such as a pot and so forth— does not find existence within duality, it is not rendered devoid of scope by the [scripture] based on the prior cutting-off.

The meaning is that, just as the scripture on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) finds its scope in other applications, so too here, the existence of Brahman— which serves as the substrate for duality— can find its scope in things other than the duality of jars and the like.
Regarding the claim that the existence of the very nature of Brahman is an object of perception, [the following is the] reasoning:
Intending the logical principle (*nyāya*), he says: "All," and so forth. Being known by all cognitions is the qualifier of "Being" (*sat*).

For in the world, if one holds the position that there is only one "Being" everywhere—regardless of whether a particular object is present in the mind—then since neither empirical being (*vyāvahārikasattva*) nor illusory being (*prātibhāsikasattva*) would exist, one would necessarily have to seek another object for the perception of "Being."

Just as when a subsequent burden is placed [upon a scale], all that is perceived as "existent" (*sat*); therefore, the existence (*sattā*) of the entire world—which is known through all cognitions—is none other than the existence of Brahman, the substrate of all, and not something distinct from it, because of the logical fault of unnecessary complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). How was it previously...?
He now raises the objection indicated by the word "yat tu" (as for what was said): "In the case of the jujube fruit.

Just as in that case, first a dark form arises, and subsequently, following the destruction of that prior form, a red form arises; likewise, by means of the prior cause, the duty occasioned by that cause arises immediately upon birth.

The meaning is that [the subsequent duty] arises even when there is no cause, and that the production of the duty occasioned by the latter event occurs preceded by the destruction of the duty to be performed previously.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Like the cognition of two forms. And thus, even in the case where a subsequent contradictory sublation occurs...

The sense is that since there is no lack of authority for the scripture regarding the prior occasional rite (*pūrvanaimitika*) during the sacrifice, it is precisely the preservation of its authority that serves as the basis for such a [subsequent] arrangement. To provide support for the claim that the duty of the prior occasional rite existed as a reality prior to the performance of the subsequent occasioned rite, he says: "Therefore, previously... and so forth.
The meaning is: "In reality, it is precisely because of that admission.

For prior to the occurrence of the dismemberment (*avapāta*) of the *pratihartṛ*, the sacrifice—which in fact ought to be performed without a sacrificial fee (*adakṣiṇa*)—is subsequently [performed] otherwise, namely with a total fee (*sarvavedasa*), once the occasion (*nimitta*) consisting of the dismemberment of the *pratihartṛ* has arisen.
The meaning is that it should be performed with the right hand, according to the intention of Śaṅkuka.

In that case, while being a constituent part (*aṅga*), there is no requirement for performance; furthermore, in a sacrifice where there is a subsequent cutting off of the *pratihartr*, the expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) occasioned by the prior cutting off of the *udgātr* does not possess the status of a constituent part (*aṅgatva*). This is because the scriptural injunction regarding the *āhavanīya* fire applies to acts other than the *pada-homa*.

Just as [the rule] regarding the object of the *homa* applies, so too the scriptural injunction concerning the *udgātṛ* pertains to a sacrifice that occurs after the *pratihartṛ* has been excluded from the dismemberment (*paścheda*). For it is stated in the *Nyāyaratnamālā*: "Of that which is common..."

In the analysis of the sublation of what is obtained (*prāptabādha*)— as defined by the statement that "the restriction of a scriptural rule (*śāstra*) through its specific scope and so forth constitutes a sublation of what has been established"— it being thus, the meaning of the scriptural injunction is as follows: for one who is devoid of the subsequent cutting off (*apaccheda*) of the *udgātṛ*, there occurs the cutting off of the *pratihartṛ*.
It should be understood that for the *kratu* sacrifice, which is the primary limb of all the Vedas, this same principle applies even in the case of the cutting off of the *mudgātra*.

As for the statement from the *Śāstradīpikā* that was cited, it means that although the knowledge regarding the previous expiation has already arisen, it becomes false because it is sublated; however, such is not the case for the subsequent one.
There is some sublation because it is read at the conclusion of the treatise as demonstrating that the prior duty is to be sublated.
In a sacrifice where two mutually contradictory [prohibitions] are present in sequence, there is no inference regarding the necessity of performing the prior occasional rite (*naimittika*);

for in that case, the prior expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*), and there is an absence of any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to indicate its status as an auxiliary. Furthermore, the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) concerning the prior occasional rite is not the means of knowledge for that [subsequent rite]. This is because...

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the intention that, because [the general rule] has scope in other applications, it likewise lacks the capacity to convey the subsidiary [element] in those cases. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) and "Āhavanīya":

the general rule, which is engaged in enjoining the *āhavanīya* fire for all oblations (*homa*) in the statement "one offers in the *āhavanīya*," [is set aside] by the specific location in the form of the word [denoting] a particular type of oblation.

The meaning is that, by virtue of a specific injunction, the Āhavanīya fire is prescribed for all oblations other than the *padahoma*, just as it is for those [specific ones]. Regarding the phrase "because it has the sacrifice (*kratu*) as its object": in such a sacrifice alone, [the rule applies] based on the occasion of the *udgātṛ*'s fall.
The meaning is that [the rule] serves as a means of cognition because it has not yet arrived [at its application]. He states the consensus regarding this point, saying "For it has been said.

The restriction of a general scriptural injunction—such as "one offers in the Āhavanīya fire," which has an established form, is established by perception, and applies to all oblations—by means of a specific injunction is called "sublation of what has already obtained" (*prāptabādha*).

Just as when there is a conflict between two general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*) regarding a particular subject, that which is obtained later sublates the one previously obtained due to its posteriority— just as in the case of the two rules concerning the occasion of cutting [the sacrificial grass] when they are in conflict— so too, in cases such as "from the specific subject" (*viśeṣa-viṣayāt*) and so forth, the term "posteriority" (*paratva*) and so on is used for the purpose of inclusion.

The meaning of the verse is as follows: "In that very case, [it is] thus" (*tatraivaṃ tu*) means when, in the instance of a subsequent disconnection (*apaccheda*), the prior cognition is sublated by a subsequent cognition. "It should be observed" (*draṣṭavyam*) means that for one who has suffered a disconnection of the *pratihartr* priest, but not of the *udgātṛ*, the completion of the sacrifice—since it would otherwise be without sacrificial fees (*adakṣiṇa*)—is a necessary constituent part (*aṅga*) of the rite.

The meaning is that it must be understood [in this way]. He states "that too" (tad api), explaining that even the statement from the *Śāstradīpikā* does not intend the meaning you favor, because it contradicts the preceding text; furthermore, since your cited passage—which serves as a conclusion to the meaning of the preceding text—must be interpreted strictly in accordance with that preceding text.

The connection is that even having performed that [action], it is merely for the sake of reflection (*cintāmātraparam*). He states the reason why it is "merely for the sake of reflection" with the words beginning "by that" (*tena*).
The meaning of "by that" (*tena*) is: "by the previously established occasional scripture" (*kḷptapūrvapravṛttinaimittikaśāstreṇa*).
The term "occasioned" (*naimittika*) refers to that which exists prior to the arising of a cause; it means that even when there is an absence of the arising of a cause,

the duty remains as something to be performed otherwise— this is intended merely as a conceptual consideration, for in reality, the duty occasioned by the preceding cause does not exist prior to the subsequent arising of that cause.
The word "was" (*āsīt*) is not [the correct reading], because it would contradict the context of the preceding text.
Let alone the conventions of the Mīmāṃsakas; even by the logic of black and red forms, [the sequence] is successive.

If it is accepted that two [types of] *kartavyatā* (obligatoriness) arise, what contradiction is there? It is asked: what is this *kartavyatva* (the state of being an obligation) which ceases upon the arising of another conditional (*naimittika*) *kartavyatā*? First of all, it cannot be the fitness for accomplishment by effort (*kṛti-sādhyatva-yogyatva*) belonging to the prior conditional [act], because that does not disappear even afterwards. Nor can it be the face of the *kala*... [text fragment].

[The definition of an auxiliary is] being something to be accomplished, because it does not come into existence even prior [to the performance of the rite]; nor is its status as an auxiliary or its being an auxiliary defined by the fact that in its non-performance there would be a deficiency in the sacrifice.
He states the meaning of the previously cited passage, following the earlier text in the *Śāstradīpikā*:

"without the arising of a new occasion" (*nimitopajananaṃ vinā*). In a sacrifice characterized by two successive contradictory exclusions (*apaccheda*), if a second occasion were not to arise, then [the rite] would have to be performed otherwise on account of the first occasion.
The meaning is that this sacrifice might indeed exist, but this [proposed interpretation] does not; for this purpose, the subsequent portion of the text exists.

It refutes the meaning of that statement as intended by the opponent. [The opponent asks: "But surely... [The author replies: "Let the Mīmāṃsakas stand aside, who perceive what has been shown; what inconsistency could there be in the meaning of the scripture as conceived by us, the skillful ones?"

He raises a doubt: "Let it be so. [The opponent argues: Since the duty arising from a subsequent occasion (*uttara-naimittika*) cannot destroy the duty arising from a prior occasion (*pūrva-naimittika*)—as this is the view of others—the nature of that prior duty remains unestablished. To explain: what is that [nature]?

Is it the fitness for being accomplished by an effort (*kṛtisādhyatvayogyatva*), or is it the state of being accomplished by an effort as a consequence of the result (*phalamukha-kṛtisādhyatva*)? Or is it [the capacity] for the sacrifice (*kratu*)...?

Alternatively, one might hold in the mind the following options regarding the nature of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*): whether it consists in the performance of that which is the counter-positive to the non-performance of what prompts the option, or something else entirely; having thus formulated the options, he refutes the first with the words "Not, first of all. [He says] "Because it is not a means," and so on; and thus, the subsequent contingent duty (*naimittika-kartavyatā*) follows.

The sense is this: even if one persists in the prior duty at the [proper] time, there is a contradiction in the acceptance of their sequential occurrence—just as in the case of the dark and red stripes on a variegated fruit—since those two [dark and red parts] are mutually destructive. He refutes the second [position] with: "Nor [is it] the effect..."

"Because it does not arise. Thus, the idea is that the knowledge of the prior occasional duty (*naimitikakartavyatā*)—whose status as an error is established within the boundaries of the Mīmāṃsā system—results in nothing other than error; it does not possess the validity (*prāmāṇya*) that you [the opponent] desire for the knowledge of blackness. He refutes the third and fourth [alternatives] with the words: "Nor that which... and so forth.

The meaning is that the essence [of the rule] results in the state of possessing an action that is the counter-positive to the non-performance of those actions which, in their absence, cause a deficiency in the sacrifice; that is, it results in the performance of those very actions. This refers to a case where first there is the disqualification of the Udgātṛ and subsequently the disqualification of the Pratihartṛ.

In this regard, one who asserts that the non-performance of the expiation for the cutting off of the Udgātṛ constitutes a cause for the deficiency of the sacrifice (*kratu-vaikalya*), and that its expiation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that sacrifice, must state:
does the non-performance of the preceding expiation constitute a cause for the deficiency of the sacrifice?
Does it consist in being the producer of a deficiency, or its pervader, or its pervaded?

Not the first, because it is impossible for non-performance, which is of the nature of an absence, to be a producer; and because even a deficiency in the sacrifice, being of the nature of the prior non-existence of the sacrificial aid, cannot be produced by that [non-performance]. Nor is it the second.
In a sacrifice where there has been a disconnection (apaccheda) of the Udgātṛ alone and the expiation for that has been performed,
even if a deficiency in the sacrifice occurs due to some other cause,
there is no deviation (vyabhicāra), because there is an absence of non-performance of the expiation for the Udgātṛ's disconnection; therefore, the third [alternative] is correct.
With the intention that something remains, he says:
Because, since non-performance functions as the cause of a deficiency in the sacrifice by way of being a specific restrictive rule (*niyamaviśeṣa*),

and since [the performance] functions as a cause by way of being either an auxiliary to the ritual action (*karmāṅga*)— either as a remote aid (*phalopakārin*) or as a direct constituent (*sannipatyopakārin*)— it is impossible for these two states to be merely occasional (*kādācitka*).

In order to establish its inherent nature, the occasional *mārga* (expiatory rite) prescribed for a prior interruption of the sacrifice must be performed in that very same sacrifice which lacks a subsequent contradictory interruption; otherwise, it would cause a deficiency (*vaikalya*) in the sacrifice. Thus, it must be qualified as applying to a sacrifice where a later interruption has not occurred.

Because, regarding the contingency of the cutting of the northern part [of the sacrificial post], it is impossible— prior to the occurrence of the subsequent cutting of the southern part— for that [northern cutting] to either constitute a lapse in the performance of the sacrifice or to cause a deficiency in the sacrifice;
for it cannot be said that something exists pervading a certain period of time and subsequently does not, or that it is a cause for a certain period of time.

Nor is it observed anywhere that [the self] comes later, nor is such a thing logical; furthermore, one should not postulate some other distinct entity called "name" (nāman) as a property subject to appearance and disappearance, for there is a lack of evidence.

"By way of being a specific form of restriction" means by way of being the nature of pervasion (*vyāpyatva*). "Being an auxiliary to the result" means being a cause with respect to the result in the form of the supreme *apūrva* through the medium of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and others; and "being an immediate auxiliary" (*sannipatyopakārakatva*) means being that which produces the very essence of the sacrifice, as in [the case of the materials].

If it is argued that the nature of the previously mentioned forms belongs to the substances, deities, and so forth of the *stutis*, then it must be stated here: in a sacrifice characterized by two successive and mutually contradictory *apacchedas*, the capacity to cause optionality— consisting in being pervaded by the deficiency of the sacrifice resulting from the non-performance of the prior expiation (*prāyaścitta*)— belongs to the prior expiation.

And as for the second characteristic, whether the state of having departed from its proper place continues even after the production of the [new] sign, or not: in the first case, there would be the necessity of performing the previous expiation, which consists in the performance of the counter-positive to the non-performance that causes the deficiency of the ritual (*kratu*).

Furthermore, this would result in the collapse of the accepted principle that the obligation (*kartavyatā*) consisting of the primary and subsidiary parts of a penance is destroyed by the performance of a subsequent occasion for penance (*uttara-naimittika*). In the second alternative, the non-performance of the prior penance would not entail a deficiency in the sacrifice (*kratu-vaikalya*), as it would be restricted to the second occasion.

It results that [the duty] exists prior to the occurrence of that [event], but does not exist after its occurrence; likewise, it results that the obligation (*kartavyatā*) consisting of the performance and non-performance of the first expiation exists prior to the occurrence of the second cause for the first expiation, but does not exist afterwards. And thus:
One would have to admit that pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) and causality (*kāraṇatva*) are occasional (*kādācitkatva*) with respect to their own substrata;

however, as he will state immediately following this, that is not possible—beginning with the words "For not... (*na hi*). Therefore, in order to establish the inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) of these two, which consists in their persisting as long as their substrata exist, [one must rely on] the exclusion of successive contradictions (*kramika-viruddha-apacheda*).

He states that the qualifying attribute which serves to differentiate [the two cases] applies as a defect in both instances: "occurring later" (*paścādbhāvī*) and "due to impossibility" (*asaṃbhavāt*). The implication is that, in a ritual sacrifice where successive contradictory options are excluded, the cognition of the prior contingent duty (*naimittika-kartavyatā*) is nothing but an error. He provides the reason why those two [options] cannot be occasional (*kādācitka*): "For not... (*na hi*), as in the case of smoke and so forth.

The meaning is that the heat pervading fire and so forth, as well as the causality of smoke and so forth in relation to fire and so forth, are not observed to be merely occasional (*kādācitkatva*). Now, one might object: "Even if it is not observed, if it is logical, it should certainly be accepted. To this he says: "Or [it may be] logical" (*yuktaṃ vā*). The word "or" (*vā*) is not intended to include the previous point; rather, it refers to the position that those two are indeed occasional.

In the case of smoke and so forth, there would arise the undesirable consequence that fire and so forth possess a limiting condition (*upādhi*) that necessitates their occasional absence from being pervaded by smoke; likewise, since fire and so forth might occasionally lack causality toward smoke and so forth, one who seeks the effect— smoke and so forth— would not employ fire and so forth as its material cause.

Furthermore, due to the doubt that it lacks such a cause, there would be no unshakable engagement [in action]; therefore, the occasional nature of those two is untenable—this is the meaning. He refutes the fifth [possibility] with "Nor also...
[He says: "Immediately after the production of the first efficient cause, it is not suitable for me..."
The meaning is that immediately after the production of the second sign, one becomes fit for the states of woe.
Because a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is possible for two contradictory teachings, just as in the case of the rules regarding the *padahavanīya* fire;

therefore, the statement concerning the simultaneous arising of two successive duties is without foundation. But surely, according to the principle of the section on the "commencement" (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), because it is not yet contradicted, [the former] is indeed directly perceived—
Could it not be that the general rule (*gamāt*) is stronger? It is replied: where a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) is perceived, there the meaning must culminate in a single sense;
for if a difference in meaning were perceived, it would entail the destruction of the established syntactical unity. Therefore, in that case, that which first arises...

When, by means of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) similar to a "deed of another" (*parakṛti*), such as the opening passage "Prajāpati led Varuṇa away by means of the *varamanī* [sacrifice]," the notion that the merit belongs to the giver has been instilled,
then [the prohibition] "as many [cows] as he might accept" serves as its opposite.

"One should offer cakes on four potsherds to Varuṇa"— since the collection of words (*padajāta*) occurring in the *upayaj* (subsidiary offerings) has arisen as an opponent [to the primary injunction], it does not achieve syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by merely conveying the literal meaning; therefore, for the sake of establishing that syntactic unity, the sense of the suffix (*ṇij-artha*) [is required].

In cases where a mutual syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is not perceived, there is the predominance of the introductory statement (*upakrama*), because [the subsequent part] attains its own nature only by being included within that [introductory statement] and in accordance with it.

Even if it disregards what has occurred previously, a sentence that lacks an established nature and possesses a contradictory meaning does indeed convey its own intended sense; therefore, there is no superiority for that which has occurred previously. For this very reason, the sentence regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, disregarding what had occurred previously, [supersedes] even that sentence regarding the cup.
It is accepted as being subversive of its own purpose.

Because it has been stated that, like the *pūrvanaimitika* scriptures and the *grāvahānīya* and other such texts, there is scope for [the latter] elsewhere, and because such a [subsequent] dharma cannot serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that [prior one], he says, "contradictory" (*viruddha*). This refers to the knowledge of the duty (*kartavyatva*) based on a prior occasioning cause (*nimitta*) in a sacrifice (*kratu*) characterized by successive, contradictory exclusions (*apaccheda*).

He concludes with the words "Therefore," intending to show that since validity is impossible [in the case of the former], when there is a contradiction and the subsequent cognition sublates the prior cognition, the principle of *apaccheda* (the later annulling the earlier) indeed serves as an illustration.
Now, one might object: by the principle of *apaccheda*, it is understood that scripture possesses greater authority than perception.

He raises an objection with the intention that, by the principle of the section concerning the commencement (*upakramādhikaraṇa*), even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is understood to have greater force than scripture (*śruti*); thus, there is a lack of decisive evidence regarding which of the two should be sublated and which should be the sublater. He objects, saying: "But surely... and "It is known by the ignorant. Just as at the time of knowing the meaning of the initial statement...

Because there is no manifestation of contradiction due to the absence of knowledge regarding the meaning of the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*), the initial passage (*upakrama*) remains free from contradiction; likewise, at the time of the engagement with duality,
because there is an absence of the experience of the meaning of the scriptures that teach the falsity of duality.

Because there is no manifestation of contradiction; the meaning is that perception possesses non-contradiction with respect to what has not yet arisen. He refutes [the objection] by means of a disparity in the example, saying: "It is said. Now, regarding the phrase "that which was done by Manu": the meaning is "one who has performed [it]. *Parakṛti* refers to the performance or execution of another, namely Prajāpati; thus, the term *parakṛti*.

The meaning is that it refers to a sentence intended to establish that [fact], by way of an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) of a similar nature. It is stated that "it has that form" because, since Prajāpati lacks the qualification for ritual action, it does not constitute a contradiction, as it actually establishes that [form].
Regarding the word "of the giver": in the opening passage, "He saw this four-potherd offering to Varuṇa; he offered it."
The meaning is "because of being heard. By the word "he" (saḥ), the Prajāpati under discussion is referred to;
for, since the opening and the conclusion both touch upon the single subject matter consisting of the Varuṇa-sacrifice, it is understood that these two form a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatva).
To preserve this unity, it must be stated that these two culminate in a single intended meaning.

The meaning is that if one accepts the literal sense of the sentence, there would be no recognition of a single unified statement (ekavākyatva), because the commencement [of the action] would belong to the donor and the conclusion to the recipient. Regarding the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the phrase "one should receive" (*pratigṛhṇīyāt*) means "one should cause [the other] to receive" (*pratigrāhāyet*). However, the perception of a single unified statement occurs only in cases where the latter [clause] follows immediately.

Having stated "in view of what precedes" for the sake of strengthening the meaning, he says "But where... with the intention that in a case where there is no perception of syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*), the preceding [text] need not be respected by the subsequent.
However, because there is no other alternative for both [the means of knowledge],

the performance of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in that very [state] is accepted out of necessity. And thus, since there is no possibility of the non-dual scripture being in agreement with perception, one should disregard even what has been previously established.

The capacity to convey its own meaning is unimpeded; and in producing the cognition of that object, it arises without being sublated by what precedes it, because the subsequent [cognition] has not yet arisen.
Since the subsequent [cognition] cannot arise otherwise [than through sublation], the first [cognition] cannot possibly exist without sublation. Thus, [the argument is established].

The principle of annulment (*chedanyāya*) alone applies here, not the principle of commencement (*upakramanyāya*). For this very reason, even in the world, the initial perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is sublated by the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*). Now, one might object: "Even so, the superiority of perception based on its status as that which is depended upon (*upajīvya*) is difficult to avoid; for [in the case of] the two rules regarding the suspension of the *praiṣa* and the *anupraisa*..."

It is not logical for the latter to sublate the former on the grounds that the former is not dependent upon the latter; however, in this case, because perception is the basis upon which scripture depends— since scripture grasps the intrinsic nature of letters, words, and so forth— it is scripture alone that possesses the falsity which contradicts that [perception].

Sublation in the form of being a cause of awakening is appropriate. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction with what is presupposed (*upajīvya*), because even if the portion consisting of the reality of letters, words, and so forth were sublated by the scripture declaring falsity, there would still be no sublation of the portion consisting of their essential nature as a basis for cognition; for [this is not so] because of such scriptural passages as, "Here there is no diversity whatsoever."
Because it brings about the realization of the non-existence of the phenomenal world by its very own nature.
[The opponent] objects: "But how can two sentences be authoritative, since the taking of the *ṣoḍaśī* cup and its absence are contradictory within a single *rātri-sattra* sacrifice?

[The author] replies with the words "But what... and provides a resolution of the contradiction through a difference in application (prayoga-bheda) with the words "Of both... [The opponent] then asks: "But surely..."
One might ask: "Why could the statement of acceptance and the statement of its prohibition not be established as distinct through a difference in intention (*vakratva*)?
To this he replies: "Because there is no other subject matter.
This means that those two statements belong to a single context (*ekaprakaraṇa*). [The word] "having reached" (*agatya*)...
The meaning is: "also because of the impossibility of a combination. "In that very [case]" means: "in the *atirātra* sacrifice itself. "And thus" means:
"provided that the principle of the introductory statement (*upakramanyāya*) has as its object a text consisting of a single syntactical unity (*ekavākyatāka-grantha*).
"Because there is no doubt" means: "and thus, there would be a suspicion of the superiority of what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) over the Vedic revelation (*śruti*)."
The author concludes by defining the application of the principle of *apaccheda* (simultaneous sublation) through doubt and its resolution:
"tadarthe" and "pūrvam. This refers to a sacrifice characterized by successive, contradictory instances of *apaccheda*.

The meaning of the word "prior" (*pūrva*) is the knowledge of the duty to perform the expiation caused by the first transgression. The meaning of the word "subsequent" (*para*) is the knowledge of the duty to perform the subsequent conditional rite. He states the reason why there is no sublation of the subsequent by the prior: "because it has not yet arisen. This means that the subsequent [knowledge] does not exist otherwise than as a sublation of the prior knowledge.

The meaning of the verse is that since it is impossible for the first [cognition] to arise without sublation, there can be no possibility of the subsequent one occurring without the sublation of the former.

He provides an example of even a previously functioning perception being sublated by a subsequent verbal testimony (śabda) with the words "ata eva" ("for this very reason"). The meaning is "precisely because of its posteriority. As for the objection beginning with "nanu" ("but"): although this doubt does not...

And thus, having relied upon this, [the objection] that there is a contradiction with perception and so forth has already been refuted. Nevertheless, in order to challenge the solution stated by him (Takka), the doubt and its resolution are written again. "Nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) means: even though perception possesses intrinsic superiority just like scripture (*āgama*). [Objection: But surely, by the logic of the *apaccheda* [of sacrificial errors],...

The opponent raises the following objection: "The superiority of Śruti is also difficult to resist; thus, in the absence of a sublater, there is indeed a lack of a decisive criterion (vinigamanāviraha). Who would not accept the establishment of their own position? For it is accepted by them that Śruti is sublated by perception. Anticipating this, the opponent demonstrates the non-application of the principle of the *apaccheda* (simultaneous performance of rites) to the present case.

Regarding the phrase "for [there is a conflict] between the Apastamba-Dharmasūtra and the Śāstra": this recalls the previously stated resolution in the event of a suspicion regarding a contradiction with that which is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*).

The phrase "and not by the scripture on falsity" means that such a resolution would be appropriate only if the scripture negated merely the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); however, it negates the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the phenomenal world itself. And thus:
He says, "Not so," because since the very nature of letters, words, and so forth does not exist [in Brahman], the contradiction with that upon which [the Vedas] depend is unavoidable.
The meaning is: "In this [Brahman], there is not even the slightest thing that is manifold or differentiated."

On this point, some say: since one observes the occurrence of verbal valid cognition even in cases such as "bring the bull," where the sentence "bring the bull" was heard by someone who [due to a defect in hearing] perceived it in the form of "bring the ox," direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the phonemes, words, and so forth is not the cause of verbal valid cognition.

Since only that which is common to error is required, there is no contradiction with the basis [of knowledge] even when the non-dualist scripture subverts the very nature of the perception of letters, words, and so forth; thus, there is no conflict with what must be accepted as foundational. Others, however, say: even though the verbal cognition of truth does not depend on the establishment of the actual nature of letters, words, and so forth— [The rest of the passage continues: ...there is no contradiction with the basis, because the scripture merely negates the superimposed forms such as "this is a letter" or "this is a word," while leaving the substratum untouched, just as the cognition "this is a snake" is negated by the cognition "this is a rope" without negating the rope itself. Furthermore, since the validity of the scripture is established by its own intrinsic nature (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it does not require corroboration from other means of knowledge. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the basis. As for the objection that the scripture contradicts perception regarding the existence of the external world, that is not a valid objection, because the scripture teaches non-duality through a process of gradual instruction (*krama-nirdeśa*) intended for those whose minds are not yet fit for the direct realization of the ultimate reality. Thus, there is no contradiction with the basis. And as for the claim that the scripture contradicts inference, that too is not a valid objection, because the scripture negates only the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of duality, whereas inference establishes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Since the two have different objects of focus, there is no contradiction. Moreover, the scripture is more powerful than inference because it is free from defects and possesses the capacity to negate all conceptual constructions. Therefore, the non-dualist scripture is indeed authoritative. It is said: "The scripture, being free from defects and possessing the power to negate all conceptual constructions, is more powerful than inference; therefore, it is authoritative. Thus, there is no contradiction with the basis. And as for the claim that the scripture contradicts the Vedic injunctions regarding ritual action, that too is not a valid objection, because the scripture negates only the imagined nature of the agent and the action, while the injunctions establish the dependent nature of the ritual procedure. Since the two have different objects of focus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the scripture is more powerful than the injunctions because it reveals the ultimate goal, liberation (*mokṣa*), which is superior to the temporary results of ritual action. Therefore, the non-dualist scripture is authoritative. It is said: "The scripture, revealing the ultimate goal, liberation, which is superior to the results of ritual action, is more powerful than the injunctions; therefore, it is authoritative. Thus, there is no contradiction with the basis. Consequently, the non-dualist scripture is established as the supreme authority. It is said: "The non-dualist scripture is the supreme authority, for it is free from defects, possesses the power to negate all conceptual constructions, and reveals the ultimate goal, liberation, which is superior to the results of ritual action. Thus, the non-dualist scripture is established as the supreme authority. Since valid cognition does not arise from an incompatible word, there is a requirement for the establishment of the essential nature of compatibility (*yogyatā*).

Even when such compatibility is required, there is no contradiction with that which is to be relied upon (*upajīvya*). For even though the Śruti text "There is no diversity here" negates plurality, it refers to that [plurality] which persists as long as the knowledge of Brahman has not yet arisen.

This is because we accept the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as being distinct from the unreal and consistent with empirical activity; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception, which function within the realm of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), would be devoid of objects.
Nor does the negation of its nature preclude the phenomenal world from attaining its own existence.
It should not be argued that there is a contradiction because the counter-correlate of a negation consists in the form of its rejection.

Having approached [the point of] refutation, he resolves the contradiction with the basis [of the opponent's position] by stating, "On this point, some say... Even on the view that the world is real (*prapañca-satyatva-pakṣe*),

in accordance with the example "Bring the bull," it is held that verbal cognition, which is common to both error and valid knowledge, is what is relied upon by the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

We must state, however, that according to the authority of the Śruti, there is a distinction: in all cases—whether in perceptual or verbal cognition, or in other types of worldly activity—the cause is exclusively of the nature of error; thus, there is no contradiction with what is presupposed (*upajīvyavirodha*), because the nature of the word itself is not something that is presupposed. This is the meaning. [Regarding] the contradiction with what is presupposed...

He offers a rebuttal by way of another approach: "But others say... First, he demonstrates the lack of internal consistency in the previous position: "In the verbal cognition... and "...even in the case of non-dependence... Here too, it is indicated that there is no dependence in reality, even by means of the word; for such is the case in the previous position.
It has been stated that the objects characterized as letters, words, and so forth—which serve as the basis for mere perceptual cognition—are not themselves dependent (upon anything else).

That is incorrect, because perception cannot exist without an object; therefore, the very nature of letters, words, and so forth must indeed be accepted. Thus, the meaning is that the previous resolution does not hold when there is a contradiction with what is foundational.

"It exists. And thus, since the dependence upon fitness (*yogyatā*) is unavoidable, the contradiction with that [fitness] is necessary in the previous view; this is the sense. Nor should it be said that, by this much alone, the nature of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as intended by the opponent is not established, for [it is established] in accordance with the effect characterized as verbal cognition (*śābdapramiti*).

The intention is that just as the capacity distinct from Brahman is established despite its own essential nature being unestablished, likewise the essential nature of the jar and other objects is also established in accordance with their functions, such as carrying water. Now, if the entire world is accepted as distinct from consciousness, then [it follows that] perception and other means of knowledge, which possess objects, must be accepted as foundational (*upajīvya*) for the apprehension of that [world].

To address the objection that this contradicts that [scripture], he says: "Even though there is dependence on that. The sense is that since we also accept the nature of the phenomenal world (prapañca) which is not contradictory to the meaning of the prohibitive scripture, there is no contradiction with our own foundational basis (upajīvya) in our view.
[He now states] the subverting argument against one who follows the previous doctrine regarding the non-acceptance of a nature distinct from the unreal (asat).

He replies with the words "otherwise. The proponent of the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca) raises an objection with the words "if not. Anticipating the question, "But let the phenomenal world and its negation both reside in Brahman; what is the fault? he says: "of the negation," [referring to] the existence of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) of the absence of a jar or the like upon the ground or similar substrates.
The meaning is "because of the observation of contradiction. "Due to contradiction" means "due to the contradiction with its own nature as a negation."

And because of the conformity to both cognitions— that "this is silver" and "this is not silver"— the absence of the superimposed object residing in the substrate persists until the point of sublation (*bādha*).

This is because it is accepted that [the world] possesses its own nature as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) which is distinct from reality (sad-vilakṣaṇa). By this, the objection that "if the world were negated in its own nature, it would be non-existent like a hare's horn" is refuted; for there is no inconsistency, since its nature is admitted to be that which is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman. Not... [end of fragment].
Furthermore, when that which is superimposed is negated in its own form within its substrate,
its negation in its own form elsewhere follows automatically; thus, since it would result in being the counter-positive of a negation related to all places and times,
its non-existence (asatva) is unavoidable.

It should not be argued that non-existence is defined solely as being the counter-positive of a negation related to all places and times, because it is impossible to define it in any other way; for [the case of] the non-existent...

For one who accepts that [the self] is the counter-correlate of a negation pertaining to all places and times, since it is impossible to establish such a status through perception— given that perception cannot perceive all places and times— and since it is impossible to establish it through scripture— given the non-apprehension of any such scripture— it must be established by inference alone.
"It must be established as a means of valid cognition. Regarding that inference, they say that the logical mark (*liṅga*) to be stated is that which is excluded from existence;

for it is only of that [mark], when first perceived, that the definition of non-existence is possible, [and not] of an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a conceptual object (*kalpita-padārtha*), [which would have to reside] elsewhere than in its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Even though the substratum is eternally opposed to its counter-correlates, it is postulated that its nature is the capacity to tolerate the presence of a counter-correlates for some time; nor is there a lack of evidence for such a postulation, because the perception apprehending duality and the scriptural prohibitions possess authority, just as [the existence of] the absolute non-existence of a jar is accepted in the view of others.

Although an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) such as conjunction generally negates its counter-positive within its own locus, it is nevertheless accepted—on the strength of perceptual experience—that in certain cases it does not negate the counter-positive within its own locus. "In that same way" (*tadvat*):
keeping this intended solution in mind, [the author] provides an example established by his own school.
He speaks with justification, saying "in the case of mother-of-pearl. He explains the meaning of this word [“this”] by saying "the knowledge of Brahman.

Regarding the phrase "due to dissimilarity," the meaning is "due to the dissimilarity with [non-existent things such as] a hare's horn and the like. Regarding the phrase "elsewhere," the meaning is "in a place or time other than that of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna).
Now, let it be granted that non-existence can be defined in another way; and so, in the case of the phenomenal world (prapañca) —

He says "no" because the consequence of its non-existence does not follow from the absence of that [definition]. He explains: "by another mode. For when the well-known non-existence of things such as a hare’s horn is established by the aforementioned definition, then since the world (prapañca) would also possess that same definition, it too would result in being non-existent; therefore, it is improper to state a distinction based on the prior admission that the world is different from those [non-existent things].

That very point can be doubted because there is a lack of proof (*mānābhāva*). If it is asked, "How is there a lack of proof?", it must be stated in response: regarding that [non-existence], is there direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it scripture (*āgama*), or is it inference (*anumāna*)? Having kept these alternatives in mind, the first two are refuted.

The third [alternative] mentioned previously is set aside by the passage beginning with "of that which is non-existent" (*asataḥ*). The connection is: "[because] perception and scripture cannot be established as valid means of cognition. By the phrase "of such a kind," it is meant that there is no apprehension of a scriptural statement whose form is: "the rabbit's horn and so forth are the counter-correlates of negation related to all places and times."
This is the meaning. [Objection: Let it be then that the remaining means of knowledge, namely inference (*anumāna*), is the authority there.

[Reply: No, he says: "In that inference... [The word] "that" (*yat*) means "the state of being devoid of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvarūpatva*). [The word] "must be stated" (*vācyam*) has "by you" as its ellipsis.
He removes the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā-viraha*) by saying: "of that which is first perceived. [The word] "because of the logical necessity" (*upapatter iti*). And thus:
The sense is that because the nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is accepted as being removable by knowledge,
it does not possess the kind of non-existence characterized by a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatva*); thus, the statement regarding its difference from things like a hare’s horn is made.

Others, however, maintain that the intent of such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here" is solely the negation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in its state of being an entity (*sattva*), and not a negation of it in its own nature (*svarūpa*).

For if a negation did not exclude the thing's own nature, it could not be considered a negation of that thing; yet if it were to exclude its own nature, it would contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor is this the case...

It should not be argued that since reality (*satyatva*) is also established by perception—such as in the cognition "the jar exists"—its negation is therefore untenable even in its own nature; for it is logical that perception, in order to avoid contradicting scripture, has as its object a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasatya*) which is merely an appearance of reality. And this being so, [the objection does not hold].

Since absolute reality (*pāramārthika-satya*), which resides in Brahman, cannot possibly apply to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it is impossible to negate the world in its form as absolute reality. Just as the very appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell constitutes the "application" (*prasakti*) of real silver, and thus that silver is negated, so too [is the world negated]. Therefore, [the statement] is: "This is not silver, but rather that."
"This is not my cow; rather, it is that very one, and Caitra is not here, but in the inner room.
