In this way, the existence [of the object] elsewhere is understood from what is being negated. Thus, since the very perception of an appearance of reality constitutes the contingency of reality, its negation is logically established. Therefore...

They say that because there is no suspicion of subverting the essential nature [of the Veda] regarding the suitability of phonemes, words, and so forth, there is no contradiction with that which must be accepted as foundational (*upajīvya*).

He refutes the contradiction with the foundational [text] by another method, saying: "But others... and "Because of the impossibility. The sense is this: because the counter-correlate cannot possibly exist in the locus itself; thus, the absence of the world in Brahman—the locus of the world—is not something to be understood through the negative scriptures (*niṣedha-śruti*). [Objection: But since the world exists in Brahman as truth...
Even regarding the view that it is a negation (*niṣedha*), is what is intended to be expressed as the absence of the world qualified by reality in Brahman?

Or is the negation intended to be expressed in Brahman as having the mere world as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), while not being delimited by the property of reality? Neither of these two is possible when the locus of the counter-correlate is the same as the locus of the negation.

If it is argued that this is because the non-existence of that [truth] is not admitted, and because, by not admitting the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it is impossible for it to enter the category of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) or to be the delimiting factor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), we reply: the intention of this view is that the purport (*tātparya*) of the Śruti is the negation of reality with respect to the phenomenal world as the locus (*dharmin*). It is not, however, as follows:

The intent of this doctrine concerns the meaning of what has been heard; for this very reason, he will state that the very perception of the appearance of truth constitutes the contingency of truth, and thus its negation is established. For in this sentence, the negation of truth regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) alone is clearly perceived; therefore, in this doctrine, there is no counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

There is no room for the suspicion that these two absences could coexist in a single substratum. Now, it may be argued that just as the nature of the phenomenal world (prapañca) exists in Brahman as established by perception and other means of knowledge, so too does its reality exist in the phenomenal world itself,
likewise established by perception and other means.
He raises an objection, saying "If not," [meaning]: even if that [duality] is negated, it is impossible to assume that the Śruti has that as its purport.

The reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is apprehended by perception and other means of knowledge, is not ultimately real in the same way that the reality of Brahman is. If that were the case, then there would be many [scriptural passages] whose purport regarding their own literal meaning is established through the introduction (upakrama) and other criteria.

He offers a rebuttal with the words "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*), stating that because there would otherwise follow the consequence of the prohibitive scriptures (*niṣedha-śruti*) being devoid of an object, one must instead postulate for them a nature such as conventional reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*); thus, the negation of [absolute] reality is not untenable. With the words "and this being so" (*na caivam sati*), he means the acceptance of the conventional reality of the world-appearance (*prapañca*).
He states the connection by means of an illustration: "Just as it has been said... It must be stated that the perceptual negation "this is not silver" has as its object the negation of real silver;
for, according to this view, the absence of imagined silver in a piece of mother-of-pearl—which serves as the locus for illusory silver—is [the object].

The meaning is that by [the opponent's] own admission, it is impossible for the sublation to have that [silver] as its object, because it is a perception. He states the restrictive rule regarding the fact that the silver being negated in the mother-of-pearl and so forth must reside in another location: "For this very reason," etc.

Others, however, do not accept a threefold division of reality; they maintain that Brahman possesses ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*), while the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) possesses empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), and thus is not of the nature of a mere appearance. They hold that the illusory reality (*prātibhāsika-satyatva*) found in cases such as nacre-silver is even more inferior than that. [This is because] the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*)...

Because the conceptualization of a mere appearance of unreality— arising from the justification of the conceit of reality regarding a jar through its permeation by the ultimate reality residing in Brahman— is devoid of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, [the claim of] reality in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)...

Furthermore, since Brahman has attained identity with the dependent entities, the appearance of that [Brahman] within the phenomenal world (prapañca) due to non-discrimination is logically established; thus,
there is no contradiction with the foundational principle (upajīvya-virodha) by negating the reality of the phenomenal world, nor is there a negation of what has not been previously apprehended.

It must be explained why one accepts the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell as something distinct from the real silver that is spatially remote, given that in the case of the world, there is no appearance of existence apart from the ultimate, eternal existence residing in Brahman;
for it is impossible for that which is remote and not in immediate contact to be directly perceived, and [the theory of *anyathākhyāti*] is adopted to account for this.

Because that [error] is admitted. Now, one might object: in the case of the delusion of a reflection as well, one would have to accept the production of an appearance of a face in the mirror as something distinct from the face located on the neck;

for even though it is possible to have direct perception of the region delimited by the nose through the face located on one's own neck, [the appearance in the mirror would still require a separate origin].
Because it is impossible for regions such as the eyeballs and the forehead to be directly perceived [in that manner], and because, in the case of the delusion of a reflection,
the eyeballs and other such regions are observed to be directly perceived.

In response to the objection that a negation is untenable because the possibility of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikasatyatva*) does not apply to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), a solution was shown by relying on the doctrine of the threefold existence (*sattvatraividhya*). Now, he removes the doubt regarding the lack of possibility under the view that "Being" (*sat*) is one and the same everywhere, with the words: "But others... First, [the nature of] Being...

He refutes the position of the threefold nature with the words beginning "In Brahman" (*brahmaṇi*). Regarding the phrase "residing in Brahman": although ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattā*) has the nature of Brahman, the expression "residing in it" is used by way of a conceptualization of difference (*bhedakalpanā*). The phrase "precisely because of the interpenetration" (*anuvedhād eva*) means "because of the very cognition. And "if this is so," [it refers to] the existent (*san*). In cognitions such as "the jar," [the object] is that which has attained identity (*tādātmya*) with the jar and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: when "existent" (*sat*) is cognized, it refers to Brahman itself in its aspect as the existent reality (*sad-vastvaṃśa-rūpa*). Just as in the cognition "the jar is clay," the cognition has "clay-ness" as its object regarding the clay-aspect, so too, because of the cognition of existence in Brahman, the practical usage of "existence" (*sattva-vyavahāra*) occurs in relation to jars and the like. This being established, as for that which is stated by the proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*):

It is argued that a negation of falsity regarding the world (*prapañca*) by means of scripture is not possible, because it contradicts the perceptual cognition whose object is the reality of the world. To this, he replies: "Because the reason [for such a negation] is unestablished.
Regarding the claim that this is a "negation of the unattached" (*aprāptapratiṣedha*), he says: "Through identity with That" (*tādātmya*). The word "That" (*tat*) refers to the jar and so forth.

However, due to the non-apprehension of the difference between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and Brahman, that very perception of reality which exists in Brahman results in the attribution of reality to the phenomenal world; and it is on this basis that worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) therein is grounded—this is the meaning.

Thus, there is no contradiction with what must be accepted as foundational (*nopajīvyavirodha*). This refers to the letters, words, and so forth, which are the foundation for the realization of the falsity of the world as taught in the Śruti.
The sense is that this is because perception is admitted to have an objective basis (*sālambanatva*), and [the theory of illusory manifestation] does not subvert that. Now, one might object:

"If the empirical usage of existence in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) such as jars and so forth is established by the very existence of Brahman, and no separate existence is postulated for them—since there is a lack of evidence for such a postulation and because of parsimony (*lāghava*)—then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would follow. Thus he raises the doubt with "na" (no).

"And so forth. The intention of the objection is: "For what purpose [is this postulation]? Since such a postulation involves complexity (*gaurava*), it follows that indeterminate silver and the like would not be established. He refutes this with the thought that complexity is not a fault when it is supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇikatva*).

[The terms] "of the remote" (*vyavahitasya*) and "of the non-proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭasya*) mean, respectively, "that which is devoid of identity with manifested consciousness" (*abhivyakta-caitanya-tādātmya-śūnya*).
"Is it not thus?"—the meaning is: [it would follow that] one must admit the production of an appearance of non-remote silver. [Objection:

Even though a reflection is non-different from the original object (*bimba*), the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of the reflection is possible; therefore, that [appearance] need not be accepted. To this he says: "one's own," [referring to] the face; the ellipsis is "endowed with the status of being the original object. "The nose, etc."—this refers to the contact in that respect.
The meaning is "because of its occurrence."

Nor is it acceptable to accept that the reflection is something distinct from the original object (*bimba*), for that would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*): namely, that the individual soul (*jīva*), as a reflection of Brahman, would be different from it and thus fall into the state of being illusory (*mithyātva*). Regarding this, the followers of the *Vivaraṇa* say:

Since the superimposition of the face's being located in the mirror, its facing backward, and its difference from the original object (the *bimba*) is possible through the defect of proximity to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of the mirror while the face remains actually in the neck, it is not necessary to postulate a superimposition of the face upon the mirror; for that would be unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*). Thus, [it is said]: "The face does not exist in the mirror."

If it were a separate false object, there would be a sublation of its very nature (svarūpa-bādha) because of the sublation of the mere contact [with the mirror], as in the case of the cognition "this is my face. Furthermore, there is the recognition of non-difference from one's own face in the form: "My face appears in the mirror. Nor is it the case that...
It is impossible for the face situated in the neck to be directly perceived [as the locus of the reflection].

If the direct perception of a reflection is possible in the case of one's own face reflected [in a mirror] because there is no difference between the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*), then let the reflection be distinct from the original object and indeed illusory;
such is the objection raised by the proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*). To this, the opponent [the proponent of the previous view] states "no," [anticipating] the loss of that position.

[The author] demonstrates this: "As a reflection of Brahman. The individual soul (*jīva*) [is distinct] from Brahman because it is a reflection of Brahman in its essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). In a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), it is like a reflection of a face; therefore, the soul is false (*mithyā*) because it is different from Brahman, just like a jar or similar objects—this is the meaning. [This is established] by the worldly observation of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

He offers a rebuttal, stating that "because there is no difference, the aforementioned fault does not apply," by referring to the *Vivaraṇa*. Now, it might be argued that it is improper to postulate even the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the face upon the mirror due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*); however, this is incorrect, because in the case of the reflected face, there is the cognition "the face is in the mirror" based on its being located in the mirror, and likewise, the reflected face [is perceived as] the face located on the neck.

This is because one experiences [the reflection] as facing oneself; for on the view that the face and its reflection are non-different, it would be impossible for that very same face to face itself, and because the difference between the two is clearly experienced.
Therefore, in accordance with these three types of experience, one must accept the superimposition of an indefinable reflection upon the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Anticipating the objection that "reverence [for the scripture] does not entail a fault because it is authoritative," he states the alternative proof for those three experiences: "it is indeed situated in the neck. The intention is that the postulation of multiple attributes is more parsimonious than the postulation of a substratum possessing those attributes. Now, as for the reflection...

Anticipating the objection that [the reflection] is false because it is subject to sublation (*bādhadarśanāt*), he states the establishment of the reason (*hetusiddhi*) with the words "in the mirror" (*darpaṇe*). The word "only" (*mātra*) signifies the absence of sublation regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the reflection.
Following the word "sublation," the ellipsis (*śeṣa*) is: "the falsity of the relation (*saṃsarga*) consisting in being located in the mirror, and the reality (*satyatva*) of the reflection."

He states the defect in the opposing view: "In the case of being another false entity. Now, one might object: "In that case, even in the cognition 'there is no jar on the ground,' only the absence of the relation with the jar would be cognized. This is not so, for such a consequence is acceptable. But then, it may be argued, the absence of the jar on the ground would not be established. This is not so, because of the cognition: "The ground possesses the absence of the jar."

The intended meaning is that [the reflection] arises from that [original object]. The recognition of non-difference in essential nature (*svarūpābhedapratyabhijñāna*) also supports the mere conceptualization of a distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). [This is seen in the thought: "In the mirror, it is mine.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to combine [this point] with the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*). Alternatively, [it refers to the view that] the reflection is real (*satyatva*).

Intending the non-difference from the original object (*bimba*) as the reason, he states the proof for that: "In the mirror, [it is] mine. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a conjunction with the absence of sublation (*bādha*). Thus, the reflection is not false because there is no sublation, and because it is non-different from the original object; such is the meaning. In this way, regarding the reflection in the world...
By establishing the non-difference and the reality of the reflection and the original object, the undesirable consequence that the individual soul (*jīva*),

as the reflection of Brahman, would be different from Brahman and unreal, is refuted. As for the objection raised against the position of their non-difference— that because there is no contact of one's own eyes with regions such as the eyeballs, the reflection of pleasure residing in the throat [could not be perceived]— [this is addressed as follows]:

It has been stated that direct perception [of the reflection] as a whole is not possible; restating that, he refutes it with the words "na ca... and so forth, ending with "...adhiṣṭhānasya. The meaning is: of the substratum for the conceptualization of the various distinctions of the reflection—namely, its being a reflection, its facing inward, its being situated in the mirror, and so on.

This is because it is accepted that the rays of the eye, obstructed by an adjunct (*upādhi*), turn back and grasp the reflection, as in the case of a creeper and similar objects. For if this restriction were not accepted, there would follow the absurdity of a visual illusion of a reflection even for a large object situated behind a wall or other obstructions, such as atoms. It is not so.

Nor should it be argued that there is a rule stating that a visual reflection is merely an illusion occurring only when there is an unobstructed gross and manifest color, and not otherwise; for even though the grossness and manifest color residing in the original object (bimba) may be accounted for as being useful by producing a visual cognition, [the reflection would still arise].
Because it is impossible to conceive of its utility through any other mode.

Regarding the statement "and there is no impossibility," he states the reason: "obstructed by the limiting adjunct" (*upādhi-pratihata*). The rays of the eyes, having emerged from the eyeball and reached the limiting adjunct such as a mirror, are not obstructed;
rather, returning again, they come into contact with the face and its parts situated at the neck, and thus [perceive] that which is facing them.

The direct perception of one's own face located on one's own neck is possible through the direct perception of another person's face. Nor should it be argued that such a postulation here is burdened by unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), since in other cases the entry [of light] via the pupil through the rays of the eyes turned back has already been established.
The meaning is that even for one who maintains the theory of the production of a reflection, since it must be stated that the object of the visual contact is indeed the original object (*bimba*),
that person too must accept the aforementioned rule; therefore, because this is mutually agreed upon, the complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault.

[Objection: Surely, for one who maintains that the reflection is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the status of being the original object (*bimba*) is not admitted for that which is in close proximity [to the mirror]. Therefore, since there is no requirement for contact with one's own eyes in order to establish the status of the face on the neck as the original object, this rule need not be observed by him. To this, he says: "because that rule is not accepted."

If the proximity of the object (*bimba-sannikarṣa*) were the sole cause for the superimposition of a visual reflection (*cākṣuṣa-pratibimba-adhyāsa*), then it would follow that even a concealed object could produce a visual reflection. Without this qualification, since any object whatsoever could result in a reflection, it would follow that even atoms (*paramāṇu*) or air (*vāyu*) would produce such a reflection; this is the meaning. Regarding the superimposition of a reflection...

The proponent of the theory of superimposition (adhyāsa) of the reflection avoids the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) by stating "and not when there is no intervention" (*na cāvyavahite*), even without [positing] that the proximity of the object (*bimba-sannikarṣa*) is a cause. Thus, the meaning is that there is no undesirable consequence of visual reflection for things such as a face obstructed by a wall, nor for atoms or air; for visual perception of a substance [requires unobstructed contact].

Just as the causality of the magnitude residing in each substance and of manifested color has been established, and likewise the obstructiveness of walls and the like toward external-object perception— by way of disrupting the sensory contact—

has been established, so too, in the view that the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are non-different, it is the visual perception of the original object itself [that is obstructed].

Because the reflection is an object of visual perception, there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the view that the grossness and manifest color residing in the face and other things—which constitute the original object (*bimba*)—need not be postulated as causes for anything other than their own established visual perception. This is unlike the case of shell-silver and the like, which are manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi*). However, in the position that the reflection arises as a distinct entity...

Since it is not accepted that proximity to the original object (*bimba-sannikarṣa*) is the cause for the superimposition of a reflection, [the conditions] of largeness and manifest color residing in the substance that serves as the original object are required— just as in the case of visual perception of the substrate itself— in order to preclude the visual perception of reflections of air or atoms.

Furthermore, there is the complexity of having to postulate causality even for the production of the superimposition of the reflection, which is caused by the original object (*bimba*) in the form of a substance residing in its own substratum. Likewise, in the preferred position regarding the original object and its reflection, [this applies] to the rays of the eyes.

Since it is accepted that there is a connection with the reflection through its reversal [into the mirror], the contact with the original object (bimba) must be considered a cause even in cases where there is the illusion of a reflection; thus, just as in the visual perception of a jar or similar objects, in the visual perception of a reflection as well,
the obstructive nature of a wall or such barriers must be postulated only by way of disrupting the contact.

Regarding the parsimony [of the theory], however, since we do not admit that proximity to the original object (*bimba*) is the cause of the superimposition of the reflection, it is impossible to claim— given that the obstruction of proximity by a wall or similar object is already established— that such an object acts as a direct impediment to the erroneous superimposition of the reflection in cases where a reflection is perceived.
Therefore, [the wall] must be considered a direct impediment to the superimposition of the reflection itself.

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the intention that it would involve the conceptual burden (*gaurava*) of having to postulate a [separate principle] to prevent the reflection of an object that is spatially separated.
He says: "By the bulk of the original object" (*biṃbasthaulya*), etc. "In another manner" (*vidhāntareṇa*):
[this refers to] the postulation of utility in the production of the superimposition of a reflection by means of the substance that serves as its own substratum.
The meaning is "due to the arising of sin."
If a barrier such as a wall were an obstructer here merely by disrupting the connection of the visual ray with its object—

even without the obstruction of the visual ray itself— then it would be possible for such a thing to be an obstructer in cases of the perception of a jar and so forth as well; thus, [the opponent's view] would result in the [redundancy of postulating] mere contact of the eye.
Furthermore, because it would entail the loss of [the mirror's] status as a cause, even for one who asserts the false superimposition of a face upon a mirror,

the prior experience must be accounted for by postulating that the rays of light sometimes turn back and grasp one's own face, in order to establish the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) included among the three causes.

And because it must be established [as such]. Nor can the manifestation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arise solely from a prior experience delimited by regions such as the nose; for by that much alone, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of reflections of the eyeball and so forth would be untenable. This is even in the case of water in a pond.
For, in a place where there is the superimposition of the reflection of a person never before seen upon the surface [of the mirror],

it is impossible in any way to describe a prior experience [of that reflection]. Thus, it must necessarily be admitted that the rays of the eye, obstructed by the limiting adjunct (upādhi), reach the original object (bimba) and thereby apprehend it.
When struck by fruits, walls, mirrors, and so forth, [the eyes] reach the reflection and thereby acquire the capacity to perceive it. However,

those [rays] obstructed by stone and the like do not reach it, and those obstructed by copper and other materials that are not perfectly transparent fail to grasp the specific configuration of the face due to the defect of association with an impure limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
For those who have not yet turned back after reaching the limiting adjunct (upādhi), just as for those desiring to reach the sun directly,
there is no such obstruction by the solar brilliance when beholding the reflected sun; thus, as in the case of beholding the sun itself, it is not impossible [to behold the Self].

The word "here" (iha) means the locus of the delusion regarding the reflection. He states that not only is there the fault of the unnecessary assumption (*kalpanā-gaurava*), but another fault also follows: "In that very way," etc. This means even without the dissolution of the sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*). Thus, in order to avoid faults such as the aforementioned *gaurava*, one must accept the rule that [the cognition] occurs by turning back [from the object].

The meaning is "for the sake of contact with the original object" (*bimba*). This is because even you must admit that contact with the original object exists in cases where there is the error of a visual reflection. He states that the restriction "by turning back" is not an unproven factor:
"In the mirror, [the reflection is] false," and so on. Regarding "the three causes": [they are] defect (*doṣa*), conjunction (*saṃprayoga*), and...

The meaning is: by means of the three causes, namely mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), form (*rūpa*), and cause (*kāraṇa*). Since it is never possible to have a direct perception of one's own face by means of the contact of one's own eyes with it [without mediation], there must be an object similar to the superimposed [face]—which serves as the cause for the superimposition—once [the face] has been projected onto a mirror or the like.

Because the impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior experience would not be obtained, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the form of a reflection and so forth could not arise; therefore, the aforementioned rule must be observed in order for one's own face to obtain contact with one's own eyes—this is the sense. "By that much alone" means: not merely by a prior experience delimited by a location such as the surface of a mirror.
He states that even this is difficult to find in some cases, beginning with the words "taṭāke" (in a pond). The phrase "adṛṣṭacare" means never seen before.

The phrase "evaṃ ca" means in the manner described. He avoids the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the stated rule by saying "phalabalāt" (by the force of the result), as in the case of a mirror and so forth.

The meaning is: "because of the non-obstruction of the fruit characterized by the perception of the delusion of a reflection. He states what is excluded by the word *eva* (only): "not in stone and so forth. The intention is that reflections are not perceived in stone and such materials. [Objection:
But surely, since copper and the like—which are not transparent—possess the quality of receiving reflections, they do indeed differ from stone and other such things.

If those [rays] were obstructed—just as visual rays are obstructed by mirrors and the like—they would fail to grasp the face and other objects in their entirety; therefore, he says: "due to a stained limiting adjunct" (*malinopādhi*). A specific configuration, such as the eyeball and so forth, is postulated as the nature of the object in accordance with the results [of perception]; by this, other defects are also [accounted for].
He says they are "rejected" by means of the words beginning with "directly. "Directly" (sākṣāt) means "by looking directly at the sun.

Now, [one might object]: if it is accepted that the rays of the eyes, having been reflected by the water which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for the reflection, reach the location of the original object (*bimba*); [then what?]

There is no fault in the following conceptualization: when there is contact with limiting adjuncts such as water, although some [rays] are obstructed by the adjunct and reach the original object (*bimba*), others perceive the sand and other things contained within it, and so forth. However, the authors of the *Advaitavidyā* [hold that] the reflection...

They state that this is the intention of Vidyāraṇya, Guru, and others who accept falsity and maintain the doctrine of the three kinds of souls: [the reflection] is clearly perceived in a mirror by those standing nearby as being similar to Caitra, yet distinct from the face of Caitra itself.

That reflection is distinct from the object in its manifestation, yet it is false in its own nature, just as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is false when compared to the silver in one's own hand. Nor is there any contradiction with the cognition of non-difference from the original object in the thought, "My face appears in the mirror," for there is a clear perception of difference and duality.

Because non-difference is impossible due to the contradiction with the cognition of facing westward and so forth; and because the designation "my face in the mirror" is figurative, just like the designation of one's own face applied to its reflection. Nor can it be argued that, due to the contradiction with the cognition of non-difference, the designation of difference itself must be figurative.

One might suspect that sand and other such things contained within water would not be perceived due to the absence of sensory contact; however, he states "due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as water" to show that this objection is also refuted. [Objection: But surely, for those [rays] which are obstructed by the limiting adjunct...

If it is argued that when the object's location is no longer reached [by the mirror], there would be the undesirable consequence of a reflection appearing on the back surface, even for objects obstructed by other things—this fault does not apply. This is because, based on the evidence of the observed result (*phala*), one must assume a specific kind of proximity (*sannikarṣa*) among the various parts of the body; with this intention, he says:

Thus, regarding the aforementioned conceptualization: the Master Sureśvarācārya has stated that the visual rays, having turned back, grasp the reflected image. He says: "The vision, struck by the mirror, turns back and pervades one's own face; thus, facing [the reflection], it shows the face as reversed."
Having first refuted the position that the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are distinct, the position of their non-difference was established.
Now, having refuted that non-difference, he establishes the position of their distinction:
"But those who have composed the Advaita-vidyā [state]... and "of three kinds..."—namely, the ultimate (*pāramārthika*), the conventional (*vyāvahārika*), and the illusory (*prātibhāsika*).

The position that the individual soul (*jīva*) is threefold by way of division should be understood as having been established in the first chapter. "In this manner" means in the way that will be explained hereafter. Regarding "Caitra": when Caitra looks at his own face in a mirror, then, while the face existing on the side of the object (the original) remains on Caitra's neck, [the reflection] appears in the mirror.

The meaning is that the reflection of Caitra’s face is experienced as being both distinct from and similar to [the actual face], without doubt or error. This is just like mother-of-pearl silver, which is experienced as being distinct from the real silver held in one's own hand and yet as being similar to it.

The meaning is that it is distinct from that [the mirror] and false, just like that [silver]. He states that the cognition of non-difference is unestablished. The sense is that, as expressed by the word "clearly" (*spaṣṭa*), no cognition of non-difference between the two pieces of silver cited as examples is observed. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes facing forward, being located on the neck, being located in the mirror, independence, dependence, and so forth, which are present in the actual object. If that is so, then...
"What is the status of the designation of non-difference, which is established by universal experience?
Anticipating the objection that "the designation [of non-difference] must be preceded by knowledge," he says:
"In the mirror, 'mine'... The point is that when there is a clear cognition of difference, a designation of non-difference is untenable. But surely...
"My face shines in the mirror," "my face appears dirty," "my face appears long"— yet the face remains situated in the stone [of the original] alone, not in the mirror and so forth.
Because there exist many clear experiences of non-difference, there is the designation of non-difference.

The primary [point] is that, because it contradicts the experience of non-difference, the experience of difference itself is impossible. One might suspect the opposite— that the mere designation of difference remains undifferentiated, and since that is possible even in the absence of actual non-difference between the original and its reflection due to the existence of an imagined difference— and thus he refutes this with "No."
By the words beginning with "ceti," etc.

Because it is impossible to deny the capacity for causal efficacy— extending up to the attainment of the desired goal— which serves as the means for removing the delusion of another person [being the object] in the reflection of fools; and because even discerning people (prekṣāvantaḥ) resort to mirrors and the like in order to fully recognize the specific features of their own faces.
It must be stated that even the cognition of non-difference arising from perception culminates in purposeful action (*arthakriyā*); for even when there is difference,
the production of that [cognition] is possible solely through the thorough knowledge of the specific restriction that a reflection possesses a form identical to that of the original object (*bimba*).

He provides the decisive argument that the perception of activity and so forth regarding a reflection cannot be established without its being distinct from the original object (*bimba*), stating: "Children [flee]... Children, seeing a terrifying reflection in a body of water or similar place, flee, leaving it behind; whereas they approach a pleasant, delightful reflection.

It is established by universal experience that upon seeing it, they desire to grasp it and go toward the location of the reflection. This was stated by the teacher Karṇāmṛta: "A young child crawling on his knees upon a jeweled floor, desiring to seize his own reflected lotus-face, [is distressed] by its non-attainment..."

Out of distress, the nurse looked at his face and wept. Thus it was said: the infant Humāra, whose form is that of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, while crawling on his knees upon a pedestal made of pure jewels, saw his own reflection there; he was adorned with various ornaments such as earrings and the like.

Having obtained his own lotus-face, which was endowed with boundless beauty, captivating to the hearts of the cowherd women, and always desirable even to Brahmā and the other gods, he followed the worldly behavior of a child; then, out of a desire to give, he engaged his hands in activity for a long time.

When he did not obtain it, then, out of distress at not having received even that little, he looked at his nurse’s face and wept with a loosened throat, meaning that he acted with the intention: "Having taken this, you must give it to me."

Anticipating the objection that non-dual cognition (*abheda-jñāna*) likewise possesses efficacy up to the point of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), he refutes it with the words "And not... and so forth.

If there were indeed a real difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), then it would be necessary for investigators to determine that difference; thus, for them to determine the specific distinction residing in their own faces—

The meaning is that the taking up of mirrors and so forth would not occur for them either, since they too must be said to have a determination of non-difference upon seeing [the reflection]. He states that their activity is established otherwise: "even though there is difference" means even though there is a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). Precisely because they are investigators (*parīkṣaka*).

The meaning is that for them, the possession of certainty regarding difference and the possession of knowledge of specific rules are possible through the aforementioned arguments. [Objection: But even for children, activities such as the removal of a reflection are possible solely due to the delusion that the reflection resides in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the original object (*bimba*); thus, there is an alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*). [Reply: That [objection] is equal [in force] in this case as well.

And thus, since the experiences of difference and non-difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), as well as the purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*) resulting from those differences and non-differences, are equal, it is more logical— due to parsimony (*lāghava*)— to postulate that non-difference is intrinsic; for the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established by scripture through their relationship as the original object and its reflection.

Since the conceptualization of the non-difference between the reflection and the original image serves a practical purpose for spiritual practice (*pratipatti*), and since this non-difference is further supported by scriptural texts on non-duality (*abheda-śruti*), it is possible for the individual soul (*jīva*) itself to be the reflection that is non-different from Brahman; therefore, [a reflection] distinct from that...

Furthermore, the conceptualization of a jīva delimited by ultimate reality is burdened by the fault of unnecessary complexity (gaurava). This is because the mantra beginning with "This self consisting of light, like the sun," possesses its natural consistency only under the view of their non-difference;
for in that context, just as the multiplicity of the sun and so forth is due to being reflected in various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it is not inherent.

It is established that the unity of consciousness is due to its being reflected in many limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), while its plurality is merely apparent and its true nature is unity; however, this is not possible on the view that there is a difference between the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*),
for according to that position, the original consciousness would be one while the reflections would be many.

Since it is impossible for the multiplicity of a single entity to result merely from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), therefore, in the view that accepts the reflection of consciousness, [it applies] to Caitra in the world.

As for the claim that in the case of "this is not a face," there is a sublation of the mere contact with the face in the mirror but not of the face itself— that leads to the absurd conclusion that in the case of "this is not silver" as well, there would be a sublation of the identity with silver only in the object "this" (idam-artha), but not of the silver itself. If, however, [it is argued that] in the portion "this"...

Because of the superimposition (adhyāsa) of silver through identity (*tādātmya*), there is the sublation (*bādha*) of the silver itself through identity in the form "this is not silver," but not the sublation of identity alone; likewise, because of the superimposition of the face in the mirror through relation (*saṃsargitā*), there is the sublation of the face itself through relation in the form "the face is not here."

It is the same regarding the claim that it does not apply to mere contact. As for the objection that there is excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating the superimposition of even the substrate (*dharmin*), that is no fault, because the postulation of the appearance as silver is likewise supported by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

Furthermore, in the case of the delusion of a reflection in one's own eyeball and so forth, there is no need to postulate the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of the original object (*bimba*), since such a thing does not exist.

For if one imagines that the rays of the eyes, though obstructed by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), nevertheless reach the object, this contradicts perception and leads to many difficulties. For how could it be that, upon contact with water, some of the eye-rays enter within unobstructed while others, despite being in contact with the water, [are obstructed]?
Being excessively obstructed, these delicate rays, having overcome the mass of light that strikes all eyes, would enter the full lunar disc situated in their midst.

If it is argued that regarding the locus of the reflection (*bimba*), the position of the non-difference between the original object and its reflection is indeed superior and is what is intended by the *Vivaraṇa* and other such works— this is true from the perspective of subtle insight; for this very reason, even though there is non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, the *Bhāmatī*, the *Nibandhana*, and other texts maintain that because a superimposed difference exists— just as between a worldly original object and its reflection— there is a distinction in their attributes (*dharma*).

"Vyavasthā" refers to universal convention. However, masters such as Śrī Vidyāraṇya have established the theory of the arising of reflections (*pratibimba*) for the sake of those with dull faculties, so that reality may ascend into their understanding.

For those of dull faculties, just as there is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) which is the locus of transmigratory existence—consisting of agency, enjoyership, and so forth—[the same applies to the reflection of Brahman].

Furthermore, that [individual self] is illusory in nature, whereas the Self, being of the nature of unattached consciousness, is not the substratum of transmigratory existence; thus, through this method, one arrives at the truth. However, the Brahman-hood of the Self—which is the reflection of Brahman—is not established by itself, due to its identification with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

Regarding "being the locus of saṃsāra": according to the [Advaitic] system, one either ascends to the state of Buddhahood or remains [in saṃsāra]. This is because, in the world, while the mixing of contradictory properties is evident in cases where the substrata are distinct, it is not so manifest in cases where the substratum is non-different;
and this is their intended meaning. As stated in the *Kūṭasthadīpa*: "By whichever..."

This is clear from the example given in the *Vārttika* statement, "bhavet puṃsām" (it may be for males). And that statement has already been cited and explained at the very beginning; this is the summary. Having restated what was said regarding the reflection-case—namely, that there is only the appearance of a relation such as being located in a mirror—the object of the rejoinder (*prativandyā*) [is now addressed].
He establishes the sublation (*bādha*) of the nature of the reflection by means of the passage beginning with "yat tu" and so forth. Regarding the word "āpatteḥ":

the sense is that, in that case, the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the silver in the mother-of-pearl—which is accepted as the established doctrine—would not be established. Although here, even if only identity (*tādātmya*) were subject to sublation...

Since it has been stated that the production of an indefinable silver is unavoidable, and that perception [of it] as non-different from the object present before one is untenable because the silver located in another place is not non-different from consciousness,

nevertheless, thinking that the sublation (*bādha*) of the shell-silver can still be established, [the author] says: *...* (The text continues with the argument regarding the sublation of the illusory object.)

The proponent of the non-difference of the reflection (*pratibimbābheda-vādī*) raises an objection: "If [it is argued]... and "as being related" (*saṃsargitayā*). The meaning is "by way of being the superstratum" (*ādheyatayā*).

Regarding the phrase "because it is authoritative" (*prāmāṇikatvāt*): the meaning is that, just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, there is no difference in the fact that the burden of postulating a superimposition (*adhyāsa-kalpanā-gaurava*) is rooted in the existence of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the reflection.

Furthermore, since it is impossible for the reflection of one's own eyeballs and so forth—which reside within one's own mouth—to be perceived directly under the theory of non-difference (*abheda-pakṣa*), the assumption of such a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) involves an unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, he states: "One's own eyes... and so on, reiterating the previously mentioned argument to refute it. [He says: "Of the rays of the eyes," meaning "of the collection of light rays."
The meaning is: a mass of sunbeams.

And how is it that, just as when looking at the moon itself, there would not be a refreshing nourishment for the eyes manifested through coolness— even though there is no difference in the proximity to that cool disc when looking at its reflection? And how could this occur even through a connection with water?

Being obstructed by contact with stones and the like, they would not be obstructed; or, upon being turned back by that obstruction, they would not come into contact with the eyeballs and so forth; or, if they were to come into such contact, why would they not cause that which is contacted to be directly perceived? For even by a defect...

It is observed that only the apprehension of the specific attributes is being obstructed, and not even the apprehension of the nature of the proximate substratum itself. However, in the case of the theory of superimposition of a reflected face, there is nothing whatsoever contrary to empirical experience.

For it must be so conceived; for we observe that the superimposition of grossness and manifest color upon the eye occurs only when those very qualities—grossness and manifest color residing in the reflection—are established as the causes for the direct perception of their own substratum. Thus, [the reflection] depends on its own substratum...
The status of being a cause exists even in the case of superimposition as a reflection.

Now, it is not imagined here that water possesses the quality of resistance; rather, it is because of the sand and other substances within the water that there is no absolute softness. Just as the rays of the sun and other luminaries, though they lack the power to burn grass and such by themselves, possess that burning power when reflected from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta-maṇi), so too is this case.

[The opponent argues: "Even though the rays of the eyes do not inherently possess the quality of obstructing the rays of the sun, it is logical to postulate an excellence of capacity for them to overcome those [sun-rays] when they are obstructed by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) that serves as the locus of the reflection. Thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "And how could there be no nourishment? (kathaṃ cāpyāyanaṃ na syāt). This implies: "How could it be that [the moon] is not nourished [by the sun's rays]?"

The connection [is as follows]: the meaning is that there is no distinction from proximity to the orb of that moon, which is as cooling as nectar. "Nourishment" (*āpyāyana*) refers to the alleviation of heat. When a person, with his face turned downward, gazes continuously at the reflection of the lunar disc in a reservoir of water or similar place—

Then, there would be the manifestation of coolness in the eyes and so forth; the meaning is that because the reflection and the original object are non-different, the contact with the reflection itself constitutes the contact with the original object. Now, one might object: the manifestation of coolness in the eyes is not caused by contact with the moon and the like, but rather—
And because the continuity of contact with the moon's rays is established for those two [the eyes], there is likewise pleasure below;

yet, due to the absence of that [contact] in the eyes, even though the proximity of the moon is perceived, there is no consequence such as the manifestation of coolness. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"And how [is it] that they do not strike?"—the connection is "how would they not be obstructed?

meaning that they would indeed be obstructed. To this he says: "By being struck by that. The connection is "how would they not come into contact with the eyeballs and so forth? To this he further says: "By coming into contact with that."

If, at the time of perceiving a stone or other object, the visual rays are reflected by that stone and so forth and thus come into contact with one's own eyes, such as the eyeballs located on one's face— then how could those visual rays not cause the contact with the eyeballs and so forth to be directly perceived? The meaning is that they would indeed cause it to be directly perceived.

[Objection: "But surely, due to the power of defects (*doṣa*), even if [the object] is in contact, they would not cause direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he says: "For even by a defect... and so on, ending with "...is seen. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "even in cases of error such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver. And thus, at the time of contact with a stone or the like, there is a direct perception of one's own face, either in the form of the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "facedness" (*mukhatva*) or as the face itself.

The sense is that this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*). In reality, however, it should be understood that the quality of being an obstacle is accepted only for a clear substance—whether distinct from the result or conjoined with it—that is capable of producing a reflection;
therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. This is so in the view that there is a distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*).

Having first shown the abundance of contradictions with perceived experience from a superficial standpoint, he establishes the position that the superimposition is of a reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*), stating:

"But in the case of the position of the superimposition of a face [as a reflection]... The connection is that both causality and obstructiveness would have to be postulated. Regarding the term *svāśraya* ("its own substratum"): [the reflection's substratum is the mirror].

The meaning is that, regarding the visual perception delimited by being the locus of large, manifested color, [the cause] is established as two [factors], such as the pot and so forth. In the second case, even its own term refers to "grossness" and "manifested color.

Regarding the phrase "even in superimposition," it means that just as the face or other object which serves as the prototype (bimba) is visually perceived, so too is the face or object which is its own substrate.
Superimposition (adhyāsa) has the nature of a reflection; its production means the appearance [of that reflection].

Since a material object such as a wall acts as an obstruction, it functions through reaching [the object]—according to the principle of the sense of touch—and thus, by way of obstructing the contact of the eye, it renders an intervening object [unperceivable].

Since it has been established that [ignorance] acts as an obstacle to direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), its status as an obstacle must likewise be postulated— even in the case of the superimposition of a concealed reflection— without requiring any other intervening medium. In this regard, what contradiction is there in postulating causality or similar functions elsewhere for that which has been established as having such a function in one instance by the force of the observed result?

By this, the objection that there would be no possibility of visual reflection for an object obstructed by a medium— since the rays of the eye are blocked— and for an object hidden from view or devoid of manifest color and so forth, because it cannot reach the mirror-surface, is refuted. Furthermore, how could the aforementioned fault not follow even if one were to accept [the existence of such a reflection]?
Just as in the direct gazing at the sun, when the water is viewed without the movement of the eyes by one with bowed head, the rays of the eye, being reflected from that water,
possess the capacity to grasp the solar disc as it rises upward, even though [the sun] is actually positioned obliquely.
Just as when looking into a mirror with a steady gaze— without the movement of the eyes— the rays of light reflected from it grasp the face situated at the side, so too,
even in the absence of turning the face, the rays obstructed by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) grasp the back part that is otherwise concealed.

First of all, the status of being a perceiver is difficult to avoid, because the rays of the eyes— whose outward movement is obstructed by an adjunct— do not merely turn back, but proceed to the very place where the reflected image is located.
As for what was said— that if one accepts that the wall and so forth act as direct obstructors to the superimposition of a reflection,

then by the same logic it would follow in other cases as well, resulting in the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of sense-object contact (sannikarṣa)— that is not so; for, in accordance with the evidence establishing that contact is a cause [of perception], it is precisely through the mediation of the disruption of contact [that the wall acts as an obstructor].

With the intention of asserting that [the absence of contact] is a perceptual impediment, he indicates the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the causality of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) by saying "the sense of touch" (*tvagindriya*). This is because it is observed that the sense of touch produces the perception of its object only when it has reached that object; by this example, the same applies to the eyes and other senses as well.
The meaning is that it is understood to have the property of reaching its object (*prāpyakāritva*). The word *vyavahita* is to be split [as *vyavahita-pratibimba*].

In the case of the superimposition of a reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*) of a face or the like that is obstructed by a wall or similar barrier, the direct obstructiveness of that barrier must be postulated; otherwise, in the view that a reflection actually arises, there would be no contact with the original object (*bimba*).

The meaning is that, since it has already been shown that the undesirable consequence of a reflection—even of something separated [from the cause]—follows from not accepting its status as a cause; the connection is "what contradiction is there in that assumption?
(tatra kalpane), which means "in that assumption. [This refers to the presence of] non-separation, grossness, and manifest color in the face and so forth.
He states the purpose of postulating the utility of the superimposition of a reflection with the words "by this" (*eteneti*). The word "etc.

(*ādi*) is for the purpose of including grossness (*sthūlya*). The phrase "as stated" (*uktā*) means that the contingency of [the reflection being] a distant prototype (*vyavahita-bimba*) and so forth has been mentioned. One who is ignorant of the manner of this contingency asks, "How? To him he replies, "Directly" (*sākṣāt*).
The meaning is that without the shifting of the eyes toward the sun situated in the sky;

"with head bowed" means with face turned downward; "sideways" means that at the time of perceiving one's own reflection in a mirror facing oneself, there is also the perception of the reflection of a person standing at one's side.

At a time when no reflection is present, there is a lateral movement of one's own eyes to perceive a person standing at one's side; for it is observed that a person standing at one's side cannot be perceived by the eyes directed straight ahead in the same way as a person facing oneself can be perceived. And so it is with a mirror facing oneself.

The meaning is as follows: just as a mirror, when struck by rays of light, becomes the perceiver of a person standing at its own side without requiring the eyes to cast a lateral glance, so too [is the case here]. Regarding the word "vadan" (face):
it refers to the turning of the face, such that the eyes do not perceive what is obstructed by one's own back.
The activity of speaking conducive to the apprehension of the meaning of words. Regarding "the restriction of turning back":
this means the restriction of those [rays] that have been reflected from objects facing the eyeballs toward re-entry into the interior of the body via the gateway of the eyeballs.

Likewise, in the case of a reflection of a fair face in a dirty mirror, although the fair color residing in the original object (bimba) exists, it is not utilized in the visual cognition; thus, by the logic of the error of a yellow conch, the superimposed form—
Just as the visual perceptibility of the face in the mirror cannot be established except through its association with the blackness of the mirror's substrate,

so too it is unavoidable that even an inherently formless object can become the object of the visual illusion of a reflection through its association with the blackness of the mirror as an adjunct (*upādhi*). This holds true even for that which is itself devoid of color.
Since the sky is admitted to be perceptible by the eye precisely because of its specific quality of blueness superimposed upon it,
therefore the position that the face is superimposed in its own essential form is indeed superior.

Now, even in the view that there is no rule regarding the return [of the rays], there is still a requirement for the absence of any obstruction that would disrupt contact with the object; for instance, when looking at a mirror with straight eyes while the sun is overhead, the rays of the eyes from one whose head is bowed strike the mirror.

And in a place where a person standing at the side is reached, the attainment [of that person] is possible because of the absence of anything that obstructs proximity; however, in the present case, because of the existence of the body and its parts as intervening obstacles, there is no such attainment for those [rays] reflected by the mirror.
Because there is a lack of logical consistency in the claim that "there is an attainment of an object obstructed by the rear part [of the body]," he says: "In the same way.

This means that under the view where there is no fixed rule for the return of ocular rays obstructed by an adjunct (*upādhi*), there would be the occurrence of visual reflections not only of formless things like wind and sound, but also of objects obstructed by the rear part, just as there is the occurrence of reflections.

The word "tathā" (likewise) has the sense of adding another refutation. Now, it might be argued that even for something formless, such as sound or speech, it is unavoidable that it becomes the object of the error of a visual reflection by assuming the form residing in an adjunct such as a mirror; thus, [the claim] that this is impossible for a substance is untenable.

Anticipating the objection that in the visual illusion of a reflection, the color of the original object (*bimba*) must also be a cause because it possesses manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), [the author] replies "not so," stating that in a visual illusion of a reflection whose object is a substance, the color residing in the original object is of no use. He says: "In a dirty mirror... (*maline*). In a dirty mirror...

When there is a reflection of a fair-faced person, that reflection is perceived as dark rather than fair; thus, the visual perception of the fair-faced person—though it is actually superposed upon that [reflection] by means of the superposed form of darkness—is thereby established. In some cases, a substance is [perceived] solely through its superposed form.

He provides an example for its being visual [perception] with the words "yellow conch. The sense is that, in the context of explaining the poetic theory (*kāvyamata*), it was stated that in cases of error, the visual nature of the conch exists only when it is qualified by the superimposed yellow color, and not otherwise. In reality, however, regarding the visual perception of a substance...

Since it is only the manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) residing in a substance that serves as the cause [of visual perception], it does not follow that a colorless substance could be the object of the delusion of a visual reflection; for instance, in the case of the reflection of a fair face in a dirty mirror, or in the case of the delusion of a yellow conch and the like, the face appears dark.

In the erroneous cognition "the conch is yellow" and the like, since it is not established that the color of the object— such as yellow or white— which serves as a cause for superimposition (*adhyāsa*), functions as a cause within the prior cognition of the substratum (*dharmijñāna*); this is because there is no rule that visual perception of a substance must have color as its object, as demonstrated during the commentary on the works of certain logicians (*kavitārkika*).
It should be understood that this is because the possibility of the illusion of a yellow conch arises from its being thus demonstrated.
Furthermore, since visual perception occurs only when [an object] is qualified by the form of the superimposed [attribute], he provides another example, beginning with "naturally" (*svataḥ*).
The phrase "due to common consensus" (*saṃpratipatteḥ*) refers to the fact that, at first glance, the sky is the objective domain of visual activity.

This is accepted only by mere poets and logicians, but not by the ancient teachers (*pūrvācāryas*). In the view of the ancient teachers, however, at the time when the consciousness delimited by light is manifested through the visual function whose object is the solar light pervading the sky, there is also the manifestation of the consciousness delimited by the sky as it follows along with that light.

It should be understood that by accepting the superimposition (adhyāsa) of blueness upon the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), which is manifested as delimited by space, the sky characterized by blueness and so forth is cognized by the witness alone. Therefore, the sense is that there is no sublation consisting of a contradiction with perceived experience, and because it is indeed a proof. "Śreyān" [means]... [the rest of the sentence].
For those of dull faculties, the reality is understood through faith.
Nor is there any difficulty regarding the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience even in that case; for,

just as in a dream there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a person never before seen based merely on the latent impression of the experience of the universal "person," so too [is there the superimposition] of the face based on the experience of the universal "face."
For the superimposition of a specific face upon a mirror is possible through mere mental construction (*saṃskāra*). However, this is the distinction:

in dreams, the superimposition of a specific human form occurs in accordance with what has been seen as the cause of good or evil; here, however, it occurs in accordance with the proximity of the original object (*bimba*).

Regarding the statement "it is a superimposition of a specific facial form": the objection that if the reflection were false by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), it would follow as a defect that the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a reflection of Brahman, must also be false, is not valid;
for even if the reflected soul (*pratibimbajīva*) were thus [false], the delimited soul (*avacchinnajīva*) remains real.

Regarding the phrase "because it is established that [the soul] partakes in liberation": as for the view held by some that a reflection in mirrors and the like is indeed real, being a specific kind of shadow (*chāyā*) of the face—that is not so;
for what is called a "shadow" is that which occurs when the light, which was pervading a certain location, is obstructed by the various limbs of the body and so forth.

In each respective place, it is merely a subtle darkness and not a pearl, ruby, or the like; for it is not logical that a reflection—which possesses forms such as white or red that are contrary to darkness—should have the nature of a shadow consisting of darkness, nor is it tenable that a reflection such as the eye, which is devoid of the nature of a shadow consisting of darkness, should possess such a nature. Is this not so?
If it is argued that, since the nature of shadow as a reflected form is impossible,

darkness must be a distinct substance— because it is logical to postulate darkness as a separate substance not included among the established categories, just like a banyan tree— then what is that other substance?
The perceived form, size, configuration, and specific qualities— such as facing toward the side or the front, and so forth—

would have to be either endowed with those attributes or devoid of them. Therefore, the claim that the perception of a reflection is accounted for by a distinct substance composed of specific forms and other qualities is redundant.
That is the ritual procedure for that [rite].

Having restated the argument that for those obstructed by an adjunct (*upādhi*), since the attainment of the reflection is impossible, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—which serves as the cause for superimposition—is untenable because it is impossible to experience a prior experience of an object belonging to the same class as the face being superimposed, he refutes it with the words: "And not even there... (*na ca tatrāpi*).

The meaning is that even the difficulty regarding one's own latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) does not apply to the theory of superimposition upon a reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*). Regarding the phrase "never before seen" (*adṛṣṭacareti*): it means never having occurred at any time. Now, if the latent impression produced by the experience of a face-in-general were the cause for the superimposition of a reflected face, then when Caitra’s face and a mirror are in proximity, [it would follow] for anyone...

There is the possibility of superimposing a face [upon another]. Anticipating the objection that, as in a dream, there is no fixed rule that the superimposition of a face must occur facing forward, he states the settled distinction with the words, "But this much is the difference. The ellipsis to be supplied is "between a dream and a superimposition of a reflection. By the qualification "first, for those who maintain three kinds of souls," [he indicates the context].
He reveals the solution indicated [in the previous verse]: "The reflection is that of the individual soul (jīva).

To refute the view that the reflection is real—for the sake of strengthening the position that the reflection's non-difference from Brahman is unreal—he restates the opponent's argument with the words "As for what [was said]... [Now, an objection: But since a blueness is observed in the shadows of trees and so forth, [how can this be applied to] reflections?

In order to dispel the doubt that the reflection cannot be of the nature of a shadow because it generally lacks the characteristic of blueness found in shadows, the word "viśeṣa" (distinction) is used; thus,
although the appearance of the face and so forth is distinct from the original object, it is not merely illusory like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
However, the meaning is that [the reflection] is real like the original object (*bimba*), because it is admitted to be a specific form of shadow (*chāyā*).

He refutes this by first describing the nature of shadow, saying "that is not so," on the grounds that since shadow is invariably characterized by the color blue, it is impossible for a reflection to be a specific form of shadow, as in the case of the body and so forth.

The meaning is that it is well known that shadow is indeed darkness and nothing else. What [is meant] is that when a place is occupied by the body and its limbs—which pervade that space—[then shadow occurs]. Furthermore, it is not logical for a reflection such as a pearl or crystal, which possesses a white form, to have the nature of shadow, which is of the nature of darkness opposed to that [whiteness].

Likewise, since the reflection of rubies, gold, and so forth is considered to possess red, yellow, and other colors, it is not logical for it to have a shadow that is their opposite; thus, one should apply this by distinguishing [the cases]. The meaning is that since there is no shadow at all in the eye and other such organs, it is altogether untenable for their reflection to be of the nature of a shadow. "Like darkness" (tamo vat).

The meaning is that just as, in the established doctrine (siddhānta), darkness— since it cannot be included within the [previously] enumerated substances— is postulated as the tenth substance, so it is here.

First, how can there be the establishment of the reality of multiple reflections of large dimensions appearing simultaneously and without confusion in a single mirror of very small dimension? And how [is it possible] in a mirror whose parts are densely interwoven?

While the [mirror] remains exactly as it was, there arises another substance possessing numerous concave and convex regions such as the interior and the nasal cavity; furthermore, when a reflection possessing various colors such as white, red, and yellow arises,
that which is situated within the mirror is not present there in such a manner.

There is a reason for this. If it were argued that reflections possess only such dimensions as are capable of resting within the confines of their limiting adjuncts (upādhi), then the cognition of large dimensions and the cognition of such features as depressions and elevations would be mere error, just as in the case of a mirror previously described.
If it is argued that some cause must be postulated which is capable of producing such a reflection without contradicting the persistence of its own parts,
then even the silver in the mother-of-pearl must be real; for in that case as well, [the mother-of-pearl remains] as before.

For it is possible to explain the restriction that this silver is grasped by the sense organ only when accompanied by a cause regarded as a defect, by postulating some cause capable of producing that very silver which has already been established as having attained identity with the substrate.

The connection [of the sentence] is: "How can truthfulness be maintained in the first case? To ward off the doubt that if even a single mirror were large, it would be possible for multiple reflections to reside therein without being intermingled, he says: "small" (*alpa*). Even for those of small dimensions...
He says "in one" to show that even when there is a multiplicity of mirrors, it is not the case that a single reflection remains unmixed within each individual mirror;
for even in a single mirror of very small dimensions, multiple reflections can exist in succession without being confused with one another.
To the objection that "that too does not exist," he says: "simultaneously. As for the falsity of the reflection, this fault does not apply;

for just as in the state of dream, there is the superimposition of objects such as chariots and elephants, along with their appropriate vastness, within the very small internal space of the body, so too [is it] in the case of a mirror of small dimensions.

The sense is that because multiple reflections are not mutually confused, there is the possibility of superimposing upon them an appropriate spaciousness. The connection [of the phrase] is "and how could there be the production of another substance?"—the word "real" (*satya*) being understood as the ellipsis. Furthermore, its production does not occur due to the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*). He states that it is indeed possible [to show why]: "Moreover... (kiṃ ca).
If there were a rule that whatever color belongs to the mirror is the same as that of the reflection,
then it would be possible for some cause endowed with that color to exist within the mirror; however, this is not the case, for reflections possess various forms distinct from the form of the mirror.

He says it is not from experience [of the original object], stating "aneka" (multiple). He says that the various reflections possessing multiple colors such as white, yellow, and red cannot be the cause, stating "situated within the mirror. Even if those [colors] were instrumental causes (*nimitta*), they cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) at the location where the reflection arises.

The meaning is: "due to their absence. Regarding the phrase "of such a kind": it means that at the time of the emergence of the reflection, there is necessarily no cause endowed with various colors such as white, yellow, red, and so forth, because such a thing is not perceived.
For the reflection exists within the mirror, not on the back part of the mirror.
It is experienced as being situated within the mirror, and not—as if it were the color, dimension, or other qualities residing in the mirror—on the upper surface of the mirror;

thinking that for this reason it must also exist right there [within], it is said to be "situated within" (darpaṇamadhyastha) and "in proximity" (tatsannihita) to the mirror. Here, the word *madhya* has the sense of "inside," referring merely to the essential nature of the reflection itself.

It is true that in that case, the properties being perceived are indeed merely imagined; thus, one who clings to their reality raises this doubt: "If it were said... [The opponent argues: In reality, only reflections capable of resting within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) are produced, and within those, qualities such as great dimension appear through delusion.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "it must be postulated": just as the parts of rice (*nīvāra*) are postulated by the Mīmāṃsakas to be the parts of *ūrbrāhma* (barley), so too the parts of the reflection (*pratibimba*) conjoined with the parts of the mirror must be postulated;
this is the meaning. He states the counter-argument (*prativandī*) with the words "then indeed" (*tarhi*), keeping the previously mentioned example in mind.

It postulates a cause even for the silver in the mother-of-pearl; that is to say, even in the case of the silver-in-mother-of-pearl. Now, if one were to accept that the silver in the mother-of-pearl is real, then because it would always exist in the mother-of-pearl, it too would necessarily be perceived at the time of the perception of the mother-of-pearl; yet it is not so perceived. Therefore, it lacks reality.
He dispels the doubt that [it] might arise with the words "of that" (tasya).
Is it not the case that, according to the maxim of the "half-old woman" (*ardhavajaratīya*), the silver in the mother-of-pearl is unreal while the reflection is real?

And if that were so, would it not follow that when the mother-of-pearl—which is perceived as silver—is cast into fire, it would undergo liquefaction like silver? [This is not so], as in the cases of camphor, musk, and the like.

Just as a reflection lacks bulk, fragrance, and so forth, it is established that the silver in mother-of-pearl lacks the capacity for liquefaction and is unreal. Now, if it is argued that this silver is not real because it is sublated by the universal consensus that "this is not silver; it was only silver that appeared," and thus the silver in mother-of-pearl is not true—then [the following applies]:

The face does not exist in the mirror; it is merely a falsehood that "the face is here in the mirror. Since all such [claims] are sublated by established experience—such as the perception of the sun and so forth—it is logical that even the reflection is not real. Therefore, the doctrine asserting the reality of reflections is inconsistent. Now, one might object: "But the doctrine of falsity is also untenable, just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell."
Because no cause characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been identified, nor its counteragent, knowledge (*jñāna*). On this point, some [object]:

To this he replies: "What [is gained] there?"—that is, "By what means? He says: "By the logic of the 'half-old woman' (ardhajaratīya). The meaning is as follows: just as one might desire only the face of an old woman, while not desiring her lower body, so too is this [case]; it is like a paramour who seeks only another [woman].
