Now, [one might argue that] well-known silver, when cast into fire, becomes liquid...

"But silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not like that"; thinking that it is indeed false, he raises an objection. "And if that were so" means "if its reality were established. He supports the counter-argument with the words "not so," etc.

Although, in the view that maintains the reality of reflections, the very point [of the opponent's objection] is accepted since even things like "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" could be real, nevertheless, it should be understood that the intent is to establish the falsity of even such things as "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" under the guise of a *pratibandi* (counter-objection). He now raises a doubt regarding the resolution of this *pratibandi*.
The proponent of the reality of the reflection might be asked this. He states the parity of the refutation: "Then [it would follow that] here [the reflection] is indeed false.

It should be understood that, on the view that the original object (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*) are non-different, the experience of the falsity of the reflection has as its object the reflection insofar as it is qualified by the state of being a reflection, and not in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, if that is so—

If it is argued that even the experience of the falsity of "silver in the mother-of-pearl" must be understood as the cognition of silver having attained identity with the object "this," and not as the cognition of its own intrinsic nature— and that consequently it would follow that the identity between the silver and the object "this" is merely imagined while the silver itself is unimagined— then we reply: no, because if the silver were not produced in the mother-of-pearl, [its cognition could not be so explained].

Since perception is untenable due to the absence of non-difference from consciousness, its production therein is unavoidable; and since it is not produced [from anything else], by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it follows that the cause is precisely indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*) and nothing else.
This is because, as previously established, such a cause is admitted to be false.

The sense is that, just as there exist valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing the non-difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) according to the method previously stated, so too—due to the absence of any unestablished means of knowledge proving the reality of the silver in the mother-of-pearl—the experience of the falsity of the "silver in the mother-of-pearl" can be accounted for as having the nature of the silver itself as its object; therefore, it is false. Thus [it concludes with] "tasmāt" (therefore).
The meaning is that there is no evidence for the reality of a reflection distinct from the original object (*bimba*). As for the objection beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*):
in the view that the reflection is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), its material cause (*upādāna*) must be stated as ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that is not possible;
because [the reflection would be sublated] by the direct perception of the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*), such as the mirror, in its entirety.

Because ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by a mirror or the like has not been removed, it is impossible for the superimposition of the reflection— which persists even when such direct perception occurs— to be sublated by that [perception]; furthermore, no other knowledge is observed that could serve as its sublater.

The intention of the objection is that since its falsity is untenable without being removable by knowledge alone, the doctrine of its falsity is also inconsistent; just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the prior determination was made regarding the ignorance of the shell—which is its cause—as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus [the text continues].

The literal meaning is as follows: in the case of the superimposition of a reflection, when there is ignorance (ajñāna) regarding the mirror or other such substrates, there is the superimposition of the reflection; in the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of that [superimposition]. Since no such cause characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) can be identified, and since the knowledge that would remove it cannot be identified, [the theory is untenable].
He refutes [this]. Regarding this, some say:

Even though, although the superimposition of a reflection— which occurs even after the knowledge of the substrate in its entirety— has ignorance as its material cause by way of obscuring the substrate,
the knowledge of the specific aspect of the substrate does not remove it.

Nevertheless, although the portion consisting of the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) of the ignorance regarding the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) has ceased, it is possible for that very [ignorance] to persist through the portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*); therefore, that [ignorance] alone is the material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, knowledge of the substrate, aided by the cessation of the proximity of the reflection’s limiting adjunct (*biṃba-upādhi*), [destroys] that [ignorance] together with its material cause.

"It is the remover of that [ignorance]. Others, however, maintain that the capacity of the knowledge of Brahman to remove only the portion consisting of the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), while leaving aside the portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*), is not inherent; rather, it is like the knowledge of a shell [as silver] removing the *avasthā-jñāna* (empirical ignorance).

Otherwise, if only the obscuring power (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) were removed, there would be the undesirable consequence of its projecting power (*vikṣepa-śakti*) persisting at all times; nor is that [obscuring power] of the nature of the proximity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) which serves as the substrate for the reflection.

Since the cessation [of ignorance] is brought about by the removal of obstacles, and since it is already perceived through direct perception that the reflection— the face of Caitra— is present in the mirror even before the proximity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi), or that there is an absence of the face of Caitra in the mirror due to the absence of contact with the mirror, the portion consisting of the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti) must necessarily also cease.

For if they were present at that time by way of their actual existence, it would follow as an absurd consequence that there could be no delusion of a reflection due to the absence of a material cause (upādāna).
He restates the intended meaning of the objection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).

This means that although there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of this [shell] as "this-ness" (*idantva*) prior to the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver upon the shell, there is no direct perception of it through its specific nature (*viśeṣātman*), such as "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*).
In that case, ignorance— which is the material cause— is understood as the veil over the specific aspect of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

However, in the present instance, since there is a direct perception of the mirror— even in its specific nature such as "mirror-ness"— prior to the superimposition of the reflection upon the mirror that is in contact with the eye, the substratum exists in its entirety.

The meaning is that since there is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), and because ignorance—which is the obscuration of the specific locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—has been removed by that [realization], it is entirely logical that such a material cause (*upādāna*) cannot possibly exist. The particle *api* is used for emphasis, signifying "the remover"; the words "of the superimposition of the reflection" (*pratibimbādhyāsasya*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. If so, how then is the acquisition of a material cause and so forth obtained?
Regarding this, he says: "Even so," and "that very [substratum]. The meaning is that the substratum is indeed knowledge itself.
Even through the direct realization of the substratum in its entirety, there is only the cessation of a single portion of ignorance, and not its total removal.
The sense is that [the distinction] is postulated by the force of the result. He defines the knowledge that brings about cessation with the words "in the original object" (*bimbe*).

The meaning is that it is precisely the knowledge—"the face does not exist in the mirror"—assisted by the removal of the proximity between the original object (*bimba*) and its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that is the remover of the superimposition of the reflection. [This applies to] that which constitutes the material cause, such as the mirror.

There is one primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) which is removable by knowledge, such as that of a mirror and so forth; there is also another ignorance, which is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāvarūpa*).
In this regard, just as primordial ignorance is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the mirror and so forth, it is likewise the material cause of the superimposition of reflections.

He states another resolution: "But others," and so forth. Now, one might object: according to the previously mentioned view, since it is possible for the superimposition of a reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*)—just like mother-of-pearl appearing as silver—to be a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the ignorance of a particular state (*avasthājñāna*), what is the purpose of postulating that [transformation] of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)? He says "no" with the words beginning "of knowledge," and so forth.

Is the capacity of knowledge to remove merely the veil [of ignorance] inherent in its nature, or is it caused by the presence of sattva which obstructs the removal of the portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*)? It is not the first; the reason for this is stated:
"By the knowledge of Brahman... and "Of that... [referring to] the absence of a remover for both types of ignorance, [the power of] projection...

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of [the intellect] persisting even in the state of disembodied liberation (videha-kaivalya), because it is accompanied by the power [of karma]. He restates the second [position] with "na ca" (nor). "Tat" means the capacity to remove only the veil [of ignorance].
When the destruction of the prārabdha-karma—which acts as an obstacle to the removal of the portion of ignorance possessing the power of projection (vikṣepa-śakti)—has occurred...

Thinking that the aforementioned defect does not apply because the cessation of the portion consisting of distraction is possible through the mere consciousness qualified by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the knowledge of Brahman, he states the defect [as follows]:
"Prior to the proximity of the reflection and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)."
The meaning is: "at the very preceding moment" due to the proximity characterized by the facing toward one another of the original object (*bimba*) and the substrate (*upādhi*).

Even in the view that there is no difference between the original object and the reflection (*pratibimba*), although there is no production of a reflection, the face of Caitra—which serves as the original object—is [perceived] as having the nature of a reflection because of its presence in the mirror and so forth.
By accepting the production of that which is expressible (nirvacanīya),

its cause must be stated as the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by Caitra’s face; and that [ignorance] exists at that time when Viṣṇumitra is looking at Caitra’s face before it has been turned toward the mirror.
And due to the absence of any impediment, by means of Viṣṇu who is the object of Caitra's perception.
Therefore, it is only root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) that is the material cause for the superimposition of a reflection;

nor is there any equality with the aforementioned defects here, because the transformations of the mental modes directed toward external objects [occur] in the region of consciousness delimited by their respective objects.

Even though it overcomes a portion of the power of the veil of fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), it does not remove its portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) that even the empirical projections situated in that same location would be dissolved. Furthermore, if the reflection were an effect of fundamental ignorance...

[Otherwise] there would be the consequence of [the reflection] being merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*). This is because being produced by no defect other than ignorance (*avidyā*) is the defining condition for being empirical. In the present case, however, since there exists the defect consisting in the proximity of the upādhi of the original object (*bimba*)—which is distinct from ignorance—it is logically established that the reflection is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). And this being so...

It should not be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the knowledge of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna), even when produced simultaneously with the removal of the proximity of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) such as the mirror, would fail to remove the superimposition of the reflection, because it lacks the power to remove the ignorance (ajñāna) that is the root of that [superimposition].

Through the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the third [truth], it ceases along with the power of distraction (*vikṣepa-śakti*). At that very next moment, when Caitra’s face is facing a mirror, Viṣṇumitra develops the delusion of a reflection, thinking, "Caitra’s face is in the mirror. In that case, there is no production of qualities such as being situated in the mirror within Caitra’s actual face.
He says "because of the absence of a material cause" (*upādānābhāvāt*). Regarding the term "the original object" (*bimba*):
"contact with the mirror" means its being located in the mirror; the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include such qualities as facing inward.
Thus, the connection is: "even though it is perceived by direct perception in the absence of contact and so forth."

The manner of understanding that "the face of Caitra does not exist in the mirror" and so forth should be understood [as follows]. Regarding the view that the superimposition of a reflection arises in the mirror, he states the manner of understanding with the words "in the mirror.

According to the view of the superimposition of a reflection, since it is accepted that the reflection itself is superimposed as being in contact [with the mirror], [the phrase] "in the mirror" [is used].

The meaning is that by the statement "Caitra’s face does not exist," the absence of Caitra’s face in the mirror is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣataḥ*). Thus, for the very purpose of demonstrating the difference in substrates and the difference in their respective direct perceptions according to different viewpoints, [the author] mentions Caitra’s face and the mirror separately.

The seventh [case] is used in the sense of "indifference" (*nirdveṣa*), and the particle *ca* is for the purpose of indicating sevenfold division. "At that time" (*tatkālam*) means: at the second moment following the arising of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) which removes ignorance, occurring together with the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) upon the substratum—the face of Caitra—and upon the mirror. "Of those two" (*tayor*) refers to the face of Caitra and the mirror.

He states the reason for the consequence that the perception of a reflection—such as "Caitra’s face is in the mirror"—would be impossible for Viṣṇumitra, who possesses direct realization of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) while [the object] is present, with the words:
"due to the absence of material cause" (*upādānābhāvena*). He states the reason for that [absence] with the words: "of even the portion of the power of projection" (*vikṣepa-śakty-aṃśasyāpi*).

"By the necessity of [the reflection] ceasing. "From this" means that because the knowledge of the state [of the face] cannot be the cause for the superimposition of a reflection. Now, even in this view, due to the proximity of the original object (bimba) and the limiting adjunct (upādhi), by means of the direct perception of Caitra’s face produced in the preceding moment—

One might object: "Since the root ignorance (mūlājñāna) which veils the consciousness delimited by Caitra’s face and so forth has also been removed, the defect of the absence of a material cause (upādānābhāva) is equal [in both cases]; and if that [root ignorance] were not removed, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-manifestation of Caitra’s face and so forth, because some degree of obscuration (āvaraṇa) would still exist. Anticipating this, he says: "No."
And here too [the phrase] "also" [is used]. It is the knowledge of Brahman alone that removes the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*);

however, as for the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of mental states (*vṛtti*) directed toward insentient objects, they remove only that portion of the root ignorance which constitutes the veil residing within the consciousness of their respective objects.

The meaning is that only the mere sublation of that [object] and the manifestation of the object as far as it extends are admitted; however, unlike the removal of the portion consisting in the obscuration and projection (*vikṣepa*) of the state-level ignorance (*avasthājñāna*), there is no removal of the portion consisting in the obscuration and projection of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). "Otherwise" means:

The meaning is that when the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) residing in the consciousness of the object is removed by the knowledge of that object, there would follow the destruction of the empirical effects—termed "distortions" (*vikṣepa*)—such as mirrors and the like, because their material cause has been destroyed. The word "like" (*iva*) implies "just as in the case of illusory distortions. Now, [an objection]: [Text continues...]

Since objects such as mirrors, which are effects of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), are observed to be empirical (*vyāvahārika*), one might suspect that the superimposition of a reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*)— being likewise an effect of that [root-ignorance]— would necessarily share that status. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And not," etc., showing that being an effect of root-ignorance is not the determinant for empirical reality.

Because even in the case of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*) and the like, there is the status of being conventionally real (*vyāvahārikatva*) despite the absence of that [being produced by ignorance]. However, he states that the cause for that is something else entirely: "distinct from ignorance" (*avidyātirikteti*). The meaning is that although beginningless ignorance and the like lack the property of being produced by ignorance, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because they possess the property of being produced by a defect other than that [ignorance]. This concerns the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a reflection (*pratibimba*).
He states that even the effect of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) does not possess empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), because its causal basis is absent;
this is expressed by the words "And in the present case" (*prakṛte ca*). The meaning is "in the case of the superimposition of a reflection" (*pratibimbādhyāsa*).
And as for the phrase "this being so" (*na caivaṃ sati*), it refers to the state where the superimposition of a reflection is an effect of root-ignorance.

The meaning is "being existent. The phrase "having that as its root" implies that it is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the mother-of-pearl and so forth—which serves to remove the root ignorance—that is observed to be what removes the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver and the like; this is the intended sense.
Because there is no contradiction. Even though [the knowledge of the individual self] does not remove ignorance regarding Brahman,

it is established that the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate— when accompanied by the absence of obstacles— is capable of removing that [ignorance], since its object is opposed to the superimposition of the reflection which has that [Brahman] as its material cause.

Even on the view that the ignorance of the particular state (*avasthājñāna*) is the material cause [of the world], it must be admitted that it possesses the same object as the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) which is the transformation of the prior knowledge of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Since it is impossible to remove [the reflection] by means of a cognition of the substrate occurring at a time when the obstructing factor is absent, one must accept that only the superimposition of the reflection itself is what is to be removed by that [cognition]. Alternatively, let this superimposition be something to be removed solely by the knowledge of Brahman, which removes the ignorance (ajñāna) that is its own material cause.
They say that the status of being empirical is refuted by the fact that it is produced by defects other than ignorance (*avidyā*).
Likewise, the superimposition in dreams also occurs upon the unconditioned consciousness as qualified by the *ahaṃkāra*, which is devoid of the ignorance that constitutes the state [of waking].

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of contradiction": the root ignorance has Brahman as its object, whereas the knowledge of the mirror and so forth—which serves as the substrate for the superimposition of the reflection—has the consciousness delimited by the mirror and so forth as its object. Thus, because there is an absence of the commonality of object, which would be the cause of contradiction between the two, [there is no contradiction].

The meaning is: "even though the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate does not remove the ignorance regarding Brahman because there is no contradiction [between them]. The word *tat* (that) refers to the ignorance regarding Brahman, by virtue of having a contradictory object. For example, [the cognition] "there is no face in the mirror," and so forth.
The meaning is that the superimposition of a reflection has as its object the non-existence of the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum of form. Now,
[one might ask] regarding the position that the superimposition of a reflection has the nescience of the state (*avasthājñāna*) as its material cause (*upādāna*):

It is established that the knowledge of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna), when conjoined with the cessation of the proximity of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the reflection (bimba), is the remover of its material cause, which is ignorance (ajñāna). Thus, knowledge is the remover of ignorance alone,
whereas the cessation of the effects of ignorance occurs through the cessation of their material cause, which is ignorance itself.

Anticipating the objection that this is consistent with what was stated by the author of the *Pañcapādikā*, he says: "avasthājñāna" (the ignorance of the state). Regarding the word "tasya" (of that), it means "of the ignorance of the state. The phrase "prācīna" (prior) refers to the knowledge of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) which preceded the superimposition of the reflection (*bimbādhyāsa*), and by which [the error] was sublated in the form "there is no face in the mirror," and so forth.

The meaning is: "of that [consciousness] which has such a state of ignorance characterized by the power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). Being the object of ignorance means being veiled by ignorance; and upon the destruction of that concealment, because the consciousness delimited by the mirror and so forth no longer possesses the state of being an object of ignorance, it is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

The meaning is that the state of knowledge reaching the state of non-knowledge does not constitute a contradiction in terms of having the same object; thus, [the objection] is refuted. The word "obstructive" (pratibandhaka) refers to the proximity of the original object (bimba) and its limiting adjunct (upādhi);
the connection is that it is impossible to remove that [proximity]. [This is expressed by the phrase] "its removal."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: even in the view that the knowledge of the state (*avasthājñāna*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of that [ignorance], one must accept that only the superimposition of the reflection (*pratibimbādhyāsa*) is what is to be removed by that [knowledge of the state];
thus, there is no contradiction with the *Pañcapādikā*.
The sense is that this is equally true even under the view that the substrate-consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the state of the superimposition of a reflection.

He states the method that is not inconsistent with that [view]: "Or else" (*athavā*). The word "its own" (*sva*) refers to the superimposition of the reflection. "Is indeed to be removed" (*nivartya eva*): at the time of the proximity or departure of the original object (*bimba*) and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the subtle state (*sūkṣmāvasthā*) of the superimposition of the reflection [is what is meant].

He says "no" to the objection that even when the [illusory] characteristics are destroyed, there would still be the consequence of it being merely empirical (*vyāvahārikatva*). The connection is as follows: the word "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "the consequence of being empirical, however" serves to emphasize that [this objection] has already been refuted. The proximity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to the original object (*bimba*) is the defect. He extends this same reasoning to other cases with the word "in the same way" (*evam*): "In the same way, [the status of] the superimposition in a dream is also..."

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: its status as *prātibhāsika* (illusory) is due solely to its being produced by defects such as sleep, which are distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is an effect of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). The meaning of the word "only" (*eva*) is not that it is *prātibhāsika* because it is an effect of the knowledge of a state [of consciousness]. He states the reason why the knowledge of a state does not serve as the material cause (*upādāna*) for a dream.

"Because of superimposition upon that which is empty of the ignorance of the nature of the state. By way of different philosophical views, he states the difference in the substrata for the superimposition of dreams:

"Likewise, there is no cessation in the form of sublation; rather, that [cessation] depends solely on the knowledge of Brahman, because that [knowledge] alone is the remover of the ignorance that is the root of its material cause"—this is the sense. Now, regarding the knowledge of Brahman...

Just as in the case of the jar and other objects that are sublated, so too for that which is sublated by it— namely, the Brahman-consciousness unconditioned by the ego (ahaṃkāra)— there is a state of being devoid of [empirical] knowledge because it is the locus of only the root ignorance (mūlājñāna);
whereas the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), which is conditioned by the ego, possesses [empirical] knowledge.
The intended meaning is that because the obscuration of the substratum of pleasure and so forth is not admitted, there is a state of being devoid of knowledge.

The darkness called deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the seed of both dreaming and waking— since the Teachers have stated that the dream and waking worlds share a single cause in ignorance— this [knowledge] is the subverter of its own material cause by virtue of being the effect of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

Some maintain that the appearance-nature (*prātibhāsikatva*) of these [objects] belongs solely to their being produced by defects such as sleep, which are distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus they are sublated exclusively by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*). Others, however, hold that this bondage consists of the non-distinction between the Self and the body, based on the statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "And these chariots and so forth seen in a dream are sublated upon waking."

Because it is an adversary [to the superimposition], like waking consciousness (*jāgradbodha*); this is seen from the *Vivaraṇa*, and because one who has awakened experiences the falsity of the dream.
Thus, waking consciousness is the sublater of the superimposition of the dream.
That which is sublated by a cognition other than the knowledge of Brahman possesses only phenomenal reality (*prātibhāsikatva*). It is not...

It must be explained how knowledge that does not have the true nature of the substratum as its object, and which does not remove the ignorance that is its own material cause, could remove superimposition;
for in that very case, the superimposition of a snake on a rope is removed by the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum itself, which removes the ignorance that is its own material cause.
They say that cessation is observed even through the error of a staff arising immediately after [the perception of] a snake.

Here, by describing the superimposition of dream—which is an effect of ignorance—upon consciousness devoid of cognition, it is implied that [dream] is an effect of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). Regarding this, he states another reason:
"called deep sleep" (*saṣuptyākhya*). This is because deep sleep consists of a state of ignorance.

The meaning is as follows: it has been stated that ignorance (ajñāna) is called "sleep" by virtue of the speaker's intention; its seed or material cause (upādāna) is awakening, which is the waking world (prapañca).

The point is that it is universally accepted that this [waking world], being distinct from the shell-silver (śukti-rajata) and similar illusions, is the effect of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna). This connects with the phrase, "and because of the statement of the Teachers."

It is established that the cessation of the superimposition of one's own feet in a dream is achieved solely through the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman. It should be understood that even when the subtle state of the dream-phenomenon arises at the time of waking and its form is destroyed, its cessation in the form of sublation (*bādha*) is achievable only through the knowledge of Brahman. Furthermore, being produced by a defect other than ignorance (*avidyā*) is the defining condition for the status of being merely apparent (*prātibhāsikatva*).
According to the view that the superimposition of dreams— which is produced by defects such as sleep— is *prātibhāsika* (illusory),

he establishes that status by showing that being sublated at the time of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*) is the defining characteristic of *prātibhāsikatva*. Regarding the phrase "others, however" (*anye tu*), the word *prabodhe* found in the Bhāṣya is in the locative case.

Since bondage is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), it consists of ignorance; [the phrase] "contrariety" means the state of being an antidote or a remover, and the remainder [of the sentence] is that this applies to the knowledge of Brahman immediately following the fifth [state].

The meaning is: just as the cognition of a jar and so forth occurring during the waking state removes the bondage of a dream, so it is here. Regarding the word "of one who has arisen": [it refers to one for whom the dream was] merely false.

The meaning is that he experienced falsity because he perceived, "I saw a gathering of a great multitude in a dream; yet there is no such gathering of a great multitude. If the falsity of the dream-phenomenon were caused solely by its being sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, then one who has awakened from the dream would not experience that falsity.
Because prior to the knowledge of Brahman, one does not observe the experience of falsity in objects such as jars— which are sublated by that [knowledge]—
it must be stated that the sublation of the dream-world occurs through something other than the knowledge of Brahman, namely, through waking consciousness itself. Therefore,
like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and so forth, its status as *prātibhāsika* (illusory) is due solely to sublation occurring at the time of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*).

And the time of empirical usage (*vyavahārakāla*) is prior to the knowledge of the reality of Brahman; this is the sense. By the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), the meaning is knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman. He indicates the reason for its lack of power to remove the superimposition of dreams by the word "its own" (*sva*): the material cause (*upādāna*) of one's own superimposition of dreams is root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).
The meaning is that it does not remove that [superimposition]. He indicates the reason for its failure to remove it with the words "of the substrate" (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
The meaning is that it is not in contact with the true nature (*yāthātmya*)—namely, the undivided Brahman-consciousness and so forth—of the aforementioned substrate of the dream.

The point is that there is a rule that only the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) brings about the cessation of superimposition (adhyāsa) by way of removing ignorance. He refutes this by pointing out the failure of the stated rule with the words "rope-snake," etc. Here, the word "own" (sva) refers to the superimposition of the snake; [the refutation is shown by the fact that] it is not by knowledge alone—such as "this is not a snake, this is a rope"—[that the superimposition is removed].
The meaning is "by knowledge alone. "In that very place" means "in the rope itself," which is the substratum of the superimposition of the snake.

"By 'itself'" means by the cognition "this is not a snake, it is a staff," which arises immediately after the delusion of the snake. "Because cessation is observed" means because sublation (bādha) is observed.

Others, however, maintain that when the karma that bestows the experiences of the waking state ceases, the empirical individual soul (jīva), which is a reflection and the perceiver of the waking world,
is enveloped by a state of sleep that arises, concealing even the perceived waking world.
The state of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) is the cause of the distinction [of states] and the material cause (*upādāna*) for the superimposition of the dream-world;
it is not the case that root-ignorance is not the cause, nor is there a lack of evidence for sleep being a form of state-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*),
[considering] the empirical individual (*vyāvahārikajīva*) who, while veiled by this root-ignorance, perceives the waking world.
For one who conceives of their own self without doubt or error— as "I am a human," "I am a Brahmin," "I am the son of Devadatta," and so forth— that self,
through long-standing familiarity, remains at all times unobscured and uniform in nature, even upon the passing away of one's grandfather and other such events.
And if there were no obscuration whatsoever at the time of dreaming regarding the reality of the waking world, then just as in the waking state,
there would likewise be in dreams such delusions as "I am a tiger," "I am a Śūdra," "I am the son of Prajñadatta," and so forth, as well as the delusion of one's grandfather being alive and so on.

Furthermore, because it would otherwise entail the consequence of non-existence, it is established that sleep itself is a particular state of the ignorance (ajñāna) that veils the living being during its engagement with the empirical world produced at that time. Nor does this imply that the living being (jīva), being likewise veiled, would lack the capacity to be a perceiver of the dream-world.
Although there is a rule that only the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) can remove superimposition (*adhyāsa*),
[the author], considering that this does not lead to an inconsistency in the present context, states another view consistent with it, beginning with "Others, however. In this view,
the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) individual soul (*jīva*) is the perceiver of the dream-world, which is illusory (*prātibhāsika*).

The locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the dream-phenomenal world is precisely the waking phenomenal world itself, and not the unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*) or the like; furthermore, through the two-fold veiling of these two loci,
the ignorance pertaining to the state of sleep— which consists of the twofold nature of the seer and the seen— is perceived.

The material cause of the dream-phenomenon is not root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because that [root-ignorance] veils only the Brahman-consciousness and lacks the capacity to veil the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth.
Consequently, the locus of the awakening regarding the empirical individual soul and the world is—

The intended meaning is that, because [the knowledge] consists of the realization of reality as it is (*yāthātmya-jñāna*), the sublation of the superimposition of dreams is not possible [by mere non-perception]. The connection is that [this occurs] when action has ceased. By the words "repeatedly" (*āvṛttyā*) and "taking up" (*upādānena*), [the text refers to] sleep.

The definition of ignorance (ajñāna) has been stated as the state of possessing the power of veiling and projection; thus, since its status as ignorance is established, its nature as being a state [of the substrate] is proven because it possesses the quality of having an origin. For in this system, it has been stated in the first chapter that all forms of ignorance as states possess a beginning.

The state [of being]. He elaborates upon the meaning stated in the summary by raising an objection, beginning with the words "And not of sleep," and so forth. [He explains that] at the time of dreaming, there is no obscuration whatsoever for the empirical individual (vyāvahārikajīva), who is veiled by the various forms of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna) and whose experiences consist of the waking world.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: since there is an absence of the delusion "I am Yajñadatta’s son" and so forth, as well as the absence of the experience of one's own grandfather during his lifetime, it follows by implication that sleep itself is established as being of a non-dual nature.
He states that during the waking state, when the status of being a Brahmin and so forth exists, there is an absence of doubt and error.

Regarding the term *asaṃdigdha*: it is an adjectival qualifier of the act of conceit (*abhimāna-kriyā*), signifying that it is distinct from doubt and error, insofar as it occurs for one who conceives [the object] in a manner that is both non-doubtful and non-erroneous.

He states the reason for the persistence of the waking world-process—such as the death of one's grandfather—in a uniform manner toward Devadatta’s son, despite its being constantly veiled by [the son's] own experiences: "Because of his... For Devadatta’s son, having first experienced the death of his grandfather and so forth, subsequently [experiences it] every month and every year.
He performs ancestral rites such as the libation (*tarpaṇa*) and so forth. Consequently,
through the repeated practice of experiencing and remembering the perception of his father’s death and other events, and by virtue of that long-standing familiarity,
there arises for him— beginning with his own grandfather and others— a state of non-veiling characterized by the constant absence of doubt and the like.

The meaning is that it exists in a single form. The implication is that, just as in the waking state there is an absence of delusions such as [seeing] a tiger for Devadatta’s son, and an absence of experiencing the state of his grandfather while he is alive, so too would there be an absence [of such things] in the dream state. Regarding the phrase "at that time": this refers to that which is produced at the time of the empirical [world], once the [dream] has ceased.

The meaning is that the specific state of ignorance which veils both the world and the individual soul is established as being of the very nature of sleep (nidrā), and not of anything else; for it is sleep that is present by virtue of possessing the powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa), whereas no other [entity] is present. Nor is this so, because sleep is merely empirical (vyāvahārika).
The meaning is: "this being established as having the nature of a particular state of ignorance that veils the individual soul (jīva) and so forth."
Because the witnessing individual soul (*jīva*) is also a phenomenal superimposition along with the dream-world, so too,
when awakening arises from karma that bestows the experiences of the waking state,
it results precisely from the knowledge of the empirical nature of the *jīva*, which removes the ignorance in the form of sleep that is its own material cause.
The sublation of the dream-phenomenon. Nor should it be argued that, in this way, if the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) individual soul— the seer—
is also sublated by that [waking state], there would be no subsequent recollection such as "I experienced an elephant in my dream," for [the soul remains] empirical (*vyāvahārika*).

Because the empirical (vyāvahārika) individual soul is superimposed upon the illusory (prātibhāsika) individual soul, there would be the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of its continuity even when one accepts the experience of that [illusory soul].

Now, [one might object]: "In the case of the unconditioned consciousness (anavacchinna-caitanya), or rather, in the case of the consciousness conditioned by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra-avacchinna-caitanya), [the dreamer's experience occurs]..."
The two positions previously stated regarding the superimposition of phenomenal diversity (*prapañca-adhyāsa*) are both untenable. In the first case,
since dream-elephants and the like possess a location distinct from the Witness (*sākṣin*)— which is conditioned by the *ahaṃkāra*—
they do not require contact with a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), unlike friends and other external objects, for their manifestation.

Because the eyes and other sense organs have ceased [their activity], it is impossible for a modification (*vṛtti*) to arise; thus, since there can be no contact with them, illumination is impossible. In the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), just as one might say "this is silver," or "I am an elephant," or "I am happy," or "I possess an elephant."

With the intention that there is no room for this objection because another individual soul (jīvāntara), in the form of a reflection of consciousness within the illusory internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), is admitted, he says:
"together with the dream-world. And by the words "in this way," he refers specifically to the empirical (vyāvahārika) individual soul and the world.

The meaning is: "this being established" refers to the fact that the dream-world of living beings has been proven to have its locus in [the Self]. "Awakening from karma" means awakening produced by karma, which is to say, the waking state. "From the knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul (jīva)" means from such forms as "I am a human," "I am a Brahmin," "I am the son of Devadatta," and so forth; this is merely an illustration.
It should also be understood that [the phrase] "due to the knowledge of the death of one's grandfather" and so forth applies here;
the word *sva* refers to the dream-phenomenon (*svapnaprapañca*), and not to "this" (*idam*). He states the meaning of the word *eva* as follows: "by the seer of that" (*tadṛṣṭeḥ*).
This means by the seer of that dream-phenomenon, who perceives his own self in such forms as "I am a tiger," "I am a Śūdra," and so on.
The meaning is "of one who considers [it as such].

"From that" means from the knowledge of the empirical nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). "It would not be" is because it is impossible for one person to remember what was experienced by another; this is the underlying sense. "By that which is superimposed" (*adhyastayā*); and thus, in the empirical [context]...

The meaning is that because there is an identity (*tādātmya*) between the two types of living beings—the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) and the foundational (*adhiṣṭhāna*)—it is possible for the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) living being to have a recollection of dream objects based on the experience of the illusory living being as the agent. Regarding the phrase "lest there be an over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*): [this refers to] the case of an object experienced by Yajñadatta...
The meaning is that for Viṣṇumitra as well, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in the context of investigation;

the sense is that there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between those two. Now, one might object: according to the view of the threefold nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), since the empirical soul (*vyāvahārikajīva*) and others—which are accepted as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of dreams consisting of the seer and the seen—are themselves false (*mithyātvena*).

Due to its insentience (*jaḍatā*), it is not possible for it to be the illuminator of the manifestation of the dream-world. Nor should it be said that consciousness (*caitanya*) alone is its illuminator; for if that were the case, since consciousness itself would be the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it would be possible for it to consist of the fulfillment of existence (*sattāpūrti*), and thus it would be illogical to accept an insentient entity as the substratum. If so, [then...]
If it is argued that "let that very [unconditioned consciousness] be the substrate," he says "no" because even there an inconsistency exists, beginning with the words "But surely...

In the view that unconditioned consciousness itself is the substrate, one must state that dream-elephants and the like exist outside the body; and if that is so, is their manifestation by the Witness due to being perceived by the senses? Or is it something else?

Or rather, he says "not today" and so forth. By the phrase "of the witness" (*sākṣiṇaḥ*), using the ablative case to express separation, the absence of contact between the witness—who possesses the dream-elephant and so on—and those [objects] is shown.
This is because the manifestation of the dream-elephant and so on does not depend upon contact with a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).

The connection is: "because it does not require contact with that [object], and because manifestation [otherwise] would be impossible. The two words "by that" (*tena*) refer to the Witness (*sākṣin*).

Just as pleasure and the like do not manifest without depending on contact with a mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) whose object is that pleasure and so forth, so too [is the case] for the elephants and other things in a dream by means of that [Witness].

The meaning is "due to the impossibility of illumination. He refutes the second [position] with the words "of the eyes, etc. By "the second," he means the position that the consciousness qualified by the *ahaṃkāra*, which is the object of the experience of "I," is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of dreams. Is the superimposition of the elephant and so forth there [in the dream] by way of identity (*tādātmya*), or rather as the supported (*ādheya*) upon the support (*ādhāra*)?

The first [type of superimposition] is refuted by the fact that it is sublated through contact with the real object, as in the case of saying "this is silver. The second is rejected by the example "I am happy," and so forth. The construction is as follows: in the second case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of superimpositions such as "I am an elephant" or "I possess an elephant."

On this point, some support the first position: they maintain that consciousness (caitanya) unconditioned by the ego (ahaṃkāra) is not accepted as the substratum for the dream-world outside the body, but rather only within it;
for this very reason, it possesses a dimension appropriate to what is perceived.

The illusory nature (*māyāmaya*) of dream-elephants and the like is asserted because of the absence of the perfection of place (*deśasaṃpat*). Likewise, because the internal organ lacks independence outside the body during the waking state, it must produce a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward external objects such as the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) of mother-of-pearl.
Even when there is dependence on the eyes and other organs, because the activity of that independent instrument [the internal organ] can occur by itself within another body,
[that body] serves as the locus for the undivided consciousness manifested through the activity of that instrument in another body.
There is no lack of application here. Therefore, just as in the waking state,

the ignorance residing in the consciousness delimited by the "this" portion of the mother-of-pearl— manifested through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by sensory contact— undergoes a transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of silver,
so too in the dream state, within the body, there occurs a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

In the Vivaraṇopanyāsa, it is stated that when [the self] is possessed of defects such as sleep, the ignorance (*avidyā*)— in which consciousness is manifest and accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of various objects awakened by unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)— undergoes a phenomenal transformation (*vivartate*) into the form of the world (*prapañca*).

Regarding the statement of Bhāratītīrtha: others, however, maintain that unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*), when manifested by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is not the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the dream-world; for it is impossible for a modification directed toward unconditioned consciousness—which is not rooted in the scriptures—to arise. [Mūla...]

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "unconditioned by the ego-sense" (*ahaṃkārānavācchinna*): here, the consciousness of the Lord (*īśvaracaitanya*) existing as the prototype (*bimba*) within ignorance (*avidyā*) is intended by the term "unconditioned consciousness.
This is because it is the consciousness of the Lord alone that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for all things; it does not refer to the form of the reflection (*pratibimba*) in ignorance.
It should be understood that the consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*) is not its material cause (*anupādānatvāt*).

He states the restrictive factor for why only the internal consciousness (*antaracaitanya*) serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*): "For this very reason" (*vyata eva*). This means: precisely because the internal consciousness is accepted as the substrate. At the time of dreaming...

Because there is an absence of the necessary internal space within the bodies of elephants and other beings that possess the dimensions we perceive, their [existence] is described as merely illusory by the authors of the Sūtras and others;
for if consciousness were to reside externally to the body as its substrate, then [the state of those beings] would be like that of elephants seen in a waking dream.

The meaning is that even dream-elephants and the like would possess empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) due to their occupying a suitable location; thus, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtras and other authorities. "If this were so" (*evam ceti*) means: provided that the internal consciousness alone is established by proof as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of dreams. Now, [an objection]:
Because Brahman-consciousness, even when it has entered the body,

remains uncontracted, there would follow the consequence that the elephants and other objects superimposed therein would not appear. Nor can it be argued that their appearance is possible once the veil is destroyed by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), since in dream the eyes and other sense organs have ceased to function.
Nor should it be said that, due to the impossibility of [other] mental modifications (*vṛtti*), the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) arises by itself at that time;
for if that were so, it would follow by implication that this occurs even during the waking state, and consequently, there would be no dependence on the eyes and other sense organs even then.
Therefore, he says: "of the internal organ" and "by itself," meaning without depending on the eyes and so forth. Not...

The meaning of "some [say]" (*kācit*) is as follows: by accepting that the internal consciousness itself, manifested through the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is neither an impossibility of the appearance of the dream-phenomenon nor an impossibility of its being merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*). [This is] because of the consciousness manifested by the modification of the internal organ...

He states the consensus regarding its locus with the words "for this very reason. Since consciousness manifested by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is always easily accessible, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of dreams occurring at all times; therefore, he says "sleep, etc.
The meaning of the word "etc. includes the excessive drinking [of wine] and so forth. It is that consciousness which is manifested when the mental modification is afflicted by defects (*doṣa*).

In this context, the meaning is "ignorance that exists therein. He states the cause for the manifold variety of the dream-world: "by various objects," and so forth. In the waking state, latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) produced by the experience of various kinds of objects reside within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); together with these, when awakened by unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), [they produce the dream].

The meaning is that [avidyā] transforms itself into the form of the manifold diversity of the world (vidyā-vicitra-prapañca-ākāreṇa). Now, he states another view according to which the locus (adhiṣṭhāna) is the undivided consciousness of the individual soul (jīva-caitanya), which exists as a reflection within avidyā;
this begins with "Others, however" (anye tu). He points out the inconsistency in the previous view with the words "undivided consciousness" (anavacchinna-caitanya).

The word "consisting of the image" (bimbabhūta) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding the phrase "not rooted in sound": the sense is that, just as in the case of pure Brahman, the consciousness of the Lord (īśvaracaitanya) is also accessible solely through scripture.
Since the arising of a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of "I" is observed only within consciousness (caitanya) as delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and so forth, therefore,
the consciousness that is not delimited by the ego-sense and the like is self-evident and is the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) of that [ego]. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*:
"An erroneous cognition whose object is an immediate form must have an immediate substratum as its basis, whether that [immediacy] arises through the mind itself,
through the eyes, or as is well-known in cases such as dream-delusions. By this verse, the immediacy of the substratum required for immediate superimposition is [established].

Having stated that [cognition] occurs sometimes through mental activity and sometimes through the activity of the external senses, it was said that [these objects] are inherently beyond direct perception (*parokṣa*). Nevertheless, in this case of delusion, a form and appearance arises here; the mind is the cause in dreaming, appearing again and again even without the object of the eye, having its own locus.

Just as in the case of Ambaṭṭha, an error regarding form—which is accessible to the mind—is perceived in many ways through distinctions such as white and so forth by the power of its direct manifestation; likewise, an error such as "moving" occurs regarding what is accessible to the eye.
This is stated in the subsequent verse concerning the superimposition of dreams.

It has been stated that the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) is directly manifest by its own nature; nor should it be said that the mere consciousness unconditioned by the ego (ahaṅkāra) is veiled, such that its manifestation could not occur without a mental modification (vṛtti).

For it is accepted that the consciousness of Brahman itself, when veiled, is the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya) reflected in ignorance; and although this [individual consciousness] is not delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), it is nevertheless unenveloped.

[Objection: But surely, even in the case of the individual consciousness (jīvacaitanya), which is a reflection [of Brahman] in undifferentiated ignorance (avidyā), we observe the arising of a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of "I" independent of words; why then should it not be the same in the case of the consciousness of Brahman?
[Reply: No, he says: "in the consciousness delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)," etc. This is a locative case denoting the object (viṣayasaptamī).

The word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including the body and other such things; however, the particle "eva" (only/itself) means that [the self] is not the limited individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). The intention is that the all-pervasiveness of the individual consciousness is to be understood solely through the scriptural texts that purify the meaning of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*) and through the reasoning favorable to them; thus, the proof by way of an illustration is established. Therefore...
The meaning is that it is impossible for the undivided Brahman-consciousness, which serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), to be the reflected image (*bimba*).

"By itself" (*svataḥ*) means that it is manifested even without a mental modification (*vṛtti*). Regarding "consciousness" (*caitanya*): the ellipsis is that, as in the previous view, it is strictly internal.
"For this very reason" refers to the fact that [the object] is consciousness itself, which is directly manifest by its own nature.

The meaning is: precisely because [the dream object] is accepted as the locus for the superimposition of the dream. Or rather, the meaning is: that cognition in the form of an error regarding an object such as nacre-silver, which possesses a non-apparent (non-empirical) nature, occurs in dependence upon a locus that is apparent (empirical). Alternatively, it means: that cognition in the form of an error regarding an object such as nacre-silver, which possesses an apparent nature.
And by what means does that direct perception of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) occur? To this he says: "By the mind," and so forth;

the construction is: "either by itself or by means of the eye. He states the proof for this: "because it is perceived as such in dreams, delusions, and the like. The meaning is: because it is perceived in that way through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). For instance, in the case of the "this-portion" (*idamaṃśa*) of a mother-of-pearl shell:

Through the methods of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that when there is contact with the eyes, the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) required for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver occurs, and not otherwise; thus, in some cases, the immediacy of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) arises from the eyes. Likewise, [this applies] to the superimposition of the blueness of the sky, which requires [such immediacy].

It is understood that the direct realization (*aparokṣya*) of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is consciousness delimited by space (*gaganāvachinnacaitanya*), is possible through the mind (*manas*). By the word "mind" (*matrasā*), what is intended is a visual modification (*cākṣuṣa-vṛtti*) whose object is the ether (*ākāśa*) and so forth, which are co-extensive with consciousness delimited by space; it is not a visual modification whose object is the formless ether.
Because a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is impossible [in the case of the sky], the perception that "the sky is blue" and so forth occurs immediately after the opening of the eyes and not otherwise;

furthermore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the visual modification is instrumental in the manifestation of the consciousness of the ether (*gagana-caitanya*). And thus:

It should be understood that, by the force of the result (*phala-bala*), it is maintained that even through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having one form, there occurs the manifestation of consciousness delimited by another [object]; this has been explained in detail in the *Advaitadīpikā* and other works. He states the purport of the cited verse with the words "by this verse.
Regarding the phrase "herein": in the present context, within the delusion consisting of the superimposition of a dream, which is directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) in itself...

The meaning is that consciousness (*caitanya*) is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, the connection is as follows: in the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, regarding the superimposition of dream, the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of the substrate-consciousness is cited as being established by itself (*svataḥ*). This refers to the objection concerning the self-evident nature of the immediacy of the consciousness that serves as the substrate for the superimposition of dreams.

He demonstrates this through the two [verses] beginning with "samādhi" and "na cāhaṃkārānavacchinneti. The word *mātra* signifies "entirety"; thus, the intended meaning is that even the consciousness located within the body is indeed veiled.
As for the term "vṛtti," it has been stated previously that even a mental modification (*vṛtti*) cannot have an unconditioned object without the aid of words.
"The object of meditation is unobstructed. The meaning is that this very [consciousness] is the substratum for the superimposition of dreams. Now, an objection may be raised:

if the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*), which is all-pervading, were unobstructed, then because it would always exist in the location of objects such as jars, there would follow the undesirable consequence that all objects would be manifested at all times, even without depending on visual or other mental modifications (*vṛtti*). To this we say: no, because [the consciousness] is not everywhere...

Even though that [consciousness] exists, because it does not serve as a material cause (*upādāna*), there is no connection with objects such as jars; and since the requirement for a mental modification (*vṛtti*)— for the sake of establishing a connection—
is already resolved by the principle of the restriction of cognition to each specific object (*pratikarmavyavasthā*), [there is no need for further explanation].
And thus, when dream-objects such as elephants are superimposed upon consciousness that is not delimited by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra),

there arises the empirical usage "I see this" even with respect to the consciousness of the knower, due to the manifestation of difference produced by a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti) directed toward the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) which is co-extensive with those objects.
Thus they say. Others, however, support the second position:

that the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is consciousness delimited by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). In this view, the ego-sense is not admitted to enter the category of the substrate as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*), but rather as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Since the substrate is merely consciousness in the form of its reflection, there is no contingency of experiencing [the world] as "I am an elephant" and so forth; in this same way, even silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is superimposed upon the internal organ, which possesses a modification that is a reflection of consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearl.

Some maintain that if there were a superimposition upon the universal mirror-consciousness (bimbacaitanya) as delimited by the "shell-silver" (śuktīda-asaṃśā), it would follow— just as in the case of pleasure and so forth— that it could not be perceived by anyone other than its own locus.

Now, if it is granted that the superimposition of dreams occurs upon the consciousness of the individual soul— which is a reflection of knowledge, resides within the body, is independent of the ego (ahaṃkāra), and is designated as "unconditioned" (anavacchinna) by virtue of being either a qualifier or a limiting adjunct— then that very consciousness would be the seer during the time of the dream.

But this is not the case for the knower (*pramātṛ*), because that [dream-object], having attained identity with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), is distinct from it as delimited by that [ego]. Nor is this a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would contradict the experience of the knower during the time of dreaming—namely, "I see Śrī Kṛṣṇa"—which establishes the dreamer's status as the perceiver of the dream-objects. Therefore, he says: "And thus," [and] "by itself."
The meaning is: "provided that there is the status of being the substrate for the consciousness of the living being which is beyond the senses. Regarding the phrase "co-extensive with that":

at the very moment that an elephant or the like is superimposed, there arises either a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ or a modification of ignorance (*avidyā*) directed toward that substrate;
and thus, [this applies] to the consciousness that is the substrate of the dream-elephant and so forth.

The meaning is that when the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*) is attained through the connection of the internal organ with the enclosure and the door of the enclosure, it is possible for the knower to be the perceiver of that [object]. "By the manifestation of non-difference" means by the manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness of the knower and the object in the manner described. "The second" refers to...

The meaning is that this refers to the position [of some] that the locus of the superimposition of dream-consciousness is the limited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*). To prevent the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that there would arise cognitions such as "I am an elephant" in place of the cognition "this is an elephant," the status of the ego-component (*ahaṃkāra-aṃśa*) as the locus is not accepted.

He raises an objection, fearing that if this were the case, it would follow that there is no difference from the previous view, since the locus would then have become undivided. He asks: "But what [is the case]? [The answer is: Only that individual consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) which consists of the reflection of consciousness in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is accepted as the locus; and that is indeed limited, because its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is limited.

He refutes [the objection] by saying, "pervaded by the ego-sense" (*ahaṃkāropahita*). The meaning of "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which consists of the ego-sense and serves as the activator (*prayojaka*) of the notion of "I," does not enter into the category of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
This is because the Brahman-consciousness, which exists as the original image (*bimba*) in ignorance (*avidyā*), is reflected within that [ignorance].

Alternatively, according to the view that the consciousness reflected in the individual soul (*jīvacaitanya*) is the substratum for the superimposition of the dream-world, since those two [the individual soul and its reflection] are common to all subjects, the dream-world would also have to be common to all. This is the case if the consciousness reflected in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-pratibimba-caitanya*) is held to be its substratum.

It should be understood that this second position is undertaken with the intention that the fault of over-extension (*sādhāraṇya-prasaṅga*) does not apply. Now, one might object: "In this case, the uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*) of shell-silver and the like would not be established, because the consciousness (*caitanya*) which serves as their substrate is common (*sādhāraṇa*) to all. Anticipating this objection, he states the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*) by saying "evam" (thus).

Regarding the phrase "the internal organ as the substrate": when the modification (*vṛtti*) is conjoined with the "this-ness" portion of the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), the reflection of the Brahman-consciousness delimited by that "this-ness" portion of the mother-of-pearl is superimposed upon that [modification].
And that reflection resides precisely within the modification, because of the metaphorical identification (*abheda-upacāra*) between the modification and its substrate.

It should be understood that the statement regarding the modification (*vṛtti*) being located within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is for the purpose of clarifying its non-cognizability by anything else.

With the intention of pointing out the unavoidable consequence of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) that would arise if one did not accept the reflection of Brahman residing in the modification as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the silver in the mother-of-pearl, he says: "limited by this [objective] aspect of the mother-of-pearl" (*śuktīdamaṃśāvacchinna*).

The meaning is that there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-existence of that which is "cognizable by none other" (ananyavedya), just as in the case of pleasure and so forth.
The sense is that pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so on belonging to Devadatta are not perceptible to anyone other than Devadatta; thus, they are "cognizable by none other."

Some, however, accepting that superimposition occurs upon the consciousness of the reflection itself, establish its non-cognizability by others by arguing that it is perceptible only to the one whose ignorance serves as its material cause, and not to another individual soul (*jīva*).

But [an objection may be raised]: in the case of the superimposition of silver on mother-of-pearl, there is the experience of its being visual, which directly contradicts [the claim of non-cognizability].

Or, if it is argued that [the dream experience] is possible because it depends upon cognition, then how is the experience of the visual nature of the elephant and so forth in a dream to be accounted for? It is said in reply: first of all, for the sake of accounting for that, one cannot claim that the sense organs exist in the dream state just as the dream body and the objects do.

An illusory manifestation (*prātibhāsika-vivarta*) cannot be asserted, because there is no such thing as an "unknown existence" (*ajñāta-sattva*) for that which is merely illusory; furthermore, whether the sense organs are perceptible or imperceptible, their existence must necessarily be admitted as an unknown existence. Nor...

It can be asserted that the very empirical sense organs, having emerged from their respective physical sockets and taken recourse in the dream body, function as the perceivers of their respective objects;
for it is heard in scripture that at the time of dreaming, they are in a state of cessation characterized by the absence of activity.

He says that although the consciousness (*caitanya*) that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is common to all, the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like are unique because the ignorance (*ajñāna*) which is their material cause (*upādāna*) is unique; thus, the silver in the shell and so forth are unique. Regarding the phrase "some, however," [it means] that the reflection resides in the mirror-consciousness (*bimbacaitanya*) itself.
The meaning is "the consciousness reflected [in ignorance]. Alternatively, it means "the reflection in ignorance.

Regarding the Brahman-consciousness that has become a reflection, the meaning is "as delimited by the 'this' portion of the mother-of-pearl. The word "eva" (only) signifies that it is not the reflection in a specific mental modification (*vṛtti*). As for the phrase "if [it were]," it refers to that silver which belongs to a particular person.
The meaning is that since it is logically consistent to conceive that [the superimposition] has knowledge as its material cause and is perceived by that very person alone and not by anyone else,
there is no possibility of the commonality [of perception] that would apply to such things as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Thus,
having defined the substratum for the superimposition of the dream-world, [the author proceeds to discuss] the experience of dream-objects.

In response to the doubt as to whether [the object] is perceptible by the senses (*aindriyaka*) or of the nature of a witness (*sākṣirūpa*), he introduces the objection for the sake of a definitive conclusion with the words "nanu" and "sākṣād vā. It should be understood that this [objection] regarding the perceptibility of shell-silver and the like follows a particular philosophical school; however, he speaks [here] according to the view that shell-silver and the like are manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*).

The phrase "by means of the knowledge of the substrate" (adhiṣṭhānajñānadvāra) means by means of the knowledge of the substratum (dharmijñāna), because [the error] depends upon the eye, as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. How so? For the experience of dream-elephants and such as being visual must occur either through sense organs consisting of latent impressions (vāsanāmaya), or through empirical sense organs (vyāvahārika), or through subtle sense organs (sūkṣma).

Alternatively, it is conceived as something to be established by way of superimposition; thus, the meaning of the question is: "In what manner is it to be so established? He promises its establishment by means of the fourth method with the words, "It is said.
He refutes the first three methods with the passage beginning with "Not, for instance," [and so on], [arguing that] they consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

First, he refutes the manner in which the experience of visual perception is justified by means of illusory sense organs with the words "like the dream-body. Just as dream-objects and illusory objects are accepted as being transformations (*vivarta*) of consciousness, so too are the sense organs [accepted].

The meaning is that an illusory manifestation (*prātibhāsika-vivarta*) consisting of consciousness as its very nature can be accepted. Regarding the phrase "because of being denotable" (*vācyatvāt*): the sense is that since those [objects] are observed to be invariably existent when unknown, and because conceptual construction follows what is observed, [the object must be real]. He refutes the second alternative with the words "nor even" (*nāpi*). Now, [an objection]: [Text fragment: ...svarūpabhūtaścaitanyavivartaḥ prātibhāsikobhyupagaṃtuṃ śakyate ityarthaḥ | vācyatvāditi | teṣāmajñātasattvaniyamasya darśanād dṛṣṭānusāritvācca kalpanāyā iti bhāvaḥ | dvitīyaṃ prakāraṃ nirākaroti | nāpīti | nanu... ...the meaning is that an illusory manifestation (*prātibhāsika-vivarta*) consisting of consciousness as its very nature can be accepted. Regarding the phrase "because of being denotable" (*vācyatvāt*): the sense is that since those [objects] are observed to be invariably existent when unknown, and because conceptual construction follows what is observed, [the object must be real]. He refutes the second alternative with the words "nor even" (*nāpi*). Now, [an objection]:...

Anticipating the objection that there is no basis for establishing how objects such as elephants seen in dreams can be experienced through visual perception by means of empirical sense organs—since those [dream-objects] reside in the sleeping body and not in the waking body—he says: "Because of the scriptural statement, 'each in its own... regarding those who are asleep.

Regarding the phrase "while waking," etc., there is a textual ellipsis (*śeṣa*) in the Śruti; immediately after the word "while [others] are sleeping," the word "instruments" (*karaṇeṣu*) is to be supplied.

The "withdrawal" (*svāya*) of the instruments means their cessation of activity, and this occurs precisely at the time of dreaming in the form of a lack of operation; it should be understood that this is not the cessation of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), for the cessation of their nature is heard of only in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Furthermore, because it is impossible for the empirical tactile organ to pervade the entire dream body— which is of a greater dimension than itself— within this body that lacks the presence of its own appropriate empirical location.

Moreover, if that [heat] were to reside in only one part [of the body], it would be impossible to account for the sensation of cold touch pervading the entire body produced by immersion in dream-water. For this very reason,
even though the waking sense organs have ceased their activity during sleep, those [organs] which are employed in the functioning of the Taijasa [dream state] remain active.

The objection that the dream objects possess the nature of being perceived by the senses because there exist subtle sense organs which constitute the parts of the subtle body is also refuted, since subtle sense organs distinct from those of the waking state are not established. Furthermore, in this regard:

Since the self-luminosity of the Self is difficult to discern during the waking state— due to its intermingling with external lights such as the sun and the movement of the functions of the eyes and other senses— the text addresses the state of dreaming to establish the self-luminosity of the Self therein, stating: "The person is self-luminous."

He states another defect regarding the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*) alone: "of the empirical" (*vyāvahārikasya*). This refers to that which is situated within the interior of the body—a region devoid of the presence of the empirical location appropriate for one's own tactile organ—and is [thus] in comparison to the dimension of the empirical tactile organ.
At times, it might not pervade the entire dream-body if that body were of a larger dimension;
