this refers to the sense of touch (*tvag-indriya*). Due to the absence of the specific requirements of appropriate place and time for the empirical organ of touch, its movement into the interior of the body for entry into the dream-body is simply impossible.
It has been indicated that [the tactile organ] exists.

If there is no connection because the empirical tactile organ cannot pervade the entire dream-body, then let it reside merely in one part of the dream-body; what is the fault in that? To this he says: "In one part of that," etc.; "of that," etc.

The meaning is "of the tactile sense organ. He refutes the third alternative with the words "for this very reason. Since it is impossible for the empirical tactile sense organ itself to pervade the entire dream-body, which is of a greater dimension than itself, [it must be] the subtle tactile sense organ that constitutes its constituent part.

The meaning is: "all the more so," because it is impossible for [the subtle body] to pervade the dream-body. The *taijasa* is the individual soul (*jīva*) that has entered the state of dreaming; by the term "subtle body" (*sūkṣma-śarīra*), the eleven empirical sense organs (*indriya*) are denoted.
Having shown the defect in the case of the tactile organ alone by way of extension, he states the common defect:

Regarding the phrase "jāgrat-indriya" (the waking senses): one might object that even [senses] not [actually] present are postulated during the time of dreaming in accordance with the experience of objects as being visual and so forth;
anticipating this doubt, he says, "not so, because of contradiction with scripture. Furthermore, regarding the word "atra" (here) in the scripture: [he explains] by the word "atra" in the scripture.

He states the purport of the mention of the dream state: "In the waking state," etc. In the waking state, the sun and other luminaries serve as the means for the functioning—characterized by sitting, moving about, coming, and going—of the collection of causes and effects [the body and senses], together with the objects being experienced.

The meaning is that the modifications (*vṛttis*) produced by the eyes and other senses proceed toward the location of the object precisely for the purpose of accomplishing empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), being situated in such a way as to be mixed together. "Intermingling" (*vyatikara*) means contact or conjunction.
The connection is with the phrase "difficult to discern in the waking state. "Difficult to discern" means difficult to determine with certainty.

The meaning is that for one who finds it difficult to distinguish [the Self], it is impossible to determine [its nature] without effort. What is called the self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) of the Self is its fitness to be the illuminator of everything other than itself, while not being illuminated by anything else;
and that [fitness] cannot be grasped during the waking state, because [in that state] there exists something distinct from the Self.

It cannot be asserted that everything is illuminated solely by the self, because in the world, luminaries such as the sun and cognitions produced by the eyes and other senses are well known for illuminating the universe; likewise,
since the self is the illuminator of the cognition "I," it follows that it is not unilluminable by anything else.

And because of the doubt that [the self] cannot be described; for if it were impossible to refute [this doubt] during the waking state, it would be impossible to determine its self-luminosity (svayaṃjyotiṣṭva) while awake. However, in the state of dream, [there is the absence] of the well-known lights such as the sun and so forth, as well as the cognitions produced by the eyes and other senses that occur during waking.

And because of the absence [of other illuminators], it is possible to conclude that the dream-world is illuminated solely by the consciousness of the Self (*ātma-caitanya*). Likewise, it will be stated later that the cognition "I" (*aham*), being of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), is not the illuminator of the Self.
Thus, [the definition of consciousness is] the state of being capable of illuminating the entire world while not being illuminated by anything else.
The meaning is that one's own self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) can be determined by means of the dream state as its witness.
Now, an objection may be raised: "The scripture intends the literal sense—that his self-luminosity exists only in the state of dreaming and not in other states."

Otherwise, since it is self-luminous at all times, [the scripture stating that it shines] in this state would be redundant. In that case, if one were to assume the movement of the functions of the eyes and other senses even in dream, then its self-luminosity would be as difficult to discern there as it is in the waking state; thus, the cited scripture would be contradicted. Now, [one might object]:

Since it is admitted that in a dream there is the conceptualization of the cessation of the eyes and other [senses], the existence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as a non-ceased instrument is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*); therefore, there is no proof of self-luminosity (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*). Do not say so; for according to the manner explained in the *Nyāyanirṇaya* under the section "The agent [is the Self] because of the meaningfulness of the scriptures" (*kartā śāstrārthavattvāt*), [it is the Self]. Regarding the internal organ...
Alternatively, because it does not serve as a means for knowledge independently of other instruments such as the eyes,
it exists as the object of knowledge through its own transformation into the form of an elephant and so forth within a dream, according to the method stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*.

This is because, at that time, it is impossible for [the mind] to be a means of knowledge; thus, the conclusion follows by elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Nor is there an impossibility of the subsequent recollection of an elephant or other objects seen in a dream by one who has awakened—due to the absence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) during the dream—given the mental modification of ignorance (*avidyāvṛtti*) already established for deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Because that is logically established: in deep sleep, it is the very nature of consciousness (svarūpacaitanya) as conditioned by that state which is the manifestation of ignorance, pleasure, and so forth; and the subsequent recollection by one who has awakened occurs through the mental impression (saṃskāra) produced by the destruction of the conditioning state.
Furthermore, according to the view favored in the Vedāntakaumudī, which maintains that there is no modification (vṛtti) of nescience during deep sleep, here too—

in the case of the appearance of illusory elephants and so forth in a dream— the subsequent recollection is possible due to the latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by the destruction of the dream state itself, which serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for the consciousness manifesting those dream-objects.

To the question, "Why might this not be so? he says, "No; otherwise. This means that the self’s self-luminosity (*svayañjyotiṣṭva*) is based on its being the witness (*sākṣin*) of the state of dream, according to the scripture (*śruti*). "He [the self] discerns" refers to the failure to grasp the intended meaning (*tātparya*). By reflecting upon such scriptural passages as "Everything shines only after Him who shines," it follows that [the self's luminosity] exists at all times.

The sense is that [it is so] because of the certainty of its being self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭa*). Regarding the phrase "here" (*atra*): since the qualifier "here" would be redundant as it lacks any thing to exclude (*vyāvartakatva*), the intention is not to take the meaning according to the literal reading, but rather the intention lies in the meaning already stated. Having thus determined the intention of the scripture, [one considers] the eyes and other [senses] at the time of dreaming...

He states that the postulation of activity is refuted therein. Regarding the phrase "therein": the meaning is that once it is established that the intention of the Śruti is that self-luminosity is easily understood through its being the witness of the dream state, then [the objection is addressed]. Now, [an objection]:
He raises the objection that the previous statement—that the dream world and the waking world are manifested by the Self alone because there is no other manifestor—is incorrect.

[The objection begins with] "But surely" (nanu). [The phrase] "it remains unceased" implies that since it is possible for the mind itself to be the manifestor of the dream world, the argument based on the *pariśeṣa* (method of elimination) regarding the absence of any other manifestor is undermined.
The meaning is "accomplishment. [The opponent objects: "In the state of dream, its status as the instrument of cognition is unestablished;

therefore, since it is impossible for it to be the illuminator of the dream-world, the conclusion follows by elimination. [The author] refutes this, saying: "Not so. Let the Self be the agent; for if that were the case, [it would follow from such texts as] "the agent is the conscious self (vijñānātman), the person," and so forth.

The meaning of the sūtra is that the treatise (śāstra) possesses purposefulness. "By the stated method" means by the method already explained, namely, that because the mind (*manas*) is the material cause (*upādāna*), it does not inherently possess the status of being an instrument of cognition (*jñānakaraṇa*). "By the method stated in the *Tattvapradīpikā*" means that in a dream, the mind itself—characterized by various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) into the form of the dream-world; [it is not the case that...].

The meaning is that, according to the reasoning already stated, that ignorance lacks the capacity to transform into various objects because it cannot serve as a substratum for the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Regarding the phrase "as an object" (*karmatayā*):
the meaning is that since [ignorance] is exhausted merely by being an object, it lacks the nature of an illuminator (*prakāśaka*) which consists in being a subject (*viṣayin*).

By the word "then" (tadānīm), it is indicated that although [the mind] may be the cause of knowledge during sleep or wakefulness, nevertheless, that is not accepted in the case of a dream, because [in a dream] it exists solely as an object. The phrase "it is untenable" (anupapattiḥ) means that there is an absence of latent impressions (saṃskāra). Now, one might object: even in deep sleep (suṣupti), the veil of ignorance (avidyāvṛti) need not be postulated.

Although the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is eternal even during states such as deep sleep, because the state of deep sleep— which is manifested by that witness— is perishable, it is possible for a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) characterized by destruction to arise in the witness insofar as it is qualified by the object, namely the state of deep sleep; thus, the recollection of the bliss of deep sleep and so forth is logically established.

He says: "In deep sleep," [meaning] that even for the witness of a dream, since a latent impression (saṃskāra) characterized by destruction is possible in the form of being qualified by the illusory object, the recollection of the elephant and so forth seen in the dream is logically established.

"That state" refers to deep sleep (*suṣupti*), meaning the manifestation of ignorance, pleasure, and so forth; that is to say, the experience of ignorance and the like. "Even here" means even in the state of dreaming. "Having become an adjunct" (*upādhibhūta*) means having become an adjunct by way of being an object.

Alternatively, let it be that this very *sattva* by which one sees a dream is the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) having as its object the elephant and so forth in the dream, according to the manner stated by Kalpataru, based on such scriptural passages as "that *sattva* by which one sees a dream. Nor does this much fail to establish the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), because the internal organ, which is grasped as "I," cannot be [the self] in its entirety.
Because, through the perspective of worldly experience, its distinction from the Self—superimposed as a unity with the individual soul—is not established;
for, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), there is required merely the absence of activity in the eyes and other organs.
This is because there exists the certainty that "whatever is established as merely an object of sight is fit to be illumined by the Seer."

Because it does not depend on anything else for its remaining [objects], therefore, since the operation of the eyes and other senses is in every way impossible in a dream, the experience of visual perception and so forth regarding dream-elephants and the like is nothing but an error.
Now, one might object: even in a dream, the experience of elephants and such occurs when the eyes are open, and when they are closed, as in the waking state.
If it is argued that the experience of an elephant and so forth is perceived as following upon the opening of the eyes and other such acts, [we reply:
like the experience "I see silver with my eye," this too will be some kind of dream-delusion, since it occurs in the form of the pure witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone.

In the experience of an elephant and so forth in a dream, the conformity to the eyes and other senses— and the cessation resulting from their non-conformity— is sublated; for what indeed is too difficult for Māyā to produce as an illusion, especially when she has transformed into the form of sleep, by whose power [this occurs] in a dream?
A chariot is perceived as a man in one moment, and that same [man] is perceived as a cat in the next;

yet for the dreamer, there is no synthesis of the contradiction between the preceding and succeeding moments, just as in the waking state. Therefore, even in a dream, the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) whose object is the elephant and so forth is accepted as being nothing other than that [modification]. Hence, it is not [the case that the dream object is external].

There is room for the doubt that [the experience] might be merely a mental construction (*saṃskāra*). Nor should it be said that the proof by elimination (*pariśeṣa*) fails because of the existence of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) at that time;
for even the proof by elimination is established from the perspective of worldly experience. Thus, he states another opinion:
"Or rather" (*athavā*), where the third case ending refers to the internal organ denoted by the word *sattva*.

The meaning is as follows: according to the method stated in the *Kalpataru*, the scripture reveals that [the dream state] possesses the instrumentality for producing cognitions whose objects are dream-elephants and the like; thus, on account of the authority of scripture, even though there is an absence of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) produced by the eyes and other senses during a dream, there exists a mental modification (*mānasavṛtti*). Therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). The phrase "by that much" refers to the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).

The meaning is: "by its mere existence. Since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is superimposed in its entirety upon the single consciousness of the living being (*jīvacaitanya*), it is apprehended as the seer in such forms as "I see";
yet, from the perspective of the ignorant, that internal organ [is distinct] from that conscious Self (*cidātman*).

The meaning is this: since the distinction [of the self] from the immediate presence [of the organs] is not established, and because for the sake of establishing the "remainder" (pariśeṣa), one must depend on the very absence of activity in the instruments and so forth—which are distinct from what is commonly perceived as the "seer"—the establishment of the remainder is not achieved by that much alone.
What is being said here is that activity, characterized as a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is in reality [an activity of] the instrument.
The activity [of the internal organ] is also to be understood as the activity of the Seer, because the internal organ is grasped by people as the Seer;
thus he shows the method for determining its self-luminosity.
Regarding the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*), it refers to what was previously indicated by the phrase "it is said," concerning dream-objects.
He now elaborates upon the course of the experience of visual perception and so forth, explaining the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*) with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

He explains the phrase "in every way" (*sarvathā*) as meaning "by all the aforementioned modes as well. Having raised the objection that if the experience of a dream were of the nature of the Witness (*sākṣin*), it would contradict the dependence [of perception] on the eyes and other organs, he resolves it by means of an illustration.

By the words beginning with "svapna" (dream), [it is meant that] "tadanuvidhāyinī" (conforming to that) does not have its literal meaning as it stands— namely, that the well-known function conforming to the eyes and other senses during the waking state is superimposed upon the witness of the dream—
because that would result in the fallacy of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension). Rather, [it means] "that which is this sattva by which one sees the dream."

The meaning is that, according to the *Śruti*, the author of the *Kalpataru* maintains that a mental modification (*mānasavṛtti*) having an elephant or similar object as its domain is superimposed upon that [witness-consciousness], or rather, that conformity with such [external objects] is superimposed upon it. And thus, in the experience of dream-elephants and the like, which consists solely of the nature of the witness (*sākṣin*), either a modification conforming to the eyes and other senses is superimposed there, or— since it is so stated— [the aforementioned].
The meaning is that it is merely an illusion (*bhrama*). Anticipating the objection that such an illusion is difficult to establish, he says:
"What indeed is difficult for Māyā to accomplish? The connection is:
"What, by way of what example, does Māyā not perform? What example exists for Māyā in its performance of the impossible?"

The meaning is that it does not exist. On the contrary, its capacity to produce such effects is well-known in the case of the illusions of magicians (*aindrijālika*) and the like; this is the sense of the word "hi" (for/indeed). Furthermore, Māyā, which is the cause of error regarding space and so forth, brings about the illusion of the world (*prapañca*)—even though it is difficult to reconcile—in a stable form; however, when she has transformed into the form of sleep, she [produces] from that...

Thinking that it causes a delusion of a distinct nature, the word "specifically" (aviśeṣataḥ) was stated. The phrase "of which" (yasyāḥ) means of that [nature] which has transformed into the form of sleep.

Therefore, although the cognition of conformity with positive and negative concomitance is equal in both cases, only the experience of the elephant and so forth during the waking state is produced by the eyes and other sense organs, whereas the experience of the elephant and so forth in a dream is not. For the proponent of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*, however, it is untenable for that which is imagined to have an existence unknown [to the subject]; thus, [he maintains] the entire waking phenomenal world...

Having reached the view that creation is simultaneous with perception, [one considers] the cognition following the contact of the eye with the pot and so forth, which would be inconsistent prior to the perception of the pot because of the non-existence of the pot at that time.

They say that even the experience of an elephant and so forth during the waking state is not visual, as it is established as being just like a dream. Now, if one accepts the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) and thus admits that the entire waking world is a mental construction (*kalpita*), then who is the creator? Is it the Self (*ātman*) without attributes (*nirupādhi*), or is it the Self conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*)? It cannot be the former.

Even in liberation, because the postulating subject (kalpaka) would still exist independently of any other means, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it would not differ from saṃsāra due to the continued persistence of the phenomenal world (prapañca). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because since even ignorance (avidyā) must be postulated, one must state how the postulating subject is established prior to that postulation of ignorance. On this point, some say: "Previously..."

That which is conditioned by previously imagined ignorance is the projector of subsequent ignorances; and because this stream of projecting and being projected has no beginning, there is no fault of infinite regress.
Nor is it improper for ignorance to be a mere mental construction—like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—simply because its beginninglessness is admitted.

He concludes the determination of the explanation regarding the experience of visual perception and so forth in a dream with the words, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that in a dream, the operation of the eyes and other sense organs is impossible. However, those who are qualified [practitioners], having attained unsurpassed [results] through the performance of various kinds of knowledge and rituals...
Sages whose inner organs have been rendered exceedingly pure by the majesty of the grace of the Supreme Lord do not perceive any difference between waking and dreaming;
[this work] is intended for those who desire the knowledge of Brahman concerning the entire universe.

Following the scriptural texts that establish origination (*prabhava*) and dissolution (*pralaya*) in the states of waking and sleep, the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) was formulated by the ancient teachers; he now demonstrates that this [doctrine], having entered the intellect through the investigation of dreams, is as follows:
"As for the proponents of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*," that [creation] whose timing is identical to the time of perception.

Regarding the phrase "having accepted such a view of the entire waking world," the author provides the reason in the preceding sentence with the words "of that which is imagined. This means it is like the world of dreams. He establishes that the perception of conformity experienced in the vision of jars and other objects—being otherwise inexplicable—is, like a dream, merely an illusion.

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: the reason for its being inconsistent is "because of the perception of the prior absence of the jar and so forth. In that context, the meaning is that the creation occurs at the same time as the perception; it is not visual (*cākṣuṣa*), but rather, like a dream experience, it is purely of the nature of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). "Acceptance of its being imagined" means acceptance of its being of an illusory appearance (*prātibhāsika*) nature.

He shows the conceptual alternative indicated by the word "kaṃ" (which): "nirupādhiḥ" (without adjuncts). He refutes the first alternative—that the conscious self (*cidātman*) alone, being independent (*nirapekṣaḥ*), is the creator of transmigratory existence—by stating "mokṣe 'pi" (even in liberation) and "anuvṛttyā" (by persistence); the meaning is "by way of persistence. [He then addresses] "avidyāyā api" (of ignorance too): if one accepts that even that [ignorance] is occasional (*kādācitkatva*).

The meaning is this: since the conscious self (cidātman), which is conditioned by ignorance (avidyopahita) and is the conceptualizer of knowledge (vidyā) and so forth, must be spoken of as existing even prior to the creation of ignorance, the creation of ignorance and the rest is impossible in the absence of that [self].
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that saṃsāra would never be perceived at all. Now, even if this were so...

Regarding the question of what brings about the first ignorance (*avidyā*), he says "anidam" (not this). Since there is no "firstness" [in the absolute sense], there is no such thing as a "first ignorance"; therefore, the objection does not arise. Now, fearing that this might lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), [the author] states that it is not a fault, because the Self, conditioned by ignorance, is the creator of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

With the intention that there would be no possibility of establishing [the world] as its conceptualizer in the absence of a preceding ignorance for an already established [world], he says: "There is no fault of infinite regress. But [it may be objected]: "The individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), pure consciousness (viśuddhā cit), the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, ignorance (avidyā), and the connection between that [ignorance] and consciousness—these six are beginningless for us."

He raises an objection, stating: "If not [so]," because the postulation that ignorance (*avidyā*) is beginningless by way of its stream contradicts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*); for in the summary verse of the doctrine (*siddhāntasaṃgrahaśloka*), it is perceived as being beginningless in its very nature (*svarūpa-anāditya*), just like consciousness (*caitanya*).
Otherwise, it must be said that the distinction between things with a beginning and so forth would be untenable. Just as in a dream,
some imagined objects such as gate-towers are conceived as having existed previously,
while others are conceived as being produced right now, so too in the waking state, some imagined object is conceived as having a beginning.
It is postulated that by the mere fact that something is "otherwise" [than its appearance], the distinction between having a beginning and being beginningless is established.

By this, the division of causes is also explained, according to others. However, others say that in reality, ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are indeed beginningless; therein, the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*) is not accepted, but rather that it applies only to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) other than that [ignorance]. But even if this were so—
Who is the creator of the sequence of creation beginning with space (viyat) and so forth, which is merely perceived through scripture? None at all.
On what basis, then, is the scriptural statement "from the Self, space was produced" and so on founded?
Know that it is based upon the non-duality of the Self and Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal manifestation (niṣprapañca).

He states the fault even in proceeding by transgressing the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: the non-acceptance of the beginninglessness of the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest. Regarding the phrase "due to impossibility" (*anupapatteḥ*): the sense is that the aforementioned distinction is established by both common worldly experience and the scriptures (*śāstra*). [This applies to] pure consciousness (*viśuddha-caitanya*), which is to be understood solely through scripture (*śruti*).

Having accepted the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) regarding everything that is distinct [from consciousness], he states an analogy for a specific type of error, based on the support of worldly and Vedic means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which establish the distinction between the beginningless and the beginningless-in-time, as well as established doctrinal traditions, using the words "Just as... and so forth. "Something else otherwise" means that something such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like is otherwise.
The meaning is that it is conceptualized as being without beginning by means of a self conditioned by each preceding ignorance.

By this much, the meaning is "by mere conceptualization. Now, an objection: since the object is a cause for perception, a jar or the like must be said to be unknown prior to its being seen; otherwise, the distinction between cause and effect would not exist. Thus...

If the single conscious self (*cidātman*), conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), were the sole creator of the world within itself, then—since the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) would be one—there could be no distinction between teacher and disciple, nor any distinction between gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
Therefore, he says: "By this. This means: by explaining the establishment of the distinction between that which has a beginning and that which is beginningless. Thus it is explained.

Thus, although in reality the object is not a cause of perception, it is nevertheless postulated as its cause; likewise, everything else should be understood in the same way, like a dream—this is the meaning. To avoid the infinite regress of the postulator who is conditioned by ignorance (avidyā), and to ensure the consistency of the distinction between that which has a beginning and that which is beginningless, he states a limitation of the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi): "Others..."

"Indeed" (tviti) means "in reality" (vastutaḥ), that is, "by its own nature" (svarūpataḥ). Then, one might object: "In that case, the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) cannot be accepted anywhere because there is a lack of evidence. To this, he replies: "It is not so," because the fact that the entire phenomenal world (*kāryaprapañca*) undergoes dissolution and origination during sleep and waking is established by numerous scriptural texts (*śruti*).
"Other than that" (*tato'nyatra*)—the remainder of the phrase is "from ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth. The word *mātra* signifies "entirety.

Now, even in the view that the creation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) occurs at the very moment of perception, it is intended by the word "perception" (*dṛṣṭi*) that there is only direct apprehension (*pratyakṣa-pratīti*), and not indirect apprehension (*parokṣa-pratīti*). [This is because] it is immediate...

Cognition itself constitutes the object, because it establishes an illusory object even in the absence of actual existence; whereas indirect cognition (*parokṣa-pratīti*) does not possess such a character.
This being the case, he anticipates an objection: "But even so... The meaning is:
even though the Self conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita-ātman*) functions as the creator of perceptible objects. If the creation of space and so forth...

If it were perceived through scripture (*śruti*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then, by the force of that perception, its status as being merely illusory (*prātibhāsikatva*) could be established—just as in the case of a jar or similar objects—but since that is not the case, the word "merely" (*mātra*) has been employed with the intention [of excluding such perception]. The first term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is for the purpose of including air and the rest; [the second] refers to the dissolution of ether and the rest.

The phrase "from the second [verse], there is no sequence" is for the purpose of summarizing that sequence; the meaning is that a creator (kalpaka) simply does not exist. Regarding the absence of a creator, the proponent of the theory of "creation as perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivādin) states, "no one [exists]. If that is so, then the creation of ether and the rest, along with its sequence—which is taught in the scriptures concerning the beginning of creation—would be like the horn of a hare.

He raises the objection that the scripture might lack authority due to the absence of a referent (*ālambana*). He answers with "And [there is] certainty," for since the object intended by the purport (*tātparya*) exists, there is no resulting lack of authority;
thus, through the methods of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), the realization of Brahman devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*) occurs.

If it is proclaimed in the *Bhāṣya* and other works that the presentation of creation and dissolution in the *Śrutis* is merely as a means (*upāya*) for attaining that [Brahman] and not with [ultimate] intent (*tātparya*),

then it would follow that the *Śrutis* concerning the creation of ether and so forth, as well as their sequence, found in the *Viyan-māna* and *Prāṇa* sections, would be purposeless in the absence of such intent.
Effort toward resolving mutual contradictions is not in vain,

for one must accept an intended meaning (tātparya) for the sake of understanding the principles of logic, since that [effort] is undertaken for that purpose. For it has been stated in the *Śāstradarpaṇa* that the intended meaning of the Śrutis pertains to creation.
Having accepted this, it has been stated here that because those [Vedic texts] have as their primary purport the identity of Brahman and the Self, they exist for that purpose alone;
the accomplishment of the fruit results from the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites as enjoined by the Śruti.

Now, one might object: "Is it not improper to abandon the literal meaning of the passages concerning creation and so forth and instead assume an intention regarding a non-literal meaning? Rather, it is more appropriate to assume the creation of the world and its creator in accordance with what is heard [in scripture]. To this, he says: "Superimposition," etc. As in the world...

Someone engaged in awakening others to the reality of space first causes them to grasp space as endowed with superimpositions such as blueness and vastness; subsequently, by means of the negation of those [superimpositions], stating that "this is not actually possessed of blueness and so forth," they teach that the reality of space is formless, all-pervading, and neutral.

It awakens [the mind]. Likewise, the Vedāntas also first cause Brahman to be perceived as the cause of the creation, dissolution, and so forth of bipeds, quadrupeds, and the like, through sentences concerning creation and so on; having thus apprehended Brahman by way of its association with superimposed creation and the rest, they subsequently [proceed] by means of negating sentences (*niṣedhavākya*) through the sublation (*apavāda*) of that superimposed creation and so forth.
The Upaniṣads establish the non-duality of Brahman and the Self. Likewise, passages concerning creation and so forth—
being subordinate to prohibitory statements by providing the objects to be negated, and thus forming a single syntactical unit with them—
have as their sole purpose the establishment of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self, and not the creation and so forth for their own sake.

Since their purpose is fulfilled merely by [establishing] the [proposition], and because there is no fruit in the communication of their own literal meaning— as is the case with explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like— it is impossible for the Veda to have its purport (*tātparya*) in a fruitless matter; therefore, it is indeed logical to assume that, by abandoning their own literal meaning, the purport lies in the non-duality of Brahman and the Self, which is free from phenomenal plurality (*niṣprapañca*), as that is what is to be attained.

Since the fact that liberation is the fruit [of knowledge] is established by scripture itself, it is thus that first, through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), there occurs the realization of that very Brahman as the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); subsequently, through the negation (*apavāda*) of the phenomenal world, there occurs the realization of that same Brahman as being devoid of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcatva*). Furthermore, the former realization is merely a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) for the latter realization.

The essential point is that [the world] is independent; the detailed elaboration is to be found in the Bhāṣya and other works—this is the meaning. He raises an objection: "It is useless. The explanation of the word "then" (tarhi) is "absence of purport"; the ellipsis is "regarding the creation of ether and so forth, and their sequence. The ellipsis for "effort is useless" is "of the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya."

The sense is that even if there is a contradiction with scripture (*śruti*) regarding what is not the intended meaning (*tātparya*), it is of no consequence. He refutes [the objection] by saying, "It is not useless. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the principles" (*nyāya*): the meaning is for the purpose of understanding those established principles (*siddhānta-nyāya*) determined in the various topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) contained within the two chapters on space (*viyat*) and breath (*prāṇa*). Of these...

The intention behind the activity of the author of the Sūtras and others is as follows: even though the logical principles (*nyāya*)—such as those concerning creation and so forth—are not required for determining the meaning of the Vedic sentences regarding the purport of the Śruti, they will nonetheless be useful for resolving contradictions that may occasionally arise in that very context; it is with this aim that they have been undertaken. This is the meaning of the phrase "for the sake of their application" (*tatpravṛtteḥ*).

The meaning is that the commencement of the section beginning with "Ether" (viyatpāda) proceeds precisely by accepting that the scriptural texts concerning creation and so forth have their primary purport (*tātparya*) in their own literal sense. Regarding this point, he states the consensus of the author of the *Kalpataru*:
"For it has been said..."—meaning, "this [is the resolution of the contradiction]. "In this regard" (*iha*) refers to the present context.

The meaning is: "in the case of the ether (viyat) and the vital breath (prāṇa). The word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis. Because those scriptural passages concerning creation and so forth have as their primary purport the identity of Brahman and the Self, they have no purport at all regarding [creation] itself; for if they had a purport even toward their own literal meaning, it would result in a split in the sentence (vākya-bheda). Furthermore, there is an absence of any fruit (phala) in the literal sense—this is the meaning. Thus, [the view of] "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭi-sṛṣṭi)...
In this discussion, having refuted the charge of being without a basis (*nirālambanatva*) regarding the Vedic texts on creation and so forth,
he now refutes the charge of being without a basis regarding the passages concerning ritual action (*karma*) and meditation (*upāsana*), beginning with the words "Jyotiṣṭoma," etc.,
by means of the scriptural authority of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such rites.
The meaning is that the attainment of results such as heaven occurs through the performance of sacrifices and the like, which have been taught as the means for achieving heaven and other goals.

The procedure for establishing the theory of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) is as follows: just as there is a correspondence between the results produced by the performance of rites enjoined by dream-revelations and those results themselves, so too the Vedic injunctions regarding the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and other rituals possess no lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), because their ultimate purport (*tātparya*) lies in Brahman, mediated by the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*).
This and similar points constitute the method of exposition for *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*.

The detailed exposition of this should be sought in the original source itself. This one view is the *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* (the theory that the world is created by perception), according to which the creation of the universe occurs simultaneously with its perception;

another [view] holds that the creation of the universe is indeed its perception, because there is no evidence for a difference between the object perceived and the act of perceiving it. The wise declare that this entire world is of the very nature of consciousness.
"Other people of false vision perceive the nature of objects within themselves," according to the *Smṛti*.

Thus, the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) has been shown in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*. Some teachers, however, finding no mental conviction in either of these two types of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* doctrines, [state as follows].
They take pleasure in the doctrine of creation-as-perception.

"Belonging to oneself" (svām) means that indeed someone, at some time, having imagined a Vedic injunction such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, perceives a specific means from it and obtains the fruit through its performance; the meaning is that the attainment of fruits such as heaven is similar to that even in the case of waking. However, in reality:

It should be understood that just as the creation of space and so forth, along with its sequence, is intended to be non-existent because it is perceived through scripture alone, so too the fruits such as heaven are intended to be non-existent because the absence of a creator (kalpaka) is equal in both cases. [Objection: In that case, those [scriptures] would lack authority (*apramāṇya*).

"No," he says, "and [the injunctions] of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other [rites]. For one who performs the rites and meditations enjoined by the ritual sentences and the sentences concerning meditation, there arises purification of the inner being (*sattvaśuddhi*). And for the qualified seeker whose inner being is purified, the Vedānta scripture produces the valid cognition of Brahman. Thus it is said:

The intention is that since the sections on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) and meditative worship (*upāsanākāṇḍa*) are subordinate to Brahman by way of preparing the qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*), their purport lies in that [Brahman] alone and not in their own literal meaning— such as being a means to attain heaven— and thus there is no contingency of them lacking authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Nor is it the case that the Vedāntas [are incomplete] in their entirety...

It must be stated that there is no evidence for the claim that Brahman is not the primary object of inquiry; for there are thousands of scriptural passages, such as "All this, having seen, meditate upon that state" and "Brahmins desire to know That through the study of the Vedas," which serve as evidence for that very point. With this in mind, he says: "and so forth."

The detailed exposition of the process for establishing the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception) is as follows: the connection is that "this one [doctrine] is called *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* because of being creation upon perception.
Another [version], however, is that which has been shown in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* and other works; the connection there is that it is the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*.
He describes the second [type] with the words "of perception alone" (*dṛṣṭereva*). Here, *dṛṣṭi* means seeing (*darśana*).

The meaning is that its essential nature is self-luminous knowledge (*svaprakāśajñānasvarūpa*). This is what is being said: the very nature of knowledge, having attained identity with the visible phenomenal world (*dṛśyaprapañca*), as delimited by the first moment of the world, is called its "creation. Now, [one might object]: how can there be a state of non-different existence between the seer and the seen, which are distinct?

Anticipating the objection that identity (*tādātmya*) is unestablished, he says: "of the perceptible" (*dṛśyasya*). "Vision" (*dṛṣṭi*) means cognition; the meaning is: "in the case of difference," that is, in the state of having distinct natures. Otherwise, [there would be no distinction] between cognition, which is of the nature of existence, and the jar and so forth, in the form "the jar exists" and so on.

The meaning is that there would be no cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In the *Smṛti*, the word "that" (*tat*) means that which is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "the nature of the object" (*arthasvarūpa*): the word "object" (*artha*) refers to that which is independent;
"those of false vision" (*kudṛṣṭayaḥ*) means those whose knowledge is corrupted by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*). And thus, other [beings] of false vision perceive this world...

The meaning is that, because the latter half [of the verse] shows that deluded people perceive the world as non-different from the reality whose nature is consciousness (*jñānasvarūpa*), and because the denial of the perception of difference establishes that the two possess the same ontological status (*satākatva*), [the world is not different from Brahman]. Regarding the phrase "and from Smṛti":
the word "and" implies "and from Śruti"; one should cite such Śruti passages as "All this is indeed Consciousness" (*cidvīdaṃ sarvam*). It should be understood thus.
The meaning is: "not obtaining conviction"—that is, mental trust or the certainty that [the scriptures] are authoritative.

And the reason for not obtaining that is as follows: the acceptance of even the waking world as being merely illusory (prātibhāsika), the denial of the creation of ether and so forth, and the dependence on the performance of the duties prescribed in the sections concerning ritual action (karma-kāṇḍa) and meditation (upāsanā).

It should be understood that [the opponent's position] includes such claims as: "There is no departure from the heavenly world, the world of Brahmā, and so forth," and "The perception of following after the eyes and other senses while awake is an error."

In accordance with the sequence shown by the Śruti, the universe, created by the Supreme Lord, is indeed endowed with an unknown existence; thus, upon the introduction of the respective means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding each object, that specific object is established through perception. Nor does this imply a lack of the world's being imagined (*kalpita*), for it possesses creation, dissolution, and so forth as understood from the Śruti and other sources.
It must be stated that since it performs a causal function (arthakriyā) as perceived through perception and other means,
its very reality would have to be admitted; [however, this is not the case], because—
like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell— it arises from the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) through the form of sensory contact, mental impressions, and defects.

Alternatively, because it is not produced by the three causes— namely, cognition, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and defects— it is [defined as] conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Even in the absence of simultaneity with cognition, it possesses the nature of being removable by cognition alone,
and the nature of being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent, as well as its presence within the locus of apprehension (*pratipannopādhigata*).
Alternatively, this is because we accept that falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of a negation at all three times.
Since, on the view of reality, there is an absence of such falsity in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), it follows that [the world] is distinct from that [Brahman].
He explains the term "creation-as-perception" (*sṛṣṭidṛṣṭi*) with the words beginning with "not so" (*neti*) as shown in the Śruti. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).
He raises an objection: "And not thus. This means that if the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is accepted according to the aforementioned reasoning, [the opponent argues as follows].

The connection is: "In the absence of being imagined (*kalpitatva*), reality itself would have to be admitted. The phenomenal world is real because it is established by scripture (*śruti*), just like Brahman. Nor can it be said that for that which is established by perception, scripture...

It should be stated that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*). For while its nature is established through perception, it is established by the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other authorities as being characterized by creation, dissolution, and so forth. Likewise, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is real because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just like Brahman, which performs causal efficiency such as creation and so on. Nor is there a lack of establishment of the logical reason (*hetu*).

The sense is that its existence in earth, water, and so forth is established through perception and other means of valid cognition. With the intention of resolving the objection by suggesting that the two reasons for the ultimate reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—being like Brahman—are non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*), and therefore no contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) arises, he replies: "In the case of mother-of-pearl... (*śukti*).

The phrase "like silver and so forth" means that although the view of the proponents of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception)—namely, that the world of ether and so forth is coeval with its conceptual construction like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—is absent here, there is still an acceptance of falsity (*mithyātva*), which is the opposite of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*). This is the connection [of the argument]. [This applies to] ether and so forth.
In the case of conceptual construction regarding the world (*prapañca*), the reason for the absence of simultaneity with its object is that it is not produced by the three causes [of perception].

This is because sensory contact (*saṃprayoga*) does not pervade illusions such as dreams. Therefore, in place of sensory contact, one substitutes the knowledge of the general substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-sāmānya-jñāna*). Thus, it says: "the knowledge of the substrate."

He demonstrates the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*) in three ways, beginning with the words "kṣānaika" and so forth. This means [falsity] consists in being removable by the knowledge of the reality of the substrate alone. Being merely different from the real (*sad-vilakṣaṇatva-mātra*) over-extends (*ativyāpta*) to non-existence (*asat*); being merely different from the non-real (*asad-vilakṣaṇatva-mātra*) over-extends to the real Brahman. Therefore, both...

The meaning is that the fact that the substrate (*pādāna*) of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is distinct from both [the real and the unreal] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the term "pratipanna": it refers to that which is apprehended, perceived, or superimposed upon Brahman;
its negation throughout the three periods of time (*traikālika-niṣedha*) occurs within that Brahman, which is the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) having Brahman as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
The meaning is that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is accessible through scripture (*śruti*), and its status as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) [of Brahman] remains intact.

In this regard, even at the first moment, since there exists the state of being removable by the cognition "I am destroying the jar" and so forth, the word "only" (*mātra*) has been provided; for those who maintain the doctrine of reality (*satyatva-vādin*) do not admit that which is removable by cognition alone [to be real]. It is not [so].

There is no distinction from the position of [the world's] reality; for likewise, since others accept that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has the nature of existence (*sadrūpatva*), they do not accept its being different from existence. Furthermore, even regarding the second definition, there is no distinction from the position of reality, because the world is established in its material cause, Brahman, just as a jar or other objects are established in their material causes according to our own school's conclusion (*siddhānta*).

Since others do not accept the negation of jars and the like throughout the three periods of time, [the author] says, "In the case of the position that [the world] is real," with the intention that even in the third definition there is no difference from the opponent's view. Now, one might object: "In this way, would not the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and its attributes also possess the aforementioned form of falsity?"

If it is argued that since [the ego] is established even in the absence of being imagined like space and so forth—as stated in the *Bhāṣya*, *Ṭīkā*, and *Vivaraṇa*—then the effort to establish the three causes for its superimposition is useless; [we reply:
because the ego and the rest are also cognizable solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

The teacher Citsukhācārya maintains that [the world] is intended to be merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*); this is a mere *abhyupetyavāda* (a concessionary argument) regarding the consciousness (*caitanya*) which is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-dual Brahman-self as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so forth—
referring to the section of the text establishing the three causes of that [consciousness]— insofar as consciousness is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*).

The teacher Rāmādvaya holds that [this view] is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*), because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of fragmenting the conceptualization of the Vedānta as the instrument of realization (*karaṇa*) and so forth. Now, one might object: since both in the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*) and in the doctrine of "perception of creation" (*sṛṣṭidṛṣṭivāda*) there is agreement regarding the falsity (*mithyātva*) [of the world], how [can there be such a distinction]?
We maintain that even that which is false possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just as in a dream. Now, one might object:

"The causal efficiency consisting of activities such as bathing in water and so forth, which is accomplished by dream-water and the like, is indeed unreal; however, the causal efficiency accomplished by waking water and the like is real."

The proponent of the theory of "creation through perception" (dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivādin) raises an objection: "But if this were so... This means: provided that being removable by knowledge alone constitutes the very nature of falsity. The connection is as follows: even for the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and its attributes, falsity in the aforementioned sense would be established, just as it is for ether and the other elements. [This holds] "even in the absence of being imagined" (kalpitatva).
The meaning is: "even in the absence of being merely apparent" (*prātibhāsikatva*). The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth;
the meaning of the word "and so on" (*ādi*) is the establishment of the fact that the conscious self (*cidātman*) is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so on. Regarding the phrase "is accepted":
the words "of the Commentator [Śaṅkara] and others" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. And thus, the effort to bring that about and so forth is fruitful.

[The opponent's] position: Although the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and its attributes are cognizable solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), it is improper to describe them as merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, because no sublation (*bādha*) is perceived at the time of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, even though they lack the status of being merely apparent from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*vastugati*),...
He states another resolution, saying "having accepted" (*abhyupetya*), to show that effort was made by them to accomplish the three conditions of the cause.

The meaning is that the statement in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts is merely an acceptance of the appearance (*prātibhāsikatva*), and does not follow the actual state of reality. [It serves as] the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the non-dual foundational Brahman-self.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because the *prauḍhivāda* (bold assertion) nature of the text contained in the *Ṭīkā*, *Vivaraṇa*, and so forth—namely, that "consciousness (*caitanya*) is [the self]"—is evident. He states the justification for its being a *prauḍhivāda*:

"Insofar as consciousness is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramākaraṇatva*)," which means "insofar as Brahman is the instrument of valid cognition. [This is] its character as being established by the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*).
The meaning is that, in accordance with scripture (*śruti*), it is only the Vedāntas that are postulated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman.
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the postulation of the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of the valid cognition of Brahman produced by the Vedāntas.

Previously, it was indicated that if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were ultimately real, then its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) would not be an irrelevant factor; however, that [position] is untenable.

Having considered that false things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell are not observed to perform causal functions such as [obtaining] water-jars and the like, he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but surely). He refutes this by stating "as in a dream," showing that the capacity for causal function does not deviate from reality; for in the case of dream-water and so forth, there exists the performance of causal functions in the form of bathing and the like.

The meaning is that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) because [the reason] lacks truth (*satyatva*). Now, one might object: "It is not merely the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) that is the reason; rather, it is the capacity for *true* causal efficiency. And since that does not exist in the case of dream-water and the like, there is no deviation. To this he replies with "Now, [it is]... The meaning is: "It is indeed non-existent, but not existent. In the reading *asatyaiva*, it means "it is non-existent, but not..."

The meaning is "it is true. Then, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) states the proof for the reason in the argument: "In that case, the phenomenal world (prapañca) is real because it performs real purposeful action (arthakriyā). He says: "But what... The connection is: "Is the purposeful action accomplished by waking water and so forth real? The word *tu* is used for emphasis; the word *kim* expresses a challenge or objection (*ākṣepa*). It is not unreal.

The meaning is that it indeed exists. Therefore, in order to avoid the objection regarding the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*), one must state that the mere capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the determinant of reality; and since that [capacity] exists even in the case of dream-water and the like, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains as it was—this is the intended sense.
Some maintain that there is no distinction between the two cases, as both possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) within their own respective levels of existence.
However, the masters of Advaita-vidyā say: "The objects of a dream do not merely perform causal efficiency that is sublated upon waking; [for instance,] a dream-woman..."
For it is observed that even for things such as serpents, they produce pleasure, fear, and so forth, which are not subsequently sublated.
Indeed, even in the case of pleasure, fear, and the like produced by objects in a dream, no sublation is experienced after waking;
on the contrary, even after waking, there is a clarity of mind.
Because the persistence of the subtle body (*śarīraka*) is observed even prior to [the present life], its existence is determined to be real even then.

For this very reason, it is possible for living beings to experience a desire for objects that produce pleasure within a dream, as well as aversion toward such [objects] in a dream. And this occurs within the dream state itself.
The arising of pleasure, fear, and so forth consists in the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which are colored by knowledge.

[Objection: But surely, even though dream-water and the like lack the capacity for real causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), they nonetheless possess the capacity for causal efficiency regarding effects that share the same level of reality as themselves; therefore, since that [capacity] exists for the waking world as well, does this not establish the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatyatva*) you desire? With this intention, he replies: "It is indistinguishable. (*aviśiṣṭam iti*)

"In both cases as well" means in both states of waking and dreaming. Regarding the resolution that "we say it is like a dream," where some raise the objection of a discrepancy— namely, that in a dream the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is not real, whereas in the waking state it is real— we offer a counter-objection (*prativandyā*).

The reconciliation has been shown. Now, he states another resolution to the effect that there is no disparity in the example, because even objects such as those in dreams are seen to perform real causal functions:
"Advaita... [etc.]. Causal function that is sublated upon awakening is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*); it is the causal function that is not sublated by awakening [that is real].

Even actions occurring during sleep are indeed conventionally real; such is the distinction. Thus, dream-objects do not merely possess the capacity for illusory causal efficiency (*prātibhāsika-artha-kriyā-kāritva*), but also possess the capacity for conventional causal efficiency (*vyāvahārika-artha-kriyā-kāritva*).

The point is this: the capacity of dream-women and the like to perform even conventional purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) is established by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*); therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding their performing purposeful action even within the position that they are false (*mithyātva*). [Objection: But surely, since objects such as the snakes and women in dreams are seen to be sublated upon waking...

Anticipating the objection as to how fear, pleasure, and so forth—which are effects of that [dream]—could be sublated by waking, he says: "By dream-objects," etc. This is because we observe that even dreams of snakes and the like produce pleasure that is not sublated by waking, and they likewise produce fear and trembling that are not sublated by waking; and thus, it is so.

The meaning is that the objects of the empirical waking state are indeed interrupted; for after awakening, during the time of dreaming, pleasure, fear, and so forth are no longer present, and thus the sublation (*bādha*) of pleasure, fear, and the like is experienced.
On the contrary, the effect of the experience of present pleasure is mental clarity (*manaḥ-prasāda*), while [the effect of] present fear is...

The effect of the experience of suffering consists of bodily tremors and so forth; therefore, the indicators [of that experience] persisting after awakening are the clarity of mind (*manas-prasāda*) and so on, as well as fear and the like which persist immediately thereafter. This is because they are real, and thus existed even prior to the awakening.

The meaning is that its reality is established. Even pleasure, fear, and so forth occurring during the time of a dream are conventionally real—just like the pleasure of the waking state—and not merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), because there is no sublation (*bādha*) after awakening, and because they continue to persist even thereafter; such is the conclusion.

He states another reason for the reality of dream-pleasure, fear, and so forth: "For this very reason" means precisely because dream-fear and the like are not merely illusory (*aprātibhāsika*). The underlying sense is that there is a rule that desire (*rāga*) and aversion (*dveṣa*) must have real pleasure and pain as their objects. Now, [an objection is raised: "In a dream, everything..."
Because it consists of mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*). To the question, "How can there be the occurrence of fear and so forth in that which is real? he says: "And it is possible.

This is because the authors of the *Kalpataru*, following the scriptural statement, "That being by which one sees the dream," accept that knowledge is of the nature of a mental modification (*mānasavṛtti*).
The sense is that empirical fear and the like, which consist of transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), are possible;
for it is accepted that only those objects distinct from that [internal organ] are of the nature of illusory appearances (*prātibhāsika*) as transformations of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Nor should it be argued that it is the cognition of the dream-woman and so forth itself that generates pleasure and the like, and that this [cognition] is indeed real;

for even that [cognition], which consists in the functions of seeing, touching, and so on, is superimposed upon the witness of the dream-phenomenon and is established merely through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Not so.
For one whose senses have ceased [to function], the operations of the eyes and other organs do not exist;

nor can it be said that the mere direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of their objects produces happiness, since that [perception] is of the nature of the Witness (*sākṣin*), and "He is that. This is because [happiness arises] from seeing, touching, or even the foot-touching of a beloved woman.

Since it is established by experience that there is a specific pleasure when a snake is touched by the hand at a non-vital spot, and a specific fear when it is touched at a vital spot, even in a dream,
that specific pleasure, fear, and so forth must be produced by specific imagined instances of seeing, touching, and so on.

Because it must be so stated: likewise, in the waking state, just as light capable of illuminating a jar or similar object is observed by other persons present there, so too for a person who has just entered a room,
the deep darkness imagined [there] possesses the capacity for objects appropriate to well-known deep darkness.

Some also maintain that its capacity for action is observed; for instance, when a lamp or similar object is brought near, there is the removal of obstructions such as jars and the like, and when it is taken away again, there is the re-occurrence of the obstruction, as seen in such instances.

One might object: "Is it not the case that fear and so forth in a dream are not produced by objects such as snakes or women, but rather by the cognition having those as its object? Thus, since cognition is real, it is untenable to claim that even a real effect can be produced from the unreal, as this is seen to occur in dreams? To this, the author responds with the words "na ca" (and not), by one who asserts that "that [dream-object] is indeed real."

It must be stated: is that [cognition] of the nature of a modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the mind alone, or of the nature of a modification produced by the eye and other [senses], or of the nature of the pure witness (*sākṣin*)? Even regarding the first [option], is it the mere modification that is the cause of fear and so forth, or is it the modification as qualified by a specific object such as a real or imagined serpent? Not the first.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of fear and so forth even from a cognition whose mode of operation (*vṛtti*) has some object as its domain; nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because even if the mere mode of operation were real, the object itself is unreal, and thus that which is qualified by it must also be merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). Consequently, since empirical causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arises from an apparent cognition, this very case indeed serves as an illustration.

Having considered the first three alternatives, he refutes the second with the words "tasyāpi" (of that too). This means "of knowledge as well. Now, one might ask: why is it not accepted that the true knowledge consisting of the functions of seeing, touching, and so forth, is produced solely by the eyes and other sense organs? To this, he replies: "nahi" (for not...). He then raises the third alternative: "na ca tad ati... (nor is it that...).

He refutes this with the words beginning "from seeing" (*darśanāt*). The connection is as follows: from seeing a woman, there is the experience of a specific pleasure (*sukhaviśeṣa*) established by perception when touching her, and likewise when not touching her feet with the hand; however, this is not the case when touching a serpent on a non-vital spot, such as its tail, as opposed to a vital spot.
The connection [of the phrase] is as follows: "by the fact that the touch on the head is established by experience as a specific fear. Regarding the words "even in a dream":

just as in the waking state, the production of specific pleasure, specific fear, and so forth, arises from the immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) of an object qualified by specific modifications (*vṛtti*) such as seeing or touching, and not otherwise.
The state of being produced solely by the immediate presence (*aparokṣya*) of an object cannot serve as a determinant for a specific effect, because that immediacy alone is uniform in nature.

This is likewise the case in dreams; thus, even though the immediate presence of various objects—which is of the nature of the Witness (*sākṣin*)—is real, [it does not entail the reality of those objects].

The meaning is that because the immediate manifestation (*aparokṣya*) of various objects— which is characterized by specific mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as perception and so forth, and which generates pleasure, fear, and the like— is itself illusory (*prātibhāsika*),
it is possible for empirical (*vyāvahārika*) pleasure, fear, and so forth to arise from that which is illusory. Thus...

Having illustrated the performance of a true purpose by means of what is unreal during the state of dream, he illustrates it in the waking state as well with the word "tathā" (so too). The meaning is: that which is capable of illumination and possesses light being observed by other persons staying within the inner chamber (*apavaraka*). An *apavaraka* is a small room.

He elaborates on this point—that the qualification "being observed by another person" was seen in order to exclude the doubt that there might be no people present there—with the words "by that. This means "by dense darkness. The word "api" (also) is to be connected with the phrase "even while awake."

Others, however, maintain that for an action such as drinking or bathing, it is only the mere nature of the water and so forth that is useful; the reality inherent in it is of no use because it lacks both causality and the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*). If this were the case, then [the same would apply to] the water of a mirage in the desert.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even mother-of-pearl, silver, and the like would perform the appropriate causal functions (arthakriyā) characteristic of water and so forth.

Furthermore, since the universal "water-ness" (*udakatva-jāti*) does not exist in a mirage or similar phenomena, the fact that an error regarding such an object is expressed by the word "water" must be due to its being produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience that was itself expressed by that word.

Regarding the claim that [the universal] is "applied," this is because in the *Tattvaśuddhi* and other works, it is argued that since there is no universal such as "water-ness" (*udakatva*) which serves as the cause for performing the relevant purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such a consequence does not arise. Even in that case, the universal "water-ness" and so forth must exist; otherwise—

Because it would contradict the error that involves the manifestation of such a distinction, and because it would entail the undesirable consequence that those seeking water and other such things would not act toward it.

Regarding the phrase "others, however," even those who maintain the reality of the world cannot claim that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) alone constitutes reality; for if that were so, it would follow that objects such as jars would be unreal during states when they do not perform a causal function. Rather, it must be said that reality is the cause of causal efficiency. And if that is the case, what [is the nature of this reality]?

He states that [the opponent's] intended "existent" (*sat*) is neither the cause of purposeful action (*arthakriyākāraṇa*) nor the delimiting property of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), by means of the passage beginning with "drinking" (*pāna*). It should be understood that the term "water" (*jala*) and so forth includes water-ness (*jalatva*) and other such properties as well.
Regarding the word "useful" (*upayogin*): it refers to the nature of water and so forth as the cause, and the nature of water-ness and so forth as the cause.

The distinction is that [truth] is [the cause] by virtue of being the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) of causality. He states what is excluded by the word "only" (mātra): "not residing therein" means that truth is not the cause because it is distinct from the essential nature (svarūpa) of water and so forth; furthermore, since it would otherwise over-apply (atiprasakta), it lacks the status of being the delimiting condition of causality. "What is the use of that? means "what is the use of truth? And thus:

The sense is that even in the absence of reality (*satyatva*), the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is possible in the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); therefore, there is no contradiction with its falsity (*mithyātva*). Now, one might object: although reality is necessarily associated with the performance of specific causal functions, it does not pervade causal efficiency in general.
Since [the objection] is applicable, he anticipates the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) that it would otherwise be a limiting factor (*avacchedaka*) by saying, "And this being the case...
This means: while truth (*satyatva*) is not a general limiting factor for causality, such being the case, there is no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
Thus, it is not so.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "like the water of a mirage," and so forth.
"Mirage-water" refers to the water superimposed upon the rays of the sun that have come into contact with a desert land;
because it is a mere appearance of water, water-ness does not exist therein. How then is there the cognition, "This is water, this is water"?
Anticipating the objection that [the cognition] involves the verbal expression of a word, he states its establishment otherwise:
"of the error regarding that object. This means: of the error regarding water in a mirage. The prior experience involving the verbal expression of the word "water" has as its object real water.

The meaning is that because it is produced by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) generated by that [previous perception], the fact that it is expressed by that word is caused by it. Regarding the term "causal factor" (*prayojaka*): in the case of well-known water, the universal of "water-ness" (*udakatva-jāti*), characterized by its performance of appropriate purposeful action such as drinking and so forth, is the causal factor.

The meaning is as follows: since drinking and other such functions are not observed in things other than water, and since well-known objects like silver are seen to perform their appropriate causal functions (arthakriyā) such as [forming] bracelets and the like, it is the quality of "silver-ness" (rajatatva) and so forth that is the determining factor (prayojaka) in those cases; for otherwise, one would observe the causal functions of bracelets and the like even in intoxicants (madau) and similar substances. Thus, [the opponent's position] would lead to the undesirable consequence (aprasaṅga) of such an occurrence.

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [marīci-water and the like] performing the appropriate causal functions (*arthakriyā*) such as providing water, which they do not actually do. Even if one were to accept a genus (*jāti*) as the determinant of causal efficacy in the case of mirage-water and so forth, he avoids the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) with the words "even there," etc.; the meaning is "even in the case of mirage-water and the like. The phrase "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means:

In that context, "in the absence of the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) and so forth" is the meaning. The point is that in cases such as the water of a mirage (*marīcikodaka*), the activity of one desiring water would not be possible there without the appearance of the qualification of *jalatva*, which is the intended delimitor (*iṣṭāvacchedaka*).

This is according to the view of those who maintain that even in the case of an illusory object (*prātibhāsika*), there must be conformity with the linguistic usage of being of the same class as what was previously perceived.
In some cases, there occurs the cessation of superimposition along with its root through the knowledge of the specific substrate;

in other cases, there is the destruction of mere superimposition through the subsiding of the knowledge of the general substrate; and in some cases, such as in the instance of an elephant and so forth.
Furthermore, in cases where there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of fire and so forth upon the eye,

since the hot touch and other qualities that cause burning, cooking, and the like are not superimposed there, the absence of those specific purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) is logically established; moreover, it is because only certain purposeful actions are desired in certain instances.
Furthermore, since that form which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and which distinguishes [silver] from a mirage or water must be stated,

one must set aside— because it contradicts scripture and is difficult to apprehend through perception and other means— the quality of being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time; rather,

[the required form] is simply the "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) and so forth, which is not produced by any particular defect and is suitable for the purposeful action appropriate to silver and the like.
And because it can be so stated; therefore, since the capacity for causal efficiency is possible even in the case of falsity, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is indeed false and not real.

Furthermore, since there is no single universal such as "silver-ness" (rajatatva) in both the case of illusory silver and real silver, the usage of "similarity to what was previously perceived" found in the Bhāṣya and other texts regarding illusory superimpositions would be untenable.
