With the intention that a universal must therefore be admitted there in accordance with those texts, he says: "In the case of the illusory," etc., and "in some cases."

After the delusion of water in a mirage has receded, when one approaches it for the purpose of bathing and so forth, and upon the perception of its specific nature— the realization that "this is not water, it is merely rays of light"— the superimposition of water, together with its own root-ignorance (*ajñāna*), [is simultaneously sublated].

The meaning is that, because of its destruction, it is impossible to bring about causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) from it. Regarding the phrase "in some cases, upon the substrate" (*kvacid adhiṣṭhāne*):

after the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver onto mother-of-pearl and the like, where there is a perception of the specific difference (*viśeṣadarśana*), the previously mentioned method applies; however, where that is not the case, there is [the requirement of] the cognition of the general nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhānasāmānyajñāna*).

The meaning is that since the mere superimposition of silver can be destroyed by the destruction of its cause, even in that case it is impossible to bring about the production of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). By saying "as in a dream," we mean that according to the previous text beginning with those words, even illusory objects possess causal efficiency.
He states that even the acceptance of the undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) has already been shown in the discussion of the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), saying: "in some cases, of some [things].

Now, even while conceding that illusory objects lack causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), he says that reality (*satyatva*) need not be stated as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for causality: "the water of a mirage, etc. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (even).

The phrase "śruti" means the scriptural teaching on falsity. For you, existence (*sattva*) must be apprehended as the limiting factor for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*) by means of perception accompanied by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), based on the fact that effects such as bracelets can arise from real silver, whereas they cannot arise from illusory silver which is distinct from it.
And such an entity does not possess the nature of being unsublated throughout the three periods of time—which is the opposite of falsity.
Since it is not capable of being perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one must state some other defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) for it;
with this intention, he says "by direct perception and so forth. Here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes inference (*anumāna*) and the rest.

It should be understood that for the sake of summary, it was stated that even by means of inference and so forth— despite their contradiction with direct scripture— the existence of the phenomenal world (prapañca) in the form of non-sublation throughout the three periods of time cannot arise; therefore, its nature is difficult to grasp even through such inference and other means.

The phrase "of silver-ness and so forth" refers to snake-ness and other such qualities that are free from sublation at the time of conventional usage; this is the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Therefore, the meaning is that "truth-ness" (*satyatva*) is not a causal factor with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Now, if the falsity (*mithyātva*)—which is a property of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—were real, then the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) would be compromised; therefore, that falsity must also be declared as false. In that case, how could there be a loss of the reality of the phenomenal world? According to your own reasoning, that falsity of the phenomenal world belonging to Brahman does not contradict Brahman’s state of being devoid of the phenomenal world (*niṣprapañcatva*).

Because the falsity of that which is false does not contradict its reality. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Advaitadīpikā*: "Falsity has the same nature as the phenomenal world (prapañca) such as space and so forth; and that [falsity] is a property that negates the reality of the substratum."

For when it comes to the exclusion of properties contradictory to itself, what is established for both parties is that the substratum (*dharmin*) must be equally real; ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) is not the criterion. This is because we do not admit the ultimate reality of "pot-ness" and so forth in relation to that which excludes "non-pot-ness" and the like. [This applies] to Brahman...
The statement that "the subject (dharmin) possesses both reality and unreality by virtue of being phenomenal" does not negate phenomenality itself.
Therefore, the objection— that if falsity were merely conventional, then its opposite, the non-illusory reality of the world, would have to be ultimately real— is refuted.
He raises an objection regarding the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) from another perspective with the words "Now, it must be said... (*nanu vaktavyam iti*).

The word "no" (*na*) is to be supplied as the response from the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*). [The opponent objects: "But even though falsity (*mithyātva*) is itself false, it nonetheless excludes its opposite—reality (*satyatva*)—from its own substrate, namely the phenomenal world."
Fearing that the destruction of truthfulness would be unavoidable, the author of the Siddhānta refutes this by means of an example accepted [by all parties]:

"That which is illusory," and so forth. "Possessing the world" (*saprapañcatvam*) means identity with the world; "being devoid of the world" (*niṣprapañcatvam*) means possessing the absolute non-existence of the world, and that is real in the ultimate sense (*vāstavam*) and conventional (*vyāvahārikam*).

The sense is this: since the absolute non-existence of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) in Brahman is accepted as its ultimate reality, just as there is no contradiction between the states of being with phenomenal proliferation and being without phenomenal proliferation in one and the same substratum, so too there is no contradiction between falsity and truth. Thus, [the world] is "falsely situated" upon the ground of falsity.
He establishes [his position] by adopting the very same side, stating: "It has been said here" and "having a common nature.
This means having a common existence (*satā*). The sense is that the world-phenomena (*prapañca*), such as space and so forth, possess a conventional existence (*vyāvahārikī satā*).
Now, one might object: [what of] superimposed properties like "pot-ness" upon their own substratum, which serves as the locus of superimposition?

Anticipating the objection that— since we do not observe potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like to exclude their own opposites, it must be admitted that potness and so forth are indeed real insofar as they exclude contradictory properties within their own substratum— how could false falsity (*mithyātva*) exclude reality (*satyatva*) from its own locus, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the property" (*dharmasya*): according to the perspective of the opponent, reality (*satyatva*)—in the form of ultimate existence (*pāramārthikatva*)—resides in properties such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

Likewise, it is agreed upon by both schools that the property possesses the same degree of existence (*samānasatākatva*) as its substratum (*dharmin*). Thus, when a property such as "pot-ness" excludes a property contradictory to itself within its own natural substratum...

The meaning is that, when there is an expectation for a motivator (*prayojaka*), one should postulate only that which is already accepted as such, not that which is contested. He refutes the example with the words "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). [He says] "the subject" (*dharmin*); because Brahman is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

The sense is that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is of a conventional nature (*vyāvahārika*). Now, if one maintains the position that the falsity (*mithyātva*) residing in the phenomenal world is itself false, then it must be said that such falsity is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*); for it is impossible for a property of falsity—which is to be removed solely by the knowledge of Brahman—to be either illusory (*prātibhāsika*) or ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
If, however, [the world] were merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), then the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) pertaining to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be established;

for that [reality], which is proven by perception in such cognitions as "this is not a jar" and which persists until the attainment of the knowledge of truth, cannot be considered merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). This is because the phenomenal world possesses the attribute of empirical falsity (*vyāvahārika-mithyātva*).

Furthermore, because its conventional reality is untenable, if the attribute of reality belonging to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were established as ultimate, then the ultimate reality of the substratum— the phenomenal world itself— would also be unavoidable; thus,
the objection raised by some that this would result in the destruction of the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita-kṣati*).
He says "for this very reason" to indicate that [the objection] has been refuted by the reason that will be stated hereafter.

For the property (*dharmin*) is equal [in status] to its falsity; since there is a rule that if the falsity of something is conventional, the property-bearer (*dharmin*) must also be conventional. Alternatively, whatever property belongs to something as long as it is not removed by a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) whose object is not itself, that [property] exists therein.

This is because we observe a systematic distinction: in the case of mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), the exclusion of its own contradictory property—the identity with mother-of-pearl—is not removable by the direct perception of that object and is incompatible with non-mother-of-pearlness; whereas in that very same place, the identity with silver—which is removable by that perception—is incompatible with non-silverness. Thus it is. Likewise...

And even though falsity (*mithyātva*) is imagined, it is not removable by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*); thus, it indeed excludes the reality (*satyatva*) [of the world]. However, the state of Brahman being accompanied by the phenomenal world (*saprapañcatva*) is removable by the direct realization of Brahman; therefore, it is not [the case that it does not exclude reality].

Regarding the phrase "rejecting the state of being a conceptual proliferation" (*prapañcatva-pratikṣepaka*): by this, it must be stated that if Brahman, which is accessible through words, is real, then the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the word and the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of the verbal cognition must also be real;
for [otherwise], a conventional object could not be established by the statement of a reliable person (*āpta-vākya*) when that statement possesses only a phenomenal fitness.

For, by means of a sentence such as the *agnihotra* injunction— which pertains to the conventional level— there is no capacity for establishing a real (tāttvika) object; this is because it is a rule that the establishment of the meaning of a word occurs only when that meaning possesses an equal degree of reality (*samānasatāka*).

The meaning of "by necessity" (*niyamāt*) is as follows: since the property of falsity (*mithyātva*) must be admitted as having a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) because it shares the same ontological status as its locus (*dharmisamānasattākatva*), it is impossible for that [property] to result in the truth of the world (*prapañca-satyatva-paryavasāyin*)—the locus of falsity—because this would contradict the establishment of the world's truth as being ultimately real (*pāramārthikatva*). It is not [possible].

Nor should it be argued that, since ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-satyatva*) is absent in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), and since the two types of apparent reality (*prātibhāsika-satyatva*) have already been refuted, there is a contradiction with the experience of existence therein; for by accepting only empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-sattva*) in the phenomenal world, there is no contradiction with experience. Nor [is there a contradiction] with falsity (*mithyātva*).
It should not be said that there is a contradiction between reality and unreality when they possess the same level of existence (*samānasattāka*) within a single locus;

for it has been stated more than once that the object of perception and other means of knowledge is that which is characterized by *satva*—defined as having an essential nature (*svarūpa*) free from sublation and not opposed to falsity. This is the intended meaning.

Thinking that the resolution— that "the same level of reality as the substratum (dharmin) is the governing factor"— is not possible in the view that everything is perceived solely as the reality of Brahman, and that there is no other empirical or illusory reality apart from it, he states another resolution with the words "Or else" (athavā). [Regarding] the property (dharma)...

The point is this: when a property excludes its own contradictory property, what is postulated as the determinant is the state of not being removable by the direct perception of its own substratum, because that is commonly accepted; it is not ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), for we do not accept that [ultimate reality] in such cases. Whatever property belongs to whatever substratum is the object of that [perception].
It is not to be removed by direct perception; that is the property (dharma) in that locus (dharmin)—such is the literal meaning.

He states another reason for the aforementioned prover: "In the mother-of-pearl," etc. The word "that" refers to the mother-of-pearl; "opposed to non-mother-of-pearl-ness" means that which rejects non-mother-of-pearl-ness. "In that very [locus]" means in the mother-of-pearl itself, in the form of identity with silver.

The dharma [of silverness] exists, and it cannot be a sublater (*pratikṣepaka*) of its own opposite—namely, the non-silverness or the difference from silver residing in the mother-of-pearl; this is the sense of the qualifying phrase "that which is to be negated" (*tannivartyam*), which contains a reason within itself. This means it is not something to be negated by the direct perception of the mother-of-pearl. Thus it is said.

The meaning is: when it has been ascertained by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that a property which cannot be sublated by the direct perception of its own substratum is incompatible with the presence of a property contrary to itself in that same substratum. The term "unsublatable" (*anivartyam*) is used because, just as the identity with mother-of-pearl (*śukti-tādātmya*) is not sublated when there is the direct perception of mother-of-pearl, so too [the identity] is not sublated when there is the direct perception of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in the form of jars and the like.

The meaning is that the falsity established by scripture and reasoning does not cease. He states, "By this," that another objection also is refuted by the reason about to be mentioned. Regarding the point that if Brahman, which is accessible through words, is real, then the fitness residing in the words must also be declared to be real, he provides the reason for this.
"Whose is this equal reality?"— this establishes the rule that the sentence-meaning and the fitness residing in the sentence possess equal reality. "Possessing an illusory fitness"—
the connection is with the phrase "due to the absence of the establishment of a conventional object."
Furthermore, because it is impossible for an object to be real if the validity consisting in non-sublation were unreal; and thus,

since there would necessarily be duality due to the existence of a real entity other than Brahman, the claim that the phenomenal world (prapañca) such as space and so forth is also real is refuted by [the fact that] the capacity for causal efficiency belongs only to the conventional level.

Because the establishment [of categories] entails that even conventional fitness can lead to the proof of the reality of Brahman; for while words such as "real" (satya) exist within the Vedānta texts devoted to Brahman,
thereby establishing the reality of Brahman, such words are absent from sentences concerning the Agnihotra and other rituals.

Even if that [the object] exists, its non-establishment follows precisely because it contradicts the powerful Vedic texts on the non-duality of Brahman; for this constitutes a valid distinction. This is because there is no evidence for a rule that the word and its meaning must possess an equal degree of reality (*satā*), just as the validity of the cognition of a jar depends upon the jar-ness [which exists at a different level of reality].
Furthermore, even the validity of the knowledge of Brahman as the reality must be admitted to be composed of elements other than that [Brahman], and thus its falsity is established.

He states the reason for the claim that if Brahman, which is accessible through verbal testimony, is real, then the validity residing in the verbal knowledge whose object is Brahman must also be real: "because its nature is non-sublation. Thus, in order to preserve the reality of Brahman, the subject matter of the Vedāntas, the validity of the means of knowing it [must likewise be maintained].

The sense is that reality must be asserted [of duality]. Now, one might object: even if the reality of the aforementioned fitness and so forth—distinct from Brahman—is established, how can the reality of the entire duality as intended by the opponent be proven? To this, he says: "And thus," meaning that the necessity of duality [would follow], which implies the necessity of the destruction of non-duality (advaita).

Is the reality of the fitness for the Vedāntic verbal cognition required for the sake of establishing its causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) in the form of verbal comprehension, or for the sake of establishing the reality of Brahman? It is not the former; thus he says: "Of the empirical [world]. The word "of the phenomenal world" (*prapañcasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder.

The ablative case in "yogyatāyāḥ" [is used in the sense of "from"]. In the second [alternative], he states that even in the absence of the reality of fitness (*yogyatā*), Brahman is established through verbal cognition; thus he says, "brahmaparaḥ. Here, the word "ādi" (and so forth) is for the purpose of including terms such as "cit" (consciousness).
If that is so, then even a subject (*dharmin*) such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice would be real...

He says "no" to the claim that truthfulness (*satyatva*) would be established [by this]. He states: "The Agnihotra, etc. Now, one might object: since the word "truth" (*satya*) is indeed applied to *dharma* in the Śruti in the passage, "That which is *dharma* is indeed truth," he replies: "Even though that [word] exists, there is no proof for it. This is because the statement, "That which is *dharma*," serves to establish the ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) of the Agnihotra and other such rites.

The meaning is that because the marks of *tātparya* (the intention of the text) are absent, that which is not intended [by the scripture] cannot be established as its primary purport; thus, due to the sublation by the powerful non-dual Śruti, it is not established that dharma possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) in the same way as Brahman.
This is because, in the Śruti, the Agnihotra and other rites are understood as being for the sake of realization (*avagati*).

It should be understood that by intending *satyatva* (truthfulness) as the state of being practiced and *dharmatva* (dharma-ness) as the state of being performed, the non-difference between truth and dharma is stated in the passage, "That which is dharma is indeed truth. This occurs when Brahman, who is Truth, is established by means of a Vedāntic statement possessing conventional fitness.

He states the conclusion with the words "of word and meaning, and of fitness. Even though Brahman is real, the reality of that [cognition] whose authority consists in the removal of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired is not established;
for it lacks the nature of being solely Brahman. He says this with the words "the cognition of a jar" and "distinct from that," [meaning] that which possesses the nature of Brahman.

The meaning is that even the validity (*prāmāṇya*) consisting in the nature of an experience whose mode (*prakāra*) is Brahmanhood is constituted by the qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) of Brahmanhood as something distinct from Brahman. And if the validity residing in the knowledge of Brahman consists in the nature of an experience of an uncontradicted object, and that [validity] is intended according to the specific distinction [stated].

If it were argued that the validity [of cognition] culminates in the mere nature of the object as being incapable of sublation, and that for a validity culminating in that alone— as in the non-dual Vedāntas which have the undivided (akhaṇḍa) as their meaning— the result is simply Brahman alone and not a composition of anything beyond that,
and thus the truthfulness of the validity of the knowledge of Brahman would be possible; then:
Even if the validity of the verbal cognition whose object is Brahman were true, your desired conclusion would not be established;
for the point is that, since it consists of Brahman alone, no real entity distinct from Brahman is thereby established.

Therefore, by the logic stated in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, the falsity of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) beginning with space is established as being as firm as adamant. Now, although the falsity of the insentient phenomenal world beginning with space is established through the word "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*) and other such reasons, [what of] the sentient beings who partake in liberation?

Because of the impossibility of falsity, the concordance [of the Vedas] with the non-dual Brahman is not tenable. Nor is the previously mentioned non-difference of those [individual souls] from Brahman tenable, because it is impossible for those which are mutually distinct to be non-different from a single Brahman. Furthermore, their difference is not unestablished, as evidenced by pleasure, pain, and so forth.

If it is argued that [the distinction] is established through a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*), we say no; for even though there is no difference between those [entities], such an arrangement is possible precisely because of the difference in their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Now, one might object: "Even when the adjuncts differ, how can there be an arrangement if the non-difference of those [entities] does not cease? For contradictory properties cannot fail to be produced by a difference in their substrata."
The confusion [of experiences] is established by the admission of some distinction belonging to something other than that [single self]. On this point, some say:
"The regulation of pleasure, pain, and so forth is indeed established through the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); [for it is said:
desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith..."

For through such scriptural passages as, "Fortitude, lack of fortitude, shame, lack of shame, fear—all this is indeed the mind; it is consciousness that performs the sacrifice," the fact that the mind alone is the substratum of all misfortunes is established; likewise, [it is taught in texts such as] "This person is indeed unattached" and "Being unattached, he does not cling."
Furthermore, because the scriptures establish through various means that the conscious Self, as the universal witness, is indifferent (*udāsīna*),
there is no contradiction with the experience of agency and other attributes of bondage being co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with consciousness, even this being the case.

"Therefore" means because there is no contradiction. It has been established that, on the view that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is illusory (*mithyā*), there is no contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge. Now, he introduces the context to examine the objection that, on the view that the Self is one in all bodies, there would be a contradiction regarding the distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

The phrase beginning with "nanu" and ending with "apavarge" means that since the individual souls (*jīva*) would be sublated by the knowledge of their own falsity according to their true nature, liberation (*mukti*) for them would not be possible. [Objection: But surely, the non-difference of the individual souls from Brahman, which is established by the authority of the Vedānta, was stated at the conclusion of the first chapter.

Having raised the objection that the non-duality [of Brahman] is untenable because of [the existence of] Brahmā, he refutes it with the words, "Nor [is there such a thing] for them. Having raised the doubt that the difference between the individual souls (*jīva*) and the Supreme is not established, he says, "Nor is that... When what they call the ether (*kha*) belongs to one, then happiness belongs to another individual soul; thus, the distinction between pleasure and pain [is maintained]. In this way...

He states that the mutual distinction between passion, hatred, and so forth is established by the fact that they are determined as being experienced and perceived; thus he says: "Sukha... (pleasure, etc.). Now, with the words beginning "āraṃbhaṇa...
(merely a name), he rejects the position that there is a difference in the self for each body, saying: "No," because of logical consistency (*upapatti*). There is no plurality of selves.

The meaning is "one who possesses authority" (*prāmāṇika*). Regarding the phrase "non-difference from that" (*tadabheda*): the meaning is "non-difference from the self" (*ātmābheda*). He states the logical inconsistency indicated by the word "not" (*na hi*) as follows: "of something other than that" (*tadatiriktasya*) means "of some object of the experience of 'I' (*aham-anubhava*) which is distinct from [the self] and characterized by contradictory qualities such as pleasure and pain."

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone is the locus of bondage and the object of the experience of "I," but not the Self (*ātman*), because the latter is immutable (*kūṭastha*). Thus, he resolves that the distinction between properties arises precisely from the difference in their loci. Regarding this, some say: "It is the mind (*mana*) alone"—that is, the mind as the internal organ [is the locus] of desire, volition, and so forth.

Because it is a transformation of that [intellect], there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*): consciousness expands—that is, performs—the sacrifice, which is scriptural action; by the word "etcetera," such scriptural passages as "Desires reside in his heart" are to be understood. He states the proof for the immutability of the conscious Self: "For this [Self] is indeed unattached."

"Unattached" (*asaṅga*) means that it does not cling, because it is incapable of attachment; this is the meaning. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is a collection of scriptural passages such as: "The Witness, the Knower, solitary and devoid of qualities," and "Another, not eating, looks on. And "this being so" means while the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone is the locus of bondage. [I] think "I am doing."

The meaning is that there is a contradiction [with the doctrine of non-duality] because consciousness, whose nature is apprehension— as in the form "I am happy" or "I am miserable"— is experienced as being in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with bondage consisting of agency, pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is superimposed upon consciousness through identity, it is possible to experience its attributes as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with consciousness. Nor should it be argued that if the internal organ were the locus of bondage such as agency and so forth, the conscious self would not be the transmigrating subject (*saṃsārī*).

The transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of that [Self] consists precisely in its state as the locus for the superimposition of identity with the knot of egoism (*ahaṃkāra-granthi*), which is the substratum for bondage such as agency and the like; therefore,
through the cessation of that [superimposition], the fearfulness residing in the locus of the superimposition of identity with the snake ceases by that much alone.
For just as one has the conceit that "this [king] is terrifying" with respect to a king and so forth, the conceit that the Self is the locus of misfortune is likewise possible;
and because of scriptural passages such as, "As if thinking, he trembles," and "The self deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer,'" this is indeed the intended meaning. It is not otherwise.

Furthermore, it must be stated that even so, the systematic distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth— based on the conceit (abhimāna) within the self due to the superimposition (adhyāsa) of various internal organs upon that very same single self— is not established.

Just as there is an experience of the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "this-ness" (*idaṃtva*) and silver-ness (*rajatatva*) when silver is superimposed through identity upon this "this" portion, so it is here; thus he resolves [the objection] with the words "of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇasya*).
In the phrase "of its properties" (*taddharmāṇām*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the internal organ. This is what is meant:

Even though the Self is of the nature of consciousness, consciousness is considered an attribute of the Self through the conceptualization of difference. Thus, when there is the superimposition of identity between the Self and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the attributes of these two—consciousness, agency, and so forth—attain co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya); therefore, there is no contradiction with that experience.
"Conscious" (cetana) means that the transmigrating self (*ātman*), which is the substratum of consciousness, would not possess attributes such as agency and so forth; this is the meaning.

For even though consciousness itself does not inherently serve as the substratum of transmigratory existence, it is possible for the transmigratory state—which actually resides in the intellect (*buddhi*)—to be superimposed upon the self, as it is experienced by the witness (*sākṣin*).

He refutes [the objection] that there is the state of being the locus of transmigratory existence superimposed [upon the Self] by stating "agency, etc. The meaning is: the very fact of being the substratum for that superimposition (adhyāsa) which consists in identity and is like a knot between the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and consciousness (cetanā). "Of that" means "of that consciousness. "Transmigratory existence" refers to the cause of the error regarding the state of being the locus of transmigratory existence.
The meaning is: "because of such an admission. "By that much alone" means: by the mere fact that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the locus of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

"Terrifyingness" is the state of being a cause of fear, and that is a property of the snake. "Mistaken identification" (*abhimāna*) is an error (*bhrānti*). Nor should it be argued that if the locus-ness of transmigratory existence residing in another were superimposed upon the Self, it would result in the fallacy of *anyathākhyāti* (the theory that an object is perceived as something else).

The meaning is that this undesirable consequence does not arise in cases where there is a superimposition upon what is being experienced, because it is accepted that an indefinable relation between the object of superimposition (*āropya*) and its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) comes into existence. The phrase "this [is so]" means precisely with the intention of superimposing the transmigratory state residing in the intellect (*buddhi*) onto the Self (*ātman*). [This applies] to the intellect...

When that [intellect] meditates, the Self appears as if it were meditating; when that very [intellect] is moving or flickering, the Self appears as if it were moving. However, in reality, the Self is not the substratum of meditation and so forth—this is the meaning of the word "as if" (*iva*).
The mention of "meditation and so forth" is intended to indicate all the attributes of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), by means of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

Having fallen into the superimposition of identity with the delusion associated with the locus of agency, that [Self] thinks, "I am the agent," "I am the doer. This conceit of agency is intended as an illustration for the conceit of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).

Now, it may be objected: is it not the case that the intellect (*buddhi*) is inherently the locus of transmigratory existence, while for the conscious Self (*cidātman*), its being so is established only through delusion?

Regarding the point that [bondage] has saṃsāra as its locus: even if, by accepting a distinction [between selves], the establishment of the distribution of those attributes is achieved because the intellect (*buddhi*) differs for each body, nevertheless, since there is no difference between selves for each body,
the bondage residing therein [would not be restricted].

He raises the objection that the systematic order [of experience] is thereby established: "Nor [is it possible] in one alone. Because the various internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serve as the substrata for diverse pleasures and pains, are superimposed upon a single Self, there arises within the Self a sense of ego-identification (*ābhimānika*).
The meaning is that the determination of pleasure, pain, and so forth for that [self] is not established. "Even so" means even when the determination of the attributes of cognition is established.

Just as the multitude of evils residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—with which the Self has attained an identity through superimposition (*ādhyāsika-tādātmya*)—is [regarded as its own] by way of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*), so too is the mutual distinction residing therein; for the determination of that [Self] is established through such a distinction, which appears as an evil to the Self. By this, [the objection is answered].
The argument that— even though pleasure, pain, and so forth are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— the experience of them is of the nature of the witness (*sākṣin*),
and therefore the establishment of the distinction of experiences such as pleasure and pain follows from the unity of that witness,
is refuted; for [the distinction] arises through the difference between respective internal organs due to the internal organ's attaining identity with those [respective objects].

Others [hold] that it is indeed the witness (*sākṣin*) who is the agent, because the determination of that [agency] is also possible through its nature as the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Still others [hold] that agency and so forth cannot belong to the insentient (*jaḍa*), as it is impossible for the insentient to be the locus of bondage; therefore, the agent is [the witness].
If it is argued that [bondage belongs to the conscious self] because the scripture teaches its meaningfulness, [the reply is:

by the sūtra establishing that the conscious self alone is the locus of that [bondage], it is shown that the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the locus of bondage; and this [reflection], being unreal and distinct from the original (bimba), [is not the true self].

Due to the difference in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is the established distinction between the wise and the ignorant, the happy and the miserable, the agent and the non-agent, and so forth.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that there is no lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*), because it is accepted that the self superimposes upon itself not only the state of being the locus of bondage—which resides in the intellect—but also the state of being the locus of mutual difference.
He says: "Superimposed... Having raised the objection, "But how can there be a systematic order based on a difference that is merely superimposed? [the author proceeds].

He states, "of such a kind," [meaning] that because it is superimposed upon the Self, that sort of difference cannot be the establisher [of distinctions]. Although there is no difference between the Self and the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), he has refuted the fault [in his position] by postulating a difference and thereby attributing the experience of a single pleasure, pain, or the like to the Self, which is the locus of that imagined bondage.

Now, having raised the objection that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) would incur a defect due to its oneness across all bodies, he refutes it with the words "by this" (*eteneti*). This means: by the reason that is about to be stated. "The experience of that" (*tadanubhava*) means the experience of pleasure and so forth. "Pleasure" (*sukha*) refers to that very experience of pleasure belonging to Devadatta.

The meaning is that if [the self were identical], then at the time when Devadatta experiences pleasure, Yajñadatta would also experience that very same pleasure, resulting in the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) that Yajñadatta too would think, "I am happy," by taking up that very experience of pleasure.
Just as the distinction residing in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is superimposed upon the Self, so too [is it superimposed] upon the Witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya).

He refutes [the objection] that there would be no distinction in experience by stating, "those [experiences] belong to him," because even when pleasure and so forth are experienced, one admits the superimposition of distinctions residing therein. Regarding the phrase "by means of difference": the meaning is that [the experience belongs] only to that which is qualified by a difference superimposed upon the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) through the distinction of this or that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The instrumental case here is used just as in the expression "wealthy by means of grain" (*dhānyena dhanavān*).

The cause for the superimposition of distinctions upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is its attaining identity [with the Self]. Regarding the objection of the opponent—that if the Self were one in all bodies, there would be no regulation of pleasure and so forth—he states another solution:
"But others... This refutes the previously mentioned view that the intellect (*buddhi*) is the locus of bondage. [He says] "of the insentient," because [bondage] is untenable [for it].

The sense is that [this view] contradicts the well-established fact that bondage is a property of the conscious being (*cetana*). He says "the agent" (*kartā*) to refute the Sāṃkhya position—which holds that agency belongs only to the intellect (*buddhi*) and not to the conscious being because the latter is immutable—and to establish, in accordance with the Sūtra, that agency belongs to the conscious being alone. Thus: "The conscious being is the agent. It must be the conscious being that becomes the agent.

Thus, it is indeed appropriate that the scripture stating, "The conscious self (vijñānātman) is the person who is the agent," is meaningful as a proof for the agency of consciousness; otherwise, it would be purposeless—this is the meaning of the Sūtra.

Regarding the term "reflected consciousness" (cidābhāsa): it is not the conscious self itself directly [that is the agent], because its nature is immutable (kūṭasthatva), and thus it cannot be subject to bondage.

The sense is that this is due to the connection with transformation (*pariṇāma*). To the question, "Even though the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is the locus of bondage, how is its systematic establishment (*vyavasthā-siddhi*) possible?", he replies: "And of that... Although there is no difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), a distinction between reflections is obtained in relation to each internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), determined by the distinction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Even though a conceptual distinction is admitted for reflections as well, nevertheless, because of the falsity of the reflection, its status as the locus of bondage is inherent; thus, the doctrine of its falsity has been adopted.
Nor does the fact that this unreal [reflection] is the locus of bondage lead to the fallacy of a difference in substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between bondage and liberation;
for this reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), when delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is real in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and thus [remains the locus] of liberation.

They say that bondage is the state of being the locus of the superimposition of identity with the *cidābhāsa* (the reflection of consciousness), which—while being superimposed upon the ultimate Self—is the substratum for agency and other attributes.
Others, however, maintain that "the wise declare the Self, when joined with the body, senses, and mind, to be the enjoyer. Along with this...

Because the conscious self is heard in scripture to be the enjoyer when it is joined with the body, senses, and mind through its agency, there is no identity between them. Furthermore, since there is a distinction between the internal organs and the distinctness of the qualified [self], there is no such fixed rule that bondage belongs to the qualified self while liberation belongs to the pure self; for if that were so, there would be a lack of coordination (vaiyadhikaraṇya) regarding what pertains to the qualified self.
They say that because there is no lack of connection with the qualificand (viśeṣya) in the case of a compound, the qualified entity (viśiṣṭa) is not something distinct [from its constituents].

"And not thus" means: assuming a difference between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*). And "while the real consciousness of the original object (*bimbacaitanya*), characterized as Brahman, is the substratum of liberation"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Even in liberation, there is no [liberation] for the limited consciousness (*avacchinnacaitanya*) which constitutes the original object by its own nature.

He says "of this" (asya) to show that there is no fault of lack of co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because even though transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) lacks a real locus, its having such a locus is possible through the power of delusion (*bhrānti*). He states the reason for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the bondage residing in the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) onto the conscious Self (*cidātman*)— namely, the superimposition of identity (*tādātmya-adhyāsa*) between the conscious Self and the reflection of consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "by way of being superimposed" (*adhyastatayā*): the connection is that this reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) is superimposed upon the *jīva*, which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

"Its bondage" (*tasya bandhaḥ*) means it is the cause for the imposition of bondage; this is the intended meaning, because according to the literal text, the status of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of superimposition does not itself constitute the nature of bondage, [but rather] pleasure and so forth do.

It should be understood that this is also because [the self] has the nature of being bound (*bandha-rūpatva*). Although the conscious self (*cid-ātman*) is one and the same in all bodies, it is not accepted that the pure (*kevala*) self alone is the locus of bondage. Rather, it is the conscious self as qualified by the intellect (*buddhi-viśiṣṭa*) that is so;
and since such a qualified entity, which is the locus of bondage, is distinct in each body, pleasure, pain, and so forth do not [transmigrate].
He states another view, namely that there is a confusion [of categories], with the words "But others... He provides the proof for the qualified [self] being the enjoyer, stating:

"The self... Here, the word *ātman* refers to the body; in the scripture, the word "the self" (*ātmānam*) is supplied as an ellipsis, and the particle *iti* has the same sense as the accusative case. Consequently, [the text refers to] the self as being endowed with the body, the senses, and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The meaning is that the wise call [the Self] the enjoyer. Now, it may be argued that the body cannot be included within the category of the enjoyer because it serves merely as a limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) for the Self with respect to experience; furthermore, since it is an instrument, even the sense organs cannot be included within the category of the enjoyer.

Since they are merely instruments, and since enjoyment is observed even in the absence of those [instruments] during a dream, one might suspect that the scriptural statement regarding the self's status as an enjoyer when joined with the body and senses is untenable. Anticipating this, he demonstrates the "joining" (yoga) denoted by the word "joined" (yukta) according to its appropriate application, stating: "by way of acting together. First, with respect to the self:
Desires, volitions, and so forth are experienced, and these are established by scripture as being attributes of the mind (*manas*).

Thus, without the identity of the self with the mind that possesses desire and so on, it would be impossible for the self to be the substratum of desire and the like. Therefore, through such identity, that which is qualified by those [mental states] is the enjoyer.

With the intention that this is logical, he says: "by way of identity" (*tādātmyena*). Now, one might object: the self qualified by cognition (*buddhiviśiṣṭātmā*) is distinct from the unqualified self (*kevalātman*), because it is perceived that the qualified is not the unqualified; furthermore, there is a rule that a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the unqualified, residing in the qualified, must reside in the substantive (*viśeṣya*). And thus, [the difference] residing in the qualified self...

Even though bondage inheres in the qualified [self], it does not inhere in the liberated one; thus, since it does not inhere in pure consciousness (*kevalacaitanya*), the fault of "residing in different substrata" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) remains as before. To this he says: "Of the qualified.
The meaning is that the qualificand, which is included within the qualified, is not distinct from the pure [consciousness]. This is the intended sense: in the world...

Because the identity of the pure person (*kevalapuruṣa*) with the person qualified by a staff (*daṇḍaviśiṣṭapuruṣa*) is recognized through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and because there is no sublation of that recognition, the natural oneness of the qualified entity as a whole and its constituent substratum— the pure entity— is established; meanwhile, the difference between them, characterized by being "qualified" and "unqualified," is merely conceptual (*kālpnika*).
And thus, it is established that the bondage residing in the qualified— which is connected with the qualifier—
also inheres in the pure self alone.

But others [hold] that let the pure consciousness alone be the locus of bondage such as agency; for, according to the analogy of the redness of a crystal, since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) or that which is qualified by it possesses agency and so forth, agency and the like are superimposed upon consciousness as well due to its proximity. Nor is it the case that...

Because it is a single entity, its [distinct] arrangement would be untenable; however, that is established precisely through the difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor should it be argued that the arrangement of contradictory properties in one thing cannot result from the difference in another, for [it is observed] by means of the mere limiting adjuncts of the forms of the root and the tip.
Because we observe the determination of conjunction and its absence in a tree [with respect to different observers],
space— which, through the distinction of limiting adjuncts such as the ear-cavities of various individuals, attains the state of being the auditory organ—
is the cause of the perception and non-perception of sound therein, as well as its qualities of being high or low, pleasant or unpleasant.

They say that this is because of the observation of diversity, such as the capacity to perceive sound and so forth. However, some maintain that if the establishment of contradictory attributes must be explained solely through a difference in substrata, then let the conceptualization of difference due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) apply only to the limited conscious entity; for in the case of the [supreme] unconditioned, there is no imagined difference in substrata at all.
The claim that [the distinction] is caused by a formal arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is nowhere accepted;

for even though a distinction is imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as a jewel, a pearl, a sword, and so forth, there is no [actual] division of properties such as dark, bright, round, or long in the face.

They say that, due to the distinction imagined through the limiting condition (upādhi) of support by a finger, there is the establishment and mutual recognition of properties such as being posterior or anterior in the case of a lamp.

He states the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of bondage and liberation as being direct (*aṃjasā*). Regarding the phrase "But others," he says "Like crystal. Just as, due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower or the like—which is the locus of redness—there arises in a crystal another redness that is a reflection, in dependence upon the redness belonging to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), so too [is it here].
The meaning is that, by disregarding the bondage consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth which resides within the conscious self (*cidātman*), one accepts another bondage—

namely, agency and the like— which is of the nature of illusion (*bhrama*). Nor [is there any contradiction] in the fact that the bondage experienced by the witness (*sākṣin*) in the intellect and so forth [belongs to the conscious self].

It should not be said that the assumption of the arising of bondage—consisting primarily of agency and so forth, which resemble the agency residing in the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties—is not authoritative, because the doubt regarding a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) can be resolved by accepting the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) based merely on contact;
for it is stated: "Indeed, the lower [self] is no larger than the tip of an awl through the quality of the intellect."

By demonstrating in the Śruti that the soul— referred to by the term "inferior" (avara)— possesses a minute dimension expressed by the phrase "the size of the tip of an awn," which is caused by the dimension attributed to the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), it follows by parity of reasoning that agency and other such attributes likewise arise in the Self as if they were properties of the intellect. This is the meaning of the Śruti.
Because [the Self] is authoritative by virtue of being universally accepted. "And not of that" means:

of the Self, which is the substratum for the superimposition of agency and so forth. Regarding the phrase "at the root," according to the opponent's view (*paramata*), these two examples are not established; however, in our own system (*siddhānta*), they refer to the tree delimited by its root and the tree delimited by its top.

It should be understood that the determination of conjunction and its absence is accepted solely by admitting a conceptual distinction, and because it is accepted that the auditory organ (*śrotra-indriya*) is composed of the element of space (*dig*). Regarding "tāra" (high-pitched):
this refers to the capacity for perceiving a high-pitched sound, the capacity for perceiving a low-pitched sound, and the capacity for perceiving a pleasant sound.

The meaning is: because we observe a variety characterized by the perception of distinct sounds and so forth. If the opponent were to argue that in the two examples there is a difference in the trees and other objects as conditioned by a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then with the intention that the same should apply to the case at hand, he says: "But some... and "inferior... and so on.

The meaning is: in the conscious self (cidātman) as qualified by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), but distinguished from it—that is, as conditioned (upahita) by it. Now, one might object that the distinction alone is the determinant of the [individual] arrangement; to this he says: "unimagined" (akalpita). The meaning is that we do not accept even the reality of distinctions such as those between jars and other objects.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that only an intrinsic difference (*svābhāvikabheda*) is the determinant for such a distinction, and not a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikabheda*)? Anticipating this, he says: "Like a gem," and so forth. For indeed, in the case of a face, a distinction between its dark and bright aspects is perceived through the difference produced by a stained gem or a mirror; likewise in the case of a sword, a gem, or a pillar made of crystal.

The meaning is that the determination of circularity, length, and so forth occurs through the distinction produced by [the limiting adjuncts], because of the common recognition [of them as the same]. Nor should it be asked:

"If the identity between the reflection and the original object is natural, how is it established that the distinction is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and on the basis of that, how is their determination also established? How, indeed, is their identity itself proved? For that...

The sense is that this has already been established previously. Under the view that [the difference] is delimited (*avacchedapakṣa*), he shows the consensus regarding the fact that adventitious difference (*aupādhikabheda*) is the determinant [of distinction], by means of the example "the finger" (*aṅguli*).

Thus, while it is possible to establish the distinction [between souls] on the basis of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), one must determine what the specific adjunct is that serves as the cause for the mutual experience of pleasure and so forth among individual souls (*jīva*).
On this point, some say: "It is the non-difference of the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*)."
The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that serve as the causes for the connection with or non-connection with those [experiences] are [the respective parts of the body],
because an experience delimited by the body is connected with that which is delimited by it,
whereas an experience delimited by the foot is not connected with that which is delimited by the hand.
This is because there is no such cognition as "I, whose hand has been cut off, experience pain in my foot.
How then does the hand move to extract a thorn stuck in the foot?
This movement of the hand is not due to a synthesis (*anusandhāna*) with the hand that was cut off; rather, it is [due to...].

Thus, because there is non-difference between the two parts—the foot and the body—due to the existence of non-difference between the foot-limited sensation and the body-limited "I," the sensation in the foot is constantly integrated with [the sensation in] the body; this is because of that integration. And so it is.
Because there is no identity between the bodies of Caitra and Maitra, the sensation delimited by Caitra’s body is not experienced by that which is delimited by Maitra’s body;
nor is it experienced by something delimited by a further whole (avayavin) that permeates both bodies.
Since there is no single composite whole (*avayavin*) that permeates both [bodies] to serve as the locus of experience,
it does not follow that a thorn pricking Caitra’s body would cause pain in Maitra’s body.

When the systematic distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth among individual souls (*jīva*) is established—either through the difference of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or through the difference produced by those adjuncts—it follows that there is no evidence for their mutual distinction in reality; thus, the non-difference of all from the one Brahman is established. Once that is established, [the conclusion follows] regarding Brahman, which is non-different from the individual souls and devoid of phenomenal manifestation (*niṣprapañca*).
It has been established that the systematic concordance (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta is proven. Now, he begins another inquiry.

The word "thus" (*evam*) means "in the manner described. Regarding the connection and non-connection [of the self with the body], are the non-difference and difference of the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) the determining factors, or rather the non-difference of the locus of the distinct objects of experience?

The meaning is that the response to the question—"Are these the non-difference and difference of that [the Self]? or "Are they the non-difference and difference of the body? or "Are they the non-difference and difference of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)? or "Are they the non-difference and difference of ignorance (ajñāna)?"—must now be determined. Among these, taking the first position:

He examines the reply. Regarding this, some say [as follows], and therein he establishes the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) by means of the phrase "delimited by the body" (*śarīrāvacchinna*). For the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) is the body, which is the substratum of experience through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*);
and with the intention that its parts, such as the hand and so forth, are also [such loci], he says "the foot" (*caraṇa*), etc.

He demonstrates precisely this lack of connection. Regarding the phrase "severed from the hand," he raises an objection against the absence of the capacity for the self delimited by the hand to experience the pain residing in the self delimited by the feet:
"How then [is there such experience]? This [experience] does not arise from the connection of the one delimited by the hand with the activity of the hand.

However, the connection is with the phrase "due to the recollection of that. This means: because of the recollection of the sensation located in the foot by that [self] which is delimited by the body. Now, one might ask:
how can a sensation located in what is delimited by the foot be recollected by that which is delimited by the body?

Because of the difference between the part and the whole. Even if one were to admit the connection [of memory] despite this difference, the sensation delimited by Caitra’s body would also be connected by one delimited by Maitra’s body, since the difference is no different [in both cases].
And thus, when a thorn is stuck in Caitra’s body, it would follow as a natural consequence for Maitra’s body as well.
An undesirable consequence would follow; therefore, he says: "of the part and the whole.

The meaning is that even though there is mutual difference between the parts, identity (*tādātmya*) is admitted between the body and its parts. "And in this way" means that there is a recollection of the pain delimited by the foot in [the self] delimited by the body.

The meaning is: provided that identity (*tādātmya*) with respect to each individual body is the regulating factor. Now, even though that which is delimited by the hand lacks the capacity to synthesize the experience of that which is delimited by the foot, [the pain] occurs through the thorn stuck in the foot.
Even if one were to perform an action with the hand out of friendship,
since there is an absence of a unifying consciousness that synthesizes the pain residing in Caitra’s body (as delimited by his own body),
it is impossible to avoid the undesirable consequence that the hand of Maitra would move because of a thorn stuck in Caitra’s body.
To this he replies, "Nor even... The meaning is that [the pain] is not permeated through both bodies of Caitra and Maitra.

The connection is as follows: a sensation delimited by Caitra’s body is not experienced as permeating both [bodies], even by one delimited by another whole (avayavin). Therefore, the sense is that the example is not analogous.
Others, however, maintain that it is indeed the distinction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) being non-severed that is the cause of the unification of experience;

and thus, there is no fault even if one accepts the unification of the sensation of the foot by one delimited by the hand. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that an embryo in the womb would unify with the mother’s pleasure.

Because the term "separated" (*viśliṣṭa*) is intended to refer to two things that have not entered into one another as parts within a whole; for it is said that such is the case with the mother’s womb and the body [of the fetus]. And they were not [merely] those whose arms were like clubs of weapons, but rather those seeing with their own fallen heads and eyes.

It must be stated that even when there is separation, a connection [of perception] is understood through the Mahābhārata statement, "The head and the trunk, though enemies, joined together here. For even in that case,
the head and the trunk have entered into a single substratum as constituent parts.
Because it is a matter of experience: if, immediately following the head [being struck],

either fainting or death necessarily occurs, then such a statement— whose meaning contradicts what is observed— is, by the logic of "how much more so" (*kaimutya-nyāya*), a praise for the excellence of the warrior's extraordinary zeal.

Because it is external [to the Veda]; because, although it is a statement of an existing fact (*bhūtārthavāda*) by virtue of having as its object a particular person endowed with such power, there is no contradiction with the Nirukta’s etymological derivation; and because it depends upon the intention [of the speaker] and is free from obstruction. For this very reason, it has been said [and will be said] regarding the various positions concerning yogis and those who remember their past births (*jāti-smara*).
The occurrence of a fault [arises] from the pursuit of the internal affairs of another body.

When a thorn is stuck in the foot, it is accepted that the person who experiences the pain delimited by the foot is the very same one whose hands are engaged in the act of removing it from the door; for if that were not the case,

the difference between the locus of experience (the body) would not be a cause for the lack of recollection, since there would be a deviation in the case of the difference between the foot and the hand.

This must be stated. Thinking that it is appropriate to provide a qualification in order to maintain that [point], he defines the second condition (*upādhi*) with the words "But others... Here, the word *upādhi* refers to the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*). [He says] "there is no fault" because, although there is a difference between the two loci of experience—the hand and the foot—there is no disjunction (*viśliṣṭatva*) between them.

The meaning is that there is no fault of deviation (vyabhicāra) in that case, because of the absence of a factor that would prevent the reconnection of the divided locus of experience. "This being so" means when the qualification of "being divided" is provided.
[It refers to] the mother's body, which is the locus of experience for the embryo—that is, for the living being (jīva).

The sense is that there is no disjunction [between the parts]. He refutes [the objection] by stating that for one who does not recognize the distinct objects, there is "movement and so forth at the beginning," and by saying, "in one [entity]," because of its being such. The meaning is: because it has not entered into a state of non-penetration within a single composite whole (*avayavin*) consisting of parts. And thus, because there exists a distinction of separate limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is not [the case that] the embryo is situated [within].
The sense is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the soul (*jīva*) being connected with pleasure and pain.
He raises the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the stated cause of non-connection by saying "If it is not [the case]... "Arms" refers to the trunks of trees;
"bodies" refers to those whose heads have been severed; "here" means in this battle, on the ground, or in this statement, O Caitra.

The meaning is that there is a deviation from the rule (vyabhicāra): just as in the case of Caitra and Maitra whose bodies have become separated, even though there is a division of the head, one perceives in the one whose head has been severed the quality of being a cognizer and a unifier (anusandhātṛtva) belonging to the one whose body was previously delimited by Caitra. Having accepted the fact of such unification in that case, he resolves the objection by pointing out the difference between the bodies of Caitra and Maitra.

Regarding the phrase "even there" (*tatrāpi*), it means "because it has already entered previously. With the intention that no doubt of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is even possible—since this statement lacks any lack of authority regarding its own meaning—he abandons his initial position by saying, "immediately after the severing of the head. [The implication is: "If even headless trunks (*kabandha*) cause them to fall, how much more so others?"

The meaning of these words is that he praises the extraordinary enthusiasm of the warriors. Now, one might object: even after the severing of their heads, it is possible for some—through the power of yoga, through their own greatness, or through the power of a boon—to continue engaging in battle and so forth. Therefore, this [statement] would merely be describing an existing fact.
Anticipating the objection that this is merely a statement [of a rule], he addresses the deviation by accepting the principle of "reconnection" (*anusaṃdhāna*) and stating:

"Such [a case]. This is because the general rule (*utsarga*) is accepted as being that the distinction between separate bodies of experience is not a cause for the absence of reconnection; thus, the instance cited as one of reconnection is admitted to be a case where that general rule is set aside (*apavāda*).

The meaning is that in such cases, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not a fault. "For this very reason" means precisely because it is accepted as being of the nature of a general rule (*utsarga*). "There is no occurrence of a fault" [is said] because, if one were to accept the rule that the diversity of the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana-bheda*) and so forth necessarily causes a lack of recollection (*ananusaṃdhāna*), then [such a fault would apply] to yogis, those joined in yoga (*yukta*), and those who remember their past lives (*jātismara*).

The meaning is that even though the four causal factors— the diversity of the sense-bases for experience and so forth— are present, there would be no occurrence of the fault of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to the absence of non-continuity (ananusaṃdhāna).
Others, however, maintain that the connection between the unity and difference of the body is due to the presence or absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);

for we observe the connection between experiences of childhood and other lives, as well as their absence, depending on such adjuncts. Nor should one suspect a difference in the body even between childhood and youth, because of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Nor...

The cognition of its difference [in size] arises from the difference in measurement; for just as there is a distinction between the root and the top of a single tree, it is possible for multiple measurements to coexist in a single entity through the distinction of time.
[Objection: But surely, there can be no difference in measurement without an increase in parts (*avayava*), and parts...
If it is argued that those arriving later do not occupy the body already established by the former [occupant],
and thus a difference in size necessarily implies a difference in the body— this is not so,
because when a lamp is lit, there is a simultaneous expansion of a circle of light pervading the interior of a palace.

Because we do not accept the theory that initiates the process of atomic dimensions— which would fail to account for contraction and so forth at the same moment as their covering— [we instead follow] the Vivarta (illusory manifestation) doctrine.

Some say that, just as in the case of the body displayed by a magician (*ceṇdrajālika*), the growth of the body occurs through illusion (*māyā*) even without an increase in its constituent parts. Others, however, explain the distinction between the continuity of experience and its absence through the non-difference or difference of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And this is the position [of the latter].

This has been established previously. However, some, accepting that there are multiple ignorances (*ajñāna*) which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) for the various individual souls (*jīva*), assert that the distinction between the experience of unity and the lack thereof is determined by the difference or non-difference of those [adjuncts]. Regarding this, some others say:

The intended meaning is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the young and so forth, because it is intended that a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) serves as the cause for the non-connection [of memory] with the diversity of the body—the locus of experience—and other such factors resulting from actions performed together. Taking up this third position, he provides the response, beginning with "But others... He states the proof for that [position] with the words "From childhood... (*bālya*).

The recollection of what was experienced in childhood is observed in old age because of the continuity of the body between childhood and old age. The meaning is that precisely because of such [physical] difference, the recollection of what was experienced in another birth is not observed in this present life. Thus it should be suspected.

The sense is that [the body] differs in size and so forth. He refutes [the objection] by stating that there is no difference in the body, because we observe recognition in the form "this is that very same body" even when there are differences in states such as childhood and so on. Having raised recognition and the like as the seed of doubt, he states that they are established otherwise (anyathāsiddhi).

And by the words "na ca" (not [so]), etc., he raises an objection by resorting to the theory of new production (*ārambhavāda*). [The objection begins with] "nanu" (but surely), [and continues with] "na pūrvasiddham" (it is not previously established).

Because it is impossible for a previously established body to serve as the material cause (*upādānatva*), [the body must arise] after the destruction of the previously established body, through the conjunction of its constituent parts and the accumulated parts.

The meaning is that since the body must be produced through a sequence beginning with dyads (dvyaṇuka) and triads (tryaṇuka), a difference in size necessarily entails a difference in the body; furthermore, recognition will have as its object the general property of "bodiness" (śarīratva-sāmānya). The term "simultaneous" is an adjective qualifying the expansion, and "time" (samaya) refers to—
The two [atoms] are to be understood as having the nature of moments (*kṣaṇa*). That term refers to their supreme radiance;

the meaning of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the substratum of their material cause" is as follows: [it refers to] the "non-compliant" ones, because in the position that gross composite wholes (*avayavin*) arise through the sequence of dyads (*dyaṇuka*) and so forth, a delay would result.

Furthermore, because it contradicts the experience of simultaneous occurrence, even if light and so forth were to perish through the sequence of the destruction of atomic conjunctions, a delay would result; moreover, in the theory of causal origination (*ārambhavāda*), since one must admit an absolute difference between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*), this contradicts the experience of their coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

The meaning is that such a doctrine must indeed be rejected. [Objection: If one does not accept the commencement of another body through the sequential accumulation of parts, how can there be the conjunction of contradictory dimensions within a single body?
To this, he provides a reply by adopting the fourth position—that it is due to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*): "But others... and so forth.
"Previously" means the section of the text that establishes the arrangement of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

He states the fifth position with the words "some, however," [referring to] the proof for the difference in ignorance for each individual soul, which was shown during the occasion of investigating the definition of Brahman; thus [it stands] in the doctrine of non-dualism (*aikātmyavāda*).
Having established the systematic order [of the world], he states the impossibility of that systematic order in the doctrine of manifoldness (nānātvavāda) with the words: "In this case... (atra).

Following the method of the *sūtra* and its commentary in the section beginning with "A part [of Brahman], because of the designation of diversity" (*aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*), and specifically the *sūtras* "Because of the lack of restriction regarding unseen merit" (*adṛṣṭāniyamāt*) and "If it be argued that this is likewise in the case of intention and so forth, we say no, because of their being included within [the self]" (*abhisaṃdhyādiṣv api caivam pradeśād iti cet nāntarbhāvāt*), [it is established that] within a single Self, by means of the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-bheda*).

They state that even in the doctrine of the plurality of selves according to the system of Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika) and others, the lack of a systematic order is equally untenable. For instance, when a sensation arises in Caitra due to a thorn pricking his foot, why would a sensation not arise simultaneously in other selves as well? [This would occur] for all selves...

Because [the self] is omnipresent, there is no distinction in its being included within the body of Caitra; nor can there be a fixed rule that pain such as the prick of a thorn occurs only in the body of the one who experiences it and not in others,
since the body arises in the proximity of all selves and thus belongs to one alone and not to others.

Because it is impossible to restrict [the body], there is no rule that "whatever body is produced by a particular unseen force (adṛṣṭa) belongs to that [specific] self," since the restriction of the unseen force itself is not established. For when the mind, in order to produce that unseen force, comes into conjunction with one soul, it likewise comes into conjunction with others; how then [could there be a restriction]?

If the causes were common to all, that [result] would arise only in some specific case. But surely, even though the conjunction with the mind is common to all, the determination—such as "I shall obtain this fruit," or "the volitional effort conducive to the action that produces the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa)"—is established as restricted; therefore...

If it is argued that there will thus be a restriction based on the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no; for since intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) and the rest also arise from the common conjunction with the mind, a fixed determination [of agency] cannot be established. Now, if it is claimed that the conjunction with one's own mind is the cause of intention and so forth, then the conjunction with the mind alone would be the factor of non-commonality.

It will not be so; for it is impossible to restrict the mind—which is eternal and connected to all selves—to belong to any one person alone. Nor can the relationship of ownership between a specific self and the mind be established on the basis of a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), because, as in the previous case, the stability of that *adṛṣṭa* itself cannot be proven.

The individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman, because the scriptures speak of the difference between the individual soul and Brahman. Nor should it be asked how the individual soul can be a part of Brahman, who is partless; for just as the delimited space (*avacchinna-ākāśa*) is a part of the great space (*mahākāśa*), so too is the individual soul a part of that which consists of undivided consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanyarūpa*).

The meaning of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "because of the admission that [the individual] is a part of Brahman" is as follows. An explanation of the three Sūtras beginning with "adṛṣṭāniyamāt" will follow. For the followers of Kaṇāda and others have resorted to the distinction of selves, on the grounds that the established order of experience would not be possible if there were no difference between selves in each body; they argue that even if the Self were one, such order could be accounted for by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

It must be said that their recourse to a distinction between those [minds] is futile, because an arrangement based on adventitious conditions (upādhi) is cumbersome. Therefore, for the sake of establishing an arrangement directly, they have resorted to a distinction between selves; such is this doctrine.

He refutes [the objection] by saying "according to the system of Kaṇabhuj (Kaṇāda) and others. The meaning is that they state the equality of the absence of systematic consistency (*vyavasthā*). That is to say, just as it is for Caitra, so it is for others as well.
The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "pricking with thorns, etc. is intended to include being struck by a sword and other such things.

He refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that the specific self residing in the body is not established as being unique [to that body], saying "in the proximity of all selves. He introduces the sūtra, "Because of the lack of restriction regarding the unseen" (*adṛṣṭāniyamāt*), with the words "when the unseen...
He explains the sūtra with the words "even of the unseen... He establishes the lack of restriction with the words "for when..."
