The meaning is that at that time, it also conjoins with other selves (*ātman*). It should be understood that the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "mere conjunction" (*saṃyogamātra*) is intended to exclude [the self's role as] a common cause such as intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) and so forth, but not to exclude its being an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), intention and the desire for its fruit are included.

He provides the answer by applying the sūtra, which states that there is a "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) of the knowledge of being an effect produced by an agent and of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), and that this is likewise the case for intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) and so forth. With the words beginning with "no" (*na*), he raises the objection regarding the mind’s lack of commonality (*asādhāraṇya*) and refutes it. [The opponent asks: "But [how can it be] one's own? [The author replies: "And thus, from its conjunction... (*tatsaṃyogāt*).

The sense is that everything having an inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) will be unique (*asādhāraṇa*). To this he says "How so?"—the meaning is that [the sound] would not be unique because its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), namely the conjunction of the self with the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*), and its inherent cause, the self (*ātman*), are common [to other instances]. (35) truṭat.
Now, even if selves are omnipresent, it may be argued that only specific locations (pradeśaviśeṣa) of those selves undergo bondage;
thus, because other selves lack such specific locations within Caitra’s body, the distinction between pleasure and so forth will be maintained.
In whatever place Caitra, having experienced pleasure and so forth,
has departed from that place, if Maitra arrives at that very same place, one observes pleasure, pain, and so forth in him as well, despite his being a different body.

Because even a specific internal region of the self is included [within the self], therefore, even if there were a plurality of selves, the systematic arrangement [of experiences] would be difficult to justify. And if it is somehow justified, then— given both conformity with scripture and parsimony— one should accept the oneness of the self (*ekātmya*) and justify that arrangement within that very unity.

"It is proper to do so. [Objection: "Let it be then that the selves (*ātman*) are indeed atomic (*aṇu*); for if they were all-pervading (*vibhu*), there would be no basis for the distinction [between one self and another]. [Reply: It is not so; for if the selves were atomic, the simultaneous arising of pleasure throughout the entire body, as well as the presiding over the hands, head, feet, and other limbs, would be impossible. As for the modern conceptualization regarding this...

The individual souls (jīvas) are indeed atomic, because their passing away, going, and returning cannot otherwise be accounted for, and because their atomic nature is directly heard in such scriptural passages as: "This self is indeed atomic," "This one, verily, moves from this world, [carrying] both merit and sin," and "It is subtler than the hundredth part of the tip of a hair."

While explaining the sūtra, "If it be argued that [the distinction] is due to location (pradeśa), no, because of inclusion," he anticipates and refutes the position established by those who rely on location. He begins with the words, "Now, as for the selves... [The opponent argues: "Bondage, such as pleasure and pain, is restricted to specific locations belonging exclusively to each respective self. This is the meaning of the word "if" (cet) in the sūtra.

The meaning of the words [of the verse] is as follows: he refutes [the opponent's position] by stating that the restriction—that in a single body there is space for only one self and not for other selves—is unproven. This is expressed in the words "not in which" (*na yasmin*).
Since unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), pleasure, and so forth do not exist pervasively, that part of the self which is the locus of the unseen merit and so on—

This is the meaning of the term "location" (*pradeśa*) here. Thus, in whatever location, such as a seat, Caitra’s body is situated, that becomes the locus of pleasure and so forth for Caitra. In that very same location, immediately after Caitra’s body has departed, Maitra’s body arrives and remains; it then becomes the locus of pleasure and so forth for Maitra.

It is observed [that this occurs]. Therefore, in that case, it follows that the body which has subsequently arrived would result in the experience of both Caitra and Maitra, because the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in the respective soul-regions (*ātmapradeśa*) of Caitra and Maitra have entered into that body. Furthermore, at the time of departing from the previous body—
It should not be argued that the portion of Caitra’s self residing in that body might also depart [with it],

because, since the self possesses spatial divisions (*pradeśa*) and is stable, the movement of such a division is logically impossible; furthermore, one should infer that for other selves as well, there would be a confusion of experiences resulting from the overlapping of their respective spatial divisions.

"Therefore" means because the pervasiveness of the selves is accepted. Anticipating the objection that "just as in the view of the unity of the self, some kind of systematic arrangement is admitted even in the view of their plurality," he says: "The scripture," meaning the scripture concerning the unity of the self. "In that very [place]" means in the single self alone. [This refers to] the indicator of the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Relying upon scripture and reasoning, he again raises an objection regarding the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, beginning with "Let them be.
He refutes this with "Not so. Regarding the phrase "of the substrate," the meaning is: of the simultaneous impelling of the hands and other limbs.
He raises a doubt, suggesting that even if the individual soul is atomic in size, experiences such as pleasure that pervade the entire body are possible, with the words "As for what is here."

The manner of their conceptualization will be explained in the passage beginning with "even though they are atomic" (*aṇutve'pi*). First, he states the proof for its atomicity: "In departing" (*utkrānti*). The sense is that in such scriptural passages as "when it departs" (*utkrāmantaṃ*), departure and so forth are heard. [Objection: But what of one who possesses a medium size?

If the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) is postulated because its departure [from the body] and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable, then its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) must likewise be postulated because the scriptural teaching of its identity with Brahman would otherwise be inexplicable; since there is no difference in the nature of this presumption based on scripture (śrutārthāpatti). Anticipating this objection, he cites scripture as well: "For it is atomic," and so forth.
Regarding the self that these [actions] bind from here, he says what it is: "both merit and demerit.

The meaning is that this self is atomic (*aṇu*). The statement, "the individual soul (*jīva*) is to be known as the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided [into a hundred]," is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*). It refers to the hundredth part of the tip of a hair.
The meaning is that the soul is that portion which results when that [space] is divided into a hundred parts, being equal in measure to such a part.

Even though these [qualities] such as knowledge and pleasure are minute, by the analogy of the light of a lamp, they pervade a specific location distinct from their substrate; thus, as qualities, they are experienced throughout the entire body, resulting in the perception of pleasure and so forth extending over every limb. Droṇa.
Because, in accordance with the Smṛti passages beginning with "the portion of Bṛhaspati," there exists a constituent part (*aṃśa*) of the individual souls (*jīva*);

thus, there is no contradiction regarding the simultaneity of pleasure, pain, and so forth in those [souls] that have entered into hands, heads, feet, and other limbs, nor regarding the diversity of experience among yogis who have entered into multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*).

There is some inconsistency. And thus, because the individual souls (*jīva*) are atomic (*aṇu*), there is no confusion [of experiences], which accounts for the systematic distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth; furthermore, this establishes the difference between them and the omnipresent Lord (*īśvara*).
Regarding this, it is stated in the *Advaitadīpikā*: "Even so, how is the establishment of this systematic order achieved? In the case of Caitra..."

For just as one experiences pleasure and pain occurring in different parts of one's own body— such as pain in the feet and pleasure in the head— it is equally unavoidable to experience the pleasure and pain associated with others through the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Indeed, Caitra is no different [from himself].

Furthermore, there is a distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and its parts (*aṃśa*), as well as between them and the friend; for in the case of the multiplication of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), since the parts—

which are capable of migrating elsewhere after being separated from the soul— must necessarily be distinct from the soul, you yourself must admit both difference and non-difference between the part and the whole (*aṃśāṃśin*).
And because of the [scriptural] passage beginning with "gamāt. Nor should it be argued that pure difference (*śuddhabheda*) is not the cause for the lack of mental synthesis (*ananusaṃdhāna*).

For "purity" (*śuddhatva*) must mean either the absence of concomitance with the relation of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*) in the case of difference, or the absence of concomitance with non-difference (*abheda*).

He demonstrates a modern mode of conceptualization that follows the means of proof establishing the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*). Regarding the phrase "even though they are atomic": just as light, having left its own support—the lamp—pervades other regions, so too do knowledge and the other qualities [leave] their own support, the atomic self.
The meaning is that [the soul] is sometimes conceived as abandoning its pervasiveness of the body. Now,
if the self were pervasive of the entire body,
then pleasure, effort, and so forth, arising simultaneously, would be possible within it by means of differences in limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*).

But if that [body] were atomic, how could their simultaneity be maintained? To this he says: "droṇam" (the heap). After "anugateṣu" (in those who have entered), the word "jīvāṃśeṣu" (in the portions of the individual soul) is to be supplied. After "vyūhaḥ kāyavyūhagateṣu" (the array in those who have entered into an array of bodies), the word "jīvāṃśeṣu" (in the portions of the individual soul) is likewise to be supplied. [This concerns] the enjoyments.

The meaning is that for yogins, the diversity of the pleasures and other experiences being enjoyed, their simultaneous manifold nature, and their simultaneous presiding over multiple bodies are possible through their own parts (*khāṃśaiḥ*).
Under the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic (*aṇu*), there is not merely a lack of logical consistency; rather, there is a total absence of possibility. However—

He says, "There is also a gain," meaning "if this is so. This means: given that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic (*aṇu*). "Due to non-confusion" means: because there is no entry of all souls into a single body. "Of the all-pervading" (*vibhoḥ*): if the soul were also all-pervading, then due to the absence of any difference in characteristics, its distinction from the Lord (*īśvara*) would not be established; whereas [if it is] atomic, [the distinction is] absolute.

The sense is that difference is easily understood due to their distinct characteristics (*vailakṣaṇya*). He refutes the modern [Advaitin] hypothesis with the words "it has been said here. The phrase "even so" means even if one postulates that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic and possesses parts. [In that case, there would be] the individual soul's awareness of the pleasure and so forth residing in its own parts, but no awareness of the pleasure and so forth residing in other individual souls.

Moreover, by you who accept this, it must indeed be stated that non-difference (*abheda*) is the cause of synthesis (*anusandhāna*), and that difference (*bheda*) is the cause of the absence of such synthesis.
In that regard, is the cause of the absence of synthesis mere difference, or is it pure difference (*śuddhabheda*)? In the first case:
Caitra does not experience the pleasure and so forth residing in his own [other] parts because of the existence of the distinction that serves as the cause for non-connection;

for if he were to experience what resides in his own parts despite the presence of such a distinction, then he would also experience the pleasure and so forth residing in another person, Gautama. Thus he says: "Of Caitra... and so on.

Anticipating the objection that the distinction between the part and the whole (*aṃśa-aṃśin*)—which serves as the basis for their non-connection—is unestablished, he proves it with the words "the network of bodies" (*kāyavyūha*) and "being separated" (*viyujya*). The meaning is: having attained separation from the whole. "Elsewhere" (*anyatra*) means:
in a network of bodies other than the yogi's own body. The distinction between those two is not [unestablished] by us.

With the intention that this must be established, he says: "of the part and the whole. Now, it might be argued that mere difference is not accepted as the cause for the lack of recollection; for if it were, the Jīva would not recollect pleasure and so forth even when they belong to its own part. And if it were to recollect them, then it would likewise recollect what belongs to another Jīva.

One might object that if one were to connect [the two] in that manner, the fault of duality would follow; however, he raises a second objection, suggesting that there is rather a specific distinction, by saying "na ca" (but not).

The first alternative is not tenable, because the Śruti, Smṛti, and Sūtras— such as "This is indeed a portion of Me, the Supreme," and "In the world of living beings, [the soul] is a portion [of Brahman], for there is the designation of diversity"—
establish that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Brahman; thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion of experiences between Brahman and the individual soul.

Now, one might object: "Just as the individual souls (jīvāṃśas) are parts of the individual soul (jīva), why not say that the individual soul is a part of Brahman? Rather than being a literal part, its 'part-like' status is merely figurative, consisting simply in its similarity to Brahman while being smaller than it—just as Jupiter’s orb is a hundredth part of the moon’s orb. If this is your view, what is the point of this [distinction] beyond such a claim?

The primary status of being a part (aṃśatva) is here attributed to the individual souls (jīvāṃśas) with respect to the [Supreme] Soul (jīva), based on their non-perception [of the Whole] while residing within the body.
It cannot, however, consist in being a material cause (ārambhakatva) of the soul, as is the case of various beings with respect to a cloth, because the soul is beginningless (anādi).
Nor can the great space (mahākāśa) possess the nature of being a spatial part, as in the case of the space within a jar and so forth,

nor the nature of being a fragment, as in the case of pieces of stone broken by a hammer; for it is partless due to its atomicity (in the sense of being indivisible), and because it is incapable of being cut.

If it is argued that "part-ness" (aṃśatva) is intended to mean being both different and non-different in substance, this is not so; for if that were the case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion of experiences between the Lord and the individual souls, as well as among the individual souls themselves.
This is because you yourself accept that although they are inherently distinct, they are also non-different by virtue of their consciousness and other such qualities.

Furthermore, according to your view as one who maintains both difference and non-difference between the aggregate and its constituents, there is also a mutual non-difference among the individual souls contained within a single aggregate.

In the first [view], because the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is accompanied by the relationship of part and whole (aṃśāṃśibhāva), it is a pure difference; therefore, there would be no mutual experience of pleasure and so forth between the two. Thus he says: "Not the first. He states the proof for the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Lord: "For the part... [of the Supreme].

The "world of living beings" (jīvaloka) refers to the world characterized as the individual soul (jīva) in relation to the Supreme Self (paramātman). Now, it may be argued that purity does not consist merely in being accompanied by a relationship of part and whole (aṃśāṃśibhāva) based on difference; rather, it must be accompanied by a primary relationship of part and whole. However, such a primary relationship of part and whole does not exist between the individual soul and the Lord.

He raises an objection, saying "But surely," [thinking]: "In the primary view, since there is a difference between those two, and because the purity consisting of being co-existent in the form of the relationship between the principal and its part exists, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
Thus, with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*), there is a primary relationship of part and whole between the soul and its parts.

The sense is that since concomitance (*sahacaritatva*) itself is non-existent [in that case], there is an absence of the purity consisting in concomitance; therefore, the connection (*anusaṃdhi*) is not possible. After the word "part-ness" (*aṃśatva*), the word "face" (*mukha*) is to be supplied as the remainder, meaning "possessing luster.
In this regard, the distinction between concomitant entities based on a primary relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*) is not the cause for the connection.

He states that the relationship between the primary whole and its parts is difficult to define, asking: "What is that? The construction is as follows: "Apart from this [primary part-ness] which is introduced here into the body that serves as the cause [of the whole], what else is it? Is primary part-ness the state of being a constituent atom (*ārambhakāvayava*), or being a spatial location (*pradeśatva*), or being a fragment (*khaṇḍatva*)?

Or is the meaning of the word [the soul] that it possesses a substance that is both different and non-different? Regarding this, he first refutes the initial [position] with the words "Not, for one... He then sequentially restates and refutes the second and third [positions] with the words "Nor also... and so forth; for since the individual soul (jīva) is atomic, spatial divisions are impossible, and thus its bifurcation occurs precisely by way of its atomicity.

The meaning is "and because of suitability. He raises the fourth objection: "distinct-and-non-distinct" (*bhinnābhinna*). The primary sense of being a part (*aṃśatva*) intended here is that the portions of the individual souls (*jīvāṃśa*) possess the nature of a distinct substance (*bhinnadravyatva*) in relation to the [Supreme] Soul;

and it is precisely this [nature] that is assigned as the cause for the lack of recollection (*ananusaṃdhāna*) within the body. And thus, because of the nature of being a distinct-and-non-distinct substance...

The conclusion is that the distinction based on association is a pure distinction, and that [pure distinction] is what necessitates the lack of non-consideration (ananusaṃdhāna). Regarding this, he states the refutation: "If that were so," because you admit that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) are substances that are both non-different and different. Their distinction...

It is not a pure difference (*śuddhabheda*). Likewise, since you accept that the individual souls (*jīvāṃśa*) possess a nature that is both different and non-different from one another, their difference also is not a pure difference. Thus, due to the absence of the causal factor for non-recognition (*ananusaṃdhāna*), [there is no such recognition] between the Lord and the individual souls, nor among the individual souls themselves.

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of a confusion of enjoyments (bhoga-sāṃkarya). The word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "by being conscious and so forth" (cetana-tvādinā) is intended to include [the properties of] being sentient (sattva) and being a substance (dravyatva). He states another refutation: "of the aggregate" (samūha). This means that while the aggregate and its constituent members (samūhin) are mutually distinct...
In your view, which accepts difference (*bhinnatva*), it is necessary that even those things forming a collection (*samūhin*) must be mutually distinct.

Consequently, since there exists a state of non-distinct substantiality (*abhinnadravyatva*) among the individual souls (*jīva*) who have gathered together in one place during festivals and the like— despite being mutually distinct— their mutual difference is a "pure difference" (*śuddhabheda*).

It does not possess a nature that is both distinct and non-distinct, because [such a nature] is accompanied by [the logical fault of] being a single substance; and thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of their mutual recollection of pleasure and so forth—this is the meaning.
Because it would be impossible to avoid the non-difference of the thing itself [from its parts], since it is non-different from the collection that is non-different from itself.

If conjunctions and the like, as well as universals (*jāti*), were to reside in multiple substrates, then there would be non-difference between quality and the qualified (*guṇa-guṇin*) and so forth; consequently, even a cloth, which is non-different from a conjunction that is non-different from a jar, would [be non-different from the jar].

Furthermore, [your objection] that "the non-difference from the jar would follow," and so forth, is invalid, because you yourself have accepted the rule that what is non-different from something non-different from X must itself be non-different from X. Nor [does this apply] to another individual soul, because of its inclusion within a single collection characterized by the uniformity of attributes such as being a sustainer and being conscious.

If it is argued that there exists another form of non-difference between part and whole— distinct from the non-difference already employed— which serves as the cause for their synthesis despite their difference, and which must be specified here to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), then it follows that this very [non-difference] must be specifically defined.
If it is argued that the distinction between the part and the whole consists in the fact that they are not joined together because they possess the same single form, namely *dharma*.

[The opponent] objects: "Even though the members of a collection are distinct from the collection itself, in our view they are not mutually non-distinct; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Anticipating this, [the author] says: "svābhinnetyādi" (by that which is non-different from itself).
Devadatta is a single member himself; the collection is non-different from him; and Yajñadatta is non-different from that [collection]. By that [reasoning...]
The meaning is that even for Sahasva and Devadatta, their non-difference would be unavoidable in his view,

because you have accepted the rule that "that which is non-different from what is non-different from x is itself non-different from x. He establishes the acceptance of this rule against the opponent with the words beginning "yadi" (if), [referring to] the genus of quality and qualified.

This passage beginning with "yadi" and so forth is intended as a refutation directed at one who maintains the non-difference between individuals, specifically the proponent of the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*). Having accepted the non-difference between quality and the qualified, if it were admitted that a quality—
such as conjunction, disjunction, or duality— is dependent upon multiple substrates, then [the following would ensue].

If, having accepted the non-difference between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), one were to admit that the universal resides in multiple individuals, then it would follow as an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even a cloth (*paṭa*) and so forth would be non-different from a jar (*ghaṭa*). Regarding this, he states a qualifying term containing the reason:
"non-different from the jar. The meaning is: because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is non-different from the jar, the cloth and so forth are likewise non-different [from it]. Now, [an objection]:

The non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the non-difference among the individual souls—which are a collection of parts that are themselves non-different from the soul—is based on attributes such as sentience and on their belonging to a single collective whole.

Apart from those, there exists another distinct non-difference between the individual soul and its parts; therefore, even though they are mutually different, there is mutual recollection (*anusaṃdhāna*) between them.

Because there is no such identity between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), nor between the individual soul and the aggregate of souls, there is no mutual recollection (anusaṃdhāna), even though there is non-difference based on their common nature as consciousness and so forth.

And thus, according to that established doctrine, difference coexisting with non-difference in substance is the "pure" difference; and since that [pure difference] is not a cause for mutual awareness, it follows that only a distinct kind of non-difference— which is intended to be the cause of mutual awareness between the individual soul (*jīva*) and its part (*aṃśa*)— is actually involved here.

He refutes the objection that there is no such over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because, in the case of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), there exists a difference that is not accompanied by the state of being a substance that is both different and non-different (bhinnābhinnadravyatva)—a state constituted by such non-difference—as is the case between the soul and its parts. He says: "Not so," because [the property] such as sentience (cetanatva) is common to other individual souls just as it is to the soul and its parts.

The meaning is that non-difference is distinct from that [non-difference] which is conditioned by the uniformity of nature (*dharmaikarūpya*) and conditioned by being included within a single aggregate (*ekasamūhāntargati*), and so forth. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including the secondary relationship of part and whole (*amukhyāṃśāṃśibhāva*) existing between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), even though there is a difference between the part and the whole.

The construction is as follows: there is no other distinct difference between those two that could serve as the basis for their connection, such that another form of non-difference—distinct from [the absolute non-difference of] the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—might be intended as being included within the category of "different-and-non-different substance" (bhinna-abhinna-dravyatva) in order to avoid over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Now, one might ask: why [is there] no other form of non-difference?

Anticipating the objection that [the part and the whole] do not exist, he says, "that being so," meaning that while there is non-difference characterized by distinctness between the part and the whole,

he explains the specific nature of the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and its part— the Lord (*īśvara*)— in contrast to the non-difference between the *jīva* and the Lord, as being "not caused by the identity of attributes" and so forth.

Nor [is there non-difference] between the living being and the body, because even though they possess a single uniform nature in terms of attributes— such as the quality of being capable of movement— and because they exist as a single aggregate when multiple bodies are unified in a *kāyavyūha*,
it is possible that their non-difference is merely conditioned by that uniformity of attributes and so forth.

If it is argued that, although there exists another non-difference conditioned by the oneness of nature (dharmaikarūpya) and so forth, the non-difference that grounds the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (jīva) and its part (the Supreme Self) is not conditioned by that [oneness of nature], we say: no.

Because for those two, there is no absence of duality or non-duality; for in your own view, when the substratum is one, you do not admit that either difference or non-difference can be manifold through a difference in counter-correlates or a difference in their forms.
Therefore, in the first case, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) remains firmly established. By this very reasoning, the second case is also refuted.

If non-difference (*abheda*) were the cause for the non-recognition of the difference between co-existent entities, then according to the reasoning already stated, such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would be unavoidable in your own view, since non-difference exists both between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, as well as among the individual souls themselves. [Objection: But surely, the perception of non-difference is the governing factor (*tantra*) in recognition; therefore, [recognition does not occur] in its absence.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the identification [of one's own self] with oneself, the non-difference from oneself, and the non-difference from one's own parts are perceptual?

Therefore, although there exists non-difference from another individual soul (*jīva*), there is no identification with that other soul’s suffering and so forth, because that [other soul] is not perceptual for [the first soul].

He states the non-establishment of the specific [reasoning] mentioned: "Not the individual soul," etc. For the individual soul (*jīva*) and its parts, there exists a uniformity of properties such as sentience, existence (*sattva*), and substantiality (*dravyatva*); likewise, for the individual soul and its constituent parts at the time of entering a single body.
Just as a collection exists by way of delimitation from that body, so too,

when there is sometimes a conjunction of those bodies belonging to the yogic souls who have entered into the multiple bodies designated as a "body-array" (kāyavyūha), the collection exists together with the yogic soul as the whole; and thus, there is non-difference between the soul and its parts.

The meaning is that because it is possible for [the non-difference] to be conditioned by the uniformity of attributes such as being conscious (*cetana*), the claim that it is not so conditioned is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, even if non-difference exists among individual souls (*jīva*) due to their uniformity of attributes such as consciousness,

since they stand in the relation of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*), that non-difference which is the cause of the part-and-whole relationship is distinct [from the former], and that [latter] does not [apply here].

He raises the objection that [the identity] is caused by the uniformity of attributes (*dharmaikarūpya*) and so forth. Since even the non-difference common to other individual souls (*jīvāntara*), which is caused by the uniformity of attributes and the like, cannot be avoided,
when that too is accepted, two types of non-difference between the individual soul and its part would be accepted according to the opponent's view.
It follows [by implication]. To the opponent who says "yes," he replies: "Not of those two. This means "not of the part and the whole.
"In that form" (*tadākāre*) means "in the form of the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogyākāre*); that is to say, "as delimited by the counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
The presentation of the non-acceptance of the manifoldness of difference is for the sake of providing an illustration. "Because of that" (*tasyāt*).

The meaning is that, apart from the relationship of part and whole previously established between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), it is impossible to establish a relationship of part and whole between the face and its reflection; and thus,
since the difference between the individual soul and the Lord is accompanied by the aforementioned relationship of part and whole, [it cannot be otherwise].

The meaning is that, in the absence of purity in the form of non-concomitance with that [impurity], there is no pure difference that could serve as the cause for non-contemplation; consequently, the defect consisting in the contingency of a mutual confusion of enjoyments between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) remains constant. Regarding the "first position," this refers to the state of being non-concomitant due to the absence of the relationship between part and whole.

"Purity" (śuddhatvam) means the position [that purity belongs to difference]. He refutes the position—that purity belongs to difference because it is not co-present with non-difference—by means of the reason to be stated later. "By this very [reason]" means by the aforementioned method; namely, [the reason of] sentience and so forth.

The method [of resolving objections] has been stated as being uniform with respect to *dharma*. Now, even while accepting the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—as well as among individual souls—just as there is non-difference between the individual soul and its parts (*aṃśa*), [the author] raises a doubt to avoid the previously mentioned over-extension, beginning with "But surely...

(*nanu*). The word "his own" (*svasya*) means "of the individual soul who is the whole" (*aṃśin*). The phrase "by another individual soul" (*jīvāntareṇa*) is to be construed with "his own" (*svasya*).

If it is argued that everything is consistent— since for one who remembers their past lives, there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of non-difference even from their former self, and thus they can recollect the events of that life, whereas others cannot because they lack such perception— then the same applies to the doctrine of the unity of the self (*aikātmyavāda*).

Because Caitra’s direct perception of the non-difference between himself and Maitra is obstructed by the ignorance that veils the state of being the Self of all, it follows that the entire system of worldly distinctions is established from that very [ignorance]; thus, your acceptance of a difference between selves—which contradicts the Śruti—is useless. Moreover, this is not so even for you who maintain the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

The establishment and maintenance [of the world] belongs to the omniscient Lord; for if he were necessarily subject to the direct perception of the non-difference between himself and other individual souls (*jīvas*), it would follow that he would experience suffering within those souls just as they do, such that he would have the experience "I am suffering. In our view, however, the Lord perceives the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) in the soul as non-different from himself.
Even though one perceives impurity as if before one's face, one does not grieve because of the certainty of [its] falsity; thus, this undesirable consequence would not apply,
lest there be a division of parts in the Śaṅkara-body-manifestation consisting of the head, feet, and so forth.

If it is argued that the pervasive radiance of knowledge—the non-departing light of the lamp of the Self—is the substratum, and that by means of that alone all things will have their substratum, [we reply: no.

"Of one who remembers their births" (jātismarasya) means of one possessing the recollection of previous lives. "The all-" (sarva-) refers to that ignorance which veils the state of being the Self of all; the meaning is "due to the obscuration caused by that [ignorance]. "Precisely for that reason" (tata eva) means precisely because there is an absence of direct perception of the mutual non-difference among all [beings], such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, [which would otherwise establish it].
The meaning is that the non-connection with pleasure and so forth would be untenable.

Having accepted that the perception of non-difference is the cause of connection, [the author] has demonstrated—in accordance with the view of the opponent—that the hypothesis of the non-difference of the self involves conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) and contradicts scripture; and [he now proceeds] to [show] that in the opponent’s view...

He states that even the status of being a prompter (*prayojakatva*) is not possible due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), saying: "Nor even in this way. The meaning is: even by the assumption that the perception of non-difference is the prompter for the [Lord's] volition. For it is necessary that the Lord possess the perception of that non-difference of other individual souls (*jīva*) which is real and ultimate; otherwise—

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [the Lord] not being omniscient. Now, one might object: "Even in your own system (*siddhānta*), since Brahman possesses both omniscience and non-difference from the individual soul (*jīva*), the aforementioned defect follows"—to this he replies, "In our view.
As for the claim that because individual souls possess parts (*sāvayavatva*), there are portions of the soul located in the hands, head, and feet;

The simultaneous occurrence of pleasure, pain, and so forth is possible for yogins in their manifold bodies (*kāyavyūha*), and the diversity of the simultaneous experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth among the constituent parts of a yogin’s soul is also possible; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
That [objection] regarding the soul with respect to the parts of the soul...

Since even the status of being a "portion" (*aṃśatva*) has been refuted, and since— given that those portions are similar to the individual soul (*jīva*)— even a figurative portionhood consisting in having a smaller dimension than the soul is contradicted under the view that the soul is atomic; therefore,
the atomic dimension alone [is established] in comparison to all other dimensions.
Because they possess a smaller magnitude than that [the soul], and because there is no magnitude even smaller than that, and because, while being similar, their nature as parts—

consisting in being smaller than that— functions as the cause of absolute difference from the soul (just as the parts of the moon's disc are distinct from the heavy disc itself), [there is a distinction] for the soul.

Furthermore, because it is impossible for [the yogin] to experience the pleasure and so forth residing in his own parts, and because it would follow that the yogin’s own soul— which is absolutely distinct from the individual souls (jīvāṃśas) presiding over the array of bodies—
could not be the presider over that array of bodies; such is the case for the soul that presides over the body.

Because the portions of the individual soul (*jīvāṃśa*) that preside over the various parts of the body, such as the head and feet, would be entirely distinct from one another, there would follow the undesirable consequence of multiple experiencers within a single body; furthermore, since there is no evidence for the soul having parts, and because of the scriptural statement, "O Bṛhaspati, the *droṇa* measure is the portion of [the soul]," [the soul is partless].
Because, according to the manner described, there is no intent to state that [the sages] were actually parts [of Viṣṇu],

but rather that Bṛhaspati and others merely assumed other bodies for the sake of divine tasks— such as the removal of the earth-demon (Bhūtāra)— through the power of yoga; by this, the divinity of Śrī Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others [as portions of Viṣṇu] is also explained.

The conventional usage has also been explained. Therefore, since it is established in the intention of the preceding text that it is impossible for a specific portion of the individual soul (jīvāṃśa) to be the presiding agent over the hands, head, feet, and so forth, or to be the presiding agent over a plurality of bodies (kāyavyūha), the author raises an objection with the words "syādetat" (it might be so) and "adhiṣṭhānam" (presiding).
It will be argued that the soul (jīva) is the impeller; for although the soul itself is atomic and resides in only one part of the body,
by means of its all-pervading knowledge— which is coextensive with itself— it presides over the hands, head, feet, and so forth, as well as over a plurality of bodies (kāyavyūha).
The point is that even though the individual soul (jīva) is partless, its presiding over the entire body and so forth is not logically untenable.
It is not [the case] that the experience of pleasure and pain belongs to the self as something like knowledge;

for if it were dependent solely on knowledge, it would follow that there could be no diversity of experience— just as there is no diversity of bodies in the case of one who possesses a plurality of bodies through the differentiation of limbs such as hands and feet.
If one accepts that the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is a property of cognition alone and not a property of the self,

then even though a distinction among the cognitions— which are qualities of the self— is established by their diversity, the non-distinction of the self is not thereby established; thus, the diversity of experience and the like cannot refute the oneness of the self.

Because the self (*ātman*), which is the substratum of enjoyment and so forth, is atomic (*aṇu*) by virtue of yoga, it is partitioned in each body; thus, there arises the consequence of a confusion of attributes (*dharmasaṃkara*), as if one were asserting its omnipresence or its non-difference [from other selves]. Furthermore, this would result in the abandonment of your own tenet. Therefore, it is proper to establish the systematic order by accepting the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Nor is it logical for him to establish the soul's difference from God on that basis, because you— who assert that the individual soul (jīva) is atomic due to scriptural statements regarding its departure [from the body] and the direct hearing of its atomicity— must admit that [the Lord], having created it, entered into that very thing, as in the text: "He entered within."

Because of scriptural passages such as "The Teacher of men has entered the cave" and "He is beyond my highest reach," and because of the hearing of words like "entering" (*praveśa*), and because of the scripture stating his direct atomicity (*aṇutva*): "This is that subtle essence; this is my Self within the heart, subtler than a grain of rice or a grain of barley."

Since even the other [the Supreme] would be established as merely atomic through hearing [of its size], how can the distinction between the Supreme and the individual soul be established on the basis of their being all-pervasive and atomic respectively?
Is it not said that "He is all-pervading like space and eternal, and greater [than all]"?
Because of scriptural statements such as, "From heaven, from the intermediate space, from the sun," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "relying on cognition": for if pleasure and so forth were properties of cognition, their production would occur within cognition itself; consequently, cognition would be all-pervasive, and it would follow that the experience consisting of pleasure and so forth—which relies upon that cognition—would arise simultaneously in the hands, head, feet, and so on, as well as in a plurality of bodies (kāyavyūha). But this is not accepted by you.
The meaning is as follows: pleasure and so forth are held to be attributes of cognition (*jñāna*).

Since it is admitted that these, like cognition itself, are attributes of the self (*ātman*), even if cognition were all-pervasive, a simultaneous variety of experiences in the hands, head, feet, and in a manifold body (*kāyavyūha*) would not be possible.
Regarding the phrase "surrounded by an array of bodies," the word "yogin" is to be supplied as the subject. And his diversity of enjoyments is recorded in the Smṛti:

"He may cast them forth again like the multitude of rays from the sun. The "power of the selves," that is, of the bodies, refers to the capacity produced by yoga. [Objection: In that case, let pleasure and so forth be properties of cognition itself, provided that they possess the nature of being its attributes.

To this, he says: "the diversity of experience such as pleasure, pain, and so forth. The meaning is that it is not established [as a proof], because since the diversity of experience—which resides in knowledge, which is a quality of the self—is located in a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇatayā*), it cannot possibly serve as a prover of the plurality of selves. [Furthermore,] pleasure and the like are properties of all-pervading knowledge.

And he says that it is contrary to his own view: "of the substratum of experience and so forth. This means [it is contrary] both to the view of the Naiyāyikas and others, as well as to the Advaita view. "Therefore" means because it is impossible to conceive of qualities of the self, such as knowledge and pleasure, as being all-pervasive. Regarding the acceptance of the atomicity of the *jīva*, the following is the position of the opponent:

Another purpose [is stated]: "O bull among the Bharatas, having attained power, a yogin may create many thousands of selves and move about with all of them; with some he may enjoy sense-objects, and with others he may perform severe austerities. This is contradicted and refuted by the scripture: "Nor does he possess it through that [power]."

The meaning is that [the soul] is not atomic. He refutes [the opponent's position] by stating "because of departing, etc.," on the grounds that according to your own view—which asserts the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) based on scripture and logical necessity—the same two [sources of knowledge] would also unavoidably establish the atomicity of the Lord (īśvara). Consequently, the omnipresence (vibhutva) of the Lord cannot be established; and if that is not established, your desired conclusion is not achieved.
The connection is that even according to your own position, it must be established that [the Self] is indeed atomic (*aṇu*). Regarding the two words "having created that" (*tat-sṛṣṭvā*):

the world is the referent; the Supreme Self under discussion, the creator of the creation and so forth, is "within"—the word "in bodies" (*śarīreṣu*) being understood as the ellipsis; He is the "ruler" (*śāstā*), meaning the controller. "Supreme" (*parārddhya*) means worthy of the highest place, that is, most excellent.

The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) have entered the cave characterized by the intellect within that space of the heart (*hārdākāśa*). Regarding the phrase "because of entering," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to such qualities as being situated inside the body;
this [subject] under discussion at the beginning is present here. The suffix *aṇ* in the term *aṇimā* does not intend to convey the sense of atomicity (*aṇu-bhāva*).

The meaning is that this Self, whose qualities are described as being "of the nature of light" (*bhāk*) and so forth, exists within the heart; and compared to rice and other such things, it is even more minute (*aṇutara*). [The opponent] objects to the omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the Lord on the basis of the Śruti and other texts that cannot be explained otherwise: "But surely... [The reply is: "Greater than the great" (*jyāyān mahattaraḥ*).

Furthermore, because the Supreme is the material cause of all phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*), its omnipresence is established; therefore, scriptural passages concerning its atomicity (*aṇutva*) should be understood as intended for the purpose of meditation or as referring to its being difficult to grasp, and scriptural passages concerning its "entry" (*praveśa*) are to be explained by means of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body. Nor do the scriptural passages concerning the departure (*utkrānti*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth [contradict this].

It might be suspected that [the self] cannot be led out by means of the intellect (*buddhi*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); however, this is not so, because of the statement: "As he departs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs after him," which indicates that the departure of the living being (*jīva*) occurs even before the departure of the intellect known as *prāṇa*. Likewise: "The knower, liberated from name and form, [reaches] that which is higher than the high..."
Furthermore, because it is heard that there is a movement even after the liberation from name and form,
as in the passage: "Just as a man, well-prepared, sets out while making a sound, even so this embodied self, mounted upon the conscious self (prājña), sets out while making a sound."
If you argue that this is because of the stated analogy of the cart as the substratum for its natural motion, this is not sound;

for [the scriptures state]: "This indeed is that great, unborn Self, who consists of consciousness," and "Just as when a jar containing space is being carried, the jar is carried but the space is not, so too the individual soul (jīva) is like the sky. And so forth.
Because the scriptures also declare that the individual soul (jīva) possesses all-pervasiveness.

He states the indicative mark for the omnipresence of the Supreme in the words "sarva" (all). He states the alternative proof for the scriptural passages concerning atomicity in the words "tadaṇutva" (its atomicity).

The meaning is that such scriptural passages as "smaller than a grain of rice" are intended for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). The meaning is that such scriptural passages as "this very [Self] is the subtlest" are intended to express its being difficult to grasp (*durgrahatva*).
The sense is that these [meditations] do not belong to the context of worship (*upāsanā*).
The particle *vā*, expressing an optional alternative (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*), states that the scriptural mention of "entering" and so forth is established otherwise.
And as for the scriptural texts concerning "entering," they refer to the Supreme Lord’s assumption [of forms] by His own will.
The meaning is that "entry into the body" refers to entry into the interior of bodies, conditioned by the [individual] body and senses. Now, one might object:

since even the scriptural texts and indicative marks regarding the atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) can be interpreted otherwise, why should the soul not possess inherent omnipresence? And if that were so, its atomicity would not be established.
The proponent [of the Siddhānta], having restated the objection of the opponent, refutes it with the words "And not...

and so forth, citing the passage "as he departs... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2). Even though this Śruti mentions the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) prior to the departure of the individual soul (*jīva*), the departure of the soul alone is not thereby established. This is because of the intellect (*buddhi*).

It should not be argued that [the soul] departs because it is distinct [from the intellect], for the distinction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is unestablished; rather, their non-distinction is established by scripture.
Thus says the Śruti: "That which is the vital breath is indeed wisdom, and that which is wisdom is the vital breath."
With the intention that [the soul] is of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), he says: "The one called *prāṇa* [is the soul], because of its departure.
Even after the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) designated by the terms "name and form," the soul's return to Brahman is heard in scripture.
And thus, just as it is not possible for departure to be a means [to liberation], so too [is it not possible for the soul to be the agent of action].

With the intention that it is not possible for motion to be non-contingent upon an adjunct, and that therefore the soul (*jīva*)—which possesses a middling dimension—must be admitted to have inherent atomicity (*aṇutva*), he says: "Thus the knower... [and so on].
This is because the soul's being the substratum of motion is inherently impossible unless it is non-inherent [in its own nature] relative to the supreme Hiraṇyagarbha.
With the intention that otherwise the specific illustration would be inconsistent, he says:
"It is as follows" (*tadyathā*). In this context, an illustration for the soul’s departure toward the next world is stated:
a cart (*anaḥ*), well-stocked with household utensils and making a creaking sound while moving along, might depart.

The meaning is that just as [the chariot] moves, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), mounted upon and impelled by the Lord (*īśvara*), goes to the other world. Thus, once the inherent atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the soul is established,
the distinction between the soul and the Lord is proven by their respective states of atomicity and omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

The proponent [of the view] refutes this, saying: "This is not sound. With the intention that just as the omnipresence of the Supreme Self heard in the context of the Paramātman cannot be interpreted otherwise, so too the omnipresence of the individual soul (jīva) heard in the context of the Jīva cannot be interpreted otherwise, [the text begins with] "Which is the Self? and so forth.

He cites a statement occurring in the section concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), beginning with "That indeed," etc.; the meaning is that because the scripture declares the pervasiveness of the soul—stating that the soul, which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), is the "Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*)—it is pervasive. By the phrase "like the sky," the inherent omnipresence (*vibhutva*) of the soul is expressed; this scriptural passage has already been explained previously.

In your view, since only *prakṛti* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, Brahman lacks the status of being the material cause of the world. Furthermore, even if the individual soul (*jīva*) were atomic (*aṇu*), it could still be the material cause of the world—just as it is the material cause of the pleasure and pain experienced by multiple bodies in a *kāyavyūha* (multiplication of bodies). Consequently, its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) is not established. [This leads to] its entry...

For, if one were to assume that the Śrutis [teaching the soul's size] refer to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body, it would be possible to likewise accept that the Śrutis concerning the soul's departure (utkrānti) and so forth refer to the limiting adjunct of the intellect (buddhi); this is because the Sūtra-bhāṣya on the passage "It has five functions like the mind" establishes the difference in the effects of the intellect and the prāṇas.

When the individual soul (*jīva*), which has the intellect as its limiting adjunct, first departs, it is logical that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows after; for there is no contradiction in the scriptural teaching of the attainment of Brahman— following the liberation from name and form— occurring with respect to the Brahman to be attained, just as it does with respect to the attaining soul, since [Brahman's] omnipresence is not compromised.
Immediately after liberation from ordinary name and form,
in the view of those who maintain that Brahman is to be attained through the assumption of adjuncts such as a non-material body and so forth,
there exists for the attaining individual soul (*jīva*) as well a non-material body, sense organs, and so on; by means of that [non-material] adjunct, [the soul attains Brahman].

Because there is no contradiction with the scriptural teaching on the attainment of Brahman; for, while the soul's natural motion might be established merely by hearing the analogy of the cart as the basis for such motion,
[the case here is different] due to the mention of the soul in conjunction with its natural entry, in the phrase "the two who have entered the cave."
Since it is possible for even Brahman to possess an innate capacity for entry [into the body],

he refutes the mutual evidence of omnipresence cited by the other [party] after stating that such scriptural claims are otherwise established through [Brahman’s] all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*). He does so with the words "In his view," meaning that *prakṛti* (primordial matter) is *māyā* belonging to the Supreme Brahman.

He says that even by accepting its status as the material cause of all phenomenal manifestation (*sarvaprapañcopādānatva*), that does not prove its omnipresence; this is expressed by the words "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*).

The word "atomic" (*aṇoḥ*) is to be supplied [to *jīvasya*]. Therefore, the meaning is: "because of its being the material cause of everything. He further states that the interpretation of the scriptural texts and indicative marks regarding the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīvāṇutva*) is likewise equal [in force] by saying "its entry" (*tatpraveśa*).

Regarding the word "śruti": it means "entry into Brahman. That primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) which possesses five functions characterized as prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, is designated as "pañcavṛtti-prāṇa" in the scriptures. And the illustration "like the mind" is given merely on account of its possessing multiple functions.
It should be understood that the functions of the prāṇa, apāna, and so forth, as well as exhalation (ucchvāsa) and the like, constitute a single effect.

Thus, by way of the relationship between the illustrative example and the subject illustrated, the distinction between the intellect (buddhi)—denoted here by the term "mind" (manas)—and the vital breath (prāṇa) is specified in the Sūtra. Furthermore, this [distinction] pertains to the objects of the functions of the cognitive faculties (buddhīndriya), in relation to the eyes.

The meaning is that it has been established in the Bhāṣya by such means as the observation of effects in the form of activities such as inhalation and exhalation—which are distinct from [the self]—that the vital breath (prāṇa) is different from the intellect (buddhi) and so forth. This is despite the fact that in the scriptural text "That which is prāṇa is indeed prajñā," there appears to be a non-difference between prajñā and prāṇa; [however, this refers only to] that which is conditioned by prajñā and prāṇa.

The sense is that there is no contradiction with scripture, because it has been established in the *Pratardana-adhikaraṇa-bhāṣya* that, since the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is one, the identification of those two [the individual soul and Brahman] as primary with respect to the conditioned self (*upahita*) is not contradictory. As for the scriptural statement regarding the individual soul’s return to Brahman after the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of name and form— that refers to the soul...

The claim that [the soul's movement] is opposed to omnipresence is incorrect; for since that [movement] would also be opposed to the omnipresence of Brahman, it would follow as an absurd consequence that Brahman itself could not be established. He says, "Name and form," because in the world one observes a rule that only that which is limited can be a destination. Now, in the opponent's view, Brahman, being all-pervasive by its very nature, cannot be the object to be reached by the liberated.

However, one might object that being "to be attained" (prāptavyatva) occurs through a conditioned form—being delimited by specific worlds and so forth—and not by the very nature of Brahman itself, because its nature as all-pervasive has been understood. Anticipating this, he says that the same applies to the individual soul (jīva) in your own view:
"In the scripture [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1], 'The knower is freed from name and form,' it is said to be freed from *prakṛta* (material) name and form."

By postulating this meaning, you— by accepting that even the conscious individual soul (jīva) possesses non-material name and form— demonstrate that although the jīva is inherently all-pervading, its capacity to reach Brahman is possible when it is delimited by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of non-material name and form; therefore, the scriptural texts concerning its all-pervasiveness need not be interpreted as referring to the jīva.
This is the meaning.
The term "entry" (praveśa) must be explained as having a single uniform sense— namely, that it pertains to both Brahman and the individual soul (jīva). Consequently, according to the opponent's view,

since the established distinction between the all-pervasiveness of Brahman and the atomicity of the jīva cannot be maintained, no proof for their difference can be established from any source whatsoever.

In our view, there is hope because subordinate statements must be interpreted in accordance with the Great Mahāvākya concerning the non-duality of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmaikya*); thus, the soul (*jīva*) is omnipresent in its essential nature (*svarūpa*), while its limitation is due to its conditioned form (*aupādhika-rūpa*), and so forth. Regarding the soul...
The reconciliation of the scriptural texts regarding the non-difference of Brahman is clearly established in the Bhāṣya and other works.

Therefore, because the insentient phenomenal world (prapañca) is illusory and because the sentient phenomenal world is non-different from Brahman, the Vedāntas have as their sole object of knowledge the non-dual Brahman, which is the one thing to be attained.
"There is no contradiction whatsoever with the doctrine of samanvaya.
[Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha*. || 2 ||
Now, one might object that in the phrase "the two have entered," the word "entered" (praviṣṭa) signifies an inherent entry in the case of the individual soul (jīva), whereas in the case of Brahman,

it signifies an entry effected by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body; however, if that were so, there would be a contradiction regarding the meaning of the word "entered," which is heard only once [in the text].

Thinking that this would lead to the consequence of a lack of uniformity (*vairūpya*), he says: "Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, if—on the basis of scriptural authority and other means—it is assumed that the word "entered" refers merely to the act of entering by virtue of Brahman's omnipresence, then surely it must also refer to the specific qualities residing therein; for the same applies to the individual soul (*jīva*) in accordance with the scriptural texts concerning its omnipresence.

In the illustration of the cart, it is intended merely that there is a similarity regarding movement and so forth, but not that [the soul] possesses inherent motion or the like as its substratum; thus, the inherent atomicity of the individual soul (jīva) is not established. Or, if that were established for it, the atomicity of Brahman would also be unavoidable due to a lack of a determining factor (vinigamanāviraha); this is the sense. "Therefore" refers to what has been stated.

The meaning is "because of the established distinction. Now, an objection: since, according to the opponent's view, there is no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) regarding the scriptural texts and indicative marks (*liṅga*) concerning their all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) and atomicity (*aṇutva*), and since there is likewise no difference in the way the scriptural texts and indicative marks for the atomicity of both could be otherwise explained, then either the atomicity or the all-pervasiveness of both would be established by those very [texts] equally, rather than belonging to one alone.

Just as the fault would arise that the established distinction between the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the other [the Supreme Self] and the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the other [the individual soul] would be undermined, so too,
even when [the soul's nature] is established, because there is no difference between the scriptural texts and indicative marks regarding the soul's limitedness and its all-pervasiveness,
the distinction that its all-pervasiveness is innate while its limitedness is adventitious (*aupādhika*) would not be established.

The objection [that this] follows as a logical consequence is not so; he says, "In our view. Since the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self is the means to liberation, the sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), which generate that [knowledge], are the Great Sentences (*mahāvākya*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of the meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* serves as the cause for the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence.

The intermediate sentences (*avāntaravākya*)— namely, those statements that establish the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) and those that establish the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*)— serve as counter-evidences;
because they are supplementary to the great sentence (*mahāvākya*), they relate to the meaning of the words.

The phrase "of the subordinate sentences" means that subordinate sentences must be interpreted in accordance with the principal sentence. Regarding the term "in its own nature": if the individual soul (*jīva*) were atomic by its very nature, the non-difference from Brahman—which is not taught by the Great Sentences (*mahāvākya*)—would be untenable; and [the same would apply] to Brahman in its own nature.

The sense is that in the absence of fullness, there would be contradictions with such qualities as being "one who has heard much" (*bahuśrutya*) and so forth. He concludes the meaning of this chapter, which consists of the establishment of the non-contradiction of the Vedānta concordance regarding the non-dual Brahman, with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He explains the two locative endings (*pañcamyanta*) by means of the two ablative endings (*pañcamībhyām*), beginning with "of the insentient" (*acetanasya*). Thus.

Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgrahavyākhyā* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Essence of the Tenets of the Scriptures), composed by Acyuta Kṛṣṇānanda Tīrtha, who has become like the dust clinging to the divine lotus feet of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya, Śrī Svayaṃprakāśānanda Sarasvatī. || 2 ||
Oṃ, salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now, what is this liberation while living (jīvanmukti), which occurs through the persistence of a trace of ignorance (avidyā-leśa)?
It is the state [attained] when the root ignorance (mūlāvidyā)—which possesses the powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa)—is [rendered inactive] by means of prārabdha-karma.

Some maintain that the portion consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*) is the cause for the persistence of the present body and so forth; others hold that the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance is comparable to the lingering scent of garlic in a washed pot;
while still others assert that it is simply the root ignorance itself persisting according to the analogy of a cloth.
But for those whose teacher is the Omniscient One (Sarvajña), since even a trace of the persistence of ignorance is impossible upon the arising of direct realization, [the two are] contradictory.
Oṃ, salutation to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ! I go for refuge to Hari, the unborn and eternal, by remembering whom a person does not fail to become a vessel for all auspiciousness.
When that Hari is remembered— meaning, when He is kept in mind— may He,
who wanders very slowly while leaning on Nanda’s hand with His own hand, His eyes slightly opened, and the sound of His golden tinkling bells continuous, bestow auspiciousness upon my body.
May that Bhāratī, by the mere remembrance of whom the power of speech unfolds, dwell for a long time and eternally within my mouth.
By the mere remembrance of Him who is named Śiva and of that Goddess who is the source of all auspiciousness, men attain victory and prosperity in every respect.
O Lord of Obstacles, saluted by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Sun, the Moon, Indra, and Upendra; salutations to you, O Gaṇapati, the Brahman of the Brahmas, O Lord of the Veda!
Now, regarding "Then [the section] on Liberation":

in the third chapter, the means to liberation, which consists of the knowledge of Brahman, along with its auxiliary factors, was described; now, liberation, which is the fruit thereof, is being described. And thus:

In the investigation of the fruit for the other [type of aspirant], it is stated in the fourth [chapter] that the word "tat" (that) in the *smṛti* refers to Brahman; the remainder of the sense is that this is according to such scriptural passages as, "By that [path] goes the knower of Brahman and the doer of merit. Thus, by the combination of both knowledge of Brahman and merit, one goes—that is, one attains—Brahman.
The meaning of the scripture is as follows: [the author] approves of the scriptural statement that the combination of knowledge and action is the cause for attaining Brahman, saying "True.
This is supported by another scriptural passage which establishes that the attainment of Brahman is accomplished through knowledge alone, together with reasoning.

With the intention that, because of the contradiction, the scriptural mention of their combination and the Smṛti statements based upon it must be interpreted as referring to a sequential combination rather than a simultaneous one, he says: "There is no other path. In relation to the knowledge of Brahman, "another" refers to a path—meaning a means—consisting either of the combination of knowledge and action or of action alone.

The meaning of the Śruti is that liberation exists for those intent upon it. The attainment of Brahman—which is eternally established as the very nature of the Self—is of the nature of the cessation of errors such as the delusion of non-attainment; and the cessation of such errors is seen in the world to be achievable through knowledge alone, just as [the discovery of] a necklace already around one's neck.

When the golden garland has been forgotten, for one who undergoes various distractions due to the delusion that it has not been obtained, the attainment of the previously established golden garland— consisting in the cessation of the delusion of non-attainment through mere knowledge produced by the instruction of a reliable authority— occurs.

The meaning is that since the attainment of Brahman—which is eternally established and identical to that [Self]—does not require any means other than knowledge (*vidyā*), and since [karma] lacks the capacity to remove error (*bhrama*) and the like other than that [knowledge], [karma is useless for liberation]. He asks, "Then where [is its use]? in order to elaborate upon the utility of actions (*karman*) for liberation through an indirect sequence (*paraṃparayā*). "Then... [he says].

The meaning is that, since they lack the status of being direct causes of liberation like knowledge (*jñāna*), their function is to serve as means toward some form of inquiry or knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the phrase "that very" (*tam etam*): the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the previously mentioned Supreme Self (*paramātman*), while the word "this" (*etat*) refers to the eternally immediate individual self (*jīva*). Thus, [it refers to] the Supreme Self who is non-different from the individual self.
The meaning is that they desire to know [Brahman] through the recitation of the Vedas and so forth.

To exclude asceticism characterized by fasting and the like, the qualification "by non-fasting" (*anāśakena*) is used for *tapas*. Thus, it is understood that what is intended here is asceticism in the form of eating what is beneficial, moderate, and pure. But [one might object]:

To the question, "How can there be an application [of ritual action] to *vividiṣā* (the desire to know), which is not itself a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*)?", he replies: "By means of the accomplishment of knowledge. Thus, the meaning is that its status as a secondary human goal (*gauṇapuruṣārthatva*) is possible. Now, since it is proximate to liberation, [one might ask] regarding that very knowledge...

Why is *viniyoga* (application) not postulated? And since there is no difference in their being directly stated (*śrutatva*), one might think that because heaven and so forth—stated as the objects of desire—are accepted elsewhere as the fruits of action, [the same applies here]; thus, having considered this, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). In sentences such as "one desiring heaven," once the sacrifice and so forth are understood to be means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhana*) by means of the injunctive suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), what [is there to object to]?
Therefore, it is desired as a qualification.
It would not [be so]. Because the meaning of the suffix is primary; because of its association with knowledge (*vidyā*);

because the means to knowledge, such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*), are proximate, whereas sacrifices and the like are more remote due to their association with the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); and also because of the commentary on the section concerning the dependence on all [works] (*sarvāpekṣādhikaraṇa*). But [an objection may be raised]: "Is it not so..."

For one who performs sacrifices and other rites for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), since that desire to know would already be established once there is a longing for the object of knowledge, it is impossible for there to be a desire for the desire to know itself as a means to knowledge in its absence; thus, the performance of sacrifices and other rites for the sake of the desire to know is not tenable. Nor [is it tenable] for sacrifices and the like...

If it is argued that its application (*viniyoga*) is appropriate for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), we say no; for instance, when one has become emaciated through aversion to food, even though there exists a longing characterized by a yearning for the object of food in order to remedy that condition, [the result does not follow] due to factors such as restlessness or indigestion.

However, because of the fault of inequality when applied [in that way], a lack of relish for the practice does not arise until its completion; therefore, it is like a medicine prescribed to induce an appetite.

When there is a desire [to know], since neither of the two— desire nor heaven— which are heard as qualifiers of the person, possesses verbal predominance, one must necessarily resort to that which possesses predominance by implication; and between these, it is heaven alone that is so, because it is inherently a human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

In other cases, the sacrifice is accepted as being construed as the means to the fruit—namely, "the sacrifice is the means to heaven"—but not so for the desire for knowledge. However, in this case, it is appropriate that the desire for knowledge itself be construed as the fruit, because it is the primary element according to the word;
therefore, considering that proximity to the fruit and such factors are irrelevant here, he provides the resolution: "It would not be [the case]."

He cites the consensus of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the point that the meaning of the word "condition" (*pratyaya*) is "a true condition," and that its application is specifically to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*). [The phrase] "due to connection with knowledge" means "because they are the means to knowledge.
[The phrase] "proximate" means "to be practiced until the arising of knowledge. [This constitutes] the distinction from tranquility (*śama*) and the other [internal disciplines].

It demonstrates the nature of karma by stating, "because of its connection with the desire to know" (*vividiṣā-saṃprayogāt*). The meaning is: "precisely because it is a means to that [desire]. The phrase "until the rise of the desire to know" (*vividiṣodaya-paryantam*) means that these [rites] are to be performed only up to the point when the desire to know arises. This refers to the section (*adhikaraṇa*) which establishes that all ritual actions are required for the arising of knowledge (*vidyotpatti*).
He raises an objection against the application [of sacrifices] to the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) by another method, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).

If the desire for knowledge were the fruit of sacrifice and so forth, then the performance of sacrifice and so forth would have to be said to be prompted by a desire for the object of that desire for knowledge; and since the desire for knowledge itself lacks intrinsic fruitfulness, it must [lead to its fruit] through the mediation of knowledge (*vedana*).
Or rather, it must be stated that liberation is the fruit [of knowledge]. And thus the sequence is as follows:

first, from the knowledge that liberation is an end in itself (*puruṣārtha*), there arises a desire for liberation; then, from the knowledge that knowledge is the means to liberation, there arises a desire for knowledge; then, from the knowledge that [the sacrifice] is the means to that desire for knowledge, there arises a desire for [the performance of] knowledge; and by means of that [desire], there is the performance of sacrifices and other rites.

And likewise, for one who is engaged in the performance of sacrifices and other rites with the desire to know (*vividipā*)—which consists of the desire for knowledge—as the objective, does that desire for knowledge exist as a fruit when the result is the knowledge of Brahman, or not? If the former, then the performance of sacrifices would be useless; having this in mind, he says: "In the sphere of knowledge," etc.

The sense is that the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) is indeed nothing other than the longing for the sphere of feeling (*vedanā*). The connection [of the argument] is that, since [knowledge] is already established, it is impossible to perform sacrifices and other rites for the sake of desiring knowledge.
