It is not the second [alternative], because if there were no desire for the result—namely, knowledge—there would likewise be no desire for the desire-for-knowledge itself; therefore, [the rites cannot be performed] with the desire-for-knowledge as their objective.

He states that there is no possibility of performing sacrifices and so forth [once knowledge has arisen], saying: "In the absence of that. This means that when the desire for knowledge has ceased, there is an absence of the desire directed toward knowledge. For one who performs sacrifices and so forth for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), the desire for knowledge certainly exists; however, this much alone does not constitute the performance of those [sacrifices].

The desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is not rendered useless, because it admits of two types. For the desire to know consists of two kinds: that characterized by an inclination toward knowledge (*vidyā*), and that characterized by a taste for it (*ruci*). Of these, the former exists even prior to the performance of sacrifices and the like, and even while one is still seeking knowledge; therefore, taking that [first type] into account...

Since desire arises with regard to the longing for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) which serves as the means to [attain] direct realization (*vedanā*), it is logical that the performance of sacrifices and other rites is for the sake of that longing; however, since the second [type of desire] has sacrifice and the like as its fruit and occurs immediately after their performance, the application of sacrifice and the like to the longing for knowledge is indeed appropriate.
Intending to provide a clarification, he says: "No.
Regarding the desire for knowledge, he provides an illustration in the context of the performance of sacrifices and so forth, stating: "By means of aversion to food.
This refers to the intense desire for the consumption of food directed toward the avoidance of emaciation, which serves to prevent that [aversion].
The meaning is "even when there is truth.

The word "utsakā" means "excessive. The word "ādi" (and so forth) is used for the purpose of including things such as extreme fasting, which cause an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). "Therein" means "in the eating of food. "It is not born" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that this is established by direct experience.

In the sense that Brahman is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss and that knowledge is the means for its attainment— for a person who possesses faith acquired through the power of the purification of the mind, earned by performing obligatory and occasional rites throughout many previous births without desire for their fruits—

Even though there exists a longing characterized by intense yearning for the attainment of Brahman and for knowledge, the inclination of a theistic seeker who is nonetheless a lustful man— due to the defect of numerous sins accumulated through beginningless existence— is directed toward the enjoyment of sense objects, just as it is toward actions that ought to be abandoned.

Because an inclination reaching as far as engagement in the means of knowledge, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), does not arise due to obstacles, it is logical to enjoin sacrifices and other rites that accomplish those means after first removing such obstacles. However, those who follow the *Vivaraṇa* say: [regarding] the meanings of the root and the suffix...
The meaning of the suffix is primary, according to the general rule.
It is incorrect to say that a person who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*)— a *brāhmaṇa*—
having understood through the Upanishads (*vedāntaiḥ*) that knowledge consists of the nature of unsurpassed bliss and that it is the means for attaining that [bliss],
would thereby possess perfect conviction regarding that matter; for even among those of such a kind...

Anticipating the objection that "in many men, there is no observation of the attainment of faith regarding that [highest] goal," he says: "In former [lives]," etc. This refers to those obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites performed in many previous births, which were devoid of desire for fruits.

The meaning is: "by the greatness of that specific purity" (*śuddhiviśeṣa*), which has been produced and accumulated by them. And so says the *Smṛti*: "Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection. The word "scarcely one" (*kaścit*) means one who possesses the aforementioned clarity of mind (*cita-prasāda*). The sense is that not everyone strives for perfection—that is, for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā-lābha*). Now, [an objection]:

Even when there exists an intense desire for the attainment of Brahman and for the knowledge that is its means, one might not find a taste for hearing about those means and so forth that culminates in actual engagement; thus, it was argued that such a person has no need for the performance of sacrifices and other rites. To this, he replies: "Anādi" (beginningless). Due to the obstruction caused by the defect of past demerit (*durita*), taste does not arise.

The connection is with the word "is born" (*jāyate*). Now, one might object: "How can it be possible for even the most devout believer—who has attained conviction regarding the knowledge of Brahman and so forth through the power of the previously mentioned clarity of consciousness—to have an inclination toward the enjoyment of sense-objects, which abound in misfortune? Anticipating this doubt, he makes its possibility conceivable by means of an example established by experience. [He says: "O believer... (*āstika*)...
Regarding the phrase "of the lustful one": from the performance of prescribed duties, prosperity necessarily arises;

and from the commission of prohibited acts, great misfortune necessarily follows. This is the certainty based on the authority of the scriptures. Or, even for an atheist, there may arise in someone an excess of passion for forbidden sexual intercourse and the like.

The meaning is that just as a tendency toward evil arises from specific sins, so too does it arise for one seeking liberation (umukṣu), as previously stated. Regarding "obstruction" (pratibandha): the meaning is an obstruction caused by the defects of numerous misdeeds accumulated throughout beginningless existence. Regarding "that which brings it about" (tatsaṃpādaka): [this refers to] hearing and so forth, which are designated as the desire to know (vividiṣā).

The meaning is that [the text] expresses a lack of satisfaction with the culmination in worldly activity (*pravṛtti*) and brings about that [lack of satisfaction]. To the question, "In what case, then, is there utility for ritual actions?

he introduces another response: "In knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the word "explanation" (*vivaraṇa*), previously, sacrifices and so forth were understood through the force of the instrumental case-ending as being means [to knowledge].

When there is an expectancy for an object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) itself that connects as the thing to be accomplished; for that [desire] is primary according to the word, and it is a rule of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) that in all cases, such as "bring the king's servant" or "wash his feet," it is only the word-meaning that is primary according to the word that connects with other co-uttered word-meanings.

With the intention that [the means] are already established, it was stated that sacrifices and so forth are enjoined for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). Showing the lack of satisfaction with that view, he establishes their application to knowledge (*vidyā*) itself by stating: "In the base... That is to say, between the meanings of the verbal root and the suffix—the knowledge and the desire for it—it is the meaning of the suffix, the desire to know, [that is primary].

Because the suffix (*pratyaya*) denotes the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it possesses primacy in terms of the word (*śabda*). Consequently, the general logical principle well-known from examples such as "bring the king’s man"— wherein that which is primary according to the word is indeed what is connected [as the object]— serves as the reason for the fact that only the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is construed as the fruit of sacrifice and the other duties.
The meaning is as follows: [the connection] consists in the relation between the action and its factors (kāraka) as expressed together [in the sentence].

Therefore, when there is an expectancy for a specific desired object regarding a sacrifice and so forth—which is understood through the injunctive suffix (vidhipratyaya) as being a means to what is desired—the connection of heaven as the fruit is established, even though it lacks grammatical predominance (prādhānya).
This is the meaning.

Since the connection with being a means for a verbal cognition occurs only when something is understood through words as the object of a desire, the established principle of specific [grammatical] rules in sentences such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is more powerful; thus, in common usage such as "he wishes to go by horse" (*aśvena jigamiṣati*) or "he wishes to strike with a sword" (*asinājighāṃsati*), the means consisting of the horse and so forth [is connected as such].

In such Vedic usages as "That is to be sought," "That indeed is to be desired to be known," and "That is to be meditated upon," because the suffix *tavya* denotes an injunction (*vidhi*), and because it is a matter of linguistic convention that the connection of the object of desire— expressed by the desiderative suffix *san*— is understood only with respect to an action such as going, and not with respect to knowledge which is expressed by the verbal root itself; [knowledge] remains the object of the injunction.

[This concerns] the application of sacrifices and other rites. [Objection: But if that were so, since the performance of ritual action would follow as long as knowledge has not arisen, the status of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—which consists in the abandonment of action established by such scriptural passages as "one who abandons [action]" and "the ploughing of what is beneficial"—as being for the sake of knowledge would be undermined.

If it is argued that ploughing is not performed before the seed exists, or that there is no ploughing after [the seed has been sown], and thus the production of rice and other crops does not occur through two acts of ploughing—[we reply: for the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the cause;
for him who has ascended to yoga, tranquility (śama) is the cause.

In accordance with such statements as "The cause is being declared," it is understood that knowledge is accomplished through both the performance of action and its renunciation; for one performs action until the arising of an inward inclination toward direct realization, such as the desire to know (vividiṣā), which results from the purification of the mind, and thereafter follows renunciation.

To the question—"Since there is no difference in the absence of verbal primacy, why is it not assumed that the desire itself is construed as the fruit (phala)?"—he says: "Because of being the object of desire. This means that since being the object of desire is what indicates the status of being a fruit, it is heaven (*svarga*), which is perceived as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), that is the fruit, and not the desire. Now, [an objection]:...

Since being the object of desire is common to liberation as well, why should that [liberation] itself not be postulated as the fruit of sacrifices and the like? To this, he says: "That which is understood from the word. For, according to the maxim that "verbal expectancy is satisfied by a word alone," there is no over-extension [of the term]. Thus, when there is a co-occurrence with that which is desired (*iṣyamāṇa*), [the sacrifice becomes its means].

Since it has been established through the principle of specific exception (*viśeṣanyāya*)— namely, that in sentences connected with desire (*kāmopabandha*), the primacy belongs to the object desired and not to the desire itself— that the general rule (*sāmānyanyāya*) is set aside,
so too in the case of the phrase "desiring to know" (*vividiṣanti*), the primacy of the desire to know is not necessitated by its being the meaning of the suffix.

The meaning is that one should abandon the primacy of the word and instead attend to the primacy of the cognition itself. Even though desire (*icchā*) is the primary meaning of the suffix when it occurs in conjunction with verbal roots in both worldly and Vedic usage, one must transcend that desire and [attend] only to its objects.
And he says "because we see the connection with other word-meanings expressed in proximity," using the example "with a horse.

"That is to be sought" means that Brahman, known as the ether of that day, is to be investigated. "It is to be desired to be known" means that very Brahman is to be meditated upon. "It is to be intensely contemplated."

The meaning is that the Self is to be meditated upon. Now, if it is argued that in the cited examples the desire [for knowledge] is abandoned because it cannot logically connect with the means such as horses, then in the present case as well, since the desire for the knowledge of Brahman cannot logically connect with those [means], and since the knowledge of Brahman...

The sense is that since [knowledge] is capable of being connected as a fruit by way of being the direct realization of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda-sākṣātkāra*), the connection with sacrifices and other rites belongs to *vidyā* (knowledge) itself, not to the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); thus, the position is equal. He raises an objection regarding the application of the rites to knowledge (*vidyā-viniyoga-pakṣa*) by saying "But not... [referring to the fact that] the seeker of liberation must abandon ritual actions. Of one who abandons them...

The meaning of the scripture is that one’s own inner self-nature, which is the state of Brahman, is to be directly realized, and not abandoned. Furthermore, by another scriptural passage beginning with "Then [he becomes] a wandering mendicant" and ending with "he became fit for becoming Brahman," it is shown that the renunciation denoted by the word *parivrāj* leads to what is termed "becoming Brahman."

It has been stated that [renunciation] is the cause for the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*). One should understand the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) with the intention that this is likewise found in other Vedic texts. He demonstrates, along with an illustration and authoritative evidence, that there is no contradiction between the statement regarding the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*) and the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-vidhi*), by saying "not before" (*na prāk*). In that statement, there are two words denoting the cause.

It should be understood that the explanation of the word *yoga* in this statement from the Gītā refers to tranquility (*śama*), renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), and the inward orientation toward the Self in the form of purity of mind, the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), and so forth— all of which relate to what is to be accomplished.

For it is said in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "Once the intellect has been directed toward the inward [Self], the ritual acts, having accomplished their purpose, set like clouds at the end of the rainy season. Even according to the view that ritual acts are for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), they serve only up to the point of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).
If it is asked, "What is the difference from the position that the performance of ritual action is for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)?"— the difference is this:

according to the position that actions are for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), even after the desire to know— which serves as the means— has been accomplished and has ceased, the actions continue until the attainment of the final fruit.
By obtaining a distinguished guru, one accomplishes the means for hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption— namely, the practices beginning with renunciation—
and there is a rule that this leads to the arising of knowledge. However, according to the view that [the sacrifice] has the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) as its purpose,
it serves merely to produce an intense longing capable of generating engagement in hearing and the other practices.

The phrase "having accomplished the purpose" does not necessarily imply a fixed rule regarding the production of knowledge; for according to the root text of the Smṛti stating, "for whom these forty-eight sacraments [exist]," the rites serve to remove impurities and bestow qualities that produce fitness for the knowledge of the Self.
They say it is like the position that [the word] has the purpose of expressing a characteristic (lakṣaṇa) or a refinement (saṃskāra).

Regarding the statement that the performance of ritual action continues until the arising of direct orientation toward the Self—characterized by the purity of consciousness consisting in the absence of passion and other defects, the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), dispassion, and devotion to the Guru, the Deity, and so forth—he cites the consensus of Sureśvarācārya, saying: "For it has been said... through purity. The meaning is: "by means of purity."
"They go to their setting" means they go to abandonment;
that is to say, they become things that must be relinquished because their purpose has been fulfilled. He provides an illustration for the cessation of those whose purpose has been fulfilled:
"at the end of the rainy season," meaning at the conclusion of the monsoon period. This refers to the view that [the knowledge of Brahman] is employed for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*).

There is no dispute that the performance of sacrifices and other rites continues until the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) arises; even under the view that they are employed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), one might object: "If this is so, what is the difference between the two? To this, he says: "Of the ritual acts" (*karmaṇām*). Although there is no difference in their performance, there is a difference in terms of their result; thus he says: "This is the difference. The meaning is: "as will be explained."

The phrase "ceased" (uparatau) means even upon their abandonment; the words "by way of the unseen potency" (adṛṣṭadvārā) are to be supplied as the remainder. For, according to the view that [sacrifices] are enjoined for the purpose of generating the desire to know (vividiṣā), the unseen potency produced by rites such as sacrifice perishes after having generated the inclination termed "desire to know," which culminates in the engagement in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; this is because the unseen potency is destroyed once its single fruit has been realized.

Immediately after the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), provided that there is an absence of the evil deeds (*durita*) which obstruct hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, one attains knowledge (*vidyā*) by accomplishing hearing and the rest through the power of that very desire to know alone. However, if the evil deeds obstructing hearing and the rest are present, then even if effort is made, one determines— due to the failure to obtain hearing and the rest— that they exist.

If one does not practice the means for its cessation, or if one fails to practice those means that would turn it away, or if there is an abundance of obstacles even when practicing them, then knowledge does not arise because hearing and the other [limbs of yoga] are impossible;
just as, despite the potency of a medicine, [the desired result] does not occur if there is no appetite for consuming it.
If he obtains food without obstruction, he attains the cessation of emaciation by eating it; but if he does not obtain it, he exerts himself to obtain it,
and even when effort is made, if he does not obtain it, then he attains the cessation of emaciation [through that very lack].

Intending to show that it is the same here as well, he says: "Not necessarily. He provides an illustration for the position that [the duties] are employed for the sake of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) by means of the position that actions are employed for the sake of purification (*saṃskāra*): "Of whom... That is to say, of whichever person these forty-eight purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), consisting of the duties prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti, exist.

And the perfection of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth also exists. For that qualified seeker of knowledge (*vidyādhikārī*) who has been refined by ritual actions (*karma*), the attainment of the Supreme Brahman occurs through the door of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) once there is the perfection of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
And in the absence of that [perfection], there is the attainment of meritorious worlds. Thus it is, according to the view that ritual actions serve as purifiers (*saṃskāraka*).
There is no fixed rule that it produces knowledge, since it merely generates a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

Now, with respect to which actions is this application by means of the Śruti intended to be understood? On this point, some have said: "By the recitation of the Vedas" refers to the duties of the student; "by sacrifice and by charity" refers to the duties of the householder; and "by austerity and fasting" [refers to the duties of the forest-dweller].

Since the duties of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) serve as an illustration, it follows that the application of knowledge pertains specifically to the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama*). For this very reason, in the *Śārīraka-sūtra* (Brahma-sūtra), the term "duties of the stage of life" (*āśrama-karma*) is employed in reference to those actions performed for the sake of knowledge; thus it is stated in the *Kalpataru*.
The application of knowledge is not restricted solely to those whose duty is defined by the stages of life (āśrama-dharma).

The meaning is that, since actions whose purpose has been fulfilled have no further operation until the arising of knowledge, the same applies even under the view that they serve the purpose of generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). The fitness for self-knowledge resides in the aggregate of causes and effects (the body), and it is the [actions] that bring about that [fitness].

The meaning is that, in the view that [the Vedas] have that [knowledge] as their purpose, the two purificatory acts (saṃskāra) are characterized by the removal of impurities and the instilling of virtues.

Although there is an equal lack of certainty regarding the arising of knowledge in both the view that ritual actions have the desire to know (vividiṣā) as their purpose and the view that they have purification as their purpose,
in the case of the view that they have the desire to know as their purpose, the arising of knowledge is the general rule, just as [the attainment of food is certain] when there is an intense hunger.

This is because a firm desire to know (*vividiṣā*), through every effort, is capable of bringing about the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*). However, in the view that [the rites] serve as purificatory acts (*saṃskāra*), even though the mere fitness for the knowledge of Brahman is established, since the desire to know itself is not certain, the arising of knowledge does not occur even as a general rule (*prāyikī*).

The sense is that even in the two views regarding the purpose of the *vividiṣā-saṃskāra*, the distinction must be inferred. Regarding the question "of which [acts]?"—the meaning is: is it only the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*), or is it others as well?
Now, one might object that even among all the duties of the stages of life, there is no mention of them in the *vividiṣā* passage.

Since it is not possible to apply all of those [means] there, he says: "By the recitation of the Veda" (*vedānuvacanena*). "Recitation of the Veda" (*vedānuvacana*) means the instruction following the word of the teacher, which is the study of the Veda;
and since that is the primary among the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), all those duties are thereby included.

This is the meaning. In the same way, primacy is to be understood in what follows as well. The intention is that here, by the conventional usage of the word "tapas" (austerity), asceticism in the form of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and so forth—which is common to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*)—is what appears. He who performs the action that must be done without depending on the fruit of the action.

In such Smṛti texts, it is established that whatever duty is to be performed by those in the permanent stages of life (*nityāśramin*), he who performs all that action having abandoned attachment to its fruits attains the state of Yoga previously mentioned— namely, the inward orientation consisting of the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) and the purification of the mind; therefore, [this is] the root of that [Yoga].

It should be understood that even in the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), it is appropriate for all duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) to be indicated; thus, he states the indicative mark from the Sūtra regarding the fact that the application belongs to the duties of the stages of life alone. "For this very reason" refers to the duties of the stages of life alone.

The meaning is: "precisely because of the acceptance of its application. Since the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karmāṇi*) have been enjoined for the sake of knowledge and so forth by the *vividiṣā* passage, there arises the doubt that an inhabitant of a stage of life who lacks the desire for such [knowledge] need not perform the duties prescribed for his own stage. In response to this, the Sūtra states: "Even by him, it must indeed be performed."

The meaning of the Sūtra should be understood as follows: because [the rite] has been provided for, otherwise there would be the consequence of sin (*pratyavāya*). He first shows that the position regarding "the application (*viniyoga*) of others as well" pertains specifically to obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) alone. Regarding the phrase "in the Kalpataru," the connection is: "it is stated in the Kalpataru. There exists [an application] even for those things distinct from the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*).

The claim that the application of knowledge (*vidyopayoga*) is according to the opinion of the author of the *Kalpataru* is incorrect; for it contradicts the Sūtra’s statement that there is no application [of knowledge] in the case of rites for specific purposes (*kāmyakarman*) or rites pertaining to the stages of life (*āśramakarman*).

Nor is there a contradiction [with the Sūtra], since the term "rites pertaining to the stages of life" (*āśramakarman*) in the Sūtra can appropriately be understood through a non-exclusive indication (*ajahallakṣaṇā*) to include even the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*).

Thus it should be stated. Anticipating the objection that there is no evidence for metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā) [in this case], he shows the determining factor therein: that the duties of the stages of life (āśrama-dharma) alone are not what serve the purpose of knowledge (vidyopayoga).

Furthermore, in the section beginning with "But even in the interval, because that is seen," it is established that even the actions performed by those such as the *vidhura* who are devoid of an *āśrama* are of use for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*). Nor is it the case that for those such as the *vidhura* who lack an *āśrama*, [knowledge arises] solely from sacrifices and other rites performed in previous births.
That section merely aims to define the qualification for those desiring to know (vividiṣā) regarding hearing and other means of attaining knowledge;
it does not, however, concern the utility of the rites performed by them for the sake of that knowledge.
It should not be suspected that this is intended as a definitive determination.

He states the reason for the emphatic particle *eva*—that even those duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) distinct from the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) have utility for knowledge—in the words: "And also in between... [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.5.1]. This addresses the question of whether there is eligibility for those not belonging to a stage of life (*anāśramin*) regarding external means to knowledge, such as ritual action, or regarding internal means, such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that when such doubt exists, there is no qualification [for knowledge], because the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-karman*) alone are enjoined for the sake of knowledge, and those [who lack them] are devoid of the duties of the stages of life; furthermore, qualification for hearing and so forth belongs only to one who is endowed with the fourfold means (*sādhana-catuṣṭaya*),
and for those not belonging to a stage of life, [the means] included within the fourfold means are absent.

In the absence of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which is denoted by the term *uparati*, there is no ownership of that [knowledge] because of the lack of its own master. However, in the sūtra, the word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The word "in between" (*antarā*) indicates the intermediate state between the stages of life, namely the state of being without an āśrama. And thus, even while existing in that state of not belonging to an āśrama—

A person is qualified for rites performed for the sake of knowledge, such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; why? Because it is observed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis that even those outside the stages of life (anāśramin), such as Raikva, Vācaknavī, and others, possess knowledge; and because, although the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) has the primary qualification for hearing and so forth, those outside the stages of life are likewise qualified, just like householders and others.
Because there is the possibility of a secondary qualification (*gauṇādhikāra*). And thus, in that very section, the Bhāṣya says: "And knowledge has a visible purpose;
it qualifies even one who merely desires [it] through the absence of a prohibition, because of the scriptural injunction to hear [it]. The cessation of ignorance is the visible fruit of knowledge.
The meaning of the Bhāṣya is that it accepts as qualified seekers those who desire direct realization—which removes ignorance—just as it does for a Śūdra;

for there is no prohibition against those outside the stages of life (anāśramins) regarding the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth. The word "mere" (mātra) is used because, in the case of a secondary qualification, there is no requirement for renunciation (saṃnyāsa). This is the sense of the commentary.

Furthermore, the section beginning with "And even in the interval" (antarā cāpi tu) is intended solely to establish the eligibility of those not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramin) for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth; it does not, however, establish that the duties of those not in a stage of life are also useful for knowledge. Thus, regarding the term "duties of the stages of life" (āśrama-karma) in the Sūtra:
Thinking that the status of being characterized by the duties of one's caste (*varṇadharma*) is not established [for them], he raises an objection: "And not for widowers and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that—since for those [widowers] there is an absence of ritual action aimed at knowledge (*vidyārthakarma*), the arising of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is impossible, and thus it is improper to define the qualification for hearing (*śravaṇa*) for those who do not belong to an order of life (*anāśramin*)—he says: "In a previous birth... and so on.

Furthermore, that particular section (adhikaraṇa) is intended to determine the qualification for hearing (śravaṇa) regarding those who, though not belonging to any stage of life (anāśramin), possess the desire to know (vividiṣā) generated by the performance of duties in a previous birth, yet have fallen from their primary eligibility due to the absence of the intense dispassion (vairāgya) that is the cause for renunciation; it does not concern all those who are merely outside the stages of life.

The meaning is: "precisely because it is impossible for those who do not desire to know [Brahman] to engage in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. This is to be connected with the phrase "and thus it is not to be doubted."

Furthermore, because it is explicitly stated in the sūtra and its commentary on that section (*tad-adhikaraṇa-sūtra* and *bhāṣya*)— namely, "and also the duties of the stages of life" (*āśrama-karma ca*)— that even those duties consisting solely of caste-specific practices such as recitation (*japa*), when performed by those [in the stages of life], are of use for knowledge (*vidyopayoga*). This is because the term "duties of the stages of life" (*āśrama-karma-pada*) in that sūtra refers to them.
Intending to show that the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) are also implied by this, it was stated:

"There is also a utility for knowledge (*vidyā*) even for those [duties] distinct from the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*). However, it is only for those that are obligatory (*nitya*) that their fruit—the destruction of evil (*duritakṣaya*)—depends upon knowledge."
The fruit of the optional rites is not heaven and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that in the sūtra "But even for those in between" (3.4.36), the fact that Raikva, Vācaknavī, Vidura, and others— who were not in any [formal] stage of life (āśrama)— are seen to possess knowledge in the Śruti and other texts was stated as the reason for the eligibility of widowers and others for the rites aimed at knowledge;
however, that is incorrect, because [the knowledge of] Raikva, Vācaknavī, Vidura, and the rest [was acquired] in another birth.

Since the doubt may arise that knowledge is produced solely by the power of performing the practice of the means of knowledge (*vidyāsādhanānuṣṭhāna*), the observation of those [householders] possessing knowledge regarding the utility of knowledge for the duties of those outside the stages of life (*anāśramikarma*) does not constitute a conclusive indicative mark (*liṅga*); therefore, because this is unsatisfactory, [the author provides] a non-alternative [proof].

This was stated with another established reason in mind: "And there is the favoring by specific qualities. By "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaiḥ*)—meaning specific attributes such as recitation (*japa*) and so forth, which pertain even to mere caste (*varṇa*) such as Brahminhood—there is a "favoring," that is, an assistance, to knowledge through the mediation of purification (*vitta-śuddhi*) and the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), just as there is assistance to knowledge through the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*).

How could it be possible? For there are such scriptural statements as: "A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; of this there is no doubt," and "By merely bathing in the Gaṅgā one is liberated; of this there is no doubt," and "By the mere remembrance of whom... and so forth. By these words, [the efficacy of] religious acts such as recitation (*japa*), bathing at sacred fords (*tīrtha-snāna*), and meditation on the deities is established.
The meaning of the sūtra is that [the sūtra] establishes that [these acts] are means for attaining knowledge (vidyā) by way of purification and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of those performed by them": the referent of the word "them" (tat) is those who do not belong to an āśrama.
Thus, even for those whose duties are not those of an āśrama, the utility for knowledge has been clearly stated by the author of the sūtras himself.

With the intention that, since [the status of the householder] has already been established, the term "duties of the stages of life" (*āśramakarma*) in the Sūtra must be understood as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the duties of the castes (*varṇadharma*) as well, so as not to contradict that, he says: "In the Sūtra.
Having thus described the intention of the authors of the *Kalpataru*, he establishes their view.

By the words "the duties of the stages of life" (*āśramadharma*) and so forth. Now, one might ask: when the application (*viniyoga*) of sacrifices and other rites is being postulated, is it postulated as common to both optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory rites, or only for the obligatory ones? It cannot be the first [option], because the fruits of optional acts, such as heaven and the like, are not required by knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, those [optional acts] could not serve as auxiliaries to knowledge.

Because it is possible [for them to be required]. Not the second [alternative], because there is no evidence that the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*)—even the destruction of evil (*duritakṣaya*)—requires knowledge (*vidyā*) as something to be accomplished by means of valid cognition; therefore, their application to knowledge (*vidyāviniyoga*) is untenable. He raises an objection: "But what [is the case]? He provides the resolution: "Only through the obligatory [rites] does knowledge arise in men from the destruction of sin."

The statement beginning with "of action" (*karmaṇaḥ*) indicates, by the word "for" (*hi*), that it serves as a scriptural authority for the fact that the destruction of evil (*duritakṣaya*), which is the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), is required by knowledge (*vidyā*). The intended meaning is that since even knowledge produced from valid means of cognition can be obstructed by evil, it is logical that there is a requirement for the destruction of evil.

He accepts that optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) do not assist in the attainment of knowledge. He says: "No. Nor should it be argued that optional rites, like obligatory ones (*nityakarman*), may also have the destruction of evil (*duritakṣaya*) as their fruit; and thus, it is possible for them too to produce the assistance characterized by the destruction of evil required for knowledge. For those [optional rites]...
The sense is that, since there is no evidence for their having the destruction of evil as their fruit, it has not been established that they assist knowledge (*vidyā*). In this regard,

just as when there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the subsidiaries whose assistance is already established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), one does not postulate an assistance in addition to that which assists the archetype, so too it is with those [subsidiaries] enjoined for the sake of knowledge.

In the *Saṃkṣepaśārīraka*, it is stated that there is no basis for postulating an auxiliary benefit common to both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites— such as sacrifices— that exceeds the destruction of sin, which is the established constant fruit of such rites.

However, the application of both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites has been stated because there is no distinction in the use of terms such as "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and so forth. It is not the case that the connection of ritual elements (*padārtha*), whose auxiliary functions are established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), with the modified forms (*vikṛti*) occurs through extension (*atideśa*) by way of merely extending those established archetypal auxiliaries.
However, since the assumption of an auxiliary function occurs only after the transfer (*atideśa*) of the constituent elements (*padārtha*),

there is no possibility here of assuming an auxiliary function that exceeds the original (*prākṛta*) one. But in this case, for sacrifices and the like which have been first enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*)— just as if they were explicitly taught— subsequently...

Why should an auxiliary function, though not explicitly prescribed, not be postulated for the sake of fulfilling the application understood from the initial [textual] statement— a function common to all obligatory and optional rites alike, as conveyed by the general term?

Regarding the application of ritual acts (*karma*) to knowledge (*vidyā*), he provides an illustration for the fact that the injunction is fulfilled by the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) alone, which provide the requisite assistance; this is expressed in the phrase "In that case, just as... Alternatively, even though the destruction of sin as the fruit of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) is not established from any other source, there is still the application of sacrifices and so forth [to knowledge].

"Let that [assistance] be postulated for them by force alone"—to this he says "no," meaning "therein. This means that since the assistance required by knowledge (*vidyā*) is already established through optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), there is no need for further assumption. He says "not obligatory" (*na nityam*); the sense is that it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, he refutes the position that there is an application of even those duties distinct from the duties of the stages of life (*āśramakarman*).

He shows that [the injunctions] are common to both optional and obligatory rites: "In brief, because there is no distinction. This is because words such as *yajña* (sacrifice) and so forth are equally established (*rūḍha*) in reference to obligatory sacrifices and optional sacrifices alike; therefore, just as with the obligatory ones, there is an application (*viniyoga*) of the same for the optional ones as well.
The meaning is that, having heard [the term] "it shines," the assistance of the ritual acts is postulated as being common to them alone.

Thinking that it is not possible to postulate an assistance suitable for knowledge (vidyā) by way of its being common to optional rites (kāmya), because such a postulation would contradict the logic of the *Pūrvatantra*, the subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) prescribed for the modifications (*vikṛti*) [are applied].

He states that those examples cited in the *Kalpataru* as illustrations are not suitable for being cited as illustrations for sacrifices and the like: "In the archetype" (*prakṛtau*). This means that in the archetypal sacrifices such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, there is a well-established auxiliary benefit (*upakāra*) of the ritual elements; first, there is the extension (*atideśa*) of that [benefit].

By way of following upon that [sublation], there is an extension (*atideśa*) of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) into the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), such as the *saurya* animal sacrifice; however, it is not the case that the utility (*upakāra*) of those elements is postulated there after their application (*viniyoga*) into the modifications through extension from the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*). Thus, it is not so in that case.
The meaning is that there is an attachment to another benefit by abandoning a benefit whose utility has already been established. This is what is being said:

in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*), the determination of the benefit occurs after the application (*viniyoga*) of the sacrifice and other elements; however, in the case of extended application (*atideśa*), the application of the archetypal elements to the modified forms (*vikṛti*) occurs after the benefit has been established and the determination of that benefit has taken place.
Therefore, [the opponent claims] the example is dissimilar. To this, [the author replies]: "But here... This means that the point of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*) is being addressed.

He states an example consistent with the subject at hand: "Of those things taught... That is to say, regarding the ritual items heard in the contexts of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and elsewhere, [their application] to the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* and so forth is determined by direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), and other such criteria.

Just as for those things already enjoined, a visible or invisible benefit (upakāra) is postulated as appropriate to fulfill the injunction first understood, so too must a benefit be postulated even when it has not yet arisen;
however, it is not proper to abandon the injunction first understood, for that would constitute a sublation of the Vedic revelation which makes no distinction regarding sacrifices and the like.

The meaning is "by way of incidental connection" (prasaṅgāt). Regarding the phrase "the word for the general": it means the word "sacrifice" (yajña) and so forth, which is common to both obligatory and optional rites.

For even by those who are not Mīmāṃsakas, in the case of sacrificial rites (*adhvara*), it is established that the application of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) occurs first by way of their mutual assistance;

and as for the restriction regarding the specific assistance rendered, if one were to postulate the assistance only after the application of the constituent elements has already taken place, then even an unestablished assistance must be postulated as being consistent with the constituent elements already enjoined.

Having thus established the point, for the sake of proving the commencement of the definition of *vādha* (annulment), it was demonstrated in the first section of the tenth book (*Daśamādhyāya*) that the application of archetypal elements (*prākṛtānvaya*) to modified rites (*vikṛti*) occurs through the medium of assistance (*upakāra*).

Just as the non-assumption of an auxiliary benefit beyond that which has been established is stated by the author of the *Kalpataru* and is accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas, so too is the assumption of an unestablished auxiliary benefit in accordance with the application first understood; thus he says: "In the sacrifices (*adhvareṣu*)," meaning even by the ritual Mīmāṃsakas.
The connection is that even the Mīmāṃsakas of the *Adhvara* school have unanimously supported the application of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements;
this is the sense. "Only in the case of the syntactical connection of word-meanings" means: only in the context of the syntactical connection of word-meanings.
"The restriction of established assistance" means: the non-imagining of an assistance other than that which is already established. The particle *eva* [indicates this exclusivity].

He states the exception: "after the syntactic connection of the word-meanings. This means: in cases where a supplementary benefit (*upakāra*) is postulated. "Having fully accepted" means: having indeed admitted it. "Characterized by sublation" means: for the purpose of establishing the commencement of the chapter on sublation (*bādhādhyāya*). "The archetypal connection" (*prākṛtānvaya*).

Thus, these are the constituent elements (padārthas) that serve as subsidiaries (śeṣa) in the archetypal sacrifice (prakṛti-yāga) and so forth; the meaning is that their application in the modified sacrifices (vikṛti-yāga) and so forth occurs through extended application (atideśa). What is being said here is this: in the tenth chapter of the *Pūrvatantra*, it is established that when the assistance (upakāra) already determined for the archetypal sacrifice is impossible for the subsidiaries extended to the modified sacrifice, there is sublation (bādha).

And that determination of sublation is not established under the view that the determination of auxiliary benefits occurs after the application of constituent elements (*padārtha*) through extended application (*atideśa*) to the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*),
because visible benefits are impossible for those constituent elements that have been applied to the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛti*) by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and so forth.

It is like the postulation of an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭopakāra*). When the visible benefits of the constituent elements (*padārtha*) prescribed by extension (*atideśa*) in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) are impossible, there is a necessary performance of all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) for the sake of accomplishing them through the postulation of an unseen benefit.

Since the non-performance of certain constituent parts would result in a sublation (*bādha*) consisting of the invalidity of their extended application (*atideśa*), it was established in the first section of the tenth chapter that the connection of archetypal elements in modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) occurs precisely through the mediation of the assistance already determined in the archetype. Thus, for the sake of defining sublation, [the author] has proven that the archetypal elements are connected to the modifications by way of the assistance established in the archetype.

And thus, it is understood that the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that wherever the postulation of an auxiliary benefit occurs subsequent to the application of ritual elements (*padārtha*), there the postulation of an unestablished benefit is for the sake of fulfilling the application first apprehended according to the capacity of each respective element. If...

Even in a case where the letter *u* is postulated immediately after the application (*viniyoga*), if a postulated benefit (*upakāra*) is impossible, the only course is the abandonment of the applied item; it would not be acceptable for them to postulate a benefit that has not been established.
If that were their view, then the section (adhikaraṇa) devoted to defining that the extended application (*atideśa*) of items occurs solely by way of the benefit would be undermined.

It would be useless; for even if there were an extended application (*atideśa*) of the very substances such as *śrayaṇa* (boiling) and so forth, since the visible benefit (*dṛṣṭopakāra*) consisting of softening and the removal of husks— which belongs to the *kṛṣṇala* coins and other items in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*)— is already accomplished [by other means], [the extended application] would be redundant.

Since that which is established in the world does not exist [in this context], and since one does not accept the postulation of an unestablished benefit (*upakāra*), there is the possibility of sublation (*bādha*)— characterized by non-performance and so forth— of the *āśraya* (substratum) and other elements as will be determined in the tenth chapter;
therefore, for that purpose, the extension (*atideśa*) of ritual items (*padārtha*) occurs solely by way of their benefit (*upakāra*).

Because no specific determination is required, once it is first understood through the *vividiṣā* injunction that there is an application common to both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites without distinction, it is indeed proper to postulate an as-yet-unestablished auxiliary function (*upakāra*) for the sake of fulfilling that application.

Furthermore, if one accepts that this application (viniyoga) belongs exclusively to the obligatory rites (*nitya*) because they lack any [previously] established auxiliary benefit (*kḷptopakāra*), then this application is rendered useless; for if the destruction of evil (*duritakṣaya*) resulting from those obligatory rites, or the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*) from them, is already established by other means, such an application is redundant.
Conversely, if it is not established by other means, then the capacity to produce the auxiliary benefit required for knowledge does not exist in the obligatory rites.

Since it is stated simply as "prepared" (*kḷptam*) without qualification, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that its application (*viniyoga*) is common to both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites. Now, although it is established from other sources that obligatory rites have as their sole purpose the destruction of evil (*durita*), it is not established that they specifically destroy the evil that acts as an obstacle to the arising of specialized knowledge (*jñāna*). Rather, [the following applies]:

If this application (viniyoga) exists, then for one who performs the obligatory rites (nitya-karmans) with knowledge as their objective, knowledge will necessarily arise. Otherwise, there would be mere purification and the arising of knowledge would be uncertain; thus, if you argue that this application is meaningful, then even for the obligatory rites, [the result] remains unestablished.
The nature of [the rite] is the removal of evil deeds that necessarily obstruct the arising of knowledge.

In reality, however, the assumption that even obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) produce an assistance required by knowledge (*vidyā*) is unestablished; thus he says, "Furthermore," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "due to non-attainment": the word "in the case of optional rites" (*kāmyeṣu*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The status of obligatory rites as causes of knowledge—either through the door of destroying sins (*duritakṣaya*) which is required by knowledge, or through the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)—is not established from any source other than the scriptural statement concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*).

Whether [the utility] be established (*siddha*) or unestablished (*asiddha*), the first alternative is not tenable, because it would result in the redundancy of the scriptural statement regarding the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); thus he says:

"From the obligatory rites" (*nityebhyaḥ*). Regarding "application" (*viniyoga*): the meaning is a word that conveys application in the form of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*). In the second case, even for the obligatory rites, the fact of being an auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyopakārakatva*), which has not yet been established, must be postulated.

He states that it is indeed proper to assume an auxiliary function common to both the obligatory (*nitya*) and the optional (*kāmya*) rites: "In the case of its non-attainment from another source. This means: in the case of the non-establishment of the obligatory rites as auxiliaries to knowledge. Taking the position that they are established from another source, he raises an objection regarding the meaningfulness of their application: "But surely... First, demerit (*durita*) is of two kinds [obstructing] the arising of knowledge...

An obstacle is neutral toward the arising of knowledge yet bestows [rebirth in] hell and other such states; thus, there is no evidence for the claim that when obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) are not employed for the sake of knowledge, they merely destroy the demerit (*durita*) that obstructs knowledge—as in the statement, "One dispels evil through dharma; sacrifice, charity, and austerity likewise."

Since eternal scriptural and traditional injunctions (śruti and smṛti), such as "They purify the wise," are intended solely to convey that [these acts] are causes for the destruction of general demerit (*durita*), the fact that obligatory rites (*nitya-karman*) are causes for the destruction of the specific demerit that obstructs knowledge is not established from any other source; therefore, this must be understood through these [injunctions].
The meaning is that this application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of attaining that.

If, by way of the statement regarding the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-vākya*), the obligatory rites (*nitya*) are applied to the attainment of knowledge through the door of the destruction of evil (*durita-kṣaya*) via sacrifices and so forth, then one asks: how is it that the destruction of precisely that evil which obstructs knowledge is obtained from the performance of the obligatory rites? What [is the reason]?

Regarding the word "thus" (*tviti*): he explains the manner of attaining that [knowledge] with the words "in this" (*asmin*) and "necessarily" (*avaśyam*). The meaning is that when the demerit (*durita*) which obstructs knowledge is destroyed through constant practice (*nityānuṣṭhāna*), knowledge necessarily arises from the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) once it is free from obstructions. Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*itarathā*): it refers to the absence of this application (*viniyoga*).

This is the meaning: there occurs an impurity consisting of the destruction of sins in general, but not necessarily that specific purification consisting of the destruction of those sins which obstruct knowledge, because the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) is for the sake of [attaining] knowledge. And thus, even for one whose habit is the performance of obligatory rites throughout many births, [knowledge does not arise].

The meaning is that knowledge does not arise by necessity; rather, it occurs only occasionally through the power of destiny (*daiva-yoga*), because there arises a complete destruction of the mass of sins that obstruct knowledge. Thus, the production of knowledge is non-necessary (*aniyata*). Furthermore, the assistance required for knowledge has been established as existing in the case of eternal [entities].

Intending that the mind is without a supporting object (*nirālambana*), [the author] refutes [the opponent's view] by stating that the assumption of an unestablished auxiliary function is equal in the case of obligatory (*nitya*) rites as it is in the case of optional (*kāmya*) ones. "In that case" (*tahi*) means: if the necessity of the mind being an auxiliary to cognition in the case of obligatory rites is not established.

Furthermore, one must postulate an unseen potency (*apūrva*) that brings about the hearing, reflection, and so forth, which result from obtaining a Guru distinguished by his means of knowledge; thus, because there is no need to postulate an unestablished auxiliary benefit, the general application (*viniyoga*) established by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), which is common to both obligatory and optional rites, should not be set aside. Now, even if this is so—

How, then, is the traditional teaching (smṛti) beginning with "For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone" to be reconciled? Nor can that [text] be interpreted as being intent upon the performance of rituals for the sake of knowledge, because in the passage concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*), the term "Brāhmaṇa" is used, [indicating that] it applies only to Brāhmaṇas.

Since the qualification for the action aimed at knowledge (*vidyārthakarman*) is thus understood, one might argue that the actions performed by Janaka and others must be said to contribute directly to liberation; this is not so, because in the scriptural passage concerning the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣāvākya*), the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an illustration for all three social classes (*traivarṇika*).

But even so, there is simplicity of the injunction (*vidhi-lāghava*) in the view that only the obligatory (*nitya*) rites are enjoined; for in that view, the removal of the evil that obstructs knowledge is already established by other scriptural statements and thus need only be understood through an injunction of restriction (*niyamavidhi*). However, in the case of optional (*kāmya*) rites...

If it is argued that, since the capacity to destroy the evil that obstructs knowledge has not been attained by all [the rites], there is an unavoidable weightiness of intent (*tātparya-gaurava*) for the injunction even in the case of employing the optional (*kāmya*) rites, [we reply]: True; nevertheless, the employment of the optional rites as well is necessary to avoid the sublation (*bādha*) characterized by the restriction of the scriptural texts concerning sacrifices and the like.

It should be understood that the intended meaning lies precisely in the word "necessary" (*āvaśyaka*). Even though one attains a specific purity consisting of the destruction of the demerit (*durita*) that obstructs knowledge through the obligatory rites (*nitya*), knowledge does not arise from that alone;
for there still exist perceptible obstructions in the form of doubts regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth. Therefore—

He states [the following] regarding the phrase "means of knowledge" (*jñānasādhana*): since it is already established that the performance of excellent teachers and the hearing, reflection, meditation, and so forth dependent upon them—which are useful for the removal of that [ignorance]—produces a visible result, it must be inferred that even for obligatory rites (*nitya*), the production of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) is to be understood by virtue of their application (*viniyoga*) through the scriptural injunction [to seek knowledge]. Thus, [they serve] in the production of ignorance (*avidyā*) by means of the desire to know.

Having determined the application of the various actions, he demonstrates the relevant context by means of an objection in order to establish that the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) possess the qualification for them. He begins with "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth, up to "even so" (*evam api*).
The phrase "knowledge and action are said to be the cause for attaining that, O Great Sage" refers to the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*).

The meaning is that the recollection of the means of instruction can be reconciled by taking it as referring to a sequential combination (*kramasamuccaya*), wherein knowledge is the direct means for attaining Brahman, while ritual action is the means for attaining it through *vidyā*, without contradicting the *vividiṣā* passages. Here, by the use of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), [the author] establishes perfection.

The meaning is that because liberation through mere hearing (śabdita-mukti) excludes any means other than [the hearing of] the respective [Vedic] actions, it is understood that the actions performed by Janaka and others have a direct utility toward liberation. However, since this contradicts the *vividiṣā*-sūtra, the justification of this traditional teaching—just like the traditional teaching on the combination [of knowledge and action]—is not established. This also applies to...

The desire to know (*vividiṣā*) anticipates an objection based on a meaning favored by the Siddhāntin that would contradict the scriptural statement, and [the author] refutes it with the words, "Nor is it for the sake of that [knowledge]," and "for the sake of knowledge. In this Smṛti passage, the word *saṃsiddhi* refers to knowledge; thus, the sense of the Smṛti is that one attains knowledge through action itself by way of purification. Of that...

He states the reason why recollection (*smaraṇa*) does not have as its purpose the performance of ritual acts for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the phrase "in the *vividiṣā* statement," the meaning is:

because the three castes (*traivarṇika*) lack the qualification (*anadhikāra*) for those ritual acts which are the means to knowledge, as understood from the *vividiṣā* statement. [The phrase] "because it is an indicative mark" (*upalakṣaṇatvāt*)...

And thus the Bhāṣya states that the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is for the sake of illustration; for the qualification is not restricted [to him alone], as it applies to all three castes. Furthermore, since there is qualification for those who seek knowledge, for those performing rituals, and for those born of noble lineage, the Smṛti text "By action alone" [is established].

The sense is that since [the scripture] teaches only that the performance of ritual acts is for the sake of knowledge, one cannot, on the strength of that, claim—contrary to such scriptural passages as "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death;
there is no other way"—that rituals have a direct utility for liberation.
This is the intended meaning.

As the venerable authors of the Vārttika have said here: "The mention of the Brāhmaṇa here is an indication for the twice-born [in general], because the qualification is not restricted, as the realization of the Self belongs to all. Indeed, in the injunction regarding the qualification of one who desires knowledge, it is not the case that the word *vidyākāmaḥ* (one desiring knowledge) should be modified to *yajñādīn anutiṣṭhet* (he should perform sacrifices and so forth).

It is appropriate that the word *brāhmaṇa* functions as a qualifier for the person entitled [to the rite], because a qualification cannot apply to the objective (the thing to be enjoined). Nor, in the injunction of the Rājasūya within the context of one desiring self-sovereignty (*svārājya*),
such as "One desiring self-sovereignty should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," can it be [that the term applies] to one desiring self-sovereignty who has a king as the performer.

Just as in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," because it is impossible for one who is not a king to accomplish a Rājasūya sacrifice whose performer must be a king— since the king is enjoined as a qualification of the specific sacrifice by virtue of being its agent— the king is included in the category of those entitled to perform it (adhikārī) by implication;
so too here, because a Brāhmaṇa is enjoined as the agent of the sacrifice and other rites, he is included in the category of those entitled to perform them by implication.
It is appropriate to say "the entry into ten million."

In this context, "bhavantaḥ" means "those who are worthy of honor. Regarding "ātmabodhane," the meaning is "in rites such as sacrifice, which are the means for the realization of the Self. This should be understood because the subject under discussion is precisely the qualification for rites performed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārthakarma*). Now, [one might object]: in the *vividiṣā* passage, the word "brāhmaṇa"— [The text continues: ...is used in the sense of the three twice-born classes (*dvija*), because the term "brahmin" is employed in its primary sense (*mukhyārtha*) with respect to the three castes. Furthermore, since the qualification for rites is established by the very nature of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*), there is no need to separately state that the three castes are qualified; for the eligibility for rites is already implied by the fact that they are enjoined for them. Therefore, the word "brāhmaṇa" here refers to the three castes. Once it is established that the term [brāhmaṇa] is indicative of the three castes (traivarṇika), it follows that all three castes, without distinction, possess the entitlement to perform ritual actions for the sake of knowledge (vidyā). Since it is thus established that all [castes] have an equal entitlement,
the fact that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is merely illustrative (upalakṣaṇa) is thereby proven in accordance with that principle.
If it is argued that this leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatva*), we say no;

for the mention of the "twice-born" (*dvija*) as a qualification for the act of smelling is intended—as in the *Vārttika*—merely to indicate all twice-born persons who possess the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for rites aimed at knowledge, without depending on that very act of smelling. Now, as for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*)...

If it is argued that since the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" in the scriptural injunction implies that only a Brāhmaṇa possesses the qualification for rites performed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārtha-karma*), how can a common qualification for all three castes be established? This need not be said, [for] does the word "Brāhmaṇa" serve merely to provide a specific qualifier for the subject (*uddeśya*) in the injunctions for sacrifices and the like?

Does [the text] establish the qualification for the Brāhmaṇa alone by way of providing the agent for the injunction, or does it establish that qualification for him alone merely by its own proximity (*svasaṃnidhi*) even in the absence of providing both [the act and the agent]? Since there is no other alternative, [the author] states that the first case is not so: "Not indeed," etc., regarding sacrifices and the like.
In an injunction whose primary purpose is the application [of a means] to the fruit characterized by knowledge,

the qualification of one who desires that [fruit] is indeed established; thus, it cannot be maintained that the word "brāhmaṇa" is intended to convey a qualification of the qualified person (adhikārin) in order to state that the qualification belongs to one who desires knowledge and is distinguished by being a brāhmaṇa, because [the word] is not something to be enjoined.

Since the objectivity (uddeśyatā) established by sacrifices and other rites can possibly terminate in the mere desire for knowledge (*vidyākāma*), the qualification "being a Brāhmaṇa" is not required; thus, it cannot be construed as a further qualification of those desiring knowledge. This is because it would be improper to construe it as such, given that one is postulating the qualified entity as the object of the injunction.

Furthermore, because of the respect [due to the injunction], if both "desire for knowledge" (*vidyākāma*) and "brahminhood" (*brāhmaṇya*) were each intended as the object of the injunction, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). The meaning is that one who desires knowledge and so forth should remain [in study], while a brahmin should perform sacrifices and the like. Having raised the second alternative along with an illustration, he refutes it with the words "Nor... (*nāpi*).

In the sentence concerning the desire for self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), since it is impossible for the word "king" (*rāja*) to function as a qualifier of the desire for self-sovereignty according to the method previously stated, the meaning is that by accepting its status as an injunction regarding the agent, the qualification of one who is already a king and desires self-sovereignty within the *Rājasūya* sacrifice is established.

The connection is that [the injunction] is like the appointment of a minister by the king for the sake of wealth. He clarifies the *arthāpatti* (presumption) expressed by the word "for the sake of" (*arthāt*). "By the king as the agent"—here, "here" means in the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*).
"Of that which is to be enjoined"—namely, that a Brāhmaṇa desiring knowledge should perform sacrifices and so forth; thus [it is said].

The meaning is "of which [the performance] is prescribed. By the word "by implication" (arthāt), the meaning is that sacrifices and the like, for which a Brāhmaṇa is the performer, cannot be accomplished by one who is not a Brāhmaṇa.

In every respect, it has been established in the sūtra *ubhayaliṅgāt* that in the sentence concerning the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-vākya*), there is an injunction regarding the connection with a specific result for sacrifices and other rites already prescribed elsewhere, and not an injunction for new sacrifices and so forth;
thus, in a single sentence, there is a reference to the sacrifices and other rites already obtained.

Because there would be the fault of syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) due to the injunction of two things— the injunction of the agent’s form and qualities, and the injunction of the connection with the result—
nor [is it possible] under the view that in the *Rājasūya* sentence the king is not to be enjoined as the agent.

Just as the status of a specific agent is obtained merely through the co-utterance with the word "king" (*rājapada*), so too here, even though the Brāhmaṇa is not enjoined as the agent in order to avoid a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), the status of the Brāhmaṇa as the agent is obtained merely through the co-utterance with the word "Brāhmaṇa."

Thus, it is logically established that [the injunction] terminates with that specific qualification. For it is appropriate that sacrifices and other rites—already established elsewhere as having the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) as their qualified agents, and now being enjoined here for the purpose of the knowledge of the Self (*ātma-vidyā*)—should likewise have the three classes as their qualified agents; this remains consistent even in the absence of a connection with a formal injunction [to that effect].
Considering the disparity with the illustrative example— that because the mere mention of the word "Brāhmaṇa" alongside [the word "study"] does not allow for a restriction of eligibility,

the word "Brāhmaṇa" must be taken as a mere indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of all those entitled to knowledge as they are already established, and thus its inclusion within the category of eligible persons occurs by implication (*arthāt*)—
this too is not tenable.

He states the reason with the words "In every way" (*sarvathāpi*), and so forth. Whether one holds the view that sacrifices and the like are duties belonging to the stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) or the view that they are auxiliary to knowledge (*vidyā-sahakāritva*), those very duties such as the Agnihotra and others which are enjoined in the scriptural passages concerning "as long as one lives" (*yāvajjīva*) must be performed. Why? Because of the evidence of both Śruti and Smṛti. First, the Śruti is the passage concerning the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā-vākya*).
The scriptural passage beginning with "gata-yajña" refers to well-known sacrifices and the like, as well as well-known acts of charity and the like,

because they are recognized through re-cognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Since this would contradict re-cognition if it were intended to enjoin entirely new sacrifices and so forth, [the passage] merely establishes a connection with a result by way of restating well-known sacrifices and the like.

Furthermore, because of the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) in the act of cognition, and because it is not perceived that the word "sacrifice" (*yajña*) and so forth are here intended as the objects to be enjoined— since they are already established as the means for sacrifices and the like— and because the Smṛti states,
"The fruit of action belongs to one who does not rely [on the Veda]," it refers only to those sacrifices and so forth that are not well-known [from the Veda].
The meaning of the Sūtra is that it demonstrates that knowledge (*vidyā*) functions as a cause even for those [rites] performed without an intention for a specific fruit (*phalābhisaṃdhi*).

Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": this means in the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), other than the passage concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣāvākya*). Regarding the phrase "because both are enjoined":

in the Rājasūya passage, however, since it is accepted that the injunction pertains only to a new rite (*apūrvakarman*) qualified by attributes such as the agent and so forth, [there is no contradiction].

The sense is that, since the contingency of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would arise [otherwise], it is appropriate for the word "king" (*rāja*) there to enjoin the quality of being the agent. He also anticipates and refutes a third possibility with an illustration, beginning with "Nor... (*nāpi*). Even though the king is not enjoined as the agent by the word "of the king" (*rājñaḥ*), the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the Rājasūya is established for the king alone.

The meaning is: in the view of those for whom the injunction is not accepted as having the king as its agent—on the grounds that, by the proximity of the word *rājan*, the term *svārājyakāma* (desiring self-sovereignty) is understood to refer to a Kṣatriya, otherwise the word *rājan* would result in being redundant. This is the intended sense.

He states the reason why it is also untenable to claim that [the qualification] concludes with the section concerning Brāhmaṇas. "Elsewhere" means in the *karmakāṇḍa*. "Here too" means even in the *vividiṣā* passage.
"The knowledge of the Self has the three castes as its qualified subjects" means that it applies to both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well as Brāhmaṇas.

The meaning is that there is no distinction in their qualification, characterized by the desire for knowledge (*vidyā*), and because, as in the case of a *śūdra*, there is no prohibition against those two [the king and the Vaiśya] performing sacrifices and other rites for the sake of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "by way of being appropriate": the sense is that the non-restriction of the qualified persons (*adhikārin*) serves to establish the authority of the injunction, characterized by its non-annulling nature (*anapodhatva*).

Anticipating the objection that— since the three grounds for justification such as "being established elsewhere" (kḷptatva) apply— the eligibility of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, even though it has been attained, is set aside by the word "Brāhmaṇa," he says: "lacking connection with an injunction" (vidhisaṃsargahīna),
[meaning] either by way of providing the subject matter (uddeśya) or by way of providing the thing to be enjoined (vidheya).
The meaning is that it is not useful for the comprehension of the syntactic connection of the meaning of an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*). However, in the case of the *rājasūya* sentence,

since the *rājasūya* itself is what is to be enjoined here, and because its eligibility for the three social classes (*traivarṇika*) is not established elsewhere, it is appropriate that it lacks a connection with an injunction (*vidhi-saṃsarga-hīna*).

The sense is that the restriction to the king as the agent follows merely from the co-occurrence with the word "king. Now, it may be objected: by the logic already stated, even in the absence of the word "Brāhmaṇa," since the eligibility of the Brāhmaṇa for rites performed for the sake of knowledge is established—just as it is for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya—the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" would be entirely redundant.

If it is argued that [the text] is redundant, the sense is that this is not the case, because its purpose is established as being to indicate that the Brāhmaṇa has the primary eligibility for rites performed for the sake of knowledge; thus, there is no possibility of futility.

If it is objected: "But if [the qualification] is merely an indicator for anyone entitled to knowledge (vidyā), then since even a Śūdra might possess the desire for knowledge and so forth, it would follow that he too has the entitlement to perform rites for the sake of knowledge"—we say no. For eligibility for Vedic matters belongs only to one who possesses the knowledge of their meaning derived from the Veda as studied through formal instruction.

Thus, because the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning those who are not Śūdras) prohibits a Śūdra— who is devoid of the study of the Vedas, the hearing of Vedic sentences, and so forth— from the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*), and because of the Smṛti text, "One should not impart instruction to a Śūdra," his greatness [is established] even from that perspective.

Some say that because the means for [understanding] speech do not exist [for him] and because his desire for that [knowledge] is untenable, he has no qualification for Vidyā; others, however, say that even a Śūdra indeed possesses qualification for performing rites for the sake of Vidyā, even though for him the recitation of the Vedas, the Agnihotra, and so forth are impossible.
