Because the recitation of the King of Mantras, the venerable five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara), which is explicitly taught as being for the benefit of all castes, and other such practices— along with austerity, charity, cooking, and sacrifice— are possible causes for the destruction of sin; and because of scriptural statements using distinct instrumental case endings, such as "by the recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity," [these means are available] even for widowers and others.

Because [the scriptures] acknowledge the performance of even a small portion, such as a single virtuous act or a single syllable, and because [liberation] does not depend on the combination of practices such as the recitation of the Vedas.
He raises an objection regarding the view that the mention of the *brāhmaṇa* is merely illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*).
For when knowledge is not something to be enjoined (*avidheya*), the qualification (*adhikāra*) consists merely in the desire for knowledge;
and since that is possible even for a *śūdra*, he too would have a qualification for those rites intended for the sake of knowledge, just as a *kṣatriya* or others do.

The meaning is that they are difficult to prevent. Having raised the doubt as to whether a Śūdra has the qualification for hearing the Vedāntas and other means for the knowledge of Brahman with attributes (saguṇa) and the knowledge of Brahman without attributes (nirguṇa) as declared in the Śruti, it was determined in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* that he lacks such qualification.
And regarding his lack of entitlement [to such knowledge], the reason is set forth in the Bhāṣya: "because of the absence of Vedic study.

Having raised the objection—namely, that even if a Śūdra lacks Vedic study due to the general prohibition against both pronouncing and hearing the Veda, why should he not perform the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*) and so forth, which constitute the meaning of the Veda?—[the author] addresses this by means of study...

It has been stated that because knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas—which is produced by the Vedic injunctions—is restricted to the performance of Vedic rites, one who is devoid of study lacks such knowledge; therefore, he has no qualification for the practice of either saguṇa or nirguṇa vidyā. And thus, because they share the same purpose—

The meaning is that there is no eligibility even for those actions which serve as means to knowledge (*vidyārthakarma*). Now, one might object: although a Śūdra lacks eligibility for Vedic sacrifices and the like, since it is possible for him to perform the actions that are means to knowledge according to the method to be explained, a Śūdra might also [engage in them] out of a desire for knowledge.

Anticipating the objection that their performance [of rituals] is possible, he states that for such a person, even the desire for knowledge is not possible: "Not for a Śūdra. This means that the Śūdra lacks the *mati*—the understanding of the meaning of the scriptures—and the greatness of knowledge, which consists in its being the means for attaining Brahman, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss.

Regarding the point that the inclusion of the qualification for the rite of learning (*vidyārthakarma*) would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "But others [hold]... That which has the qualification of all castes (*sarvavarṇa*) explicitly stated (*kaṇṭhataḥ*) is such a thing; this refers to the recitation (*japa*) of the *vidyā* and so forth.
The *vidyā* is specifically the venerable five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣara*), the king of mantras; and the word "and so forth" (*ādi*)...
For the purpose of collecting other mantras from the Āgamas and Purāṇas, it is likewise stated in the Brahmottara-khaṇḍa:

"What is the use of many mantras for him, what use are sacred fords or austerities and sacrifices, for whom the mantra 'Oṃ Namaḥ Śivāya' has entered the range of his heart— that which is the king of kings among mantras?"

This six-syllabled Śaiva mantra is the crest-jewel of all Vedānta and the treasury of all knowledge; this very five-syllabled mantra is remembered as being preceded by the *praṇava* (Om). It is meditated upon by women, Śūdras, and those of mixed castes who desire liberation. [In the phrase] "pākayajñādī," the word "etc. (*ādi*)...
This is for the purpose of including service to twice-borns, chanting of names, bathing at sacred fords, and so forth. Now,

although in the *vividiṣā* passage the duties common to all castes are indicated by implication, because sacrifices and other such acts are mentioned together in a single sentence, it appears that their collective performance constitutes a means to knowledge, as seen in the context of sacrifices and the like.

Anticipating the objection that since the combination [of rites] is precluded for a Śūdra, how can he have the qualification for ritual action for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), the author refutes this by pointing out the failure of the reason, stating: "By the recitation of the Vedas" (*vedānuvacanena*). They desire to know through the recitation of the Vedas.

Since each [means] is perceived as an independent instrument in such forms as "they desire to know through sacrifice" (*yajñena vividiṣanti*), there is no requirement for their combination; for if that were intended, the sentence would have been "they desire to know by means of Vedic recitation,
sacrifice, charity, and austerity" (*vedānuvacana-yajña-dāna-tapobhir vividiṣanti*), using the instrumental case of separate application.

The sense is that even in the case of the *pravaṇa* [passage], there may be a sentence joined with the particle *ca* for each individual item—such as "by the recitation of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by giving, and by austerity"—just as in the case of "to Agni and to Prajāpati," and so forth. Furthermore, it is not impossible for a Śūdra to have a desire for knowledge (*vidyā*), for it is said: "One should cause the four castes to hear [the Purāṇas]."

Because, by the traditional recollection (*smṛti*) that all four castes have the right to hear the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*—beginning with the passage "having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the head"—it is possible even for such a person (a Śūdra) to seek knowledge, since the greatness of knowledge is understood from the *Purāṇas* and other sources; and because of the traditional law: "One should not impart instruction to a Śūdra."
This is because [the passage] is intended to prohibit knowledge of rituals such as the *agnihotra*, which are not applicable to its performance; otherwise,

since there would be no means for him to understand even his own caste-duties (*svavarṇadharma*), it would follow that the Śūdra— the fourth caste, consisting of a single birth— would lack truthfulness, freedom from anger, purity, and the practice of ritual sipping (*ācamana*).

Otherwise, there would result the invalidity— characterized by non-implementation— of those scriptural statements that distinguish their respective duties, such as: "Only the washing of hands and feet," "The performance of ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the maintenance of servants, contentment with one's own wife, and service to superiors," and so forth.
And this being so, the section concerning those who are not *paśu* or *śūdra* does not become devoid of subject matter;

for that section concerns the *śūdra*, who— according to the Smṛti stating "there is no sin whatsoever in a *śūdra*, nor is he entitled to sacraments"— is devoid of the sacrament of initiation (*upanayana*), which is known as the "approaching of the teacher" and is an auxiliary to the knowledge [of the Veda].
Because it is intended to prohibit eligibility for the means of both saguṇa-vidyā and nirguṇa-vidyā, such as the hearing of the Vedānta and other practices.

As for the objection that, since the greatness of knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot be understood at first glance, there is no possibility of a means [to attain it], and thus the qualification characterized by the desire for knowledge (*arthitva*) is untenable—having restated that, he refutes it:

"And [the rule] 'one should cause the Śūdra to hear' [is not applicable]; the word "Brāhmaṇa" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. When one would not cause a Kṣatriya or others to hear [it], then...

He states the distinction: "by means of [the knowledge of] what is to be done" (*kṛtya*), etc. The meaning is: that *śūdra* by whom the greatness of knowledge has been understood through the *Purāṇas* and other such means; it belongs to him. He shows the limitation of the prohibitory statement regarding "intellect" (*mati*) with the words "not for a *śūdra*" and "otherwise."

The meaning is that [the prohibition] is intended solely to forbid the mere giving of knowledge regarding the meaning of the scriptures. The meaning is that since for a Śūdra there is a natural prohibition against reading the Purāṇas and so forth, if he were also prohibited from hearing the Purāṇas and so forth from others, it would be impossible for him to understand his own dharma. Anticipating the objection that this is an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says:

By the passage beginning with "The Śūdra is the fourth caste," etc., [the meaning is as follows]: *jāti* means birth; the sense is that he is devoid of the second birth known as the initiation (*upanayana*). The force of the particle *eva* in "only washing" (*prakṣālanaṃ eva*) is to exclude such things as the sipping of water (*ācamana*) or touching the limbs. Regarding the phrase "of the subsequent ones," the meaning is "of the twice-born" (*dvijānām*). It does not apply to a Śūdra.
Although the Smṛti statement "one should punish" is intended solely to prohibit the giving of mere knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures, [it is further stated]: "In times of prosperity,
one must support one's mother and father, as well as a virtuous wife and an infant son, even if they have committed a hundred improper acts."

Based on the observation of statements such as "he said," there is no inconsistency whatsoever; for those Brāhmaṇas who, for the sake of profit, engage in reciting the Purāṇas and other texts before Śūdras— provided they possess at least the aforementioned characteristics and are capable of protecting the wealth required for such purposes— it is possible for them to attain an understanding of the majesty of knowledge and their own duty (*svadharma*).
It should not be thought that this is so; the meaning is that one would thereby be accepting the eligibility of even a Śūdra for ritual acts performed for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārthakarma*).

As for the phrase "it would be without a subject" (*nirviṣayatvam*), the intention is that the said section (*adhikaraṇa*) is intended to negate the eligibility of a Śūdra. True, that section [negates] the eligibility of a Śūdra...
However, that [passage] is intent upon prohibition; it does not intend to prohibit the qualification for ritual action (*karma-adhikāra*).
He refutes [the objection] by stating "He is not a Śūdra," etc., because that [passage] intends to prohibit the qualification for hearing the Vedānta.
If there were an absence of qualification for hearing the Vedānta and for the meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*), [the following would apply].

He states a qualification containing a reason: "called approaching the teacher. He provides the authority for the Śūdra’s lack of sacramental refinement: "not a Śūdra. Regarding the term "sin," it means that which is committed by eating what is forbidden to eat and so forth. [The initiation] is characterized by the *upanayana*, which is a constituent part of Vedic study.

He prohibits both types of consecration characterized by the initiation (*upanayana*) that is a limb of learning (*vidyāṅga*). This is expressed in the phrase "he does not deserve consecration. Initiation as a limb of learning consists of the teacher’s act of accepting someone as a disciple and placing them near himself; and that...
Because it is preceded by the disciple’s approaching the teacher, it is called "approaching the teacher" (*gurūpasadana*).

And this approaching the teacher is enjoined as an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to knowledge in such passages as, "For the sake of understanding that, he should approach a teacher alone," and likewise in the Śruti, "Then he initiated him."
The sense is that initiation (upanayana) is understood as being an integral part of sacred knowledge (vidyā). The meaning is that the teacher initiated that seeker of knowledge.

In the case of knowledge devoid of qualities (*nirguṇavidyā*), even for a *śūdra*, it is impossible to prohibit the desire for it prompted by the beauty of the object; furthermore, since that knowledge is not something to be enjoined, there is no possibility of a qualification other than that [desire], and thus a prohibition of it is untenable. Nor is it the case for him...

It should not be said that even if the performance of rites for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārthakarmānuṣṭhāna*) is possible when the hearing of Vedānta (*vedāntaśravaṇa*) is impossible, such performance of rites is useless because knowledge does not arise; for the Blessed Teacher [Śaṅkara] stated that even though he lacks the qualification for hearing Vedānta, "he should cause the four [castes] to hear... [in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*].
Regarding the phrase "the castes," since the Smṛti texts establish that all four castes have the right to study the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, it is settled that Śūdras lack the right to study the Vedas;
this is stated in the concluding commentary of the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* concerning the identity of Brahman and the Self.
Because it has been shown that one possesses the qualification for the means of acquiring knowledge through the hearing of the Purāṇas and other such texts.

Now, one might object: why is it that the *Paśu-adhikaraṇa*— which is intended to prohibit the qualification [of Śūdras] for meditations on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) as taught in the Śruti, and likewise for the hearing of the Vedānta and so forth which are the means to the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*)— does not apply to the knowledge of the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇavidyā*) itself as well?

It might be argued that, due to a lack of a determining factor (*vinigamakābhāva*), if there were no qualification for the knowledge of the attributeless (*nirguṇa-vidyā*), then the qualification of Śūdras for the ritual acts that are its means would not be established; therefore, he says: "In the knowledge of the attributeless.
[This refers to] the excellence of the object characterized by the knowledge of Brahman, namely, its being the means to liberation.

The meaning is that for one engaged in that knowledge, the qualification characterized by the desire for knowledge (*vidyā*) cannot be negated by the logic of that specific section (*tad-adhikaraṇa-nyāya*). [Objection: But even if the Śūdra possesses the qualification characterized by the desire for knowledge, there is something other than that...

Since there is an absence of other qualifying attributes such as having studied the Vedas, one might ask: how can he have the qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*)? To this, he says: "in that which is not a matter of injunction. The word "and" (*ca*) is for the purpose of dispelling doubt.
"Beyond that" means beyond mere desire (*arthitva*). It is like the experience of heaven.

Since the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā), which consists of the experience of the bliss of Brahman, is of the nature of a fruit, it is not something to be enjoined; for a fruit is not an object of injunction. Thus, just as in the case of the fruit such as the experience of heaven, the qualification for it consists merely in the desire for that fruit, so too it is with respect to the knowledge of the attributeless Brahman.
The meaning is this: the mere desire for that [knowledge] is itself the qualification (*adhikāra*), and that cannot be denied;

however, regarding the enjoined practices such as meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like, the scripture has specified a dependence on other previously mentioned qualifications for the qualified person—thus, the example is dissimilar. As for the term "impossibility," it refers to the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*.

The meaning is: "provided that it is impossible according to the rule. Even though for him (the Śūdra) the hearing of the Vedāntas is impossible, since the commentary (*bhāṣya*) has shown his eligibility to hear the Purāṇas and other texts concerning the non-duality of Brahman and the Self, the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*) is possible even for a Śūdra; this is the meaning. In the commentary, however, the word "tu" (but/however) serves the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇārtha*).

Although the Śūdra is permitted to hear the Purāṇas and other texts by the statement, "One should cause the four castes to hear," there is no permission for him to engage in reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Therefore, his practice of reflection and so forth is not established [by that alone]. Nor can it be argued that because reflection and the rest are auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) of hearing, they do not require a separate permission.

It must be stated that, as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is no authoritative means (*pramāṇa*) in the present context to establish a relationship of subsidiary and principal (*śeṣa-śeṣibhāva*); therefore, the designation of "subsidiary" and "principal" regarding hearing and so forth is merely figurative.
Consequently, even if a *śūdra* hears portions of non-dualistic texts such as the Purāṇas, the arising of knowledge (*vidyodaya*) is impossible.

Since the futility of performing rituals for the sake of knowledge remains exactly as it was, he states [the following] out of his own inclination: "fit for the arising of knowledge. Alternatively, based on the statement, "One should augment the Veda by means of Itihāsas and Purāṇas," [he refers to] that portion of the Itihāsas and so forth which concerns the supreme non-duality of Brahman and the Self.

It is determined that [the study of grammar] serves merely as an auxiliary to the knowledge of the meaning of Vedānta produced by the hearing of Vedānta; it does not, however, independently generate the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self without depending upon the hearing of Vedānta. Only when this is the case does the first half of that statement become consistent.

"The Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, 'He might lead me astray. This is the meaning: that person by whom only a small portion of the Veda has been heard and investigated is one of little learning (alpaśruta)."

Thinking that it will serve the purpose of liberation by means of producing a pure body suitable for the arising of knowledge, the performance of ritual action by those of the three higher castes— which has the fruit of gradual liberation— is like the hearing of Vedānta [for the purpose of attaining] that qualified knowledge.
Since it will serve the purpose of generating knowledge by means of producing the bodies of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*),
and because there is no contradiction in a Śūdra performing ritual acts for the sake of knowledge, therefore, in the sentence concerning the desire to know (*vividiṣā-vākya*),
the word "Brāhmaṇa" functions as a mere indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for anyone who is eligible for knowledge as established by the context.

Thus, it is established that even for a Śūdra, there is indeed eligibility for ritual action for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*). Now, while it may be granted that rituals are useful for knowledge by way of purifying the mind (*citta-śuddhi*), what is the means (*dvāra*) through which renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is useful for it? Some say it is the removal of evil deeds (*durita*) which obstruct the arising of knowledge.

Since [ignorance] is not something infinite, is there anything to be removed by the performance of sacrifices and the like, or is there something to be removed by the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)? Thus, like ritual action, renunciation too is useful for that [liberation] only through the mediation of the purification of the mind.

Therefore, the Veda heard by that person fears him. How it fears is stated here: "Mā. This person of little learning might cross over me—the Veda—by means of Mīmāṃsā, which consists of inquiry into me, due to suspicions such as the presence of fallacious reasoning (nyāyābhāsa) and so forth, [thereby] making even me refer to something else.

One should honor [the Veda]. The word "iti" has the sense of a reason. Thus, because deception is possible for this reason, one should properly augment the Veda by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas—by means of the statements of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas that follow the Mīmāṃsā. In that [Mīmāṃsā]...

One should establish the Veda upon the meaning determined by Mīmāṃsā by means of accomplishing a firm certainty regarding its logical validity. And thus, even for a Śūdra who is excluded from hearing the Vedānta,

there is indeed the possibility of renunciation through hearing the Itihāsas and other texts which, being devoted to the identity of Brahman and the Self, serve to augment the understanding of the Vedāntic meaning.

The statement, "There is no arising of knowledge; one should cause the four castes to hear [the Vedas]," is intended to grant permission for the Śūdra’s hearing of non-dualistic Purāṇas and similar texts for the sake of unseen spiritual merit (adṛṣṭārtha);
likewise, in the commentary on the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*, there is a description of the Śūdra’s hearing of non-dualistic Purāṇas and so forth.
The statement "one fears the person of little learning" does not imply that [the Śūdra] has failed because he did not perform [the study], for there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya;

furthermore, since knowledge is to be accomplished solely through the hearing of the Vedānta, it would not be established for a Śūdra in its absence. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "fit for the arising of knowledge," and "for the sake of liberation."

The phrase "the meditation on Brahman endowed with qualities" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding the statement "for the purpose of the arising of knowledge": the meaning is that it is possible for a Śūdra to perform those duties because he has the certainty that they will serve as the means for the arising of knowledge. Therefore, [it follows] for the Śūdra...
The meaning is that there is no obstacle to the performance of the rites for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the phrase "only those qualified for knowledge" (*vidyādhikārimātra*):

the word *mātra* signifies that the term "Brāhmaṇa" does not refer exclusively to Brāhmaṇas alone, nor does it refer exclusively to the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) alone. Alternatively, if the word "Brāhmaṇa" is intended as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the twice-born (*dvija*), [this is] as stated in the Vārttika...
The reason has been stated: because there is no distinction regarding the eligibility for the three [classes] in respect to self-knowledge, the means of knowledge, and ritual action;

the sense is that this reason applies equally to the Śūdra. "By what door?"—does the application of knowledge occur through an unseen (adṛṣṭa) door, or through a seen (dṛṣṭa) door? Not the first, because [knowledge] arises from...

The first position is untenable because, since the obstructing evil (durita) has already been removed by the merit (apūrva) produced from the performance of sacrifices and other rites, there would be no evil remaining to be removed by the merit produced by renunciation (saṃnyāsa); thus, renunciation would result in being purposeless. Nor is the second [position] tenable, because such [an obstructing evil] is not perceived—this is the intended meaning of the objection. Regarding these, as for the first position...

He provides a justification, saying, "Some say... [The objection]: But surely the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) cannot be the cause for the arising of knowledge, since we observe that some who are not renunciants also perform hearing and other practices with knowledge as their goal;
and because it is established by authoritative means of knowledge that for some, the arising of knowledge occurs even without renunciation. To this, he replies:

And likewise, for householders and others who practice hearing [the scriptures] and so forth during the intervals between ritual duties, the attainment of knowledge does not occur in that very birth; rather, it occurs in another birth only after they have obtained renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
However, as for those householders such as Janaka and others in whom knowledge is observed even while remaining householders—[for them...]

Because the attainment of knowledge [occurs] through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) in a previous birth, there is not even the slightest suspicion of a deviation of knowledge from renunciation in the past. Others, however,
[hold that it is attained] because it is subsumed under the term "withdrawn" (*uparata*) in such scriptural passages as, "peaceful, self-controlled, withdrawn," and so forth.

Because renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is included within the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), the commentary on the Sūtra "an injunction for another auxiliary" states that for the renunciant who possesses knowledge, this third stage of "munitude" (*mauna*) is enjoined in view of childhood (*bālya*) and scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*). Therefore, it says, "A Brāhmaṇa [should practice] scholarship," and so forth.
In the Śruti, it is established that one should "wander for alms before that," because this indicates the qualification for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
The phrase "and likewise" (tathā ca) means that since no visible means for the acquisition of knowledge through renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is perceived,

it is established by the injunction of renunciation that it is a cause for attaining knowledge only through an invisible means (*adṛṣṭa*). Nor is it unestablished that there is no visible means, because [renunciation is required] for one whose mind is distracted by worldly and Vedic activities.

It should not be argued that the renunciation of all actions (*sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa*) serves as a cause for ignorance (*avidyā*) through the visible means of removing distraction (*vikṣepanivṛtti*), because [renunciation] arises from the dawn of knowledge (*vidyodaya*). For even among certain preeminent men who possess both worldly and Vedic actions, there occurs [the absence of] dejection and joy.

The sense is that since the cessation of distractions characterized by anger, fear, and so forth is established through direct experience, there is no need for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for that purpose. However, adhering to the view that renunciation functions through the medium of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), [the author] explains the utility of knowledge by way of the prior state of renunciation being a qualification for those entitled to hearing (*śravaṇa*) and other practices.

He states this with authoritative proof: "Others," "peaceful," and so forth. The remainder of the Vedic scripture says: "Having become patient, composed, and full of faith, one should see the Self in the very self. Here, *śama* is the restraint of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), *dama* is the restraint of the external organs (*bāhyendriya*), and *uparati* is the renunciation of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*). Now, [an objection]:

If it is argued that the scriptural injunction for *uparati* (cessation from action) is redundant because the mere performance of ritual acts (*karma*) has already been prohibited by the terms "tranquility" (*śānta*) and "self-control" (*dānta*), we say no; for the scriptural injunctions regarding tranquility and self-control are general rules, whereas the injunctions for obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) are specific rules. Therefore, [the former] refers to actions other than the obligatory and occasional rites (*naimittika*).

Since there would be no abandonment of obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) if [the term *uparati*] were restricted to the mere cessation of the activities of the external and internal organs, the abandonment of obligatory duties is understood through the scriptural mention of *uparati*; thus, it is not redundant. Furthermore, one who is patient—enduring the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat—and composed, possesses the mental state required for hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

"One possessed of concentration" means one who has devotion toward the deities, the Guru, and the Vedāntas; "having become one whose mind is imbued with faith"—this [phrase] is to be construed with each [term]. The meaning of the Śruti is that one should perceive within the Self alone—that is, within this very aggregate of cause and effect—the Self who is the witness of the aggregate, thinking, "I am Brahman."

The "fourfold means" (sādhanacatuṣṭaya) consists of: discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, dispassion toward enjoyments of this world and the next, the hexad of tranquility and so forth (śamādi), and the desire for liberation (mumukṣā). The sense is that these four means were established in the first sūtra as the specific qualifications for one who is entitled to [engage in] hearing (śravaṇa) and the other [limbs of inquiry].
He states another reason for the fact that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is a qualification for the preceding [state],
with the passage beginning "because of the injunction of another concurrent duty" and ending with "on account of the teaching.
The meaning of the portion of the Sūtra, *atha muniḥ* ("then the sage"), is that there is an injunction regarding *mauna* (the state of a sage), which is another means toward knowledge (*vidyā*).

The word *tadvataḥ* in the Sūtra is explained as *vidyāvataḥ*, meaning "one who possesses the preliminary knowledge (*āpātajñāna*) suitable for the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth. Regarding the phrase "for one who possesses that, there is an injunction for another task along with it," the term refers to the renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*).

He states how it is obtained there: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is indeed a Vedic term; because the Brāhmaṇas of the past, having known Brahman as the Self even at first sight, performed renunciation—designated by the term "withdrawal"—for the sake of the direct realization of reality, therefore even a Brāhmaṇa of the present time [should do likewise].

The meaning of the Śruti is that one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), having renounced scholarship and the rest, should practice for the sake of the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra). "Scholarship" (pāṇḍitya) refers to hearing (śravaṇa), and "mauna" refers to meditation (dhyāna); the phrase "therefore [he is] a Brāhmaṇa" implies that this occurs prior to that [realization].

Furthermore, as stated in the *Vārttika*: "Only for one who has renounced all actions, who desires to abandon transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and who seeks to know the identity of the Self (*ekātmya*), is there eligibility with respect to the [Upanishads]," it follows that the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) serves as a qualification for the person eligible for the hearing of the Vedāntas and other means of knowledge. This is its [function].

Some say that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is useful for knowledge (vidyā). Others, however, hold that since the fruit of renunciation is the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) as a subsidiary element of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, its utility for knowledge consists in its performing the accomplishment of hearing and the rest through undivided attention; this is by way of a visible means (dṛṣṭadvāra), according to the statement in the Vivaraṇa.
For it is impossible to assume the unseen [as a cause] when [the result] can be accounted for otherwise; however, if for a wise man of noble character,
even while residing in another stage of life (āśrama),
the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth is accomplished during the intervals between ritual duties.

He states another reason, in the form of agreement with the Vārttika, for the fact that the unprecedented state of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa-apūrva*) serves as a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikārin*), beginning with the word "having abandoned" (*tyakta*).

In the Vārttika, the first qualification refers to renunciation; therefore, by means of the particle *ca* (and), which signifies a conjunction of renunciation, the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), and the desire to know (*jijñāsā*).

The sense is that, just like the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutva*) and so forth, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) also appears to be a qualification of the person entitled (*adhikārin*) to the hearing of the Vedānta and other such practices. Regarding the phrase "of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) of renunciation": since renunciation, being an action characterized by relinquishment, cannot persist [in its own form], it must be pursued until it culminates in the production of an *apūrva*.
He supports the second position—that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is applied to knowledge (*vidyā*) through a visible means—by stating, "But others...

Having raised the objection that the statement in the *Vivaraṇa* is untenable because, while there is scriptural evidence (*śruti*, etc. for understanding renunciation as an auxiliary to knowledge, there is no such authority for it being an auxiliary to hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth:

He states its intended meaning: "By means of having no other activity. Occasional hearing [of the scriptures] and so forth are not the means for immortality through the arising of knowledge; rather, it is constant abiding in Brahman—according to such Śruti and Smṛti as, "One who is established in Brahman attains immortality," and "From the time of sleep until death, one should spend one's time in reflection on the Vedānta."
Likewise, by enjoining the performance of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth with undivided attention for hundreds [of years], the scripture implies the renunciation of householders and others,
since it is impossible for those constantly preoccupied with the duties prescribed for their own stage of life (āśrama) to perform hearing and so forth at all times. Thus:

Even though the scripture ordains renunciation as a means for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyā*), it requires the constant practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth as its instrumental medium (*dvāra*),
because renunciation lacks direct efficacy as a means to knowledge; this is so provided that a visible medium is possible.

Furthermore, it is untenable to assume an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) as the means [to liberation]. In that case as well, since hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth manifest the reality, they are primary by implication; however, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), due to the absence of the aforementioned reason, remains subordinate. Such is the injunction regarding hearing and the rest.

And since the injunction for renunciation and [the injunction for hearing] have attained the status of a single syntactical unit through the force of their mutual dependence, it is established that hearing— accompanied by reflection and meditative concentration— is enjoined as having renunciation as its constituent part; thus, renunciation, by virtue of being an auxiliary to hearing and so forth, results in the fruit of self-knowledge.

This is the meaning; or rather, this is the intention expressed in the Vivaraṇa: the injunction for hearing (śravaṇa-vidhi) requires, as a means to hearing, both the cessation of distraction and renunciation (saṃnyāsa), which is the cause thereof, because it is impossible for one whose mind is distracted to engage in the performance of hearing and so forth. And this applies to householders and others as well.

Because distraction necessarily occurs even at times other than those for performing the duties of one’s own stage of life (*āśrama*) due to the multiplicity of objects; and because the injunction for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) ordains renunciation as a means for accomplishing ignorance (*avidyā*) by effecting hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth through the visible door of the cessation of distraction.

Since it is possible for [the text] to have a direct purpose (*cāritārthya*), it is impossible for it to enjoin renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) as a means to knowledge (*vidyā*) through an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, as in the previous case, it is established that renunciation results in the fruit of knowledge only by being an ancillary (*aṅga*) to hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, and not through an unseen potency; this is the conclusion of this interpretation.

The intended meaning of the phrase "by means of having no other activity" is "through the cessation of distraction. The word "of that" means "of renunciation. Now, an objection may be raised: it is untenable to say that renunciation, having become a subsidiary element (*aṅga*) to hearing and so forth through the cessation of distraction, serves as a means to knowledge (*vidyā*).

He raises the objection with the words "yadi tu" (but if), suggesting that for some qualified candidates for hearing (*śravaṇa*), the cessation of mental distraction may occur even without renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*). The term "analasasya" means one who is not indolent; that is to say, one in whom the quality of purity (*sattva-guṇa*) predominates. The term "dhīmataḥ" means one whose nature is to perceive the defects in sense-objects; that is to say, a preeminent person (*puruṣadhaureya*) [who has turned away] from sense-objects.
The meaning is: "of one who is capable of restraining [the senses] from their respective objects."

In that case, one must accept the restrictive rule that within the four stages of life (*āśrama*), the practice of hearing the Vedānta and so forth occurs only through the adoption of the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*). Now, in these two positions, how can Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas carry out the practice of hearing the Vedānta and so forth, since renunciation [is not permitted for them]?

Because the section concerns Brāhmaṇas; for in the injunctions regarding renunciation, such as "A Brāhmaṇa should attain detachment," "A Brāhmaṇa, having risen above [worldly life]," and "A Brāhmaṇa should go forth [into the forest]," the term "Brāhmaṇa" is used. The mention of "Brāhmaṇa" is for the purpose of identifying the specific qualified person, because the injunction for renunciation is not [restricted] in the Śruti.

If it is argued that this is because of the statement in the Vārttika, "of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya," some here reply: "Or otherwise, one may renounce even from the stage of studentship, or from the household, or from the forest"— since there is no distinction made in the revealed scripture (śruti), it applies to both the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya as well.

Or a Vaiśya may renounce from his house; for, since the eligibility of both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas for *saṃnyāsa* is established by the Smṛti statement— "Having studied the Veda, there are four stages of life (*āśrama*) for the three castes"—
the mention of the Brāhmaṇa in other Śruti texts [is merely illustrative].

This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of all three [castes]. For this very reason, in the *Vārttika* as well, after stating the intention of the *Bhāṣya* with the verse beginning "of the specific qualified person" (*adhikāriviśeṣasya*), it is stated that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) applies without distinction to the three [castes].
It is heard in the *Śruti* that the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" would be for the purpose of such an elliptical indication.

Others, however, maintain that by the immediately following verse, the eligibility for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is shown to belong to both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in his own view, thereby establishing their right to perform hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and other such practices. Yet others, in many [texts]...
Since the term "Brāhmaṇa" is mentioned in the scriptural injunctions regarding the rite of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*),

even though the term "Brāhmaṇa" does not appear in the cited Jābāla-śruti passage concerning the injunction for renunciation, it is established that the eligibility for it belongs exclusively to Brāhmaṇas, as confirmed by other Vedic texts.

Furthermore, because of the reference to "Brahmin" in the statement, "How can one who lacks the sacrificial thread be a Brahmin? during the state of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), it follows that only a Brahmin has the qualification for renunciation.
By these qualifiers, the absence of the causes of distraction is indicated; thus, the cessation of distraction is stated.

Since the absence of distraction—which is the fruit of renunciation—could be obtained from sources other than renunciation, [the text] establishes the cessation of distraction required for hearing and so forth, as an obstacle to the intended renunciation.

Thus it is understood that there is attainment in one case and non-attainment in the other. And so, let it be granted that the injunction for the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsāśrama*) is not an original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*), but rather it may be a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*). [The phrase] "by means of that" refers to by means of possession alone; the ellipsis is "as a means for the cessation of distraction. Now, regarding these two alternatives...
The meaning is: in the view that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is a qualification for eligibility, and in the view that it is an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of hearing (*śravaṇa*).

[The question] "How so? [is asked]. The intention is: because of the absence of renunciation. He states the reason for the absence of renunciation in those two cases with the words: "of renunciation. He states the authoritative basis (*pramāṇa*) for the Brāhmaṇa's eligibility for renunciation with the words: "the Brāhmaṇa."
The meaning is that one should perform renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), which is the act of laying down (*nyāsa*), preceded by detachment (*vairāgya*) and characterized by world-weariness (*nirveda*).

This is because, since detachment denoted by the word *nirveda* constitutes the complete causal complex for it, renunciation is necessary when that [detachment] exists. The intention is that this very [verse] is the injunction for renunciation.

"Having emerged" (*vyutthāya*) means "having renounced" (*saṃnyasya*). Since the mention of the word "Brāhmaṇa" in the scripture is for the purpose of identifying the specific qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), the interpretation of the *Vārttika* is that there is no rule for the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas. Regarding this, some maintain that the performance of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth is established for those two castes as well.

The connection [is as follows]: "Having completed his student life (*brahmacarya*), he should become a householder; having been a householder, he should become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); then he should renounce" (*gṛhī bhavet... pravrajeta*).

Thus, the previous scripture establishes the combination (*samuccaya*) of all four stages of life (*āśrama*). Then, by saying "or else otherwise" (*yadi vetarathā*), it shows their optionality (*vikalpa*). The phrase "or else" refers specifically to the stage of the student (*brahmacarya-āśrama*).

The meaning is: "if dispassion has arisen. Regarding that, he says "or from [the householder's] stage" (*grahāt*) when it has not arisen even in that stage; and he says "or from the forest" (*vanāt*) when it has not arisen even there. "Without distinction" (*aviśeṣeṇa*) means being devoid of the specific distinctions such as being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth.
For this very reason, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is common to the three castes, according to the Śruti and Smṛti.

The meaning is: "precisely because it is already established. When the words "yadi vā" (or if) are heard in the scripture (*śruti*), the connection is that they would then serve as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark). "Others, however" means those who follow the *Bhāṣya*. "Established by another scriptural passage" means established by another scriptural passage such as "A Brāhmaṇa, having renounced," and so forth.
"Having established [the point]" means that all the scriptural injunctions regarding the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) are syntactically unified under the heading of the *vidyā* (knowledge).
How so?
Because, in the case of the *paramahaṃsa* renunciation, your sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and other such items serve as indicators of your status as a Brahmin.

The meaning is also because of the mention of "four" [castes]. If renunciation were intended here for the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, then just as it is said "how [does] a Brāhmaṇa," one would likewise have heard "how [does] a Kṣatriya" and "how [does] a Vaiśya"; yet this is not heard. Therefore, the sense is that renunciation is not intended by the Śruti for those two castes.

Because, according to the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*), only the meaning of a Smṛti that is not contradicted by Śruti is to be accepted. As for the statement from the Vārtika regarding renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) being an entitlement for all, that refers to the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*), and not to the renunciation of the sick person or of one desiring knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*).

If it is maintained that the realization which severs all eligibility is intended to convey an eligibility contrary to the purport of the Commentary, then how can a restriction of eligibility be forcibly imposed upon one who has emerged [from samādhi]? This is addressed by the subsequent verse concerning the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) immediately after the dawning of the knowledge of Brahman.

Because, when *vidvatsaṃnyāsa* (the renunciation of the knower) is being performed, the restriction regarding eligibility (*adhikāra*) is discarded. And thus, while for Brāhmaṇas alone renunciation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the practice of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas there is eligibility for hearing and so forth even without that [renunciation]. Therefore, for those two...

Regarding the fulfillment of the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth: even on the view that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is required for hearing, it cannot be established as a rule that hearing alone requires it,
since one who has attained the state of being a deity through saguṇa-upāsanā— which has gradual liberation as its fruit— engages in hearing and other practices.
Because it must necessarily be stated that there is no dependence on renunciations.

Thus, since there is unanimity among the rules for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), he states that the Smṛti statement, "whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya," is not authoritative because it is rooted in ignorance of the intended meaning of the Jābāla Śruti; this is according to the principle of the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).
The principle established in the section on contradiction (*virodhādhikaraṇa*) is that a statement in a Smṛti which contradicts direct Śruti is not authoritative.
Therefore, in accordance with the qualification for renunciation found in such Śruti passages as "A Brāhmaṇa, having become learned... and so forth, a Brāhmaṇa should renounce.

This is because the meaning of the sentence is obtained as "one should practice scholarship and so forth. Furthermore, it is the opinion of the venerable commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) that when renunciation for the sake of knowledge (*vidyārtha-saṃnyāsa*) is being performed by one desiring to know (*vividiṣu*), the qualification belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone,
provided that the statement of the Vārtika-kāra is based on authoritative evidence and does not contradict the opinion of the Bhāṣyakāra.
In that context, just as the scriptural statements of Smṛti establishing the universality of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) would have to be rejected, so too would the statement of the Vārtika;
therefore, he says that the Vārtika statement has a meaning not contradicted by the Bhāṣya: "That [refers to] the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*)."

Regarding the phrase "the object": he states another reason why it is not possible for the *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa* (renunciation of the seeker) to be intended as establishing universal eligibility. He says, "universal eligibility," etc.
This is because even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the realization of truth (*tattvajñāna*) is the goal; therefore, the latter [type of renunciation] is not [intended] for Janaka and others.
There is no contradiction with the scriptures that establish the possession of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*),

because for both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas as well, there occurs the renunciation of the learned (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*)— which consists in the cessation of all ritual action— once the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth, which is the prerequisite for eligibility for ritual action, has been removed by the knowledge of reality.

The sense is that, because it is impossible to prevent [the arising of knowledge], just as in the case of the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*), even in the renunciation of the knower (*vidvat-saṃnyāsa*) there can be no restrictive rule (niyama) that only a Brāhmaṇa is qualified; for what reason could such a restriction be forcibly imposed? The meaning is that no such force exists. And "if this is so" (*evaṃ ceti*) means either as a subordinate element of hearing (*śravaṇa*) or as a qualification of the agent.

The meaning is: "this being established"—namely, that only a Brāhmaṇa has the qualification for the renunciation of the seeker (vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa) as a means to the realization of knowledge (vidyā-sādhana).
Now, [an objection is raised]: whether saṃnyāsa is required for hearing (śravaṇa) as a qualification of the qualified person or as an auxiliary factor (aṅga),...

Since it is understood that mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) depends upon renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), it follows as a conclusion that there is no performance of hearing for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who lack the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*); it does not mean, however, that hearing for them is independent of renunciation. And so, how could [hearing] belong to them?
The fulfillment of the practice of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth [is required]. To this, he says "not" (*na hi*). Regarding the phrase "one who has attained the state of a god":

even for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā as a meditator on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsaka*) and has attained the state of a god through that meditation, when hearing and other practices are being performed by the meditator for the sake of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the unqualified Brahman (*nirguṇabrahman*), [there is no requirement for] renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

It should not be argued that this is an inconclusive deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because since the direct realization of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) is possible through the power of the knowledge of the qualified (*saguṇa-vidyā*) alone, there would be no need for the performance of hearing and other practices (*śravaṇādi*).
For in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*, it is primarily the meditator who has attained the state of divinity through the knowledge of the qualified who is the subject.

Since it has already been established during the discussion on the injunction for *śravaṇa* that the qualification of gods and others for *śravaṇa* and so forth depends upon their assuming the form of a human subject (*viṣayākṛti*), and since it was previously shown at that time that even for them knowledge does not arise without the performance of *śravaṇa* and the rest, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is therefore not [required] there, as there would otherwise be an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*).

The meaning is that while [hearing] is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to knowledge], it is specifically hearing performed by a Brāhmaṇa that is the required auxiliary; thus, even though Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas lack the right to renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), their performance of hearing and other practices is still possible.

They say that renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), which consists of the total abandonment of attachment to the performance of rituals, is impossible for the gods because such engagement is inherent to them. Others, however, maintain that it refers to that state of being "established in Brahman" (*brahmasaṃstha*) mentioned in the scripture— "one established in Brahman attains immortality"— which is a complete absorption in Brahman characterized by the absence of any other activity.
Devotion to that [Truth] constitutes one’s primary qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices.

As it is said: "Whether walking or standing, waking or even dreaming, he whose mind is not intent on inquiry is called dead. And: "One should spend the time from birth until death in reflection upon the Vedānta," and so forth.

Because the *Smṛtis* always enjoin non-deliberation [on the Self], and that state of being established in Brahman is not possible for one residing in another stage of life (*āśrama*) without renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), due to the distraction caused by the performance of duties prescribed for their respective stages; therefore, it is not possible for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who lack renunciation.
The primary qualification for hearing [the teachings] and so forth.

[Objection: But how can there be an absence of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) even for the gods? To this he says: "Of the gods. [Objection: If there is an instance of deviation regarding the stage of renunciation in the case of hearing performed by the gods, then let the stage of renunciation be the cause for hearing performed by human beings of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), but not otherwise.
For there is no evidence for such a restriction [to Brahmins alone] when the agency belongs to Brahmins in general;

indeed, it was already stated previously that among the four stages of life (āśrama), the hearing of scripture and so forth must be accomplished specifically by undertaking the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), and that this division of stages is common to all three castes (varṇas) and does not pertain to Brahmins alone. And thus...

Because it is impossible for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who lack renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to have the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth—just as it is for a Brāhmaṇa who possesses renunciation—the author states "But others... out of this sense of inconclusiveness. The connection is that he who is capable of the state of being established in Brahman (brahma-saṃsthā), which is enjoined by the Śruti, has the primary qualification.
The explanation of *saṃsthāpada* is "completion," and its further explanation is "non-otherness.
He also cites scriptural statements (*smṛti*) regarding the necessity of continuous inquiry for one who desires immortality: "whether walking" and "whether sleeping."

The meaning is "of one who is lying down. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including such scriptural statements as, "He lives whose mind lives by thinking alone," and so forth. The meaning is that one devoid of such thinking—that is, reflection on reality—is dead even while living. Furthermore, he states that this primary qualification belongs only to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) with the words "And that... (*sā ca*).

"Due to distraction" (*vaiyagryāt*) means "due to being preoccupied. The sense is that for those who have not renounced, the cessation of mental wandering (*vikṣepa*) does not occur at all times. "Not primary" (*na mukhyaḥ*) means there is no scriptural qualification (*adhikāra*). This is the sense:
by the Śruti text, "One established in Brahman attains immortality," just as by the Śruti on learning (*pāṇḍitya*), [renunciation is required].
It has been established that the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsāśrama) is ordained as having the dharma of being grounded in Brahman (brahmaniṣṭhā),
because the state of being grounded in Brahman— denoted by the term *brahmasaṃsthā*— is possible in the stage of renunciation, whereas it is impossible in the other stages of life.

Furthermore, since steadfastness in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhatva*) is prescribed as a duty of the renunciant order (*saṃnyāsāśrama-dharma*) in the *Bhāṣya* on the section concerning renunciation (*saṃnyāsādhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*) and other texts, steadfastness in Brahman is the inherent duty (*svadharma*) of a Brāhmaṇa who is a renunciant; thus, the renunciant possesses the primary qualification (*mukhya-adhikāra*) for that [practice]. Of him—

Furthermore, because it is understood that there is a transgression (pratyavāya) upon the violation of steadfastness in Brahman, it is likewise heard in the *Paramahaṃsa Upaniṣad*: "He who carries a wooden staff (*kāṣṭhadaṇḍa*), eats all things, and is devoid of knowledge, goes to the terrible hells known as Mahāraurava. Here, [the term] refers to one characterized by the wooden staff.

He by whom the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsāśrama) has been undertaken or accepted— being a "consumer of all" (sarvāśī), meaning one whose habit is to eat or enjoy the entire range of sense objects; that is to say, one who is devoid of mastery over the external and internal organs— and is "devoid of knowledge" (jñānavarjita), meaning lacking the practice of wisdom— who, having renounced [the world], is yet devoid of tranquility (śama) and the other [virtues]...

The meaning is that one who does not practice steadfastness in Brahman goes to an evil state. For example, there are injunctions for renunciants regarding steadfastness in knowledge, such as: "Having renounced, one should engage in hearing [the scriptures]," and "Whether walking or standing, from sleep until death, throughout time," and so forth.

There are thousands of Smṛti statements [to that effect], and likewise there are also thousands of Smṛti statements that declare one to have fallen (pātitya) upon abandoning them; for since renunciation of all actions is ordained by Śruti for the sake of discriminating the meaning of the word "Thou," he who abandons it becomes fallen.

"An ascetic who abandons his obligatory duties (*nityakarman*) and exists without listening to the Vedānta certainly falls; there is no doubt. These and other such statements apply to all stages of life (*āśrama*).
However, since knowledge has a visible purpose, it qualifies even one who merely lacks a prohibition as a seeker for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;
thus, according to the principle stated in the commentary on the section *antarā cāpi tu tad-dṛṣṭeḥ*,
it is by means of that which brings about knowledge in another body— just as in the case of the *śūdra* or those such as the *vidhura* for whom [knowledge] is not prohibited.

It cannot be maintained that the qualification for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, as accepted for Viśvāmitra and others who were not in a formal stage of life (anāśramin), is a primary one based merely on their status as principal figures; for it has been established in the section beginning with "But even in the interval, because of the observation thereof" that such a qualification exists.
It is recorded in the tradition that even for one in the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha), there is great harm in abandoning one's own duty (svadharma), even if it is deficient;
as in such passages as: "Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed; death in one's own duty is better;
the duty of another is fraught with fear," and so forth, as stated by the Commentator himself in the *Sannyāsa-adhikaraṇa*.

Intending all of this, it is stated explicitly that for a renunciant who does not perform the cultivation of hearing [the scriptures] by means of being free from other activities, there is a fall from grace;
and thus the Commentary [says]: "For his state of being established in Brahman alone is augmented by tranquility and the other [virtues]."
Just as ritual acts such as the sacrifice (karmayajña) prescribed for one’s own stage of life (āśrama) are incumbent upon others, and there is sin (pratyavāya) in their transgression, so too,
because hearing (śravaṇa) and the rest are prescribed for the mendicant (bhikṣu),

and because it is understood that the mendicant incurs sin by transgressing them, the renunciant (saṃnyāsin) possesses the primary qualification (adhikāra) for hearing and the other [means of knowledge].

However, for those who have not renounced the world (*saṃnyāsa*), since hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth are not prescribed for them, and since no transgression (*pratyavāya*) is understood to arise from their non-performance, there is no primary qualification (*adhikāra*) for them. To this, one might object: "Why is it not simply stated that, in the absence of injunctions for hearing and so forth directed toward Kṣatriyas and others, they lack qualification altogether? Thus he raises the doubt.

"But what [is the case]?"—the commentary provides the answer: "Even though a primary qualification in the form of a permanent obligation (*nityādhikāra*) is impossible, it is not so because a secondary qualification in the form of a voluntary obligation (*kāmyādhikāra*) is possible. And:
"And [the study] has a visible purpose. But is the inference of hearing the Vedas (*śravaṇa*) and so forth based merely on this secondary qualification?

The connection [of the inquiry] is as follows: Just as the act of eating has a visible fruit consisting in the cessation of the affliction of hunger, so too knowledge (vidyā) has a visible fruit established by scripture consisting in the cessation of ignorance (avidyā), which is the root of all evils;
and thus, for those who desire the cessation of evil in that knowledge...

The qualification characterized by the desire for [knowledge] is possible for all indeed. Thus, when the qualification for hearing the Vedānta and so forth would follow without distinction for all those qualified for knowledge, it was stated in the *Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa* that the Śūdra lacks such qualification because of the prohibition against hearing the Veda and so forth.

The meaning is that, because there is likewise no prohibition for Kṣatriyas and others, their eligibility for hearing the Vedānta is accepted by the Bhāṣya, just as in the case of widowers and similar persons. Now, one might object: even when hearing and other practices are performed by those who are only secondary eligible candidates, they must necessarily produce knowledge.
Otherwise, it must be stated that the Bhāṣya, which aims to define the secondary qualification (*gauṇādhikāra*), would be rendered purposeless.

Furthermore, if the production of knowledge were inevitable [even for those with secondary qualifications], then the qualification for optional rites (*kāmyādhikāra*) could not be considered secondary, since there would be no difference between primary and secondary qualifications regarding the result; therefore, he says: "in another body."

The point is this: for the primary qualified aspirants, hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, performed daily with undistracted application and accompanied by unrestrained celibacy, non-violence, tranquility, self-restraint, and the like, generally results in the production of knowledge (*vidyā*) in this very life.

However, for those who are not primary qualified candidates (*amukhyādhikārin*), hearing and the other means of knowledge do not result in the production of wisdom in this very life, because they lack the state of being single-mindedly devoted to such practice and because they are joined with a restricted observance of celibacy and other vows;
rather, in many births, they must accomplish hearing and the rest in whatever measure is possible.

Thus, by coming together [in this life], one may produce such knowledge in some future body; therefore, there is a great difference in the results between the secondary and primary forms of qualification. And so says the Smṛti: "Having attained perfection through many births, he then reaches the supreme goal. This means that in some birth, one becomes perfected through the merit of many births, such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth.
The meaning of the Smṛti is that one who has produced knowledge and is constant attains liberation through the power of perfection (*siddhi*). Now, an objection is raised:

"It is incorrect to say that for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, widowers, and so forth, there is a secondary qualification (*amukhya-adhikāra*), because the supporting example is not accepted. To this, he says: "Indeed not," which connects with the statement that "it cannot indeed be said [otherwise]."
Therefore, because the author of the Sūtras himself clarified that their qualification is secondary by stating, "But the other [is] superior on account of the indicative mark" (Sūtra 3.4.37),
it is not the case that only their qualification for hearing is denied there; rather,
it is their [specific] ritual actions that are addressed.

It cannot be suspected that [the study] serves as a support for knowledge (*vidyā*), because this would contradict the commentary on that very section (*adhikaraṇa-bhāṣya*) which states that knowledge has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Nor can it be argued that, due to the absence of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, they possess only a secondary qualification; for by that same logic, the same would apply to the gods as well.

In the case of hearing [the Vedas] and so forth, the qualification would be non-primary; and thus, for those who, having attained the state of divinity through qualified knowledge (*saguṇavidyā*) which has gradual liberation as its fruit, perform hearing and other practices,
it must be stated that there is a subsequent birth as a Brahmin— fit for renunciation— for the sake of attaining excellence.

It should not be argued that this contradicts scriptural texts and sūtras such as, "He attains Brahman and does not return; there is no returning" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.15.1), because for the gods, since there is an absence of neglect in the performance of their duties, it is possible for them to possess a state of non-other-directed activity by their very nature;
thus, [the path] leads to the fruit of liberation in due order.

They say that even the injunction for knowledge with attributes (saguṇavidyā) is established by the authority of the scriptures as having primary eligibility for those [householders] even without renunciation (saṃnyāsa).

Although it has been established previously that only renunciants (saṃnyāsins) possess the primary qualification, and thus the secondary qualification of widowers and others is already established by the mere absence of renunciation for them, [the author] nevertheless states the reasoning—though already summarized in the Sūtra—for their secondary qualification: "But from this, the other [is established]. From this, [it follows that the path] is practiced even by those who do not belong to any [specific] stage of life (anāśramin).
In comparison with the means for attaining knowledge practiced by those belonging to other stages of life (*āśrama*),
the performance of rituals such as hearing the Vedas (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— which are means for attaining knowledge— performed by one in the householder stage (*vānaprastha*) is more excellent;

the word "but" (*tu*) is used for the purpose of determining this superiority, based on both the indicative mark of the Śruti and the indicative mark of the Smṛti, as expressed in the phrase "by that he goes."

The statement "the knower of Brahman is a doer of merit" (*brahmavid puṇyakṛt*) is an indicative mark from the Śruti. The statement "a twice-born man should not remain even for a single moment without belonging to an āśrama," and so forth, is an indicative mark from the Smṛti. Therefore, the meaning of the Śruti is that by means of the knowledge of Brahman obtained through merit, one goes to Brahman—that is, one attains Brahman. In this Śruti passage, [it is understood] by way of its being merit...

Since it is established that the very duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*)— as they are well-known— are specifically taught to be the means for attaining Brahman, there is a special favor accorded to those who do not belong to a stage of life; thus, by the logic stated in the Sūtra, even those [duties] conducive to knowledge appear to be inferior, and that inferiority pertains to the ritual acts performed by widowers and others for the sake of knowledge.
It must be stated that [the lack of qualification] regarding hearing and so forth is indeed caused by the absence of primary qualification;
for, since there is no other state [of life] apart from the [four] stages of life (āśrama), and because the state of being without an āśrama is censured,
one who is primarily qualified for action (karma) and knowledge (jñāna) is not fit for censure— this is the intention of both the author of the Sūtras and the author of the Bhāṣya.

This is the meaning. Now, an objection is raised: in the *Vidhurādhikaraṇa*, it was stated only that actions performed by those such as the *vidhura* (those lacking a wife) are means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*), but it was not established therein that such persons also possess the qualification (*adhikāra*) for hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*). And thus, regarding the qualification of the *vidhura* and others for hearing and so forth—
Anticipating the objection that there might be consideration of primary and secondary status regarding the support [of the meditation], he refutes it with the words "And not there.
This means in the section concerning those without a spouse (*vidhurādhikaraṇa*). "Precisely from that" means precisely because of the absence of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).
To the objection that one might attain birth again as a Brāhmaṇa, he says: "The world of Brahman. "He does not return again."

The meaning is that having attained the world of Brahman (brahmaloka), one does not return again to this world. He cites the aphorism which has this very scripture as its source: "Non-return" (anāvṛti). "Non-return" means the absence of return. The meaning is that for those meditators who have gone to the world of Brahman, there is no return, according to the cited scripture.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) is used for the purpose of including such sūtras as "And because of Smṛti," and likewise there is the Smṛti: "When the dissolution arrives at the end of the highest [Brahmā], all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state along with Brahmā. These are the inhabitants of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).

Those who worship Brahman are such that, during the *pratisaṃcara*—the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—they have realized the Self of the Supreme Hiraṇyagarbha, the lord of the Brahma-world, as their own essence.

Now, one might object: "Even if other activities are possible for them, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) does not exist [for them]. Anticipating this, he says: "In the case of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*)."

The meaning is that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the primary determinant of eligibility only among human beings, because the division of social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama) pertains exclusively to humans.

But surely, for one who is not a primary qualified candidate (*amukhyādhikārī*), how can the investigation of Vedānta— which is undertaken for the sake of understanding the meaning of the sentences that constitute its unseen fruit (*adṛṣṭaphala*)— be useful toward the attainment of knowledge in another birth, given that it is like an investigation into other scriptures not prescribed [for that purpose]? Indeed, the investigation does not [bear fruit] on another day...
It is logical that [the hearing of scripture] is a cause for comprehension through inquiry; nor should it be argued that its causality pertains to a distant future birth,
because even when performed by a wandering ascetic (parivrājaka), who is the primary qualified candidate, the hearing has a visible purpose alone,
since in all cases comprehension resulting from inquiry yields a visible fruit, just as in the case of [other worldly activities].

This is because it has been determined in the relevant section (*adhikaraṇa*) that karma in the form of a specific *prārabdha* (commenced) action, which does not produce its fruit in this life due to an obstacle, produces its fruit in another birth once the obstacle has been removed; for such a phenomenon is observed even in the case of obstacles pertaining to this life.

Thus, it might also apply to that which is performed by one who is not authorized (*anadhikārin*). For, in the view that [the injunction] is an *apūrva-vidhi* (an original injunction), the scripturally enjoined hearing (*śravaṇa*)—when conjoined with its auxiliary factors (*aṅga*)—produces an unprecedented transcendental result (*apūrva*) culminating in the fruit;

whereas in the view that it is a *niyama-vidhi* (a restrictive injunction), it produces the unseen merit of restriction (*niyamādṛṣṭa*). And that [result] is the state of remembering one's past births (*jātismaratva*).

Since the means of attainment, like perception, awaken the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous birth and thereby establish the utility of the inquiry rooted therein for knowledge in another life,
it is held that hearing (*śravaṇa*) devoid of the scriptural auxiliaries does not produce *adṛṣṭa*; how then could such [hearing] [be effective]?
The utility of knowledge from a previous birth is established; for, were it not for the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) acting as a connector,
there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting that the operation of a means of valid cognition from a previous birth is the cause of comprehension in another birth.

Regarding the term "not prescribed" (*avihita*): the meaning is that it is like the investigation of the *Nyāya-śāstra* and other such systems. [The author] confirms, by means of a *kaimutika* (a fortiori) argument, the impossibility of the investigation of Vedānta performed in this life being a cause for the comprehension of the meaning of Vedānta in a future life. It is not... [the case].

The word "indeed" (*khalu*) serves to raise an objection: by means of the example of the inquiry performed by the primary qualified seeker (*mukhyādhikārī*), one might suspect that even for the secondary qualified seeker (*gauṇādhikārī*), hearing and so forth may be of use toward knowledge acquired in another birth. To this, he says: "And it should not be said," and then, to explain what follows from that, he says:
"Of that," meaning that just as for that hearing performed by the primary qualified seeker, there is [an effect] in this life due to the absence of obstacles.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: it should not be argued that just as knowledge, though failing to produce its fruit in this life, produces the fruit in another birth, so too even the hearing performed by one who lacks primary qualification would produce the fruit in another birth.

He states the authority for the claim that the birth of knowledge occurs in the next life when there is an obstacle to the hearing performed by one who is primarily qualified [for it]: "Even in this life" (*aihikam api*). This means that when no obstacle is present to what has been undertaken, the birth of knowledge occurs even in this very birth; from the word "even" (*api*), it follows that when an obstacle is present, it occurs in another birth. Why? Because that is observed (*taddarśanāt*). Of that...

The meaning is that, due to the influence of obstacles, the arising of knowledge in another birth is observed in the case of Vāmadeva and others. He provides an answer by pointing out the disparity with the illustrative example: "joined with scriptural auxiliaries" means joined with the scriptural auxiliary, namely renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*); that is to say, it is being practiced by one who has renounced.

And thus, in the view that the injunction for hearing (*śravaṇa-vidhi*)— which is accompanied by the scriptural auxiliaries— is an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*), it itself produces an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) culminating in the fruit characterized as knowledge.
However, in the view that the injunction for hearing is a restrictive injunction (*niyama-vidhi*), hearing performed by one such as myself, being qualified by that restriction, [produces the result].

The meaning is that [the practice] produces an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) by way of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) until the attainment of the fruit. And "that" refers to the unseen merit produced by hearing (*śravaṇa*). Regarding the word "birth" (*jāti*): *jāti* means birth; therefore, just as the unseen merit that brings about the recollection of births (*jāti-smaratva*) arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of events in a previous life, so too [in this case].

Just as [the Guru] awakens [the latent impression] in this birth and thereby effects the recollection of the events of the previous birth through that awakening, so too, by awakening the latent impression produced by hearing and other means in a prior existence,
he establishes the utility of that very hearing— which served as the cause of that impression— for the acquisition of knowledge in the future birth.

The meaning is that it brings about [the result]. Regarding the phrase "devoid of scriptural auxiliary factors" (*śāstrīyāṅgavidhura*): the idea is that the hearing (*śravaṇa*) performed by Kṣatriyas and others who lack renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) does not produce the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because hearing and so forth have not been prescribed for Kṣatriyas and the like.
[Objection: But it has not been prescribed...

Even though hearing [the scripture] does not produce an unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), it is possible for it to generate a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). One might ask: "By the power of that [impression] alone, why could it not be the cause of knowledge in another birth?
To this he says: "without the *adṛṣṭa* that acts as a facilitator. This is because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding what was experienced in another birth.
The meaning is that it would entail the undesirable consequence of remembering all objects simultaneously.

It is said: even by one who is not a primary qualified candidate (*amukhyādhikārī*), but who has generated the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*), the hearing (*śravaṇa*) performed is impelled by the *apūrva* (unseen potency) produced by the performance of ancient sacrifices and other rites which generate that very door-like desire for knowledge; thus, it is that same *apūrva* which extends until the fruit in the form of realized knowledge (*vidyā*).
