There is no inconsistency, for [the effort] being exerted serves to bring about the assistance of one's own hearing (śravaṇa) even toward knowledge acquired in another birth. However, in the view that there is no injunction regarding hearing and so forth, even that which was performed prior to renunciation—

Since hearing (*śravaṇa*) does not produce an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), its status as a cause for knowledge in another birth must be explained in this very way when an obstacle exists. The Teachers (*ācāryas*), however, maintain that even under the view that it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*), this same explanation applies to one who practices hearing repeatedly.
Because the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from that discipline does not arise if one dies before attaining the fruit,

since that merit is to be accomplished through the performance of the discipline of hearing (*śravaṇa*), which has the quality of functioning until the attainment of the result; for the discipline of hearing, which generates the unseen merit of discipline, is not something to be repeated until the end of the fruit.
By the mere commencement of which [hearing], [the result] is accomplished;
by which it is possible that even the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced thereby arises prior to the completion of the hearing, until its fruit is reached.
He offers a rebuttal by relying on the position that there is an application of ritual actions toward knowledge (*vidyā*). He says: "It is replied. The meaning is as follows:
when knowledge is to be accomplished through sacrifices and other means, there is the desire to know (*vividiṣā*) which serves as the gateway;
[the result] is produced by that previous performance of sacrifices and so forth for the sake of knowledge. Thus, it is born from that.
In the view of Vācaspati, the term *svapadam* (one's own state) refers to the *apūrva* (unseen merit) produced by the performance of sacrifices and other such rites;

he states this with the intention of providing an illustration, namely that even for one who has performed hearing (*śravaṇa*) as a primary qualified person, its fulfillment occurs solely through the *apūrva* of sacrifice and so forth. However, in the case where there is an absence of injunctions regarding hearing and the rest, [he says] "but in the case of the absence of injunctions regarding hearing and so on. — Vivaraṇa.
He states that the explanation is exactly the same even for the other [view] with the words, "But the Teacher... The intended meaning is as follows:

the removal of doubt regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*); the removal of doubt regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the fruit of reflection (*manana*);
and the removal of contrary notions (*viparītabhāvanā*) is the fruit of meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*). And thus...

For that primary seeker in whom hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other means have reached completion— characterized by the removal of the threefold obstacles and culminating in the fruit— the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the observance of rules (*niyamādṛṣṭa*) has indeed arisen. Likewise, even for one who has fully prepared the means for knowledge (*vidyā*), if knowledge does not arise due to the force of obstacles, then [the unseen merit remains].
When the obstacles are destroyed through the attainment of another birth, knowledge arises without even requiring further inquiry,

as was the case with Vāmadeva, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others. However, for one who has died in the interim before the repetition of hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth— extending until the removal of the aforementioned obstacles— has occurred, even if he is a primary qualified candidate (*mukhyādhikārī*).

The unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the observance of rules (*niyama*) does not arise [in this life]. Furthermore, in another birth, having practiced hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth until the cessation of the aforementioned obstacles, by virtue of the unseen merit of the rules of hearing and so forth—

When the impurities that obstruct knowledge have been destroyed, one attains knowledge. As it was said by the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa: "There he regains that same connection with wisdom belonging to his former body, and from there he strives even further toward perfection, O Joy of the Kurus. Thus, when that auspicious birth has been obtained in a previous body...

Now, this existence, continuing in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), attains a connection with the intellect through the conjunction of the intellect—that is, a connection with the understanding that hearing and so forth are duties. Even in this life, by means of the removal of obstacles, there arises the realization: "This hearing and so forth must be performed for the sake of the dawn of knowledge."

The meaning is that he becomes endowed with discernment (*buddhi*). Therefore, the meaning is that whatever is "more" (*bhūyaḥ*)—that is, greater—than his wife from a previous birth, that [effort] is for the sake of his perfection (*saṃsiddhi*). And thus, regarding this one who has fallen from yoga (*yogabhraṣṭa*), who is devoid of hearing and other practices characterized by repetition until the attainment of the fruit:

Since there is no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restrictive rule (*niyama*), the accomplishment [of the goal] must proceed solely from the unseen merit of the sacrifice (*yajña*) and so forth. He states the reason why the unseen merit of the restrictive rule does not arise prior to the attainment of the fruit, which consists in the removal of obstacles, with the words "of that" (*tasya*). This means "of the unseen merit of the restrictive rule. For the unseen merit of the restrictive rule is not produced by mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone.

However, that [result] is produced by the restriction (*niyama*) of hearing (*śravaṇa*); and that restriction is accomplished only when there is a repetition of hearing and so forth until the attainment of the fruit. Thus, the meaning is that prior to the arising of the fruit, because the restriction of hearing and so forth does not exist, the production of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction does not occur. He elaborates on what has been stated: "No."
By the words beginning with "hi," etc.

Just as in the case of threshing and other such acts, since it is only the hearing characterized by repetition that is heard to be the means for attaining the fruit, any statement regarding the necessity of that [hearing] prior to the accomplishment of the ritual act which is the means to the fruit would be without a basis.

They say that if the completion of the restriction (*niyama*) were achieved merely by the initial commencement of acts such as hearing or threshing, then the performance of the restrictive injunction would be accomplished by that alone; consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-deficiency even when those acts are not repeated. However, some [hold] that even for that which has a visible purpose...
On the day of Śravaṇā, by hearing the Vedānta with devotion—

obtained through service to the Guru— one obtains the fruit of eighty *kṛcchra* penances; according to the authority of such scriptural statements, it also possesses the capacity to produce an independent unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), just like [the performance of] fire-sacrifices (*agni*).
Since the act of kindling (*ādhāna*), which has the purpose of consecration (*saṃskāra*), is enumerated among the consecrations of the person, it also serves that purpose.

Thus, by the force of the scriptural statement, its dual purpose is established; and so, through the very power of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by daily recitation, it serves as a means for knowledge pertaining to the hereafter.
They say [this refers] to the means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*). Thus,

this being established as a point universally accepted— that the attainment of knowledge occurs through the mediation of the practice of means such as hearing and reflection— Bhāratītīrtha, in his *Dhyānadīpa*, states:
They also state that there is another means for the attainment of knowledge.

Regarding the fact that the rule of hearing (*śravaṇa-niyama*) is not fulfilled by the mere commencement of hearing, he states the reason: "like threshing, etc. This refers to the fact that threshing is characterized by repetition (*āvṛtti*).

The sense is that the fact of [hearing] being the means for achieving the result characterized by the production of rice is established by worldly experience. Prior to that—meaning, while there is repetition of hearing alone until the result is reached—the restriction (niyama), characterized by the fulfillment of unattained portions of the hearing, becomes accomplished; it is not [otherwise].

The meaning is that [the rule] refers to what precedes that; or rather, once the mere commencement of hearing (*śravaṇa*) has occurred, or even after only a few repetitions have taken place, the statement that "the rule of hearing is fulfilled" is without support because its object is non-existent.
The phrase "even when there is no repetition" means that having begun the performance of hearing, threshing, and so forth, one performs the hearing and other such acts.

The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of no contradiction with the rules of discipline even when one engages in activities such as scratching with the nails, having abandoned the study of grammar, composition, and so forth. [This applies] to the hearing of the Vedānta being performed daily by the primary qualified practitioners.
Some, however, offer this resolution: just as [the study of scripture] produces a visible result in the form of the removal of obstacles, it also produces an invisible result (*adṛṣṭa*);

and thus, by the power of that [invisible result], the utility of inquiry for the sake of knowledge in another birth is possible. "Result" here means a result in the form of merit (*puṇya*). As for the statement: [The text continues: "But in the statement..."

And the word "ca" (and) [is used] with respect to the object. Thus, the sense is that the word "tu" (but/and) signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the hearing of Vedānta, as well as with devotion toward the deities, the teacher, and the subject matter of Vedānta, and with service to the teacher—both those already undertaken and those not yet undertaken—as well as with tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), celibacy (*brahmacarya*), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), and so forth. [The term] "svatantra" (independent).
The meaning is that the hearing of Vedānta possesses the capacity to produce *adṛṣṭa* independently.

It should be understood that "independence" refers to the hearing's lack of dependence on the injunction for hearing—which prescribes its application toward knowledge—for the generation of *adṛṣṭa*. Regarding the case where a single thing serves both purposes:
He states an illustration:

"Just as [the injunction] 'one should establish the fires' (agnīn ādadhīta) implies that the act of establishment (*ādhāna*) is accepted as a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *āhavanīya* and other fires—this is the sense. Regarding the refinements of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāreṣu*)."

The meaning is that even the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is included within the aphorism beginning with "the establishment of the fire" (*agnyādheya*) and "the fire-oblation" (*agnihotra*), which summarizes the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of a person. Regarding the phrase "by the power of the unseen" (*adṛṣṭamahimnaiva*):
it refers to the fact that the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by hearing the Vedānta is, by its very nature, applied exclusively to knowledge (*vidyā*).

The sense is that, by virtue of being subject to discourse [on these matters], there is the utility of knowledge pertaining to other births through the power of that [discourse]. Thus, having described the path of Sāṃkhya for the superior and middling qualified aspirants (adhikārin), he begins to describe the path of Yoga for those who are unable to follow that, namely the extremely dull-witted qualified aspirants. He does so with the word "evam" (thus).
"Sarvasaṃpratipanna" means correctly understood or ascertained in all the Śrutis and Smṛtis;
"āhuḥ" means they have properly determined.

The cause of that [liberation] is attained through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, for as seen in Śruti and Smṛti— according to the statement, "That state which is reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is also reached by the followers of Yoga"— Sāṃkhya is the investigation of Vedānta, designated by the term *śravaṇa* (listening), which, when accompanied by *manana* (reflection) and so forth, is the means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*).

Thus, even the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma), which is designated by the term "yoga," exists. Nor should it be doubted that there is no such thing as meditation on the attributeless [Brahman], for in the Praśnopaniṣad, in the inquiry of Śaibya, it is stated: "But he who meditates upon this Supreme Person with the three-moraed syllable Om..."
Since the meditation on the attributeless [Brahman] alone is being propounded,

immediately thereafter— in the statement regarding the fruit of that meditation, "He beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the highest, beyond the mass of living beings"— that [Brahman] is indicated as the object of the act of beholding (*īkṣati*).
That which is the qualityless Brahman is the very same object of meditation even in the meditative injunctions; one does not meditate on one thing and perceive another,

because of the rule that meditation (*dhyāna*) and perception (*īkṣaṇa*), standing in the relation of cause and effect, must have a single object— this being accepted by the author of the Bhāṣya and others in the section concerning the perception of action (*īkṣatikarmādhikaraṇa*).
However, one should not be deluded into thinking that [the Sāṃkhyas] imagined this as something newly invented; for it is established by the Śruti and other authorities.

The meaning of the Śruti passage is that Brahman—characterized by its causality, which is the subject at hand—is attained through knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, in a direct and immediate manner (*pratyak*). This is understood by the Sāṃkhyas who are devoted to hearing [the scriptures] (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.

The meaning is that the state which is the nature of Brahman is reached—that is, attained—by yogins and upāsakas through the means of knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even by yogas," it should be understood that this indicates the status of the path of yoga as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
The word "also" implies that "knowledge" is to be supplied as the means of attainment; thus, the meditation on the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma-upāsana*) is the authority.

Anticipating the objection that [the world] is empty, he refutes it with the words "And not," and so forth. Now, this doubt is indeed not appropriate, because the Sāṃkhyas have already cited Śruti and Smṛti at the very outset as authoritative evidence for that [position]. Nor is it the case that the word *yoga* found in the cited Śruti and Smṛti refers to the meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman.
It should not be said that the doubt arises because of the possibility of [the two] being different;
for since there can be no causal relationship between meditation and direct realization when they have different objects,
it follows necessarily that the yoga which is the cause of the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa-vidyā) must itself take the form of meditation on the attributeless.

It should not be argued that the claim that the word *yoga* in the phrase "and by the Sāṃkhyas" refers exclusively to meditation (*upāsti*) is unproven, because it has been explained in the *Gītā-bhāṣya* as referring to the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). For the statement "that which [is attained] by the Sāṃkhyas," while in fact referring to the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), was [interpreted] by the Blessed One...

Because Śrī Kṛṣṇa has cited this regarding the subject of action (*karman*), it is appropriate that it is explained accordingly in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*). Since the word *yoga* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) in the sense of meditation (*dhyāna*), it does not actually have action as its primary meaning. Furthermore, in the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) which is the source of that statement, namely "that is the cause" (*tatkāraṇam*), [the context supports this].

Furthermore, since the term *yoga-pada* has been explained in the *Śārīrakabhāṣya* as being synonymous with meditation (*dhyāna*), it is possible that the Blessed One cited this statement regarding action (*karman*) in order to make it known that the yoga of action is a means for attaining Brahman through the gateway of the primary yoga, and not directly; and because such an illustration by the Blessed One is indeed possible.

If it is argued that doubt is not appropriate because there is a lack of authoritative evidence (*māna*), we say no; for such a doubt arises from the intention that, apart from the Śrutis and Smṛtis cited, nowhere else is the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman observed. It is precisely for this reason that the meditation on the attributeless is seen in all the Śrutis.

The Ācārya has stated that even one of dull capacity [attains the goal] by means of the *praṇava* (Oṃ), citing the *Praśnopaniṣad* and other texts. In the phrase "by means of the three-syllabled" (*trimātreṇa*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, it refers to the *oṃkāra* which possesses three *mātrās* known as *a*, *u*, and *m*.
Regarding the point that in the *oṃkāra* one should meditate upon Brahman itself—which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)—as non-different from it, there is the commentary (*bhāṣya*) and so forth.

He states the consensus: "Immediately thereafter" is the meaning. The "jīva-mass" (jīva-ghana) is the dense form of the Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness limited by adjuncts (upādhi), like the space within a jar; "higher than that" refers to the Person (puruṣa), the unconditioned Supreme Self. That meditator [perceives] Him as the witness of the intellect within the space of the heart in the city [of the body].

"He beholds" (*īkṣate*) means that he directly perceives (*sākṣātkāroti*). "In the passage concerning meditation" (*upāsanā-vākye*) means in the sentence "one should meditate upon the Supreme Person" (*paraṃ puruṣam abhidhyāyīta*).
[The term] "resulting from action" (*kārya*) is used because the passage concerning beholding establishes the direct perception that is the fruit of meditation.

The meaning is that because of the syntactical unity of the injunctive statements, the relationship of cause and effect between the two meditations is understood. Regarding the phrase "due to the restriction": the meaning is that [the result follows] from meditation on one thing and not from the direct realization of something else. Furthermore, this has been elaborated elsewhere in other scriptural passages such as the *Tāpanīya* and the *Kaṭhavallī*.

Therefore, even by the author of the Sūtras, in the section on the "Combination of Attributes" (*Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda*)— which was commenced for the purpose of delimiting the attributes to be meditated upon— it is stated in the sūtra, "Bliss and so forth [belong] to the Principal even in the case of the attributeless," that there is a "comprehension of the attributes consisting of positive entities such as knowledge and bliss," and so on, as well as the "restraint of the cognitions regarding the Imperishable" (*akṣara-dhiyām*).

Furthermore, because the scripture has demonstrated the inclusion of qualities such as "not gross" (*asthūlatva*) and others which are of the nature of negation; [one might object: "But if there is an inclusion of qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*), then the object of meditation would not be *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities)," [we reply:
no.

Because it is impossible to practice meditation upon Brahman as being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*) without destroying [the very nature of] that which is characterized by bliss and so forth, and by qualities such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so on—as in the realization "I am Brahman, the indivisible single essence"—[an objection is raised]:
"But surely the Supreme Brahman is not to be meditated upon, for the Śruti says: 'Know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship.'"
Volition.
Now, it might be argued that in the *Kalpataru*, because the person to be meditated upon resides within the sun—
according to the statement of the *Sūryasaptati* that "he becomes merged in that splendor of the sun"— the qualifying attribute was provided; thus,
the authors of the *Kalpataru* do not accept that the person to be meditated upon in the syllable *Oṃ* is of the nature of the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.

If it is argued that [the soul] "attains" [the sun], we say no; for in the fourth chapter, it has been established that the statement regarding the "attainment of the sun" intends the attainment of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*), and not the attainment of the sun itself or the Lord residing within it.
This is also the view of the authors of the *Kalpataru*, as can be seen by considering other statements of theirs.

The sense is that the *Parimala* has established that there is no intention in the scripture to provide the qualification of "being situated within the sun" because the text is devoted to the path (*mārga*). Furthermore, the *Ātmapurāṇa* (or *Ātmanopaniṣad*) Śruti begins: "The gods indeed said to Pratipad: 'Explain this Self to us as the syllable Om, subtler than the subtle'"; thus [it speaks of] the subtle.

The meaning is that this Supreme Self, who is subtler than the subtle, whose nature is immediate, and who is accessible through the syllable *oṃ*, is difficult to know. For this very reason, there is the Kaṭha Upaniṣad scripture beginning with "This imperishable is indeed Brahman," and the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad scripture beginning with "All this is this imperishable syllable *oṃ*"; [and it is said] "Meditate thus upon *oṃ*."

The *Muṇḍaka-śruti* passage beginning with "the Self" (*ātmānam*) refers to the primary subject matter. He cites the consensus of the author of the *Sūtras* regarding the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman by stating, "by the author of the *Sūtras* as well.

The connection is that the author of the *Sūtras* has demonstrated the inclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) of attributes even in the case of the attributeless; thus, there is an inclusion of attributes within the attributeless.

To exclude the doubt that this section aims solely at the knowledge (*pramiti*) of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*) and not at the meditation (*upāsti*) upon it, the author qualifies the section by stating: "for the purpose of determining the qualities of the object of meditation. "Determination" (*pariccheda*) means ascertainment; thus, the description of the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāra*) regarding the attributeless Brahman has as its fruit even the meditation upon that attributeless reality.
The sense is that otherwise, it would follow that the investigation [of those qualities] would lack connection with the respective sections (*pāda*).

Attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, though heard in one place, must be brought over (*upasaṃhartavya*) to other places as well, because the primary object of knowledge, Brahman, is the same.

The meaning of the sūtra is that because the knowledge of Brahman is one and the same without distinction across all Vedāntas. It should be understood that the qualification "of those [attributes] consisting of positive entities" is intended to avoid redundancy with the section on "Bliss and so forth" (*ānandādayaḥ*) within the section on the "cognitions of the Imperishable" (*akṣaradhiyaḥ*), as these pertain to the Imperishable Brahman.

The meaning of the portion of the Sūtra is that those negations— which constitute the referents expressed by words such as "not gross" (asthūla) and so forth— must indeed be included, that is, subsumed, within the other Vedānta texts; for the intention is that the prohibitions of grossness and so forth serve as the cause for the realization of Brahman as devoid of phenomenal manifestation (niṣprapañca).

An objection is raised: "But surely... [The author] replies: "It is not admitted that qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) are included within the category of the object of meditation, by which the Brahman to be meditated upon would become possessed of qualities (*saguṇa*); rather, it is accepted that they serve merely as a means for the meditation on the qualityless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman, by way of determining that the object of meditation is indeed qualityless."

No; for what is intended by the "combination" (*upasaṃhāra*) of qualities such as bliss (*ānanda*) and qualities such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) is the simultaneous utterance of the words denoting them. Thus, by means of words like "bliss," which denote consciousness qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [one understands] that which is qualified by the absence of grossness and so forth.

The meaning is that by means of words denoting consciousness, such as "not gross" (*asthūla*) and so forth, that which is the indivisible and immediate Brahman—pervading all denoted objects—is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); for otherwise, meditation in the form "I am He" would not be possible. And it has been said in the *Dhyānadīpa*:

"One should meditate thus: 'I am He who is indicated by [attributes] such as bliss and the like, and by [negations] such as not coarse and the like, and who is the indivisible single essence. Here, "in this" means in the Vedāntas. Having thus established through both scripture and aphorism that the Nirguṇa Brahman is the object of meditation, [the text proceeds to discuss] the meditation upon the Nirguṇa.

He anticipates and resolves the contradiction with another scriptural passage, beginning with "But that very [Self]," and so forth. The phrase "that very" means the witnessing-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) itself, such as the intellect (buddhi) and so on.

Because of the scriptural statement, "It is indeed other than the known, and also other than the unknown," there arises the contingency that even its status as an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) is unestablished. Since the knowledge of Brahman is well-known in other scriptures, the scriptural passage regarding its being unknowable must be intended to mean that it is unknowable in reality (*vāstavāvedyatva*). Thus says the Atharvaṇa.

Since its worship is well-established, even the scriptural statement regarding its non-worshipability must be understood as referring to the ultimate reality (*vastuvṛtta*). And thus, from the scriptural passage:

"He who is not obtained for hearing even by many," [it follows that] there are those who, due to dullness of intellect or because they have not obtained a qualified teacher skilled in the exposition of logic, do not hear it.

The former is not possible; for those who, through the study of the Vedas they have mastered, have attained a superficial understanding of the identity of Brahman and the Self, [there would be liberation] even without inquiry into that [identity],
based on the texts of the sages such as the *Praśna Upaniṣad* and others, and the *Brahma*, *Vāsiṣṭha*, and other *kalpas*.

Furthermore, having ascertained from gurus who know the tradition alone the method of practicing the meditation on the attributeless [Brahman]— which, like the Agnihotra and other rites, has its mode of performance determined in the Kalpasūtras by synthesizing all the various matters scattered across numerous branches such as the Pañcīkaraṇa— one should proceed.
Through the performance of that [practice], by worshipping in due order, the direct realization of the attributeless Brahman as the true reality is accomplished.
He says, "It is indeed other," because just as the status of Brahman is denied for that which is to be worshipped, so too is the status of Brahman denied for that which is to be known;

thus, even the knowledge of the Supreme Brahman would not be established. When it is stated that Brahman is other than the object of knowledge, it follows by implication that Brahman is not something to be known.

The meaning is that it is established. The sense is that the purport of the prohibitive scriptures (*niṣedha-śruti*) is that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), neither the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) nor the state of being an object of meditation (*upāsyatva*) exists in Brahman. He shows the qualified aspirant for the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇopāsana*):
"If this is so" means, provided that the meditation on the attributeless is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For some...

He states the authoritative proof for those desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) when hearing [the teachings] is impossible: "The Supreme Self, whom many seekers of liberation are unable even to hear—of that which remains unheard, direct realization is cast far away. This means that if hearing is not attained by many, direct realization is considered impossible by the Śruti.
He shows the reason with the words "of those who. Regarding the word "intellect," it is stated in the *Dhyānadīpa*:

"Because of extreme dullness of intellect, or because the collection of [necessary] means is impossible, he who does not obtain inquiry should worship Brahman constantly. Therein, he explains the absence of the collection of means with the word "Nyāya" (logic).

The meaning is that for those whose intellect is so extremely dull that hearing [the teachings] and so forth are not possible, and for those of even virtuous intellect for whom hearing and so forth are not possible due to a lack of the necessary conditions (*sāmagrī*). "Distinction" (*viśiṣṭatva*) should be understood as characterized by such qualities as having unmixed noble boundaries (*ārya-maryādā*) and being compassionate (*kāruṇikatva*).

He states the reason for their desire to know Brahman: "adhyayana" (study), etc. The meaning is: those by whom the nature of Brahman as the Self has been made known—that is, understood—are so described; for them, direct realization is attained simply by learning it from teachers and then practicing it, even without an inquiry into it.

The connection [of the text] is as follows: the meaning is that [liberation occurs] even without an inquiry into the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇabrahma*), solely through the meditation (*upāsanā*) upon the attributeless Brahman.

Now, one might object: "In the *Praśnopaniṣad* and other such texts, only meditation is mentioned, but not the method for its performance. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the scriptures of the Ṛṣis" (*ārṣagrantheṣu*). One might further object: "In the *Pañcīkaraṇa*..."

Having first described the dissolution of the entire phenomenal world—which consists of the measures of the syllable *praṇava*—into that which is the goal of Vedānta, the indivisible single essence, one should meditate thus: "I am That which is the indivisible single essence," by abiding in non-duality through the realization "I am Brahman. This is what is called *samādhi*.

Furthermore, from such cited passages as the *Dhyānadīpa*, it is intended that the subject at hand is the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman in the form of "I-grasping" (*ahaṃgraha*). However, in the question of Śvetaketu within the *Praśna Upaniṣad*, the contemplation of the attributeless Brahman upon the symbol (*pratīka*) in the form of the syllable *Oṃ* is intended; likewise also in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is a sentence such as a question cited as an authority for the meditation under discussion? [the answer is: It is not so, because it is intended that only the Tāpanīya, Māṇḍūkya, and Muṇḍaka Śrutis are the authorities for the meditation under discussion. As for the citation of the Praśna and Kaṭhavallī Śrutis, however—
The sense is that there is no contradiction on the grounds that the worship of the *nirguṇa* (attributeless) is observed elsewhere as well;
the connection is that [the method] has been determined for practice in works such as the *Pañcīkaraṇa*.
In this regard, he provides an illustration: "in many branches," meaning because it is scattered across many Vedic recensions (*śākhās*).
The meaning is as follows: just as there is a determined method for the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* through the synthesis of entities that exist in a fragmented state,
so too is the method for the performance of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) obtained from teachers who know only that [method], which constitutes the tradition (*saṃpradāya*).
The meaning is "having ascertained from his presence. And it was said by the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa in the section on the Nirguṇa:
"Having heard from others, they worship"—the sense being "in due order," that is, according to the sequence of the maturation of their practice (*upāsanā*).

Even in the case of a practice based on a method of delusion (*vibhrama*), there is the possibility of it culminating in valid knowledge (*pramā*) at the time of the result, because it is non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādin*). For example,
when someone has covered five cowries in their hand and is asked, "How many cowries are in your hand?",
the answer given is, "Five cowries."

Just as the cognition of a specific number— which serves as the basis for a speaker’s use of speech— may be factually correct even if it is a mental superimposition lacking a foundational means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too is the meditative cultivation (*upāsanā*) of the qualityless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahman*) factually real,
despite being independent of a definitive foundational *pramāṇa* that discriminates its objective reality.
Just as in the case of the meditation on the "small one" (dahara) and others,
even for that which is performed by relying solely upon the scripture, because it is in fact true to reality,
there arises through the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa)— just as through the meditation on the "small one"— a direct realization (sākṣātkāra) of its own object.
Furthermore, because [the meditation] necessarily has as its object the true nature of reality, just like the direct realization produced through the sequence beginning with hearing;
[one might ask: "But how can the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) culminate in a direct realization characterized by valid cognition? To this [it is replied]:...

He said: "Non-contradictory. This is the meaning: for a person standing at a distance who sees the reflection of the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—which is situated as an original object (bimba) within a particular house—outside that house, the delusion arises that "this is Śrī Kṛṣṇa" with respect to that reflection; by means of that delusion...

It is well known in the world that for a person who has gone near the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the superimposition of a reflection, there arises a valid cognition (*pramā*) whose object is the real Śrī Kṛṣṇa. In that context, the error regarding the reflection as being the original (*bimba*) Śrī Kṛṣṇa is a "discrepant error" (*visaṃvādī-bhrama*); "discrepancy" (*visaṃvāda*) here means the absence of the [expected] result.

Devoid of that [contradiction], it is a non-contradictory error; that is to say, it is an error that bears fruit. Just as for one who has engaged in that error, at the time of attaining the fruit characterized by the realization of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, there arises a valid cognition (*pramā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, so too for one who has engaged in the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), at the time of attaining the fruit characterized by the realization of Brahman, there arises a valid cognition of the attributeless.

Thus [it is said]. Now, it may be objected that the conclusion reached by the example of a "corresponding error" (saṃvādibhrama)—that the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) results in valid knowledge—is untenable due to a disparity between the example and the case at hand; for in that instance, after approaching closely, there occurs the sensory contact of the eyes with the real Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
It is not merely because of a concordant error (*saṃvādibhrama*) that [the result] arises from the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa;

for in the present case, the worship of the *nirguṇa* (devoid of attributes) lacks the capacity to produce valid knowledge (*pramā*), and since no other causal complex (*sāmagrī*) exists, how could it culminate in valid knowledge? Anticipating this objection, [the author states] that of the worship of the *nirguṇa* itself...

In order to establish the possibility of its capacity to produce a valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding an object identical to its own, he states its truthfulness along with an illustration: "In the hand," and "having covered. The phrase "unknown to the subsequent speaker" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding "the subsequent speaker":
it means that by a stroke of fate, there happen to be exactly five cowries in his hand; such is the meaning for the subsequent speaker.
The connection is that even the meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa) is, in reality, "in accordance with the truth" (yathārtha).

The sense is that because there is no sublation of the object, the meditation—which consists of a continuous stream of the realization "I am Brahman, the partless, single essence"—is indeed in accordance with the truth. Now, [an objection]:

Because the meditation under discussion is preceded by the knowledge of reality free from doubt, its correspondence with reality is possible—just as in the case of *nididhyāsana* (meditative concentration) which occurs subsequent to *śravaṇa* (hearing) and *manana* (reflection). Why is its correspondence with reality established here through the force of destiny (*daivayoga*)? To this he says: "In the state of being such of the object," meaning the state of being such (*tathātva*) of the object, which is Brahman.

The meaning is: "of that which is independent of the primary means of knowledge in the form of Śruti"—that is, the root authority which is decisive, determinative, free from doubt, and devoid of any suspicion of having another purpose, and which distinguishes [the Self] as being of the nature of immediate presence and free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca). This refers to the present meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa), just like the meditation (nididhyāsana) itself.
Because it is not preceded by inquiry (*vicāra*). The sense is that its truthfulness is not necessitated by being preceded by a definitive determination of reality free from doubt.
[Objection: But if there is no determination of Brahman as non-different from the inner self (*pratyagātman*) preceded by inquiry...
He explains how the meditation in the form of a continuous stream of cognition—"I am Brahman"—is to be practiced:

"In the case of the *dahara* [the small ether] and so forth. Just as, even in the absence of a definitive ascertainment of one's non-difference from the Lord with attributes (*saguṇeśvara*) following inquiry, one must perform the contemplation of one's own identity with the Lord with attributes—such is the nature [of this practice].

The meaning is that, just as meditation on the qualified (saguṇa) is performed by relying on the scriptural injunctions for the practice of saguṇa-upāsanā, so too is the meditation on the unqualified (nirguṇa) practiced by relying solely on the scripture whose nature is the injunction that "nirguṇa-upāsanā must be performed. [This applies] to the case where nirguṇa-upāsanā is the cause of direct realization (sākṣātkāra).
He states an illustration: "Just as by the meditation on the small [space] and so forth. "Because it must necessarily occur" means:
because of the power of meditation having the same object and because the object is not sublated.

However, this is the distinction: for a person free from obstacles, the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman through the channel of hearing and so forth is accomplished instantaneously; thus, the path of Sāṃkhya is the primary method (*mukhya-kalpa*), whereas the path of Yoga, which proceeds by means of meditation (*upāsti*), is the secondary method (*anukalpa*) due to its delay. Now, in both of these two positions—

Regarding the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), some say that the instrument is *prasaṃkhyāna* itself, which consists of the repeated practice of cognitive states (*pratyayābhyāsa*). This is because such [practice] exists in the form of meditation (*upāsanā*) from the very beginning on the path of Yoga, and in the form of contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) following reflection (*manana*) on the path of Sāṃkhya. It is not [the case that it does not exist].

Furthermore, there is no evidence for its being the cause of making [the object] one's own (brahmasātkāra); for it is heard in scripture that "one sees the partless [Self] while meditating upon it. [Otherwise], there would be the absurd consequence that even the direct perception of a beloved woman by one afflicted by desire would result from *prasaṃkhyāna*.
However, [this is] because of the non-imagining of a cause and because [the result] has not been reached; for even in that case, it is observed [as such].

This is established in the section [beginning with] "There is an option, because of the distinction of the fruits," and in the section [beginning with] "Because of the meditation on the 'I' in the small [space]," etc., since the meditators on the qualified Brahman accept the direct realization of the object of meditation through *prasaṃkhyāna*. Now, one might object: [The objection continues: "But..."
Furthermore, because *prasaṃkhyāna* (repeated meditative reflection) is not included among the instruments of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),

the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) produced by it would not be valid knowledge (*pramā*). Nor can it be argued that, like a forced cognition of a specific number of cowrie shells that happens to coincide with reality, it is valid because its object is not sublated.

The establishment of its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) follows from the fact that what is not rooted in a valid means of knowledge cannot possess the nature of a true cognition (*pramā*); for even though a mental act of willful assumption (*āhāryavṛtti*), like the act of meditative worship (*upāsanāvṛtti*), has an object that is not contradicted by reality, it is not admitted to be a true cognition because it is distinct from knowledge (*jñāna*) and is of the nature of an action, like desire and other such states.
This [verse] dispels the delusion that the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga are of equal status. "But this much," etc.:

for one who is free from obstacles such as dullness of intellect and so forth, and who has obtained a distinguished teacher and the like, the path of Sāṃkhya alone is to be practiced, because it is the cause of accomplishment with speed. However, in the absence of [such] Sāṃkhya—

The meaning is that this is an alternative method (*anukalpa*) because yoga is to be practiced; however, "not in this" means not even in both the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. [Objection: But surely, in the path of Yoga, there is the meditation on the attributeless (*nirguṇa*), as well as the meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa*).

Since it was stated immediately prior that [meditation] is the cause of direct realization by means of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one might argue that the question is inappropriate because it applies equally to both positions. This is not a fault; for the question is appropriate with the intention of seeking the authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for meditation being the cause of direct realization. For this very reason, in that context...

He will state the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the words beginning "and not... (*na ca*). Alternatively, in the preceding section, by means of the example of meditation on the qualified (*saguṇa*), only the causality of meditation on the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) was stated, but not its status as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, the intention of the question—namely, whether in the path of yoga (*yogamārga*) meditation itself is the instrument, or whether it is something else—is appropriately consistent.

The state [of being]. He describes the persistence of *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) at the time of the arising of direct realization in both paths, beginning with the words "In the path of yoga" (*yogamārge*). The meaning is that one who meditates upon the partless, undifferentiated Supreme Self (*paramātman*) perceives It through that meditation. Regarding the phrase "one afflicted by desire":
The meaning is: in the case of the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a beloved woman who is not in proximity for one afflicted by desire.

In that situation, because the eye cannot function as the instrument due to the absence of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), and because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects, the idea is that the practice of contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) directed toward the beloved woman alone is the cause.

The meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇopāsana*) must be repeated until the moment of death. Why? Because even at the time of death, the contemplation of Brahman by the yogin is established by both Śruti and Smṛti; for without constant practice, such contemplation would be impossible at the time of death—this is the meaning of the Sūtra. Regarding meditations involving the identification with the Self (*ahaṃgrahopāsana*), there is an option (*vikalpa*).

The meaning of the sūtra is that because the fruit—characterized by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the deity—is identical, and because it is well-established that there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding things having the same purpose. Even though the direct realization of Brahman is not produced by an instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its status as valid knowledge (*pramātva*) is not denied, because its object is not sublated. Thus, having raised the doubt regarding its validity, he refutes it.

"And not 'like the crow and the palm fruit' (kākatālīya)" means accidental. With the intention that for that which is produced by a fabricated instrument, there is not even the status of being knowledge (*jñānatva*), let alone the status of being valid cognition (*pramātva*), he says: "of that which is not rooted in a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāmūlakasya*).

He states that even for a forced cognition (*āhāryavṛtti*) whose object is a specific number of non-contradictory cowries, the status of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is unestablished. Regarding the phrase "and of forced cognition," he says this because he considers that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in being a cognition of an uncontradicted object, and not merely having an uncontradicted object, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); thus he says: "desire, etc. (*icchādi*).
Thus it is said.

Do not say so; for even if it is not rooted in the instruments of valid cognition as previously established, its status as valid knowledge (*pramātva*) is still possible— just like the Lord’s [knowledge] or the concealment by *māyā*— because there is equality in the non-sublation of the object in both paths,
since the practice of contemplation (*prasaṃkhyāna*) has been thoroughly investigated.
Furthermore, because it is rooted in the realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self derived from the Vedānta scriptures as they have been investigated,
even the direct intuition of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) produced by *prasaṃkhyāna* is based upon a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For it has been stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru*:
The immediate cognition born from the cultivation of knowledge arising from the statements of Vedānta does not fall into error due to the firmness of its foundational source;
nor does it entail the consequence that its validity is extrinsic.

This is because it follows the purity of the root [text] in order to refute objections. Others, however, hold that based on such scriptural passages as "This subtle Self is to be known by the mind" and "But it is seen by the highest intellect," the mind alone is the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman; [they argue that] its function regarding the self with adjuncts is the notion of "I."
This is because it is established as the instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the form of a veil;

likewise, it is stated in the *Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇa* passage beginning with, "of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the means of knowledge for the cognizer and so forth, which are the opposite of the dream-world."
Because of the demonstration.
Now, he refutes the objection raised by the words "nanu ca prasaṃkhyānasya" (But surely, of the prasaṃkhyāna... with the words "maivam" (Not so).

He says "māyāvṛtivat" (like the veil of māyā). Nor should it be said that the veil of māyā also lacks the nature of knowledge; for if that were the case, [it would contradict] the scriptural passages concerning the veil of māyā belonging to the Lord, such as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and so forth.

The sense is that it would follow that [the self] lacks the nature of being the object of knowledge (*jñā-dhātvartha*). Regarding the phrase "due to parity" (*taulyāt*): one should not argue that there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to desire (*icchā*) and so forth, because the definition is qualified by the condition of being "distinct from those. This is the sense. Prasaṃkhyāna is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a produced direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), because [only] that which is rooted in a means of valid cognition possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*).

He states another solution: "In both paths. Regarding the phrase "because it is not based on inquiry": this means that the realization of Brahman derived from the Vedānta and other sources is intended here as being based on the path of Yoga (*yogamārga*), since it is rooted therein. Nor should it be asked: "If the realization of Brahman has already arisen from what has been inquired into, then for what purpose is *prasaṃkhyāna*?"

The sense is that prior to *prasaṃkhyāna*, because one has not yet attained the realization of Brahman—which is unimpeded and which sublates ignorance—that [practice] is necessary for that purpose. He cites an authoritative statement in support of the view that even that which is not produced by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) may still be considered valid cognition (*pramā*) simply by virtue of being prompted by a means of valid knowledge: "For it has been said... *Jñānabhāvanā* refers to the form of the repeated practice of knowledge.

The meaning is that it is immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) produced by *prasaṃkhyāna*. It should be understood that the primary means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*) is the Vedāntic statement; the firmness of the validity produced by that consists in its having a status of authority that is not contested.

He raises the objection that if, in order to ascertain the validity residing in the direct realization produced by *prasaṃkhyāna*, one must depend upon the ascertainment of a foundational means of knowledge (*mūlapramāṇa*), then a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) would result. He says: "And not...
[The validity] residing even in the direct realization born of *prasaṃkhyāna* is necessarily...
Since it is manifested solely by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) which apprehends its own substratum,

there is no need to seek out a fundamental means of valid cognition (*mūlapramāṇa*) for the sake of ascertaining its validity; rather, this is because we do not observe the lack of validity in the direct perception of a beloved woman that arises from *prasankhyāna*, even though it is temporally remote [from its object].

The sense is that even in the case of the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) produced by *prasaṃkhyāna*, the possibility of a doubt regarding its invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) may occasionally arise;

therefore, the pursuit of the original source of authority (*mūlapramāṇa*) in order to dispel that [doubt] does not constitute a violation of our established tenet (*apasiddhānta*). Regarding the term "apavāda": an "apavāda" is a doubt concerning invalidity.

He shows the view that *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative discernment) is not the sole means, nor even the direct instrument for realization; rather, it is the mind, aided by that [discernment], which is the instrument therein. Regarding the phrase "others, however": "subtle" (*aṇu*) means difficult to perceive; "the state of being fire-like" refers to being refined by *prasaṃkhyāna*;
and scriptural passages such as "it is to be perceived by the mind alone" constitute the meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
He states the consensus regarding the mind being the instrument for the direct realization of the Self in the verse beginning with "svapna" (dream).
The meaning is: in comparison to the illusory dream-world (*prātibhāsika-svapna-prapañca*), the empirical world of the knower and so forth (*vyāvahārika-pramātr-ādi*) is its opposite;

[the compound] refers to that which is the means for the knowledge of such [an empirical world]. The word "ādi" (and so forth) is intended to include the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and other factors. "Tathā" (so it is).

The meaning of the word "thus" (tathā) is that the mind functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the direct realization of the Self with its adjuncts, which is designated by the term "knower" (*pramātṛ*).
For it is stated in the Śruti: "He thinks, 'I am indeed all this; I am everything'—this is his supreme world.

Furthermore, it is universally accepted that the mind (*manas*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*) occurring during dreamless sleep, as no other instrument exists for that [realization]. Prasaṃkhyāna, however, is the mind.
It functions as an auxiliary cause;
for the internal organ, accompanied by the ripening of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of the sentence,
[realizes] the immediate reality of the referent of the term *tvam* (*tvaṃpadārtha*) through the negation of the forms of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
This is because of the statement in the *Bhāmatī*: "It manifests itself as the referent of that word (*tatpadārthatāmāvibhāvayati*).

Furthermore, in the Śruti passage, "But he who has a pure sattva through the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*) sees Him, the partless one, while meditating," it is precisely by virtue of being the cause for the one-pointedness of consciousness—designated by the term "clarity of knowledge"—that [the Self is seen].

Because it is the instrument of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Now, one might object: "Prasaṃkhyāna itself is an instrument; for it has never been established anywhere that it is an instrument of knowledge. Even in cases such as the direct perception of a beloved woman by one afflicted with passion, it is the mind alone, assisted by prasaṃkhyāna, [that acts as the instrument]."

They say that because the status of being an instrument is established [for the teacher], it is impossible to postulate another unestablished instrument for knowledge. Others, however, [cite] such scriptural passages as "He showed him the further shore of darkness," "The man who has a teacher knows," and "For him there is delay only so long," which [indicate] that immediately after the teacher's instruction...

Because it is heard that liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) occurs upon the arising of the direct realization of Brahman, and because it is heard that there is no further desire for other knowledge in the statement "those who have well-ascertained the meaning through the wisdom of Vedānta," and because [the Upanishads speak of] "the Person who is known from the Upanishads" (*tattvopaniṣadam puruṣam*).

Furthermore, because it is heard in scripture that Brahman is accessible solely through the Upaniṣads, the great Mahāvākya alone is the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman, and not the mind; for the passage "that which one does not perceive with the mind" prohibits the mind from being an instrument for the knowledge of Brahman.
He states that the mind’s status as an instrument is established even in the direct realization of the unconditioned Self:

"I am indeed [all]" (*ahameva*). The meaning is this: "I am that very Brahman, which is the Self of all and is experienced as the existent nature (*sadrūpa*) in every object; therefore, 'I am everything'—thus the knower of Brahman thinks in his dream. Now, one might object:

One might ask: since the contemplation of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) can occur even in a dream for those who know Brahman, why should the sentence itself not be the instrument [of realization]? To this, he says: "At that time. Because the contemplation of the Great Sayings in a dream is not constant, the sentence does not produce immediate intuition (aparokṣadhī).
The sense is that [the Self] is not accepted as being a cause; thus he cites the consensus of authorities with the words "of the meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*).

This means "of the meaning of the Great Sentence" (*mahāvākya*). That which is the referent of the term *tvam* (*tvaṃpadārtha*), consisting of self-luminous consciousness, has been purified by means of negation through such sentences as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*) regarding the adjuncts of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies.

The meaning is that the manifestation of its fullness is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the removal of veils (*avṛti*). As for the claim— that by intending the construction "meditating upon Him who is partless,

one sees Him through that meditation," the status of meditation as the instrument for direct realization is established by scripture— that he refutes with the words "by the clarity of knowledge" (*jñānaprasādena*).

The meaning is that, based on the etymological derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*), the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to consciousness (*cit*); thus, "clarity of knowledge" (*jñāna-prasāda*) signifies one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*).

Consequently, the intended construction is: "meditating, he sees by means of the clarity of knowledge obtained through meditation. The decisive factor for this construction is the previously cited [scriptural] evidence regarding the mind's status as an instrument (*karaṇatva*).
Intending that [the means] consists solely of the words of the instructor, he refutes the view that mere *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative meditation) is the instrument.
He says, "But not... He states the opinion of others, namely that the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) alone is the instrument there, with the words, "Others, however...
The meaning is: "From the instruction of this father, he knew—that is, directly realized—that Brahman; indeed! (*ha kila*)."

The meaning is that for that wise one, Brahman—which has become the supreme support—there is only as much delay toward disembodied liberation (videha-kaivalya) as is required until he is released from his prārabdha karma. Regarding the term "Vedānta":
here, it is precisely from the knowledge born of the Vedāntas that the reality characterized by the identity of Brahman and the Self [is realized].

By the statement that [the meaning] is "well-ascertained" (*sunirṇīta*), it is understood that the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna* is not required after the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. And this independence from it is consistent with the position that immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) arises from the sentence alone;
otherwise, [it would not be so].

Since that [knowledge] is required for immediate realization (*aparokṣajñāna*), its dependence on anything else is not tenable. Therefore, the meaning is that it is determined that the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) alone, through the hearing of the Vedāntic knowledge, is the instrument for immediate realization. Thus, "the great sentence alone" [is the cause], even when considering the practice of the Sāṃkhya path.

Or, it should be understood that when all obstacles characterized by [false] views are destroyed through the practice of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, the true word itself produces direct realization as something free from bondage; thus, one should not suspect the futility of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga on the grounds that the word alone functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*). This is the view of the world.
The construction is as follows: "O knower of Brahman, know that very consciousness which the mind does not perceive to be the Self."

Nor is this [Brahman] an object for an unripe mind, because in the supplementary statement, "that which is thought by the mind," the term "mind alone" (*manomātra*) is used. Nor should it be suspected that, by the phrase "that which is not expressed by speech," the status of speech as its instrument is also being denied; for even by one who maintains that the mind is its instrument...

Since it is accepted that verbal testimony is the instrument for indirect knowledge devoid of particularity (*nirviśeṣa-parokṣajñāna*), its status as such an instrument is negated by way of its power (*śakti*)—which consists in the reaching of the word’s object—in accordance with the scriptural text: "From which speech turns back, along with the mind, not having attained it. This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

It cannot be argued that its status as an instrument is not contradicted by defining it through the characteristic of being an "inexpressible relation" (*vaktavyatayāśakya-sambandha-rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); nor can it be said that the instrumentality of the mind (*manas*) therein— established by the scriptural text "it is to be perceived by the mind alone" (*manasaivānudraṣṭavyam*)— cannot be set aside.

Even in the production of verbal direct perception (*śābdasākṣātkāra*), since one-pointedness of mind (*tadaikāgrya*) is required, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is justified on the basis of its being a mere cause; for it is seen thus in such passages as "for with the mind alone one sees, with the mind one hears," and so forth. This is the view of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) regarding the mind in his *Gītā-bhāṣya*.
They say that the statement regarding its being an instrument proceeds from the perspective of another school of thought.

Regarding the statement "it does not think," he provides the reason why this negates only the capacity of an impure mind to be the instrument for the knowledge of Brahman. He says, "by which they say... (yena...

āhuḥ); because it is impossible to state in the remainder of the sentence that the mind—which is thought of or illumined by that consciousness—is itself the object of consciousness, [it follows that] there, the mind...

The inclusion of the term "only" (*mātra*) is necessary for the sake of consistency; thus, the meaning is that even in the preceding sentence, "mind-only" (*manomātra*) is to be understood as the intended object. "And not so" means: if one accepts the negation of mind-only being the instrument of knowledge regarding Brahman. "Not experienced" means: not manifested.

Nor should it be argued that the word "or" (*vā*) here refers to words other than those of the Vedānta; for even in this context, since the supplementary statement "by whom speech is uttered" establishes that all speech whatsoever is illumined by consciousness, the author— intending to maintain consistency with that— states that the word "or" (*vā*) in the preceding sentence must likewise refer to speech in general.

"Of sound also" means that it is not only of the mind alone, but of sound alone as well. While it is true that [the text] denies that sound alone is the instrument for the knowledge of Brahman, nevertheless, that statement intends to deny that sound is the instrument for the knowledge of Brahman by way of its primary power (*śakti*), and not even by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Intending the resolution that the scriptural statement regarding the Upaniṣadic nature [of Brahman] is aimed at negating its being an instrument, lest it result in [Brahman] being without a support, he indicates a subverting argument against the opponent even in the case of the contrary position:
"Even by one who maintains that the mind is the instrument," and so on. [This applies] even to the Vedāntas through their secondary (lakṣaṇā) sense.

The meaning is that if it were not admitted that [the Vedic sentences] cause the knowledge of Brahman, then Brahman itself would result in non-establishment; therefore, even by those who maintain that the mind is the instrument [of perception], it must be admitted that these [Vedic sentences] are instruments for the knowledge of Brahman. However, [that knowledge] is produced by the sentence (*vākya*).

With the intention of stating that, in your view, the knowledge of Brahman is indirect (*parokṣa*), whereas in our view it is direct (*aparokṣa*), he says: "indirect," etc. This refers to the statement, "that which is not manifested" (*anabhyudita*), which aims to negate the Vedāntas' capacity to convey the cognition of Brahman [in its direct form].

It corroborates another scriptural passage regarding this established position with the words "of that" (*tasya*). Alternatively, the meaning is that it is a prohibition of the statement [that Brahman is] "not manifested.

By the phrase "without reaching" (*aprāpya*), the scripture negates the application of words toward Brahman as their object. And that application is indeed the word's *śakti* (potency), because that potency is the inherent, natural capacity of words.
The state [of being]. "By way of being the means of expression"—the ellipsis here is "even by those who maintain that the mind is the instrument.

"Of that" means "of the word. "That" means "in the direct realization of Brahman. Being the instrument for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is Brahman is not the meaning of the instrumental case heard in the scripture, because it would contradict the scriptures cited previously. Rather, [it is as follows]:
He says that the meaning of that [word] is merely its being a cause by way of being the basis for the one-pointed mind.

This is because he says, "even in the production of verbal direct perception (*śābdasākṣātkāra*). The point is that in cases such as visual cognition, since the mind lacks the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is not seen even when it functions merely as a cause. [This applies to] tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth.

He resolves the contradiction with the statement in the *Gītā-bhāṣya*—that the conditioned mind alone is the instrument for the perception of the Self—by saying "the Gītā" and "in another system. This means "according to the view of the author of the Vṛtti"; it is not stated according to his own view, because it would contradict the aforementioned authorities. This is the intended meaning.
If it is objected that even so, it is not consistent for a word, whose nature is to produce indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*),

to produce direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), some reply here: although a word is inherently incapable [of producing such knowledge], it becomes capable through the cultivation of mental impressions (*pratyayābhyāsa*) preceded by scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).
Supported by the mirror of consciousness attained through one-pointedness on Brahman—which is itself acquired through the accumulation of purificatory disciplines—immediate knowledge arises;
this is postulated just as a sacrifice performed upon a substrate refined by scriptural rites produces the *apūrva* (unseen potency). Thus, one crosses over.
"One who knows the Self is free from grief," according to the authority of the scriptures;

for since the superimposition of agency and other attributes is immediate, it cannot be removed without the knowledge of the immediate substratum. Furthermore, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) operates with respect to Brahman as taught in the Upaniṣads.

They say that if direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) were impossible even from verbal testimony (*śabda*), it would follow that liberation could never occur. Others, however, argue that when accompanied by the accumulation of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāpracaya*), the mind—though incapable of perceiving external objects on its own—is seen to produce the direct perception of a beloved woman who has passed away; thus, through the accompaniment of profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*), [the mind can perceive Brahman].
They argue, in accordance with the supporting example, that it is also logical for verbal testimony to produce immediate, direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).

The phrase "nanu tathāpi" (but even so) means that although there is no contradiction with the Śruti or the Bhāṣya on the view that verbal testimony is the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman, the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) cannot be the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman because it contradicts the inherent nature of verbal testimony as a means of valid cognition (*śabda-pramāṇa*). This is stated precisely by conforming to the very nature of verbal testimony.
He establishes that [the mind] is the instrument for direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*). Regarding the phrase "here some say": "accumulation" (*pracaya*) means a collection;

the meaning is that the mirror is the mind itself, which is supported by that one-pointedness toward Brahman obtained through such accumulation. Just as the eye, although inherently incapable of producing the experience of a reflection, [requires assistance].

The phrase "the mirror of consciousness" (*cit-darpaṇa*) indicates that, just as [an object] reflected in a mirror produces the experience of that [object], so it is here according to the scripture. For instance,
a sacrificial oblation (*homa*) performed in a primary locus (*agryadhikaraṇa*) that lacks the purificatory impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by rites such as *ādhāna* does not generate the *apūrva*.

The meaning is as follows: since a mere oblation performed on the *agrya* [upper] vessel does not possess the inherent nature of producing a transcendental result (*apūrva*), it produces its own *apūrva* only when it is an oblation performed on the *agrya* vessel as qualified by scriptural consecrations;
it is just like that. [Objection: But in the illustrative example, such a thing is accepted on the strength of scripture; how can it be so in the present case?
Since the scripture is not perceived [as stating this], he says: "He crosses over. Now, one might object:

by this scriptural passage, it is stated that the cessation of the superimposition—characterized by sorrow and consisting of agency and so forth—which is superposed upon the conscious self (cidātman), occurs through the knowledge of the Self; but it is not [stated] that...

To [address] the objection that verbal testimony is not a means for immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), he says: "Of that which is immediate" (*aparokṣasya*). Just as in the example, because it is heard that the fire which is the locus of the oblation (*homādhikaraṇa*) has been consecrated by rites such as *ādhāna*, it follows that the cognition of the fire is produced by the sense-organ aided by scriptural consecration (*śāstrīyasaṃskāra*).

The meaning is as follows: it is postulated that the instrument (karaṇa) produces the action first; likewise, because the direct realization (*aparokṣa-adhyakṣa*) of the Self is heard in scripture to be that which removes [ignorance], and since this would otherwise be inexplicable, it is postulated that the Vedāntas themselves—which generate the knowledge of the Self—are the instruments of that direct knowledge. This is because [otherwise] there would be no connection (*ayogāt*), even though...
Because one does not observe the cessation of the superimposition of agency and so forth through the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by hearing [the scriptures],
and because it would follow that the injunctions for reflection (*manana*) and so forth would be useless if the cessation of superimposition occurred through mere indirect knowledge,
[liberation cannot occur] without the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the true nature of such things as the delusion regarding directions, which consist of immediate superimpositions.
The meaning is that [liberation occurs] because one does not perceive [the world] once [ignorance] has ceased. Now, an objection is raised:

"Surely the knowledge consisting in the direct realization of the reality of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), which removes the superimposition of agency and so forth, is possible through the mind alone; what is the use of postulating the Word (śabda) as its instrument? To this, he says: "Aupaniṣadaḥ" (known from the Upaniṣads).

The sense is that if Brahman were accessible through the internal organ (manas) as a means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), it would entail the sublation of those scriptural passages which establish that Brahman is knowable through the Upaniṣads alone. [Objection: But surely, this contradicts the scriptural teaching regarding its being known through the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣadatva*).

Since no other means of knowledge operates with respect to Brahman, it is impossible for the word itself to function in generating the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman, due to a contradiction in its very nature as a linguistic sign. And thus, since the instrument for the direct realization of Brahman cannot even be obtained, one might object: "Let there be no such direct realization. To this, he says:

"Even from verbal testimony" (śabdād api). The sense is that, in order for the scripture on liberation (mokṣaśāstra) to be authoritative, it must be postulated that verbal testimony alone is the instrument for direct realization (sākṣātkāra).
Thus, he establishes that verbal testimony is the instrument for immediate knowledge even without depending upon the authority of the scripture.
"But others," however, [say].

Others, however, maintain that the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of knowledge consists in its having an immediate object as its domain, since no other definition is possible; yet the immediacy of the object does not consist in being the domain of an immediate cognition—
which would result in circularity— but rather in its non-difference from the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the respective person.

Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its attributes are superimposed upon the Witness (*sākṣin*), they possess non-difference from it. Furthermore, for external objects such as jars, which are superimposed upon external consciousness, there is no lack of non-difference from that [consciousness], because their non-difference from the consciousness belonging to that person is manifested through the modification (*vṛtti*) of that external consciousness. Thus, [the objection] does not hold.
In some cases, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti).

Now, since it is established that the very nature of sound is to produce indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*), another view is stated [by the author]—namely, that the Vedāntas possess the capacity for direct realization (*sākṣātkārakaraṇatva*) regarding Brahman, which is eternally immediate—without any exception.
This is introduced with the words "But others... [The opponent objects: "But surely, [the cause of realization must be] the state of being a cognition produced by the senses, and so forth..."

Since verbal knowledge concerning Brahman lacks immediacy (*aparokṣatva*), it is not immediate; therefore, he says: "because of the impossibility of defining it otherwise. The sense is that [definitions] such as being a cognition produced by the senses have already been refuted at the conclusion of the first chapter.

But surely, the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of an object consists in its being the object of immediate cognition; since nothing else can be defined [in this way], there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*):

the cognition of the immediacy of the object depends upon the cognition of the immediacy of the cognition, and the cognition of the immediacy of the cognition depends upon the cognition of the immediacy of the object.

Anticipating the objection that "cognition" (*jñapti*) is thus [defined], and intending to show that such a definition is unestablished because it cannot be precisely stated, he says: "But the immediacy of the object...
that very thing. This means that for each respective object, its immediacy with respect to each respective cognizer consists in its non-difference from the consciousness of that specific cognizer.
The meaning is that for a given knower, there is a cognition whose object is non-different from the consciousness of that knower;

that is, there is immediate (aparokṣa) cognition regarding an object that is non-different from the consciousness of that knower. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of uniformity (ananugama) regarding the immediacy of objects and so forth, because there exists a uniform character of immediacy residing in the cognition itself.

The sense is that since both "birth-form" (*jātirūpa*) and "limiting-adjunct-form" (*upādhirūpa*) have already been rejected, a common "directness of the object" (*arthāparokṣya*)—even in the sense of its non-existence—is impossible; therefore, that [definition] is a defect.

Now, [one might object]: even if directness of the object consists in non-difference from the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*), [how could it apply] to an insentient object that is directly present?

Since the pervasion [of the relation] between consciousness and the insentient is sublated due to their being one, he says: "Because of the existence of non-difference with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This means because of the existence of non-difference with the cognizing consciousness designated by the term *sākṣin*. Thus, in the definition of the immediacy of an object, what is intended is a non-difference that is common to both the imagined and the unimagined.

The point is this: although there is no non-imagined (akalpita) identity between the insentient object and the sentient knower— as there is between the consciousness of the knower and the consciousness of Brahman— nevertheless,

because an imagined (kalpita) identity exists, as established by the experience of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the form "the insentient is existent," there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).
