Having established the non-difference of the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛ-caitanya*) from internal insentient objects, he now establishes it with respect to external, perceptible objects.

[The word] "external" [is used] because of the existence of non-difference between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its attributes [on the one hand], and on the other, [the non-difference of the consciousness of the knower from] jars and so forth.
The connection is that because there is non-difference from that [consciousness], there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) anywhere, even in the case of internal objects.

He states the reason for the existence of the non-difference of jars and so forth from the consciousness belonging to their respective persons: "by means of the manifestation of the non-difference of external consciousness from the consciousness belonging to their respective persons. Now, [one might ask] regarding the external consciousness belonging to their respective persons...

And although consciousness is in reality always non-different [from the self], from what cause does its manifestation arise? To this he says: "By means of a mental modification (vṛtti). When there is contact with the external consciousness delimited by an object—[contact] occurring when a mental modification has gone out through the door of the eyes and so forth—then, because of the non-difference between the modification and that which possesses the modification, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is the possessor of the modification, also comes into contact there.

It is obtained. And thus, the meaning is that external consciousness, when conjoined with a mental modification (*vṛtti*), becomes the consciousness belonging to a particular person through its connection with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); in this manner, the manifestation of non-difference between the external consciousness and the consciousness belonging to that particular person is produced by the mental modification. Now, [one might object] according to the aforementioned method...

Raising the objection that even if the non-difference of external consciousness from the cognizing consciousness (*pramātṛ-caitanya*) is established, the non-difference of jars and other objects from the cognizing consciousness remains unestablished, he says: "Of those imagined in external consciousness. To begin with, the non-difference of jars and other objects from external consciousness is already established; therein—

The meaning is this: because they are imagined (kalpita), and likewise because of the manifestation of the non-difference of external objects from the consciousness belonging to a particular person— which is produced by the mental modification (vṛtti)— it is established that even jars and other such things are non-different from the consciousness belonging to that particular person.

Nor does it follow that mental dispositions (*saṃskāras*) of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) would likewise become directly manifest, on the grounds that they are equally superimposed upon the Witness (*sākṣin*)— just like cognitions and other qualities of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—
because those [dispositions] are unmanifest (*anudbhūta*), whereas only that which is manifest [can appear directly].
The insentient [nature] is non-different from consciousness, because it is admitted that [consciousness] is immediate (*aparokṣya*). And thus,
because it is non-different from the consciousness of all persons, it is established by the scriptural text, "Brahman is that which is directly perceived and immediate," as being Brahman.

They say that since Brahman is indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*), it is logical to maintain that even the verbal knowledge of Brahman is immediate, because its object is an immediate thing. However, the teachers of Advaita Vidya maintain that the immediacy of a cognition does not consist in its having an immediate object as its domain.

Because [the self] is not pervaded by a knowledge that has the form of the direct manifestation of the bliss of its own nature; for the self-luminosity characterized by having itself as its object is denied. Rather, just as the directness of an object consists in its non-difference from the consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage, so too—
The immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of cognition is the non-difference between consciousness and the respective object, which is conducive to the corresponding empirical usage (*vyavahāra*).

Thus, this immediacy is indeed a property of consciousness itself; it is not a property of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), as is the case with inferentiality, desire, and so forth.
Fearing that the definition characterized by the direct perception of the object (*arthāparokṣya*) might be over-extensive (*ativyāpti*), he refutes it with the words beginning "And not" (*na ca*).

The point is that even for properties such as *dharma* and so forth, there exists non-difference in the form of identity (*abhinnasattākatva*) with the consciousness of the cognizer (*pramātṛcaitanya*), which serves as their substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This is provided that [the cognition] is manifest (*udbhūtatve sati*).

The non-difference from the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*), which constitutes the immediacy of the object, and its "manifestness" (*udbhūtatva*)—which is a specific nature to be inferred from the result—are [the criteria]. And since that [manifestness] does not exist in the case of *dharma* and so forth, this is the sense of the rebuttal. Thus, regarding the direct realization of Brahman through the word (*śabda*).
Having provided an introductory discussion (*upodghāta*) for the purpose of establishing [Brahman] as the instrument (*karaṇa*), he shows the subject at hand with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

The meaning is: "given that [the knowledge] is conditioned by its being immediate (*aparokṣya*). Regarding the phrase "because of non-difference": the sense is that the non-difference of the cognizer in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman is established by scripture. And this non-difference of Brahman from the individual soul—

With the intention that the non-difference of the insentient from the consciousness of the knower (*pramātṛcaitanya*) is not merely conceptual, but rather constitutes an actual identity, he says: "By itself" (*svata eva*). He cites scripture regarding the non-difference of Brahman from the eternally immediate consciousness of the knower: "That which [is] directly," and so forth. Brahman is not like the insentient.

It is not immediate (aparokṣa) in relation to a cognizing subject's consciousness that is distinct from itself; rather, the meaning is that it is immediate precisely because its nature is that of the cognizing subject's own immediate consciousness.
He now defines the immediacy of knowledge and the immediacy of the object by means of another method.

"The teachers of Advaita-vidyā, however," [they say]. This refutes the previously stated definition of the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of knowledge on the grounds of its being under-extensive (*avyāpti*). The meaning is that the term "not non-immediate" (*nāparokṣa*) does not extend to the self-knowledge whose nature is the immediacy of the bliss of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-sukha*). Now, [one might object]: regarding the experience of the bliss that is the very nature of the Self...

Because it is admitted that the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), being of the nature of consciousness, is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*); and because self-luminosity consists in having itself as its object; and because the state of having one's own essential bliss as its object is indisputable in the case of the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpajñāna*) which is of a direct (*aparokṣa*) form—for this reason, he says: "characterized by having itself as its object. [This applies] to a single consciousness.
The meaning is this: there can be no relation characterized by the state of being an object between [the self and consciousness], because a relation must reside in two things (*dviniṣṭhatvāt*).

Furthermore, self-luminosity has been established in the authoritative treatises as being characterized by not being an object of doubt and so forth, which is brought about by its own existence even without having itself as an object. What, then, is the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of knowledge?
He asks: "But what [is it]? By means of a counter-example, he first defines the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of an object, providing a definition of the immediacy of knowledge. [He says: "Just as...

The immediacy of an object consists in its non-difference from the consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage (*vyavahāra*); and such [immediacy] exists in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The identity of those objects with the witnessing consciousness—which is conducive to their own empirical usage—exists because they are superimposed upon it. Likewise, even for objects such as a jar, there exists identity with the consciousness that has the jar as its substrate, which is conditioned by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the jar and is conducive to the jar's own empirical usage. Thus...

Furthermore, even Brahman possesses non-difference from the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya)—which is conditioned by a mental modification (vṛtti) within its own sphere and conforms to its own manifestation; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) anywhere. As for objects such as a jar, which are superimposed upon consciousness, their non-difference from consciousness exists at all times, yet their immediacy (aparokṣatva) does not exist at all times.

It has been stated that [consciousness] is "conducive to empirical usage" (vyavahārānukūla); thus, it is only during the state of a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward an object such as a jar that the consciousness which is the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) of that jar becomes conducive to the empirical usage of the jar, and not at all times.
Therefore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Now, regarding the consciousness conducive to such and such empirical usage...

Granted that "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) may indeed consist in being non-different from its respective object, nevertheless, the immediacy of cognition has not yet been explained, because cognition in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) is distinct from consciousness (*caitanya*). To this, he says: "And thus" (*tathā ca*). The meaning is: when it is intended that consciousness alone is conducive to the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding its respective objects. And thus:

The point is that in the expression "directness of knowledge" (*jñānāparokṣya*), the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers exclusively to consciousness (*caitanya*) and not to cognitive modification (*vṛttijñāna*); thus, there is no fault of omission.

For this very reason, there is immediacy (*aparokṣya*) in the witness (*sākṣin*), whose nature is the manifestation of pleasure and so forth, and in consciousness (*caitanya*), whose nature is the manifestation of the bliss of one's own essence (*svarūpasukha*). Nor is there any contradiction with experience regarding the manifestation of jars and other objects through sensory modifications (*indriyaka-vṛtti*); for experience consists in the immediacy residing in the consciousness delimited by such a modification.

Because it is logically established that [the Self] is an object [of knowledge]. Now, an objection is raised: if the immediacy (*āparokṣya*) of both cognition and its object were to depend on the verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*) whose sphere is the heart and so forth, then it would follow too far, as it would apply even to those two objects [of such a modification]. In that case, when by chance a contact between the modification and the object occurs, there would be [a unity] of the consciousness delimited by the modification and the consciousness delimited by the object.
If it is argued that this is because the manifestation of non-difference is unavoidable, we say no;

for the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward an object beyond the senses lacks the capacity to remove ignorance regarding the consciousness delimited by that object. Thus, the object-consciousness remains covered by ignorance [in that state], while [the consciousness] is not covered [by the modification].
Because there is no manifestation of non-difference with the witness-consciousness delimited by the mental mode (vṛtti), immediacy does not result.

He states the reasoning for the fact that the immediacy of cognition (*jñānāparokṣatva*), which consists in being non-different from a particular object while being conducive to the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding that object, is a property of consciousness (*caitanya*) alone. "For this very reason" means:
precisely because it is accepted as a property of consciousness. However, if it were a property of the mental modification (*vṛtti*),...

The meaning is that there would be a contradiction with the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth as being immediate (*aparokṣa*), because one does not accept a direct modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is pleasure, pain, and so on; and because the property of immediacy cannot exist in the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) which illumines pleasure, pain, and so forth. [Regarding the definition: "Truth" (*satyam*).

Since it is indeed the living consciousness (jīvacaitanya), as conditioned by a mental modification (vṛtti) directed toward fire, that has become conducive to empirical usage, the qualificand (viśeṣya) is included [in the definition] to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) to that [consciousness]. Because the mental modification directed toward inference does not travel to the location of the object, the consciousness delimited by that modification is not non-different from the fire; thus, there is no over-extension.
In the state when there is an absence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having a jar or the like as its object,

although the jar or other object is non-different from the consciousness delimited by that jar, the quality of being directly perceived (*aparokṣatva*) is absent; therefore, in order to maintain that [non-difference],
it is said that "it exists" because at that time that consciousness is veiled (*āvṛta*) with respect to the jar and so forth.
Because it would lack conformity with common linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), one should not consider this to be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*). As for the phrase "na ca" (nor):

if the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of cognition were an attribute of consciousness (*caitanya*), it would contradict the experience of immediacy in the form "I directly perceive the jar," which occurs during a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward an object such as a jar. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that because of the identity (tādātmya) between the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and consciousness (*caitanya*), the experience of the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the modification is logically accounted for as having a non-indirect object (*aparokṣa-viṣayakatva*) residing in consciousness. Now, an objection: a verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*) directed toward objects such as the heart, the channels (*nāḍī*), or the qualities (*dharma*) arises as something pervading the interior of the body.
If, by the conjunction of destiny, [the mental modification] should arise in a region of the internal organ delimited by the heart, the channels, and so forth, then—

in the case of objects such as a jar, once there is contact between the mental modification and the object— an unavoidable manifestation of non-difference must occur between the consciousness delimited by the form of the object (such as the heart) and the consciousness delimited by the verbal mental modification directed toward that heart.

Because it is accepted that there is a manifestation of non-difference between consciousness delimited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and consciousness delimited by its object, so too, in the case of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)— which consists of consciousness delimited by a mental modification such as verbal cognition or inference directed toward the heart and so forth—

there exists a notion characterized by the immediacy of knowledge (*jñānāparokṣya*), which is non-different from the object (the heart, etc. and conducive to the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the heart and so forth.

[The opponent] objects: "There is over-extension (ativyāpti). For instance, in the case of an object such as the heart, which is beyond the senses (parokṣa), [your definition] would over-extend because that object is non-different from the consciousness delimited by verbal and other cognitive functions that are conducive to one's own practical activity (vyavahāra). Thus he raises the doubt with the words, "But it has been said."

And for those two consciousnesses whose non-difference is intended to be manifested, it is required that both be unobscured; for when one of the two consciousnesses is in a state of obscuration, the manifestation of their non-difference—characterized by direct perception—is impossible. And thus:

He offers a rebuttal, stating that there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases where there is a verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*) having the heart and so forth as its object, because in those cases the consciousness of the object remains veiled.

He says: "Not [in the case] of a remote modification (*parokṣavṛtti*)," meaning that because direct manifestation (*āparokṣya*) is not applicable to an object such as the heart that is remote (i.e., known through verbal testimony).
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "and of the indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna) consisting of consciousness delimited by a verbal modification (śābdavṛtti) whose object is the heart and so forth.

And thus, [the meaning is that there is a causal relationship] between the indirect knowledge consisting of consciousness delimited by a verbal modification whose object is the heart and so forth, and the linguistic usage regarding the heart and so forth.

Even though there is knowledge of the shore, because there is no identity with the object such as the heart due to a lack of manifestation [of that object], the immediacy of cognition— defined as being a knowledge conducive to the practical usage of that object while being non-different from the manifested form of that object— is absent.
Similarly, although the object such as the heart also exists in non-difference from the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) as delimited by a verbal function conducive to its own empirical usage,
there is no manifestation of that non-difference; thus, there is no manifestation of non-difference from the consciousness conducive to its own empirical usage.

The meaning is that there is no direct perception of an object in the form of "being rice" (śālitva). Furthermore, although the non-difference between the witness of pleasure and so forth— which has the form "I am happy" or "I am miserable"— and the objects consisting of pleasure, pain, and so on exists through [the power of] knowledge, it is not manifested.

This is because the relationship between the locus and the located is perceived between the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the witness of pleasure and so forth, and the pleasure itself. Furthermore, it should not be argued that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because there is no identity between the manifest object and the direct perception of pleasure, pain, and so on; for in the manifestation of a jar within the form of the direct perception of a jar, the jar manifests.
Just as the manifestation of non-difference from objects such as a jar occurs by taking up the experience in the form "the cloth manifests," so too, in the perception of pleasure, pain,
and so forth, it occurs precisely by taking up the experience in the forms "pleasure manifests" and "pain manifests."

This is because there exists the manifestation of non-difference from the object, such as pleasure. Nor should it be argued that in the experience "the jar manifests" (*ghaṭaḥ sphurati*), what appears is merely the jar's being the substratum of manifestation, and not its non-difference from manifestation;
for in the usage "the jar manifests," [the jar] is non-different from the agent of manifestation, just as Devadatta is non-different from the agent of going in the expression "Devadatta goes."

Just as in the sentence "the deity has been given," [the object] is non-different from the locus of manifestation; so too, since it must be stated that the meaning of the sentence "the jar is non-different from the locus of manifestation" applies even to the experience underlying the usage "the jar manifests"—
namely, the experience "the jar manifests"— the jar is [non-different] by virtue of being non-different from the conscious self (cidātman) which constitutes the locus of manifestation.

Because manifestation necessarily exists. Nor should it be argued that even if the non-difference between the jar and the substratum of manifestation is revealed, the revelation of the non-difference of manifestation itself has not yet been established; for the perception "the nature of the jar" reveals the jar alone.
Just as it makes the jar its object by way of the jar's own nature,

so too the perception "the jar manifests" [makes manifest] during the state of the jar's manifestation none other than the unobscured conscious self (cidātman) which serves as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) for the jar and so forth.

By accepting that [the Self] makes [the object] its own object through the mode of manifestation (sphuraṇa) residing in the self-luminous conscious Self, the manifestation of non-difference— whose locus is the manifestation in the jar— is itself the manifestation of non-difference from that manifestation.
What is meant by this is that the very use of the expression "the nature of the jar" is the jar...

The difference between the pot and its own-nature (svarūpa) appears [only conceptually], but not in the perception that takes the pot's own-nature as its object; otherwise, that perception would result in being an error, because there is no difference between the pot and its own-nature. Nor can its status as an error be admitted.

This is possible because there is no sublation [of such a claim]. Thus, when the verbal expression "it shines forth" (*sphurati*) is employed, the shining forth of the self-luminous nature occurs, and the manifestation of difference arises by virtue of being its substratum; however, in the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that "it shines forth," there is no shining forth [in that sense], because duality is not perceived therein. Nor is it the case that...

Since it is observed that a verbal modification (*śābdavṛtti*) whose object is Brahman— which is connected with its own objective content— is capable of removing ignorance regarding that very object, how can a similar capacity belong to a verbal modification whose object is the heart and so forth,
given that there is no difference in its connection with its objective content? How could [ignorance] residing in the consciousness that is its own object [be removed by it]?

It cannot be said that [verbal cognition] lacks the capacity to remove ignorance; for even when there is a connection with the object in the case of a verbal operation directed toward the heart and so forth,
the capacity to remove ignorance is established in that operation due to the absence of any obstacle to its removal of ignorance, as concluded at the end of the first chapter.

The meaning is that this has already been demonstrated. For this very reason, although the soul is in reality non-different from Brahman during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), it remains indirect (*parokṣya*) at that time; for the difference created by the veil of ignorance (*ajñāna*) still exists.
Nor does it follow from this that Brahman would also lack direct intuition (*aparokṣya*) of the soul and thus become non-omniscient.
Because ignorance, by veiling the Lord, does not bring about a difference between Him and each individual soul;

for that ignorance which veils a particular [subject] brings about a difference in its own substrate only with respect to that [subject]. For this very reason, when Caitra’s knowledge [arises], his ignorance regarding the jar [is removed].

When Caitra’s [consciousness] is veiled, Maitra’s un-veiled ignorance produces a differentiation of the object-consciousness specifically with respect to Maitra; thus, there is no impossibility of Caitra’s direct perception of the jar either.

He states the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the following point: that the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of an object consists precisely in its possessing a manifestation of non-difference from consciousness that is conducive to its own empirical usage, and not merely the possession of such non-difference. He says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).
This means: precisely because it is accepted that the manifestation of non-difference alone is the cause of immediacy. [The term] "saṃsāra... [is used].

The meaning is: "prior to the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). By the phrase "even though there is non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman," the intended sense is:

"even though Brahman is non-different from the consciousness of the individual soul that is conducive to its own empirical usage. And thus, during the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), [it is] conducive to its own empirical usage...

The point is this: although Brahman is non-different from the consciousness of the living being (jīvacaitanya), it must be stated that Brahman lacks immediacy (aparokṣatva) with respect to the individual soul precisely because the manifestation of their non-difference has not occurred; therefore, it is logical that the manifestation of non-difference is the necessary condition for immediacy. Not [otherwise].
"And thus" means that the difference created by ignorance acts as an obstacle to the manifestation of non-difference.

Regarding the phrase "due to impossibility": the cognition conducive to the empirical usage concerning the individual soul (jīva)—expressed as "I perceive the jīva" or "the jīva is beyond my perception"—is Brahman as conditioned by a modification (vṛtti) of Māyā.
And thus, although the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the object of worldly activity performed by Brahman,
exists as non-different from that very consciousness of Brahman which is conducive to such activity,
there is no direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of Brahman by the soul, because it lacks the state of possessing a manifested non-difference.

It is possible. Nor should it be argued that even if direct (aparokṣa) knowledge regarding the individual soul (jīva) is impossible for Brahman, its omniscience is not thereby destroyed, because that [omniscience] is possible through mere indirect (parokṣa) knowledge regarding the soul;
for the point is that indirect knowledge is not admitted for the Lord (Īśvara). For ignorance (ajñāna)...

This is because there exists the experience of difference from Brahman in the form "I am not Brahman," which establishes a difference where the soul is the subject and Brahman is the counter-correlative;

however, it does not establish a difference where Brahman is the subject and the soul is the counter-correlative, as there is no evidence for such an experience as "Brahman is not I, the soul. And thus, with respect to each individual soul, [the difference] from Brahman...

He offers a rebuttal, stating that the aforementioned defect does not apply because of the absence of the differentiation caused by ignorance—which is the obstacle to the manifestation of non-difference from Brahman. Regarding the phrase "of ignorance": since there is no evidence for the experience of the Lord thinking "I am ignorant," ignorance does not serve as an obscuration to the Lord with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*). Nor [is this the case] for the Lord himself.
It must be stated that it is understood from his own words during the period of worldly activity— preceded by his *līlā* body— that there is an experience of his own ignorance; for,
as established in the fourth chapter, his words indicating his own ignorance are otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddhi*).

The meaning is that this will be explained later. Regarding the word "him" (tam): it refers to Īśvara, because [the difference] does not serve as the cause for the difference between Him and each individual soul (jīva).
To the objection—namely, why should that which veils each soul not also be the producer of the difference between souls?—he says: "yaṃ" (Him).

The meaning is as follows: regarding the cognition (*pratīti*), it is accepted that for whatever individual soul (*jīva*) there exists an ignorance (*ajñāna*) which veils the consciousness of the object, that very ignorance brings about a difference relative to the consciousness of the object—which serves as its own substrate. In this established arrangement, [the following applies].
He states the restrictive rule: "For this very reason. The connection is as follows:

precisely because one accepts the established rule that "ignorance belongs to whomsoever [it is directed] toward which object," it is also not the case that Caitra’s experience of the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of a jar is untenable. This refers to the consciousness (*caitanya*) delimited by the jar.

Just as ignorance exists that veils the consciousness of the jar with respect to Caitra, so too does ignorance exist there that veils the consciousness of the jar with respect to Maitra. And thus, by Caitra’s knowledge of the jar,

[that ignorance]— which resides in Caitra— is brought to an end, while the ignorance regarding the jar remains for Maitra, which brings about a difference relative to the consciousness of the object (the jar) that serves as its own substrate (Maitra).

When [the ignorance] belonging to Caitra has been removed by his cognition of the jar, the Maitreya-ignorance— which resides in the consciousness of the jar and remains unremoved with respect to Maitra—

produces a difference relative to the consciousness of the jar (which is its own substrate) only for Maitra; however, that Maitreya-ignorance does not produce such a difference for Caitra with respect to the jar.

[The jar] is also non-obscuring of consciousness; it brings about a difference, relative to Caitra, with respect to the consciousness residing in its own substrate (the jar). This being so, when Caitra’s ignorance regarding the jar is removed by Caitra’s cognition of the jar, even though the difference caused by that [ignorance] is removed, there remains [the distinction between] Caitra and the consciousness of the jar.

Since there is no manifestation of non-difference for Maitra due to the existence of difference produced by his own ignorance, it would follow that Caitra could not have the experience of perceiving a jar as "not-Maitra. Therefore, Maitra’s ignorance does not, with respect to Caitra, bring about a difference in its own substrate [the Self] in the same way it does with respect to Maitra himself. With respect to Caitra, it does not produce a difference in its own substrate.
It should be stated that [ignorance] does not obscure consciousness; thus, as it has been said, the established order is proven—this is the meaning.
Now, if immediate perception— characterized by the manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness of the modification (*vṛtti*) and the consciousness of the object—

is produced by the cessation of ignorance residing in the object-consciousness, then it would be impossible for that [perception] to be the cause of that cessation; therefore, knowledge alone is the remover of ignorance.

If it is argued that this must be so, we say no; for the qualification is made that only that cognition which, upon arising, arises already in contact with its object through the power of its own cause is the remover of ignorance. This is the case for sensory cognitions as well.

Because of this, even though the knowledge of Brahman arises from the word [of scripture], it arises as already conjoined with the Brahman-consciousness which is its own object and the material cause of all; thus,
its capacity to remove ignorance consists in the removal of that ignorance.
Thus, it is perfectly logical that direct perception (*āparokṣya*) arises from the dissolution of the difference rooted therein.
Now, one might object: "In that case, why would direct perception not also arise through the knowledge produced by the study of the Vedānta, which likewise removes the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)?"
Now, it cannot be argued that, according to the principle that "mediate knowledge removes ignorance," directness (*aparokṣatva*) is the necessary condition for a cognition to remove ignorance;
for the very directness residing in the cognition is itself dependent upon the removal of ignorance. Nor should it be said: "Let it not be so."
It must be stated that the immediacy of knowledge (*jñānāparokṣya*) is the cause for the cessation of ignorance (*ajñānanivṛtti*).

Anticipating the objection that if this were so, it would follow that every kind of knowledge—even indirect knowledge—would have the power to remove ignorance simply by being knowledge, the author raises the following doubt: "But if this were so... (nanvevam). Thus.

He states the meaning of the word: "In the case of the function (*vṛtti*)," which means that in the knowledge consisting of consciousness delimited by the function (*vṛttyavacchinna-caitanya*) and in the object such as a jar, there is the manifestation of the non-difference between the consciousness delimited by the function and the consciousness delimited by the object; this is the sense of the phrase "consisting of [the manifestation of] that. Regarding the phrase "having the removal of ignorance as its purpose": [it refers to] the knower (*pramātṛ*).

The meaning is that immediacy (*āparokṣya*) is necessarily preceded by the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it has been stated that neither the object nor the cognition can become immediate without the removal of that ignorance which, through its veiling of the consciousness of the object, brings about a distinction relative to that object-consciousness.
There is no loss [to our position] even if immediacy (*āparokṣya*) is not the determinant factor for knowledge’s capacity to remove ignorance;
for another determinant has been shown at the end of the first chapter—this is the intention with which he replies: "No.
[He says this] because of its being so, that is, by the power of the cause in the form of proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*), [knowledge] exists precisely as conjoined with the object.

The meaning is "because it is in the process of arising. It should also be observed that there is no over-extension [of the definition] because mental modifications such as inference (*anumiti*) and so forth are not like that. Now, one might object: just as the mental modification consisting of an inference regarding fire and the like has [its own nature], so too does the verbal modification regarding Brahman [have its own nature] by virtue of its own object.
Because there would be no contact with the Brahman-consciousness, the cessation of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) would not occur;
and consequently, even after the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the direct perception (*aparokṣya*) of Brahman would not arise. To this, he says: "In this way" (*evam ca*).
This means "in exactly this manner. That is to say, just like the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward Indra. [This refers to] the mental modification whose object is Brahman.

He states the reason for the restriction [of a mental modification] to its own object: by the phrase "being the material cause of all," he intends that since there is a restriction of everything being born to contact with Brahman—Brahman being the material cause of all—what need is there to mention the restriction of a mental modification directed toward Brahman to its own object? It is with this intention that the term "the material cause of all" was used.

The meaning is that because there is a rule regarding the connection between an effect and its material cause (*upādāna*), the mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is Brahman is not equal to an inferential cognition whose object is fire and the like.
And as for "immediacy" (*āparokṣya*): [the opponent objects] that, on the view where the immediacy of knowledge is not the instrumental cause for the cessation of ignorance...

If it is argued that the demonstration of the immediacy (*aparokṣatva*) of the knowledge produced by Vedānta is useless in this doctrine of verbal immediacy (*śabdāparokṣavāda*), we say no; for the rule that "knowledge which removes ignorance must be immediate in form"—
a rule observed in the case of cognitions produced by the eyes and other senses— is equally applicable to the knowledge that removes ignorance regarding Brahman.

For it is established that the means [of knowledge] is purposeful insofar as it serves to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding verbal cognition whose object is Brahman; for verbal cognition whose object is Brahman— which removes the root ignorance—
is characterized by immediacy (*aparokṣya*), according to such scriptural passages as "seeing this very [Brahman]" (*tad vaitat paśyan*).

The meaning is that [the existence of Brahman] is established by the experience of the wise who say, "I directly realize Brahman," and because it would otherwise be inexplicable without establishing it there. In the case of a jar or similar objects, perceptibility exists only at the time of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that jar;
however, when that modification ceases, one again encounters a distinction created by another layer of ignorance, which is conducive to one's own empirical usage.

Because there is no manifestation of the non-difference from consciousness, there is no immediacy [of Brahman] [during the state of ignorance]; however, in the case of Brahman, once the root-ignorance has ceased, since the difference caused by the veil can never again arise, there is always immediacy after the knowledge of Brahman—this indicates the distinction. [The word] "tarām" (more so). Now, [the objection]: "Even so, that which is grasped through study... [This refers to] the knowledge [obtained] by rule.

The meaning of the word "iti" (thus) is as follows: it is accepted as a rule that knowledge which arises in conjunction with an object indeed removes ignorance; the sense is that even knowledge acquired at first sight (āpātajñāna) arises precisely through its own connection with Brahman.
Nor should it be argued that because that [knowledge] lacks the nature of certainty, it does not remove ignorance;
for even so, since ignorance would be removed by the doubt-free verbal knowledge of one who has performed *śravaṇa*, it would follow that *manana* and the rest are useless. This is not so.
Even though knowledge free from doubt arises from hearing (śravaṇa), because it is obstructed by the defect of mental distraction (cittavikṣepa),
ignorance is not removed; therefore, the performance of the injunctions for reflection (manana) and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana) is purposeful for the sake of dispelling that [ignorance].

They say this because direct realization of Brahman is sought through mere instruction for one whose mental distractions have been dispelled by the practice of meditation and other means performed in previous lives; and furthermore, even so,
for one who has already performed *nididhyāsana*, [realization occurs] through the knowledge of Brahman arising from the Vedānta alone.

Why should the ignorance regarding Brahman not also be removed by the cognition of a jar and so forth? Nor should it be argued that because that [cognition] does not have Brahman as its object, there is no removal of the ignorance regarding Brahman from it; for it is admitted that the mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) in the form "the jar exists" has as its object Brahman in its nature as Pure Being (sadrūpa). Nor, in that case...

When the ignorance regarding that [object] is removed by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of a jar or the like, the consciousness delimited by it shines forth as "existent" simply through its own self-manifestation; therefore, it should not be said that it has the jar or the like as its object via the mental modification. In the absence of that [manifestation], there would be no cognition of the jar.

Knowledge has as its object the consciousness delimited by that [object], whereas ignorance is not so; therefore, since their objects are distinct, it is impossible for knowledge to remove that [ignorance]. Furthermore, because there is no function of veiling (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to what is insentient (*jaḍa*), a jar cannot be the object of ignorance. Nor is this the case...

It should not be argued that, although the modification (vṛtti) regarding a jar or similar object has as its object the consciousness delimited by it, the fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna) is not removed by it because it lacks the form of undivided bliss (akhaṇḍānanda).

He raises an objection, suggesting that even the state of being "existent" (*sat*) is a qualification of the sublating cognition, and therefore there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): "Nor is that... The meaning of the word "that" (*tat*) is the knowledge produced by the Vedānta texts acquired through study prior to inquiry. Having accepted this qualification, he states the over-extension nonetheless: "Even so..."

He provides the resolution: "Nor even [the quality of] being unobstructed," meaning that since this too is a qualification of the specific knowledge that brings about cessation, the aforementioned over-extension does not occur. [Objection:

But if [practices] such as reflection (*manana*) are for the purpose of removing doubt (*asaṃbhāvanā*) and contrary conviction (*viparītabhāvanā*), which are designated by the term "distraction" (*vikṣepa*)...

For that qualified seeker of knowledge (*vidyādhikārī*) whose entire defect of distraction has been dispelled through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) accompanied by reflection (*manana*) and so forth from previous births, the unobstructed knowledge of Brahman in the form of certainty arises even by means of mere instruction. And thus, for him, in this very life—

He says "bhavāntarīyā" (pertaining to another life) because [otherwise] the cessation of root-ignorance and the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmāparokṣya*) would occur even without the performance of hearing, reflection, and so forth; the sense is that such an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*) would follow. Then, "even in this way... [he says].
The meaning is: even when there is a dependence on reflection (*manana*) and so forth for the purpose of removing the defect of distraction;

for a qualified person who has already performed *nididhyāsana*, why should the cessation of root ignorance not occur even through the knowledge of a jar or similar object, just as it does for one qualified for the meditation (*dhyāna*) upon a jar? For the mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding a jar and so forth is also [of the nature of consciousness].

The intention of the objection is that there is no difference between [the knowledge of a jar] and the knowledge whose object is the consciousness that is the locus of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna), because both have consciousness as their object. The author of the Siddhānta refutes this by restating the doubt and showing that the claim that root-ignorance and the knowledge of a jar have the same object is unproven. He begins with "And not of that," which means "of the knowledge of a jar and so forth. From that...

The meaning is "from the cognition of a jar and so forth. The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) raises an objection, stating that the claim that the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) in the form "the jar exists" and so on has Brahman-consciousness as its object is unproven; this is expressed by the words "And not there... and so on.
Regarding the three words beginning with "tatra" (therein), the word "tat" refers to the jar and so forth; "tasya" means "of Brahman.

The proponent of the previous view establishes that the consciousness delimited by the jar and so forth is the object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding the jar and so forth, starting with the phrase "in the absence of that" (*tadabhāve*).
This means: "given that there is an absence of the consciousness being the object of the mental modification regarding the jar and so forth. Now, [an objection]:
If the cessation of ignorance regarding consciousness delimited by the jar cannot occur through a cognition whose object is merely the jar—
because there is an absence of identity of object between the two— then [what is the relationship] of that ignorance with the cognition of the jar?

The proponent [of the opposing view] says "no" to the claim that ignorance (*ajñāna*) must also have only insentient objects such as jars as its domain in order to achieve identity of objective referents (*samānaviṣayakatva*). He states: "insentient.
This is because, precisely due to the insentience of the insentient, its non-manifestation is logically established even at a time when no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been applied to it.

The meaning is that for an insentient object (*jaḍa*), the postulation of an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) is impossible because it is not of the nature of light (*aprakāśātmatvāt*). Furthermore, regarding the purpose or fruit (*phala*):

just like the knowledge produced by the Vedānta, the knowledge of a jar or similar objects must necessarily have the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacaitanya*) as its object; therefore, it possesses the same object as the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

It is thus established that by that [reasoning], the consequence of its cessation would follow. To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) objects with the words "na ca" ("but not so").
Because even in the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) produced by the Vedānta, that [duality] is absent;

for in that case, there is no such qualifier as "partlessness" (*akhaṇḍatva*) or "bliss-ness" (*ānandatva*), since that would entail the loss of the defining characteristic of the Vedāntas as having "indivisible meaning" (*akhaṇḍārthatva*), which consists in their being a means of valid knowledge whose object is not a relational complex (*saṃsarga*). Not so.

Nor should it be said that there is a rule that its cessation occurs only through the knowledge produced by Vedānta; for since the established causal factor for the removal of ignorance exists in other types of knowledge as well, it is impossible to restrict it in such a way. Nor...
Since the delimited consciousness (avacchinna-caitanya) which is the object of the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of a jar and so forth is itself imagined (kalpita),

it lacks the status of being the object of that true, undelimited consciousness (anavacchinna-caitanya) which is the object of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna); therefore, the mental modifications regarding jars and the like are not intended to be what is to be removed [by knowledge].
It must be stated that the postulated causal factor— characterized by having the same object as the cognition— does not exist at all;

for even though the delimiting portion (*avacchedakāṃśa*) therein is imagined, the delimited portion (*avacchedyāṃśa*) consists of consciousness (*caitanya*) which is the object of the non-imagined root-ignorance.
If that [ignorance] were imagined (*kalpita*), then, like a jar, it would be insentient (*jaḍa*); consequently, it could not be the object even of the ignorance regarding its state.
Therefore, one must assert that the ignorance regarding the state has as its object the non-imagined consciousness (*caitanya*).
For this reason, even the knowledge of a jar or the like, which removes that [ignorance], [must likewise have that same consciousness as its object].

Since it is inevitable that [the cognition] has that as its object, the undesirable consequence— that the primordial ignorance (mūlājñāna) would be removed by that [cognition] even in that case— cannot be avoided.
The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvavādī) objects: "In that case, even the knowledge produced by the Vedānta would not be the remover of ignorance regarding Brahman.
[The author] replies with the words "produced by the Vedānta" (*vedāntajanya*). [This is because] indivisibility (*akhaṇḍatva*) means being unconditioned (*anavacchinnatva*);
for if it were admitted that the knowledge produced by the Vedānta apprehends a qualification by attributes such as indivisibility, [it would no longer be the remover of ignorance].
He states the objection: "Of the Vedāntas... Since this [knowledge] removes the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), the qualification "being produced by the Vedāntas" is also intended;
therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the knowledge of jars and the like. With this intention, he restates and refutes the doubt.
The proponent [says]: "And not by the Vedānta," etc.

This refers to the characteristic of that which is postulated as the knowledge produced by the Vedānta—namely, its capacity to remove root-ignorance—which consists in having the same object as the root-ignorance, being of the nature of a certain conviction (*niścaya*), and being unobstructed.

At the time of the maturation of *nididhyāsana*, even though cognitions of jars and the like produced by the eyes and other senses exist, it is improper to restrict [the cessation of ignorance] to the knowledge produced by the Vedānta alone as the cause for the cessation of the root-ignorance, rather than to the cognition of the jar and so forth; for the quality of being produced by the Vedānta is equally present in that [Vedāntic knowledge] as it is in the nature of being a certain conviction (*niścaya*) and so on.
The sense is that [the opponent objects] because there is both complexity (gaurava) and a lack of evidence for [the self] being a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the instigator (*prayojaka*).

Then, the author raises an objection: "But surely the very same factor established as the instigator in the knowledge produced by the Vedāntas is absent in the knowledge of jars and the like," [expressed in the words] "na ca ghaṭādyākāra... and so forth.
The meaning is as follows: being delimited (*avacchinnatva*) is the reason for being imagined (*kalpitatva*), while being undelimited (*anavacchinnatva*) is the reason for being real (*satyatva*).

This is because the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) directed toward jars and the like have as their object the imagined consciousness (*kalpitacaitanya*), and thus lack the real Brahman as their object. [Regarding] the consciousness delimited by a jar and so forth...

Regarding the term "imagined" (*kalpita*), one must consider whether the intended meaning refers to the aspect of consciousness (*caitanyāṃśa*) being imagined or not imagined. It is not the first case;
thus he says: "Therein. This means "in the limited consciousness" (*avacchinnacaitanya*).
The aspect of consciousness that is delimited—which has objects such as jars as its content—is not imagined.
The meaning is that [the vṛtti] has the same nature as the Brahman-consciousness which is the object of the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna).

Thus, the intended ground for the sublation of even a vṛtti whose object is the consciousness delimited by a jar or the like is present in the knowledge produced by the Vedānta; namely, the fact that it possesses the same objective referent as the root-ignorance which is to be removed—this is the point.

Demonstrating that even in the second alternative (kalpa) there exists an established causal factor for the occurrence of a jar and so forth, he refutes that alternative with the words: "Because of its being imagined" (*tasya kalpitatve*). This means: "of the portion of consciousness that is delimited" (*avacchedya-caitanya-aṃśasya*). By the phrase "because it must be stated," [he implies] that under the view that the delimited portion of consciousness is imagined, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍatva*).

Since it is impossible for that insentient [effect] to be the object of ignorance, one must state that the Brahman-consciousness, which is the object of the fundamental ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), is itself the object of the ignorance regarding that state;
for ignorance cannot exist without an object. And thus:

In order for [cognitions] to remove the ignorance regarding the state [of the world] that has Brahman-consciousness as its object, it is unavoidable that even the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) directed toward jars and the like must have as their object the Brahman-consciousness which is the object of the root-ignorance; for if the mental modifications directed toward jars and the like did not have the real Brahman as their object, they could not remove that ignorance.
The meaning is that because there is an absence of identity between the two objects, those [states] would not have the capacity to remove the ignorance regarding those states.

Regarding the phrase "its remover": the word "that" (tat) refers to the ignorance regarding the states; in the phrase "having that as its object," the word "that" refers to the Brahman-consciousness which is the object of the root-ignorance. This applies even in that [other] view.

The meaning is that even in the second alternative, the portion to be delimited (*avacchedya*) is imagined (*kalpita*). "From that" means from the cognition of a jar or the like. "Because it is not avoided" means that the cognition of a jar or the like is [subject to the same critique] just like the cognition produced by the Vedānta.
The meaning is that [the ignorance in question] has the same object as the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna).
Regarding this, the teachers say: "Consciousness is not an object of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the eyes and other senses;
'His form does not stand within the range of vision; no one sees Him with the eye';
'The Self-existent One pierced the openings toward the outside; therefore, one looks outward, not at the inner self,' and so forth."

This is because scripture teaches that it is unfit for the eyes and other senses—just like atoms and the like—and because of the qualifying term "pertaining to the Upaniṣads" (*aupaniṣada*). Nor does this contradict the Vārttika, which states, "Nor is Brahman established as being cognizable by all means of knowledge," and so forth; for that [passage]...
When the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "pot" arises, because the veil [of ignorance] is overcome, the pot— which is essentially real like a dream—
becomes conventionally treated as "the pot exists," since it is intended to mean that it is cognizable through the metaphorical mental modification of "pot" and so forth.
Furthermore, the capacity of the cognition of a jar or the like to overcome its own veil is established precisely by its having the jar or the like as its object,

since the jar and so forth are also objects of nescience (ajñāna). This is evident from such states of nescience as "I do not know the jar" and "the nescience regarding the jar has been destroyed by the cognition of the jar."

This is because there is the experience of [the jar] as having the jar and so forth as its object. Nor should it be argued that the postulation of ignorance (*ajñāna*) in that case is improper because there is no function of concealment (*āvaraṇa-kṛtya*); for the non-manifestation of that [jar] is explained precisely by the concealment of the consciousness delimited by it (*tad-avacchinna-caitanya*), which is the illuminator of that [jar].

Regarding the phrase "here they say": the meaning is that this addresses the objection that even the cognition of a jar or similar object would remove the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because it has consciousness (*caitanya*) as its object, just like the knowledge produced by the Vedāntas; thus, they state the non-establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*). [The text continues:
"The form of this Self is visible (*saṃdṛśe*)," where *saṃdṛśa* means "within the range of vision."
Because it lacks form and other qualities, it does not abide as a fit object [for perception]. Therefore, no one sees this Self with the eye.
The Lord pierced the apertures—the sense organs—so that they were turned away from external objects;
that is to say, He created the instruments solely for the purpose of perceiving insentient objects. Therefore, it is so.

Because it is created, everyone in the world perceives only that which is external and further removed by means of the senses; they do not perceive the inner self whose nature is consciousness—this is the meaning. The scriptural passage beginning with "It is not grasped by the eye" constitutes the meaning of the word "etcetera.
The word "of that" (tasya) means "of consciousness" (caitanyasya). Now, [one might object]: if this is taught because the senses are incapable [of perceiving it], then [the Upanishads] alone...

He raises the objection that if consciousness is accepted as the object of experience residing in the pot and so forth—because it is heard [in scripture] that it is "to be gone to" (gamya)—then there would be a contradiction with the Vārttika.
He says: "Nor [is it the case that] all... If whatever object is perceived is perceived only as "existent," such is the experience.

The meaning is that Brahman, whose true nature is *valāt* (by force/essentially), is established as being cognizable by all cognitions. The Vārtikakāras maintain that the cognizability of consciousness (*caitanya*) by all cognitions is merely figurative (*gauṇa*), and not primary (*mukhya*) in the same way as jars and other objects, because that would contradict the cited scripture. Thus, there is no contradiction with the Vārtika.

He explains: "Of that" means "of the statement in the Vārttika. Just as a jar possesses the status of being an object of worldly transaction dependent upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the jar, so too does Brahman—the reality (*sat-rūpa*) which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the jar and other objects—possess [the status of being an object of worldly transaction] dependent upon the modification of the jar and so forth.

The meaning is that by stating "it exists as an object of empirical usage" (*vyavahāraviṣayatvam asti*), the author of the Vārttika asserts that Brahman, like a jar or other objects, is not perceived as having the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) through its qualities. Nor should it be argued that such a conclusion is impossible in the case of objects of indirect cognition (*parokṣa-vṛtti*), because there is no sublation of the concealment (*āvaraṇa*) in those instances.
The point is that in the *Vārttika*, the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is understood as functioning to overcome an obscuration. Now, one might object:

if a cognition such as that of a jar does not have as its object the consciousness delimited by the jar, it cannot possibly overcome the ignorance that obscures that consciousness, for [knowledge and ignorance must relate to the same object].

Because there is an absence of having the same object [of cognition], he says: "And being the subduer of the veil. He states that even an insentient object must be accepted as an object of ignorance on the strength of experience, saying: "Even of a jar, etc.
The word "state" (*avasthā*) is used to exclude primordial ignorance (*mūlājñāna*); for that [ignorance] is [expressed as] "I do not know Brahman."

Because there is the experience that [the witness] has Brahman alone as its object; the sense is that it does not have an insentient thing (*jaḍa*) as its object. Nor is it the case "there" (in the verse), meaning: with respect to an insentient entity. It is "not proper" because being the locus of ignorance is not appropriate for an insentient thing, since there is no concealment (*āvaraṇa*) there. And the absence of that [concealment] is due to the absence of a result (*phala*). [The phrase] "I do not perceive the jar... [is used].

The point is this: the experience "I know" is also possible by virtue of having consciousness as its object, due to the identity between the jar and the consciousness that is its substrate. [Objection: But if there is no concealment (āvaraṇa) of an insentient object, how can its non-manifestation be possible? Nor [is it the case that...]

It should not be said that the non-manifestation [of the insentient] is due solely to the absence of contact with the consciousness that illuminates it, rather than due to the power of an obscuration; for since the insentient is superimposed upon self-luminous consciousness, there is always a contact between it and the consciousness that makes it manifest. Therefore, the non-manifestation of the insentient is indeed [due to its own nature].
Because [the result] is the fruit of the veil of insentience (*jaḍāvaraṇa*), he says: "of its illuminator. Here, the three occurrences of the word *tat* refer to the insentient.

Although it has been stated by way of argument that the negation of insentient matter (*jaḍa*) being the direct object of ignorance does not imply that the manifestation of consciousness delimited by that insentient matter is veiled by ignorance; nevertheless,
even when there is contact with the manifestation of eternal consciousness, it is said of the insentient matter that "it does not exist" and "it is not manifested," and so forth.
The state of being fit for empirical usage [is established] because ignorance is admitted to be its object through a traditional lineage;
for it is only knowledge whose object is that which is to be obscured by ignorance—whether directly or indirectly—that possesses the causal efficacy of removing that ignorance. And it is not thus...
Since, according to the aforementioned method, even objects such as jars would be the objects of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*),
it would follow that root-ignorance is removed by the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the jar itself; however,
on the strength of the observed result (*phala-bala*), it is held that only that which has as its object something other than the effects of that ignorance can remove it.
Because it is the underlying principle.

Regarding the phrase "by the stated reasoning": the meaning is that even though the sentence—stating that "the acceptance of ignorance [as residing] in the insentient is not tenable because of the absence of the function of obscuration"—rejects both the direct substratum-hood of ignorance and the direct object-hood of ignorance in the insentient, [one might object]: "But surely that sentence [only rejects] the direct object-hood of ignorance in the insentient..."

One might ask: why is it assumed that [the scripture] aims at the total rejection [of the world], rather than merely rejecting its status as an object of ignorance common to both direct and indirect [perception]? Anticipating this objection, the subsequent passage states that if that were the case, the non-manifestation of the insentient would be established simply by the veiling of the consciousness delimited by it (tadavacchinna-caitanya), which is what illumines it; thus, [the rejection applies] even to the insentient.

With the intention that it would result in a contradiction of the accepted position that [the Self] is the object of ignorance through a traditional lineage, he says, beginning with "limited by the insentient" (*jaḍāvacchinna*) and so forth.

In the portion of the text starting from "because its non-manifestation is established" (*tadaprakāśopapatteḥ*), there exists the doubt regarding the insentient: "Does it manifest? or "Is it dear? (i.e., is it not manifest?).

By the phrase "precisely because of the veiling of consciousness," he demonstrates that the veiling of consciousness is accepted as the cause of the veiling of the insentient (jaḍa), since the veiling characterized by the unfitness for such conventional usage [as "this is consciousness"] has been admitted [to belong] to consciousness itself. [The words] "by ignorance" and "from that" [refer to this].

The meaning is: because of the obscuration of consciousness (*caitanya*). Since consciousness, by virtue of being self-luminous, possesses a state of constant, inherent luminosity that necessitates the postulation of an obscuration, so too does the insentient (*jaḍa*) possess a state of constant, inherent luminosity—due to its perpetual association with the light of consciousness—which likewise necessitates the postulation of an obscuration.
It indicates that [the two cases] are equal. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of contact with the light of eternal consciousness," the word *iti* expresses a manner or mode.

Now, according to the aforementioned method, it follows that the ignorance of a state (*avasthājñāna*), which resides in the consciousness delimited [by an object], is insentient and is the veiler of both that [ignorance] and the consciousness delimited by it. And thus:

If it were admitted that the cognition of a jar and so forth has only insentient objects as its domain, then—because it would lack identity of object with ignorance in every respect—it could not be the remover of ignorance; therefore, he says: "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
In the body of the definition of opposition, the mere fact of having an identical object with ignorance is the determining factor for knowledge.

The sense is that [the cognition] has entered [into the object], yet it does not have the same objective domain (*samānaviṣayakatva*) in all its aspects due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*). "And not thus" means that there is no insistence on the cognition and the ignorance having the same objective domain in all their aspects.
"By the stated method" means by virtue of the fact that the limited consciousness (*avacchinnacaitanya*), in its own nature, is real.
Just as the nature of Brahman is the object of the state-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*), it is likewise the object of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

Thus, by virtue of the concealment of consciousness effected by the state-ignorance, even the insentient [world] becomes indirectly the object of the state-ignorance, according to the manner previously described.

The meaning is that, by the power of the concealment of consciousness caused by root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), it would be unavoidable for insentient objects such as jars to also become the objects of that root-ignorance. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "As for the jar, etc.
Just as knowledge in its various states (*avasthā*) is not an object for the primary consciousness...

The meaning is this: since the cessation of the ignorance residing in the limited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*) occurs solely through the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of the insentient object, it would follow—by the same logic—that the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) would also cease solely through the direct perception of the insentient object, which serves as its indirect object. Thus, there arises the undesirable consequence (*āpāta*) that the root-ignorance would be removed [even without the realization of Brahman]. This is the sense of the phrase "the undesirable consequence of the removal of root-ignorance does not occur."

He states the reason with the words "by the force of the result" (*phalabalāt*) and so forth. The meaning is: even when there is direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of a jar or other objects, it is by the force of the result consisting in the persistence of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). [This occurs] in that knowledge which has as its object the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—which is the object of the root-ignorance and is distinct from the root-ignorance and its effects—characterized as having that very [pure consciousness] as its object.

The meaning is that since the capacity to remove fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna) is postulated as being contingent upon [the means], and since that [contingency] is absent in the case of the direct perception of a jar and so forth, there is no unwanted consequence of such perception removing fundamental ignorance.

Alternatively, the insentient [object] is not the object of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) itself; however, for the states of knowledge which reside in the limited consciousness (*avacchinnacaitanya*), the insentient alone is the object. Otherwise, when consciousness is manifested in a piece of sandalwood by a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*), [there would be no distinction] regarding that which is in contact with it.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the odor becoming directly perceived [even when it is not].

Furthermore, if that [consciousness] were not manifested, there would be the undesirable consequence of neither the sandalwood nor its color being revealed. Nor can it be argued that the manifestation of the sandalwood and its color occurs through the visual modification (vṛtti), because of the manifestation of the consciousness delimited by the sandalwood and its color [by that very same modification].
It must be stated that due to the absence of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having smell as its form, the consciousness delimited by smell is not manifested;

and because of that non-manifestation, there is no illumination of it. This is because, in the absence of a mental modification that doubles [the manifestation] of consciousness, the qualities of a single substance cannot pervade everywhere within their own substratum.

Since it is impossible for present objects to individually limit consciousness— just as it is impossible for them to individually limit space— they [are perceived] only by the consciousness delimited by their own substratum-dravya, just as [an object is perceived] by the consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearl.

If it were manifested through being made manifest like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, then it would follow that even the fragrance would not be manifested when consciousness is unmanifested, and likewise, even color and other qualities would fail to be manifested. Nor is there any rule that fragrance is manifested only when consciousness is colored by a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of fragrance.

To the objection that the removal of ignorance— which veils the limited consciousness— cannot occur through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is merely the insentient (*jaḍa*), because their objects are distinct, [the author replies]:
the state-ignorance (*avasthājñāna*) also veils the insentient by means of its veiling of the limited consciousness.
Thus, it has been established that the cessation of the ignorance of the states is possible even through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is merely the insentient (*jaḍa*).

Now, regarding that very doubt, he shows a resolution by another method, beginning with "Alternatively" (*athavā*). Alternatively, the objects of the various ignorances of the states are precisely those respective insentient things.
The connection [is as follows]: the sense is that [this is known] precisely from the previously mentioned experience, such as "I do not know the jar.

If that were so, then the substratum of the various states of ignorance would also have to be that very same insentient object; and if that were the case, it would contradict your own established tenet. To this, he says: "of those [ignorances] residing in the limited consciousness (avacchinna-caitanya)."

Now, one might ask: if it is accepted that the insentient (jaḍa) is the object of ignorance, what becomes of the established tenet (siddhānta) that "the insentient is not the object of ignorance"? To this, he says: "Of the root-ignorance alone.
The meaning is that the tenet regarding the insentient not being an object of ignorance refers exclusively to the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna).

"Otherwise" means: if the insentient object were not veiled. By the visual modification (*cākṣuṣa-vṛtti*) directed toward a piece of sandalwood, is the consciousness delimited by that [object] manifested or not? Regarding the first case, he states the defect: "of those things in contact with it.

This means that there would result the immediate perception (*aparokṣya*) of the fragrance residing in the sandalwood, just as there is of the sandalwood itself, because [the consciousness] is manifested.

Because the state of being in contact with consciousness is indistinguishable in both cases. However, this fault does not apply to the position that the insentient is covered; for the meaning is that the covering of fragrance is not removed by a visual modification (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*). He states the fault in the second [position]: "those [objects] are unmanifested," meaning that non-illumination would result.
The meaning is that at the time of the visual function directed toward sandalwood, there is an absence of the manifestation of the color-form (*rūpa*) of the sandalwood.

Anticipating the objection that— just as in the case of substances such as pieces of sandalwood, pots, or cloths— qualities residing in a single substance can also serve as delimiters of consciousness (*caitanyāvachedakatva*), he raises the doubt with the words "na ca" (and not).

He states that there is no difference in consciousness within a single substance due to the distinctions of color, taste, smell, and so forth, because there is a lack of evidence. Regarding the phrase "of consciousness": since consciousness is partless, it is impossible for one [quality] to exist at a certain location within a substance while another is excluded from that same location; this is the meaning. If it were one...

If odors and other qualities were to exist within a substance through spatial differentiation, then there would arise even the suspicion of a differentiation in consciousness within that same substance due to the differentiation of those odors and so forth. However, this is not the case, because odors and the like are experienced as having pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*). With this intention, he says: "pervasive" (*vyāpya*). Just as in the case of substances such as jars...
The sense is that while there is a differentiation of space [by objects], there is no such differentiation of space by smell and so forth;

for it is not the case that space is differentiated by the differentiation of smell and so forth. Thus, once it is established that there is no differentiation of consciousness (caitanya) through the differentiation of smell and so forth...
He states that the previously mentioned defects regarding the manifestation and non-manifestation of consciousness (*caitanya*) in sandalwood are difficult to avoid, saying:

"Of those... Just as in the case of mother-of-pearl, because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver upon the consciousness delimited by the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearl, the silver is manifested within that very consciousness of the "this" aspect of the mother-of-pearl.
The meaning is this: it is not the case that [color and so forth] are manifested by a consciousness delimited by itself—which would be separate from the consciousness delimited by the [substance];

rather, even color and other qualities imagined within the consciousness delimited by a substance are illuminated by that very same consciousness delimited by the substance. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But..."

He restates and then refutes the objection that even though the fragrance of sandalwood is conjoined with the manifestation of consciousness whose nature is pure awareness, it lacks immediacy precisely because there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward that fragrance;
this is expressed in the words: "Nor [is it the case] that it has the form of fragrance."

Since the very contact with light is the meaning of the term "manifesting," it would be contradictory to imagine a state of non-manifestation when the contact with light is unobstructed, even if there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of that object. And [this is so] because the consciousness which is the material cause of the fragrance has been manifested.
Because it is impossible [to speak of] the non-contact of fragrance [with that which is not a substrate], therefore, just as in the case of Caitra’s cognition of a jar,

there is the cessation of ignorance alone— which is the veiler with respect to that [object]— and thus the manifestation of the object belongs to him alone and not to anyone else; so too, through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of this or that object, there is the cessation of only that ignorance which veils it.
Because it is accepted that the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of another object belongs only to that which is unobscured, and that immediacy consists in the non-difference from consciousness; thus,
even with a difference of objects, there is [immediacy] in a single [consciousness], despite the difference of subjects.

Since it must be stated that the distinction among the various states of ignorance (avasthājñāna) consists in their having respective insentient objects, there is no inconsistency in the fact that mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as those directed toward a jar do not remove these states of ignorance, nor does it follow that they would remove the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

He states the reason for the restriction "and not [in the case of] *niyama*" as follows: "only in the case of contact with [pure] illumination (*prakāśa*). This is because the meaning of the term "manifesting" (*prakāśamāna*) does not apply to pleasure and the like when they are in contact with the witness-consciousness (*sākṣiprakāśa*) that is not accompanied by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward pleasure and so forth, even though that witness-consciousness is unobstructed and associated with a modification conditioned by [the object].
The meaning is that it would follow as a consequence that there is an absence of the manifestation of the word's meaning.

Having raised the doubt that there is no connection at all between fragrance and manifested consciousness, he says: "And of the manifested [fragrance]," where the word "and" (ca) is connected with the phrase "because of its impossibility. The term *upādāna* refers to the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
"Furthermore, because it is impossible.

The sense is that, likewise, under the view that the insentient (jaḍa) is unobscured, the immediate perception (āparokṣya) of fragrance would also unavoidably follow at the time of the manifestation of the consciousness of sandalwood. However, under the view that the insentient is obscured...

He states that the aforementioned fault does not apply: "Therefore," etc. The meaning is that because the veiling of the insentient (*jaḍa*) is established.
