Now, even on the view that the insentient is veiled, the removal of the veil over the fragrance might occur through the visual modification (*vṛtti*) directed toward the sandalwood itself, because of the identity (*tādātmya*) between the quality and the possessor of the quality. And thus, at the time when the sandalwood is directly perceived...
Anticipating the objection that the same defect applies here as well when examining the scent of that [flower], he dispels it by means of an illustration:
"Just as... The meaning of the particle *eva* (only) is that there is no cessation of the obscuring ignorance for anyone other [than the specific perceiver].
The phrase "of that very person" means that the manifestation of the jar belongs to Caitra alone, and not to others such as Maitra. "In the same way... [is the conclusion].

The meaning is that even though there is identity (*tādātmya*) between a quality and its possessor, because difference (*bheda*) also exists, it does not follow that fragrance and other qualities would become directly perceived (*āparokṣya*) simply by the occurrence of a cognition whose object is sandalwood.
Now, one might ask: how can fragrance—which is non-different from the cognition of sandalwood—be [perceived] when it is veiled?

Fearing that [the absence of] non-immediacy might be the case, he says "of the unobscured object alone" (*anāvṛtārthasyaiva*), showing that it is not so, because it is observed that the non-difference of consciousness (*saṃvidabheda*) is the cause of immediacy precisely in the case of pleasure and the like, which are unobscured.
Now, [one might object]: if the state of knowledge resides in the consciousness delimited by a single piece of sandalwood for Caitra...

He dispels the doubt that— since the covering of the sandalwood is one and since it does not cease from functioning upon the sandalwood— it would be illogical for the fragrance to be obstructed at the time the sandalwood is covered— by stating: "only by means of a difference in the cognizer."

Just as there is manifold ignorance regarding the subject (*pramātṛ*) due to distinctions such as Caitra, Maitra, and so forth, so too it must be stated that even in a single instance of consciousness delimited by sandalwood (*caṃdana*), there is manifold ignorance due to the distinction of objects such as fragrance and the like; for this is precisely because fragrance is not perceived when the sandalwood is being directly perceived. This is the point.

The reason is provided by the phrase "by means of the reflective awareness of the subject at hand. Thus, the sense is that since there is no possibility of an obscuration of the fragrance and so forth at the time of the direct perception of sandalwood, the aforementioned defect does not arise. Regarding the phrase "because it has an insentient object":
this means "because it has an insentient object as its content. There is no inconsistency whatsoever; [this refers to] the modifications (*vṛtti*) such as those directed toward a jar and so on.

In the absence of consciousness (*caitanya*) being their object, there can be no basis for contradiction between knowledge and ignorance in the form of having the same object; for those [modifications] have only the insentient (*jaḍa*) as their scope, whereas ignorance has only consciousness as its object. Thus, the aforementioned inconsistency does not apply even to the ignorance residing within itself.

Because it is admitted that [nescience] has only the insentient (*jaḍa*) as its object; likewise, there is no contradiction with established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*) even if the concealment (*āvaraṇa*) of the insentient is admitted, nor is there any logical inconsistency (*rūpānupapatti*), since the non-admission of the concealment of the insentient pertains to the object of root-nescience (*mūlājñāna*). And thus:

Furthermore, there is no logical inconsistency in the form of contradicting the established doctrine of unity by accepting the multiplicity of the ignorance that veils the insentient; for even the acceptance of that unity has as its object the root-ignorance, [and thus does not exclude] the ignorances that veil the insentient. Regarding those ignorances that veil the insentient...
Having intended [the argument] beginning with "because it has the nature of a state," it was stated that there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

He states the primary subject matter: "And not... This refers to the objection raised at the outset by the opponent (pūrvavādin), namely, that the cognitions of jars and so forth would also result in the removal of the root ignorance (mūlājñāna).

The meaning is that this [objection] does not exist at all, because it is not admitted that the functions (vṛttis) regarding jars and so forth have as their object the consciousness that is the object of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna).
Even so, there is no contingency of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of "I," which has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its object, being the remover of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*),

because that [modification] has as its object only the non-conscious element (*acidaṃśa*) conjoined with the self-luminous consciousness (*citsaṃvalita*). This is as in the case of "So 'ham" (That am I).

This is because even recognition (*pratibhijñā*), while being self-luminous consciousness, has as its object merely the qualification by prior and posterior times along with the qualification by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); thus, it lacks consciousness itself as its object.
However, some, having accepted that the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) regarding jars and so forth have as their object the consciousness delimited (*avacchinna*) by those respective [objects],...

And since all means of knowledge would otherwise apply [to Brahman], and because it is the locus of the fruits of all means of knowledge, the statement "it is to be heard" (śrotavya) was uttered with the desire to initiate [inquiry];
for, as stated in the Vārttika,
in accordance with the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) regarding the Vedāntas— the meaning of which is that "it is to be heard"— [the knowledge] arises solely from the Vedāntas.

They say that the knowledge of Brahman, when conjoined with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from observances (*niyama*), is unimpeded and is what removes [the ignorance of] Brahman; thus, there is no risk of the removal of [ignorance regarding] jars and other objects occurring through the knowledge of those things.
Others, however, [hold that] the knowledge of the identity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīvabrahmābhedajñāna*) produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*)...

Only knowledge whose object is difference (bheda) is the remover of root-ignorance (mūlājñāna), because root-ignorance has non-difference as its object; thus, there is no possibility of its removal by the cognition of a jar or similar objects, which have the mere nature of consciousness (caitanya-svarūpa) as their object.
"And even so" means that although mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as those regarding a jar do not have consciousness as their object,

the "I"-modification must necessarily have consciousness as its object, because the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is the "I," consists of a conglomeration of consciousness and non-consciousness. "Of that" refers to [the "I"-modification] itself, by virtue of its self-luminosity.

The meaning is as follows: since the "I"-form modification (*ahaṃkāra-vṛtti*) has as its object only that portion of the non-conscious which is blended with and superimposed upon the manifesting consciousness through identity with it, it does not have pure consciousness as its object; otherwise, it would contradict the Upanishadic scriptures. [Objection: But [is it not the case that] "I, who experienced Śrī Kṛṣṇa in a dream, am that same [person now]"?

Furthermore, in recognition such as "I remember that [person] from my waking state," it is necessary that consciousness be the object; otherwise, through such recognition, the permanence and the distinctness from the aggregate of the conscious self would not be established. Therefore, he says: "That I am."

Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) also, while consciousness is manifesting by itself, takes as its object not only the identification with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as "I," but also attributes such as "this-ness" (*tattā*).

However, in this system, self-luminous consciousness does not [require recognition for its manifestation], because the permanence and other qualities of the conscious Self are established solely on the strength of scripture (*śruti*).

It should be understood that this does not apply to recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For if it were argued that since the mental states (*vṛtti*) regarding jars and so forth are no different from the Vedānta-generated knowledge in their having consciousness as their object, they too would result in the removal of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), such an objection is invalid because the reason (*hetu*) for it simply does not exist. Thus, [the unwanted consequence] is not stated.

The objection (*prasaṅga*) has been answered; now he states that even if it is admitted that those [cognitions] have consciousness as their object, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) does not follow: "However, some...
and "having admitted... (*abhyupagamya*).

Nor should it be argued that by accepting this [position], there would be a contradiction with those scriptural passages that deny that consciousness is an object of the eyes and other sense organs; for those passages have as their subject matter unconditioned consciousness (*nirupādhika-caitanya*),
whereas the eyes and other senses have as their objects delimited consciousness (*avacchinna-caitanya*).

The sense is that there is no contradiction with that [scriptural authority]. For this very reason, the previously cited statement from the *Vārttika*, which establishes that the consciousness of Brahman is the object of all cognitions, is also consistent.
For validity consists in making known what was previously unknown, and it is the reality of consciousness alone that is unknown; therefore, it is that alone [which is made known].
Because it is logical to conceive of ignorance as having the self-luminous [consciousness]— which is eternally engaged in manifesting itself— as its object;
for since the non-manifestation of the insentient is possible only when the manifesting consciousness is veiled,
it is impossible to postulate a separate veil for that [insentient matter], and because ignorance is necessarily dependent upon consciousness, [it belongs to] that darkness.

Furthermore, because it is logically untenable for [an obstruction] to act as a cause of concealment anywhere other than its own substratum, so too, for the sake of establishing the validity of perception and the other means of knowledge, one must admit that they have as their object consciousness delimited by objects such as a jar,
and not merely the insentient (jaḍa) alone; thus, for all means of knowledge, that which is designated as the "fruit" [is consciousness].

Since the realization of Brahman—which is the means to attain immortality—has consciousness as its object, it follows that all means of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) could potentially serve as causes for it; therefore, in order to restrict [the means] specifically to the Vedāntas, the statement "it is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) was uttered with the intention of establishing this very point: that an inquiry into the Vedāntas alone must be undertaken.

The meaning of the *Vārttika* is as follows: although the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) regarding jars and other objects have consciousness as their object, they do not lead to the undesirable consequence of removing the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because—lacking the status of being produced by Vedānta—they are devoid of the association with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the injunction "one should hear" (*śrotavya*).
This is the intended sense. [Regarding the term] "unobstructed" (*apratibaddham*):...
The sense is that the obstructing evil has been exhausted by the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the observance of rules (*niyama*).

This is because we see the words of Nārada stating that the knowledge arising from such sentences as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is the means to liberation. [This refers to] that knowledge arising from sentences such as "That thou art," which has as its object the identity (*tādātmya*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Furthermore, from the observation of the words of the venerable Śaṅkarācārya that "this very knowledge is the means to liberation," and because root-ignorance (mūlājñāna) veils the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, it follows that this very knowledge is that which has as its object the identity characterized by the oneness of the jīva and Brahman.
He presents another solution to avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that [knowledge of anything] would be a means to liberation: "But others...

The meaning is as follows: since it is established that only the knowledge of non-difference produced by the sentence is the remover of ignorance, there is no consequence of the root-ignorance being removed by the cognition of a jar or other objects, which do not have that non-difference as their object.

Nor should it be said that since non-difference—which is cognized by the means of valid knowledge revealing reality—is not distinct from consciousness, and because duality would otherwise result, non-difference is merely consciousness;
and therefore, even the cognition of a jar or other objects within its scope must have non-difference as its object. This is not so.
We do not state that there is a distinction [between these two] on account of their objects, namely non-difference and cognition; rather, [we speak of it as follows].

Nor [is it the case that] the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman cannot be said to be distinct from consciousness; for if that were so, since the non-difference that is the intended purport of the Vedāntas would necessarily be real, it would entail the loss of the non-duality of consciousness. Furthermore, if the non-difference that is the subject of the Vedāntic purport were unreal...

The meaning is that it would result in the subversion of the validity of the Vedāntas, characterized as the revelation of reality (*tatvāvedakatva*), which is accepted in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*). Here, the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the ultimate reality (*paramārthavastu*).

[The opponent objects: "No; for even in the cognition of a jar or the like, although consciousness (*caitanya*) is the object, the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is not its object."

However, in the case of the knowledge of the meaning of the Great Sentence (mahāvākya), the non-difference between those two [subject and object] is the very object; thus, we do not claim that the knowledge produced by the Great Sentence differs from the knowledge of a jar or similar objects in terms of its object. This is for the reason that the aforementioned defect would otherwise remain as it was. But this is not the case in an error such as "this is silver."

Just as it is observed that the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like— which has as its object specific qualities such as superior color and so forth in relation to whatever degree of splendor the substrate lacks—
is the sublater of the error of silver and the like, so too is the case with "there is a jar."

In illusions such as "the jar manifests," as long as consciousness— which serves as the substratum— is the object, if one does not admit that the knowledge produced by the sentence has as its object a greater degree of non-difference [from that consciousness],
then the knowledge arising from the sentence would simply not have the power to remove the illusion; therefore, [it must be admitted] that it is the object.

He raises the objection that a distinction must be admitted. However, there is no rule that only those cognitions whose objects exceed the object of the error can remove that error, because this is contradicted by the observation that even cognitions whose objects do not exceed the object of the error can remove it. To illustrate: in reality, [the cognition] regarding the locus of the [supposed] ghost...
On the bank of the Gaṅgā, a person has the delusion that it is the bank of a pond; thus, he possesses the delusion that there is a hamlet on the bank of that pond.

When the sentence "There is a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" is uttered, from that sentence, the cognition arises for that person that "there is a hamlet on the bank of the Gaṅgā. And by that cognition, [he understands] the nature of being the bank of a pond [to belong] to the bank of the Gaṅgā.

And in that case, the error ceases; for, compared to the error, a certain specific object is observed in the cognition produced by the sentence regarding the portion of the Ganges bank which was the object of that error. Nor is there, in that cognition produced by the sentence, any specific feature such as "being the bank of the Ganges" that would exclude the riverbank [of a lake].
It should not be argued that [the word] lacks the capacity to have a specific object as its content because it is observed to have an object in general;

for there are cases where the utterance "A hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ) is employed with the intention of having "bankness" (*tīratva*) alone as its qualifier, and likewise, when a deluded person grasps that very intention, even though there is no resulting cognition qualified by "Gaṅgā-bankness" (*gaṅgātīratva*).

Because there is deviation [from the rule] due to the observation of the cessation of error; for instance, when a person possessing the erroneous notion that "rice-chaff must be removed by any and every potsherd" is addressed with the words "by means of the sacrificial cake-potsherd" (puroḍāśakapālena),
which are employed with the intention of signifying merely the nature of being a potsherd, and are understood by him as having that specific intention alone.

From the sentence "He scatters the husks with the potsherd" (*tuṣān upavapati kapālena*), the understanding arises that the scattering of husks must be performed with a potsherd; in this regard, even if there is no apprehension of a specific quality that distinguishes one potsherd from others, [the injunction applies] to potsherds other than those used for the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
Because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) even in that case, as seen in the removal of the delusion regarding husks being the means for removing [chaff]; therefore,

although the verbal cognition "there is a hamlet on the bank" lacks the specific object consisting of the state of being the Ganges-bank, at the time of the presentation of the word-meanings which is its cause, there exists a presentation of the bank as being related to the Ganges, and that presentation—

It must be stated that, by the very nature of its greatness, even that [cognition] which has an object no greater than the delusion— such as the cognition of one standing on the bank of the Gaṅgā regarding a poisonous snake— functions to remove that delusion. Likewise, although the verbal comprehension "the winnowing-basket-slip should be sown with husks" lacks an intrinsic specific object that excludes other winnowing-baskets, [it nonetheless functions to exclude them].

At the time of the mental presentation of the word-meanings that serve as the cause for such verbal cognition, since there exists a presentation of the potsherd as being related to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), it must be stated that by virtue of that presentation,
[the cognition] functions to subvert the error, even though its object is not something additional to the erroneous cognition itself; and thus, regarding knowledge...
In being the opposite of error, what is the determining factor is being produced by a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*),
and not having a greater object than the error, because of the risk of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*).

The nature of the knowledge of non-difference with respect to that [Tattvamasi] consists precisely in consciousness having that as its object, by means of a specific relation of identity which depends upon specific causes such as the reflective awareness of the two substrata (dharmin) that are the denotative meanings of the words "That" and "Thou."

For just as, although there is no difference in the fact that [cognitions] have as their objects the qualifier, the qualified, and their relation, the cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭajñāna*)— depending on specific causes such as the cognition of the qualifier—
possesses as its object those three [factors] precisely through a specific essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*), whereas a "collective apprehension" (*samūhālambana*) does not.

The state of being a qualified cognition is excluded [from doubt], just as the state of being a man—which is contradictory to the state of being a post—is excluded from the case of a permanent, artificial post. Likewise, the state of being a doubt is excluded from the object itself because the specific nature of the object cannot be determined; thus, even in the case of a jar and so forth, it is "this very jar."

The fact that such cognitions have the jar and so forth as their objects— by virtue of a specific relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*)— is precisely what distinguishes them from cognitions produced by words such as "jar";
for there is no cognition of non-difference that is distinct [from the object], since non-difference cannot be established as something additional.

Furthermore, it is established by Śruti, Smṛti, and the experience of the wise that the knowledge produced by the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) is opposed to the delusion that is the root of saṃsāra; and that the Great Sayings have as their sole function the awakening to the nature of pure Consciousness (caitanya-svarūpa).
[This is discussed] in the second chapter on the knowledge produced by the Great Sayings, which is the means to liberation.
We have established and elaborated in our treatises, by citing scriptural passages, that the determiner of the object is of the nature of mere individual consciousness; and thus,
in cases such as the illusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell,
there exists a cognition of the mother-of-pearl which possesses an object exceeding the scope of the error and which is opposed to that error.

Since it is observed that, just as having a greater object than error depends upon a specific causal complex (sāmagrī) consisting of the absence of defects and so forth, so too does the opposition of knowledge to error depend upon a causal complex— this being in accordance with the Vedānta texts whose meaning is impartite (*akhaṇḍārtha*) and in conformity with the previously cited instances of deviation.

Intending to show that it is logical to postulate only the dependence on a specific [object] as the pervasive causal factor— and not the state of having an object exceeding that of an error— he resolves the objection by demonstrating that the knowledge of the meaning of a great sentence (mahāvākya), even though its object does not exceed that of an error, is capable of subverting error.

Regarding the term *tatvam*: the two substrata (*dharmin*) are the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which constitute the denoted meanings (*vācyārtha*) of the two words *tat* and *tvam*.

First, there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of recollection through the primary power (*śakti*) of those two words, *tat* and *tvam*; subsequently, by the force of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the words *tat* and *tvam*, [the nature of] the individual soul...

The cognition of those two as being in a relationship of qualifier and qualified is that "it is non-different from Īśvara. Immediately thereafter, since the identity of the two qualified entities is not possible, there arises the perception of a contradiction. And immediately after that, through the two words *tat* and *tvam*, there occurs the non-difference between the portions of pure consciousness that constitute the referents of the substantive elements within the respective qualified meanings.

Intending the sequence that [the object] is first cognized through the secondary function (lakṣaṇā) of fitness, and thereafter there arises a verbal cognition whose scope is the non-difference between the two qualificands, [the author uses] the word "ādi" (and so forth). This refers to that specific relation of essential identity (svarūpa-sambandha) between the knowledge produced by the sentence and its own objective consciousness, which is brought about by a particular causal complex (sāmagrī).
The meaning is as follows: by virtue of its relationship [with the Self], the state of having consciousness as its object distinguishes [this knowledge] from the cognition of a jar and the like;

that very state constitutes its nature as non-dual knowledge, and it is solely by the power of that [nature] that it possesses the capacity to oppose root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), and so forth.
This refers to the knowledge produced by the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) in comparison to the cognition of jars and other such objects.

Although there is no distinction in the aspect of consciousness (*caitanya*) due to the object, he provides an illustration for the distinctness (*vailakṣaṇya*) consisting in the nature of non-dual knowledge (*abheda-jñānatva*), which arises solely from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*) compared to the cognition of a jar or the like. He says: "Just as... [and] "of the qualified cognition" (*viśiṣṭajñānasya*).

The meaning is "of the cognition 'the man with a staff'. The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the non-apprehension of the non-relation between the qualifier and the qualified. "Collective apprehension" (*samūhālambana*) means the cognition "the staff, the man, and the conjunction [between them]. This has been stated in the *Cintāmaṇi*:

The phrase "produced by causes" means that there is a distinction [in this case] produced by causes such as the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇajñāna*), when compared to a collective apprehension (*samūhālambana*) of specific knowledge. The phrase "regarding the state of being a post" refers to a certainty (*niścaya*)— namely, "one who possesses humanity, which is incompatible with the state of being a post"— that has the same object as the doubt.
The meaning is that its nature consists of an induced [cognition], which is excluded from that [other state];
it is called "induced" because, at the time of perceiving the specific features, a non-induced certainty is impossible. This is stated with respect to the object (*viṣayataḥ*).
The phrase "in a qualified cognition" implies "in a doubt such as 'Is this a post or a person? It is not merely...

He states "likewise" (tathā) to show that this method must also be followed in cases where the knowledge produced by sentences such as "this is that pot" or "this is that Devadatta" is a cognition of non-difference— even though such a cognition is distinct from the cognitions produced solely by the words "pot" or "Devadatta," provided that it is indeed a cognition of non-difference arising from the sentence *tat tvam asi*.

Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a jar, etc.": concerning the term "additional" (*atirikta*), there is no evidence for the non-difference conveyed by sentences such as "this is that" being something additional to the nature of the jar—which is the object of the cognition produced solely by the word "jar" or the word "Devadatta. Thus, in terms of the object...

Because there is no difference [in the underlying principle], even in cases such as "This is that jar," the cognition has as its object the very nature of the jar and so forth, characterized by a specific relation dependent upon a specific cause— namely, the reference to two substrata (dharmin) in the form of the referents of the two words "this" and "that," just as in the case of "That thou art."
The intended meaning is that it must be stated that the nature of the cognition of non-difference from a jar and so forth is nothing other than this.

The nature of non-existence, similarity, and so forth, when conjoined with their locus, counter-correlate, and so on, consists of a specific relation of their own nature; namely, in the case of non-existence, it is a specific relation of their own nature in the form of the relationship between locus and located with respect to the locus, and a relation with respect to the counter-correlate.

Just as one postulates a specific sub-variety within the relation of essential identity (svarūpasaṃbandha) by way of such forms as the relation between counter-correlate (pratiyogin) and non-counter-correlate (anuyogin), so too, since conjunction (saṃyoga) and identity (tādātmya) would over-extend to objects [of cognition], there must be a distinct relation of object and subject (viṣaya-viṣayibhāva) with respect to objects.
When it is impossible to determine specific objects for those [cognitions] that possess an essential relation with form,
the already established essential relation itself accounts for their mutual distinction— such as being a cognition of non-difference and so forth— through the postulation of internal sub-varieties.
And because of the [logical] consistency:
thus, since it is not admitted that the knowledge of Brahman has as its object some relation called "non-difference," the Vedāntas do not have non-dual reality as their sole purport.
They say that there is also loss.
Now, it might be argued that even for a cognition produced solely by words such as "jar," there is indeed an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) with its object;

and if so, how can the distinction between cognitions—such as being a cognition of non-difference—be established on the basis of essential relation? Furthermore, [essential relation] cannot be the factor that establishes the subject-object relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) between objective cognitions (*vṛtti-jñāna*) and their objects.

It must be stated that although there is no difference among the relations in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is possible to establish the systematic order by postulating a distinction for the opponent regarding those very relations— which consist of the object and the nature of its cognition— based on their dependence upon specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).

Since no distinction has ever been observed among relations that consist of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), such a postulation is untenable; therefore, he says: "of absence, similarity, and so forth.
Now, one might object: is it not the case that the relationship between cognitions (*vṛtti*) and their objects as object and subject is indeed established solely through essential identity?

It is so; however, [this distinction] is produced by conjunction and the like. Moreover, since their own essential relations with those [qualities] are unestablished, the postulation of a "particular" (viśeṣa) consisting of a difference among them is cast far away. Therefore, he says: "conjunction," etc.

If the conjunction with a mental modification (*vṛtti*) were the determinant of being an object of that modification, then even the eyeball and so forth would follow as objects of modifications such as those directed toward a jar, because they too are conjoined with such modifications. Therefore, identity (*tādātmya*) with the modification must be the determinant of being an object of that modification; [this applies to] that which has attained identity with the modification by virtue of being the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that modification.

Even though consciousness delimited by a jar or the like may be the object of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) regarding the jar, it would follow that the jar itself—lacking identity with that modification—could not be its object; furthermore, it would follow that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the substrate of that modification, would become the object of the modification regarding the jar. Therefore, [the object must be] the transformation (*pariṇāma*).

The meaning is that [the two] are identical because they are subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*). Now, one might object: the essential relation between the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and its object consists of the nature of both consciousness and the knowledge directed toward it; in that case, even by the power of a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*), [how could there be identity]?
Since a specific distinction cannot be defined within a relation that consists of the very nature of the object itself, he says:

"In the impossibility of defining a specific distinction in the object. This means that although it is impossible to impart a specific distinction to the object—which consists of non-dual consciousness—such a distinction is nonetheless established as being inherent within the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*).

The meaning is that since the introduction of specific qualities is possible through the power of a particular causal complex (*sāmagrī*) within a relationship whose very nature is knowledge, the aforementioned defect does not apply. Alternatively, since conjunction and identity would lead to over-extension even regarding objects, it is impossible to define a specific object for mental modifications (*vṛtti*).
The connection is as follows: [the relation] belongs to those things which possess a nature consisting in the state of being an object of objects through their respective domains (*viṣaya*).

Even for entities such as absences (*abhāva*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*), which reside in their loci (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth, [the relations of] conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and identity (*tādātmya*) would be over-extended; therefore, by means of those two, [the relation of] subsistence (*vṛtti*)... [is excluded].

The meaning is that, since it is impossible for there to be a restriction to specific objects [for each sense], by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa), they possess an essential relation (svarūpa-sambandha) which serves as the cause for the state of being object and subject.
The word "rūpa" (form/essential nature) refers to the restrictor; it is the essential relation that constitutes the state of being object and subject.

Because there is no possibility for the meaning of the word "form" (*rūpa*) to be non-different from those two [the eye and the object] insofar as they are subject to regulation. Now, even if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and identity (*tādātmya*) lack the capacity to regulate the specific objects of the cognitive functions (*vṛtti*), it does not follow by process of elimination that the relation of these functions to their objects is an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*), since something other than an essential relation [is possible].
Since it is possible to assume another relation [between the two], he says: "It is indeed already established.

This is because the relation of identity (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) is already established as being identical with the nature of the substrate (*vṛtti*) and so forth. When assuming a specific relation within an already established identity-relation, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), whereas one would have to assume a different relation altogether.

The point is this: since it would involve the complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating a specific relation within that other relationship to account for the cognition of non-difference (*abheda-jñāna*), it is more appropriate that the relation between the words in the *vṛtti* and their objects is simply a relation of identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*). Now, one might object:

if the cognition of the non-difference of the individual soul (*jīva*) from Brahman is attained through the sentence "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), then [the relation] must be that very non-difference itself.

He states that this objection—that because [the object] appears through the mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhayā*), there would be a loss of the accepted status of the Vedāntas as having "indivisible meaning" (*khaṇḍārthatva*) defined as the capacity to produce a valid cognition whose scope is not relational—is without foundation. He says: "And thus...
regarding that which is produced by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).

The meaning is: since it has been established otherwise that the state of being a cognition of non-difference resides within knowledge itself, there is no dependence on the appearance of a relation of non-difference (*abhedasaṃsarga*). "There would also be a loss" means that there is no contingency of cognitions such as those of a jar being the remover of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).
The meaning of the word "also" (api) is that there is no loss of the quality of having an indivisible referent (akhaṇḍārthatva).

If it is argued that, like the cognition of a jar or similar objects, the cognition of Brahman cannot properly be the remover of primal ignorance (*mūlājñāna*), because the nature of "removal" implies a contradiction consisting in the inability to coexist with that [ignorance], and because an effect cannot possess such a contradiction with its own material cause— [we reply: no.

Although such a contradiction is not observed elsewhere between cause and effect, here there exists a contradiction induced by the cognition or non-cognition of a single object; furthermore, such a contradiction is observed even between cause and effect, as in the case of fire-contact and cloth.

Nor should it be argued that when there is contact with fire, the destruction of the cloth occurs solely through the destruction of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) conjunction via the process of the disjunction of parts, and not from the fire-contact itself; for even in the case of a burnt cloth, the persistence of its former configuration is observed.

Because the division of parts is not observed— just as in the case of a jar reduced to powder by a mallet— and because the postulation of such a division of parts therein lacks any basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
nor is it logical to claim that the destruction of the cloth occurs there through the destruction of its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) due to the burning of the threads themselves.

Because the burning of the cloth is observed simultaneously with its parts, such as the threads, it is impossible to postulate a sequential process; for it cannot be that the destruction of the lower part occurs first, since the destruction of that constituent part must be attributed solely to its conjunction with fire. [Objection: Let this be so; nevertheless...
If it is argued: "How could this knowledge of Brahman, which destroys ignorance along with its latent tendencies (*savilāsa*), ever perish, given that there is no other cause for its destruction?"

This raises an objection regarding the capacity of the knowledge born of Vedānta to remove even the primal ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). [The author] says "But surely" (*nanu*) and "of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*);
the meaning is that in the world, it is never observed that an effect contradicts the persistence of its material cause (*upādāna*).
Since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), limited by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) whose object is Brahman, is itself the material cause, [it cannot be destroyed by that very modification].

Because a counter-knowledge (*pratyajñāna*) cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*), it is possible for it to be its sublater; thinking this, he says "No. Furthermore, even while conceding that it is the material cause, he says "By the effect," etc.
The general rule (*utsarga*) is that there is no contradiction between the material cause and its product that would necessitate a relationship of sublated and sublater. And that...

In the case of the locus of the material cause (*upādāna*) of the knowledge of Brahman, that [material causality] is set aside because it is sublated by the state of being a remover; for in common worldly experience, the relationship between knowledge and ignorance— which serves as the determinant of the state of being a remover— is established as a specific form, and by that [specific relationship], the general contradiction inherent in the relationship between material cause and its effect is negated.

The meaning is: "because of the occurrence of sublation. He states that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) that in the world one does not observe a contradiction—which serves as the basis for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator—between material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*). He says: "Even in the case of cause and effect," meaning that we observe the effect, namely contact with fire, to be the destroyer of its own material cause, the cloth. Now, [the opponent objects]: "But..."

Regarding this, one might raise an objection, thinking that the observation of fire-contact as the cause of destruction is an error: "Nor [is it so] by the Vaiśeṣika method. According to the Vaiśeṣika method, from the contact with fire there arises motion in the threads; from that, their disjunction; from that, the destruction of the conjunction that is the non-inherent cause of the cloth; and from that, the destruction of the cloth.
He states that the very process of disjunction among the threads is rooted in delusion: "Even in the case of a burnt cloth.

He provides the example of the state of being conjoined with a previous configuration as a counter-example: "By means of a mallet," etc. Just as disjunction is observed among the parts of a jar that has been pulverized by a mallet, so too [is it in the case of the cloth].

The meaning is that after the cloth has been burnt, no disjunction (*vibhāga*) is observed among the burnt threads. The word "therein" (*tatra*) means "among the threads. He states that even another Vaiśeṣika method is rooted in delusion, beginning with the words "nor indeed," etc.; "therein" (*tatra*) means "at the place where the cloth has been burnt."

Since it is necessary that the conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) in some cases acts as the destroyer of the material cause (*upādāna-dravya*), he states that its capacity to destroy the cloth also belongs to that very [conjunction] alone. This is because, prior to the destruction of the dyad (*dvy-aṇuka*), there is no destruction of the atom (*paramāṇu*), which is the part of the dyad; [this applies] in that dyad.

Since it must be stated that the destruction of the dyad (dvyaṇuka), which serves as the material cause of that [triad], results from the very conjunction with fire already present, one cannot argue there that the destruction of the dyad occurs solely through the destruction of the conjunction of two atoms via the process of the separation of parts; for the process of the separation of parts and wholes has already been refuted. Likewise...

The sense is that the observation of the destruction of its own material cause (the cloth) upon contact with fire is not an illusion. Now, one might object: "Let this be so. This means that the knowledge of Brahman likewise destroys its own material cause, namely ignorance (*ajñāna*), by way of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nevertheless—[regarding] the knowledge of Brahman together with its manifestations...

The meaning is: "even though it is the destroyer of knowledge. The point is that the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman—which destroys ignorance along with its effects and remains at the time of that destruction—cannot be established, because it is impossible for something to destroy itself, and no other destroyer remains.
Just as the powder of the *kataka* nut, by not uniting with the water,

produces the disjunction of other particles previously united [with it] while also producing its own disjunction; so too, the knowledge of Brahman, superimposed upon the Self, brings about the cessation of the entire phenomenal world previously superimposed, and brings about its own cessation as well.

Some say that it causes [the other] to cease. Others, however, cite the analogy of burnt iron and drunk water, stating that having caused another to cease, it ceases itself as well. Still others provide here the example of the burning of a heap of dried grass. And as for destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)...

The rule that [destruction] must be produced by something other than its counter-positive is not tenable, because it lacks a probative force (*aprayojakatva*) and because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the destruction of a fire that has run out of fuel, and so forth. Furthermore, if destruction were produced solely by its counter-positive, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, another cause must necessarily be asserted. [This applies even to] a fire that has run out of fuel, and so forth.

It must be stated that even in the case of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), there exist other causes such as time (*kāla*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and the will of the Lord (*īśvarecchā*); for this is not a case of failing to understand the [logical] over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor does the over-extension—that the destruction of a jar and so forth would likewise be independent of other causes—apply to destruction in general.
Because it is not stated that [the destruction of knowledge] is independent of other causes,

nor can the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman be established as depending on other causes by means of the example of the destruction of a jar. This is because, by that same example, [the dependence on other causes] would apply to both.
Because the means of proof would also entail dependence upon the falling of a hammer.
It is not accepted that there is a sequence where first everything other than the knowledge of Brahman is destroyed by the knowledge of Brahman,

and subsequently the remaining knowledge of Brahman itself is destroyed; rather, at the very moment the knowledge of Brahman destroys ignorance along with its manifestations (*savilāsa-ajñāna*), it is destroyed simultaneously with that ignorance.

It is accepted that even the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*) undergoes destruction, because it is admitted that the knowledge of Brahman itself serves as the cause for its own cessation. Nor should it be argued that it is never observed for a single entity to dissolve both itself and another; for this is seen in the case of the powder of *kataka* nut. He provides the illustration with the words "as... previously."
The meaning is that due to contact with the powder of *kataka* nuts, there occurs a separation of the water from the other particles of dust with which it was previously joined.
"Prior to the superimposition" means prior to the superimposition [of the world] by the knowledge of Brahman. "Others" [mean]:
just as water thrown into a red-hot iron ball destroys the fire residing in the iron while destroying itself as well.

The meaning is that it destroys even the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*). Since the knowledge of Brahman removes everything other than itself, at that very moment it must also remove itself; thus, they cite the illustration of water drunk with heated iron as the literal sense. Regarding the phrase "others say": just as in a heap of dry grass...

Just as a fire cast into a heap of grass, while destroying the grass, destroys itself as well, so too the realization of Brahman (*brahmapratyaya*), having arisen within the collection of ignorance and its effects, destroys them; it also destroys itself—this is the meaning. Now, one might object that according to the logic of the fire that consumes its fuel, the knowledge of Brahman must itself perish.

Thus, the argument for [the non-existence of destruction] is incorrect; for one might object that in the case of the destruction of a jar or similar objects, a cause distinct from the counter-positive (pratiyogin)—such as the falling of a hammer—is observed, and there is a rule that destruction is produced by causes other than its counter-positive. To this, he replies: "And not [so] of destruction... [na ca dhvaṃsasya...].

Regarding the phrase "without fuel" (*niriṃdhana*): the meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, immediately after the complete destruction of fuel, one observes the destruction of the fire itself; likewise, in the case of the destruction of a fire without fuel and the destruction of cognitions and so forth occurring at a time immediately preceding sleep, these are produced by the mere counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Thus it has been stated.
The proponent (pūrvavādī) avoids the charge of inconsistency by stating, "niriṃdhaneti" (regarding that which is without fuel).

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the intention that the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) itself is invalid, because the rule that destruction must be produced by a cause distinct from its counter-entity (*pratiyogin*) lacks any probative force (*aprayojakatva*).
The Siddhāntin: [This is] due to a failure to understand the over-extension [of the argument].

If it is asked, "But why is there a failure to understand?"—it should not be said so; for if the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman were not produced by anything other than its own counter-positive (the knowledge itself), then the destruction of a jar and the like would also not depend on any cause other than its own counter-positive.

Alternatively, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that [the destruction of Brahman-knowledge] would depend on causes other than its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), just like the destruction of a jar or similar objects; or, conversely, there would be the over-extension that even the destruction of the jar-knowledge and so forth would not depend on any other cause, just like the destruction of Brahman-knowledge.
Or rather, the intended point is the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that the knowledge of Brahman would perish at the very second moment of its own arising.

Regarding this, he first restates and then refutes the former position with the words "If not" (*na cet*). The phrase "mere destruction" (*dhvaṃsamātre*) means "that which is delimited by the property of being a destruction" (*dhvaṃsatvāvacchinne*). [The opponent objects: "Because of such a designation. [The author replies: "And it is not so according to the Siddhāntin."
It should not be argued that even though it is not explicitly mentioned, [the destruction] is established there at that time because there is no difference in its being a destruction (*dhvaṃsatva*);

the sense is that this is unproving (*aprayojakatva*). He refutes the second position by way of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): "Nor by the example of the destruction of a jar"—the remainder of the phrase being "by the reason of being a destruction."

Nor does it follow as an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that the destruction of the cognition of a jar and so forth would likewise be independent of other causes simply because of their commonality as being "destructions of cognition";
for even though the destruction of a fire with fuel depends upon perceived causes such as the sprinkling of water.

Just as the destruction of a fire without fuel does not depend on anything else, and just as the destruction of a cognition during the waking state— though it depends on another specific quality (guṇa)— does not depend on such a quality in the case of the destruction of the cognition preceding deep sleep,
so too is the destruction of the cognition that removes root-ignorance [independent of other causes].

Since it is established that [destruction] does not depend on that [cause], nor is there the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that destruction would occur in the very moment immediately following its own production due to independence from other causes; for this is accepted [by us]. For at the very moment of its production, by the burning away of the entire phenomenal world superimposed upon Brahman, that [destruction] which is included therein likewise occurs at that very time.

Because burning is admitted [as the destruction of fuel]; and because, according to the logic of the destruction of a fire that has consumed its fuel, there is no contradiction even if the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman is produced by other causes such as time, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), or the will of the Lord (Īśvara).

Since it is not accepted that there is a cessation of the knowledge of Brahman— which remains as the sole residue after the cessation of all phenomenal proliferation (prapañca)— therefore, at the moment immediately preceding the simultaneous burning away of everything,
[the Lord is the cause] of time, which consists either in the relationship between consciousness and ignorance or in the form of a distinct substance.
For there exist other perceived things, such as clarity (*prasāda*), which consists of a specific quality of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and so forth; nor does the contingency of the knowledge of Brahman being false arise from its dependence on causes other than knowledge, since its nature is to be removable by knowledge alone.
It should be stated that [the definition] is "falsity" (mithyātva), because its meaning is: being removable by knowledge while not being removable by a causal complex that does not include knowledge.

Having restated the third [position], he refutes it by showing its lack of probative force: "Nor is it [the case] because of similarity with the destruction of knowledge," the remainder being "by means of the example of the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman. Regarding the phrase "in deep sleep" (*suṣuptau*):
when there is the cessation of another quality that destroys the qualities such as the cognition existing prior to deep sleep, that [destruction] also...

The sense is that, lest there be the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of deep sleep (suṣupti) due to the necessity of postulating another destructive quality of the self, one must state— by way of avoiding that— that the qualities such as knowledge existing prior to deep sleep do not require any other destroyer. "That which removes the root ignorance" means the knowledge of Brahman.

He states that the fourth position is not desired by the proponent, following the objection: "Nor is there dependence on another cause," with the words "of the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman" being the ellipsis. Now, even though a deviation is observed in cases such as the destruction of a fire without fuel, where specific causes like the sprinkling of water are seen to be involved;
Since no deviation is observed among common causes, the requirement for common causes for the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman is likewise unavoidable; therefore, he says:
"according to the maxim of the destruction of a fire without fuel."

Now, if it is argued that there is a sequence such that the birth of the knowledge of Brahman occurs in the first moment, the cessation of ignorance along with its manifestations in the second moment,

and the cessation of the knowledge of Brahman in the third moment— then, since time, unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), and so forth do not exist in the moment prior to the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman, how could they [be the cause] of that destruction?
Since there is no contradiction in accepting [the Lord] as the cause, he says: "In all phenomenal manifestation" (*sarvaprapañca*), speaking according to his own view;

"consciousness and ignorance" (*cidavidyā*), speaking according to the view of others; or alternatively, even within his own view, he speaks with the intention that the Lord possesses the nature of time (*kālatva*).

By the phrase "as a distinct substance," he states that in his own system, *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen force) does not have two modes. Regarding the term "Īśvara" [in the verse], the mention of "grace" (*prasāda*) is illustrative; it should be understood that merit (*puṇya*) consists of the grace of Īśvara, while demerit (*pāpa*) consists of the wrath of Īśvara. By the phrase "of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*), [he refers to] the self according to his own system.
The sense is that [the Self] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). "And of others" means [it applies] to Īśvara, the directions (*diś*), and so forth as well.

"Nor is that the case there" means [it does not apply] to the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñānadhvaṃsa*). For "being removable by knowledge alone" does not, according to the literal reading, consist in being removable by knowledge while not being removable by anything other than knowledge.

Since the cessation of ignorance—which is to be accomplished by knowledge—has as its cause not only knowledge but also something else that serves as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), he says: "not consisting of knowledge" (*jñānāghaṭita*). This means: provided that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not consist of knowledge and yet is not removable by it. This is true even according to the view that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is real.

It might be argued that objects such as a jar possess the property of being removable by knowledge, since their destruction is observed to be preceded by a cognition such as "I am destroying the jar" followed by the falling of a mallet or similar means; however, to exclude this [from the definition], the word "real" (*satyam*) is used,
because there is no rule that the destruction of a jar or the like must necessarily be preceded by knowledge, and thus its causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not constituted by knowledge.

Because in things such as a jar, which are of a nature to be destroyed, there is an absence of the property of being destructible by a general cause that includes God's knowledge; nor, according to the opponent's view, is destruction in general produced by a causal complex consisting of God’s knowledge.

The scriptural statement, "There is no other path," also has its purport precisely in that regard. Therefore, the analogy of the fire that burns the fuel once it has been consumed is indeed appropriate. However, some maintain that the knowledge of Brahman, being of the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), does not remove ignorance or the phenomenal world rooted therein. [This is because] of ignorance...
Because it is impossible for [ignorance] to be removed by a modification (vṛtti) that is insentient in nature— given the rule that [only] what is luminous can remove [what obscures it]— rather,

the manifestation of consciousness established therein is its remover. For although in its own nature consciousness does not remove ignorance and the like since it stands as their witness (sākṣin), [it does so] when mounted upon a modification in the form of the undivided whole (akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti).

Because it is logically established that [the sun's light] is the remover of that [darkness]. For it has been stated by the learned: "Even though this solar radiance illuminates grass and other such things, it may burn the grass; one should apply that same principle there [to the case of the crystal].
And thus, just as when one climbs onto a certain piece of wood and burns a village, a city, or the like—

They say that just as fire indeed burns even that wood, so too the light of non-dual consciousness (akhaṇḍacaitanya), having ascended to the final stage (caramavṛtti) and uprooting the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), is capable of bringing about its cessation; thus, there is no logical inconsistency whatsoever in its destruction.

It should not be argued that this is not a valid definition of falsity because, in the mere sense of being removable by knowledge, there exists a state of being removable by knowledge while not being removable by a causal complex not involving knowledge; for in the definition,
the word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers specifically to the knowledge of the individual soul (jaiva-jñāna), in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to the Self (ātman).

The intended meaning is that [the term] refers to the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Now, one might object: if it is accepted that time, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth are causes for every effect, then even upon the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman, since time, unseen merit/demerit, and so forth must still be admitted as causes, [this would apply] even to liberation, which consists in the destruction of the root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*).

Time and so forth would also possess the status of being causes, since there is no distinction in their being effects; nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence, because it would contradict the Śruti text, "There is no other path. To this, he says: "There is no other path. This Śruti does not intend to convey that knowledge alone is the means to liberation, but rather that [liberation] is not constituted by anything other than knowledge.

The intended meaning here is that there is no means whatsoever [to destroy knowledge]; therefore, there is no contradiction with the Śruti—this is the sense. The word "ataḥ" (therefore) means because there is an absence of subverting factors such as contradiction with the Śruti.
It has now been stated that just as the knowledge of Brahman in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) destroys ignorance and so forth, it likewise possesses the capacity to destroy itself.

He states the view that the knowledge of Brahman in the form of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) possesses neither the power to destroy ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, nor the power to destroy itself; rather, it is the Consciousness (*caitanya*) reflected in that modification, together with the modification itself, that is the destroyer of everything. He introduces this with the words "Some, however" (*kecit tu*). Now, an objection may be raised: since Consciousness is the very means for establishing ignorance and so forth, how can it be its destroyer? To this, he replies:
Regarding the phrase "by its own nature," he demonstrates an illustration for that in a verse: "of grass and so forth.
This solar radiance, which is directly perceived, is indeed an illuminator of grass and such by its own nature;
yet, having ascended the sun-crystal (*sūryakānta-maṇi*), it burns the grass and so forth—this is established by direct perception, and this is the underlying principle.

In that regard, one should apply it to consciousness (*caitanya*). One must indeed determine that although consciousness, by its very nature, illuminates ignorance and the like, it becomes the destroyer of ignorance and so forth when conjoined with a particular mental modification (*vṛtti*). [Objection: But how can that which is the means of realization (*sādhaka*) possess the quality of being a slayer (*ghātaka*)? This is due to the impossibility [of such a thing].

The purport of the verse is that one should disregard an object established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now, it is observed that the brilliance of the sun reflected in a gem burns grass and other such things distinct from the gem, but not the gem itself;

likewise, consciousness (*caitanya*) mounted upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*) should destroy ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the like which are distinct from the modification, but not the modification itself.

And thus, in response to the doubt— “How could the knowledge of Brahman perish, given that there is no other cause for its destruction?”— he provides the resolution with the words “If this is so” (*evaṃ ceti*). This is because, in the world, the relationship between the sublated (*nivartya*) and the sublator (*nivartaka*) is observed only between light and darkness when consciousness is mounted upon a mental modification (*vṛtti*).

The meaning is that since it is logical for light to be a specific auxiliary cause [of destruction] without contradiction, [the result] is established by both [reasons]. "Unmūlayan" means destroying along with the root-ignorance. "Pragalbhate" means it comes into being. "Tannāśa" refers to the destruction of the final mental modification (*vṛtti*).
This is the meaning.

Others, however, maintain that the knowledge of Brahman is the remover of ignorance alone, because knowledge and ignorance are directly opposed to each other; whereas the phenomenal world (prapañca) perishes through the destruction of its material cause,
and thus even the knowledge of Brahman, being included within the phenomenal world, perishes for that very same reason— and not otherwise.

If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were not sublated by knowledge, its falsity (*mithyātva*) would be untenable. Even though the cessation of the phenomenal world is not produced directly by knowledge, it is nonetheless produced by knowledge—either directly or indirectly—because it is produced by the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), which itself is produced by knowledge.
Thus, the world is exclusively sublatable by knowledge, whether directly or through a mediated process.

Because it is accepted that [the world] is false (mithyātva). And thus, even upon the arising of the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra), the appearance of the body and so forth for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is logically established. Even though the direct realization of reality has arisen, due to the obstruction by karma whose effects have already begun (prārabdhakarman), [the body persists].

This is established because the persistence of the appearance of its effects— the body and so forth— is due to the non-cessation of a trace of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*), which serves as their material cause. Furthermore, this is consistent with the fact that, like ignorance itself, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is directly sublated by the direct realization of Brahman, even though it is extremely resistant [to such sublation].

They say that when there is the direct realization of Brahman (brahmasākṣātkāra), since it is impossible for prārabdha-karma to remain by itself, it cannot serve as an obstacle to the cessation of the residual traces of ignorance (avidyāleśa).
[Thus ends the third chapter in the Śrī-Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha. || 3 ||
[The author] shows the view that the destruction of ignorance (*ajñānanāśa*) is the cause for the destruction of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñānanāśahetu*), [introducing it with] "But others...

and "Of ignorance alone...". And it is stated in the *Pañcapādikā*: "Knowledge is the direct remover of ignorance alone," because the conditions for contradiction, such as having the same object, reside in ignorance itself.

The meaning is "because of its arising. "From that alone" means "from the destruction of the material cause (upādāna) alone. Whether directly or indirectly, since it is established that all that is false is sublated solely by knowledge—given that everything insentient other than the root-ignorance (mūlājñāna) is dependent upon that [root-ignorance]—it [the effect] itself...

It should also be understood that even in the absence of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) being directly sublated by knowledge, its falsity (*mithyātva*) remains established without obstruction. He demonstrates that this view is supported by the scriptures on liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-śāstra*) with the words "And thus," etc., regarding that which is distinct from ignorance (*ajñāna*).

The meaning is: "provided that there is no direct contradiction between the insentient (jaḍa) and knowledge. Now, one might object: if ignorance is destroyed by the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra), then, due to the absence of its material cause (upādāna), it would be impossible for the body and so forth to persist; how then can there be the appearance of the body and so forth upon the arising of knowledge? To this [it is replied]: [The text continues: ...Therefore... [the author] says: "In the case of the insentient... and so on. The sense is that while there is no direct opposition between the insentient and knowledge, the body and so forth continue to appear due to the force of residual impressions (vāsanā) even after the destruction of ignorance. This is because the body and its adjuncts, having been produced by ignorance, persist for some time through the momentum of their own causal efficiency (śakti) even after their material cause has ceased, just as a potter’s wheel continues to spin for a while due to the momentum of the initial impulse even after the potter’s hand has ceased its action. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the body and so forth are not real entities but merely appearances (pratibhāsa), they do not require a material cause in the same way that real objects do; rather, they persist as long as the conditions for their appearance remain, such as the non-cessation of the mind's latent tendencies. Therefore, the objection is refuted.

He says: "Prārabdha" [is the cause]. When the dawn of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*) occurs, there arises the consequence that ignorance (*ajñāna*) must cease without remainder; yet, due to the obstruction caused by *prārabdha* karma, the cessation of even a trace of ignorance is not possible.
And as long as that trace persists, even after the realization of reality, the *prārabdha* karma [continues to operate].

The meaning is that the persistence of its effects— the manifestation of the body and so forth— is also logical, due to the persistence of a trace of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*) which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for the body and so on. He states the failure to establish liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) according to the former view.

"Like ignorance" means that for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is still the appearance of the body and so forth. "The adversary" means that it is the direct adversary not only of ignorance but also of prārabdha-karma. Having meditated upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa with the mind and having prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa, this chapter has been explained.
For the complete satisfaction of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.

Thus, in the work of Acyuta-Kṛṣṇānanda-Tīrtha, whose dust has become attached to the divine lotus-feet of the venerable Svayaṃprakāśānanda Sarasvatī, the teacher of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka order...
The third chapter [is concluded] in the commentary on the *Śāstrasiddhāntaleśasaṃgraha* titled *Śrīkṛṣṇālaṅkāra*. || 3 || [End].
